paragraphs.text: The pituitary gland is formed of two portions derived from different sources: the anterior (adenohypophysis) and the posterior (neuro hypophysis) [1]. The upward invagination of stomodeal ectoderm forms the primordium of the anterior pituitary, Rathke’s pouch, while the posterior pituitary arises from the neural ectoderm of the forebrain [2]. Rathke’s pouch can be identified by the third week of pregnancy [3].
paragraphs.heading: and Function

paragraphs.text: The anterior pituitary comprises 80% of the pituitary and consists of three parts: the pars distalis (pars anterior or anterior lobe), the pars intermedia (intermediate lobe), and the pars tuberalis (pars infundibularis or pars proximalis). In humans, the pars distalis is the largest portion of the anterior pituitary and where most of the anterior pituitary hor
paragraphs.heading: and Function

paragraphs.text: mones are produced [3]. The intermediate lobe is poorly developed in humans with only a tiny remnant identifiable in adults, although more obvious in the fetus and in pregnant women [4]. The upward extension of the pars distalis onto the pituitary stalk forms the pars tuberalis, which may contain a small number of gonadotropin-producing cells [3].
paragraphs.heading: and Function

paragraphs.text: Peptide hormones produced in neurons of the hypothalamus are transported via a capil lary plexus in the pituitary stalk to the ante rior pituitary, where they regulate the synthesis and release of several hormones from special ized cell types. Somatotrophs produce somato tropin, more commonly known as growth hormone (GH); lactotrophs produce prolac tin (PRL); thyrotrophs produce thyrotropin, also known as thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH); gonadotrophs produce the two gonad otropins, follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH); and cortico trophs produce adrenocorticotropin (ACTH) [5]. Earlier studies suggested localization of the various cell types, for example, lactotrophs to the rostral and caudal regions and somato trophs predominantly to the anterolateral wings of the gland. However, the organization appears to be much more complicated with the anterior pituitary cells arranged in net works and adapting dynamically in response to the hypothalamic-releasing and -inhibiting hormones [6]. Posterior pituitary hormones are synthesized in cell bodies of neurons in the hypothalamus and transported along their axons through the neurohypophyseal tract of the pituitary stalk. These hormones, arginine vasopressin (also known as antidi uretic hormone [ADH]) and oxytocin, are then stored in, and secreted from, the poste rior pituitary [7].
paragraphs.heading: and Function

paragraphs.text: Hypopituitarism is the deficiency in vary ing degrees of one or multiple pituitary hor mones. In this chapter, GH deficiency (GHD) will be discussed, while other hormonal defi ciencies are presented elsewhere in this book. To understand GHD, an understanding of GH physiology is important and follows below.
paragraphs.heading: and Function

paragraphs.text: Growth hormone is a single-chain α-helical nonglycosylated polypeptide. The majority (75–90%) of circulating GH is a 22-kDA form consisting of 191 amino acids and two intra molecular disulfide bonds [3, 8]. There is also a 20-kDa variant form, which arises from alternative splicing during the processing of human GH pre-mRNA [9, 10]. The remainder of the GH produced by the pituitary is in the N-acetylated and desamidated forms and oligomers [3]. Secreted GH circulates both unbound and bound to binding proteins, which are portions of the extracellular domain of the GH receptor (GHR) [11].
paragraphs.heading: 1.1.2 Growth Hormone

paragraphs.text: The GH1 gene encodes for GH and is part of a 50-kb cluster of five genes located on human chromosome 17q22–24: GH1, chori onic somatomammotropin (CS)-like (L), CS- A, GH-2, and CS-B [12]. The CS-L translated protein appears nonfunctional, while the CS- A and CS-B genes encode human chorionic somatomammotropin (hCS), also known as human placental lactogen (hPL). hCS is pro duced by syncytiotrophoblastic cells and has 85% homology to GH. While hCS also con tains two disulfide bonds that occur at the same positions as in GH-N, it only has 0.5% affinity for the GHR. Interestingly, hCS does not appear necessary for fetal or extrauterine growth, nor does it appear essential for the maintenance of pregnancy or lactation [13]. The GH-2 gene product, which is known as the GH variant (GH-V), differs from GH-N by 13 amino acids. It is expressed as at least four alternatively spliced mRNAs in the pla centa and is continuously secreted during the second half of pregnancy, suppressing mater nal pituitary GH-1 gene function [14, 15].
paragraphs.heading: 1.1.2 Growth Hormone

paragraphs.text: 1.1 Infants have nonpulsatile GH secretion. There is a gradual increase in 24-h integrated GH secretion during childhood. The ampli tudes of GH pulses are increased during puberty, which may be secondary to the effect of gonadal steroids on GHRH [26–28]. Although GH production continues through out life, the levels decline in the elderly [29, 30].
paragraphs.heading: 1.1.2 Growth Hormone

paragraphs.text: There are multiple other factors that affect GH secretion. Thyroid hormone regulates GH secretion at the level of the hypothalamus and pituitary, and hypothyroidism is associ ated with a decrease in GH secretion [31]. Adiposity (in particular visceral fat) is associ ated with decreased GH secretion [32], while undernutrition leads to the oversecretion of GH but low IGF-I levels indicating GH resis tance [33].
paragraphs.heading: 1.1.2 Growth Hormone

paragraphs.text: Synthetic hexapeptides capable of stimu lating GH secretion are termed GH secreta gogues (GHS) or GH-releasing peptides (GHRP). These compounds can stimulate GH release but do not act through the GHRH or SST receptors [34, 35]; rather, they act via the GHS receptor (GHS-R), which is distinct from the GHRHR. These peptides can initi ate and amplify pulsatile GH release [35]. The
paragraphs.heading: 1.1.2 Growth Hormone

paragraphs.text: GHS-R is a seven-transmembrane G-proteincoupled receptor that acts via protein kinase C activation and is expressed in the hypothal amus and in pituitary somatotrophs [36].

An endogenous ligand for the GHS-R, ghrelin, stimulates GH release in a doserelated manner, as well as potentiates GHRHdependent secretion of GH [37, 38]. It is produced mainly by the oxyntic cells of the stomach but is also found throughout the gastrointestinal tract, as well as in the hypo thalamus, heart, lung, and adipose tissue [39]. Several studies have demonstrated that ghre lin has a wide range of effects, including act ing as a physiological mediator of feeding [40, 41].
Approximately 50% of circulating GH is bound to GH-binding protein (GHBP). GHBP is produced in multiple tissues, with the liver being the predominant source. GHBP

acts as a circulating buffer or reservoir for GH, prolonging the half-life of plasma GH and competing with the GHR for GH, prob ably forming an unproductive heterodimer. In general, GHBP levels reflect GHR levels and activity. In rodents, GHBP appears to be syn thesized de novo from alternative splicing of GHR mRNA. In humans, rabbits, and others, it is shed from membrane-bound GHR by proteolytic cleavage [11, 42].

dimerized in an unbound or inactive state [45, 46]. The GH-binding sites on the extracellular domains of the two subunits are placed asym metrically; GH binding to the constitutive dimer induces rotation of the two subunits, which allows downstream kinase activation by phosphorylation of Janus kinase 2 (Jak2) [46]. Subsequently, the Jak2 molecule induces tyrosine phosphorylation on the intracellular portion of the GHR, which then provides docking sites for intermediary signal trans ducers and activators of transcription (STAT) proteins [47–49]. After phosphorylation, STATs dimerize and move to the nucleus, where they activate gene transcription [50, 51] ( Fig. 1.2).

Many of the actions of GH, both meta bolic and mitogenic, are mediated by insulinlike growth factors (IGFs) or somatomedins, initially identified by their ability to incorpo rate sulfate into rat cartilage [52]. IGF-I, which is a basic 70-amino-acid peptide, is pro duced under the direction of GH predomi nantly in the liver [53]. It plays an important role in both embryonic and postnatal growth. Both systemic and local IGF-I have been shown to stimulate longitudinal bone growth [54–58].
Human fetal serum IGF-I levels, which are approximately 30–50% of adult levels, have been positively correlated with gestational age [59, 60]. The levels of IGF-I gradually increase

during childhood and peak during pubertal development, achieving two to three times the normal adult values [61, 62]. IGF-I produc tion during puberty is augmented by the rise in gonadal steroids leading to increased GH secretion and the pubertal growth spurt [60, 63]. Testosterone mediates its effects on GH pulse amplitude through aromatization to estrogen [64]. After adolescence, serum IGF-I concentrations decline gradually with age [60, 63].

IGFs circulate within the plasma com plexed to high-affinity binding proteins or IGF-binding proteins (IGFBPs). IGFBPs extend the serum half-life of IGFs, transport IGFs into target cells, and modulate the inter action of IGFs with their receptors [60, 65]. Six distinct IGFBPs have been cloned and sequenced [66, 67]. IGFBP-3, which is GH dependent, is the major IGFBP in human serum and transports over 90% of the circu lating IGF-I [3].

The IGF-I receptor (IGF-IR), which is structurally related to the insulin receptor, is a heterotetramer comprised of two membranespanning α-subunits and two intracellular β-subunits [68, 69]. The subunits contain binding sites for IGF-I, are linked by disulfide bonds, and are composed of a transmem brane domain, an adenosine triphosphate (ATP)-binding site, and a tyrosine kinase domain that mediates the presumed signal transduction mechanism for the receptor [3, 70].

The incidence of congenital isolated GHD (IGHD) has been reported as between 1:4000 and 1:10,000 live births [71, 72]. Congenital cranial malformations, including holoprosen cephaly, septo-optic dysplasia (SOD) spec trum, and midline craniocerebral or midfacial
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency (Box 1.1)

paragraphs.text: abnormalities, can be associated with anoma lies of the pituitary gland, including pituitary hypoplasia and/or aplasia or an ectopic poste rior pituitary gland (EPP) [7]. Clinically, they may be associated with pituitary hormone deficiencies at birth or with the risk of devel oping future hormone deficiencies. Although these conditions often have no identifiable eti ology, ongoing advances in understanding pituitary development have provided a genetic basis to account for pituitary pathology. Mutations have been found in genes necessary for pituitary development and function. The following presents a summary of reported genetic defects associated with pituitary pathology.

Subsequently, the expression of Hesx1, Isl1, paired box gene 6 (Pax6), and Six3 assists in appropriate cellular development, proliferation, and migration. Ultimately, the mature pituitary gland is marked by the differentiated cell types: somatotrophs, lactotrophs, thy rotrophs, gonadotrophs, and corticotrophs [73–75]
paragraphs.heading: Mutations

paragraphs.text: Mutations in genes involved in pituitary development may be associated with other developmental anomalies ( Table 1.1).
paragraphs.heading: Mutations

paragraphs.text: Gli transcription factors mediate sonic hedge hog (Shh) signaling, which controls cell fate specification and proliferation in multiple tis sues. Gli2/Shh signaling controls the expres sion of genes in the ventral diencephalon that are necessary for the early patterning of Rathke’s pouch, as well as the proliferation of pituitary progenitors [76]. Mice deficient in Gli2 have early forebrain, spinal cord, skele ton, and ventral diencephalon defects with variable pituitary loss. Pituitary cell types develop, but corticotrophs, somatotrophs, and lactotrophs do not proliferate [77]. Mutations in GLI2 have been found in patients with GH deficiency alone or with one or more other anterior pituitary deficiencies

with and without holoprosencephaly and in patients with holoprosencephaly with and without pituitary hormone deficiencies. When pituitary hormone deficiencies are present, the GLI2 protein is usually truncated; when pituitary hormone deficiencies are absent, there is usually a missense mutation. The anterior pituitary may be absent or hypoplas tic, and there may or may not be an EPP. Polydactyly is often an associated find ing [78].

Hesx1, a member of the paired-like class of homeobox genes originally described in Drosophila melanogaster, is one of the earliest known specific markers for the pituitary pri mordium and is a transcriptional repressor [79, 80]. Hesx1 null mutant mice demonstrate abnormalities in the corpus callosum, anterior and hippocampal commissures, and septum pellucidum, a phenotype similar to the defects seen in humans with SOD [79]. The initial report of a human HESX1 mutation was in two siblings with agenesis of the corpus cal losum, optic nerve hypoplasia, and panhypo pituitarism who were found to have a homozygous mutation at codon 53 (arginine to cysteine) in the homeodomain (DNAbinding domain) of HESX1, resulting in a drastic reduction in DNA binding [79]. Subsequently, autosomal recessive and domi nant HESX1 mutations have been found in association with SOD (although a rare cause of SOD) or with combined pituitary hormone deficiency (CPHD) [81].

Several investigators have screened patients with a wide spectrum of congenital hypopitu itarism for mutations in HESX1. Thomas et al., for example, evaluated 228 patients: 85 with isolated pituitary hypoplasia (including IGHD and CPHD), 105 with SOD, and 38 with holoprosencephaly or related pheno types. In this cohort, three missense mutations were identified [82]. In another study, approxi mately 850 patients were studied for muta tions in HESX1 (300 with SOD; 410 with isolated pituitary dysfunction, optic nerve hypoplasia, or midline brain anomalies; and 126 with familial inheritance). Only 1% of the group was found to have coding region muta

tions, suggesting that mutations in HESX1 are a rare cause of hypopituitarism and SOD [83]. As the described mutations in HESX1 present with variable phenotypes, it has been suggested hormone abnormalities may be affected by modifier genes or environmental factors [84].

Otx genes are expressed in the rostral brain during development and are homologous to the Drosophila orthodenticle (otd) gene, which is essential for the development of the head in Drosophila melanogaster [85]. Otx2 is expressed in the ventral diencephalon, where it interacts with Hesx1, and in Rathke’s pouch. Homozygous inactivation of Otx2 in mice leads to extreme brain defects, while heterozy gous inactivation results in eye abnormalities, commonly pituitary hypoplasia, and some times holoprosencephaly. Heterozygous muta tions of the OTX2 gene, which have been implicated in severe ocular malformations such as anophthalmia, have also been reported in patients with hypopituitarism ranging from GHD to multiple pituitary hormone deficien cies [86–89]. There are variable findings of hypoplastic pituitary, EPP, and Chiari syn drome [90–92].

Pitx2 is a paired-like homeodomain transcrip tion factor closely related to the mammalian Otx genes [85]. Pitx2 null mice show embry onic lethality; however, a hypomorphic allele model of Pitx2 demonstrated pituitary hypo plasia and cellular differentiation defects in proportion to the reduced dosage of Ptx2. The gonadotrophs were most severely affected, followed by somatotrophs and thyro trophs [93–95].

RIEG is the human homolog of Pitx2, and clinical mutations of PTX2 have been described in patients with Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome. This syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition with variable manifesta tions including anomalies of the anterior chamber of the eye, dental hypoplasia, a pro tuberant umbilicus, mental retardation, and pituitary alterations [96]. One group of inves

tigators described mutations in six out of ten families with autosomal dominant Rieger syndrome [96, 97]. Five of the six mutations reported were in the homeobox region, and several showed loss of DNA-binding capacity.

Lhx3 is a LIM-type homeodomain protein expressed in the anterior and intermediate lobes of the pituitary gland, the ventral hind brain, and the spinal cord. Lhx3 expression persists in the adult pituitary, suggesting a maintenance function in one or more of the anterior pituitary cell types [97]. In addition, its expression is associated with cells that secrete GH and PRL, as well as the expression of the α-glycoprotein subunit (α-GSU), sug gesting a common cell precursor for gonado trophs, thyrotrophs, somatotrophs, and lactotrophs [98, 99].

In humans, homozygous loss-of-function mutations in LHX3 have been identified in patients with hypopituitarism including GH, TSH, PRL, LH, and FSH deficiencies, ante rior pituitary defects, and cervical abnormal ities with or without restricted neck rotation [100, 101]. Among 366 studied patients with IGHD or CPHD, only seven patients from four families were found to have LHX3 mutations, suggesting LHX3 gene mutations are a rare cause of CPHD [102]. A com pound heterozygous mutation of LHX3 was described that leads to a short protein induc ing a dominant negative effect (from a pater nally derived change) and a protein with impaired transactivational ability (from a maternally derived change) [103]. As with other described LHX3 mutations, the patient presented with pituitary hormone deficien cies, in addition to deafness and limited neck rotation.

Lhx4 is a closely related transcription fac tor to Lhx3. Heterozygous sporadic and familial LHX4 mutations have been reported. Pituitary hormone deficiencies range from IGHD to panhypopituitarism, and the pitu itary may be hypoplastic with or without an EPP. Some patients also have corpus callosum hypoplasia or Chiari syndrome with pointed cerebellar tonsils [104].

In addition to the more commonly cited fac tors, several other mutated developmental factors have been reported to cause CPHD [104]. For example, patients with reported SOX2 mutations present phenotypes that include hormone deficiencies (primarily iso lated gonadotroph deficiency, but occasion ally GH deficiency), pituitary hypoplasia, and eye abnormalities [104, 105]. Sox2 is a member of the SRY-related HMG box (SOX) family of transcription factors and plays a role in the stem cell compartment and in the maintenance of the pituitary progenitor cells and their differentiation into all the pituitary cell types. Sox2 is also expressed in the dien cephalon, the developing central nervous sys tem, in the sensory placodes, inner ear, cochlea, and the developing lens, retina, and optic nerve [104].

Another interesting development has been the association of pituitary hormone deficien cies with mutations in the gonadotroph genes prokineticin receptor 2 (PROKR2), fibroblast growth factor 8 (FGF8), and FGF receptor 1 (FGFR1), which have been traditionally reported in patients with isolated hypogonad otropic hypogonadism [106]. Mutations in PROKR2, similar to those in LHX4, OTX2, HESX1, and SOX3, may be associated with pituitary stalk interruption syndrome (PSIS). Additionally, genetic variations in Roundabout, Axon Guidance Receptor and Homolog 1 (ROBO1), which play a critical function in axonal guidance, may have a role in the development of PSIS [107].

Prop1 is a paired-like homeodomain tran scription factor with expression restricted to the anterior pituitary during development [2, 108]. During pituitary development, Prop1 acts as a repressor in downregulating Hesx1 and as an activator of Pit-1 [73]. More recent evidence suggests that Prop1 may play a more central role in pituitary stem cell differentia tion than previously recognized [73].
paragraphs.heading: Transcription Factors

paragraphs.text: Bi-allelic PROP1 mutations are the most frequent genetic etiology of CPHD [109]. At least 42 heterozygous or compound heterozy gous human mutations have been described [104, 110]. The most common is a recurring homozygous autosomal recessive mutation of PROP1, delA301_302AG (also known as 296delGA) in exon 2, which changes a serine to a stop codon at codon 109 in the homeodo main, resulting in a truncated gene product. The other common mutation is 150delA [110, 111]. These mutations have been found in nonconsanguineous patients from over 21 countries worldwide, and while previously were thought to be a consequence of hot spots, they are now thought to be founder variants [112]. A considerable variation in clinical phenotypes of patients with PROP1 mutations has been demonstrated, even in patients bearing identical genotypes [108, 113, 114]. Several reports have shown that the hor mone deficiencies may be variable and dynamic; some patients may develop hypogo nadotropic hypogonadism, despite the pro gression into spontaneous puberty, or cortisol deficiency over time [108, 115–117]. Interestingly, some patients present with pitu itary hyperplasia prior to developing hypopla sia, which is speculated to be due to pituitary progenitors accumulating in the intermediate lobe rather than differentiating into more mature cell types [118].
paragraphs.heading: Transcription Factors

paragraphs.text: Pit-1 (Pit-1, GHF-1) is a member of a family of transcription factors, POU, which are responsible for mammalian development, and its expression is restricted to the anterior pitu itary lobe [119, 120]. Pit-1 has been shown to be essential for the development of somato trophs, lactotrophs, and thyrotrophs, as well as for their cell-specific gene expression and regulation [120].
paragraphs.heading: Transcription Factors

paragraphs.text: Mutations in Pit-1 in humans were described in 1992 by four different groups in patients with CPHD consisting of GHD, TSH, and PRL deficiencies and variable hypo plastic anterior pituitaries on MRI [121–124]. At least 47 different mutations have been
paragraphs.heading: Transcription Factors

paragraphs.text: described, with the majority demonstrating autosomal recessive inheritance [74]. The most common mutation, however, is an R271W substitution affecting the POU homeodomain; this leads to a mutant protein that binds nor mally to DNA but acts as a dominant inhibi tor of transcription and may act by impairing dimerization [122, 124–130]. In another single allele mutation, K216E, the mutant Pit-1 is able to bind DNA but unable to support reti noic acid induction of the Pit-1 gene distal enhancer either alone or in combination with wild-type Pit-1. This ability to selectively impair the interaction with the superfamily of nuclear hormone receptors is thus another mechanism responsible for CPHD [131]. Several other point mutations in the Pit-1 gene resulting in CPHD have been described, as well as a few deletions and insertions [110]. Some alter residues important for DNA bind ing and/or alter the predicted α-helical nature of the Pit-1, while others have been shown to or postulated to impair the transactivation of target genes [74, 132].
paragraphs.heading: Transcription Factors

paragraphs.text: Inactivating mutations reported in the GHRHR are often classified as a type of IGHD. The little mouse (lit/lit), which dem onstrates dwarfism and a decreased number of somatotrophs, has a recessively inherited missense mutation in the extracellular domain of the Ghrhr gene [133–135]. In addition to GHD and postnatal growth failure, these mice exhibit delayed pubertal maturation [135]. The first human mutation identified was a nonsense mutation that introduced a stop codon at position 72 (E72X) in two cousins who presented clinically with the typ ical phenotype of severe GHD [136]. Subsequently, a nonsense mutation was found in codon 50 in “Dwarfism of Sindh” in Pakistan [137]. Since then, more than 64 non sense, missense, and splice site mutations in the GHRH gene and deletions and regulatory
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency

paragraphs.text: mutations in the Pit-1-binding sites in the GHRHR promotor have been identified [110, 138].
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency

paragraphs.text: Four forms of IGHD have been described, and their classification is based upon the clini cal presentation, inheritance pattern, and GH secretion.
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency

paragraphs.text: IGHD Type IA results primarily from large deletions, along with microdeletions and sin gle base-pair substitutions, of the GH1 gene, which ultimately prevents the synthesis or secretion of the hormone. This condition is associated with growth retardation in infancy and subsequent severe dwarfism. Heterogeneous deletions of both alleles rang ing from 6.7 to 45 kb have been described [139–142]. In addition to GH1 gene abnor malities, a report of siblings with IGHD described two homozygous variants in the proximal GH1 promoter within a highly con served region and predicted binding sites [143]. Patients with IGHD type 1A frequently develop antibodies to exogenous GH therapy, which is attributed to the lack of immune tol erance because of prenatal GHD [144, 145]. Some patients may eventually become insensi tive to GH replacement therapy demonstrat ing a decreased clinical response; subsequently, recombinant IGF-I therapy may be an alter native option.
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency

paragraphs.text: IGHD Type IB is a less severe autosomal recessive form of GHD resulting from muta tions or rearrangements of the GH1 gene, such as splice site mutations that lead to par tial GH deficiency [140, 146, 147]. In one study, a homozygous splice site G to C trans version in intron 4 of the GH-1 gene was iden tified, causing a splice deletion of half of exon 4, as well as a frameshift within exon 5. These changes ultimately affected the stability and biological activity of the mutant GH protein [148]. Several other deletions or frameshift mutations have been described by others [149–151].
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency

paragraphs.text: IGHD Type II is an autosomal dominant condition considered the most common genetic form of IGHD. Several patients have
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency

paragraphs.text: been found to have intronic transitions in intron 3, inactivating the donor splice site of intron 3 and deleting exon 3 [147, 148, 152–156].
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency

paragraphs.text: IGHD Type III is a partial GH deficiency with X-linked inheritance due to interstitial Xq13.3-Xq21.1 deletions or microduplica tions of certain X regions. Patients may also have hypogammaglobulinemia, suggesting a contiguous Xq21.2-Xq22 deletion [157, 158].

Bioinactive GH has been reported in patients with short stature demonstrating normal GH immunoreactivity but reduced biopotency. A child with severe growth retardation, high serum GH levels, elevated GHBP, low IGF-I levels, and increased GH levels after provoca tive testing was found to have an autosomal arginine to cysteine mutation at codon 77. The child expressed both mutant and wildtype GH; however, the mutant GH had a higher affinity for GHBP, a lower phosphory lating activity, and an inhibitory or dominant negative effect on wild-type GH activity [159]. In another patient, an aspartic acid to lysine mutation at codon 112 was identified and suggested to prevent appropriate GHR dimerization [160].

There are also patients with the phenotype of growth hormone insensitivity who do not demonstrate mutations of the GHR gene, but have identified mutations in downstream GHR signaling molecules. Homozygous mutations in STAT5B, a major GH-dependent mediator of IGF-I gene transcription, have been identi fied as a cause of GH insensitivity [161, 162]. The first mutation characterized was a point mutation resulting in a marked decrease in phosphorylation of tyrosine [162], a critical step in the pathway to STAT activation of IGF-I gene transcription; while the second characterized mutation was an insertion in exon 10 leading to early protein termination [161, 163, 164]. In addition to growth retarda tion, both patients had evidence of immune dysfunction presumably because STAT5B is involved in downstream signaling for multiple cytokines. An additional 12 mutations in the STAT5B gene have been reported [110].

Laron dwarfism is an autosomal recessive dis order characterized by clinical features of severe GH deficiency along with low IGF-I levels but with normal to high levels of GH after provocative testing [165]. Several dele tions and point mutations of several GHR exons have been described [166–174]. Many of these mutations affect the extracellular domain and, therefore, lead to absent or decreased levels of GHBP [175]. Recombinant IGF-I therapy has been demonstrated to effectively treat these patients [176, 177]. It has also been hypothesized that some patients with idiopathic short stature (ISS), normal GH secretion, and low serum concentrations of GHBP may have partial insensitivity to GH due to mutations in the GHR gene [173].
paragraphs.heading: Mutations

paragraphs.text: A patient noted to have a homozygous partial IGF-I gene deletion with undetectable levels of IGF-I presented with severe prenatal and postnatal growth failure, bilateral sensorineu ral deafness, mental retardation, moderately delayed motor development, and behavioral difficulties. His evaluation did not demon strate a significant delay in his bone age, and an IGFBP-3 level was normal [178]. Subsequently, a few other cases of IGF-I mutations have been described.
paragraphs.heading: Mutations

paragraphs.text: Studies with African Pygmies demonstrate normal levels of GH but decreased IGF-I lev els and unresponsiveness to exogenous GH. Although IGF-I deficiency has been hypothesized, Bowcock et al. found no differ ences in restriction fragment length polymor phisms in the IGF-I gene in Pygmy versus non-Pygmy black Africans [179]. Furthermore, Pygmy T cell lines show IGF-I resistance at the receptor level with secondary GH resis tance [180]. In subsequent studies, it was dem onstrated that adult Pygmies demonstrate a reduction in both GH gene expression (1.8fold) and GHR gene expression (8-fold). This decrease of the GHR expression in Pygmies was associated with reduced serum levels of IGF-I and GHBP [181].
paragraphs.heading: Mutations

paragraphs.text: Abnormalities in the IGF-IR gene have also been reported and are associated with intrauterine growth retardation (IUGR) and usually postnatal growth retardation. Several heterozygous, and occasionally compound heterozygous, mutations of the IGF-IR gene have been reported, as well as an association with deletions in chromosome 15q [182–187]. Phenotypic expression is variable, even between relatives with the same mutation, although microcephaly is a specific finding [188]. IGF-I levels are often high or high nor mal at baseline, but may be low in patients with feeding difficulties; they rise markedly after starting GH therapy [188]. Walenkamp et al. have proposed that partial IGF-I resis tance is likely if a patient has three or more of the following: birth weight and/or birth length below −1 SDS, height at presentation below −2.5 SDS, head circumference at presentation below −2 SDS, and IGF-I level greater than 0 SDS [189].
paragraphs.heading: Mutations

paragraphs.text: Other post-signal transduction defects and mutations in IGF-binding proteins may occur but have not been demonstrated as of yet.
paragraphs.heading: Mutations

paragraphs.text: Hypopituitarism can be caused by anything that damages the hypothalamus, pituitary stalk, or pituitary gland. Head trauma can injure the pituitary stalk and infundibulum and lead to the development of transient and permanent diabetes insipidus, as well as other hormonal deficiencies [190, 191]. There are a number of reports suggesting an association between hypopituitarism and a complicated perinatal course, especially breech delivery [192, 193]. It is not clear if a complicated peri natal course causes hypopituitarism or if a brain anomaly leads to both a complicated delivery and hypopituitarism. The finding that some of these patients have a microphal lus at birth suggests that pituitary dysfunction may precede birth trauma [7].
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency (Box 1.2)

paragraphs.text: Infiltrative conditions can also disrupt the pituitary stalk. Diabetes insipidus can be the
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency (Box 1.2)

paragraphs.text: first manifestation of germ cell tumors, Langerhans cell histiocytosis [194–196], or sarcoidosis [197]. Lymphocytic hypophysitis, usually in adult women in late pregnancy or in the postpartum period, can result in hypopi tuitarism [198].
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency (Box 1.2)

paragraphs.text: Metabolic disorders can cause hypopitu itarism through the destruction of the hypo thalamus, pituitary stalk, or pituitary. Hemochromatosis is characterized by iron deposition in various tissues, including the pituitary. It may be idiopathic or secondary to multiple transfusions (e.g., for thalassemia major); gonadotropin deficiency is the most common hormonal deficiency, but GHD has also been described [199, 200].
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency (Box 1.2)

paragraphs.text: Hypothalamic or pituitary tissue can also be destroyed by the mass effect of suprasellar tumors or by their surgical resection. These tumors include craniopharyngiomas, lowgrade gliomas/hypothalamic astrocytomas, germ cell tumors, and pituitary macroadenomas [201]. Treatment of brain tumors, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, or acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) with cranial irradiation may also result in GHD. Discordancy between failure to pro voke an adequate GH response to insulininduced hypoglycemia and normal response to exogenous GHRH stimulation suggests that the hypothalamus is more vulnerable than the anterior pituitary [202]. The higher the radiation dose, the more likely and the earlier GHD will occur after treatment [203, 204]. Clayton et al. reported that 84% of children who received greater than 30 Gy to the hypothalamic-pituitary area had evi dence of GH deficiency more than 5 years after irradiation [203]. Higher radiation doses also increase the likelihood of the development of other anterior pituitary hor mone deficiencies [204]. Lower radiation doses preserve pharmacologic response of GH to stimulation, but there may be decreased spontaneous GH secretion [205]. Data, however, from Darzy et al. show that spontaneous GH secretion is maintained in adults after low-dose cranial irradiation, suggesting there is not GHRH deficiency.
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency (Box 1.2)

paragraphs.text: There is a normal but decreased peak GH response to stimulation testing indicating decreased somatotroph reserve. They postu lated that there is a compensatory increase in hypothalamic stimulatory input (GHRH) and suggested that “neurosecretory dysfunc tion” after low-dose cranial irradiation may only be seen in puberty during this time of increased GH demand [206]. Lifelong peri odic clinical assessment for GHD is recom mended for childhood cancer survivors who have received a hypothalamic-pituitary radi ation dose of ≥18, with the highest risk in those who have received ≥30 Gy [207]. Cranial irradiation can also cause precocious puberty leading to premature epiphyseal fusion, and spinal irradiation can lead to skeletal impaired spinal growth [207, 208]; both will further compromise adult height.
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency (Box 1.2)

paragraphs.text: Growth failure presenting in infancy and childhood is the most common sign of GHD. Children with mild GHD usually pres ent after 6 months of age when the influences of the prenatal environment wane [209]. They generally have normal birth weights and lengths slightly below average [209]. The height percentile of a child with GH defi ciency will progressively decline, and typically the bone age will be delayed. They develop increased peri-abdominal fat [210] and decreased muscle mass and may also have delayed dentition, thin hair, poor nail growth, and a high-pitched voice [209]. Severe GHD in the newborn period may be characterized by hypoglycemia and conjugated hyperbiliru binemia, as well as a small phallus in boys due to other concomitant anterior pituitary hor mone deficiencies [209].
paragraphs.heading: Hormone Deficiency

paragraphs.text: There is much debate as to the proper meth ods to diagnose GHD in childhood. It is clear that there is a spectrum of GHD, and the clin ical presentation varies with the degree of hormonal deficiency. The diagnosis of GHD should be based on the integration of auxo logical, biochemical, and radiographic crite ria.
paragraphs.heading: of Growth Hormone Deficiency

paragraphs.text: GHD should be considered in children with short stature, defined as a height more than 3 SD below the population mean or height more than 2 SD below the population mean with a height velocity more than 1 SD below the mean, and in children with a very low height velocity (more than 2 SD below the mean) irrespective of current height. In con sidering who should undergo evaluation for GHD, it is important to first exclude other causes of growth failure and then assess the patient for clinical features that can coexist with GHD. These features include hypoglyce
paragraphs.heading: of Growth Hormone Deficiency

paragraphs.text: mia, prolonged jaundice, microphallus, trau matic delivery in the neonate, and craniofacial midline abnormalities. Additionally, a history of other pituitary hormone deficiencies, cra nial radiation, and central nervous system infection, as well as a family history of GHD, should be ascertained [211]. When present, the majority of these features are seen in patients on the severe end of the spectrum of GHD. These patients are typically easy to diagnose and have low height velocity and biochemical markers of GHD, including low IGF-I levels [212] and low peak GH levels after stimulation tests [213]. Nonetheless, most patients with GHD will present with short stature without any of these other fea tures.
paragraphs.heading: of Growth Hormone Deficiency

paragraphs.text: GH induces the expression of IGF-I in the liver and cartilage. The use of age and pubertycorrected IGF-I levels has become a major tool in the diagnosis of GHD [213]. Because of little diurnal variation, their quantification in random samples is useful. However, sensi tivity is still limited due to a significant over lap with normal values. Low levels of IGF-I may be found in normal children, especially in those less than 5 years of age. Similarly, low levels are reported in children with malnutri tion, hypothyroidism, renal failure, hepatic disease, and diabetes mellitus. Serum levels of IGF-I do not correlate perfectly with GH sta tus as determined by provocative GH testing [214, 215].
paragraphs.heading: 1.4.1 IGF-I and IGFBP-3

paragraphs.text: IGFBP-3 is the major carrier of IGF-I [216]. It is GH dependent but has less age vari ation and is less affected by the nutritional sta tus compared to IGF-I [217]. Although low levels of IGFBP-3 are suggestive of GH defi ciency, up to 43% of normal short children have been reported to have low concentrations [218]. Similarly, normal values have been reported in children with partial GHD [214].
paragraphs.heading: 1.4.1 IGF-I and IGFBP-3

paragraphs.text: The combination of a low height velocity and a low IGF-I level for pubertal status may remove the need for provocative testing in patients [219] where other causes for growth
paragraphs.heading: 1.4.1 IGF-I and IGFBP-3

paragraphs.text: failure, especially malnutrition and gastroin testinal illness, have been excluded. This is particularly true in patients with CPHD.
paragraphs.heading: 1.4.1 IGF-I and IGFBP-3

paragraphs.text: GH is secreted episodically, mostly during slow-wave sleep. Between the pulses of pitu itary GH secretion, serum concentrations are typically low, even in GH-sufficient children, and thus a single sample is not useful. Thus, a variety of pharmacological tests have been implemented to assess the GH secretory capacity of the pituitary gland [220]. These tests are expensive, have side effects, and require fasting conditions, as high glucose lev els inhibit GH secretion [221, 222]. GH pro vocative tests have been divided into two groups: screening tests including levodopa and clonidine and definitive tests including arginine, insulin, and glucagon [221, 222]. There is poor reproducibility of the same and different tests in the same subject [223]. Due to their low specificity, sensitivity, and repro ducibility, in order to exclude normal children who might fail a single stimulation test, two different provocative tests are required per patient [221, 222].
paragraphs.heading: Tests

paragraphs.text: The sensitivity and specificity of these tests are also limited by the use of different labora tory techniques for the measurement of GH. Radioimmunoassays used in early stud ies employ polyclonal antibodies, which ren der low specificity and higher GH levels when compared with the more specific immunora diometric assays used today that employ two highly specific monoclonal antibodies. Discrepancies up to two- to four-fold have been reported among different assays [224]. The discrepancies between GH assays are also addressed in current guidelines, which recom mend that institutions require laboratories to provide harmonized GH assays using the somatropin standard 98/574 [225].
paragraphs.heading: Tests

paragraphs.text: Conventionally in the United States, the gold standard for the diagnosis of GHD has been a peak serum GH of less than 10 μg/L after two different GH stimulation tests. This
paragraphs.heading: Tests

paragraphs.text: cutoff is arbitrary. While very low GH peak levels on provocative testing are consistent with severe GHD and generally correlate with a favorable response to GH replacement, there is considerable overlap of GH peak lev els in patients with partial GHD and healthy subjects. Multiple studies have shown that many children diagnosed with IGHD based on peak GH levels less than 10 μg/L will have normal GH secretion on retesting both in childhood [226] and as adults [227, 228]. With newer GH assays that use monoclonal anti body testing and result in GH levels that are up to 40% lower than those obtained with older immunoassay-based testing, many experts believe that the diagnostic threshold should be lowered to a peak serum GH of less than 7 ng/mL [229].
paragraphs.heading: Tests

paragraphs.text: Guidelines from the Pediatric Endocrine Society suggest that in patients who meet aux ological criteria and have a hypothalamicpituitary insult (congenital malformation, tumor, history of radiation, etc.) and defi ciency of one additional pituitary hormone, diagnosis of GHD can be established without provocative testing of GH secretion [225]. Similarly, in newborns with congenital hypo pituitarism and deficiency of at least one additional pituitary hormone (or imaging findings of EPP with pituitary hypoplasia and an abnormal stalk), GHD can be diagnosed without formal provocative testing if GH fails to rise above 5 μg/L during hypoglycemia. In patients who do undergo GH provocative testing, their results should not be used as the sole diagnostic criterion for GHD [225].

In normal children, serum levels of GH are age and sex dependent and show a sharp puber tal increase. During the first few weeks of life, GH levels rise but are associated with low levels of IGF-I. In addition, there is a low number and immaturity of GH receptors, along with lower levels of GHBP. Newborns, therefore, show a state of GH resistance that resolves over time. Because of this, random GH levels can be useful in assessing a neonate for GH deficiency. Mamilly et al. determined that a random GH level in the first 28 days of life ≤4.5 ng/mL has 100% specificity and 83% sen sitivity in the diagnosis of GHD [230].

Immediately before puberty, GH secretion may normally be very low, making the dis crimination between GHD and constitutional delay of growth and puberty difficult. In a study by Marin et al., 61% of normal stature prepubertal children who were not primed with sex steroids failed to raise their peak serum GH concentration above 7 μg/L follow ing a provocative test [231]. Sex steroid prim ing with estrogen to prepubertal girls older than 10 years of age and either estrogen or testosterone to prepubertal boys older than 11 years of age is suggested by experts [225] and can reduce unnecessary treatment of chil dren with slow growth due to constitutional delay of growth and puberty. Priming can be achieved with β-estradiol 2 mg (1 mg if less than 20 kg) orally on each of the two evenings before the test is performed for both boys and girls or with one dose of intramuscular testos terone (50–100 mg) 1 week prior to testing in boys [225, 232]. While children with GHD might have an attenuated response, those with constitutional growth delay will have a nor mal pattern [233].

Obesity also affects the results of GH stimulation testing. There is a negative impact of adipose tissue on GH secretion [234]. These lower stimulated GH values in obese children normalize after weight loss [32, 234]. However, a lower GH peak cutoff in children who are obese has not been established.

In summary, the threshold to define GH deficiency to various provocative stimuli is arbitrary and based on no physiological data. Pharmacological tests involve the use of potent GH secretagogues, which may not reflect GH secretion under physiological cir cumstances, masking the child with partial GH deficiency. Age, gender, and body weight all affect responses. GH stimulation tests are reliable only in the diagnosis of severe or complete GH deficiency. In addition to their low reproducibility [225], a “normal” secre tory response does not exclude the possibility of various forms of GH insensitivity or par tial GH deficiency. The usefulness and reli ability of GH provocative tests for the diagnosis of GHD remain a matter of ongo ing debate.

In addition to pharmacological tests of growth hormone secretion, frequent blood sampling can be performed overnight to test for spontaneous GH secretion. The term GH neurosecretory dysfunction refers to patients with an abnormally slow growth rate and low integrated GH concentration (mean serum 24-h GH concentration) but appropriate GH response to provocative tests [235, 236]. The pathophysiology and the incidence of this condition remain unknown. Although the integrated GH concentration has better repro ducibility compared to the standard provoca tive tests, there are still significant intraindividual variations and overlapping with the values found in normal short chil dren [237]. Lanes et al. reported decreased overnight GH concentrations in 25% of nor mally growing children [238]. As sampling is required every 20 min for a minimum of 12–24 h, this test is not practical for routine clinical care. Current guidelines advise against the use of overnight GH sampling, as there are very limited data on its usefulness to dis tinguish between GH-deficient and normal subjects. Thus, it does not warrant the burden to the patient [225].
paragraphs.heading: of Growth Hormone Secretion

paragraphs.text: The evaluation of skeletal maturation is cru cial in the assessment of growth disorders, as osseous growth and maturation are influenced by nutritional, genetic, environmental, and endocrine factors. Skeletal maturation is sig nificantly delayed in patients with GHD, hypothyroidism, hypercortisolism, and chronic diseases. Children with constitutional growth delay will show a delayed skeletal age or bone age (BA), which corresponds with the height age.
paragraphs.heading: 1.4.4 Bone Age Evaluation

paragraphs.text: In children over 1 year of age, the radio graph of the left hand is commonly used to evaluate skeletal maturation. The BA is deter mined by comparing the epiphyseal ossifica
paragraphs.heading: 1.4.4 Bone Age Evaluation

paragraphs.text: tion centers with chronological standards from normal children. Several methods to determine the BA are available, with the Greulich and Pyle (GP) and Tanner- Whitehouse (TW) methods most widely used. For the GP method, a radiograph of the left hand and wrist is compared with the stan dards of the Brush Foundation Study of skel etal maturation in normal boys and girls [239]. The standards correspond to a cohort of white children, so its applicability to other racial groups may be less accurate. It is still the most popular method as it is relatively quick and easy to learn but has a high interand intra-observer variability. The TW2 method [240], updated in 2001 to Tanner- Whitehouse 3 (TW3), assigns a score to each one of the epiphyses. It is more accurate and carries less intra-observer variability, but it is also more time consuming.
paragraphs.heading: 1.4.4 Bone Age Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Several automated methods have been developed in an attempt to provide more objective, immediate results. BoneXpert is an automated computer program that analyzes 13 points of interest of the same 13 bones used in the TW3 system, and rates them indi vidually, and transforms the summary BA according to GP and TW criteria. It has been validated in different populations with report edly higher reliability and precision than traditional methods [241]. Another validated option, though not yet approved for clinical use, is the Paediatric Bone Age Calculator from 16Bit.ai, which uses artificial intelli gence (AI) and machine learning with similar results [241].
paragraphs.heading: 1.4.4 Bone Age Evaluation

paragraphs.text: The growth potential of an individual must be evaluated according to the parents’ and other relatives’ heights, as genetic influences play a crucial role in determining the adult’s height. An approximation of the ultimate adult height is obtained by calculating the midpa rental height (MPH). For girls, MPH is (mother’s height + father’s height − 13 cm)/2 and for boys (mother’s height + father’s height + 13 cm)/2. Tanner originally suggested a 95% confidence interval for target height of
paragraphs.heading: 1.4.5 Prediction of Adult Height

paragraphs.text: ±8.5 cm, but subsequently increased it to ±9 cm in girls and ±10 cm in boys [242–244]. However, more than 12,000 common variants with independent effects on height have been identified in the genome (European ancestry). It is the combined, polygenic effects of these common genetic variants that explain much of the variation in height SDS, and the MPH does not account for all the polygenic varia tion [245]. Nevertheless, when the growth pat tern deviates from the parental target height, an underlying pathology should be consid ered.
paragraphs.heading: 1.4.5 Prediction of Adult Height

paragraphs.text: Four methods to predict adult height are available: (1) Bayley-Pinneau is based on cur rent stature, chronologic age, and BA obtained by the Greulich and Pyle method [246]. This method probably underpredicts growth potential [247]. (2) The TW2 method consid ers current height, chronologic age, TW2 assessment of BA, midparental stature, and pubertal status [240]. (3) The Roche-Wainer- Thissen method requires recumbent length, weight, chronologic age, midparental stature, and Greulich and Pyle BA assessment [248]. (4) The Khamis-Roche (KR) algorithm directly calculates predicted adult height from a linear combination of the child’s height and weight, together with midparental height. Sex- and age-specific coefficients for both sexes are provided [249].

There is wide variation in predicted adult heights using height prediction algorithms, and different methods are useful under certain circumstances, with accuracy varying accord ing to subjects’ age, gender, and BA [250]. It remains unclear whether newer methods using AI will be more precise. In addition, predic tions of adult height may be of limited value in patients with underlying pathology.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain is a sensitive and specific indicator of hypopituitarism: a high proportion of chil dren with IGHD with normal or small pitu itary glands showed normalization of GH secretion at the completion of GH treatment,
paragraphs.heading: 1.4.6 Magnetic Resonance Imaging

paragraphs.text: whereas GHD was permanent in all patients with congenital anatomical abnormalities, such as pituitary hypoplasia with pituitary stalk agenesis and an EPP [227]. In a study by Hamilton et al., structural abnormalities were more common in patients with CPHD or pan hypopituitarism (93%) and in those with severe GH deficiency (80%) compared to those with IGHD [251]. Likewise, Hwang et al. reported GH values less than or equal to 5 ng/mL were associated with more severe MRI abnormalities [252]. Mass lesions such as suprasellar tumors or thickening of the pituitary stalk due to infiltrative disorders may be found in patients with acquired GHD.
paragraphs.heading: 1.4.6 Magnetic Resonance Imaging

paragraphs.text: There is wide variability in the dose of recom binant human GH used to treat GHD. Traditionally, GH dosage has been based on weight, and consensus guidelines recommend doses of 22–35 μg/kg/day given 6–7 days/week (0.16–0.24 mg/kg/week) with possible, but not routine, increase in GH dose during puberty [225]. There is great variability in response to GH therapy. IGF-I levels should be monitored and maintained within the laboratory-defined normal range for the age or pubertal stage of the patient. Treatment should be discontinued once height velocity falls below 2–2.5 cm/year [225]. Recently, long-acting preparations of growth hormone (LAGH) administered weekly have been approved with the goal of improving patient adherence. Their pharmacogenetics are differ ent from daily GH leading to prolonged GH bioactivity, and IGF-I levels with peaks postinjection and troughs pre-injection rather than a relatively stable level. There have been no safety concerns with short-term use [253]. Long-term data are not yet available.
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency

paragraphs.text: In order to decrease variability and improve adult height outcomes, two strategies have evolved to help refine GH dosing. The first strategy employs prediction models that calculate expected height velocity based on baseline parameters [254]. These prediction
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency

paragraphs.text: models are derived from large pharmaceutical company GH registries and provide impor tant insights into GH responsiveness. Peak GH levels during stimulation testing, age at onset of GH therapy, and height deficit from midparental target height have been found to be the most significant predictors of first-year height velocity [255]. This indicates that indi viduals with more severe GHD, younger age at therapy start, and greater genetic potential will have the greatest response to therapy. Height velocity in subsequent years is highly dependent on growth response in the first year. One study has shown that using individ ualized GH doses based on a prediction model decreased variability in response without compromising efficacy [256].
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency

paragraphs.text: The second strategy for refining GH dos ing involves using IGF-I levels to target ther apy. One study showed that targeting higher IGF-I levels leads to an increase in height gain without apparent adverse effects [257]. With this strategy, there is still a range of responses, which depend on the individual patient’s GH sensitivity. To date, there is no consensus on the optimal IGF-I level that results in favor able growth while minimizing long-term risk. For this reason, current guidelines propose aiming to keep IGF-I within normal range for age and pubertal status [225].
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency

paragraphs.text: Regardless of the strategy used to select a dose for initiation of GH therapy, one must assess response to therapy and make further decisions about dose adjustments or discon tinuation of therapy. Typically, response is assessed after a year of therapy, and the most important parameters are height velocity and change in height standard deviation score (SDS). Height velocity varies by age and gen der, while change in height SDS intrinsically corrects for these factors [258, 259]. In patients with severe GHD defined as a peak GH level less than 5 ng/mL on stimulation testing, a change in height SDS less than 0.4 in the first year of therapy is a poor response, while in those with less severe GHD, the corresponding value is 0.3 [259]. A suboptimal response may be indicative of an incorrect diagnosis of GH deficiency, lack of adherence to therapy, improper preparation, and/or administration
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency

paragraphs.text: of the GH, associated hypothyroidism, con current chronic disease, complete osseous mat uration, and, rarely, anti-GH antibodies. Development of antibodies to exogenous GH has been reported in 10–30% of recipients of GH. However, the presence of GH antibodies does not usually attenuate the hormonal effect, as growth failure has been reported in less than 0.1% [260]. Additionally, one can compare actual growth response to predicted growth response based on the aforementioned growth prediction models. As GH dose is included in the models, a poor actual versus predicted response indicates either decreased GH sensi tivity or nonadherence [259]. Finally, there is some evidence that underlying genetic variants in the GHR influence response to therapy [261], but this area requires further research.
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency

paragraphs.text: In summary, to evaluate the response to GH therapy, the most important parameter is the determination of the height velocity (expressed as the change in height SDS score). While monitoring of IGF-I levels has gained wide acceptance to assess safety and adherence [225], the level does not always correlate with the obtained increment in height velocity. Additionally, although rec ommended by some [262], regular monitor ing of the BA in children receiving GH therapy is questionable. Interobserver differ ences in BA interpretation and erratic changes over time in osseous maturation make the estimation of adult height inaccu rate. Similarly, predictions of adult height may be overestimated, as GH may accelerate the bone maturation in advance of any radio graphic evidence [262].
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency

paragraphs.text: Potential adverse effects of recombinant human GH (rhGH) treatment include benign intracranial hypertension, slipped capital fem oral epiphysis, and progression of scoliosis, all of which should be monitored during physical
paragraphs.heading: 1.6.1 Short-Term Follow-Up

paragraphs.text: exams on follow-up visits and require counsel ing of patients prior to the start of treatment.
paragraphs.heading: 1.6.1 Short-Term Follow-Up

paragraphs.text: This neurological complication has been described in patients receiving rhGH, but with a low incidence. A prospective study collect ing data on 3332 children in Australia and New Zealand found a low incidence of 1.2 cases per 1000 patients [263]. Data from the Kabi International Growth Study further demonstrated the incidence is lower than pre viously reported [264]. Nevertheless, an oph thalmologic evaluation is mandatory in rhGH recipients in the event of persistent headaches, nausea, visual symptoms, and dizziness. Symptoms usually resolve with discontinua tion of treatment.
paragraphs.heading: Hypertension

paragraphs.text: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) occurs with an incidence of 73 per 100,000 treatment years in rhGH-treated patients. The incidence is significantly lower in patients with IGHD (12.2) than in those with Turner syn drome (56.4), congenital GHD (54.5), Prader- Willi syndrome (PWS) (68.3), and chronic renal insufficiency (147.8), and not increased from the general population in children with ISS [264]. It occurs from 0.01 to 1.3 years after the onset of therapy in various diagnostic groups, but up to 2.5 years into treatment in other series. Typically, these children were older and heavier [260]. SCFE, however, can be associated with not only obesity, but also untreated endocrine conditions (e.g., hypothy roidism), trauma, and radiation exposure. Although the incidence of SCFE in all data bases appears to remain greater than for the general population, it is difficult to assess the risk of SCFE in the general population because of several variables (age, sex, race, and geography) [264, 265].
paragraphs.heading: Epiphysis

paragraphs.text: Rapid growth during GH treatment can worsen existing scoliosis. Scoliosis is more fre quent during GH treatment in groups with a
paragraphs.heading: 1.6.1.3 Scoliosis Progression

paragraphs.text: higher baseline incidence, such as Turner syn drome and PWS [225].
paragraphs.heading: 1.6.1.3 Scoliosis Progression

paragraphs.text: The incidence of type 1 diabetes mellitus in children and adults is not increased by GH treatment. Recombinant human GH decreases insulin sensitivity, which can result in higher insulin requirements for patients with coexist ing diabetes or result in the development of type 2 diabetes mellitus in those at risk. The increase in insulin resistance appears to hap pen early and returns to baseline with time or after discontinuation of treatment. Monitoring for impaired glucose metabolism and potential diabetes mellitus should be focused on patients at risk [266].
paragraphs.heading: Resistance

paragraphs.text: Other recognized side effects include muscu loskeletal symptoms such as edema, carpal tunnel syndrome, and muscular pain related to fluid retention which might correlate with overdosage. They are less likely to occur if the starting dose is low and titrated up as needed. GH can cause tonsillar hypertrophy and can exacerbate obstructive sleep apnea, which is a particularly important risk in patients with PWS. Polysomnography prior to initiating treatment and monitoring during treatment is recommended for those patients. Pancreatitis, although rare, is another listed side effect of rhGH, but whether there is a causal relation ship from rhGH treatment is still unknown. Lastly, increases in the metabolism of cortisol and thyroid hormone may help unmask adre nal insufficiency or hypothyroidism, respec tively after starting GH treatment [225].
paragraphs.heading: 1.6.1.5 Other Side Effects

paragraphs.text: In 2016, the European Society of Paediatric Endocrinology (ESPE), the GH Research Society (GRS), and the Pediatric Endocrine Society (PES) released a position statement to address rhGH safety: “GH exposure and treatment data throughout studies are incom plete and lack harmony in how patients are
paragraphs.heading: 1.6.2 Long-Term Risks

paragraphs.text: characterized, diagnosed, and treated, how and which risk factors are quantified, and risk metrics reported. The available evidence to date does not support an association between rhGH therapy and all-cause mortality, and there is inadequate data to reach a conclusion regarding the association to cause specific” [266].
paragraphs.heading: 1.6.2 Long-Term Risks

paragraphs.text: GH and IGF-I, which both have anabolic and mitogenic effects, have been suggested to cause the proliferation of normal and malig nant cells. GH and IGFs may favor the devel opment of tumors because they promote cell proliferation, epithelial-mesenchymal transi tion, and angiogenesis, as well as inhibit apop tosis. Therefore, the potential role of GH in tumor growth has been considered. On the other hand, IGFBPs may protect against tumor progression by inhibiting mitogenesis and stimulating apoptosis [267, 268].
paragraphs.heading: and Secondary Malignancies

paragraphs.text: Initial data from the Kabi International Growth Study (KIGS) [269] and the National Cooperative Growth Study (NCGS) [270] did not support an increased risk of brain tumor recurrence. Follow-up data by the NCGS in 2010, which comprises approximately 20 years of GH therapy and 192,345 patient-years, continued to report no increase in new malig nancies or recurrences of CNS tumors in rhGH-treated patients without risk factors [265].
paragraphs.heading: and Secondary Malignancies

paragraphs.text: The Childhood Cancer Survivor Study ini tially reported that cancer survivors treated with GH appeared to have an increased risk of developing secondary neoplasms com pared to survivors not treated of 3.21 (95% CI 1.88–5.46) [271], which decreased to 2.15 (95% CI 1.3–3.5) [272] with longer follow-up, and more recent data showed no significant asso ciation [273]. The most common secondary malignancy was meningioma. The French Childhood Cancer Survivor study showed that meningioma risk increased with higher radiation doses, but was not associated with GH therapy [274]; rather, both GHD and meningioma develop independently after radiation therapy. Thus, at most, the risk for
paragraphs.heading: and Secondary Malignancies

paragraphs.text: secondary neoplasia from rhGH is minor at best.
paragraphs.heading: and Secondary Malignancies

paragraphs.text: Including these and other observation studies, to date, rhGH therapy in childhood cancer survivors does not appear to increase the risk of primary tumor recurrence or the development of secondary malignancies [275]. Therefore, cancer surveillance is not recom mended beyond local standard practice, including in children and adults with prior malignancy [225, 266]. However, there are only a small number of subjects with longterm follow-up. The latter should be discussed with patients and families before starting rhGH therapy [266].
paragraphs.heading: and Secondary Malignancies

paragraphs.text: The statistics of the NCGS have not shown a higher incidence of melanocyte nevi or skin cancer in individuals treated with rhGH [276].
paragraphs.heading: 1.6.2.2 Skin Cancer

paragraphs.text: An association between rhGH treatment and subarachnoid hemorrhage, intracerebral hem orrhage, and ischemic stroke was found in a French Registry [277], but an increased inci dence of cardiovascular events was not seen in other European countries [278]. When the full cohort of 24,232 patients treated with rhGH during childhood and with more than 400,000 patient-years of follow-up was analyzed, low-risk patients with IGHD or ISS did not have a significant increase in all-cause mortal ity (SMR 1.1, 95% CI 0.9–1.3). In children born small for gestational age, all-cause mor tality was significantly increased (SMR 1.5, 95% CI 1.1–1.9), but this was due to the French cohort; potential confounders included family history and coexisting condi tions. However, cause-specific mortality from diseases of the circulatory and hematological systems was increased in all risk groups [279]. Another recent cohort study reported an increased risk of cardiovascular events in young adults, particularly women who had been treated with rhGH in childhood [280]. This is an association and does not prove cau sality. The absolute risk was low. Longer-term surveillance studies are needed.

paragraphs.text: Congenital anomalies or anything that dam ages the hypothalamus, pituitary stalk, or pituitary gland can result in GHD. It is now recognized that there are molecular defects at multiple levels of the GH axis that cause GHD. Diagnosis of GHD, however, remains problematic. Once it is diagnosed, GH ther apy is an effective treatment for a patient who is truly GH deficient.

### 1.1 Introduction and Background

### Information

### 1.1.1 Pituitary Gland Structure

### and Function

The pituitary gland is formed of two portions derived from different sources: the anterior (adenohypophysis) and the posterior (neuro hypophysis) [1]. The upward invagination of stomodeal ectoderm forms the primordium of the anterior pituitary, Rathke’s pouch, while the posterior pituitary arises from the neural ectoderm of the forebrain [2]. Rathke’s pouch can be identified by the third week of pregnancy [3].

The anterior pituitary comprises 80% of the pituitary and consists of three parts: the pars distalis (pars anterior or anterior lobe), the pars intermedia (intermediate lobe), and the pars tuberalis (pars infundibularis or pars proximalis). In humans, the pars distalis is the largest portion of the anterior pituitary and where most of the anterior pituitary hor

mones are produced [3]. The intermediate lobe is poorly developed in humans with only a tiny remnant identifiable in adults, although more obvious in the fetus and in pregnant women [4]. The upward extension of the pars distalis onto the pituitary stalk forms the pars tuberalis, which may contain a small number of gonadotropin-producing cells [3].

Peptide hormones produced in neurons of the hypothalamus are transported via a capil lary plexus in the pituitary stalk to the ante rior pituitary, where they regulate the synthesis and release of several hormones from special ized cell types. Somatotrophs produce somato tropin, more commonly known as growth hormone (GH); lactotrophs produce prolac tin (PRL); thyrotrophs produce thyrotropin, also known as thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH); gonadotrophs produce the two gonad otropins, follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH); and cortico trophs produce adrenocorticotropin (ACTH) [5]. Earlier studies suggested localization of the various cell types, for example, lactotrophs to the rostral and caudal regions and somato trophs predominantly to the anterolateral wings of the gland. However, the organization appears to be much more complicated with the anterior pituitary cells arranged in net works and adapting dynamically in response to the hypothalamic-releasing and -inhibiting hormones [6]. Posterior pituitary hormones are synthesized in cell bodies of neurons in the hypothalamus and transported along their axons through the neurohypophyseal tract of the pituitary stalk. These hormones, arginine vasopressin (also known as antidi uretic hormone [ADH]) and oxytocin, are then stored in, and secreted from, the poste rior pituitary [7].

Hypopituitarism is the deficiency in vary ing degrees of one or multiple pituitary hor mones. In this chapter, GH deficiency (GHD) will be discussed, while other hormonal defi ciencies are presented elsewhere in this book. To understand GHD, an understanding of GH physiology is important and follows below.

### 1.1.2 Growth Hormone

Growth hormone is a single-chain α-helical nonglycosylated polypeptide. The majority (75–90%) of circulating GH is a 22-kDA form consisting of 191 amino acids and two intra molecular disulfide bonds [3, 8]. There is also a 20-kDa variant form, which arises from alternative splicing during the processing of human GH pre-mRNA [9, 10]. The remainder of the GH produced by the pituitary is in the N-acetylated and desamidated forms and oligomers [3]. Secreted GH circulates both unbound and bound to binding proteins, which are portions of the extracellular domain of the GH receptor (GHR) [11].

The GH1 gene encodes for GH and is part of a 50-kb cluster of five genes located on human chromosome 17q22–24: GH1, chori onic somatomammotropin (CS)-like (L), CS- A, GH-2, and CS-B [12]. The CS-L translated protein appears nonfunctional, while the CS- A and CS-B genes encode human chorionic somatomammotropin (hCS), also known as human placental lactogen (hPL). hCS is pro duced by syncytiotrophoblastic cells and has 85% homology to GH. While hCS also con tains two disulfide bonds that occur at the same positions as in GH-N, it only has 0.5% affinity for the GHR. Interestingly, hCS does not appear necessary for fetal or extrauterine growth, nor does it appear essential for the maintenance of pregnancy or lactation [13]. The GH-2 gene product, which is known as the GH variant (GH-V), differs from GH-N by 13 amino acids. It is expressed as at least four alternatively spliced mRNAs in the pla centa and is continuously secreted during the second half of pregnancy, suppressing mater nal pituitary GH-1 gene function [14, 15].

IGFs circulate within the plasma com plexed to high-affinity binding proteins or IGF-binding proteins (IGFBPs). IGFBPs extend the serum half-life of IGFs, transport IGFs into target cells, and modulate the inter action of IGFs with their receptors [60, 65]. Six distinct IGFBPs have been cloned and sequenced [66, 67]. IGFBP-3, which is GH dependent, is the major IGFBP in human serum and transports over 90% of the circu lating IGF-I [3].

The IGF-I receptor (IGF-IR), which is structurally related to the insulin receptor, is a heterotetramer comprised of two membranespanning α-subunits and two intracellular β-subunits [68, 69]. The subunits contain binding sites for IGF-I, are linked by disulfide bonds, and are composed of a transmem brane domain, an adenosine triphosphate (ATP)-binding site, and a tyrosine kinase domain that mediates the presumed signal transduction mechanism for the receptor [3, 70].

### 1.2 Etiology of Growth Hormone

### Deficiency

### 1.2.1 Congenital Forms of GH

### Deficiency (Box 1.1)

The incidence of congenital isolated GHD (IGHD) has been reported as between 1:4000 and 1:10,000 live births [71, 72]. Congenital cranial malformations, including holoprosen cephaly, septo-optic dysplasia (SOD) spec trum, and midline craniocerebral or midfacial

abnormalities, can be associated with anoma lies of the pituitary gland, including pituitary hypoplasia and/or aplasia or an ectopic poste rior pituitary gland (EPP) [7]. Clinically, they may be associated with pituitary hormone deficiencies at birth or with the risk of devel oping future hormone deficiencies. Although these conditions often have no identifiable eti ology, ongoing advances in understanding pituitary development have provided a genetic basis to account for pituitary pathology. Mutations have been found in genes necessary for pituitary development and function. The following presents a summary of reported genetic defects associated with pituitary pathology.

Otx2

Otx genes are expressed in the rostral brain during development and are homologous to the Drosophila orthodenticle (otd) gene, which is essential for the development of the head in Drosophila melanogaster [85]. Otx2 is expressed in the ventral diencephalon, where it interacts with Hesx1, and in Rathke’s pouch. Homozygous inactivation of Otx2 in mice leads to extreme brain defects, while heterozy gous inactivation results in eye abnormalities, commonly pituitary hypoplasia, and some times holoprosencephaly. Heterozygous muta tions of the OTX2 gene, which have been implicated in severe ocular malformations such as anophthalmia, have also been reported in patients with hypopituitarism ranging from GHD to multiple pituitary hormone deficien cies [86–89]. There are variable findings of hypoplastic pituitary, EPP, and Chiari syn drome [90–92].

Pitx2 (Ptx2)

Pitx2 is a paired-like homeodomain transcrip tion factor closely related to the mammalian Otx genes [85]. Pitx2 null mice show embry onic lethality; however, a hypomorphic allele model of Pitx2 demonstrated pituitary hypo plasia and cellular differentiation defects in proportion to the reduced dosage of Ptx2. The gonadotrophs were most severely affected, followed by somatotrophs and thyro trophs [93–95].

RIEG is the human homolog of Pitx2, and clinical mutations of PTX2 have been described in patients with Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome. This syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition with variable manifesta tions including anomalies of the anterior chamber of the eye, dental hypoplasia, a pro tuberant umbilicus, mental retardation, and pituitary alterations [96]. One group of inves

tigators described mutations in six out of ten families with autosomal dominant Rieger syndrome [96, 97]. Five of the six mutations reported were in the homeobox region, and several showed loss of DNA-binding capacity.

Lhx3 (Lim-3, P-Lim) and Lhx4

Lhx3 is a LIM-type homeodomain protein expressed in the anterior and intermediate lobes of the pituitary gland, the ventral hind brain, and the spinal cord. Lhx3 expression persists in the adult pituitary, suggesting a maintenance function in one or more of the anterior pituitary cell types [97]. In addition, its expression is associated with cells that secrete GH and PRL, as well as the expression of the α-glycoprotein subunit (α-GSU), sug gesting a common cell precursor for gonado trophs, thyrotrophs, somatotrophs, and lactotrophs [98, 99].

In humans, homozygous loss-of-function mutations in LHX3 have been identified in patients with hypopituitarism including GH, TSH, PRL, LH, and FSH deficiencies, ante rior pituitary defects, and cervical abnormal ities with or without restricted neck rotation [100, 101]. Among 366 studied patients with IGHD or CPHD, only seven patients from four families were found to have LHX3 mutations, suggesting LHX3 gene mutations are a rare cause of CPHD [102]. A com pound heterozygous mutation of LHX3 was described that leads to a short protein induc ing a dominant negative effect (from a pater nally derived change) and a protein with impaired transactivational ability (from a maternally derived change) [103]. As with other described LHX3 mutations, the patient presented with pituitary hormone deficien cies, in addition to deafness and limited neck rotation.

Lhx4 is a closely related transcription fac tor to Lhx3. Heterozygous sporadic and familial LHX4 mutations have been reported. Pituitary hormone deficiencies range from IGHD to panhypopituitarism, and the pitu itary may be hypoplastic with or without an EPP. Some patients also have corpus callosum hypoplasia or Chiari syndrome with pointed cerebellar tonsils [104].

Other Transcription Factors

In addition to the more commonly cited fac tors, several other mutated developmental factors have been reported to cause CPHD [104]. For example, patients with reported SOX2 mutations present phenotypes that include hormone deficiencies (primarily iso lated gonadotroph deficiency, but occasion ally GH deficiency), pituitary hypoplasia, and eye abnormalities [104, 105]. Sox2 is also expressed in the dien cephalon, the developing central nervous sys tem, in the sensory placodes, inner ear, cochlea, and the developing lens, retina, and optic nerve [104].

Another interesting development has been the association of pituitary hormone deficien cies with mutations in the gonadotroph genes prokineticin receptor 2 (PROKR2), fibroblast growth factor 8 (FGF8), and FGF receptor 1 (FGFR1), which have been traditionally reported in patients with isolated hypogonad otropic hypogonadism [106].
