Because families in the relatively small area from which the Ecuadorian patients originate had intensive experience with this condition, lay diagnosis was considered reliable. Of 79 affected individuals for whom information could be obtained, 15 (19%) died under 7 years of age, as opposed to 21 out of 216 of their unaffected siblings (9.7%, p < 0.05). The kinds of illnesses resulting in death, such as pneumonia, diarrhea, and meningitis, were no different for affected than for unaffected sib lings [63]. The complete lifespan in the Ecuadorian cohort provided an opportunity to look at adult mortality risk factors. Twenty-three adults with GHRD had elevated cholesterol levels, normal HDL-cholesterol levels, ele vated LDL-cholesterol levels, and normal tri glycerides compared to relatives and nonrelated community controls. It was postulated that the effect of IGF-I deficiency due to GHRD was to decrease hepatic clear ance of LDL-C, since the triglyceride and HDL-C levels were unaffected. This effect was independent of obesity or of IGFBP-1 levels, which were used as a surrogate for insu linemia. The key pathogenic factor was thought to be the absence of GH induction of LDL receptors in the liver [64]. ### 2.3.4 Cancer Protection ### in Ecuadorian Laron Syndrome (ELS) GH-induced IGF-I is the main determinant of human growth, and GH deficiency (GHD) is associated with a diminished incidence of cancer [65, 66]. Subjects with congenital IGF-I deficiency (IGFD), which included subjects with GHD, have no malignancies, while their relatives displayed a 9–24% cancer incidence [67, 68]. In a similar observation, malignancy incidence in IGFD individuals appeared diminished when compared to their non-IGFD relatives [69]. It is also observed in subjects with a nonfunctional GH receptor (GHR) [67, 68, 70]. The Ecuadorian LS cohort (ELS), which represents one-third of the World’s popula tion with this condition, is the most geneti cally homogenous cohort on the planet since most subjects are homozygous for a splice-site mutation occurring at the 180 codons of exon 6 of the GHR (ss180/ss180 (ss180)). This abnormality renders the GHR an easily degradable peptide, incapable of proper intra cellular signaling [71]. In the first report on morbidity and mortality, there were no cancer cases in ELS subjects, while their age- and sexmatched relatives had a 17% malignancyassociated mortality [72]. Indeed, defective GHR signaling is associated with extremely low levels of insulin and IGF-I, two impor tant growth and mitogenic factors. However, in 2013, one woman did develop ovarian can cer and later died [73]. Cancer in humans has been linked to vari ous etiological causes, such as overexpression of pro-growth pathways, oxidative stress, genomic instability, DNA damage, and other cellular abnormalities [74]. IGF-I-dependent promotion of age-dependent mutations that allow transformation of healthy protoonco genes into oncogenes have been proposed as determinant influences in carcinogenic pro cesses [75]. Accordingly, while activation of stress resistance transcription factors and antioxidant enzymes contributes to protec tion against age-associated damage and chronic illnesses in men, activating mutations in RAS and AKT, two potent enzymes down stream the IGF-I/IGFIR signaling route, as well as those in the IGF-IR itself, are found in human cancers [76–78]. Furthermore, carci nogenesis might result from defective action or mutations of various enzymes in the IGF-I pathway, including mTOR, S6K, RAS, ade nylate cyclase, and PKA, which can induce ## PDF page 64 | printed page 46 DNA damage, by increasing superoxide pro duction, among other reasons [79]. As previously stated, mutations that impair GHR function are associated with a diminished incidence of human malignancies [67, 72]. Interestingly, partial loss-of-function IGFI-R gene mutations are found in Ashkenazi Jewish centenarians, suggesting an association of low IGF-IR action and enhanced life span [80]. In vitro studies dem onstrated that human mammary cells treated with hydrogen peroxide and incubated with the serum from the ELS relatives display expected DNA damage; however, those cells incubated with serum from ELS subjects had much less DNA breaks. Moreover, serum from the ELS subjects induced reduced expression of RAS, PKA, and mTOR, as well as upregulation of superoxide dismutase-2. Furthermore, pathway analysis of global gene expression of the IGF-I-deficient ELS sub jects showed that while downregulation of RAS, PKA, and mTOR occurs in these indi viduals, apoptosis-promoting genes are upreg ulated [72]. Contextually, the self-destruction of malignant cells is a well-known physiologic protective mechanism; however, IGF-I excess levels appear to diminish apoptosis and greatly contribute to carcinogenesis [81]. ### 2 The diminished incidence of cancer in the ELS subjects, who were matched by age to their relatives, showed strong links between diminished IGF-I and GHR signaling and the low malignancy incidence observed. Indeed, ELS subjects exhibit low circulating concen trations of IGF-I, diminished DNA breaks, lower expression of RAS and PKA, increased expression of SOD2, augmented expression of pro-apoptotic genes, and enhanced apop tosis. These findings provide objective molec ular links between diminished GHR signaling and the cancer protection documented in this cohort. When GHR signaling is absent, the GH counter-regulatory effects on carbohydrate metabolism are also abolished, insulin resis tance is diminished, and insulin levels decrease. In consequence, ELS subjects metabolize glucose and other nutrients more efficiently, accumulate body fat, and have an obese phenotype [82]. The most relevant effect in carcinogenesis appears to be the lower serum levels of insulin, a potent growth factor that not only turns on PI3K/AKT, its meta bolic branch but also the RAS/MAPK cas cade, its proliferative route. The cancer protection seen in the ELS cohort may be due to dual low-IGF-I/low insulin serum levels. Moreover, since rapidly dividing cells need excess energy to maintain their elevated mito genic rate, the lower other energy-supplier metabolites (glucose, triglycerides, etc.) in LS should make cell division slower and high mitogenic rate-dependent neoplasia less pos sible. This occurs because the insulin/INSR is a central site for energy generation in the form of ATP and GDP, which are indispensable for cell division, especially for fast-dividing cells [83]. In summary, lesser levels of the growth peptides (insulin and IGF-I) and energy sources should make cell division slower and less prone to errors compared to those under going a faster mitotic rate. Among 18 affected children and adolescents administered the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children, only 3 had IQs within the aver age range (90–110); of the remaining 15 sub jects, 3 were in the low average range (80–89), 3 in the borderline range (70–79), and 9 in the intellectually disabled range (<70). Sporadic anecdotal reports of patients with GHRD suggested a normal range of intelligence. The GH levels show normal diurnal fluctuation [17]. Twenty-four-hour profiles demonstrate marked GH variability among adult patients with suppression by exogenous recombinant human IGF-I [17]. Thus, the normal sensitiv ity of the GH secretion is preserved, despite lifelong elevated GH levels and lack of feed back suppression from IGF-I. Post-pubertal subjects with GHRD may have normal or elevated basal levels of GH but invariably demonstrate hyperresponsiveness to stimulation, which is even more impressive considering their obesity, which suppresses GH responses in normal individuals. This hyper-responsiveness might also be due to the enhanced insulin sensitivity seen in these subjects that could theoretically induce deeper hypoglycemia or, alternatively, that the higher insulin efficiency sensitizes GH release via other hypothalamic mechanisms. ALS mutations are associated with normal GH levels, despite very low circulating IGF-I concentrations. IGF-I receptor deficiency, which is an IGF-I rather than GH resistant state, can also be associated with normal GH levels. ### 2.5.2 Growth Hormone Binding ### Protein (GHBP) Absence of GHBP in the circulation was ini tially considered a requirement for the diag nosis of GHRD, along with the clinical phenotype, very low concentrations of IGF-I and IGFBP-3, and elevated (in children) or normal to elevated (in adults) GH levels. Chromatographic analysis for serum GHBP, however, showed measurable though reduced levels in several subjects. The ligand-mediated immunofunction assay (LIFA) used to mea sure GHBP serum levels since 1990 uses an anti-GH monoclonal antibody to measure the amount of GH bound to GHBP. As a largely functional assay, this should not detect structurally abnormal though expressed GHBP. ## PDF page 73 | printed page 55 As noted above, certain genetic defects in the GHR, those affecting dimerization or anchoring of the GHBP to the cell membrane, as well as dominant-negative mutations of the cytoplasmic domain, can result in normal or markedly elevated GHBP levels. There were no age-dependent changes, indicating that the difference in IGF values between children and adults was not related to the GHBP levels which did not correlate with stature or with serum IGF-I levels [93]. Thirty-one of the 82 patients reported by Woods et al. [109] had a genetic study of the GHR, of whom 27 had abnormalities affecting both alleles of the GHR gene, in association with clinically and biochemically unequivocal GHRD. Identification of heterozygous muta tions, however, is not necessarily helpful because, as noted earlier, polymorphisms have been described, which appear to have no phe notypic consequences. ### 2.6.1 Partial GH Resistance GH resistance might be expected to occur in an incomplete form, analogous to insulin resistance, androgen insensitivity, or thyroid hormone resistance. Affected children might have growth failure with normal or slightly increased GH secretion, variable but usually decreased GHBP levels, decreased IGF-I con centrations, but not as severely reduced as in GHD or GHRD, and might respond to sup raphysiologic doses of GH. It might also be expected, given the need for dimerization of the GHR for signal transduction, that certain mutations could have a dominant-negative effect in the heterozygous state. Over 40% were deemed IGF-I deficient, and half of these to have the novel diagnosis of “primary IGF-I deficiency,” i.e., normal GH responses with low IGF-I. What cannot be appreciated from such a cross-sectional analysis of data from hun dreds of pediatric endocrinologists is the clin ical context in which the biochemical measures were obtained. Decreased circulating IGF-I with normal or elevated GH levels occurs with chronic illness and undernutrition. Many of the children seen with what is termed ISS are poor eaters with decreased body mass index and may be receiving treatment for hyperac tivity, which can suppress appetite and growth. IGF-I levels decline substantially with fasting, which is considered a means of pro tecting against potential insulin-like effects on circulating glucose levels. Clinical investiga tions of children with ISS and varying responses to GH stimulation tests or IGF-I generation tests (in which GH is given for sev eral days to stimulate IGF-I synthesis) have indicated that GH insensitivity is, at most, an uncommon finding [128]. Substantial tissue delivery is reflected in pro found effects on adipose tissue, facies, and lymphoid tissue in treated patients (see below). This indicates that twice-daily injection pro vides more than adequate replacement of endocrine IGF-I, despite both IGFBP-3 and ALS deficiencies, which are not corrected by IGF-I treatment. The maintenance of circu lating levels of IGF-I despite severe IGFBP-3 and ALS deficiency may be the result of bind ing to other IGFBPs; IGFBP-2 is elevated in GHRD and increases further with rhIGF-I therapy [17]. If the tissue dose of IGF-I in patients with GHI treated with IGF-I is supraphysiologic, as indicated by increases in body fat and acro megalic facial changes, why then do we not see sustained growth acceleration as in GHtreated GHD? At this time, the dual effector hypothesis remains the most appropriate explanation for the inadequate growth response [14]. With a diminished ability to stimulate prechondrocyte differentiation and local IGF-I production, children with GHI can expect only partial recovery of normal growth with IGF-I replacement. Thus, rhIGF- I replacement therapy of GHI may need to continue longer than GH treatment of GHD to achieve more normal height. This goal will likely require suppressing adolescence in most children with GHI, using GnRH analogues [134]. In addition to statural attainment, goals of replacement therapy with rhIGF-I in GHI include improvement in body composition, normalization of facial appearance, and pos sible reduction of risk factors for childhood and adult mortality. All studies that have monitored body composition have verified lean mass increases, including increased bone density. Unlike GH replacement therapy, however, which restores normal lipolysis, IGF-I therapy is lipotropic, increasing or sus taining the high percentage of body fat. Normalization of craniofacial features has also been apparent [139]. Voice change has not been remarked on, but can be expected. The reduction of risk factors for higher mortality in infancy and childhood with GHRD is to be expected with rhIGF-I ther apy, but the reason for this increased risk is unknown. Leukocytes share in the general upregulation of IGF-I receptors in GHRD and appear to function normally in this con dition [140]. In a study of one affected infant (who died at 7 months with bronchitis) and 5 adults with GHRD from Ecuador, Diamond et al. [141] demonstrated a variety of immune disturbances in the infant and 3 of the adults. Children, especially boys, with constitutional delay in growth and maturation (CDGM), who do not have biochemical markers of undernutrition, may be hypermetabolic and have mean IGF-I concentrations that are only 40% of those of normal age-mates, which could lead to an inappropriate diagnosis of IGFD [143]. The off-label promotion of rhIGF-I has been based on two consider ations that are not evidence-based, that many children with ISS have partial GH insensitiv ity, and that appropriate therapy for these individuals is recombinant IGF-I. The absence of convincing evidence for this hypothesis, the limited ability of endocrine IGF-I to restore normal growth in those with unequivocal GH unresponsiveness, the sup pression of local GH effects on growth with IGF-I administration, the risk profile, and the absence of data on efficacy in other than proven severe GH insensitivity, led the Drug and Therapeutics Committee of the Pediatric Endocrine Society to conclude that rhIGF-I use is only justified in conditions approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and that use for growth promotion in other children should only be investigational [62]. The manufacturer of rhIGF-I estimates that approximately 30,000 children in the United States are affected by primary IGFD, which is also simi lar to the estimated (European Union) EU market size [128]. Considering that fewer than 200 children with GHI due to GHRD, trans duction defects, or GH inhibiting antibodies had been identified worldwide in the previous 20 years, it is apparent that there was exuber ant anticipation and extensive promotion of off-label use. Indeed, current clinical trials demonstrate the loosening of criteria from those in the approval by FDA ( www. clinicaltrials.gov). Inclusion requires height SDS ≤−2 (which is less stringent than the cri terion of SDS ≤−2.25 for GH treatment of ISS) and IGF-I SDS ≤1, along with a normal response to GH stimulation testing, and bone age ≤11 years for boys and ≤9 years for girls. In contrast to the far less com mon hypoglycemia of GHD which is cor rected by GH replacement therapy, IGF-I treatment increases the risk of hypoglycemia in children with GHRD. Hypoglycemia has been the most common early adverse event, reported in 49% of subjects in the largest series, including 5% with seizures [136]. In the 6-month, placebo-controlled Ecuadorian study, hypoglycemia was reported in 67% of individuals receiving placebo and 86% of those treated with rhIGF-I, an insignificant difference [86]. Finger stick blood glucose measurements in 23 subjects residing at a research unit indicated frequent hypoglyce mia before breakfast and lunch, which did not increase in frequency with rhIGF-I administration [136]. Five of the subjects participated in a crossover, placebo-con trolled study for 6 months with a 3-month washout period with fasting glucose determi nations performed three times daily by care givers for the entire 15-month study. The percentage of glucose values <50 mg/dL was 2.6% with placebo and 5.5% with rhIGF-I, not a significant difference. In practice, hypo glycemia associated with IGF-I treatment appears reasonably controllable by adequate food intake. Pain at the injection site is common. Injection site lipohypertrophy is frequent, affecting at least one-third of subjects; this is the result of failure to rotate injections and injection into the lumps, which can attenuate growth response. The inotropic effect of IGF-I results in asymptomatic tachycardia in all treated patients, which clears after several months of continued use [146]. Benign intra cranial hypertension or papilledema has been noted in approximately 5% of IGF-treated subjects. While headache is frequent, the placebo-controlled study found no difference in incidence between those receiving placebo injections and those receiving rhIGF- I. Parotid swelling and facial nerve palsy have been described. Lymphoid tissue hypertrophy occurs in over 25% of patients, with hypoacu sis, snoring, and tonsillar/adenoidal hypertro phy that required surgical intervention in over 10% of patients. Thymic hypertrophy was noted in 35% of subjects having regular chest radiographs. It is worth noting that some of these side effects may be more frequent than reported because they take time to develop; for example, snoring incidence in the first year for the 25 longest treated subjects in the ## PDF page 82 | printed page 64 mecasermin study was only 4%, but increased to 65% for the entire study period [136]. Anti-IGF-I antibodies have developed in approximately half of the rhIGF-I-treated patients during the first year of treatment, but these have had no effect on response [135, 136]. Urticaria has been noted in subjects participating in the trial of IGF-I in combina tion with GH. Transient elevation of liver enzymes has also been noted [135]. Coarsening of facial features with disproportionate growth of the jaw reminiscent of acromegaly has been common, particularly among those of pubertal age [134]. paragraphs.heading: Normal Variant and Idiopathic Short Stature

paragraphs.text: Short stature is defined as a height ≤2 stan dard deviations (SD) below the mean for age, sex, and population. Height in a given popula tion follows a normal Gaussian distribution; therefore, it is expected that the height of 2.3% of a population will fall 2 SD below the mean for age and sex [1]. Among this 2.3% of the population, the majority will have a normal variant of short stature or idiopathic short stature, but some may have an underlying pathological etiology.
paragraphs.heading: 3.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: Normal variant short stature is comprised of familial short stature (FSS) and constitu tional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP). These individuals attain an adult height con sistent with their target genetic height, while individuals with idiopathic short stature have predicted adult heights below their familial target height range. Frequently, FSS and CDGP are considered subtypes of ISS. The growth patterns of individuals with FSS and/ or CDGP, however, are usually consistent with that of a first-degree relative and their adult height conforms with their target height. These diagnoses, therefore, most suitably rep resent “normal variants” of growth [2].
paragraphs.heading: 3.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: Normal variant and idiopathic short stat ure are considered nonpathological short stat ure, without an organic origin, such as intrauterine growth restriction, chronic dis ease, endocrinopathy, skeletal dysplasia, or genetic disorder.
paragraphs.heading: 3.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: Frankfort plane. (From Foote et al. [3]. Reprinted with permission from Elsevier)
paragraphs.heading: Measurement

paragraphs.text: mass index should be plotted on the CDC growth charts for children ages 2–20 years [5].
paragraphs.heading: Measurement

paragraphs.text: Because birth length reflects intrauterine factors, an infant’s weight and length may cross growth percentiles during the first 2 years of life, gravitating toward percentiles consistent with their genetic potential. Thereafter, significant shifts in length or height percentiles should not occur, except for children with CDGP, who may continue to exhibit a decline in length or height percentile until ages 3–4. At that time, they maintain a normal linear growth velocity and will grow at a consistent percentile. Height measurements tend to be 1 cm less than length measure ments; therefore, length measurements need to be adjusted when plotted on a height chart. This difference accounts for the apparent decline in growth rate when a child is transi tioned from a length measurement to a stand ing height.
paragraphs.heading: Measurement

paragraphs.text: Assessing a child’s pattern of weight gain, linear growth, and gain in head circumference is important for the evaluation of short stat ure and overall health. Pathological causes of poor growth secondary to nutritional causes or chronic disease typically affect weight gain, then linear growth, and finally head circum ference. However, disorders of malabsorp tion, such as celiac disease, may sometimes initially present with normal weight gain, but poor growth. In contrast, children with endo crine disorders typically present with normal or increased weight gain and poor linear growth.

The evaluation of a child with a height 2 SD below the mean for age and sex should include anthropometric measurements of upper and lower segments, or sitting height, arm span, and occipitofrontal head circumference to assess for disproportion and possible skeletal dysplasia. Arm span is measured with the child standing in an erect position against a wall with outstretched arms. The distance between the tips of the middle phalanges is measured. In prepubertal children, the arm span is shorter than height, and after midpu berty the arm span exceeds height. In an adult male, arm span exceeds height by 5.2 cm and in an adult female by 1.2 cm. Ethnic differ ences exist as well, with longer arm spans noted in the African American population. Arm span can be measured in a sitting or supine position if the child is unable to stand. A sitting height (SH) is measured with the child seated on a chair flush against the stadi ometer. Subtracting the sitting height from the child’s standing height (HT) provides the value of their lower segment (LS). The SH/ HT ratio or SH/LS ratio can be plotted on their appropriate charts to determine whether these ratios are disproportionate and sugges tive of skeletal dysplasia. An alternative approach is to measure the child’s lower seg ment from the symphysis pubis to the floor and subtract this value from the child’s stand ing height for their truncal height. The upper to lower segment ratio decreases throughout childhood and adolescence. Due to an increased truncal length relative to limbs,
paragraphs.heading: Measurements

paragraphs.text: infants have an upper to lower segment ratio of 1.7. By age 3 the upper to lower segment ratio decreases to 1.3, by age 10 this ratio decreases to 1, and in pubertal children, the ratio is <1. Children with CDGP have increased leg length and shortened truncal height which accounts for their decreased upper to lower segment ratios of 0.8–0.9.
paragraphs.heading: Measurements

paragraphs.text: Skeletal maturation is evaluated by assessing epiphyseal maturation with bone age radio graphs, using the methods of either Greulich and Pyle or Tanner-Whitehouse. The former method compares a child’s left-hand radio graph to standard bone age radiographs of the left hands of mid-western boys and girls from birth through age 18 [7]. The Tanner- Whitehouse method assigns a value to each of the 27 epiphyses in the hand and wrist and sums these values for the skeletal maturity score, which correlates with specific bone ages as determined for select populations [8]. Bayley-Pinneau also provides a table for the
paragraphs.heading: 3.2.4 Bone Age

paragraphs.text: percent of adult height achieved at given bone ages, which can be used to calculate a child’s predicted adult height [9]. Variations in bone age readings among providers and inaccurate height measurements can limit the accuracy of a child’s height prediction.
paragraphs.heading: 3.2.4 Bone Age

paragraphs.text: Loss of the primary teeth and eruption of permanent teeth correlate with bone age but can vary due to environmental influences. Tooth calcification as determined on an orthopantomogram is less variable and corre sponds better with dental age [10, 11]. Growth hormone deficiency (GHD), hypothyroidism, and CDGP are associated with delayed dental age and bone age.
paragraphs.heading: 3.2.5 Dental Age

paragraphs.text: In the 1970s, Tanner et al. defined target height as either the addition or subtraction of 6.5 cm from the mean parental height for a
paragraphs.heading: 3.2.6 Target Height

paragraphs.text: boy or girl, respectively. Two SD represents 11 cm above or below the calculated target height [12]. The target height is used to deter mine a child’s expected adult height based on their genetic potential. Measuring the parents’ heights at the child’s visit improves the accu racy of the target height calculation. Starting in the 1990s, researchers devised alternative formulas to calculate the target height because the method of Tanner either underestimated or overestimated the height of a child with short or tall parents, respectively. These for mulas also tried to account for population trends and secular height trends. The 2008 consensus statement from the Growth Hormone Research Society, the Lawson Wilkins Pediatric Endocrine Society, and the European Society for Paediatric Endocrinology Workshop recommended using a corrected target height SD in lieu of the Tanner method. The corrected target height is calculated as 0.72 × the average of the father’s and mother’s height SD with the lower limit of the target height as the cor rected target height minus 1.6 SD [13].
paragraphs.heading: 3.2.6 Target Height

paragraphs.text: The evaluation of a child with short stat ure requires a review of their previous growth data, accurate length and/or height measure ments, a calculated target height, bone age, predicted adult height, and possibly arm span and upper to lower segment ratio. Analyzing auxologic data in conjunction with a detailed history and physical examination is essential for determining whether a child’s short stature is a normal variant or due to an underlying disorder.
In CDGP, the growth rate declines and crosses percentiles in the first 2–3 years of life. Usually, by age 3–4 years, growth resumes
paragraphs.heading: of Growth and Puberty

paragraphs.text: normal rate and the bone age is delayed (often 2–3 SD delay). Other features of CDGP include delayed pubertal onset and eventual attainment of an adult height consistent with midparental target range. Most children with CDGP exhibit a pattern of weight gain that mirrors their linear growth at less than 2 SD below the mean for age, sex, and population or at a lower percentile than their target growth percentile. Individuals with CDGP are frequently referred to as “late bloomers” and often have a first- or second-degree relative(s) with a history of delayed onset of puberty (defined as the onset of puberty for males as >13 years of age and for females as >12 years of age) and a similar growth pattern.
paragraphs.heading: of Growth and Puberty

paragraphs.text: Forty percent of children with constitu tional delay of growth and puberty also have familial short stature [14]. Even with a strong family history of CDGP, as with FSS, other identifiable causes of short stature and delayed puberty should be excluded, which is dis cussed in Sect. 3.4.
paragraphs.heading: of Growth and Puberty

paragraphs.text: Several studies report a 2:1–5:1 male to female predominance of CDGP [15, 16]. Wehkalampi et al.’s retrospective study evalu ated the prevalence of a positive family his tory in children with CDGP. The findings in this study challenge this male predominance because CDGP was equally prevalent in mothers and fathers. The authors suggest that referral bias may account for the reported male predominance in CDGP. The published data support an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance for CDGP [15–17]. Heterozygous mutations in the GH secreta gogue receptor gene (GSHR), a ghrelin recep
paragraphs.heading: of Growth and Puberty

paragraphs.text: tor gene, were identified in two females with CDGP, suggesting an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance with incomplete pene trance. Further studies are needed to better define the association of mutations in this gene with CDGP [18]. Researchers have not found mutations in the acid labile subunit, leptin, or the leptin receptor in individuals with CDGP [19, 20].
paragraphs.heading: of Growth and Puberty

paragraphs.text: Children with FSS have normal linear growth with height measurements ≤−2 SD below the mean for age, sex, and population and a pre dicted adult height consistent with their target height. They also have a bone age consistent with their chronologic age, a normal growth velocity and timing of pubertal, and short stature in at least one of the parents.
paragraphs.heading: 3.3.2 Familial Short Stature

paragraphs.text: Idiopathic short stature is defined is a height ≤−2.25 SD below the mean for age, sex, and population. ISS is distinguished from the normal variant short stature by a pre dicted adult height more than 2 SD below the child’s target height range. The term “idio
paragraphs.heading: 3.3.3 Idiopathic Short Stature

paragraphs.text: pathic” implies that the etiology of the short stature is unknown and is not due to FSS, CDGP, or another identifiable cause as dis cussed in detail in Sect. 3.4.
paragraphs.heading: 3.3.3 Idiopathic Short Stature

paragraphs.text: Since the FDA approved the use of GH for the treatment of ISS in 2003, genetic technol ogy has advanced in such a way as to be able to identify defects that had previously been unknown causes of short stature, blurring the line between what is now considered “idio pathic” short stature and genetic short stature. Alterations in the GH receptor gene, STAT 5b, acid labile subunit, and IGF-1 gene have been described in patients with a diagnosis of ISS [21]. One study utilized whole exome sequencing leading to the identification of genetic causes of short stature in 5 of 14 chil dren with prior diagnoses of ISS with a height ≤−3 SD below the mean for age and sex. Prior to whole exome testing, these chil dren had extensive evaluations, including standard genetic testing, that did not identify a cause for their short stature. Two of the five patients had the progeroid form of Ehlers- Danlos syndrome, and the other diagnoses included 3-M syndrome (overlapping features with Russell-Silver syndrome), Floating- Harbor syndrome, and a variant of the Kenny-Caffey syndrome with eucalcemia. However, in addition to short stature, these patients had dysmorphic features and/or other medical conditions that suggested a syn dromic cause of short stature [22].
paragraphs.heading: 3.3.3 Idiopathic Short Stature

paragraphs.text: Several other genetic etiologies have since been identified in which the only significant finding has been short stature. The most well known is the SHOX gene, which now has its own indication for use of GH. Mutations in NPR2, ACAN, IGF1, IGF1R, and FGFR3 have all been found to be associated with iso lated short stature [23]. Prior to the identifica tion of genes such as these, patients may have been classified as having ISS. As more altera tions in genes involved in stature are identi fied, the definition of ISS or criteria for treatment of ISS may need to evolve.
In summary, ISS is a diagnosis of exclu sion, determined after a comprehensive evalu ation fails to find an identifiable etiology for

the short stature. Rare genetic disorders should be considered as a cause for short stat ure in children with a height ≤−3 SD below the mean for age and sex, especially in the presence of dysmorphic features and/or other medical diagnoses. Debate remains about whether treatment of short stature should be offered to those previously classified as ISS who are now known to have a genetic cause of their short stature.

The evaluation of a child with a height ≤−2 SD below the mean for age, sex, and popula tion should include a comprehensive history and physical examination with anthropomet ric measurements. A detailed history should assess for risk factors for hypopituitarism, such as traumatic birth, postnatal hypoglyce mia, jaundice, and/or microphallus in male infants. A low birth weight and length may suggest short stature secondary to small for gestational age or Russell-Silver syndrome. A history of lymphedema, pedal edema, and/or cardiac anomalies may suggest Turner or Noonan syndrome. In girls with short stature, it is well established that Turner syndrome should be excluded even in the absence of overt clinical findings. A karyotype is not rou tinely done in boys but could be considered when the predicted adult height is below tar get height because 45X/46XY mosaicism may present with short stature and an otherwise normal phenotype. GH treatment can be con sidered for this condition [24]. Determining whether to test for a SHOX gene mutation is best determined by the established clinical scoring system for this condition. Rappold et al. found that an increased body mass index, decreased arm span/height ratio, Madelung deformity, short, bowed forearms, dislocation of the ulna at the elbow, and muscular hyper trophy were most predictive of this gene muta tion [25]. Children with a history of developmental delay and findings suggestive of a chromosomal disorder warrant further evaluation by a geneticist. Furthermore, the
paragraphs.heading: 3.4 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: evaluation should include an assessment for endocrine disorders such as hypothyroidism, isolated GH deficiency, and in some cases, Cushing disease/syndrome. Other causes of short stature to consider are chronic diseases, eating disorders, and psychosocial depriva tion.
paragraphs.heading: 3.4 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: If the comprehensive history, physical examination, and auxologic data are not sug gestive of a specific disorder, then screening
paragraphs.heading: 3.4 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: studies to exclude an identifiable etiology are indicated [13]. The diagnostic studies to con sider when evaluating a child with short stat ure are listed below. A retrospective chart review of 235 asymptomatic patients (defined as normal history, review of systems, and physical examination) referred to a large aca demic pediatric endocrinology center for short stature (height ≤−2 SD below the mean for age, sex, and population) demonstrated that these screening studies had a low yield for organic disease and were not cost-effective. Only 37% of the patients had prior growth records available as part of their evaluation. The authors suggest monitoring growth veloc ity over a 6-month period in asymptomatic children and then considering screening stud ies if growth is suboptimal. This differs from the earlier recommendations in the 2008 Consensus Statement on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Children with Idiopathic Short Stature (ISS) [27]. The most recent Pediatric Endocrine Society Guideline regarding GH treatment recommends shared decisionmaking with families when considering whether or not to treat a child with idiopathic short stature [28].
paragraphs.heading: 3.4 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Assessing children for GHD is an impor tant part of the evaluation when growth veloc ity is lower than expected. Since GH is secreted in a pulsatile fashion throughout the day with more frequent pulses overnight, random GH levels are typically nondiagnostic. GH medi ates the production of IGF-1 and IGF BP-3 from the liver; these levels are stable through out the day, serving as a better screening test for GHD. Normal ranges for IGF-1 and IGF BP-3 are based on age, sex, and the Tanner stage in prepubertal and pubertal children, respectively. Low or low/normal IGF-1 and IGF BP-3 levels should prompt further evalu ation with provocative GH stimulation test ing. Isolated low IGF-1 can be seen in children with undernutrition and may warrant delay ing GH stimulation testing until weight is improved. GH is measured at several time points following the administration of a GH secretagogue, such as clonidine, arginine,
paragraphs.heading: 3.4 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: l-Dopa, propranolol, glucagon, or insulin. A single GH value of ≥10 ng/mL on two pro vocative GH stimulation tests indicates GH sufficiency. Debate exists as to whether a lower GH peak should be used to indicate a normal stimulation test. In peripubertal and early pubertal children, priming with sex steroids (testosterone or estradiol), prior to the testing is indicated to prevent misdiagnosis of GHD [29–31]. An increase in GH amplitude and mean 24 h GH levels occurs between Tanner stages 2–4 and 3–5 in girls and boys, respec tively. Girls exhibit increased mean nocturnal GH levels and GH amplitude prior to the onset of breast development which coincides with the start of their pubertal growth spurt. In contrast, boys in the early stages of puberty have lower mean nocturnal GH levels and amplitude that are comparable to that of a prepubertal boy [32]. These data support the role of sex steroids on GH secretion and explain the decline in growth rate exhibited in boys prior to the onset of puberty. Saggese et al. showed that lower growth hormonereleasing hormone (GHRH) levels in children with delayed puberty may explain their sub normal GH response to stimulation tests. When retested in mid- to late puberty, these

adolescents had a normal GH response, and their GHRH levels were comparable to the control group [33]. A prospective study in Turkey evaluated the adult height of boys with a history of delayed growth and normal testosterone-primed GH stimulation studies. These boys had normal adult heights, consis tent with their mid-parental heights [34]. Müeller et al. and others showed that children with true GHD have an abnormal GH response to sex steroid-primed provocative GH stimulation tests [35, 36].

Adolescents with delayed puberty should have additional labs (gonadotropin levels, serum prolactin, estradiol, and/or testoster one) to assess for causes of pubertal delay. A girl with hypergonadotropic hypogonadism requires further evaluation with a karyotype for Turner syndrome, a common cause of pri mary ovarian failure and short stature with an incidence of 1 in 2500 live births. Fragile X testing should also be performed as girls with premutations can also have primary gonadal failure. Often, boys and girls with Noonan syndrome manifest delayed puberty, but boys more frequently have primary gonadal failure [37]. 46 XX SRY-positive males present with normal male external genitalia, short stature, and primary gonadal failure [38].

and Cushing disease/syndrome). Genetic syn dromes associated with HH and short stature include Prader-Willi syndrome and Werner syndrome. Table 3.1 shows the differential diagnosis and evaluation for delayed puberty.

Distinguishing idiopathic IHH from CDGP is often a challenge because basal and stimulated levels of gonadotropins are low in both conditions until the activation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis. Many studies, limited by a small number of study subjects, were conducted to determine whether basal and GnRH-stimulated FSH and LH levels, basal inhibin B levels, HCG-stimulated testosterone, and/or combinations of these tests can most effectively diagnose IHH. Binder et al.’s retrospective study showed that a combination of basal LH <0.3 IU/L and inhibin B <111 pg/mL had a specificity of 100% and sensitivity of 98% in establishing a diagnosis of IHH [39]. Another retrospective study determined that a peakstimulated LH of 2.8 U/L and 4-day and 19-day HCG-stimulated testosterone cutoff peaks of 1.04 mcg/L and 2.75 mcg/L, respec tively, had 100% sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing IHH [40]. Two prospective studies of basal inhibin B as a diagnostic test for IHH reported discrepant cutoff values. A meta-

analysis demonstrated a pooled sensitivity and specificity of 92% for inhibin B as a test to distinguish IHH from CDGP. However, the included studies were heterogeneous in meth odology and study size, making the results dif ficult to interpret. FSH-stimulated inhibin B levels have shown promise in distinguishing these two conditions [41]. A study examining kisspeptin-stimulated LH levels suggested that a stimulated level of 0.8 mIU/mL or greater accurately predicted puberty in all participants, whereas, in all participants with a stimulated level less than or equal to 0.4 mIU/mL, puberty did not occur by age 18. However, the study only had eight patients in each study group [42]. Further studies are needed to determine which set of tests, if any, can accurately distinguish between delayed puberty and hypogonadism [43–46].

Children with normal variant short stature and ISS are healthy and do not have an iden tifiable cause for their short stature. Management should include reassurance and follow-up to monitor growth, pubertal devel opment, and other auxologic growth parame ters to confirm that the child follows the anticipated pattern of growth. Ongoing sur veillance of the child’s growth pattern is important because, despite an extensive evalu ation, a diagnosis such as mild hypochondro plasia or pseudohypoparathyroidism may not be clinically and diagnostically evident until the child is older [47–49]. In certain cases, the option to treat may be considered and is an individualized decision that needs to be clearly discussed with the family. As peers progress through puberty and differences in pubertal development and stature become more appar ent, despite reassurance, many boys with CDGP have a difficult time coping with this discrepancy. The short stature and/or delay in puberty from CDGP can significantly impact the psychological and emotional well-being of
paragraphs.heading: Variant and Idiopathic Short Stature

paragraphs.text: an adolescent, causing poor school perfor mance and self-esteem, withdrawal from social activities, and even depression and anx iety [50]. Treatment with low-dose testoster one is an option for boys with difficulty coping with their short stature and delayed puberty [51]. Depot-testosterone enanthate or cypio nate 50 mg IM every 4 weeks for 3–6 months will frequently invoke an increase in growth rate and pubertal onset without bone age advancement. Testosterone enanthate con tains a sesame seed oil and testosterone cypi onate, a cotton seed oil, and should be avoided in individuals with allergies to these oils. The response to treatment should be evaluated within 4–6 months following the last testoster one dose. If the response is inadequate, then an additional 3- to 6-month course of testos terone at an equal or higher dose may be administered [52, 53]. Recently, other prepa rations of testosterone have been used for pubertal induction, including testosterone gel 10 mg every other day. Studies examining the use of subcutaneous testosterone enanthate and oral testosterone undecanoate are ongo ing [54].
paragraphs.heading: Variant and Idiopathic Short Stature

paragraphs.text: In contrast to boys, girls have a growth spurt in early puberty. Therefore, girls infre quently seek treatment for CDGP because their onset of puberty is accompanied by a pubertal growth spurt. In extreme cases of CDGP, a girl can be treated with either, oral ethinyl estradiol 5 mcg daily, or low-dose estradiol transdermal patch, 3.1–6.2 mcg/24 h (1/8 to 1/4 of a 25 mcg patch), to initiate puberty and stimulate linear growth.
paragraphs.heading: Variant and Idiopathic Short Stature

paragraphs.text: Oxandrolone , a weak, synthetic, and non aromatizing anabolic steroid derivative of tes tosterone is an oral treatment option for CDGP. Oxandrolone 0.1 mg/kg/day for 3–4 months can be considered for pubertal initiation and acceleration of growth. Crowne and colleagues’ double-blind, placebocontrolled trial showed comparable increases in growth velocity and testicular development in boys treated with either a 3-month course of oxandrolone 2.5 mg daily or testosterone 50 mg every 4 weeks [55].
paragraphs.heading: Variant and Idiopathic Short Stature

paragraphs.text: Increased interest in aromatase inhibitors as a potential treatment option for boys with CDGP and ISS stems from their inhibition of the conversion of androgens to estrogens. Cessation of growth depends on estrogenmediated fusion of the epiphyses; therefore, lower estrogen levels may delay epiphyseal closure, improving adult height prognosis. Mauras et al. performed a 2–3-year random ized controlled trial in 76 pubertal boys with ISS and a bone age <14.5 years comparing three different treatment arms, an aromatase inhibitor (letrozole or anastrozole) vs. GH alone (0.3 mg/kg/week) vs. combination ther apy (aromatase inhibitor and GH). Outcome measures included changes in predicted adult height, bone density, bone markers, IGF-1, lean body mass, and the degree of estradiol suppression by the individual aromatase inhibitors. The best height gain outcomes were seen in the group receiving both GH and aromatase inhibition, followed by the GH alone and aromatase inhibitor alone groups, respectively. This report did not note any adverse effect on bone, which had been previ ously suggested by another study examining boys with ISS treated with letrozole [56].
paragraphs.heading: Variant and Idiopathic Short Stature

paragraphs.text: Karmazin et al. reported that 25% of study subjects treated with letrozole developed adre nal suppression determined by a low-dose ACTH stimulation test [57]. The aromatase inhibitor, anastrozole, increases sperm count in males with infertility, yet concern exists as to whether it can affect sperm production in adolescent males. Mauras et al. analyzed sperm counts in 11 young adults, age 18, with GH deficiency treated with anastrozole for 29 months. No difference was found in the sperm counts between the treated and untreated cohorts, but low sperm counts were found in both groups [58]. Currently, due to conflicting data on adult height gain and the lack of long-term studies, a formal recom mendation on the use of aromatase inhibitors for ISS or CDGP cannot be made.
paragraphs.heading: Variant and Idiopathic Short Stature

paragraphs.text: In 2003, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved GH treatment (0.3–0.37 mg/ kg/week) for children with ISS defined as a
paragraphs.heading: Variant and Idiopathic Short Stature

paragraphs.text: height of ≤−2.25 SDS (1.2 percentile) below the mean for age and sex “and associated with growth rates unlikely to permit attainment of adult height in the normal range, in pediatric patients whose epiphyses are not closed and for whom diagnostic evaluation excludes other causes associated with short stature that should be observed or treated by other means” [59]. The lower cutoff for the normal range adult height is defined as 160 cm (63 in.) for a male and 150 cm (59 in.) for a female. This statement issued by the FDA does not clearly exclude GH treatment for children with FSS and CDGP.
paragraphs.heading: Variant and Idiopathic Short Stature

paragraphs.text: Prior to the FDA approval of GH treat ment for ISS, several nonrandomized, longi tudinal studies were published that used variable dosing regimens of GH. Metaanalyses of randomized and nonrandomized controlled studies indicated a variable response to treatment with gains in height ranging from 2.3 to 8.7 cm [60–65]. The GH adverse effect profile reported in these studies did not differ from that of children treated with GH for other conditions. Some studies suggest that adult height outcomes are opti mized with earlier initiation of GH treatment and with higher doses [66, 67].
paragraphs.heading: Variant and Idiopathic Short Stature

paragraphs.text: GH treatment requires monitoring of growth velocity and adjustment of GH dose to achieve an adequate response. The 2008 International Consensus Meeting on ISS rec ommended monitoring IGF-1 levels to assess dosing, adherence, and to prevent overtreat ment, with a goal of a level above 0 SDS and within the normal limits for age [68]. Dosing is usually started at the upper end of the dos ing range used for GHD (0.24 mg/kg/week) but may need to be titrated to as high as 0.47 mg/kg/week. There are no data that sup port doses higher than this and lack of response at this highest dose should prompt a discussion of discontinuing therapy [28].
paragraphs.heading: Variant and Idiopathic Short Stature

paragraphs.text: Lee et al. calculated a cost analysis of treating a 10-year-old child with GH 0.37 mg/ kg/week with an endpoint of a 1.9 in. gain in height over 5 years. The gain in height and GH dose used for this analysis were derived
paragraphs.heading: Variant and Idiopathic Short Stature

paragraphs.text: from the two studies that the FDA used to approve GH treatment for ISS. The analysis revealed a cost of approximately $52,000 per in. of height gain [69]. An estimated 400,000 children would qualify for GH treatment based on the FDA’s criteria for GH treatment of children with a height of <1.2nd percentile. Although the FDA statement that children with a “form of short stature that can be observed or otherwise managed by other means” refers to children with FSS and CDGP, these diagnoses are not clearly excluded from the FDA indications for GH treatment for short stature. The exorbitant cost of GH weighed against treating an other wise healthy child has generated controversy over the use of GH as a “lifestyle drug,” a term used to refer to a “pharmaceutical prod uct characterized as improving quality of life rather than alleviating disease” [70]. Debate also exists regarding whether having short stature should be considered a “medically necessary” intervention given the lack of data with respect to whether being taller improves psychological or physical outcomes. Additionally, the goals of treatment are unclear with respect to whether to treat to “normal” height or “maximal height” [71, 72].
paragraphs.heading: Variant and Idiopathic Short Stature

paragraphs.text: Conflicting study outcomes have been reported on the efficacy of a combination treatment with GH and a GnRH agonist for pubertal children with ISS and SGA. Many of the studies are small and nonrandomized and do not include control groups. Kamp and colleague’s randomized controlled study of combination treatment in pubertal children with ISS and SGA showed that predicted adult height in the treated groups improved by 8 cm in girls and 10.4 cm in boys [73]. These researchers also analyzed the adult height and bone mineralization of 32 of the 40 partici pants who participated in the original 3-year study and found that the treated group had a net gain of 4.9 cm above their predicted adult and target heights compared to the control group. The bone mineralization was similar between the treated and control groups except for a lower lumbar spine bone mineralization SD score in the treated boys (n = 6) compared to the control group (n = 2) [74].

Adult height outcome data in children with CDGP vary, with some studies showing impaired adult height and in others, an adult height consistent with target height. These studies found that the Bayley-Pinneau method as opposed to the Tanner-Whitehouse method of height prediction correlated best with the child’s adult height. Factors negatively impacting the adult height prognosis in chil dren with CDGP included a shorter period between the onset of puberty and peak height velocity, a lower peak height velocity, a shorter sitting height, and a faster tempo of puberty [75].
paragraphs.heading: Complications

paragraphs.text: Proponents of treatment advocate that short stature negatively impacts a child’s psy chosocial development [76, 77]. In contrast, others have shown that GH does not improve psychosocial health. The Wessex study, a lon gitudinal controlled study, evaluated whether short stature impacts a child’s academic, social, and behavioral development. The study and control groups consisted of 5-yearolds recruited from two school districts in the South of England. The study group had a height at or below the 3rd percentile and was matched with a control group of peers of the same sex, age, and grade with normal stature (10–90th percentile). These cohorts had test ing at ages 7–9, 11–13, and 18–20 years to determine whether their short stature affected their academic and psychosocial develop ment. After adjusting for socioeconomic sta tus, the two groups did not differ with respect to intelligence quotient, self-esteem, or behav ior [78–80]. Other studies that examined pedi atric endocrinology patients evaluated for short stature showed no effect on psychoso cial function [81, 82].
paragraphs.heading: Complications

paragraphs.text: In contrast, an observational study by González Briceno examined 74 short children with a median age of 10.2 years who were treated with GH for 1 year. This group, as well as their parents, filled out questionnaires regarding quality of life prior to treatment versus after 1 year of treatment. The study found that both parents and the treated chil
paragraphs.heading: Complications

paragraphs.text: dren reported an increase in social and emo tional quality of life after GH treatment. The study was limited in that there was no control group and although the results were statisti cally significant, it is unclear if they translate to being clinically relevant. The placebo effect could also be responsible for the increased scores as opposed to a true improvement based on GH treatment and an increase in height [83]. More studies are needed to deter mine if GH treatment increases the quality of life in children with ISS.
paragraphs.heading: Complications

paragraphs.text: The Sante Adulte GH Enfant (SAGhE) study led by French investigators reported on the long-term mortality of approximately 7000 GH-treated patients for diagnoses of isolated GH deficiency, ISS, and SGA. Mortality was evaluated 16.9 years fol lowing the cessation of GH treatment and compared to that in the general French popu lation. This study found an increase in mor tality due to cerebrovascular events and bone tumors among individuals treated with GH,
paragraphs.heading: Complications

paragraphs.text: particularly in those treated with higher doses of GH, exceeding 50 mcg/kg/day [84]. The SAGhE study design had several shortcom ings that may have influenced these findings. Mortality in the treated group was compared to the general French population as opposed to an identically matched, untreated control group. Also, the reported association between the higher dose of GH and increased mortal ity was in a small number of subjects, many of whom had a diagnosis of SGA [85]. A pre liminary report from the EU SAGhE Study conducted in Belgium, the Netherlands, and Sweden did not show an association between adult mortality in 2543 patients treated with GH during childhood for isolated GH defi ciency, ISS, or SGA [86]. Due to limitations of the SAGhe study design, the FDA, Endocrine Society, Pediatric Endocrine Society, and Hormone Research Society con cluded that it is safe to continue to treat chil dren with ISS, isolated GH deficiency, and SGA with GH [85].
paragraphs.heading: Complications

paragraphs.text: A comprehensive history, physical examina tion, current and past auxologic data, and diagnostic studies are essential for evaluating children with short stature to exclude an organic etiology. The growth patterns of chil dren with normal variant short stature typi cally reflect a familial pattern of growth in that there is at least one parent with short stat ure. Children with CDGP frequently have a family history of a first- or second-degree rel ative with a similar pattern of late puberty and growth. Often, children with CDGP also have FSS as the cause of their short stature. Children with normal variant short stature require reassurance and follow-up to ascer tain that they follow the expected course of growth and pubertal development for these normal physiologic variants of growth. Low-
paragraphs.heading: 3.7 Summary

paragraphs.text: dose testosterone treatment effectively initi ates puberty in boys with CDGP without advancing their bone age and compromising their adult height.
paragraphs.heading: 3.7 Summary

paragraphs.text: ISS is differentiated from the normal vari ant short stature in that the predicted adult height falls below the target height range for that child. These children are GH sufficient and do not have an identifiable cause for their short stature. Treatment of ISS with GH remains controversial in the medical commu nity because of the costs, variable responses to treatment, and lack of data regarding the effect on quality of life. GH treatment for ISS should be individualized and the growth expectations explained to families. Children who are treated with GH should be closely monitored for side effects and assessed for an adequate response by monitoring growth velocity.
paragraphs.heading: 3.7 Summary

paragraphs.text: Although the SAGhE study initially raised concern regarding a potential increase in long-term mortality from GH treatment of isolated GH deficiency, SGA, and ISS, the limitations of this study created an awareness that well-designed controlled studies are needed to effectively determine the long-term safety of GH and did not alter current guide lines on the use of GH.

Evan Graber and Mary M. Lee

## PDF page 92 | printed page 74

Key Points

5 Familial short stature and constitu

tional delay of growth and puberty are normal physiologic variants of growth. 5 Familial short stature, constitutional

### 3

delay of growth and puberty, and idio pathic short stature do not have a known organic etiology. Idiopathic short stature is distinguished from nor mal variant short stature in that pre dicted adult height is below the genetic target height range. 5 In 2003, the FDA approved GH for the

treatment of idiopathic short stature, a controversial decision. 5 Height outcome data for GH-treated

children with idiopathic short stature are variable with a mean gain height of 4–7 cm.

### 3.1 Introduction

Short stature is defined as a height ≤2 stan dard deviations (SD) below the mean for age, sex, and population. Height in a given popula tion follows a normal Gaussian distribution; therefore, it is expected that the height of 2.3% of a population will fall 2 SD below the mean for age and sex [1]. Among this 2.3% of the population, the majority will have a normal variant of short stature or idiopathic short stature, but some may have an underlying pathological etiology.

Normal variant short stature is comprised of familial short stature (FSS) and constitu tional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP). These individuals attain an adult height con sistent with their target genetic height, while individuals with idiopathic short stature have predicted adult heights below their familial target height range. Frequently, FSS and CDGP are considered subtypes of ISS. The growth patterns of individuals with FSS and/ or CDGP, however, are usually consistent with that of a first-degree relative and their adult height conforms with their target height. These diagnoses, therefore, most suitably rep resent “normal variants” of growth [2].

Normal variant and idiopathic short stat ure are considered nonpathological short stat ure, without an organic origin, such as intrauterine growth restriction, chronic dis ease, endocrinopathy, skeletal dysplasia, or genetic disorder.

### 3.2 Auxologic Methods to Assess

### Growth

### 3.2.1 Length and Height

### Measurement

mass index should be plotted on the CDC growth charts for children ages 2–20 years [5].

Because birth length reflects intrauterine factors, an infant’s weight and length may cross growth percentiles during the first 2 years of life, gravitating toward percentiles consistent with their genetic potential. Thereafter, significant shifts in length or height percentiles should not occur, except for children with CDGP, who may continue to exhibit a decline in length or height percentile until ages 3–4. At that time, they maintain a normal linear growth velocity and will grow at a consistent percentile. Height measurements tend to be 1 cm less than length measure ments; therefore, length measurements need to be adjusted when plotted on a height chart. This difference accounts for the apparent decline in growth rate when a child is transi tioned from a length measurement to a stand ing height.

### 3

Assessing a child’s pattern of weight gain, linear growth, and gain in head circumference is important for the evaluation of short stat ure and overall health. Pathological causes of poor growth secondary to nutritional causes or chronic disease typically affect weight gain, then linear growth, and finally head circum ference. However, disorders of malabsorp tion, such as celiac disease, may sometimes initially present with normal weight gain, but poor growth. In contrast, children with endo crine disorders typically present with normal or increased weight gain and poor linear growth.

### 3.2.2 Growth Velocity





3.2

6

### 3.2.3 Anthropometric

### Measurements

The evaluation of a child with a height 2 SD below the mean for age and sex should include anthropometric measurements of upper and lower segments, or sitting height, arm span, and occipitofrontal head circumference to assess for disproportion and possible skeletal dysplasia. Arm span is measured with the child standing in an erect position against a wall with outstretched arms. The distance between the tips of the middle phalanges is measured. In prepubertal children, the arm span is shorter than height, and after midpu berty the arm span exceeds height. In an adult male, arm span exceeds height by 5.2 cm and in an adult female by 1.2 cm. Ethnic differ ences exist as well, with longer arm spans noted in the African American population. Arm span can be measured in a sitting or supine position if the child is unable to stand. A sitting height (SH) is measured with the child seated on a chair flush against the stadi ometer. Subtracting the sitting height from the child’s standing height (HT) provides the value of their lower segment (LS). The SH/ HT ratio or SH/LS ratio can be plotted on their appropriate charts to determine whether these ratios are disproportionate and sugges tive of skeletal dysplasia. An alternative approach is to measure the child’s lower seg ment from the symphysis pubis to the floor and subtract this value from the child’s stand ing height for their truncal height. The upper to lower segment ratio decreases throughout childhood and adolescence. Due to an increased truncal length relative to limbs,


## PDF page 95 | printed page 77

Fig. 3.2 Height velocity charts for boys and girls. (From Tanner and Davies [6]. Reprinted with permission from Elsevier)

infants have an upper to lower segment ratio of 1.7. By age 3 the upper to lower segment ratio decreases to 1.3, by age 10 this ratio decreases to 1, and in pubertal children, the ratio is <1. Children with CDGP have increased leg length and shortened truncal height which accounts for their decreased upper to lower segment ratios of 0.8–0.9.

### 3.2.4 Bone Age

Skeletal maturation is evaluated by assessing epiphyseal maturation with bone age radio graphs, using the methods of either Greulich and Pyle or Tanner-Whitehouse. The former method compares a child’s left-hand radio graph to standard bone age radiographs of the left hands of mid-western boys and girls from birth through age 18 [7]. The Tanner- Whitehouse method assigns a value to each of the 27 epiphyses in the hand and wrist and sums these values for the skeletal maturity score, which correlates with specific bone ages as determined for select populations [8]. Bayley-Pinneau also provides a table for the

percent of adult height achieved at given bone ages, which can be used to calculate a child’s predicted adult height [9]. Variations in bone age readings among providers and inaccurate height measurements can limit the accuracy of a child’s height prediction.

### 3.2.5 Dental Age

Loss of the primary teeth and eruption of permanent teeth correlate with bone age but can vary due to environmental influences. Tooth calcification as determined on an orthopantomogram is less variable and corre sponds better with dental age [10, 11]. Growth hormone deficiency (GHD), hypothyroidism, and CDGP are associated with delayed dental age and bone age.

### 3.2.6 Target Height

In the 1970s, Tanner et al. defined target height as either the addition or subtraction of 6.5 cm from the mean parental height for a

![Source image](../../figures/ch003_p0095_01.jpg)

Unmatched source image; PDF page 95. Consult the original caption.


## PDF page 96 | printed page 78

boy or girl, respectively. Two SD represents 11 cm above or below the calculated target height [12]. The target height is used to deter mine a child’s expected adult height based on their genetic potential. Measuring the parents’ heights at the child’s visit improves the accu racy of the target height calculation. Starting in the 1990s, researchers devised alternative formulas to calculate the target height because the method of Tanner either underestimated or overestimated the height of a child with short or tall parents, respectively. These for mulas also tried to account for population trends and secular height trends. The 2008 consensus statement from the Growth Hormone Research Society, the Lawson Wilkins Pediatric Endocrine Society, and the European Society for Paediatric Endocrinology Workshop recommended using a corrected target height SD in lieu of the Tanner method. The corrected target height is calculated as 0.72 × the average of the father’s and mother’s height SD with the lower limit of the target height as the cor rected target height minus 1.6 SD [13].

### 3

The evaluation of a child with short stat ure requires a review of their previous growth data, accurate length and/or height measure ments, a calculated target height, bone age, predicted adult height, and possibly arm span and upper to lower segment ratio. Analyzing auxologic data in conjunction with a detailed history and physical examination is essential for determining whether a child’s short stature is a normal variant or due to an underlying disorder.

### 3.3 Etiology and Clinical

### Presentation

### 3.3.1 Normal Variant Short Stature

### 3.3.1.1 Constitutional Delay

### of Growth and Puberty

In CDGP, the growth rate declines and crosses percentiles in the first 2–3 years of life. Usually, by age 3–4 years, growth resumes

normal rate and the bone age is delayed (often 2–3 SD delay). Other features of CDGP include delayed pubertal onset and eventual attainment of an adult height consistent with midparental target range. Most children with CDGP exhibit a pattern of weight gain that mirrors their linear growth at less than 2 SD below the mean for age, sex, and population or at a lower percentile than their target growth percentile. Individuals with CDGP are frequently referred to as “late bloomers” and often have a first- or second-degree relative(s) with a history of delayed onset of puberty (defined as the onset of puberty for males as >13 years of age and for females as >12 years of age) and a similar growth pattern.

6



3.2



Forty percent of children with constitu tional delay of growth and puberty also have familial short stature [14]. Even with a strong family history of CDGP, as with FSS, other identifiable causes of short stature and delayed puberty should be excluded, which is dis cussed in Sect. 3.4.

Several studies report a 2:1–5:1 male to female predominance of CDGP [15, 16]. Wehkalampi et al.’s retrospective study evalu ated the prevalence of a positive family his tory in children with CDGP. The findings in this study challenge this male predominance because CDGP was equally prevalent in mothers and fathers. The authors suggest that referral bias may account for the reported male predominance in CDGP. The published data support an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance for CDGP [15–17]. Heterozygous mutations in the GH secreta gogue receptor gene (GSHR), a ghrelin recep


## PDF page 97 | printed page 79

tor gene, were identified in two females with CDGP, suggesting an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance with incomplete pene trance. Further studies are needed to better define the association of mutations in this gene with CDGP [18]. Researchers have not found mutations in the acid labile subunit, leptin, or the leptin receptor in individuals with CDGP [19, 20].

### 3.3.2 Familial Short Stature

Children with FSS have normal linear growth with height measurements ≤−2 SD below the mean for age, sex, and population and a pre dicted adult height consistent with their target height. They also have a bone age consistent with their chronologic age, a normal growth velocity and timing of pubertal, and short stature in at least one of the parents.

Fig. 3.3 Weight and height data for a girl with familial short stature plotted on the CDC growth chart [5]. Note the normal growth velocity along the 5th percentile







3.4



3.3

### 3.3.3 Idiopathic Short Stature

Idiopathic short stature is defined is a height ≤−2.25 SD below the mean for age, sex, and population. ISS is distinguished from the normal variant short stature by a pre dicted adult height more than 2 SD below the child’s target height range. The term “idio

![Source image](../../figures/ch003_p0097_01.jpg)

Unmatched source image; PDF page 97. Consult the original caption.


## PDF page 98 | printed page 80

pathic” implies that the etiology of the short stature is unknown and is not due to FSS, CDGP, or another identifiable cause as dis cussed in detail in Sect. 3.4.

Since the FDA approved the use of GH for the treatment of ISS in 2003, genetic technol ogy has advanced in such a way as to be able to identify defects that had previously been unknown causes of short stature, blurring the line between what is now considered “idio pathic” short stature and genetic short stature. Alterations in the GH receptor gene, STAT 5b, acid labile subunit, and IGF-1 gene have been described in patients with a diagnosis of ISS [21]. One study utilized whole exome sequencing leading to the identification of genetic causes of short stature in 5 of 14 chil dren with prior diagnoses of ISS with a height ≤−3 SD below the mean for age and sex. Prior to whole exome testing, these chil dren had extensive evaluations, including standard genetic testing, that did not identify a cause for their short stature. Two of the five patients had the progeroid form of Ehlers- Danlos syndrome, and the other diagnoses included 3-M syndrome (overlapping features with Russell-Silver syndrome), Floating- Harbor syndrome, and a variant of the Kenny-Caffey syndrome with eucalcemia. However, in addition to short stature, these patients had dysmorphic features and/or other medical conditions that suggested a syn dromic cause of short stature [22].

### 3

Several other genetic etiologies have since been identified in which the only significant finding has been short stature. The most well known is the SHOX gene, which now has its own indication for use of GH. Mutations in NPR2, ACAN, IGF1, IGF1R, and FGFR3 have all been found to be associated with iso lated short stature [23]. Prior to the identifica tion of genes such as these, patients may have been classified as having ISS. As more altera tions in genes involved in stature are identi fied, the definition of ISS or criteria for treatment of ISS may need to evolve.

In summary, ISS is a diagnosis of exclu sion, determined after a comprehensive evalu ation fails to find an identifiable etiology for

the short stature. Rare genetic disorders should be considered as a cause for short stat ure in children with a height ≤−3 SD below the mean for age and sex, especially in the presence of dysmorphic features and/or other medical diagnoses. Debate remains about whether treatment of short stature should be offered to those previously classified as ISS who are now known to have a genetic cause of their short stature.

### 3.4 Diagnostic Evaluation

The evaluation of a child with a height ≤−2 SD below the mean for age, sex, and popula tion should include a comprehensive history and physical examination with anthropomet ric measurements. A detailed history should assess for risk factors for hypopituitarism, such as traumatic birth, postnatal hypoglyce mia, jaundice, and/or microphallus in male infants. A low birth weight and length may suggest short stature secondary to small for gestational age or Russell-Silver syndrome. A history of lymphedema, pedal edema, and/or cardiac anomalies may suggest Turner or Noonan syndrome. In girls with short stature, it is well established that Turner syndrome should be excluded even in the absence of overt clinical findings. A karyotype is not rou tinely done in boys but could be considered when the predicted adult height is below tar get height because 45X/46XY mosaicism may present with short stature and an otherwise normal phenotype. GH treatment can be con sidered for this condition [24]. Determining whether to test for a SHOX gene mutation is best determined by the established clinical scoring system for this condition. Rappold et al. found that an increased body mass index, decreased arm span/height ratio, Madelung deformity, short, bowed forearms, dislocation of the ulna at the elbow, and muscular hyper trophy were most predictive of this gene muta tion [25]. Children with a history of developmental delay and findings suggestive of a chromosomal disorder warrant further evaluation by a geneticist. Furthermore, the

Assessing children for GHD is an impor tant part of the evaluation when growth veloc ity is lower than expected. Since GH is secreted in a pulsatile fashion throughout the day with more frequent pulses overnight, random GH levels are typically nondiagnostic. GH medi ates the production of IGF-1 and IGF BP-3 from the liver; these levels are stable through out the day, serving as a better screening test for GHD. Normal ranges for IGF-1 and IGF BP-3 are based on age, sex, and the Tanner stage in prepubertal and pubertal children, respectively. Low or low/normal IGF-1 and IGF BP-3 levels should prompt further evalu ation with provocative GH stimulation test ing. Isolated low IGF-1 can be seen in children with undernutrition and may warrant delay ing GH stimulation testing until weight is improved. GH is measured at several time points following the administration of a GH secretagogue, such as clonidine, arginine,

### 3

l-Dopa, propranolol, glucagon, or insulin. A single GH value of ≥10 ng/mL on two pro vocative GH stimulation tests indicates GH sufficiency. Debate exists as to whether a lower GH peak should be used to indicate a normal stimulation test. In peripubertal and early pubertal children, priming with sex steroids (testosterone or estradiol), prior to the testing is indicated to prevent misdiagnosis of GHD [29–31]. An increase in GH amplitude and mean 24 h GH levels occurs between Tanner stages 2–4 and 3–5 in girls and boys, respec tively. Girls exhibit increased mean nocturnal GH levels and GH amplitude prior to the onset of breast development which coincides with the start of their pubertal growth spurt. In contrast, boys in the early stages of puberty have lower mean nocturnal GH levels and amplitude that are comparable to that of a prepubertal boy [32]. These data support the role of sex steroids on GH secretion and explain the decline in growth rate exhibited in boys prior to the onset of puberty. Saggese et al. showed that lower growth hormonereleasing hormone (GHRH) levels in children with delayed puberty may explain their sub normal GH response to stimulation tests. When retested in mid- to late puberty, these

adolescents had a normal GH response, and their GHRH levels were comparable to the control group [33]. A prospective study in Turkey evaluated the adult height of boys with a history of delayed growth and normal testosterone-primed GH stimulation studies. These boys had normal adult heights, consis tent with their mid-parental heights [34]. Müeller et al. and others showed that children with true GHD have an abnormal GH response to sex steroid-primed provocative GH stimulation tests [35, 36].

Adolescents with delayed puberty should have additional labs (gonadotropin levels, serum prolactin, estradiol, and/or testoster one) to assess for causes of pubertal delay. A girl with hypergonadotropic hypogonadism requires further evaluation with a karyotype for Turner syndrome, a common cause of pri mary ovarian failure and short stature with an incidence of 1 in 2500 live births. Fragile X testing should also be performed as girls with premutations can also have primary gonadal failure. Often, boys and girls with Noonan syndrome manifest delayed puberty, but boys more frequently have primary gonadal failure [37]. 46 XX SRY-positive males present with normal male external genitalia, short stature, and primary gonadal failure [38].
