paragraphs.text: Skeletal dysplasias are caused by abnormali ties in genes that are important in the regula tion of skeletal tissues. As such, they are congenital and many syndromes can be diag nosed prenatally or in the neonatal period. However, some genes have subtle effects or play a role only in later development and/or growth and the phenotypic features appear later in life. The past two decades have seen great advancement in identifying the causative gene in skeletal dysplasias [1]. This has aided greatly in the classification of skeletal dyspla sias and our understanding of the regulation of skeletal tissues.
paragraphs.heading: 8.2 Etiology

paragraphs.text: When a child presents for evaluation of short (or tall) stature, the possibility of skeletal dys plasia should always be a consideration. It is unusual for patients with more significant phenotypes (such as achondroplasia) to be referred to the endocrinologist as the presence of skeletal dysplasia is obvious clinically and these patients are generally referred first to the geneticist for an evaluation. However, there are a number of skeletal dysplasias where the primary clinical feature is short stature while other features are absent or subtle. Tall stature can also be a symptom of skeletal dysplasia where the evaluation starts with the endocri nologist. A family history, anthropometric measurements, a careful physical exam, and the knowledge of what to look for are the basis for detecting skeletal dysplasia in these situations.
paragraphs.heading: 8.3 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: The skeletal dysplasias are of genetic ori gin and the majority are caused by single gene abnormalities; a thorough family history may provide valuable information regarding these syndromes. The most common syndromes have a dominant mode of inheritance, includ ing achondroplasia, hypochondroplasia, Léri- Weill dyschondrosteosis, and osteogenesis imperfecta. Except in cases of de novo muta tions, children with these syndromes will have a parent with the same condition. It is not
paragraphs.heading: 8.3 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: uncommon that an affected parent has never been diagnosed with the syndrome as the clin ical features may be subtle, such as in hypo chondroplasia, Léri-Weill dyschondrosteosis, or mild forms of osteogenesis imperfecta. With the newly available genetic tools, it is now routine that a diagnosis made in a child leads to the diagnosis being made in a parent and grandparent. Obtaining parental heights can assist with the evaluation. Reported parental heights are notoriously inaccurate; it is recommended that parents’ heights be mea sured by the provider whenever possible.
paragraphs.heading: 8.3 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: portionately short legs which suggests the presence of short-limbed skeletal dysplasia. A patient with short stature and an upper-tolower segment ratio less than the 3rd percen tile suggests a disproportionately short spine, possibly due to spondylodysplasia and/or sco liosis. Conversely, a patient with tall stature and ratio that is less than the 3rd percentile has disproportionately long legs, suggesting an overgrowth syndrome such as Marfan syn drome. A related measurement is the sitting height and the sitting-to-standing height ratio. For this measurement, the child is placed on a flat stool with his or her back against the wall. The child’s thighs should be parallel to the floor. A mark is made at the top of the head. The distance from the floor to the mark minus the height of the stool gives the seated height. Reference ranges are available [6].
paragraphs.heading: 8.3 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: suggests disproportionately short arms while a difference greater than the 97th percentile suggests a short spine. Either suggests the presence of skeletal dysplasia. Children with an excessive arm span-height difference should also be evaluated for scoliosis. An arm-span-to-height ratio of >1.05 is used in the revised Ghent nosology for the diagnosis of Marfan syndrome [8].

A head circumference (occipital-frontal circumference, OFC) is also important for detecting body disproportion. An OFC within the expected range in a child with severe short stature could suggest a skeletal dysplasia, although other diagnoses must also be consid ered.

A thorough physical examination focused on the skeletal system is important. Observation of the child while standing will give the clinician an idea of body proportion. As a rule of thumb, the fingertips should rest level with the mid-thigh. Examination of the skull should note the presence and position of the fontanelles, and the presence of asymme try, frontal bossing, and hypo- or hyper telorism. A highly arched palate is common in a number of skeletal dysplasias. The presence of a short neck, kyphosis, or scoliosis may suggest an abnormality of the spine. Examination of the arms and legs may show disproportionate shortening of the upper or lower arm or leg. Limb segment measure ments can be done. A guide such as that by Gripp et al. [6] provides measurement tech niques and reference ranges. Bowing of a limb is an important finding, as is a limitation in joint mobility. Prominent radial and/or ulnar

heads at the wrist may indicate Madelung deformity, seen in SHOX haploinsufficiency disorders (Léri-Weil dyschondrosteosis or Turner syndrome). A close examination of the hands and feet for shortening of some or all of the metatarsals, metacarpals, and phalan ges should also be done. Extra or missing dig its, syndactyly, and/or camptodactyly (inability to fully straighten a digit) are also important potential findings.

Once skeletal dysplasia is suspected, more indepth evaluation is called for. The diagnostic evaluation of a child suspected of having skel etal dysplasia requires a thorough history including a three-generation family history. Attention should be paid to signs and symp toms such as early onset arthritis or joint pain, fractures, joint replacement surgeries, dental problems, and hearing or vision abnormali ties. The physical examination should include specific measurements as discussed above to assess for disproportion, including signs of disproportion within the limb. Ranges of motion throughout are important to assess as both increased and decreased flexibilities are associated with various dysplasias. Lastly, skeletal imaging should be undertaken to look for diagnostic clues. There is not a standard dysplasia survey, as various experts and insti tutions do things differently. Our preferred evaluation includes the following: an AP image from the pelvis to the floor, standing if possible, otherwise supine (this image allows
paragraphs.heading: 8.4 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: for the assessment of anatomical alignment of the lower extremities and disproportion within the limb); AP and lateral images of the tho raco-lumbar spine (to assess for scoliosis and any vertebral body abnormalities); an AP image of the arm from shoulder to wrist; and an AP image of the hands. If osteogenesis imperfecta or another fragility condition is being entertained, AP and lateral skull images are done to assess mineralization and for wor mian bones. If any spine abnormalities are present either on clinical examination or radiograph, lateral flexion and extension views are recommended to assess for cervical spine instability. Important consideration should be given to having these images reviewed by a radiologist familiar with skeletal dysplasias in children. If no such radiologist is available locally, assistance should be available through regional skeletal dysplasia programs. Assistance is also available at the University of California, Los Angeles International Skeletal Dysplasia Registry ( www.ortho. ucla.edu/isdr) [9] and the European Skeletal Dysplasia Network ( www.esdn.org) [10], which can review patient images and provide diagnostic possibilities.
paragraphs.heading: 8.4 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Once the evaluation is completed, the information gathered from the history, physi cal, and radiographic examinations can be reviewed to try and reach a specific diagnosis. If a specific or limited differential diagnosis can be reached, molecular testing is likely available to confirm a diagnosis. Advances in genetic diagnostic techniques including thirdgeneration sequencing, multiple gene panel sequencing, and whole exome sequencing have diagnosis confirmation now possible in the majority of skeletal dysplasia syndromes [2].
Achondroplasia (MIM 100800) is the most common skeletal dysplasia with incidence estimates ranging from 1 in 15,000 to 1 in 27,000 births [11–13]. The average adult
paragraphs.heading: 8.5.1 Achondroplasia

paragraphs.text: height for men is 131 cm, with a range of 118–144 cm (3′10′′–4′9′′, height SD score −8.3 to −4.6), and for women, 123 cm with a range of 113–137 cm (3′8′′–4′6′′, height SD score −7.7 to −4.0) [14]. The clinical features of achondroplasia are distinctive enough that diagnosis can be made through clinical and radiographic means, and historically, the diag nosis was usually made at birth or shortly thereafter [15]. Due to advances in late-term prenatal ultrasound and the detection of limb shortening, achondroplasia is now commonly diagnosed prenatally [11, 13].
paragraphs.heading: 8.5.1 Achondroplasia

paragraphs.text: Achondroplasia is caused by a mutation in the fibroblast growth factor receptor-3 gene (FGFR3) [16]. Mutations that change the amino acid glycine to arginine at position 380 (Gly380Arg) of the FGFR-3 protein account for greater than 98% of all reported cases of achondroplasia. This typical G380R gain-offunction mutation results in the constitutive activation of the receptor. In growth plate chondrocytes, this receptor activates the sig nal transducers and activators of the tran scription (STAT1) pathway, which inhibits chondrocyte proliferation, and the mitogen-
paragraphs.heading: 8.5.1 Achondroplasia

paragraphs.text: activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, which inhibits both chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation. The net result of inhibited chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation is slowed bone growth [17–19]. Achondroplasia is inherited in an autosomal dominant man ner, but about 80% of patients with achondro plasia represent new mutations [13]. Given this high rate of new mutations and the inci dence of achondroplasia, the base pair of codon 380 in FGFR3 has the highest known rate of mutation in man. New mutations typi cally arise from the father during sperm for mation and paternal age greater than 35 years has been found to be a risk factor [20]. A recent hypothesis is that sperms containing a FGFR3 mutation have a selective advantage
paragraphs.heading: 8.5.1 Achondroplasia

paragraphs.text: and as men age, more FGFR3 mutant sperms are present [20].
paragraphs.heading: 8.5.1 Achondroplasia

paragraphs.text: Routine care for children with achondro plasia consists of monitoring for and the management of concerns such as genu varum, hydrocephalus, foramen magnum stenosis, obstructive sleep apnea, and ear infections from Eustachian tube abnormalities [21, 22]. A number of small studies have reported on the use of recombinant human growth hor mone (rhGH) in achondroplasia for up to 6 years [23–25]. Studies generally show an increase in height velocity during the first year of treatment, but this increase is reduced and then lost in subsequent years of treatment. There is an average net gain in height SD score of 1.0–1.6 (8–14 cm) [26]. The body dispro
paragraphs.heading: 8.5.1 Achondroplasia

paragraphs.text: portion is reported to be worsened [24] or unchanged [23, 25] by treatment and no unusual adverse effects have been reported. Because of the small gains relative to the pro found short stature, rhGH treatment is gener ally not recommended for the treatment of achondroplasia.
paragraphs.heading: 8.5.1 Achondroplasia

paragraphs.text: C-type natriuretic peptide (CNP) is a small peptide that acts in a paracrine manner in the growth plate to regulate growth (see acrome somelic dysplasia and type Maroteaux, later in the text). One mechanism of this is through the inhibition of intracellular signaling of the MAPK pathway [27]. In mice carrying the achondroplastic mutation, over-expression of CNP [28], as well as exogenous administration of CNP [29], rescues the skeletal abnormali ties, and leads to the possibility of using CNP as a growth-promoting treatment in children with achondroplasia [19, 29]. Vosoritide (pre viously named BMN111) is a peptide analog of a 39-amino acid version of CNP with a two-amino acid substitution at the aminoterminal end. This substitution reduces CNP cleavage by a specific neutral endopeptidase, prolonging its half-life in circulation, while not affecting binding with its primary recep tor, natriuretic peptide receptor-B (NPR-B) [30]. Vosoritide, given as a daily subcutaneous injection, has been shown to increase growth velocity in children with achondroplasia [31–33]. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study involving 119 chil dren with achondroplasia has been reported [32]. Subjects were monitored for 6 months for baseline growth data, then randomized to receive a placebo (n = 61) or vosoritide (n = 60) at 15 μg/kg daily for 1 year. The pri mary endpoint was the change in annualized height velocity from baseline. Treatment and control groups were well matched for sex, age, height, height SD score, and the upper-tolower body segment ratio. Treated subjects had an average age of 8.4 ± 2.4 (SD) years and showed a change in height velocity of 1.71 (1.40–2.01, 95% confidence interval) cm/year. This is compared to controls with an average age of 9.1 ± 2.5 years, with a change in height velocity of 0.13 (−0.18 to 0.45) cm/year (p < 0.0001). The change from baseline height
paragraphs.heading: 8.5.1 Achondroplasia

paragraphs.text: SD score was 0.27 (0.18–0.36) for treated sub jects compared to −0.01 (−0.1 to 0.09) for controls (p < 0.0001). There was no difference in change from the baseline of the upper-tolower segment ratio. Following this study, an uncontrolled, 2-year extension study of the same cohort was performed [33]. All control subjects were started on vosoritide at 15 μg/ mL daily and treated subjects were continued on treatment. The study showed the increase in height velocity during vosoritide treatment was maintained for 2 or 3 years, with no new adverse effects emerging. A clinical study of children from birth to 5 years of age [34] has been completed, but the results have not yet been published. No studies have yet been car ried out on final adult height. The most sig nificant adverse effect noted in these studies was a decrease in blood pressure 18–120 min following the injection. The decrease was transient and only occasionally was the sub ject symptomatic. The most common adverse effect was local injection site reactions, occur ring in 85% of the subjects. After 2 years of treatment, antibodies against vosoritide (antidrug antibodies, ADA) were detected in 35% of treated subjects. No drug-neutralizing anti bodies were detected and the clinical response was no different in the subjects who developed anti-drug antibodies. Based on these studies, vosoritide (VoxzogoTM, BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc., San Rafael, CA) was approved for use in children with achondro plasia older than 2 years of age by the European Medicines Agency in August 2021, and for children older than 5 years by the Federal Drug Administration in November 2021. The Japanese Ministry of Health, Labor and Welfare approved its use in children with achondroplasia of any age in June 2022. In the United States, the current average annual cost of treatment is $320,000.

There are currently no consensus guide lines on pretreatment evaluation and moni toring for patients who are being initiated or maintained on vosoritide. Prior to initiation, we recommend that a patient have a full evalu ation, including an in-depth review of past medical history, medications, allergies, and subspecialist evaluations. A clinical examina

tion, including detailed anthropometric mea surements, is also recommended. Radiographs to confirm open growth plates should also be obtained if a patient is undergoing puberty. A discussion that focuses on managing expecta tions as well as the impact and possible chal lenges of a daily injection for a child should be addressed. Families should be made aware of possible side effects, including injection site reactions and hypotension, and preventative tactics recommended including rotating injec tion sites and proper cleaning techniques. Having the child eat a small snack and drink at least 240 mL of fluid 30 min prior to admin istration is recommended to prevent hypoten sion [35]. Patients should be monitored at 3- to 6-month intervals, collecting anthropo metric measurements, monitoring for side effects, and discussing any challenges that may have arisen with the injections.

A second CNP-based drug (TransConTM CNP, Ascendis Pharma A/S, Denmark) has been developed where CNP is linked to an inert carrier to prolong half-life in vivo. TransConTM CNP is currently in a phase two clinical trial.

Other potential biochemical treatments for increasing linear growth in children with achondroplasia are in development. Infigratinib (previously named BGJ-398) is an FGFR 1–3 selective tyrosine kinase inhibitor that has been developed as an antineoplastic drug. In transgenic mice with the achondro plasia mutation, it promoted linear growth [36] and is currently in a phase two clinical trial [37] in children with achondroplasia. A soluble recombinant human FGFR3 decoy (Recifercept, previously named TA-46) was also effective in achondroplastic mice [38], but a phase two clinical trial [39] is currently on temporary hold due to unclear efficacy in chil dren with achondroplasia. Other drugs that show potential for increasing growth in achondroplastic mice models include the existing drugs of meclizine [40] and lovastatin [41] and using a FGFR3 monoclonal anti body that downregulates FGFR3 signaling, including FGFR3 with achondroplasia muta tion.
Like achondroplasia, hypochondroplasia is caused by gain of function mutations in FGFR3 [42]. While the mutation in achondro plasia is essentially always caused by the same
paragraphs.heading: 8.5.2 Hypochondroplasia

paragraphs.text: mutation, there is greater variability in the mutations causing hypochondroplasia. The lysine-for-asparagine substitution at codon 540 (Asn540Lys) is the most common muta tion to cause hypochondroplasia, but several others have been described. A second gene has been implicated but has not yet been identi fied [45]. When there is an established clinical and radiographic diagnosis of hypochondro plasia, FGFR3 mutations can be identified in about 90% of individuals [45]. Because there is a phenotypical overlap between achondro plasia and hypochondroplasia, and between hypochondroplasia and “idiopathic” short stature, genetic confirmation of the diagnosis is recommended [45].
paragraphs.heading: 8.5.2 Hypochondroplasia

paragraphs.text: As with achondroplasia, rhGH seems to have some effect on hypochondroplasia, although studies are small and short-term [46–50]. The largest and longest-term study [46] showed that, while improving growth velocity and height SD score, rhGH also worsened the skeletal disproportion. A metaanalysis of published studies concluded there was a positive effect of rhGH on height [51]. Surgical limb lengthening procedures (distrac tion osteogenesis) have been reported in adults with hypochondroplasia [52, 53] to increase height and decrease skeletal disproportion, but are very invasive with a high complication rate and are by no means routine practice at this time. Since gain of function mutations of FGFR3 cause most cases of hypochondropla sia, we predict that the drug interventions being explored for achondroplasia will also prove effective in hypochondroplasia. One such clinical trial using vosoritide is currently underway.
paragraphs.heading: 8.5.2 Hypochondroplasia

paragraphs.text: Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia (MED) is a rel atively common disorder with a prevalence of at least 1 in 20,000 [54]. MED is a heteroge neous disorder of bone and cartilage develop ment that results in small irregular epiphyses. Proportionate short or average stature is pres ent, as are frequently painful joints, and pos sibly a mild myopathy. MED is not
paragraphs.heading: Dysplasia

paragraphs.text: recognizable at birth and is typically recog nized after 2 years of age and in some cases not until adulthood. Typically, adults will grow to be between 145 and 168 cm (4′9′′ and 5′6′′). MED may present as a delay in walking or gait differences in a young child. Initial complaints usually include joint stiffness, pain, contractures, or limping. In some forms of MED, the fingers and toes are short and stubby, especially the thumb. Minor flexion contractures of the knees and elbows can be present. Joint pain, which could be fluctuating or episodic in childhood, tends to advance in adolescence or early adulthood. Genu valgus or varus may develop.
paragraphs.heading: Dysplasia

paragraphs.text: Key radiographic characteristics of MED include irregular epiphyses usually at the hips, knees, ankles, wrists, and hands. Bones of the pelvis, spinal column, and skull are typically normal. In middle to late childhood, the epiphyses are either flat or small. An important diagnostic sign is the epiphyses of distal tibias which are malformed laterally to produce a sloping wedge-shaped articular surface. This may be more apparent later in life. A bipartite (split) patella can be seen and if present, shortening of the long bones is mild.
paragraphs.heading: Dysplasia

paragraphs.text: Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia is a geneti cally heterogeneous condition that can be inherited in either an autosomal dominant or autosomal recessive manner. Dominant forms of MED are more common. The most com mon dominant genetic cause of MED is mutations in the gene encoding the cartilage oligomeric matrix protein (COMP) (type 1, MIM 132400). Other dominant forms are caused by mutations in any three of the type IX collagen genes (COL9A1, type 6, MIM 120210; COL9A2, type 2, MIM 600204; COL9A3, type 3, MIM 600969) or the matri lin-3 gene (MATN3, type 5, MIM 607078). These proteins are extracellular matrix com ponents found in growth plate cartilage. The autosomal recessive form of MED is caused by mutations in the diastrophic dysplasia sul fate transporter (DTDST, type 4, MIM 226900). The precise percentage of MED patients with identifiable mutations varies, but it is clear that mutations cannot be found in all patients.
paragraphs.heading: Dysplasia

paragraphs.text: There are no published studies of the use of rhGH in MED. Its effectiveness on height growth and body disproportion is unknown.
paragraphs.heading: Dysplasia

paragraphs.text: The majority of cases of LWD result from heterozygous deletion or inactivating muta
paragraphs.heading: 8.5.4 Léri-Weill Dyschondrosteosis

paragraphs.text: tions of the “short-stature homeoboxcontaining gene” or SHOX [58–60]. Genetic variances in noncoding regions both upstream and downstream of SHOX have also been implicated [61]. The SHOX protein is a tran scription factor that is expressed in epiphyseal growth plates [62], but its precise role is still being elucidated [63]. The SHOX protein has been shown to negatively regulate FGFR3 [64], raising the intriguing possibility of a common pathway disruption between SHOX haploinsufficiency and achondroplasia/hypo chondroplasia. SHOX is located on the distal ends of the short arms of both the X and Y chromosomes, in the pseudoautosomal regions. Although SHOX is located on the X chromosome, LWD is not transmitted in an X-linked inheritance pattern, but in an auto somal dominant-like pattern. Variable pene trance is seen, resulting in a wide spectrum of severity. Because of the variability of the phe notype, the prevalence of LWD is unknown. Homozygous mutations or deletions of SHOX are the cause of Langer mesomelic dysplasia (MIM 249700), a profoundly severe form of short-limbed dwarfism. Genetic test ing for SHOX mutations and deletions is now available through several commercial labora tories.
paragraphs.heading: 8.5.4 Léri-Weill Dyschondrosteosis

paragraphs.text: Large-scale deletions of the X chromo some can result in loss of SHOX, giving rise to LWD as part of a contiguous gene syn drome that may (in boys) include a number of X-linked syndromes, including ichthyosis, learning/behavioral difficulties, Kallman syn drome, chondrodysplasia punctata, and skel etal deformities with short stature [65]. By virtue of a missing X chromosome, girls with Turner syndrome have only a single SHOX gene. Although not traditionally diagnosed as having LWD, these girls phenotypically often have the findings of LWD and it is believed that the loss of the SHOX copy explains all or almost all of the short stature associated with Turner syndrome. Madelung deformity is seen in Turner syndrome but at a lower prevalence than in LWD (25% vs. 53%) [56].
paragraphs.heading: 8.5.4 Léri-Weill Dyschondrosteosis

paragraphs.text: In a recent study of prepubertal children with “idiopathic” short stature (a height less than the 3rd percentile or a height less than the 10th percentile with a height velocity less
paragraphs.heading: 8.5.4 Léri-Weill Dyschondrosteosis

paragraphs.text: than the 25th percentile) of 740 unrelated sub jects, 23 had a SHOX deletion, 5 had an intra genic SHOX mutation, and 8 had deletions proximal to SHOX [66]. This represents an incidence of 4.9% of SHOX-related abnor malities in children with “idiopathic” short stature. In the absence of other features, these children are not generally diagnosed with LWD, but rather with “SHOX haploinsuffi
ciency,” a designation that includes LWD and Turner syndrome.

Recombinant human growth hormone has been shown to be effective in SHOX haploin sufficiency disorders. Use of rhGH in girls with Turner syndrome is now routine care and one study demonstrated a near-final final adult-height increase over the predicted height SD score of 1.3 ± 0.6 [67]. Trials in LWD are
more limited but suggest an equally good response [68]. Both Turner syndrome and SHOX haploinsufficiency are FDA-approved indications for rhGH treatment [69].

disease-causing variants were detected in 248 (97%). All mutations found in OI type I were dominant and exclusively affected type I col lagen genes (COL1A1 or COL1A2). In the 342 patients with a diagnosis of moderate and severe OI (types II, III, and IV), disease-

causing variants were detected in 337 (99%). Dominant mutations were found in COL1A1 or COL1A2 (77%), or IFITM5 (9%). Recessive mutations were observed in 12% of individu als with moderate to severe OI, most com monly, SERPINF1 and CRTAP. Thus, about 20% of individuals with moderate to severe OI had mutations in genes other than COL1A1 or COL1A2 [75]. Patients with type I OI tend to have quantitative defects in their type I collagen protein arising from largescale deletions or nonsense mutations (“func tional null” alleles) in COL1A1 or COL1A2. Patients with OI types II, III, and IV often have missense mutations that alter glycine residues in either COL1A1 or COL1A2 or mutations in genes that affect collagen pro duction and processing [72].

The clinical diagnosis of OI is based on history and clinical examination, bone min eral density determination by dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA or DXA), find ings on radiographs, and bone and mineral biochemistry. Once OI is suspected, it is rec ommended that genetic testing be done not only to confirm the diagnosis but also to determine the recurrence risks. Identifying the type of OI is important for predicting the course of the disease as well as identifying other problems that are specific to certain types. For instance, patients with OI type V are at risk for hyperplastic callus formation, radial head dislocation, and abnormalities in the cranio-cervical junction [76]. Several com mercial laboratories now offer OI sequencing panels.

The most effective treatment strategies for OI are multidisciplinary: general medical management to maximize bone health by optimizing vitamin D status and calcium intake while minimizing the morbidity of fractures and pain; orthopedic management of fractures and skeletal deformities; and physical/occupational therapy to maximize strength and function. Other important healthcare providers are dentists for the treat ment of the complications of dentinogenesis imperfecta, and otolaryngologists for the monitoring of hearing loss [77, 78]. The last three decades have seen an increasing use of bisphosphonates in the treatment of OI and is

now routinely utilized for moderate to severe forms. It often falls to the pediatric endocri nologist to manage this treatment. Bisphosphonates are analogs of pyrophos phate that bind to bone minerals and inhibit osteoclast function, reducing bone resorption. Glorieaux et al. [79] reported on the use of pamidronate (a bisphosphonate given intrave nously) in OI in an uncontrolled study and noted a decrease in fracture frequency, improvement in bone mineral density, and improvement of chronic bone pain. A longerterm study [80] confirmed the results and in addition showed an improvement in linear growth and weight gain in more severely affected individuals (OI types III and IV). Other studies describe similar improvement, but also reported a case of nonunion of a tib ial fracture [81] and delayed fracture healing [82]. Two larger review studies including a Cochran review have been completed. In the first review, 10 trials (519 children) [83] and in the second, 14 trials (819 participants) [84] were included. The studies were, for the most part, at a low risk of bias. The Cochran review [84] found that for oral bisphosphonates, data versus placebo could not be aggregated. They reported that in two studies there appeared to be a reduction in fractures, but no differences were reported in the remaining three trials which commented on fracture incidence. Both reviews state that all studies investigating lum bar spine bone mineral density indicated a statistically significant increase in at least one time point as a result of bisphosphonate ther apy. There was general agreement that treat ment with oral or intravenous bisphosphonates in children with OI results in an increase in bone mineral density. Although most studies observed a significant decrease in fracture incidence and bone pain, the varied study designs did not allow this to be shown conclu sively. A number of studies suggest bisphos phonates also help alleviate pain in children with osteogenesis imperfecta, although a sys temic review concluded there was a high risk for bias in most studies [85]. The medications in general do appear to be safe and well toler ated [83, 84].
At our center, we use the protocol reported by Glorieaux et al. [79], namely, pamidronate

diluted in normal saline (0.1 mg: 1 cc NS at maximum concentration), infused over 4 h, 0.5–1 mg/kg (depending upon patient age) each day for three consecutive days, cycled every 8–16 weeks (depending upon patient age). Some centers delay infusions after oste otomies [86], although this is somewhat con troversial. Infusions are generally not delayed after fractures. The primary adverse effect is a febrile acute phase reaction that is common after the first dose. On the first day of the first infusion, we decrease the dose to one-quarter of the typical dose (0.125 mg/kg) and half of the typical dose (0.25 mg/kg) on days two and three to decreases this effect. Premedication with acetaminophen or ibuprofen before each dose during this first cycle can also be helpful. Transient hypocalcemia after an infusion is seen on occasion, especially in infants, but is rarely of clinical significance with pamidro nate in children. We perform pretreatment assessment and normalization of vitamin D status and calcium intake to lessen this poten tial effect. For infants with moderate to severe OI, we recommend pamidronate be initiated as soon as able, following stabilization of respiratory status and advancement to full feeds. Osteonecrosis of the jaw following den tal procedures is a rare but serious complica tion of bisphosphonate therapy in adults. This is of particular concern in children with OI associated with dentinogenesis imperfecta, who may require multiple dental procedures. However, no cases have been reported in chil dren with OI [87, 88].

Zoledronic acid is another IV bisphospho nate that is increasingly being used for the treatment of OI. The advantage of zoledronic acid over pamidronate is that the infusion is given over 30 min (vs. 4 h for pamidronate) and is given as a single infusion (vs. daily for 3 days for pamidronate). Small, randomized clinical trials have shown results are compa rable for both drugs [89, 90], although larger and long-term studies have not been pub lished. Our experience is that zoledronic acid more frequently causes significant hypocalce mia and acute phase reactions than pamidro nate. Until longer-term data are available, our center will continue to use pamidronate.

There is debate in the field on how long to treat OI patients with bisphosphonates. Bisphosphonates remain bound to bone for decades after administration and, although long-term studies to date do not suggest any very long-term adverse effects, there remains some uncertainty. It seems prudent to limit the exposure of these children as much as pos sible to these drugs. An observational study of 23 children with OI where pamidronate was stopped after at least 3 years of treatment showed a rapid decrease in bone mineral den sity in the radial diaphysis [91]. It has been suggested that this might create regions of localized bone weakness at the junction of the bone laid down during the treatment and bone laid down after the treatment [91]. Some centers are now decreasing the bisphospho nate dose by half once the bone mineral den sity SD score by DXA has improved to >−2.0 [76], although this approach has not been rig orously tested.

There is interest in the use of rhGH in patients with OI, both to treat growth failure associated with the more severe forms and also because of its anabolic effect on bone. Growth hormone deficiency is not part of OI, although there may be a blunted IGF-I release in response to rhGH [92]. In short-term trials, rhGH increased both linear growth and bone mineral density [93, 94]. Long-term studies have not been reported.

Radiographs show a rachitictype picture with normally appearing epiphy ses, widened growth plates, and severely disordered metaphyses with splaying, cup ping, and fraying. They also show osteopenia and subperiosteal bone resorption suggestive of hyperparathyroidism. About half of the patients with this syndrome have hypercalce mia, along with hypercalciuria, hypophospha temia, hyperphosphaturia, and increased 1,25(OH)2 vitamin D levels, a pattern strongly suggestive of hyperparathyroidism. However, parathyroid hormone (PTH) and PTH-related protein (PTHrP) levels are low normal or sup pressed [95]. In 1995, it was reported that Jansen-type metaphyseal chondrodysplasia was caused by gain of function mutations of the parathyroid hormone receptor (PTH1R) [96].
paragraphs.heading: Chondrodysplasia and Blomstrand Chondrodysplasia

paragraphs.text: In 1985, Blomstrand et al. [97] described a neonate that died within hours of birth with a form of short-limbed dwarfism with features of advanced skeletal maturation (Blomstrand chondrodysplasia, MIM 215045). This is a very rare autosomal recessive form of dwarf ism that is generally perinatally lethal, although milder forms have since been described [98]. The fetuses/neonates showed severely shortened limbs, polyhydramnios, hydrops fetalis, coarctation of the aorta, and hypoplastic lungs. Radiographs consistently showed dense bones with premature mineral ization of the teeth and all of the bones in the hands and feet [99]. In many ways, Blomstrand chondrodysplasia showed the opposite fea tures of Jansen-type metaphyseal chondro dysplasia, despite both being short-limbed forms of dwarfism. This symmetry was con firmed when Blomstrand chondrodysplasia was found to be caused by inactivating muta tions of the parathyroid hormone receptor [100].
paragraphs.heading: Chondrodysplasia and Blomstrand Chondrodysplasia

paragraphs.text: The parathyroid hormone receptor (para thyroid hormone 1 receptor, PTH1R, gene PTH1R) is a G-protein coupled receptor whose ligands are both PTH and PTHrP. In renal tubular cells, osteoblasts, and osteo clasts, PTH1R mediates the calcium-
paragraphs.heading: Chondrodysplasia and Blomstrand Chondrodysplasia

paragraphs.text: regulatory properties of PTH and is the source of the hypercalcemia found in Jansentype metaphyseal chondrodysplasia. However, in growth plate chondrocytes, PTH1R medi ates the growth-regulatory properties of PTHrP and gives rise to the dwarfism features of both syndromes.
paragraphs.heading: Chondrodysplasia and Blomstrand Chondrodysplasia

paragraphs.text: In the 1990s, through an elegant series of experiments conducted in a number of labo ratories in chicks and rodents, a major regula tory mechanism of the growth plate was described involving Indian hedgehog and PTHrP [101]. Briefly, differentiated chondro cytes within the hypertrophic zone of the growth plate produce a paracrine signaling peptide called Indian hedgehog, which dif fuses through the growth plate. Indian hedge hog is detected by perichondrium and periarticular cells, as well as chondrocytes in the proliferative and pre-hypertrophic zone. In response, these cells produce PTHrP, which inhibits the differentiation of pre-hypertrophic chondrocytes and prevents their entry into the hypertrophic phase. The reduced number of hypertrophic chondrocytes results in reduced Indian hedgehog production, closing the feed back loop. Through this feedback mechanism, the number of chondrocytes entering the hypertrophic phase of differentiation is regu lated. Several other signaling pathways, including transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) [102] and bone morphogenetic proteins (BMP) [103], are intermediates in, and modulators of, this feedback loop. The discovery of the disruption of this feedback loop as the cause of Jansen-type metaphyseal chondrodysplasia and Blomstrand chondro dysplasia confirmed the presence and impor tance of this regulatory mechanism in human growth.

Generally, these children are identified after their linear growth slows at 1–2 years of age. Adults with this syndrome have height SD scores ranging from −5 to −10 [106]. It is a rare syndrome, with a prevalence of roughly 1:2,000,000 [107]. In 2004, the cause of AMDM was found to be homozygous inacti vating mutations in the gene that encodes for the natriuretic peptide receptor B (NPR-B, gene NPR2) [106]. The ligand for NPR-B is a C-type natriuretic peptide (CNP). This obser vation was the first to identify CNP as an important regulator of human growth [108].

Both CNP and NPR-B are synthesized in the growth plate; CNP acts through a paracrineregulatory mechanism. Rodent and in vitro studies have now shown that CNP stimulates growth plate chondrocyte differentiation and hypertrophy, in part through inhibiting MAPK pathway signaling [27]. As such, CNP is a counter-regulatory mechanism to the FGFR3 and Indian hedgehog/PTHrP path ways. This effect has led to the exploration of CNP as a specific treatment for achondropla sia [19] (see discussion above).

It was observed that the parents and het erozygous carrier siblings of patients with AMDM were shorter than the general popu lation [106, 107, 109]. Heterozygous carriers of NPR2 mutations have on average height SD scores that are 1.4 lower than noncarrier family members but with no body dispropor tion or other detectable abnormalities [107]. Heterozygous inactivating mutations in NPR2 have been identified in 1–3% of children with “idiopathic” short stature [110, 111].
Interestingly, gain of function mutations of NPR2 have been found to be a cause of tall stature [112, 113], often associated with a Marfanoid body habitus.

Clinically relevant biomarkers of linear growth have long been sought. The gold stan dard for measuring height velocity is serial height measurements taken 6–12 months apart. This approach, however, depends on accurate height measurements and takes a long time to obtain a result. A biomarker that correlates with height velocity would allow for the assessment of growth at a single time point. This would be useful in the clini cal evaluation of children with short stature, distinguishing between a short child who is growing as expected and a short child who is growing slowly. Such a biomarker would also be useful during times of changing height velocity, such as when starting growth-pro moting treatment such as rhGH or vosorit ide, or starting potentially growth-inhibiting
paragraphs.heading: Biomarkers

paragraphs.text: treatment such as systemic glucocorticoids. A number of peptides have been proposed as potential biomarkers, including bone-for mation markers such as bone-specific alka line phosphatase and collagen-type I markers [114]; bone resorption markers such as uri nary deoxypyridinoline/creatinine [115]; tissue expansion markers such as procollagen-type III N-terminal propeptide (PIIINP) [114]; and unrelated markers such as leptin [116]. Blood levels of all of the mentioned potential biomarkers have been shown (at least in some studies) to correlate with increased height velocity in children starting rhGH therapy. However, none correlate with height velocity in healthy, normally growing children. With a better understanding of growth plate regula tion, two peptides have emerged that are spe cific to the growth plate and show significant promise as biomarkers of linear growth.

Besides being markers for growth, these biomarkers also provide us with new tools for studying growth plate function in syndromes of skeletal dysplasia. In children with achon droplasia, NTproCNP levels are higher than age- and sex-matched controls, despite their reduced height velocity [123]. In the same cohort, CXM levels were consistently reduced [124]. This pattern demonstrates that these children have resistance to CNP, as discussed

in the achondroplasia section above. Levels of both biomarkers still correlated with height velocity in these children. Conversely, in osteogenesis imperfecta, NTproCNP levels are reduced (unpublished observation), while CXM [125] levels are elevated compared to the general population. In this study, elevated CXM levels may be related to fractures or fracture healing at the time of sampling as we could not confirm this finding in this popula tion (unpublished observation). If true, how ever, it would suggest that the growth impairment in OI may be due to hypertrophic chondrocyte dysfunction.

This is a girl who presents with the common complaint of short stature. The patient has skeletal disproportion that is not severe and has some characteristic skeletal find ings, including cubitus valgus and Madelung deformity. The first consideration should be the diagnosis of Turner syndrome. However, this girl has none of the nonskeletal features of Turner syndrome, and finding that her father has very similar findings makes Turner syn drome unlikely. Léri-Weill dyschondrosteosis then becomes the leading diagnostic possibility, either from a SHOX mutation or deletion

inherited from her father. This family proved to have a point mutation that eliminated the start codon of the SHOX gene, eliminating all trans lation from the mRNA, and confirming the diagnosis. This patient is currently on human growth hormone treatment.

Previous growth charts are unavailable but he has always been the shortest boy in his class and the difference between him and his peers had increased in the previous 1–2 years. He is otherwise healthy with no other medical problems. There are 461 syndromes of skeletal dyspla sia. Most are readily recognized as such, but in a number, the effect on height is relatively minor, and other signs and/or symptoms are absent or subtle. It is not uncommon for these children to present to the pediatric endocri nologist for the evaluation of short stature. It is incumbent that the pediatric endocrinolo gist be able to recognize when a child might have skeletal dysplasia, to be able to diagnose the most common syndromes, and to under stand what treatment options are available.

There are currently 461 described skeletal dysplasia syn dromes. 5 The presence of skeletal dysplasia should be considered in any child pre senting with short stature, particularly if skeletal disproportion is identified. 5 A hormonal treatment for growth in children with achondroplasia, vosorit ide, is available. 5 Bisphosphonate treatment of osteogen esis imperfect often falls to the pediatric endocrinologist. 5 Growth plate-specific biomarkers may ### 8 prove useful in the clinical evaluation of linear growth. 5 Study of skeletal dysplasias will help us to better understand the mechanisms that regulate linear growth. ### 8.1 Introduction and Background ### Information The skeletal dysplasias (or more appropri ately, the osteochondrodysplasias) are genetic disorders that affect the development of the skeletal and cartilaginous tissues. They are of interest to pediatric endocrinologists not only because most have an impact on linear growth causing short stature (and occasionally tall stature) but also for what these disorders teach us about the mechanisms and regulation of growth. As of 2019, there were 461 described skel etal dysplasias, associated with one of 437 dif ferent genes [1], with more associations being made routinely [2]. Although each individual disorder is relatively rare, as a group, the inci dence of any skeletal dysplasia is roughly 1 in 5000 births [3, 4]. Making the definitive diag nosis in a child with skeletal dysplasia is important in order to screen for and treat the problems particular to each condition. Diagnosis and management generally require a multidisciplinary team approach; yet, it is often to pediatric endocrinology that these patients are first referred, due to the growth abnormalities. It is therefore incumbent upon the endocrinologist to understand the basics of this field and to recognize when a skeletal dysplasia may be present. Beyond recognizing and diagnosing skele tal dysplasias, there are now therapies avail able for a number of skeletal dysplasias to increase linear growth or bone mineral den sity and the management of these treatments increasingly falls to the endocrinologist. 8.1 8.1 ## PDF page 229 | printed page 213 Table 8.1 The vocabulary of skeletal dysplasias Acromelia Shortening of the terminal parts of the limbs (hands and feet) in relation to the upper and middle limb segments Atlantoaxial instability Abnormal extra motion occurring between the first and second cervical vertebrae (C1 and C2) Cervical Relating to the vertebrae found at the level of the neck Chondro- Relating to cartilage Cubitus valgus Deformity of the elbow in which it cannot be fully extended; As such, they are congenital and many syndromes can be diag nosed prenatally or in the neonatal period. However, some genes have subtle effects or play a role only in later development and/or growth and the phenotypic features appear later in life. The past two decades have seen great advancement in identifying the causative gene in skeletal dysplasias [1]. This has aided greatly in the classification of skeletal dyspla sias and our understanding of the regulation of skeletal tissues. ### 8.3 Clinical Presentation When a child presents for evaluation of short (or tall) stature, the possibility of skeletal dys plasia should always be a consideration. It is unusual for patients with more significant phenotypes (such as achondroplasia) to be referred to the endocrinologist as the presence of skeletal dysplasia is obvious clinically and these patients are generally referred first to the geneticist for an evaluation. However, there are a number of skeletal dysplasias where the primary clinical feature is short stature while other features are absent or subtle. Tall stature can also be a symptom of skeletal dysplasia where the evaluation starts with the endocri nologist. A family history, anthropometric measurements, a careful physical exam, and the knowledge of what to look for are the basis for detecting skeletal dysplasia in these situations. The skeletal dysplasias are of genetic ori gin and the majority are caused by single gene abnormalities; a thorough family history may provide valuable information regarding these syndromes. The most common syndromes have a dominant mode of inheritance, includ ing achondroplasia, hypochondroplasia, Léri- Weill dyschondrosteosis, and osteogenesis imperfecta. Except in cases of de novo muta tions, children with these syndromes will have a parent with the same condition. With the newly available genetic tools, it is now routine that a diagnosis made in a child leads to the diagnosis being made in a parent and grandparent. Obtaining parental heights can assist with the evaluation. Reported parental heights are notoriously inaccurate; it is recommended that parents’ heights be mea sured by the provider whenever possible. 5 8.2 ## PDF page 232 | printed page 216 portionately short legs which suggests the presence of short-limbed skeletal dysplasia. A patient with short stature and an upper-tolower segment ratio less than the 3rd percen tile suggests a disproportionately short spine, possibly due to spondylodysplasia and/or sco liosis. Conversely, a patient with tall stature and ratio that is less than the 3rd percentile has disproportionately long legs, suggesting an overgrowth syndrome such as Marfan syn drome. A related measurement is the sitting height and the sitting-to-standing height ratio. For this measurement, the child is placed on a flat stool with his or her back against the wall. The child’s thighs should be parallel to the floor. A mark is made at the top of the head. The distance from the floor to the mark minus the height of the stool gives the seated height. Reference ranges are available [6]. ### 8 7 8.3 6 8.2 ## PDF page 233 | printed page 217 Table 8.2 Guidelines for arm span-height difference Arm span-height difference Caucasian and Hispanic Prepubertal (cm) Pubertala (cm) 3rd percentile −8.2 −7.0 Median −2.5 0.4 97th percentile 2.7 8.1 a For girls, breast Tanner stage 2 or higher; for boys genitalia Tanner stage 2 or higher suggests disproportionately short arms while a difference greater than the 97th percentile suggests a short spine. Either suggests the presence of skeletal dysplasia. Children with an excessive arm span-height difference should also be evaluated for scoliosis. An arm-span-to-height ratio of >1.05 is used in the revised Ghent nosology for the diagnosis of Marfan syndrome [8]. A head circumference (occipital-frontal circumference, OFC) is also important for detecting body disproportion. An OFC within the expected range in a child with severe short stature could suggest a skeletal dysplasia, although other diagnoses must also be consid ered. A thorough physical examination focused on the skeletal system is important. Observation of the child while standing will give the clinician an idea of body proportion. As a rule of thumb, the fingertips should rest level with the mid-thigh. Examination of the skull should note the presence and position of the fontanelles, and the presence of asymme try, frontal bossing, and hypo- or hyper telorism. A highly arched palate is common in a number of skeletal dysplasias. The presence of a short neck, kyphosis, or scoliosis may suggest an abnormality of the spine. Examination of the arms and legs may show disproportionate shortening of the upper or lower arm or leg. Limb segment measure ments can be done. A guide such as that by Gripp et al. [6] provides measurement tech niques and reference ranges. Bowing of a limb is an important finding, as is a limitation in joint mobility. A close examination of the hands and feet for shortening of some or all of the metatarsals, metacarpals, and phalan ges should also be done. Extra or missing dig its, syndactyly, and/or camptodactyly (inability to fully straighten a digit) are also important potential findings. ### 8.4 Diagnostic Evaluation Once skeletal dysplasia is suspected, more indepth evaluation is called for. The diagnostic evaluation of a child suspected of having skel etal dysplasia requires a thorough history including a three-generation family history. Attention should be paid to signs and symp toms such as early onset arthritis or joint pain, fractures, joint replacement surgeries, dental problems, and hearing or vision abnormali ties. The physical examination should include specific measurements as discussed above to assess for disproportion, including signs of disproportion within the limb. Ranges of motion throughout are important to assess as both increased and decreased flexibilities are associated with various dysplasias. Lastly, skeletal imaging should be undertaken to look for diagnostic clues. There is not a standard dysplasia survey, as various experts and insti tutions do things differently. Our preferred evaluation includes the following: an AP image from the pelvis to the floor, standing if possible, otherwise supine (this image allows ### Automatic table extraction — verify rendered original |Col1|Arm span-height difference|Col3|Col4|Col5| |---|---|---|---|---| ||**Caucasian and Hispanic**|**Caucasian and Hispanic**|**African American**|**African American**| ||**Prepubertal(cm)**|**Pubertala (cm)**|**Prepubertal(cm)**|**Pubertala (cm)**| |3rd percentile|−8.2|−7.0|−2.8|1.6| |Median|−2.5|0.4|1.6|6.3| |97th percentile|2.7|8.1|10|16.1| [Original table](../../tables/ch008_p0233_1.jpg) ## PDF page 234 | printed page 218 for the assessment of anatomical alignment of the lower extremities and disproportion within the limb); AP and lateral images of the tho raco-lumbar spine (to assess for scoliosis and any vertebral body abnormalities); an AP image of the arm from shoulder to wrist; and an AP image of the hands. If osteogenesis imperfecta or another fragility condition is being entertained, AP and lateral skull images are done to assess mineralization and for wor mian bones. If any spine abnormalities are present either on clinical examination or radiograph, lateral flexion and extension views are recommended to assess for cervical spine instability. Important consideration should be given to having these images reviewed by a radiologist familiar with skeletal dysplasias in children. If no such radiologist is available locally, assistance should be available through regional skeletal dysplasia programs. Assistance is also available at the University of California, Los Angeles International Skeletal Dysplasia Registry ( www.ortho. ucla.edu/isdr) [9] and the European Skeletal Dysplasia Network ( www.esdn.org) [10], which can review patient images and provide diagnostic possibilities. ### 8 Once the evaluation is completed, the information gathered from the history, physi cal, and radiographic examinations can be reviewed to try and reach a specific diagnosis. If a specific or limited differential diagnosis can be reached, molecular testing is likely available to confirm a diagnosis. Advances in genetic diagnostic techniques including thirdgeneration sequencing, multiple gene panel sequencing, and whole exome sequencing have diagnosis confirmation now possible in the majority of skeletal dysplasia syndromes [2]. ### 8.5 Common Syndromes ### 8.5.1 Achondroplasia Achondroplasia (MIM 100800) is the most common skeletal dysplasia with incidence estimates ranging from 1 in 15,000 to 1 in 27,000 births [11–13]. The average adult height for men is 131 cm, with a range of 118–144 cm (3′10′′–4′9′′, height SD score −8.3 to −4.6), and for women, 123 cm with a range of 113–137 cm (3′8′′–4′6′′, height SD score −7.7 to −4.0) [14]. The clinical features of achondroplasia are distinctive enough that diagnosis can be made through clinical and radiographic means, and historically, the diag nosis was usually made at birth or shortly thereafter [15]. Due to advances in late-term prenatal ultrasound and the detection of limb shortening, achondroplasia is now commonly diagnosed prenatally [11, 13]. 8.4 Achondroplasia is caused by a mutation in the fibroblast growth factor receptor-3 gene (FGFR3) [16]. Mutations that change the amino acid glycine to arginine at position 380 (Gly380Arg) of the FGFR-3 protein account for greater than 98% of all reported cases of achondroplasia. This typical G380R gain-offunction mutation results in the constitutive activation of the receptor. In growth plate chondrocytes, this receptor activates the sig nal transducers and activators of the tran scription (STAT1) pathway, which inhibits chondrocyte proliferation, and the mitogen- ## PDF page 235 | printed page 219 activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, which inhibits both chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation. The net result of inhibited chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation is slowed bone growth [17–19]. Achondroplasia is inherited in an autosomal dominant man ner, but about 80% of patients with achondro plasia represent new mutations [13]. Given this high rate of new mutations and the inci dence of achondroplasia, the base pair of codon 380 in FGFR3 has the highest known rate of mutation in man. New mutations typi cally arise from the father during sperm for mation and paternal age greater than 35 years has been found to be a risk factor [20]. A recent hypothesis is that sperms containing a FGFR3 mutation have a selective advantage and as men age, more FGFR3 mutant sperms are present [20]. Routine care for children with achondro plasia consists of monitoring for and the management of concerns such as genu varum, hydrocephalus, foramen magnum stenosis, obstructive sleep apnea, and ear infections from Eustachian tube abnormalities [21, 22]. A number of small studies have reported on the use of recombinant human growth hor mone (rhGH) in achondroplasia for up to 6 years [23–25]. Studies generally show an increase in height velocity during the first year of treatment, but this increase is reduced and then lost in subsequent years of treatment. C-type natriuretic peptide (CNP) is a small peptide that acts in a paracrine manner in the growth plate to regulate growth (see acrome somelic dysplasia and type Maroteaux, later in the text). One mechanism of this is through the inhibition of intracellular signaling of the MAPK pathway [27]. In mice carrying the achondroplastic mutation, over-expression of CNP [28], as well as exogenous administration of CNP [29], rescues the skeletal abnormali ties, and leads to the possibility of using CNP as a growth-promoting treatment in children with achondroplasia [19, 29]. Vosoritide (pre viously named BMN111) is a peptide analog of a 39-amino acid version of CNP with a two-amino acid substitution at the aminoterminal end. This substitution reduces CNP cleavage by a specific neutral endopeptidase, prolonging its half-life in circulation, while not affecting binding with its primary recep tor, natriuretic peptide receptor-B (NPR-B) [30]. Vosoritide, given as a daily subcutaneous injection, has been shown to increase growth velocity in children with achondroplasia [31–33]. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study involving 119 chil dren with achondroplasia has been reported [32]. Subjects were monitored for 6 months for baseline growth data, then randomized to receive a placebo (n = 61) or vosoritide (n = 60) at 15 μg/kg daily for 1 year. The pri mary endpoint was the change in annualized height velocity from baseline. Treatment and control groups were well matched for sex, age, height, height SD score, and the upper-tolower body segment ratio. Treated subjects had an average age of 8.4 ± 2.4 (SD) years and showed a change in height velocity of 1.71 (1.40–2.01, 95% confidence interval) cm/year. This is compared to controls with an average age of 9.1 ± 2.5 years, with a change in height velocity of 0.13 (−0.18 to 0.45) cm/year (p < 0.0001). The change from baseline height ### 8 SD score was 0.27 (0.18–0.36) for treated sub jects compared to −0.01 (−0.1 to 0.09) for controls (p < 0.0001). There was no difference in change from the baseline of the upper-tolower segment ratio. Following this study, an uncontrolled, 2-year extension study of the same cohort was performed [33]. All control subjects were started on vosoritide at 15 μg/ mL daily and treated subjects were continued on treatment. The study showed the increase in height velocity during vosoritide treatment was maintained for 2 or 3 years, with no new adverse effects emerging. A clinical study of children from birth to 5 years of age [34] has been completed, but the results have not yet been published. No studies have yet been car ried out on final adult height. The most sig nificant adverse effect noted in these studies was a decrease in blood pressure 18–120 min following the injection. The decrease was transient and only occasionally was the sub ject symptomatic. The most common adverse effect was local injection site reactions, occur ring in 85% of the subjects. After 2 years of treatment, antibodies against vosoritide (antidrug antibodies, ADA) were detected in 35% of treated subjects. No drug-neutralizing anti bodies were detected and the clinical response was no different in the subjects who developed anti-drug antibodies. Based on these studies, vosoritide (VoxzogoTM, BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc., San Rafael, CA) was approved for use in children with achondro plasia older than 2 years of age by the European Medicines Agency in August 2021, and for children older than 5 years by the Federal Drug Administration in November 2021. The Japanese Ministry of Health, Labor and Welfare approved its use in children with achondroplasia of any age in June 2022. In the United States, the current average annual cost of treatment is $320,000. There are currently no consensus guide lines on pretreatment evaluation and moni toring for patients who are being initiated or maintained on vosoritide. Prior to initiation, we recommend that a patient have a full evalu ation, including an in-depth review of past medical history, medications, allergies, and subspecialist evaluations. A clinical examina ## PDF page 237 | printed page 221 tion, including detailed anthropometric mea surements, is also recommended. Radiographs to confirm open growth plates should also be obtained if a patient is undergoing puberty. A discussion that focuses on managing expecta tions as well as the impact and possible chal lenges of a daily injection for a child should be addressed. Families should be made aware of possible side effects, including injection site reactions and hypotension, and preventative tactics recommended including rotating injec tion sites and proper cleaning techniques. Having the child eat a small snack and drink at least 240 mL of fluid 30 min prior to admin istration is recommended to prevent hypoten sion [35]. Patients should be monitored at 3- to 6-month intervals, collecting anthropo metric measurements, monitoring for side effects, and discussing any challenges that may have arisen with the injections. While the mutation in achondro plasia is essentially always caused by the same ## PDF page 238 | printed page 222 mutation, there is greater variability in the mutations causing hypochondroplasia. The lysine-for-asparagine substitution at codon 540 (Asn540Lys) is the most common muta tion to cause hypochondroplasia, but several others have been described. A second gene has been implicated but has not yet been identi fied [45]. When there is an established clinical and radiographic diagnosis of hypochondro plasia, FGFR3 mutations can be identified in about 90% of individuals [45]. Because there is a phenotypical overlap between achondro plasia and hypochondroplasia, and between hypochondroplasia and “idiopathic” short stature, genetic confirmation of the diagnosis is recommended [45]. As with achondroplasia, rhGH seems to have some effect on hypochondroplasia, although studies are small and short-term [46–50]. The largest and longest-term study [46] showed that, while improving growth velocity and height SD score, rhGH also worsened the skeletal disproportion. A metaanalysis of published studies concluded there was a positive effect of rhGH on height [51]. Surgical limb lengthening procedures (distrac tion osteogenesis) have been reported in adults with hypochondroplasia [52, 53] to increase height and decrease skeletal disproportion, but are very invasive with a high complication rate and are by no means routine practice at this time. Since gain of function mutations of FGFR3 cause most cases of hypochondropla sia, we predict that the drug interventions being explored for achondroplasia will also prove effective in hypochondroplasia. MED is a heteroge neous disorder of bone and cartilage develop ment that results in small irregular epiphyses. Proportionate short or average stature is pres ent, as are frequently painful joints, and pos sibly a mild myopathy. MED is not recognizable at birth and is typically recog nized after 2 years of age and in some cases not until adulthood. Typically, adults will grow to be between 145 and 168 cm (4′9′′ and 5′6′′). MED may present as a delay in walking or gait differences in a young child. Initial complaints usually include joint stiffness, pain, contractures, or limping. In some forms of MED, the fingers and toes are short and stubby, especially the thumb. Minor flexion contractures of the knees and elbows can be present. Joint pain, which could be fluctuating or episodic in childhood, tends to advance in adolescence or early adulthood. Genu valgus or varus may develop. Key radiographic characteristics of MED include irregular epiphyses usually at the hips, knees, ankles, wrists, and hands. Bones of the pelvis, spinal column, and skull are typically normal. In middle to late childhood, the epiphyses are either flat or small. An important diagnostic sign is the epiphyses of distal tibias which are malformed laterally to produce a sloping wedge-shaped articular surface. This may be more apparent later in life. A bipartite (split) patella can be seen and if present, shortening of the long bones is mild. Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia is a geneti cally heterogeneous condition that can be inherited in either an autosomal dominant or autosomal recessive manner. Dominant forms of MED are more common. The most com mon dominant genetic cause of MED is mutations in the gene encoding the cartilage oligomeric matrix protein (COMP) (type 1, MIM 132400). Other dominant forms are caused by mutations in any three of the type IX collagen genes (COL9A1, type 6, MIM 120210; COL9A2, type 2, MIM 600204; COL9A3, type 3, MIM 600969) or the matri lin-3 gene (MATN3, type 5, MIM 607078). These proteins are extracellular matrix com ponents found in growth plate cartilage. The autosomal recessive form of MED is caused by mutations in the diastrophic dysplasia sul fate transporter (DTDST, type 4, MIM 226900). The precise percentage of MED patients with identifiable mutations varies, but it is clear that mutations cannot be found in all patients. ## PDF page 239 | printed page 223 There are no published studies of the use of rhGH in MED. Genetic variances in noncoding regions both upstream and downstream of SHOX have also been implicated [61]. The SHOX protein is a tran scription factor that is expressed in epiphyseal growth plates [62], but its precise role is still being elucidated [63]. The SHOX protein has been shown to negatively regulate FGFR3 [64], raising the intriguing possibility of a common pathway disruption between SHOX haploinsufficiency and achondroplasia/hypo chondroplasia. SHOX is located on the distal ends of the short arms of both the X and Y chromosomes, in the pseudoautosomal regions. Although SHOX is located on the X chromosome, LWD is not transmitted in an X-linked inheritance pattern, but in an auto somal dominant-like pattern. Variable pene trance is seen, resulting in a wide spectrum of severity. Because of the variability of the phe notype, the prevalence of LWD is unknown. Homozygous mutations or deletions of SHOX are the cause of Langer mesomelic dysplasia (MIM 249700), a profoundly severe form of short-limbed dwarfism. Genetic test ing for SHOX mutations and deletions is now available through several commercial labora tories. Large-scale deletions of the X chromo some can result in loss of SHOX, giving rise to LWD as part of a contiguous gene syn drome that may (in boys) include a number of X-linked syndromes, including ichthyosis, learning/behavioral difficulties, Kallman syn drome, chondrodysplasia punctata, and skel etal deformities with short stature [65]. By virtue of a missing X chromosome, girls with Turner syndrome have only a single SHOX gene. Although not traditionally diagnosed as having LWD, these girls phenotypically often have the findings of LWD and it is believed that the loss of the SHOX copy explains all or almost all of the short stature associated with Turner syndrome. Madelung deformity is seen in Turner syndrome but at a lower prevalence than in LWD (25% vs. 53%) [56]. In the absence of other features, these children are not generally diagnosed with LWD, but rather with “SHOX haploinsuffi 55 58 ciency,” a designation that includes LWD and Turner syndrome. Recombinant human growth hormone has been shown to be effective in SHOX haploin sufficiency disorders. Thus, about 20% of individuals with moderate to severe OI had mutations in genes other than COL1A1 or COL1A2 [75]. Patients with type I OI tend to have quantitative defects in their type I collagen protein arising from largescale deletions or nonsense mutations (“func tional null” alleles) in COL1A1 or COL1A2. Patients with OI types II, III, and IV often have missense mutations that alter glycine residues in either COL1A1 or COL1A2 or mutations in genes that affect collagen pro duction and processing [72]. The clinical diagnosis of OI is based on history and clinical examination, bone min eral density determination by dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA or DXA), find ings on radiographs, and bone and mineral biochemistry. Once OI is suspected, it is rec ommended that genetic testing be done not only to confirm the diagnosis but also to determine the recurrence risks. Identifying the type of OI is important for predicting the course of the disease as well as identifying other problems that are specific to certain types. For instance, patients with OI type V are at risk for hyperplastic callus formation, radial head dislocation, and abnormalities in the cranio-cervical junction [76]. Several com mercial laboratories now offer OI sequencing panels. The most effective treatment strategies for OI are multidisciplinary: general medical management to maximize bone health by optimizing vitamin D status and calcium intake while minimizing the morbidity of fractures and pain; orthopedic management of fractures and skeletal deformities; and physical/occupational therapy to maximize strength and function. Other important healthcare providers are dentists for the treat ment of the complications of dentinogenesis imperfecta, and otolaryngologists for the monitoring of hearing loss [77, 78]. The last three decades have seen an increasing use of bisphosphonates in the treatment of OI and is now routinely utilized for moderate to severe forms. It often falls to the pediatric endocri nologist to manage this treatment. Bisphosphonates are analogs of pyrophos phate that bind to bone minerals and inhibit osteoclast function, reducing bone resorption. Glorieaux et al. [79] reported on the use of pamidronate (a bisphosphonate given intrave nously) in OI in an uncontrolled study and noted a decrease in fracture frequency, improvement in bone mineral density, and improvement of chronic bone pain. A longerterm study [80] confirmed the results and in addition showed an improvement in linear growth and weight gain in more severely affected individuals (OI types III and IV). Other studies describe similar improvement, but also reported a case of nonunion of a tib ial fracture [81] and delayed fracture healing [82]. Two larger review studies including a Cochran review have been completed. In the first review, 10 trials (519 children) [83] and in the second, 14 trials (819 participants) [84] were included. The studies were, for the most part, at a low risk of bias. The Cochran review [84] found that for oral bisphosphonates, data versus placebo could not be aggregated. They reported that in two studies there appeared to be a reduction in fractures, but no differences were reported in the remaining three trials which commented on fracture incidence. Both reviews state that all studies investigating lum bar spine bone mineral density indicated a statistically significant increase in at least one time point as a result of bisphosphonate ther apy. There was general agreement that treat ment with oral or intravenous bisphosphonates in children with OI results in an increase in bone mineral density. Although most studies observed a significant decrease in fracture incidence and bone pain, the varied study designs did not allow this to be shown conclu sively. A number of studies suggest bisphos phonates also help alleviate pain in children with osteogenesis imperfecta, although a sys temic review concluded there was a high risk for bias in most studies [85]. The medications in general do appear to be safe and well toler ated [83, 84]. At our center, we use the protocol reported by Glorieaux et al. [79], namely, pamidronate ## PDF page 244 | printed page 228 diluted in normal saline (0.1 mg: 1 cc NS at maximum concentration), infused over 4 h, 0.5–1 mg/kg (depending upon patient age) each day for three consecutive days, cycled every 8–16 weeks (depending upon patient age). Some centers delay infusions after oste otomies [86], although this is somewhat con troversial. Infusions are generally not delayed after fractures. The primary adverse effect is a febrile acute phase reaction that is common after the first dose. On the first day of the first infusion, we decrease the dose to one-quarter of the typical dose (0.125 mg/kg) and half of the typical dose (0.25 mg/kg) on days two and three to decreases this effect. Premedication with acetaminophen or ibuprofen before each dose during this first cycle can also be helpful. Transient hypocalcemia after an infusion is seen on occasion, especially in infants, but is rarely of clinical significance with pamidro nate in children. We perform pretreatment assessment and normalization of vitamin D status and calcium intake to lessen this poten tial effect. For infants with moderate to severe OI, we recommend pamidronate be initiated as soon as able, following stabilization of respiratory status and advancement to full feeds. Osteonecrosis of the jaw following den tal procedures is a rare but serious complica tion of bisphosphonate therapy in adults. This is of particular concern in children with OI associated with dentinogenesis imperfecta, who may require multiple dental procedures. However, no cases have been reported in chil dren with OI [87, 88]. ### 8 Zoledronic acid is another IV bisphospho nate that is increasingly being used for the treatment of OI. The advantage of zoledronic acid over pamidronate is that the infusion is given over 30 min (vs. 4 h for pamidronate) and is given as a single infusion (vs. daily for 3 days for pamidronate). Small, randomized clinical trials have shown results are compa rable for both drugs [89, 90], although larger and long-term studies have not been pub lished. Our experience is that zoledronic acid more frequently causes significant hypocalce mia and acute phase reactions than pamidro nate. Until longer-term data are available, our center will continue to use pamidronate. There is debate in the field on how long to treat OI patients with bisphosphonates. Bisphosphonates remain bound to bone for decades after administration and, although long-term studies to date do not suggest any very long-term adverse effects, there remains some uncertainty. It seems prudent to limit the exposure of these children as much as pos sible to these drugs. An observational study of 23 children with OI where pamidronate was stopped after at least 3 years of treatment showed a rapid decrease in bone mineral den sity in the radial diaphysis [91]. It has been suggested that this might create regions of localized bone weakness at the junction of the bone laid down during the treatment and bone laid down after the treatment [91].
