or optic nerve atrophy should be evaluated for adrenal deficiency. Individuals at risk for iat rogenic adrenal insufficiency will often appear Cushingoid on examination, with round facies, thinned skin, striae, and a dorsal cervi cal fat pad due to prior glucocorticoid ther apy.

### 10.4 Diagnostic Evaluation

### 10.4.1 Baseline Hormone

### Measurements

To verify suspected primary adrenal insuffi ciency in the patient presenting with classic signs and symptoms of Addison disease, often little more is necessary than the measurement of plasma ACTH, cortisol, renin activity, and aldosterone. Elevated ACTH (>2-fold above the upper limit of the reference range) and plasma renin activity together with low plasma cortisol and/or aldosterone confirms primary adrenal failure [104]. In patients more than 6 months of age, the age at which the cir cadian pattern of glucocorticoid production has been established [105], not presenting in fulminant adrenal crisis, morning (approxi mately 8 AM) ACTH, and cortisol levels, along with electrolytes, plasma renin activity, and aldosterone, may establish the diagnosis. A fasting morning cortisol of less than 5 mcg/ dL is indicative of adrenal insufficiency, while concentrations exceeding 20 mcg/dL make adrenal failure quite unlikely [104, 106]. Those with early adrenal failure, or secondary dis ease, will often require additional provocative testing as described below. Adrenal autoanti bodies can be used to further establish the eti ology of adrenal insufficiency as an autoimmune [36, 37]. All males diagnosed with primary adrenal failure without evidence of other autoimmune pathology should have plasma very long-chain fatty acids measured to exclude X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy.

Screening for CAH caused by 21-hydroxylase deficiency on the newborn screen is universally required by law in all 50 of the United States [107]. In newborns with

ambiguous genitalia or a salt-wasting crisis where CAH is being considered, random mea surement of cortisol precursors and precursor by-products usually confirms or excludes the diagnosis. For a virilized female, where 21-hydroxylase, 11β-hydroxylase, or 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiencies are possible, a typical hormone profile con sists of measuring 17-hydroxypregnenolone, 17-hydroxyprogesterone, dehydroepiandros terone, androstenedione, testosterone, corti sol, plasma renin activity, and aldosterone. Males with undervirilization should be evalu ated for 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, 17-hydroxylase, or StAR deficiency, as well as nonadrenal etiologies of genital ambiguity, while normally virilized males with salt wast ing should be evaluated for 21-hydroxylase deficiency and aldosterone biosynthetic defects. In 11β-hydroxylase deficiency, hyper tension, hypokalemia, and a suppressed plasma renin are found in normally virilized males or virilized females. Since salt wasting due to CAH does not typically occur within the first 3 days after birth, and adrenal hor mone levels change dramatically in normal infants within this period [108–110], random adrenal hormone measurements should be obtained on the day of life 2–3. Additionally, the normal range of adrenal hormones differs for term and preterm infants and should be accounted for in the interpretation of results [111–113]. Late-onset forms of CAH and proximal lesions in the cortisol biosynthetic pathway such as StAR deficiency or adrenal hypoplasia often require cosyntropin stimula tion testing, as described below, with cortisol precursors measured in addition to cortisol.

### 10.4.2 Cosyntropin Stimulation

### Test

Direct stimulation of adrenal cortisol release by the administration of cosyntropin (1–24 ACTH; Cortrosyn) is the most commonly used diagnostic tool in the evaluation of adre nal function [106, 114]. In the standard cosyn tropin test (250 mcg cosyntropin in adults and children ≥2 years of age, 125 mcg for children


## PDF page 289 | printed page 276

<2 years, and 15 mcg/kg for infants), baseline ACTH and cortisol samples are obtained, and then cosyntropin is administered intrave nously [104]. If mineralocorticoid deficiency is also suspected, plasma renin activity, aldo sterone, and electrolytes should be obtained with the baseline laboratories. Thirty and/or 60 min following cosyntropin administration, a second plasma sample is obtained for corti sol determination. Data from the 1990s sup port a plasma cortisol concentration greater than or equal to 18 mcg/dL, along with a nor mal baseline ACTH level, as a normal response and rules out primary adrenal insuf ficiency [115]. However, more recent data using more specific cortisol antibodies sup port a cutoff of 13.5–20.8 mcg/dL, depending on the assay used, as a normal response to the cosyntropin test [116–118]. In addition, a nor mal response to this standard stimulation test also rules out long-standing, severe secondary adrenal insufficiency. To evaluate recent-onset secondary adrenal insufficiency or milder forms of secondary adrenal insufficiency, a more sensitive stimulation test employing a lower dose of cosyntropin has been devised [115, 119–121]. In this case, 1 mcg, or 0.5 mcg/ M2 of body surface area, of cosyntropin is administered intravenously, with cortisol measured at baseline and 20–60 min after administration. Plasma cortisol concentration above 13.5–20.8 mcg/dL, depending on the assay used, is considered a normal response. False-positive tests employing these criteria may be relatively frequent, however, and should be considered to prevent overdiagnosis of adrenal insufficiency [122]. The 1 mcg cosyntropin test is not recommended for diag nosis of suspected primary adrenal insuffi ciency [104].

### 10.4.3 Insulin-Induced

### Hypoglycemia

The response to hypoglycemia (blood glucose <40 mg/dL) requires the integrity of the entire HPA axis. After an overnight fast, 0.10–0.15 U/

kg of regular insulin is administered intrave nously. Blood glucose and cortisol are mea sured prior to and then 15, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90, and 120 min following insulin injection. Patients will experience some degree of dis comfort during the hypoglycemic phase of this test due to neuroglycopenia and the con sequences of catecholamine release, such as tachycardia, diaphoresis, anxiety, and tremu lousness. A plasma cortisol of above 20 mcg/ dL is considered a normal response [106, 123]. This test should be avoided in patients with a history of seizures or significant cardiovascular disease, and dextrose for intravenous rescue should be immediately accessible in the event of sustained severe hypoglycemia or a seizure.

### 10.4.4 Corticotropin-Releasing

### Hormone Stimulation Test

To directly assess corticotroph function, ovine corticotropin-releasing hormone can be administered intravenously at a dose of 1 mcg/kg or 100 mcg followed by the measure ment of plasma ACTH and cortisol levels over the next 2 h [124–126]. Flushing occurs in some patients after administration. Peripheral CRH administration provides a less robust stimulus for ACTH release than hypoglyce mia, and the normal range has been less well established. However, studies directly com paring the responses to CRH and insulininduced hypoglycemia have demonstrated good concordance in defining adrenal status. In normal subjects, plasma ACTH peaks rap idly (15–30 min) following administration and remains at an elevated level. Cortisol peaks slightly later, at 30–60 min following injection, and also persists at an elevated level for 2 h. In patients with hypothalamic lesions, an exag gerated ACTH response is often obtained with an even longer prolongation in the dura tion of elevation. In contrast, patients with pituitary lesions do not respond to CRH administration with increases in either ACTH or cortisol. CRH is no longer available for use in humans.

### 10.4.5 Glucagon Stimulation Test

The glucagon stimulation test provides an alternative to insulin-induced hypoglycemia in evaluating central adrenal insufficiency as it requires endogenous ACTH secretion to cause cortisol release [127, 128]. While gluca gon doses of 0.03 mg/kg have been routinely used as a provocative test for growth hormone assessment, studies evaluating adrenal func tion have employed somewhat higher doses (0.1 mg/kg IM; maximum 1.0 mg in children; in adult studies 1.0 mg if <90 kg and 1.5 mg if >90 kg) [129–131]. After an overnight fast, plasma is obtained at baseline, then 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, and 180 min following injection. A normal response is achieved if peak cortisol exceeds 20 mcg/dL.

### 10.4.6 Metyrapone Test

Metyrapone inhibits the activity of the enzyme 11-beta-hydroxylase, blocking the conversion of 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol. Thus, cortisol is unable to provide negative feedback at the central nervous system and pituitary sites increasing ACTH secretion. The increased plasma ACTH concentration stimulates increased production of 11-deoxycortisol and its urinary metabolites. Two general forms of the metyrapone test have been standardized: an overnight, singledose test [132] and a multiple-dose form [80]. Because of convenience, the single-dose test is more commonly performed. For the singledose test, 30 mg/kg to a maximum of 3.0 g is given at midnight with a snack to decrease the nausea associated with metyrapone ingestion. Cortisol, 11-deoxycortisol, and ACTH are measured at 8 am following the dose. A nor mal response is the increase in plasma 11-deoxycortisol to more the 7 mcg/dL [133]. Cortisol levels above 5 mcg/dL imply inade quate suppression of enzyme activity such that low 11-deoxycortisol levels cannot be taken as an index of inadequate hypothalamic or pituitary function.

### 10.4.7 Radiological Tests

In general, imaging studies should be utilized after the diagnosis of adrenal insufficiency is established by biochemical methods. The obvious exception to this rule is the patient presenting with symptoms suggesting an intracranial mass lesion. The resolution of magnetic resonance imaging of the hypothal amus and pituitary in general exceeds that of computed tomography [134] and is the initial imaging study of choice for the evaluation of documented central adrenal insufficiency. If a mass is found, computed tomography may be performed to establish whether the tumor has calcifications characteristic of a craniopha ryngioma.

In patients with primary adrenal insuffi ciency with positive adrenal autoantibodies or elevated VLCFA, establishing autoimmune adrenalitis or X-ALD as the etiology, respec tively, adrenal imaging is not required. If these entities are not established as the diagnosis, CT or MRI of the adrenal should be per formed [135–138]. Observation of calcifica tions in an older child is suggestive of tuberculosis or other granulomatous disease, while in an infant, the diagnosis of Wolman disease should also be entertained. In a lim ited number of cases, CT-assisted needle biopsy for pathological diagnosis may be required.

### 10.4.8 Diagnosing Adrenal

### Insufficiency in Critical Illness

During critical illness, activation of the HPA axis is essential for survival. Individuals with known primary or central adrenal insuffi ciency require additional steroids during criti cal illness. Since the early 2000s, there have been many studies published on adrenal func tion in the intensive care setting in patients not previously diagnosed with adrenal insuf ficiency. Patients in the ICU with unrecog nized adrenal insufficiency may experience


## PDF page 291 | printed page 278

treatment-resistant hypotension, prolonged ventilation, and increased mortality [139]. However, how to diagnose patients in the ICU with adrenal insufficiency remains highly con troversial. Intensivists in the early 2000s often diagnosed relative adrenal insufficiency if the rise in cortisol 30 or 60 min after administer ing 0.5–250 mcg of cosyntropin intravenously was less than 9 mcg/dL [140–144]. Still others use a baseline cortisol of less than 7 mcg/dL [142, 145, 146] or a stimulated cortisol of <18 mcg/dL [142, 147] in response to low-dose cosyntropin as evidence of adrenal insuffi ciency [144]. However, there are many factors that affect our ability to diagnose adrenal insufficiency in the setting of critical illness, and more recently, these are not considered appropriate diagnostic tests in the setting of critical illness [148]. During critical illness inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-α, the autonomic nervous system, and factors in the innate immunity response such as Toll-like receptors and macrophage inhibitory factor (MIF) have either been shown or postulated to play a significant role in the HPA axis response to stress [149]. Alterations in these confounding factors as well as polymorphisms in individual genes likely contribute to variations in the normal HPA axis response to each stressor. Second, it has recently been recognized that the HPA axis response to acute critical illness differs from its response to prolonged critical illness. Third, in critical illness, transcortin and albu min levels may decrease depending on the exact illness. Since more than 90% of cortisol is bound to transcortin and albumin, this change may affect the validity of measuring total cortisol, especially when albumin levels are also low. Ideally, free cortisol levels would be measured to determine the HPA axis sta tus, but these assays are not easily available. Fourth, the most readily available cortisol assay used is the immunoassay, which exhibits nonuniformity that may increase in the setting of critical illness. Lastly, in critical illness, cor tisol metabolism is reduced by suppressed expression and activation of renal 1-beta

hydrosteroid dehydrogenase 2 [148]. Thus, adrenal insufficiency in the setting of a critical illness is difficult to diagnose, but should be considered and the patient treated appropri ately when warranted by the clinical scenario.

### 10.4.9 Diagnosing Adrenal

### Insufficiency in Neonates

It has been increasingly recognized that criti cally ill neonates may have relative adrenal insufficiency [147]. Steroidogenic activity has been detected in fetal adrenal glands by 50–52 days postconception with a peak in cor tisol production at 8–9 weeks gestation and undetectable levels by 14 weeks gestation. Due to lack of 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydroge nase activity between 14 and 23 weeks and suppression from maternal cortisol in early gestation, very little fetal cortisol is produced between 14 and 30 weeks gestation [49]. Later in gestation, the placenta begins to express 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase 2, which inactivates maternal cortisol, allowing the fetal adrenal to take over cortisol production. In the infant born preterm, this immaturity of the HPA axis may lead to relative adrenal insufficiency during stress. Several studies have demonstrated that preterm infants with hypotension have lower baseline and stimu lated cortisol [150–153]. Critically ill term neonates may also be at risk for relative adre nal insufficiency for the same reasons. However, they may also be at risk because of hormonal shifts during the transition from fetal to extrauterine life. As the placenta matures, it produces more and more CRH that drives the fetal adrenal. Unlike hypotha lamic CRH, placental CRH is stimulated by cortisol. At birth, the placental CRH is sud denly withdrawn. During the transition, the hypothalamus and pituitary may be tran siently suppressed, leading to relative adrenal insufficiency during critical illness. Further studies in neonates are necessary before glu cocorticoid treatment of critically ill neonates can be recommended as a standard of care.

If gluco corticoids are used, a cortisol level should be drawn prior to initiating therapy. If treatment is initiated, the length of treatment should be minimized as much as possible.

### 10.5 Outcomes and Possible

### Complications

Children with adrenal insufficiency in general lead normal lives. However, glucocorticoid deficiency places them at increased risk for usual illnesses becoming life-threatening. If appropriate stress steroid coverage is not given during an illness, these children have the potential of dying. Therefore, for both the child and the entire family, reinforcement of stress steroid administration during illness is essential. If oral intake of medications and salt is not possible due to gastrointestinal dis ease or mental status changes, further instruc tion for emergency assistance is important. All children with adrenal insufficiency should be provided with a medical alert bracelet stat ing their diagnosis to facilitate urgent therapy if required. Other factors affecting quality of life are determined by the etiology of adrenal failure.

### 10.5.1 Polyglandular Autoimmune

### Syndromes

Children with adrenal insufficiency in the con text of one of the polyglandular autoimmune syndromes must contend with other endocri nopathies, or the anticipation of developing other endocrinopathies. Often, complicated, multidrug therapeutic regimens develop with significant financial and emotional costs to the families. The development of type 1 diabe tes mellitus, especially, places added demands on daily life. Additionally, enamel hypoplasia, nail dystrophy, vitiligo, and alopecia may be considered disfiguring by the patients with these disorders.

### 10.5.2 Central Adrenal Insufficiency

Secondary or tertiary adrenal insufficiency may be associated with insufficiency of other pituitary hormones. Similar to patients with polyglandular autoimmune syndromes, multihormone deficiency states are common and require frequent medication administration and dosage adjustment. Long-term issues with decreased fertility and excessive weight gain due to hypothalamic damage pose the most challenging concerns.

### 10.5.3 Congenital Adrenal

### Hyperplasia

Determining the etiology of ambiguous geni talia is an endocrine emergency. Sex assign ment of a newborn has obvious long-term implications, with optimization of adult sexual and emotional function being the primary goal. The timing for sex assignment and recon structive surgery remains controversial [107]. Members of the Accord Alliance propose that no reconstructive genital surgery should be performed on children before they are old enough to consent. In general though, 46, XX patients with CAH, if treated adequately, may be as fertile as adult females. Therefore, the recommendation that 46, XX patients with CAH be raised as females, with prompt recon structive surgery if needed, had been the stan dard of care. If a female infant is severely virilized (Prader score >3), it is suggested in Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guidelines that clitoral and perineal surgery during infancy by an experienced team be considered [107]. Further, for infants with a low vaginal confluence, it is recommended that a complete repair be done during infancy. However, more long-term outcome studies are necessary to make firm recommendations for surgical repair. Management of all forms of genital ambiguity benefits from a multidisciplinary approach with input from experienced endo crinologists, surgeons, geneticists, and psychol ogists, allowing the formulation of a consistent long-term plan for the child and family.

### 10.5.4 Adrenoleukodystrophy

The phenotype of X-ALD is variable with at least seven clinical subtypes: childhood cere bral ALD, adolescent ALD, adult cerebral ALD, adrenomyeloneuropathy, Addison dis ease only, and asymptomatic and heterozy gote women. All of these subtypes can be present within the same family [102]. In 6–8% of cases, Addison’s disease is the only mani festation of ALD. Any male sibling of an affected patient has a 50% chance of also being affected. Therefore, all male siblings should be screened and, if positive, evaluated for adrenal insufficiency. Any female sibling of a patient has a 50% chance of being a car rier. Screening should be offered to any female siblings to evaluate the risk of disease to their children as well as the risk of adult-onset myelopathy in the female carriers [154]. The major psychosocial consideration in this dis ease is the anticipation of progressive neuro logical deterioration, with limited interventions of proven efficacy.

### 10.5.5 Triple A Syndrome

Triple A Syndrome (TAS) was first identified by Dr. Allgrove in 1978. It is a rare genetic disease caused by mutations in the AAAS gene, which encodes the WD-repeatcontaining protein, ALADIN. It is one of the nucleoporins forming the nuclear pore com plex, but its exact function is unclear. Presentation is heterogenous but the most common symptoms seen include alacrimia, esophageal achalasia, adrenal insufficiency, and neurological disease. Alacrimia, which is present in more than 90% of people with TAS, is usually the first sign, but the diagnosis is not usually made until the patient has symptoms of adrenal insufficiency. TAS is thought to be progressive and neurological symptoms may develop over time. Alacramia is likely due to autonomic dysfunction of the lacrimal glands. Achalasia is found in 75–93% of people with TAS and usually presents in childhood. Achalasia may present with vomiting, weight loss, difficulty swallowing, and chronic cough.

Anyone presenting with alacrimia and/or achalasia should have adrenal function evalu ated. Adrenal insufficiency also usually pres ents within the first decade of life. Neurological symptoms are much more variable and although it has been reported in individuals as young as 2 years of age, it usually presents after the other signs. The autonomic system is most commonly affected with such signs as postural hypotension, heart rate instability, sweating, impotence, neurogenic bladder, ataxia, dysarthria, distal motor and sensory neuropathy, disorders of movement, and intellectual disability. Dysfunction of the pupillary muscles and hyperreflexia may also be present [66, 155].

### 10.6 Treatment

### 10.6.1 Primary Adrenal Failure

### 10.6.1.1 Chronic Replacement

Since the bioavailability of oral steroids is poor and varies from individual to individual, the recommended dose for replacement hydrocortisone therapy is a starting guide [156, 157]. For adults, consensus guidelines suggest 15–25 mg of hydrocortisone in 2–3 divided doses per day, with the highest dose given in the morning upon awakening and a lower dose later in the day. For children, the consensus guidelines recommend a total daily dose of 8 mg/M2 body surface area of hydro cortisone in 3–4 divided doses ( Box 10.2) [104]. It has been shown that twice-daily hydrocortisone produces a nonphysiological low cortisol level 2–4 h prior to the next dose [158, 159]. Therefore, younger children, who are more prone to hypoglycemia when cortisol levels are low, or children with CAH, where efficient suppression of adrenal androgens is required, should receive hydrocortisone divided three to four times per day. Although steroids other than hydrocortisone may be used, hydrocortisone is preferred in children since it has less growth suppressive effects than synthetic steroids [107, 160–162]. Hydrocortisone tablets and liquid suspension


## PDF page 294 | printed page 281

are not equivalent. Hydrocortisone drug is unevenly distributed in the suspension and is not recommended for use in children [107, 163].

Patients with primary adrenal insufficiency often do not produce adequate aldosterone. Although hydrocortisone has some mineralo corticoid activity, physiologic doses do not usually provide enough mineralocorticoid activity to prevent salt wasting in children with primary adrenal insufficiency. Thus, chil dren with mineralocorticoid deficiency are also treated with 0.05–0.2 mg/day of fludro cortisone. Since the aldosterone secretion rate after the first week of life does not increase from infancy to adulthood, mineralocorticoid doses do not vary significantly with body size [164]. Because infant formulas are low in salt, infants up to 1 year of age should be treated with 1–4 g/day of NaCl supplementation [165]. Older children and adults usually have enough salt in their diet without additional salt supplementation to maintain normal elec trolytes with the use of fludrocortisone.

It is important that treatment adequacy be monitored on a regular basis. Growth veloc ity, weight gain, blood pressure, serum elec trolytes, and plasma renin activity are the most useful tests every 3–6 months. Hyperpigmentation in non-sun-exposed areas is also an important sign that indicates inade quate therapy. Some physicians also like to monitor ACTH levels and to maintain these in the high normal to mildly elevated range. Special considerations for children with CAH are discussed below.

### 10.6.2 Central Adrenal Failure

ACTH or CRH deficiency is treated in much the same as primary adrenal insufficiency. The major difference is that while these patients do not require mineralocorticoid replacement, they do require evaluation for deficiency of other pituitary hormones. In addition, when first diagnosed, a head MRI, with special attention to views of the pituitary and hypothalamus, should be performed to look for a tumor or other anomalies.

### 10.6.3 Special Considerations

### for Virilizing Forms of CAH

### 10.6.3.1 Standard Therapy

Treatment of all forms of classical CAH con sists of replacement and, when indicated, stress doses of cortisol. Treatment of viriliz ing forms of CAH requires more than replace ment doses of hydrocortisone to prevent further virilization and rapid fusion of the growth plates. The dose required varies from individual to individual but averages 10–20 mg/M2/day divided three times per day [48, 107, 177, 178]. When the dose exceeds 20 mg/M2/day in infants and 15–17 mg/M2/ day in pubertal patients, there is evidence that final adult height is compromised [107, 179–182]. There has been controversy as to whether it is better to give a larger dose of hydrocortisone in the morning to mimic the normal diurnal rise in cortisol, or to give a larger dose in the evening to suppress the diur


## PDF page 296 | printed page 283

nal rise of ACTH. Recent data demonstrate that there is no difference in disease control or well-being of the patient [183]. Stress dosing (triple usual dose) is recommended for febrile illness (>38.5 °C), gastroenteritis with dehy dration, surgery with general anesthesia, or major trauma. However, it is not recom mended for mental and emotional stress, minor trauma, or exercise [107, 184].

Patients with CAH, with or without salt wasting, may benefit from mineralocorticoid therapy. In the salt-losing forms of CAH with elevation in plasma renin activity, the addition of fludrocortisone at 0.05–0.2 mg/day is required. In patients with mildly elevated plasma renin activity without overt salt wast ing, the addition of fludrocortisone often helps to suppress excess adrenal androgen production. Depending on the degree of enzyme deficiency, children with CAH may also have aldosterone deficiency or increased levels of antagonists of aldosterone action [185, 186]. Aldosterone deficiency causes hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, and volume depletion. Hyponatremia and volume deple tion lead to increased renin and angiotensin II. Angiotensin II not only stimulates aldoste rone secretion directly at the level of the adre nal cortex; it also stimulates ACTH secretion [187–189]. Therefore, by suppressing plasma renin activity with the use of fludrocortisone, patients may require a lower dose of glucocor ticoid. It is recommended that all neonates and infants with classical CAH regardless of salt-wasting status should be given fludrocor tisone and salt supplementation [107]. Infants with CAH require approximately 1–4 g/day of salt added to their formula or as supplementa tion to breastfeeding [165].

Follow-up evaluation should occur every 2–4 months to monitor electrolytes, plasma renin activity, growth velocity, blood pressure, 17-hydroxyprogesterone, and androstenedi one. Suppression of 17-hydroxyprogesterone and androstenedione into the normal range may compromise growth [190, 191]. In any patient where normal levels of these precur sors suppress growth, steroid doses should be reduced to maintain levels in the slightly ele vated range [107]. In patients with elevated blood pressure and/or suppressed plasma

renin activity, a reduction in the fludrocorti sone dose should be considered. Bone age should be monitored yearly to ensure that skeletal maturation is not advancing faster than the chronological age.

### 10.6.4 Newer Therapies

### 10.6.4.1 CAH

A major shortcoming in the therapy of CAH is compromised final adult height [192–194]. Inadequate suppression of 17-hydroxyprogesterone leads to relative advancement of bone age and ultimately short stature. Too much glucocorticoid also results in the suppression of growth. Bilateral adre nalectomy reduces the risk of virilization and allows the use of lower doses of steroids. However, this treatment is controversial because of the added risk of surgery, possible increased risk of adrenal crisis, and possible loss of other adrenal hormones (epinephrine, DHEA). Ideal therapy for CAH would be more physiological replacement of cortisol.

Current approved therapies for the treat ment of adrenal insufficiency do not mimic the normal circadian rhythm of endogenous cortisol. In addition, giving hydrocortisone three times per day is inconvenient and may result in missed doses. Researchers and phar maceutical companies have been trying to improve treatment of patients with adrenal insufficiency. There are currently several orphan drugs that are approved by the FDA and/or EMA for use to treat adrenal insuffi ciency in adults and one to use in children [195–197].

Plenadren or Duocort is a once-daily hydrocortisone modified-release tablet (OD) approved for use in the European Union but not in the United States. It is designed to be taken once a day in the morning. It has an outer coating that supplies a high concentra tion of hydrocortisone in the morning and an extended-release core for continuous release throughout the day. It comes in 5 mg and 20 mg doses. The immediate-release form of the drug gives physiological cortisol levels within 20 min of ingestion. The extended-

release form of the drug decreases the expo sure to steroids over a 24-h period compared to thrice-daily hydrocortisone. The safety pro file is similar to thrice-daily hydrocortisone. During times of mild-to-moderate stress, the drug should be given every 8 h. In a study of 64 patients, the patients on OD hydrocorti sone demonstrated lower body weight and blood pressure compared to the subjects on three times daily immediate-release hydrocor tisone. In patients with concomitant diabetes mellitus, there was an improvement in HbA1c after 12 weeks of treatment with OD hydro cortisone. In addition, QoL improved in sub jects at 12 weeks of therapy on the OD hydrocortisone [195].

Chronocort or Efmody is another hydro cortisone modified-release tablet (MR-HC) approved for use in the European Union but not in the United States. The MR-HC is a bilayer tablet consisting of an insoluble coat ing that covers all but one face of the pill. The unprotected face has a layer which slowly erodes to release the sustained release hydro cortisone resulting in a delayed and extended release of hydrocortisone. When given at 10 PM once daily, the peak cortisol level occurs at 6 AM the next day. In a small study of adults with congenital adrenal hyperplasia, twice-daily MR-HC, given at 7 AM and 11 PM, resulted in a peak cortisol at 7 AM and reduced androgens [196, 197].

### 10.7 Summary

3. Symptoms of primary adrenal insuffi

In summary, adrenal insufficiency is a rare disorder. It is vital, however, to consider it in the diagnostic differential of an appropriate patient, as left untreated it is often a fatal dis ease. Symptoms of adrenal insufficiency may include hypotension, hyponatremia, hypogly cemia, abdominal pain/vomiting, and/or hyperpigmentation. Treatment includes replacement steroids plus or minus mineralo corticoids and salt supplements in infants. During times of stress, patients with adrenal insufficiency need extra steroids. In males with primary adrenal insufficiency, it is critical to screen for X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy. Any patient with primary adrenal insuffi ciency of autoimmune etiology should be screened for other autoimmune diseases. Growth and development need to be closely monitored in these patients to ensure proper dosing of medication.

paragraphs.text: The congenital adrenal hyperplasias (CAH) are a group of autosomal recessive disorders associated with decreased function of the enzymes necessary for cortisol synthesis [1]. Abnormalities in each of the steroidogenic enzymes have been described. Decreased enzyme activity impairs cortisol synthesis with subsequent increased ACTH secretion due to loss of negative feedback inhibition. This results in overproduction of the hor mone precursors proximal to the faulty enzyme and deficiencies of the hormones dis tal to the aberrant enzyme [2]. In addition to adrenocortical expression, several steroido genic enzymes are also expressed in the gonads where they are involved in sex steroid biosyn thesis and, hence, associated with sex steroid hormone deficiencies.
paragraphs.heading: 11.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: The specific clinical and hormonal fea tures depend upon the particular genetic vari ant and the consequences of decreased enzyme activity, specifically which hormones are overproduced, and which are deficient. The virilizing forms of CAH present with
paragraphs.heading: 11.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: symptoms ranging from virilization of an affected female infant, premature virilization in boys and girls, or signs of androgen excess in adolescent and young adult women. Genetic variants involved in gonadal sex ste roid synthesis may present with atypical geni tal development and delayed puberty.
paragraphs.heading: 11.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: In the past, the terms “sex” and “gender” have been used interchangeably. However, these terms refer to different concepts. “Sex” refers to aspects of sexual development biol ogy, which can be subcategorized into karyo type, gonadal, hormonal, and anatomic categories. In contrast, “gender” refers to one’s psychological sense of self that only the individual can appreciate. For most individu als, biological sex and gender identity are con gruent. That some individuals experience incongruity between their biological sex and gender identity is increasingly recognized. Awareness regarding nonbinary gender iden tities has increased.
paragraphs.heading: 11.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: provides an overview of all of the enzymatic deficiencies resulting in CAH, initially focus ing on 21-hydroxylase deficiency, which is the most common, first described, and most stud ied of the enzymatic disorders.
paragraphs.heading: 11.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: The adrenal cortex consists of three distinct concentric zones with each zone primarily responsible for the synthesis of specific adre nocortical hormones. The outer zone, the zona glomerulosa, synthesizes mineralocorti coids and is principally regulated by the reninangiotensin pathway and serum potassium concentrations. The middle zone, the zona fasciculata, synthesizes cortisol and is regu lated by pituitary adrenocorticotrophin (ACTH) secretion. The inner zone, the zona reticularis, secretes C19 steroids including DHEA, DHEAS, and androstenedione, which are collectively labeled as the “adrenal androgens.”
paragraphs.heading: 11.2 Adrenal Steroidogenesis

paragraphs.text: The hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis is an essential neurohormonal sys tem that regulates cortisol concentrations within the physiologic range to maintain homeostasis for daily activities and in response to internal and external stressors. ACTH and cortisol manifest diurnal variation with the highest concentrations in the early morning. Acutely, ACTH stimulates cortisol secretion. Tonic ACTH secretion promotes transcrip tion and translation of the adrenal steroido genic enzymes in all three zones of the adrenal cortex. Through negative feedback inhibition of ACTH secretion, the HPA axis governs cortisol secretion.
paragraphs.heading: 11.2 Adrenal Steroidogenesis

paragraphs.text: Within the hypothalamus, the parvocellu lar neurons of the paraventricular nucleus (PVN) send projections to the median emi nence where they secrete corticotropinreleasing hormone (CRH) and arginine vasopressin (AVP) to regulate ACTH secre tion [3]. In the setting of stress, increases in

pro-inflammatory cytokines such as interleu kin (IL)-1 and IL-6 stimulate increased CRH secretion, leading to increased cortisol secre tion [4]. These factors also act directly on the adrenal cortex to increase cortisol secretion [5].

Acting via the ACTH receptor, the Gα-protein-coupled ACTH receptor (MC2R), ACTH stimulates cortisol secretion. Due to its lipophilic nature, cortisol is not prestored in vesicles and must be rapidly synthesized following ACTH stimulation [6]. Hence, unlike other endocrine tissues, such as the thy roid gland, the adrenal cortex does not store cortisol. Aldosterone secretion is primarily regulated by serum potassium concentrations and the renin-angiotensin system with angio tensin II acting through the Gq-proteincoupled angiotensin 2 receptor [7]. ACTH also contributes to aldosterone secretion.

An anonymous case report published in the Lancet in 1833 is likely the earliest description of a person conjectured to be an XX individ ual with simple virilizing CAH [11]. Luigi de Crecchio published the first detailed case report regarding CAH in 1865 [12]. He described an individual baptized as a girl who transitioned to a boy at age 4 years. This patient lived as a man and likely died second ary to an acute adrenal crisis. In the 1950s, Jayle and colleagues described women with nonclassic 21-hydroxylase deficiency [13].
paragraphs.heading: 11.3.1 21-Hydroxylase Deficiency

paragraphs.text: The most common form of CAH is 21-Hydroxylase deficiency, which accounts for approximately 95% of affected individuals [14]. Reported worldwide frequency is approxi mately 1:14,000 to 1:18,000 liveborn infants based on newborn screening. The frequency is higher among certain ethnic groups [15]. In this autosomal recessive disorder, deficient 21-hydroxylase activity leads to decreased cor tisol secretion, subsequent increased ACTH, and overproduction of steroids before the 21-hydroxylation step. Specifically, the decreased 21-hydroxylase activity decreases the conversion of progesterone and 17-hydroxy progesterone (17OHP) to deoxycorticosterone (DOC) and 11-deoxycortisol (S), respectively.
paragraphs.heading: 11.3.1 21-Hydroxylase Deficiency

paragraphs.text: Although CAH due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency reflects a spectrum of enzyme dys function, three categories have been arbi trarily defined: salt-losing, simple virilizing, and nonclassic. Affected XX infants with saltlosing and simple virilizing forms typically present with virilization of the external geni tal structures; normally developed ovaries, uterus, cervix, and Fallopian tubes are pres ent. Aldosterone synthesis in the zona glo merulosa is usually 100–1000 times less than cortisol synthesis; hence, the most dysfunc tional enzyme variants are associated with salt-losing CAH, whereas milder variants are associated with simple virilizing or nonclassic forms [16].

Virilized XX individuals often have a vagina that opens into a common urogenital sinus with enlarged clitoris and single perineal opening. Affected XY infants show normal external genital development but may mani fest hyperpigmentation of their genitalia. Infants with mineralocorticoid deficiency dis play poor weight gain, hyponatremia, hyper kalemia, and acidosis beginning around 5 days of age. The advent of nearly universal newborn screening programs has greatly decreased the number of affected infants pre senting with adrenal insufficiency during the first few weeks of life.

The diagnosis of 21-hydroxylase defi ciency should be considered when evaluat ing an infant with atypical genital appearance and nonpalpable gonads. Elevated 17OHP concentrations, the sub strate for 21-hydroxylase, are found in patients with CAH due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency. Individuals with simple viriliz ing CAH may present with premature pubarche, tall stature, accelerated linear growth velocity, and advanced skeletal mat uration. The mildest form, nonclassic CAH, typically presents in adolescent and young adult women with irregular menses, hirsut ism, acne, and subfertility.

This form of CAH is due to mutations in the 21-hydroxylase gene (CYP21A2), which is located at chromosome 6p21.3, in a complex genetic locus within the major histocompati bility complex (MHC) class III region [17]. The functional gene lies in close proximity (~30 kb) to a nonfunctional highly homolo gous pseudogene (CYP21A1P). These genes are arranged in tandem with the genes for the fourth component of complement, C4A and C4B. On the telomeric side, the C4/CYP21 unit is flanked by the serine-threonine kinase-19 (STK19) gene. The tenascin-X gene (TNXB) is located on the centromeric side; this gene encodes an extracellular matrix pro tein on the opposite DNA strand [18]. Detailed discussion regarding this locus and CYP21A2 expression is beyond the scope of this chapter [1, 19].
To date, over 200 CYP21A2 variants have been described; variants are listed in the

Human Gene Mutation Database (HGMD, http://www.hgmd.cf.ac.uk) and the Pharmacogene Variation Consortium ( https://www.phar mvar.org/gene/ CYP21A2). Approximately, ten singlenucleotide variants derived from the pseudo gene account for over 90% of cases. Variants have been categorized according to their con sequences on protein function. Deletions, large gene conversions, nonsense mutations, frameshift mutations, and missense variants that abolish enzyme activity are typically associated with salt-losing forms. Some mis sense variants significantly reduce but do not abolish enzyme activity. One common variant is a single-nucleotide variant located in intron 2 that alters the splice site acceptor for exon 3; this variant is associated with both salt-losing and simple virilizing forms. Missense variants that reduce enzyme activity by 30–50% are usually associated with nonclassic CAH. The estimated prevalence of nonclassic CAH is 1 in 200 in the USA [20]. Reported carrier prevalence rates in Europe are 4.0–7.5% [21, 22]. Most affected individuals are compound heterozygotes with different deleterious vari ants located on each allele. An individual’s phenotype typically corresponds to the milder variant.

Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS) is charac terized by joint hypermobility, skin hyperex tensibility, and tissue fragility. Typically, EDS is an autosomal dominant disorder associated with variants in collagen-associated genes. One type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is asso ciated with tenascin X deficiency and variants in the tenascin B (TNXB) gene. When this autosomal recessive EDS is associated with a CYP21A2 deletion extending into the TNXB gene, it is labeled “CAH-X” and represents a contiguous gene deletion disorder. Approximately 10–12% of patients with CAH have CAH-X [23–25]. In addition to the usual features associated with CAH, clinical fea tures of CAH-X include generalized joint hypermobility, subluxation, and chronic arthralgia; cardiac valve abnormalities are identified in roughly 25%.

In the mid-1970s, a microfilter paper method with dried blood spots to measure 17-OHP by immunoassay was developed to screen for 21-hydroxylase deficiency [26]. Now, 50 years later, newborn screening for 21-hydroxylase is mandatory in all 50 states and is performed in many countries [27]. The primary goal of newborn screening is the detection of infants with classic CAH, particularly male infants who have normal external genitalia, to pre vent adrenal crises and deaths. Additional benefits of screening include less severe hypo natremia, shorter hospitalizations, and earlier recognition of virilized affected XX infants [28, 29].
paragraphs.heading: for 21-Hydroxylase Deficiency

paragraphs.text: For the initial screen, an automated timeresolved dissociation-enhanced lanthanide fluoroimmunoassay (DELFIA) without ste roid extraction is generally used to measure 17OHP. Subsequently, using the screening lab’s testing paradigm, a second-tier test is performed as recommended by the 2018 Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guidelines [30]. The second tier may involve a steroid extraction phase or the use of LC/MS-MS methodology. Most screening labs use gesta tional age and birth weight to establish spe cific cut points. Immunoassays for 17-OHP determination continue to be used due to low cost, sensitivity, and technical ease.
paragraphs.heading: for 21-Hydroxylase Deficiency

paragraphs.text: Both false-positive and false-negative screening results occur [31]. To limit the num ber of false-positive cases, cut points have been established such that individuals with nonclassic CAH are not typically identified by newborn screening. False-positive results occur in preterm infants, infants heterozygous for CYP21A2 variants, stressed infants, and infants with other steroidogenic enzyme defi ciencies [32]. False-negative screening results have been reported [33, 34]. The effects of multiple courses of antenatal steroids are apparently inconsistent and may be associ ated with false-negative results [35, 36]. Specific testing for 21-hydroxylase deficiency
paragraphs.heading: for 21-Hydroxylase Deficiency

paragraphs.text: should be performed in suspicious clinical sce narios, even if screening results were reported to be negative.
paragraphs.heading: for 21-Hydroxylase Deficiency

paragraphs.text: Second-tier testing with LC-MS/MS avoids the concerns of cross-reactivity associ ated with immunoassays. Screening for 21-deoxycortisol in 21-hydroxylase deficiency may improve diagnostic specificity because of its specificity for 21-hydroxylase deficiency; 21-deoxycortisol concentrations are not ele vated in preterm infants [37].
paragraphs.heading: for 21-Hydroxylase Deficiency

paragraphs.text: Congenital lipoid adrenal hyperplasia is due to loss-of-function variants in the steroidogenic acute regulatory protein (StAR) gene located at chromosome 8p11.2. The StAR protein is a mitochondrial protein that facilitates choles terol transport from the outer to the inner mitochondrial membrane. In this form of CAH, synthesis of all adrenal and gonadal ste roids is impaired resulting in glucocorticoid, mineralocorticoid, and sex steroid deficiencies [38]. Decreased StAR protein activity results in the accumulation of cholesterol esters and sterol auto-oxidation products in the cytosol of the adrenal and gonadal steroidogenic cells, ultimately damaging the cell and disrupting StAR-independent basal steroidogenesis.
paragraphs.heading: 11.3.2 Lipoid Adrenal Hyperplasia

paragraphs.text: Affected infants typically present early in life with cardiovascular collapse, hyponatre mia, and hyperkalemia due to mineralocorti coid and glucocorticoid deficiencies. Since this enzyme is necessary for gonadal sex hor mone synthesis, in utero testosterone synthe sis is impaired leading to undervirilization of male fetuses. At birth, XY infants present with atypical external genitalia; labial masses may be palpable. External genital develop ment appears female in affected XX infants. Importantly, internal and external female genital structures are normal in affected XX individuals. Affected XX individuals may have sufficient gonadal function at puberty to feminize and experience menarche as individ ual follicles are stimulated and recruited [39]. However, over time, cholesterol esters accu
mulate in ovarian steroidogenic cells causing cell damage and, ultimately, premature ovar ian insufficiency (POI) [40, 41].

Congenital lipoid adrenal hyperplasia is more common in Korea and other countries in Eastern Asia which is attributed to a founder effect with a specific variant, Gln258* [42]. Individuals with nonclassic lipoid adre nal hyperplasia may present with adrenal insufficiency [43]. Laboratory evaluation in patients with lipoid adrenal hyperplasia reveals low levels of all steroid hormones with no response to ACTH or human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) stimulation. ACTH and plasma renin activity (PRA) are very elevated. Adrenal sonography typically reveals mas sively enlarged adrenal glands due to choles terol ester accumulation. However, adrenal enlargement can also be found in patients with cholesterol side-change cleavage enzyme deficiency due to CYP11A1 variants [44]. Congenital lipoid adrenal hyperplasia also needs to be distinguished from familial gluco corticoid deficiency, which is due to ACTH receptor (MC2R) mutations and from P450 oxidoreductase deficiency [45].

Cholesterol side-chain cleavage deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder due to lossof-function variants in the CYP11A1 gene located at chromosome 15q23-q24. This enzyme converts cholesterol to pregnenolone by performing three serial reactions including 20-hydroxylation, 22-hydroxylation, and scis sion of the C20–C22 bond. This enzyme is essential for adrenal and gonadal steroid syn thesis. Initially, this enzyme deficiency was believed to be incompatible with life due to the importance of fetal placental progester one synthesis. However, biallelic mutations are compatible with survival to term.
paragraphs.heading: Cleavage Deficiency

paragraphs.text: Affected individuals typically present in the newborn period with hyperkalemia, hypo natremia, and hypotension. Due to impaired testosterone biosynthesis, infant males are
paragraphs.heading: Cleavage Deficiency

paragraphs.text: undervirilized. Individuals with milder or nonclassic CYP11A1 variants have been described [46]. CYP11A1 variants have been reported among patients diagnosed with pri mary adrenal insufficiency [47].
paragraphs.heading: Cleavage Deficiency

paragraphs.text: Following the conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone, the enzyme 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase converts pregnenolone to pro gesterone. Two isomers exist, type 1 and type 2. The type 1 isomer is expressed in the pla centa, brain, and liver. The 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2, encoded by HSD3B2, is expressed in the adrenal cortex and the gonads where it converts the Δ5 steroids (preg nenolone, 17-hydroxypregnenolone, DHEA, and androstenediol) to the corresponding Δ4 steroids (progesterone, 17OHP, androstenedi one, and testosterone). The genes encoding both enzymes are mapped to chromosome 1p13. Loss-of-function variants in HSD3B2 are characterized by glucocorticoid, miner alocorticoid, and sex steroid deficiencies [48]. Affected XY infants are typically underviril ized, whereas XX infants may exhibit mild virilization attributed to excessive in utero androgen exposure [49].
paragraphs.heading: Dehydrogenase Deficiency

paragraphs.text: The 17-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase enzyme, encoded by a single gene, CYP17A1, catalyzes two distinct steroidogenic steps. The 17-hydroxylase activity converts pregneno lone to 17-hydroxypregnenolone and proges terone to 17-OHP. The other enzyme activity, 17,20-lyase, which is limited to the zona retic ularis, converts 17-hydroxypregnenolone to DHEA. In the zona reticularis, factors influ encing 17,20-lyase activity include P450 oxi doreductase and cytochrome b5. In human, 17-OHP is poorly converted to androstenedi one under usual circumstances.
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency

paragraphs.text: Deleterious variants in this gene, mapped to chromosome 10q24.3, are associated with glucocorticoid and sex steroid defi ciencies. Geographic localization of some variants presumably reflects ancestral founder variants [50, 51]. Affected XY infants are typically undervirilized due to in utero testosterone deficiency; female sex of rearing has been typical in the past. Sex ste roid hormone deficiency results in sexual infantilism and delayed puberty in both XX and XY individuals. Glucocorticoid defi ciency leads to increased ACTH secretion with the overproduction of adrenal cortical metabolites with mineralocorticoid activity such as 11-deoxycorticosterone and 18-hydroxycorticosterone. Affected individ uals may have low renin hypertension, hypokalemia, and hypergonadotropic hypo gonadism [52]. Individuals with nonclassic forms have been described [53].
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency

paragraphs.text: The enzyme, 11β-hydroxylase, encoded by CYP11B1 and located at chromosome 8q24.3, is expressed in the zona fasciculata and the zona reticularis. This enzyme is abundantly expressed in the zona fasciculata where it converts 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol and DOC to corticosterone. It is also expressed in the zona reticularis. Deleterious variants impair cortisol production resulting in increased ACTH secretion and conse quently increased production of 11-deoxy cortisol, progesterone, 17OHP, and DOC. Excessive DOC secretion can cause low renin mineralocorticoid-induced hyper tension and hypokalemia. Similar to 21-hydroxylase deficiency, precursors are shunted toward adrenal C19 steroids. Hence, prenatal virilization of the XX fetus occurs. Postnatally, both XY and XX individuals can develop premature pubarche, tall stature, and advanced skeletal maturation [54]. Individuals with mild variants have been reported [55].
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency

paragraphs.text: Aldosterone synthase is a closely related enzyme encoded by CYP11B2, which is located at chromosome 8q24.3 and expressed only in the zona glomerulosa. This enzyme catalyzes 11β-hydroxylase, 18-hydroxylase, and 18-methyloxidase activities to convert DOC to aldosterone. Loss-of-function CYP11B2 variants are associated with miner alocorticoid deficiency, leading to hyponatre mia and hyperkalemia. Glucocorticoid secretion is unaffected.
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency

paragraphs.text: P450 oxidoreductase protein is a flavoprotein that transfers electrons from NADPH to microsomal cytochrome P450 enzymes, including CYP21A2, CYP17A1, and CYP19A1. P450 oxidoreductase deficiency shows autosomal recessive inheritance. Lossof-function variants in the P450 oxidoreduc tase gene (POR) are associated with a spectrum of clinical phenotypes, depending on the specific POR variant [56]. In most cases, CYP17A1 activity, especially 17,20lyase activity, is affected leading to decreased sex steroid synthesis. The phenotype ranges from infants presenting with atypical genitalia to women with hyperandrogenism and men with gonadal insufficiency. In XY fetuses, POR deficiency impairs testicular testoster one secretion. In the XX fetus, the POR defi ciency causes steroid precursors to be diverted into the backdoor pathway with increased dihydrotesterone (DHT) production. In addi tion, POR deficiency impairs placental aro matase activity leading to increased fetal and maternal androgens. Mothers of affected fetuses may show progressive virilization.
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency

paragraphs.text: Glucocorticoid deficiency typically occurs but is usually mild often requiring only addi tional glucocorticoid supplementation for physiologic stress. Some patients manifest the

Antley-Bixler skeletal syndrome character ized by choanal atresia, craniosynostosis, midface hypoplasia, radiohumeral and/or radioulnar synostosis, and femoral bowing. The skeletal phenotype is attributed to decreased CYP26B1 activity, an enzyme that degrades retinoic acid.

The aromatase enzyme, encoded by the CYP19A1 gene located at chromosome 15q21.2, converts C19 androgens to C18 estrogens. This enzyme is expressed in ovarian granulosa cells, placenta, adipose tissue, brain, and testes. Due to alternative first exons and different transcriptional start sites with individual promoter elements, CYP19A1 expression is tissue-specific [57]. The pheno type of deleterious CYP19A1 variants includes maternal virilization during preg nancy and virilization of XX fetuses [58]. With the onset of puberty, affected girls typi cally present with delayed breast develop ment. They may develop ovarian cysts due to impaired estrogen synthesis with loss of nega tive feedback inhibition. Affected males pres ent with tall stature due to unfused epiphyses and low bone mass. Inheritance is autosomal recessive.
paragraphs.heading: (CYP19A1)

paragraphs.text: Due to chronic ACTH stimulation in patients with CAH, precursor steroids accumulate providing substrates for 11β-hydroxylase. Androstenedione is converted to 11-hydroxyandrostenedione. Circulating 11-hydroxyandrostenedione is peripherally converted to 11-ketotestosterone through the sequential activities of 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 and aldo-keto reductase family 1 member C3 (AKR1C3, also known as 17β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 5) [62]. In women with CAH, 11-ketotestosterone concentrations are directly proportional to testosterone concentrations. In men, 11-ketotestosterone concentrations are inversely proportional to testosterone concen trations because the 11-KT suppresses the HPG axis resulting in lower testicular testos terone secretion [1].
paragraphs.heading: 11.4.2 11-Oxo-Androgens

paragraphs.text: Specific clinical features such as atypical external genital development, androgen excess, or delayed puberty suggest a defect in adrenal or gonadal steroidogenesis. A thor ough medical history is the first step in the diagnostic process. In some instances, nonin vasive prenatal screening (NIPS) results and/ or prenatal ultrasound findings are available. Discrepancy between these prenatal tests often prompts further evaluation.
paragraphs.heading: 11.5 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Specific questioning should ascertain fam ily history, maternal virilization during preg nancy, and fetal or neonatal losses. The family history regarding pubertal development should be established. After examination for other physical anomalies, careful examination of the external genitalia is necessary to answer the following questions. Are the external geni talia and gonadal structures symmetrical or asymmetrical? Are the gonads palpable? What is the size of the phallus? Where is the urethral meatus and vaginal orifice? Is there a single perineal orifice? The physical examination provides preliminary information regarding
paragraphs.heading: 11.5 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: the possible diagnostic category and the most appropriate laboratory studies.
paragraphs.heading: 11.5 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: When conflicting results from NIPS/ genetic testing are obtained and/or atypical genital findings are evident on the infant’s exam, consultation with a multidisciplinary Differences in Sex Development (DSD) team should be promptly arranged. Members of this team should include pediatric endocri nologists, pediatric urologists/surgeons, genet icists, neonatologists, radiologists, behavioral health specialists, and pediatric nurse educa tors. Some pediatric hospitals have standing DSD committees to discuss and facilitate the decision-making and management of children with atypical genital development, including infants with CAH [63].
paragraphs.heading: 11.5 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: For the virilizing forms of CAH, affected XX infants are usually identified due to atypical external genital structures. The subsequent diagnostic evaluation identifies the etiology and discovers potentially life-threatening con ditions such as mineralocorticoid deficiency. The infant should be referred to as “your baby” to avoid terms conveying a sex assign ment. Guessing the infant’s sex is inappropri ate.
paragraphs.heading: 11.5.1 Infants

paragraphs.text: The parents need to be congratulated on the birth of their child and involved in the infant’s evaluation, especially when ques tions regarding whether the infant will be raised as a girl or a boy need to be addressed. Conversations with the parents should assess the parents’ health literacy and their level of understanding. Understanding and acknowledging the parents’ cultural back ground and religious views facilitates their full participation in this shared decisionmaking process. Members of the healthcare team can explain that it may take several days to obtain laboratory results. Parents can be informed that registration of the infant’s birth and naming of their baby can be deferred until conclusive laboratory results are available.
paragraphs.heading: 11.5.1 Infants

paragraphs.text: A thorough physical examination of the infant is essential to assess for additional anomalies such as the skeletal anomalies asso ciated with P450 oxidoreductase deficiency. The length and width of the phallus need to be measured (both a clitoris and a penis repre sent phalluses). The mean stretched penile length is 3.5 ± 0.4 cm for full-term infant boys and 2.5 ± 0.4 cm for males at 30 weeks gesta tion [64]. Symmetry, pigmentation, and ruga tion of the labioscrotal structures should be noted. Posterior labial fusion can be estimated by measurement of the anogenital ratio. In normal XX infants, the distance from the base of the phallus to the posterior fourchette should be 2/3 of the distance from the base of the phallus to the anus [65]. Careful examina tion for palpable gonads should be performed because gonads may be located in the inguinal canal or the labioscrotal folds. The external genitalia score (EGS) can be a useful tool to convey the appearance of external genital development in preterm and term infants [66].
paragraphs.heading: 11.5.1 Infants

paragraphs.text: Infants with symmetrical atypical genital appearance and nonpalpable gonads suggest the possibility of a steroidogenic defect asso ciated with virilization. The most common etiology is 21-hydroxylase deficiency. Rarer disorders to consider include P450 oxidore ductase deficiency, aromatase deficiency, and 11β-hydroxylase deficiency, which are para doxically associated with salt loss in the new born. XY infants with 21-hydroxylase and 11β-hydroxylase deficiencies show normal male genital development with hyperpigmen tation of the scrotum, whereas XY infants with P450 oxidoreductase deficiency are typi cally undervirilized. Variants in HSD3B2 are associated with virilization of XX fetuses and undervirilization of XY fetuses. Disorders affecting mineralocorticoid synthesis are associated with a risk for acute adrenal insuf ficiency, necessitating prompt evaluation. Discordance between XY karyotype on NIPS and appearance of the fetal external genitalia on ultrasound may identify XY infants with StAR, CYP17A1, and CYP11A1 variants, whereas XX infants with these disorders of steroidogenesis have normal female external genitalia and typically present with acute adrenal insufficiency [67].
paragraphs.heading: 11.5.1 Infants

paragraphs.text: Regardless of NIPS results, the infant’s karyotype needs to be immediately ordered. Chromosome studies should be supplemented with Y and X chromosome-specific FISH (fluorescence in situ hybridization) probes. In some institutions, results of Y and X chromosome-specific FISH tests may be avail able sooner than the full karyotype. Typically, infants with mineralocorticoid deficiency have normal electrolytes for several days after birth; hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, and ele vated plasma renin activity are usually evident 7–10 days after birth. Since 21-hydroxylase deficiency is the most likely diagnosis due to its higher prevalence, initial bloodwork should include 17-OHP, androstenedione, testoster one, LH, FSH, AMH, electrolytes, and plasma renin activity. Measurement of 21-deoxycortisol provides a reliable diagnos tic analyte to identify 21-hydroxylase defi ciency [37].

Elevated 17-OHP concentrations occur with both 11β-hydroxylase and P450 oxidore ductase deficiencies. Thus, if the 17-OHP value is not diagnostic for 21-hydroxylase deficiency, ACTH stimulation testing includ ing measurement of all steroids in the gluco corticoid and androgen pathways needs to be performed. For 11β-hydroxylase deficiency, 11-deoxycortisol concentrations are elevated [68]. Testing should be performed after 24–36 h of age to permit clearance of fetal ste roids.

With P450 oxidoreductase deficiency, 17-OHP values may be mildly to moderately elevated with normal plasma renin activity. Progesterone, corticosterone, 18-hydroxycor ticosterone, 11-deoxycorticosterone (DOC), and 18-hydroxy-DOC may be elevated. ACTH stimulation tests typically reveal normal basal cortisol concentrations with insufficient ACTH-stimulated cortisol concentrations [69]. Progesterone, 11-deoxycorticosterone, and corticosterone concentrations are usually elevated in 17α-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase defi ciency.

Clinical radioimmunoassays should be avoided because fetal adrenal steroids can cross-react interfering with assay reliability [70]. Specifically, 17-hydroxypregnenolone sulfate and 15β-hydroxylated compounds can

cross-react in the clinical radioimmunoassay [71, 72]. Rather, blood samples, especially for 17OHP, should be sent to a reference lab equipped for small assay volumes that utilize liquid chromatography/tandem mass spec trometry (LC-MS/MS) for steroid hormone determinations.

Ultrasound studies are helpful to ascertain the presence or absence of a uterus. Gonads may be visualized. Importantly, the inability to visualize gonads on ultrasound imaging of the fetus and neonate does not indicate gonadal absence. Gonadal structure, i.e., ovary versus testis, cannot be accurately resolved by ultrasound imaging.

The spectrum of congenital virilizing adrenal hyperplasias includes milder or nonclassic forms that present during childhood, adoles cence, and young adulthood. Typical features in childhood include premature pubic/axillary hair development, early onset of apocrine odor, increased linear growth velocity, and accelerated skeletal maturation. Adolescent and young adult women present with hirsut ism, irregular menses, and subfertility. Due to the nature of the symptoms of hyperan drogenism, an ascertainment bias favors the diagnosis of affected XX individuals whereas XY individuals are typically diagnosed through family studies.
paragraphs.heading: 11.5.2.1 Hyperandrogenism

paragraphs.text: In some instances, random steroid hor mone concentrations are diagnostic. For children with premature pubarche, early morning 17OHP concentrations, whether measured by radioimmunoassay or LC-MS/ MS, greater than 200 ng/dL have greater than 96% sensitivity and 96% specificity to detect children with nonclassic 21-hydroxy lase deficiency [73, 74]. Nonetheless, when symptoms suggest CAH, ACTH stimula tion tests should be performed regardless of morning 17-OHP concentrations [75]. Thus, ACTH stimulation tests, including the determination of all steroids in the gluco corticoid and androgen pathways, may be
paragraphs.heading: 11.5.2.1 Hyperandrogenism

paragraphs.text: indicated to confirm the specific diagnosis for most individuals. A novel approach using a machine-learning algorithm, single blood sample, and LC-MS/MS to obtain a quantitative assay of the circulating steroids has been reported to have good sensitivity and specificity to diagnose 21-hydroxylase deficiency in children with premature pubarche [76].
paragraphs.heading: 11.5.2.1 Hyperandrogenism

paragraphs.text: The Endocrine Society Guidelines sug gest that an ACTH-stimulated 17OHP above 1000 ng/dL is consistent with 21-hydroxylase deficiency [30]. ACTH stimulation tests may be helpful to assess the adequacy of cortisol response and determine when hydrocorti sone treatment can be limited to only stress dosing (see below). Using LC-MS/MS, ACTH-stimulated cortisol concentrations greater than >14 mcg/dL can be considered normal [77].
paragraphs.heading: 11.5.2.1 Hyperandrogenism

paragraphs.text: As noted above, individuals with deleterious variants in genes involved in sex steroid syn thesis may present with pubertal delay. When evaluating a child, adolescent, or young adult, cognizance of the individual’s emotions and privacy needs is fundamental because the dis covery of a DSD may shatter the individual’s self-esteem and self-identity.
paragraphs.heading: 11.5.2.2 Pubertal Delay

paragraphs.text: Family history for pubertal delay and infertility should be sought. For individuals raised as girls, has any virilization or clitoro megaly occurred? A thorough physical exami nation including blood pressure, height, weight, and assessment of any dysmorphic features is essential, followed by a complete examination of external genital structures. As in the infant, are the external genital struc tures symmetric or asymmetric? Can gonads be palpated?
paragraphs.heading: 11.5.2.2 Pubertal Delay

paragraphs.text: Loss-of-function variants in CYP17A1 impair sex steroid synthesis, resulting in delayed or absent pubertal development in both XX and XY individuals. Partial or non classic variants for several steroidogenic enzyme genes are increasingly recognized [78, 79].
paragraphs.heading: 11.5.2.2 Pubertal Delay

paragraphs.text: Evaluation for nonclassic steroidogenic defects such as P450 oxidoreductase defi ciency warrants consideration in women with
paragraphs.heading: 11.5.2.2 Pubertal Delay

paragraphs.text: infertility, ovarian cysts, and chronically ele vated progesterone and 17-OHP concentra tions [80].
paragraphs.heading: 11.5.2.2 Pubertal Delay

paragraphs.text: Genetic testing has become an important diagnostic tool due to the increased availabil ity of next-generation sequencing. Genetic testing panels for DSD and whole-genome sequencing are increasingly available. The complexity of the CYP21A2 locus compli cates CYP21A2 genetic analysis [81]. At the present time, direct sequencing with CYP21A2-specific primers is usually needed to fully interrogate for CYP21A2 variants. Ascertaining parental genotypes can be help ful to confirm the parental origin of the spe cific mutations because some alleles can carry multiple deleterious variants.
paragraphs.heading: 11.5.3 Genetic Testing

paragraphs.text: The paramount clinical objectives are to assure normal growth and development, including appropriate timing of pubertal mat uration. For patients with mineralocorticoid deficiency, avoiding acute adrenal insuffi ciency is a critical goal. To achieve these goals, the guiding therapeutic principle for CAH is replacement of deficient hormones and reduc tion of the overproduced proximal precursors. Much information related below pertains to the virilizing CAHs, especially 21-hydroxylase deficiency.

Glucocorticoids have been the mainstay of treatment since the 1950s [82]. Despite numer ous therapeutic paradigms, it is important to acknowledge the caveat that current gluco corticoid replacement regimens fail to fully
paragraphs.heading: Therapy

paragraphs.text: mimic the ACTH-cortisol circadian rhythm, as well as the HPA response to stress. Adequate suppression of adrenal C19 steroid secretion typically necessitates supra-physio logic glucocorticoid dosing and thus intro duces risks associated with excessive glucocorticoid exposure. These include adverse effects on linear growth, metabolism, and bone health.
paragraphs.heading: Therapy

paragraphs.text: Hydrocortisone (Cortef®) is the most com monly used glucocorticoid in childhood. Due to its short half-life, hydrocortisone is typi cally dosed three to four times per day in doses ranging between 8 and 15 mg/m2/day. With a median hydrocortisone elimination half-life of 58 min (range 41–105 min), dosing less than three times daily is not recommended [83]. Reverse dosing with provision of the highest dose at night has been utilized. However, recent data fail to support the use of reverse dosing [84]. One pharmacokinetic/ pharmacodynamic model suggested that changing daily hydrocortisone administration to four times per day dividing doses as 38% at 06:00, 22% at 12:00, 17% at 18:00, and 22% at 24:00 resembles the circadian rhythm of corti sol and achieves better cortisol concentrations throughout a 24-h period [85].
paragraphs.heading: Therapy

paragraphs.text: In the United States, hydrocortisone is commercially available in 5 and 10 mg tablets. For infants and young children, the tablets can be crushed and mixed with food. For infants, crushed tablets can be suspended in tiny amounts of liquids such as breast milk or formula; the crushed tablets should never be mixed with formula in a bottle. Inconsistent dosing has been reported for compounded preparations [86, 87]. One newer hydrocorti sone formulation consists of granules covered with a flavoring to mask hydrocortisone’s bit ter taste which can be administered by placing on top of a spoonful of food. These immediate-release granules are available in packets containing 0.5, 1, 2, and 5 mg (Infacort®/Alkindi®, Diurnal Ltd.). Both preparations have been approved for use in the EU and the United States [88, 89].
paragraphs.heading: Therapy

paragraphs.text: 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase activity, which means less cortisone is converted to cortisol. Hence, higher hydrocortisone dosing may be necessary during puberty [90]. Once linear growth has been completed, some adults prefer to switch to prednisone/prednis olone with twice daily dosing or dexametha sone with once-daily dosing. However, patients should be counseled that continued hydrocortisone treatment is associated with better bone mineral density and better meta bolic and cardiovascular outcomes than dexa methasone, prednisone, and prednisolone [91, 92] ( Table 11.2).
paragraphs.heading: Therapy

paragraphs.text: Mineralocorticoid replacement therapy, fludrocortisone, is added for salt-wasting dis orders. Fludrocortisone (9α-fluorocortisol) is a synthetic mineralocorticoid that is structur ally similar to cortisol with the addition of a fluorine atom at the 9-position of the steroid structure. Its duration of action is approxi mately 18–36 h. Fludrocortisone is available in tablets which, similar to hydrocortisone tablets, can be crushed for administration in infants and young children.
paragraphs.heading: Replacement Therapy

paragraphs.text: Mineralocorticoid therapy is recom mended for all infants with classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency. Due to relative mineralocorticoid resistance, antimineralo corticoid activity of elevated 17OHP concen trations, and a low sodium diet, neonates often require higher fludrocortisone doses. In addition, salt supplementation may be needed for some; recommended doses of a standard ized saline solution are approximately 4–8 mEq/kg/day in divided doses [93, 94]. The saline solution should be made by a pharma cist to assure accurate salt concentration. Frequent monitoring of blood pressure, elec trolytes, and plasma renin activity is essential for subsequent tapering of the fludrocortisone dose to avoid iatrogenic hypertension. Typical fludrocortisone doses for older children and adults range between 0.05 and 0.2 mg daily, divided into one or two oral doses.
paragraphs.heading: Replacement Therapy

paragraphs.text: Multiparticulate technology was utilized to develop a modified-release capsule prepara tion consisting of an inert microcrystalline core coated with hydrocortisone and covered with an enteric coat layer (Chronocort®, Diurnal Limited, UK) [95, 96]. Although bed time dosing successfully blunted the excessive ACTH surge in the early morning, once-daily dosing was insufficient to prevent excessive androgen secretion during the late afternoon in adults [97]. A phase III multicenter clinical trial involving adults with CAH in which the Chronocort capsules (Efmody®) were taken before bed (11 PM) and upon awakening (7 AM) showed that the capsules were not superior to hydrocortisone when judged by 24-h 17OHP profiling. Nevertheless, individu als taking Chronocort had lower 17OHP and androstenedione concentrations during the morning and early afternoon [98]. In May 2021, the European Medicines Agency (EMA) approved Efmody® for patients with CAH 12 years of age and older.
paragraphs.heading: Therapies

paragraphs.text: To better mimic HPA axis diurnal varia tion, continuous subcutaneous hydrocorti sone infusion therapy (CSHI) has been attempted. A phase II, open-label clinical trial involving eight adults with classic CAH showed improved androgen concentrations and quality of life compared to oral glucocor ticoid therapy [99, 100]. Yet, despite the attractiveness of CSHI in replicating physio logic glucocorticoid diurnal rhythm, this approach is complicated, labor-intensive, costly, and encumbered with numerous tech nical issues [101].
paragraphs.heading: Therapies

paragraphs.text: Corticotropin-releasing hormone type 1 receptor (CRHR1) antagonists are agents that interfere with ACTH secretion. These medications include the CRHR1 antagonists, tildacerfont (SPR001; LY2371712), and crinecerfont (NBI-74788). These medications do not obviate the need for glucocorticoid replacement and, if needed, mineralocorti coid treatment. Initial studies are promising that these medications could eventually be
