Upon confirmation of the diagnosis, discus sions with the parents should include patho physiology, genetics, treatments, and the need for regular follow-up evaluations. Themes from these conversations often warrant repeti tion and, ultimately, need to be discussed with the patient using age-appropriate terminol ogy. Teaching parents how to administer daily hydrocortisone and the indications for stress dosing are essential. Parents need to be capa ble of administering parental hydrocortisone sodium succinate (Solu-Cortef®). Kits for parental hydrocortisone administration should be kept at home and wherever the child spends a lot of time, e.g., grandparents’ home. All patients taking glucocorticoids need to wear Medic Alert Identification tags ( www. medicalert.org). Parents need to educate fam ily members and school personnel regarding their child’s medical needs. Children with CAH should participate in all school events and activities.
paragraphs.heading: and Monitoring

paragraphs.text: Regular follow-up evaluations to assess general health, linear growth, pubertal status, salt craving, BMI, and blood pressure are essential. Pertinent biochemical monitoring is important to assess hormone replacement therapy. For patients with classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency, regular monitoring of androstenedione, 17-OHP, testosterone, and plasma renin activity is necessary. Bone age X-rays are essential to monitor the rate of bone maturation. The goal is to titrate hor mone replacement to avoid features of Cushing syndrome due to overtreatment and signs of androgen excess due to undertreat ment.
paragraphs.heading: and Monitoring

paragraphs.text: In some instances, children develop sec ondary GnRH-dependent precocious puberty. Treatment with a GnRH agonist may be help ful in this situation [104].
paragraphs.heading: and Monitoring

paragraphs.text: This formidable topic warrants extensive dis cussion with adolescent and young adult women with CAH because many women with CAH have limited knowledge regarding their fertility potential [105]. Typically, women with 21-hydroxylase deficiency encounter difficulty achieving pregnancy and experiencing live births. Factors interfering with reproductive success include elevated progesterone concen trations, variations in urogenital anatomy, and decreased interest in procreation. Importantly, however, women with 21-hydroxylase deficiency need to be informed that they can deliver healthy infants with appropriate medical care before conception, throughout pregnancy, and during delivery.
paragraphs.heading: 11.7.1 Pregnancy

paragraphs.text: Elevated progesterone concentrations interfere with several aspects of female repro ductive function. Progesterone thickens cervi cal mucus hindering sperm motility, disrupting endometrium maturation, and impairing embryo implantation. At the level of the hypothalamus, a unified explanation for the consequences of increased progesterone and C19 steroid concentrations remains to be clar ified due to apparent opposing effects. Elevated progesterone concentrations disrupt pulsatile GnRH secretion leading to decreased LH pulse frequency and LH pulse amplitude, culminating in anovulation [106]. Yet, andro gens also impair the ability of progesterone to decrease GnRH/LH pulses resulting in increased LH pulse frequency and pulse amplitude, increased ovarian theca cell andro gen secretion, and polycystic ovary morphol ogy [107]. Other factors potentially contributing to the increased GnRH and LH pulsatility include the consequences of prena tal androgen programming on the hypothala mus and interference with neuroendocrine feedback due to persistently elevated postna tal C19 steroids [108, 109].
paragraphs.heading: 11.7.1 Pregnancy

paragraphs.text: Vaginal and urogenital sinus anatomy with a smaller vaginal introitus often contributes to dyspareunia and decreased sexual satisfac
paragraphs.heading: 11.7.1 Pregnancy

paragraphs.text: tion [110]. Women with more severe genotypes are reported to be less interested in sexual activity and experience less satisfaction with their surgical interventions [111]. Selfperceived body image, self-gender identity, sexual intimacy preferences, and quality of life impact sexual activity. Despite these fac tors, the pregnancy rate in women with classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency who wished to con ceive is over 90% [112]. Most women with classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency are delivered by Caesarian section due to prior urogenital sinus surgery.
paragraphs.heading: 11.7.1 Pregnancy

paragraphs.text: Women with nonclassic 21-hydroxylase deficiency may benefit from glucocorticoid replacement before conception and during pregnancy to improve the likelihood of con ception and decrease the risk of miscarriage [113]. Using assisted reproductive technology, a limited number of pregnancies have been reported in other forms of adrenal hyperpla sia including 17α-hydroxylase deficiency, iso lated 17,20-lyase deficiency, P450 oxidoreductase deficiency, and congenital lipoid adrenal hyperplasia [114–117].
paragraphs.heading: 11.7.1 Pregnancy

paragraphs.text: In the 1980s, prenatal high-dose dexametha sone treatment was introduced to decrease virilization of the external genital structures of XX fetuses with virilizing forms of CAH. Dexamethasone was used because it “crosses the placenta” and was not inactivated by placental 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2. The usual dexametha sone dose is comparable to 60 times physio logic cortisol concentrations at that timepoint in gestation [118]. To effectively decrease pre natal virilization, dexamethasone therapy must be initiated by 6–7 weeks of gestation. Hence, all “at-risk” fetuses must be treated until prenatal diagnosis can be performed. At that point, treatment was continued only in affected XX fetuses [119–121]. Nonetheless, eight fetuses are exposed to prenatal dexa methasone early in gestation to treat one affected XX fetus.
paragraphs.heading: 11.7.2 Prenatal Treatment

paragraphs.text: However, dexamethasone is a potent gene transcription factor that influences many
paragraphs.heading: 11.7.2 Prenatal Treatment

paragraphs.text: developmental processes in the developing fetus, raising concerns about the safety of pre natal dexamethasone exposure. In humans, early gestation dexamethasone treatment has been associated with a slightly increased risk for cleft palate and lip [122]. In rodent models, prenatal dexamethasone exposure is associ ated with decreased birth weight and aberrant fetal programming effects on brain, thyroid, cardiovascular, metabolic, and reproductive functions [123].
paragraphs.heading: 11.7.2 Prenatal Treatment

paragraphs.text: Swedish pediatric endocrinologists and colleagues have provided the most extensive human follow-up data regarding prenatal dexamethasone treatment. Their initial studies showed negative cognitive effects, especially related to working memory in a cohort of exposed unaffected XX fetuses [124]. Adverse effects on pancreatic beta cell function and higher cholesterol and LDL-cholesterol were reported among CAH unaffected dexamethasone-exposed individuals [125]. Structural brain altera tions were observed in dexamethasonetreated unaffected adults; this finding was associated with increased methylation of the promotor region of the FKBP5 gene. Though no apparent cognitive changes were detected, potential explanations included a small sample size and brain plasticity enabling compensatory mechanisms [126]. These researchers also described changes in DNA methylation after prenatal DEX treat ment [127].
paragraphs.heading: 11.7.2 Prenatal Treatment

paragraphs.text: During early gestation, neurogenesis is an active complex process with neurons migrat ing to their cortical locations. Prenatal dexa methasone appears to alter this developmental trajectory. In a mouse model, even a single dexamethasone dose-administered midgestation led to changes in brain architecture, neurite complexity in the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus, and anxiety and depressivelike behaviors in the adult mice [128]. Returning to the Swedish experience, based on their findings including a large change in amygdala size, increased size of the superior prefrontal gyrus, widespread alterations in white-matter microstructure, and epigenetic changes, these researchers reinforce ongoing safety concerns regarding first-trimester dexa
paragraphs.heading: 11.7.2 Prenatal Treatment

paragraphs.text: methasone treatment in CAH [126]. At pres ent, the Endocrine Society Guidelines state that prenatal dexamethasone treatment should be considered experimental and should only be performed through Institutional Review Board-approved research protocols [30].
paragraphs.heading: 11.7.2 Prenatal Treatment

paragraphs.text: Boys and men with CAH may develop tes ticular adrenal rest tissue (TART) in their testes. TARTs are benign lesions that com press the surrounding testicular tissue. Typically, TARTs are painless, bilateral, and generally detected near the testicular medi astinum on imaging studies such as ultra sound [129]. Reported prevalence is approximately 25% in adolescents and 46% in men [130]. Elevated ACTH concentra tions are believed to contribute to the devel opment of TARTs. However, TARTs have been identified in men with well-controlled CAH and men with nonclassic CAH [131]. TARTs are not restricted to boys and men with 21-hydroxylase deficiency; they have been identified in individuals with CYP11A1, CYP11B2, and HSD3B2 variants [132]. Although this section is focused on TARTS, ovarian adrenal rest tumors can occur in ovaries [133].
paragraphs.heading: and Men

paragraphs.text: TARTs can cause mechanical obstruction of the seminiferous tubules, as well as injury to Sertoli and germ cells. Azoospermia can occur. Treatments include optimization of glucocorticoid treatment. Testis-sparing surgery has been described, but gonadal func tion generally does not improve. Semen analy sis and sperm cryopreservation should be offered. Poorly controlled CAH is character ized by elevated adrenal C19 steroids, which suppress gonadotropin secretion, contribut ing to a secondary hypogonadotropic hypogo nadism. Boys with CAH and their families should be counseled about TARTs and the risks of infertility [134]. Screening for TARTs should begin in early adolescence for boys with CAH and be repeated every other year unless clinical concerns arise.
paragraphs.heading: and Men

paragraphs.text: Expression of adrenal-specific genes such as CYP11B1, CYP11B2, CYP21A2, and MC2R within this tissue supports the hypoth esis that TARTs are ectopic adrenal-like cells that migrate to the testes during gestation [135]. Recent detailed transcriptome studies of TARTs showed the greatest similarity to adult adrenal tissue followed by adult testis tissue with little resemblance to fetal adrenal and fetal testis. These findings suggest that TARTs may represent a mature adrenal-like cell exhibiting features of both adrenal and testicular cells [136].
paragraphs.heading: and Men

paragraphs.text: TARTs need to be differentiated from Leydig cell tumors which can become malig nant. Unlike Leydig cell tumors which tend to be unilateral, TARTs are generally bilateral. TARTs tend to decrease in size with increased glucocorticoid dosing.
paragraphs.heading: and Men

paragraphs.text: The discussion regarding pregnancy should be expanded to inform both women and men that CAH is not an effective form of birth control. Hence, contraception needs should be discussed. Effective options for women include combined hormonal contraceptives (pills, patches, or contraceptive rings). Progestin-only methods such as progesterone pills, Depo-Provera, and Nexplanon can be used despite the typically elevated circulating progesterone concentrations [137]. Adolescent and young adult men should be counseled that CAH does not typically cause infertility in men. All should be counseled to use barrier methods (condoms) to prevent pregnancy and STI transmission.
paragraphs.heading: 11.7.4 Contraception

paragraphs.text: Defects in sex steroid biosynthesis may pres ent at birth due to atypical genitalia. Other affected individuals present with delayed puberty due to impaired sex steroid biosyn thesis. Laboratory studies typically showed hypergonadotropic hypogonadism due to sex steroid hormone deficiency. Individuals with CYP17A1 variants may have hypertension.
paragraphs.heading: 11.7.5 Delayed Puberty

paragraphs.text: For girls, estrogen replacement therapy can be initiated with transdermal estradiol patches. Commercially available matrix patches may need to be cut into halves or quarters to provide an initial low estradiol dose to mimic physiologic pubertal estrogen secretion. Over 12–24 months, the estradiol dose can be gradually increased. After 12–24 months, cyclic progesterone treatment should be initiated. Regimens for hormone replacement therapy include transdermal estradiol with cyclic oral progesterone, com bined estradiol-progesterone patches, or com bined oral contraceptives [138].
paragraphs.heading: 11.7.5 Delayed Puberty

paragraphs.text: For boys with impaired sex steroid synthe sis and micropenis, low-dose short-term tes tosterone replacement therapy has been used to promote phallic growth [139]. Testosterone can be initiated to induce pubertal develop ment and maintain masculine features. Typically, testosterone esters are used and administered subcutaneously or intramuscu larly. Initially, low testosterone doses are used with a gradual increase in adult male replace ment dosages [140].
paragraphs.heading: 11.7.5 Delayed Puberty

paragraphs.text: During the early years of pediatric endocri nology in the 1950s, contemporaneous phi losophy specified that the appearance of the external genital structures needed to be con sistent with the sex of rearing. It was pre sumed that sex/gender identity was fluid at birth and was established by 18 months of age through interactions with the postnatal envi ronment. Thus, sex/gender assignment was typically based on the appearance of the external genital structures regardless of karyotype, gonadal histology, or internal gen ital structures. However, subsequent clinical experiences indicated that many factors such as prenatal hormone exposures and postnatal environment contributed to the development of gender identity obliging reexamination of the medical approach to individuals with atypical genital structures [141].
paragraphs.heading: 11.7.6 Urogenital Surgery

paragraphs.text: To address these concerns about the lack of patient/family involvement in medical
paragraphs.heading: 11.7.6 Urogenital Surgery

paragraphs.text: decision-making, nondisclosure of diagnostic details, repeated medical examinations, and questions about urogenital surgery, the 2005 DSD Consensus Conference was organized. At this conference, DSDs were defined as con genital disorders associated with atypical development of chromosomal, gonadal, and/ or anatomic sex. Specific recommendations included: (1) postponing medically unneces sary interventions until the child is competent to participate in decision-making; (2) promot ing open and ongoing communication with families; and (3) providing holistic openminded multidisciplinary care [142]. In 2016, an expert panel including clinicians and repre sentatives from patient advocacy and support groups reassessed and updated the 2006 rec ommendations [143].
paragraphs.heading: 11.7.6 Urogenital Surgery

paragraphs.text: Most girls with classic virilizing CAH are born with virilized external genital structures characterized by an enlarged phallus (clito ris), fused labioscrotal folds, a single perineal opening, and a urogenital sinus. Feminizing genitoplasty involves clitoroplasty, the open ing of the vaginal introitus, and labioplasty. Current surgical techniques attempt to pre serve clitoral sensitivity. In the past, these operations were performed during the first years of life. More recently, the need and tim ing for these operations have been questioned due to the inability of the person to consent to surgery, unfavorable outcomes, and greater acceptance of human variation. Potential sur gical interventions should be discussed with families and affected individuals using a shared decision-making process [144].
paragraphs.heading: 11.7.6 Urogenital Surgery

paragraphs.text: Individuals with CAH and other conditions affecting steroidogenesis can impact selfesteem. Parents often experience distress when their child is born with atypical genitalia or other chronic health problems. Parents should be encouraged to share the details of their health situation with children positively to reinforce the message that the child’s DSD is a part of who they are and should not be a source of shame.

paragraphs.heading: 11.8 Conclusion

paragraphs.text: Over the past 70+ years, the pathophysiology of disorders affecting steroidogenesis has been elucidated. This knowledge led to the development of therapeutic interventions. An individualized approach to care is essential accompanied by full disclosure and shared decision-making between patients, families, and the health care team. With this approach, the goal of the best life possible for patients with disorders of steroidogenesis should be achievable.

paragraphs.text: CAH results in increased production of ACTH by the pituitary gland. ACTH is derived from a precursor molecule called proopiomelanocortin (POMC). POMC is also a precursor for melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH). MSH stimulates melanocytes and can cause skin darkening. In sec ondary and tertiary forms of adrenal insufficiency, skin darkening does not occur since ACTH is not overpro duced.

Abnormalities in each of the steroidogenic enzymes have been described. Decreased enzyme activity impairs cortisol synthesis with subsequent increased ACTH secretion due to loss of negative feedback inhibition. This results in overproduction of the hor mone precursors proximal to the faulty enzyme and deficiencies of the hormones dis tal to the aberrant enzyme [2]. In addition to adrenocortical expression, several steroido genic enzymes are also expressed in the gonads where they are involved in sex steroid biosyn thesis and, hence, associated with sex steroid hormone deficiencies. The specific clinical and hormonal fea tures depend upon the particular genetic vari ant and the consequences of decreased enzyme activity, specifically which hormones are overproduced, and which are deficient. The virilizing forms of CAH present with Table 11.1 Enzymes and genes involved in the different forms of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) Enzymatic deficiency Enzyme Gene 21-Hydroxylase deficiency P450c21 CYP21A2 Lipoid CAH P450scca StAR Cholesterol side chain cleavage deficiency P450scc CYP11A1 3-Beta-HSD deficiency 3β(Beta)HSD HSD3B2 17-Hydroxylase/17,20-lyase deficiency P450c17 CYP171 11-Beta-hydroxylase deficiency P450c11 CYP11B1 Aldosterone synthase deficiency P450c18 CYP11B2 P450 oxidoreductase deficiency P450 oxidoreduc tase POR a Although some patients with lipoid CAH have been found to have mutations in P450scc, the majority of patients with lipoid CAH have mutations mainly in the steroidogenic acute regulatory protein (StAR), which promotes entry of cholesterol into mitochondria symptoms ranging from virilization of an affected female infant, premature virilization in boys and girls, or signs of androgen excess in adolescent and young adult women. Genetic variants involved in gonadal sex ste roid synthesis may present with atypical geni tal development and delayed puberty. The outer zone, the zona glomerulosa, synthesizes mineralocorti coids and is principally regulated by the reninangiotensin pathway and serum potassium concentrations. The middle zone, the zona fasciculata, synthesizes cortisol and is regu lated by pituitary adrenocorticotrophin (ACTH) secretion. The inner zone, the zona reticularis, secretes C19 steroids including DHEA, DHEAS, and androstenedione, which are collectively labeled as the “adrenal androgens.” The hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis is an essential neurohormonal sys tem that regulates cortisol concentrations within the physiologic range to maintain homeostasis for daily activities and in response to internal and external stressors. ACTH and cortisol manifest diurnal variation with the highest concentrations in the early morning. Acutely, ACTH stimulates cortisol secretion. Tonic ACTH secretion promotes transcrip tion and translation of the adrenal steroido genic enzymes in all three zones of the adrenal cortex. Through negative feedback inhibition of ACTH secretion, the HPA axis governs cortisol secretion. ### 11 Within the hypothalamus, the parvocellu lar neurons of the paraventricular nucleus (PVN) send projections to the median emi nence where they secrete corticotropinreleasing hormone (CRH) and arginine vasopressin (AVP) to regulate ACTH secre tion [3]. In the setting of stress, increases in pro-inflammatory cytokines such as interleu kin (IL)-1 and IL-6 stimulate increased CRH secretion, leading to increased cortisol secre tion [4]. These factors also act directly on the adrenal cortex to increase cortisol secretion [5]. Acting via the ACTH receptor, the Gα-protein-coupled ACTH receptor (MC2R), ACTH stimulates cortisol secretion. Due to its lipophilic nature, cortisol is not prestored in vesicles and must be rapidly synthesized following ACTH stimulation [6]. Hence, unlike other endocrine tissues, such as the thy roid gland, the adrenal cortex does not store cortisol. Aldosterone secretion is primarily regulated by serum potassium concentrations and the renin-angiotensin system with angio tensin II acting through the Gq-proteincoupled angiotensin 2 receptor [7]. ACTH also contributes to aldosterone secretion. 8 9 10 11.1 ## PDF page 312 | printed page 299 ![Source image](../../figures/ch011_p0312_01.jpg) Unmatched source image; PDF page 312. Consult the original caption. ## PDF page 313 | printed page 300 ### 11.3 Specific Enzyme Deficiencies ### 11.3.1 21-Hydroxylase Deficiency An anonymous case report published in the Lancet in 1833 is likely the earliest description of a person conjectured to be an XX individ ual with simple virilizing CAH [11]. Luigi de Crecchio published the first detailed case report regarding CAH in 1865 [12]. He described an individual baptized as a girl who transitioned to a boy at age 4 years. This patient lived as a man and likely died second ary to an acute adrenal crisis. In the 1950s, Jayle and colleagues described women with nonclassic 21-hydroxylase deficiency [13]. The most common form of CAH is 21-Hydroxylase deficiency, which accounts for approximately 95% of affected individuals [14]. Reported worldwide frequency is approxi mately 1:14,000 to 1:18,000 liveborn infants based on newborn screening. The frequency is higher among certain ethnic groups [15]. In this autosomal recessive disorder, deficient 21-hydroxylase activity leads to decreased cor tisol secretion, subsequent increased ACTH, and overproduction of steroids before the 21-hydroxylation step. Specifically, the decreased 21-hydroxylase activity decreases the conversion of progesterone and 17-hydroxy progesterone (17OHP) to deoxycorticosterone (DOC) and 11-deoxycortisol (S), respectively. ### 11 Although CAH due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency reflects a spectrum of enzyme dys function, three categories have been arbi trarily defined: salt-losing, simple virilizing, and nonclassic. Affected XX infants with saltlosing and simple virilizing forms typically present with virilization of the external geni tal structures; normally developed ovaries, uterus, cervix, and Fallopian tubes are pres ent. Aldosterone synthesis in the zona glo merulosa is usually 100–1000 times less than cortisol synthesis; hence, the most dysfunc tional enzyme variants are associated with salt-losing CAH, whereas milder variants are associated with simple virilizing or nonclassic forms [16]. Virilized XX individuals often have a vagina that opens into a common urogenital sinus with enlarged clitoris and single perineal opening. Affected XY infants show normal external genital development but may mani fest hyperpigmentation of their genitalia. Infants with mineralocorticoid deficiency dis play poor weight gain, hyponatremia, hyper kalemia, and acidosis beginning around 5 days of age. The advent of nearly universal newborn screening programs has greatly decreased the number of affected infants pre senting with adrenal insufficiency during the first few weeks of life. The diagnosis of 21-hydroxylase defi ciency should be considered when evaluat ing an infant with atypical genital appearance and nonpalpable gonads. Elevated 17OHP concentrations, the sub strate for 21-hydroxylase, are found in patients with CAH due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency. Individuals with simple viriliz ing CAH may present with premature pubarche, tall stature, accelerated linear growth velocity, and advanced skeletal mat uration. The mildest form, nonclassic CAH, typically presents in adolescent and young adult women with irregular menses, hirsut ism, acne, and subfertility. This form of CAH is due to mutations in the 21-hydroxylase gene (CYP21A2), which is located at chromosome 6p21.3, in a complex genetic locus within the major histocompati bility complex (MHC) class III region [17]. The functional gene lies in close proximity (~30 kb) to a nonfunctional highly homolo gous pseudogene (CYP21A1P). These genes are arranged in tandem with the genes for the fourth component of complement, C4A and C4B. On the telomeric side, the C4/CYP21 unit is flanked by the serine-threonine kinase-19 (STK19) gene. The tenascin-X gene (TNXB) is located on the centromeric side; this gene encodes an extracellular matrix pro tein on the opposite DNA strand [18]. Detailed discussion regarding this locus and CYP21A2 expression is beyond the scope of this chapter [1, 19]. To date, over 200 CYP21A2 variants have been described; variants are listed in the ## PDF page 314 | printed page 301 Human Gene Mutation Database (HGMD, http://www.hgmd.cf.ac.uk) and the Pharmacogene Variation Consortium ( https://www.phar mvar.org/gene/ CYP21A2). Approximately, ten singlenucleotide variants derived from the pseudo gene account for over 90% of cases. Variants have been categorized according to their con sequences on protein function. Deletions, large gene conversions, nonsense mutations, frameshift mutations, and missense variants that abolish enzyme activity are typically associated with salt-losing forms. Some mis sense variants significantly reduce but do not abolish enzyme activity. One common variant is a single-nucleotide variant located in intron 2 that alters the splice site acceptor for exon 3; this variant is associated with both salt-losing and simple virilizing forms. Missense variants that reduce enzyme activity by 30–50% are usually associated with nonclassic CAH. The estimated prevalence of nonclassic CAH is 1 in 200 in the USA [20]. Reported carrier prevalence rates in Europe are 4.0–7.5% [21, 22]. Most affected individuals are compound heterozygotes with different deleterious vari ants located on each allele. An individual’s phenotype typically corresponds to the milder variant. Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS) is charac terized by joint hypermobility, skin hyperex tensibility, and tissue fragility. Typically, EDS is an autosomal dominant disorder associated with variants in collagen-associated genes. One type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is asso ciated with tenascin X deficiency and variants in the tenascin B (TNXB) gene. When this autosomal recessive EDS is associated with a CYP21A2 deletion extending into the TNXB gene, it is labeled “CAH-X” and represents a contiguous gene deletion disorder. Approximately 10–12% of patients with CAH have CAH-X [23–25]. In addition to the usual features associated with CAH, clinical fea tures of CAH-X include generalized joint hypermobility, subluxation, and chronic arthralgia; cardiac valve abnormalities are identified in roughly 25%. ### 11.3.1.1 Newborn Screening ### for 21-Hydroxylase Deficiency In the mid-1970s, a microfilter paper method with dried blood spots to measure 17-OHP by immunoassay was developed to screen for 21-hydroxylase deficiency [26]. Now, 50 years later, newborn screening for 21-hydroxylase is mandatory in all 50 states and is performed in many countries [27]. The primary goal of newborn screening is the detection of infants with classic CAH, particularly male infants who have normal external genitalia, to pre vent adrenal crises and deaths. Additional benefits of screening include less severe hypo natremia, shorter hospitalizations, and earlier recognition of virilized affected XX infants [28, 29]. For the initial screen, an automated timeresolved dissociation-enhanced lanthanide fluoroimmunoassay (DELFIA) without ste roid extraction is generally used to measure 17OHP. Subsequently, using the screening lab’s testing paradigm, a second-tier test is performed as recommended by the 2018 Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guidelines [30]. The second tier may involve a steroid extraction phase or the use of LC/MS-MS methodology. Most screening labs use gesta tional age and birth weight to establish spe cific cut points. Immunoassays for 17-OHP determination continue to be used due to low cost, sensitivity, and technical ease. Both false-positive and false-negative screening results occur [31]. To limit the num ber of false-positive cases, cut points have been established such that individuals with nonclassic CAH are not typically identified by newborn screening. False-positive results occur in preterm infants, infants heterozygous for CYP21A2 variants, stressed infants, and infants with other steroidogenic enzyme defi ciencies [32]. False-negative screening results have been reported [33, 34]. The effects of multiple courses of antenatal steroids are apparently inconsistent and may be associ ated with false-negative results [35, 36]. Specific testing for 21-hydroxylase deficiency ## PDF page 315 | printed page 302 should be performed in suspicious clinical sce narios, even if screening results were reported to be negative. Second-tier testing with LC-MS/MS avoids the concerns of cross-reactivity associ ated with immunoassays. Screening for 21-deoxycortisol in 21-hydroxylase deficiency may improve diagnostic specificity because of its specificity for 21-hydroxylase deficiency; 21-deoxycortisol concentrations are not ele vated in preterm infants [37]. ### 11.3.2 Lipoid Adrenal Hyperplasia Congenital lipoid adrenal hyperplasia is due to loss-of-function variants in the steroidogenic acute regulatory protein (StAR) gene located at chromosome 8p11.2. The StAR protein is a mitochondrial protein that facilitates choles terol transport from the outer to the inner mitochondrial membrane. In this form of CAH, synthesis of all adrenal and gonadal ste roids is impaired resulting in glucocorticoid, mineralocorticoid, and sex steroid deficiencies [38]. Decreased StAR protein activity results in the accumulation of cholesterol esters and sterol auto-oxidation products in the cytosol of the adrenal and gonadal steroidogenic cells, ultimately damaging the cell and disrupting StAR-independent basal steroidogenesis. ### 11 Affected infants typically present early in life with cardiovascular collapse, hyponatre mia, and hyperkalemia due to mineralocorti coid and glucocorticoid deficiencies. Since this enzyme is necessary for gonadal sex hor mone synthesis, in utero testosterone synthe sis is impaired leading to undervirilization of male fetuses. At birth, XY infants present with atypical external genitalia; labial masses may be palpable. External genital develop ment appears female in affected XX infants. Importantly, internal and external female genital structures are normal in affected XX individuals. Affected XX individuals may have sufficient gonadal function at puberty to feminize and experience menarche as individ ual follicles are stimulated and recruited [39]. However, over time, cholesterol esters accu mulate in ovarian steroidogenic cells causing cell damage and, ultimately, premature ovar ian insufficiency (POI) [40, 41]. Congenital lipoid adrenal hyperplasia is more common in Korea and other countries in Eastern Asia which is attributed to a founder effect with a specific variant, Gln258* [42]. Individuals with nonclassic lipoid adre nal hyperplasia may present with adrenal insufficiency [43]. Laboratory evaluation in patients with lipoid adrenal hyperplasia reveals low levels of all steroid hormones with no response to ACTH or human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) stimulation. ACTH and plasma renin activity (PRA) are very elevated. Adrenal sonography typically reveals mas sively enlarged adrenal glands due to choles terol ester accumulation. However, adrenal enlargement can also be found in patients with cholesterol side-change cleavage enzyme deficiency due to CYP11A1 variants [44]. Congenital lipoid adrenal hyperplasia also needs to be distinguished from familial gluco corticoid deficiency, which is due to ACTH receptor (MC2R) mutations and from P450 oxidoreductase deficiency [45]. ### 11.3.3 Cholesterol Side-Chain ### Cleavage Deficiency Cholesterol side-chain cleavage deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder due to lossof-function variants in the CYP11A1 gene located at chromosome 15q23-q24. This enzyme converts cholesterol to pregnenolone by performing three serial reactions including 20-hydroxylation, 22-hydroxylation, and scis sion of the C20–C22 bond. This enzyme is essential for adrenal and gonadal steroid syn thesis. Initially, this enzyme deficiency was believed to be incompatible with life due to the importance of fetal placental progester one synthesis. However, biallelic mutations are compatible with survival to term. Affected individuals typically present in the newborn period with hyperkalemia, hypo natremia, and hypotension. Due to impaired testosterone biosynthesis, infant males are ## PDF page 316 | printed page 303 undervirilized. Individuals with milder or nonclassic CYP11A1 variants have been described [46]. CYP11A1 variants have been reported among patients diagnosed with pri mary adrenal insufficiency [47]. ### 11.3.4 3-Beta-Hydroxysteroid ### Dehydrogenase Deficiency Following the conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone, the enzyme 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase converts pregnenolone to pro gesterone. Two isomers exist, type 1 and type 2. The type 1 isomer is expressed in the pla centa, brain, and liver. The 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2, encoded by HSD3B2, is expressed in the adrenal cortex and the gonads where it converts the Δ5 steroids (preg nenolone, 17-hydroxypregnenolone, DHEA, and androstenediol) to the corresponding Δ4 steroids (progesterone, 17OHP, androstenedi one, and testosterone). The genes encoding both enzymes are mapped to chromosome 1p13. Loss-of-function variants in HSD3B2 are characterized by glucocorticoid, miner alocorticoid, and sex steroid deficiencies [48]. Affected XY infants are typically underviril ized, whereas XX infants may exhibit mild virilization attributed to excessive in utero androgen exposure [49]. ### 11.3.5 17-Hydroxylase/17,20-Lyase ### Deficiency The 17-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase enzyme, encoded by a single gene, CYP17A1, catalyzes two distinct steroidogenic steps. The 17-hydroxylase activity converts pregneno lone to 17-hydroxypregnenolone and proges terone to 17-OHP. The other enzyme activity, 17,20-lyase, which is limited to the zona retic ularis, converts 17-hydroxypregnenolone to DHEA. In the zona reticularis, factors influ encing 17,20-lyase activity include P450 oxi doreductase and cytochrome b5. In human, 17-OHP is poorly converted to androstenedi one under usual circumstances. Deleterious variants in this gene, mapped to chromosome 10q24.3, are associated with glucocorticoid and sex steroid defi ciencies. Geographic localization of some variants presumably reflects ancestral founder variants [50, 51]. Affected XY infants are typically undervirilized due to in utero testosterone deficiency; female sex of rearing has been typical in the past. Sex ste roid hormone deficiency results in sexual infantilism and delayed puberty in both XX and XY individuals. Glucocorticoid defi ciency leads to increased ACTH secretion with the overproduction of adrenal cortical metabolites with mineralocorticoid activity such as 11-deoxycorticosterone and 18-hydroxycorticosterone. Affected individ uals may have low renin hypertension, hypokalemia, and hypergonadotropic hypo gonadism [52]. Individuals with nonclassic forms have been described [53]. ### 11.3.6 11-Beta-Hydroxylase ### Deficiency The enzyme, 11β-hydroxylase, encoded by CYP11B1 and located at chromosome 8q24.3, is expressed in the zona fasciculata and the zona reticularis. This enzyme is abundantly expressed in the zona fasciculata where it converts 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol and DOC to corticosterone. It is also expressed in the zona reticularis. Deleterious variants impair cortisol production resulting in increased ACTH secretion and conse quently increased production of 11-deoxy cortisol, progesterone, 17OHP, and DOC. Excessive DOC secretion can cause low renin mineralocorticoid-induced hyper tension and hypokalemia. Similar to 21-hydroxylase deficiency, precursors are shunted toward adrenal C19 steroids. Hence, prenatal virilization of the XX fetus occurs. Postnatally, both XY and XX individuals can develop premature pubarche, tall stature, and advanced skeletal maturation [54]. Individuals with mild variants have been reported [55]. ## PDF page 317 | printed page 304 ### 11.3.7 Aldosterone Synthase ### Deficiency Aldosterone synthase is a closely related enzyme encoded by CYP11B2, which is located at chromosome 8q24.3 and expressed only in the zona glomerulosa. This enzyme catalyzes 11β-hydroxylase, 18-hydroxylase, and 18-methyloxidase activities to convert DOC to aldosterone. Loss-of-function CYP11B2 variants are associated with miner alocorticoid deficiency, leading to hyponatre mia and hyperkalemia. Glucocorticoid secretion is unaffected. ### 11.3.8 P450 Oxidoreductase ### Deficiency P450 oxidoreductase protein is a flavoprotein that transfers electrons from NADPH to microsomal cytochrome P450 enzymes, including CYP21A2, CYP17A1, and CYP19A1. P450 oxidoreductase deficiency shows autosomal recessive inheritance. Lossof-function variants in the P450 oxidoreduc tase gene (POR) are associated with a spectrum of clinical phenotypes, depending on the specific POR variant [56]. In most cases, CYP17A1 activity, especially 17,20lyase activity, is affected leading to decreased sex steroid synthesis. The phenotype ranges from infants presenting with atypical genitalia to women with hyperandrogenism and men with gonadal insufficiency. In XY fetuses, POR deficiency impairs testicular testoster one secretion. In the XX fetus, the POR defi ciency causes steroid precursors to be diverted into the backdoor pathway with increased dihydrotesterone (DHT) production. In addi tion, POR deficiency impairs placental aro matase activity leading to increased fetal and maternal androgens. Mothers of affected fetuses may show progressive virilization. ### 11 Glucocorticoid deficiency typically occurs but is usually mild often requiring only addi tional glucocorticoid supplementation for physiologic stress. Some patients manifest the Antley-Bixler skeletal syndrome character ized by choanal atresia, craniosynostosis, midface hypoplasia, radiohumeral and/or radioulnar synostosis, and femoral bowing. The skeletal phenotype is attributed to decreased CYP26B1 activity, an enzyme that degrades retinoic acid. ### 11.3.9 Aromatase Deficiency ### (CYP19A1) The aromatase enzyme, encoded by the CYP19A1 gene located at chromosome 15q21.2, converts C19 androgens to C18 estrogens. This enzyme is expressed in ovarian granulosa cells, placenta, adipose tissue, brain, and testes. Due to alternative first exons and different transcriptional start sites with individual promoter elements, CYP19A1 expression is tissue-specific [57]. The pheno type of deleterious CYP19A1 variants includes maternal virilization during preg nancy and virilization of XX fetuses [58]. With the onset of puberty, affected girls typi cally present with delayed breast develop ment. They may develop ovarian cysts due to impaired estrogen synthesis with loss of nega tive feedback inhibition. Affected males pres ent with tall stature due to unfused epiphyses and low bone mass. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. ### 11.4 Other Steroidogenic Pathways ### 11.4.1 “Alternative Backdoor ### Pathway” 59 60 61 11.1 ## PDF page 318 | printed page 305 ### 11.4.2 11-Oxo-Androgens Due to chronic ACTH stimulation in patients with CAH, precursor steroids accumulate providing substrates for 11β-hydroxylase. Androstenedione is converted to 11-hydroxyandrostenedione. Circulating 11-hydroxyandrostenedione is peripherally converted to 11-ketotestosterone through the sequential activities of 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 and aldo-keto reductase family 1 member C3 (AKR1C3, also known as 17β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 5) [62]. In women with CAH, 11-ketotestosterone concentrations are directly proportional to testosterone concentrations. In men, 11-ketotestosterone concentrations are inversely proportional to testosterone concen trations because the 11-KT suppresses the HPG axis resulting in lower testicular testos terone secretion [1]. ### 11.5 Diagnosis Specific clinical features such as atypical external genital development, androgen excess, or delayed puberty suggest a defect in adrenal or gonadal steroidogenesis. A thor ough medical history is the first step in the diagnostic process. In some instances, nonin vasive prenatal screening (NIPS) results and/ or prenatal ultrasound findings are available. Discrepancy between these prenatal tests often prompts further evaluation. Specific questioning should ascertain fam ily history, maternal virilization during preg nancy, and fetal or neonatal losses. The family history regarding pubertal development should be established. After examination for other physical anomalies, careful examination of the external genitalia is necessary to answer the following questions. Are the external geni talia and gonadal structures symmetrical or asymmetrical? Are the gonads palpable? What is the size of the phallus? Where is the urethral meatus and vaginal orifice? Is there a single perineal orifice? The physical examination provides preliminary information regarding the possible diagnostic category and the most appropriate laboratory studies. When conflicting results from NIPS/ genetic testing are obtained and/or atypical genital findings are evident on the infant’s exam, consultation with a multidisciplinary Differences in Sex Development (DSD) team should be promptly arranged. Members of this team should include pediatric endocri nologists, pediatric urologists/surgeons, genet icists, neonatologists, radiologists, behavioral health specialists, and pediatric nurse educa tors. Some pediatric hospitals have standing DSD committees to discuss and facilitate the decision-making and management of children with atypical genital development, including infants with CAH [63]. ### 11.5.1 Infants For the virilizing forms of CAH, affected XX infants are usually identified due to atypical external genital structures. The subsequent diagnostic evaluation identifies the etiology and discovers potentially life-threatening con ditions such as mineralocorticoid deficiency. The infant should be referred to as “your baby” to avoid terms conveying a sex assign ment. Guessing the infant’s sex is inappropri ate. The parents need to be congratulated on the birth of their child and involved in the infant’s evaluation, especially when ques tions regarding whether the infant will be raised as a girl or a boy need to be addressed. Conversations with the parents should assess the parents’ health literacy and their level of understanding. Understanding and acknowledging the parents’ cultural back ground and religious views facilitates their full participation in this shared decisionmaking process. Members of the healthcare team can explain that it may take several days to obtain laboratory results. Parents can be informed that registration of the infant’s birth and naming of their baby can be deferred until conclusive laboratory results are available. ## PDF page 319 | printed page 306 A thorough physical examination of the infant is essential to assess for additional anomalies such as the skeletal anomalies asso ciated with P450 oxidoreductase deficiency. The length and width of the phallus need to be measured (both a clitoris and a penis repre sent phalluses). The mean stretched penile length is 3.5 ± 0.4 cm for full-term infant boys and 2.5 ± 0.4 cm for males at 30 weeks gesta tion [64]. Symmetry, pigmentation, and ruga tion of the labioscrotal structures should be noted. Posterior labial fusion can be estimated by measurement of the anogenital ratio. In normal XX infants, the distance from the base of the phallus to the posterior fourchette should be 2/3 of the distance from the base of the phallus to the anus [65]. Careful examina tion for palpable gonads should be performed because gonads may be located in the inguinal canal or the labioscrotal folds. The external genitalia score (EGS) can be a useful tool to convey the appearance of external genital development in preterm and term infants [66]. Infants with symmetrical atypical genital appearance and nonpalpable gonads suggest the possibility of a steroidogenic defect asso ciated with virilization. The most common etiology is 21-hydroxylase deficiency. Rarer disorders to consider include P450 oxidore ductase deficiency, aromatase deficiency, and 11β-hydroxylase deficiency, which are para doxically associated with salt loss in the new born. XY infants with 21-hydroxylase and 11β-hydroxylase deficiencies show normal male genital development with hyperpigmen tation of the scrotum, whereas XY infants with P450 oxidoreductase deficiency are typi cally undervirilized. Variants in HSD3B2 are associated with virilization of XX fetuses and undervirilization of XY fetuses. Disorders affecting mineralocorticoid synthesis are associated with a risk for acute adrenal insuf ficiency, necessitating prompt evaluation. Discordance between XY karyotype on NIPS and appearance of the fetal external genitalia on ultrasound may identify XY infants with StAR, CYP17A1, and CYP11A1 variants, whereas XX infants with these disorders of steroidogenesis have normal female external genitalia and typically present with acute adrenal insufficiency [67]. ### 11 Regardless of NIPS results, the infant’s karyotype needs to be immediately ordered. Chromosome studies should be supplemented with Y and X chromosome-specific FISH (fluorescence in situ hybridization) probes. In some institutions, results of Y and X chromosome-specific FISH tests may be avail able sooner than the full karyotype. Typically, infants with mineralocorticoid deficiency have normal electrolytes for several days after birth; hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, and ele vated plasma renin activity are usually evident 7–10 days after birth. Since 21-hydroxylase deficiency is the most likely diagnosis due to its higher prevalence, initial bloodwork should include 17-OHP, androstenedione, testoster one, LH, FSH, AMH, electrolytes, and plasma renin activity. Measurement of 21-deoxycortisol provides a reliable diagnos tic analyte to identify 21-hydroxylase defi ciency [37]. Elevated 17-OHP concentrations occur with both 11β-hydroxylase and P450 oxidore ductase deficiencies. Thus, if the 17-OHP value is not diagnostic for 21-hydroxylase deficiency, ACTH stimulation testing includ ing measurement of all steroids in the gluco corticoid and androgen pathways needs to be performed. For 11β-hydroxylase deficiency, 11-deoxycortisol concentrations are elevated [68]. Testing should be performed after 24–36 h of age to permit clearance of fetal ste roids. With P450 oxidoreductase deficiency, 17-OHP values may be mildly to moderately elevated with normal plasma renin activity. Progesterone, corticosterone, 18-hydroxycor ticosterone, 11-deoxycorticosterone (DOC), and 18-hydroxy-DOC may be elevated. ACTH stimulation tests typically reveal normal basal cortisol concentrations with insufficient ACTH-stimulated cortisol concentrations [69]. Progesterone, 11-deoxycorticosterone, and corticosterone concentrations are usually elevated in 17α-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase defi ciency. Clinical radioimmunoassays should be avoided because fetal adrenal steroids can cross-react interfering with assay reliability [70]. Specifically, 17-hydroxypregnenolone sulfate and 15β-hydroxylated compounds can ## PDF page 320 | printed page 307 cross-react in the clinical radioimmunoassay [71, 72]. Rather, blood samples, especially for 17OHP, should be sent to a reference lab equipped for small assay volumes that utilize liquid chromatography/tandem mass spec trometry (LC-MS/MS) for steroid hormone determinations. Ultrasound studies are helpful to ascertain the presence or absence of a uterus. Gonads may be visualized. Importantly, the inability to visualize gonads on ultrasound imaging of the fetus and neonate does not indicate gonadal absence. Gonadal structure, i.e., ovary versus testis, cannot be accurately resolved by ultrasound imaging. ### 11.5.2 Children and Adolescents ### 11.5.2.1 Hyperandrogenism The spectrum of congenital virilizing adrenal hyperplasias includes milder or nonclassic forms that present during childhood, adoles cence, and young adulthood. Typical features in childhood include premature pubic/axillary hair development, early onset of apocrine odor, increased linear growth velocity, and accelerated skeletal maturation. Adolescent and young adult women present with hirsut ism, irregular menses, and subfertility. Due to the nature of the symptoms of hyperan drogenism, an ascertainment bias favors the diagnosis of affected XX individuals whereas XY individuals are typically diagnosed through family studies. In some instances, random steroid hor mone concentrations are diagnostic. For children with premature pubarche, early morning 17OHP concentrations, whether measured by radioimmunoassay or LC-MS/ MS, greater than 200 ng/dL have greater than 96% sensitivity and 96% specificity to detect children with nonclassic 21-hydroxy lase deficiency [73, 74]. Nonetheless, when symptoms suggest CAH, ACTH stimula tion tests should be performed regardless of morning 17-OHP concentrations [75]. Thus, ACTH stimulation tests, including the determination of all steroids in the gluco corticoid and androgen pathways, may be indicated to confirm the specific diagnosis for most individuals. A novel approach using a machine-learning algorithm, single blood sample, and LC-MS/MS to obtain a quantitative assay of the circulating steroids has been reported to have good sensitivity and specificity to diagnose 21-hydroxylase deficiency in children with premature pubarche [76]. The Endocrine Society Guidelines sug gest that an ACTH-stimulated 17OHP above 1000 ng/dL is consistent with 21-hydroxylase deficiency [30]. ACTH stimulation tests may be helpful to assess the adequacy of cortisol response and determine when hydrocorti sone treatment can be limited to only stress dosing (see below). Using LC-MS/MS, ACTH-stimulated cortisol concentrations greater than >14 mcg/dL can be considered normal [77]. ### 11.5.2.2 Pubertal Delay As noted above, individuals with deleterious variants in genes involved in sex steroid syn thesis may present with pubertal delay. When evaluating a child, adolescent, or young adult, cognizance of the individual’s emotions and privacy needs is fundamental because the dis covery of a DSD may shatter the individual’s self-esteem and self-identity. Family history for pubertal delay and infertility should be sought. For individuals raised as girls, has any virilization or clitoro megaly occurred? A thorough physical exami nation including blood pressure, height, weight, and assessment of any dysmorphic features is essential, followed by a complete examination of external genital structures. As in the infant, are the external genital struc tures symmetric or asymmetric? Can gonads be palpated? Loss-of-function variants in CYP17A1 impair sex steroid synthesis, resulting in delayed or absent pubertal development in both XX and XY individuals. Partial or non classic variants for several steroidogenic enzyme genes are increasingly recognized [78, 79]. Evaluation for nonclassic steroidogenic defects such as P450 oxidoreductase defi ciency warrants consideration in women with ## PDF page 321 | printed page 308 infertility, ovarian cysts, and chronically ele vated progesterone and 17-OHP concentra tions [80]. ### 11.5.3 Genetic Testing Genetic testing has become an important diagnostic tool due to the increased availabil ity of next-generation sequencing. Genetic testing panels for DSD and whole-genome sequencing are increasingly available. The complexity of the CYP21A2 locus compli cates CYP21A2 genetic analysis [81]. At the present time, direct sequencing with CYP21A2-specific primers is usually needed to fully interrogate for CYP21A2 variants. Ascertaining parental genotypes can be help ful to confirm the parental origin of the spe cific mutations because some alleles can carry multiple deleterious variants. ### 11.6 Therapy and Monitoring ### 11 The paramount clinical objectives are to assure normal growth and development, including appropriate timing of pubertal mat uration. For patients with mineralocorticoid deficiency, avoiding acute adrenal insuffi ciency is a critical goal. To achieve these goals, the guiding therapeutic principle for CAH is replacement of deficient hormones and reduc tion of the overproduced proximal precursors. Much information related below pertains to the virilizing CAHs, especially 21-hydroxylase deficiency. ### 11.6.1 Treatment ### 11.6.1.1 Glucocorticoid Replacement ### Therapy Glucocorticoids have been the mainstay of treatment since the 1950s [82]. Despite numer ous therapeutic paradigms, it is important to acknowledge the caveat that current gluco corticoid replacement regimens fail to fully mimic the ACTH-cortisol circadian rhythm, as well as the HPA response to stress. Adequate suppression of adrenal C19 steroid secretion typically necessitates supra-physio logic glucocorticoid dosing and thus intro duces risks associated with excessive glucocorticoid exposure. These include adverse effects on linear growth, metabolism, and bone health. Hydrocortisone (Cortef®) is the most com monly used glucocorticoid in childhood. Due to its short half-life, hydrocortisone is typi cally dosed three to four times per day in doses ranging between 8 and 15 mg/m2/day. With a median hydrocortisone elimination half-life of 58 min (range 41–105 min), dosing less than three times daily is not recommended [83]. Reverse dosing with provision of the highest dose at night has been utilized. However, recent data fail to support the use of reverse dosing [84]. One pharmacokinetic/ pharmacodynamic model suggested that changing daily hydrocortisone administration to four times per day dividing doses as 38% at 06:00, 22% at 12:00, 17% at 18:00, and 22% at 24:00 resembles the circadian rhythm of corti sol and achieves better cortisol concentrations throughout a 24-h period [85]. In the United States, hydrocortisone is commercially available in 5 and 10 mg tablets. For infants and young children, the tablets can be crushed and mixed with food. For infants, crushed tablets can be suspended in tiny amounts of liquids such as breast milk or formula; the crushed tablets should never be mixed with formula in a bottle. Inconsistent dosing has been reported for compounded preparations [86, 87]. One newer hydrocorti sone formulation consists of granules covered with a flavoring to mask hydrocortisone’s bit ter taste which can be administered by placing on top of a spoonful of food. These immediate-release granules are available in packets containing 0.5, 1, 2, and 5 mg (Infacort®/Alkindi®, Diurnal Ltd.). Both preparations have been approved for use in the EU and the United States [88, 89]. ## PDF page 322 | printed page 309 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase activity, which means less cortisone is converted to cortisol. Hence, higher hydrocortisone dosing may be necessary during puberty [90]. Once linear growth has been completed, some adults prefer to switch to prednisone/prednis olone with twice daily dosing or dexametha sone with once-daily dosing. However, patients should be counseled that continued hydrocortisone treatment is associated with better bone mineral density and better meta bolic and cardiovascular outcomes than dexa methasone, prednisone, and prednisolone [91, 92] ( Table 11.2). ### 11.6.1.2 Mineralocorticoid ### Replacement Therapy Mineralocorticoid replacement therapy, fludrocortisone, is added for salt-wasting dis orders. Fludrocortisone (9α-fluorocortisol) is a synthetic mineralocorticoid that is structur ally similar to cortisol with the addition of a fluorine atom at the 9-position of the steroid structure. Its duration of action is approxi mately 18–36 h. Fludrocortisone is available in tablets which, similar to hydrocortisone tablets, can be crushed for administration in infants and young children. Mineralocorticoid therapy is recom mended for all infants with classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency. Due to relative mineralocorticoid resistance, antimineralo corticoid activity of elevated 17OHP concen trations, and a low sodium diet, neonates often require higher fludrocortisone doses. In addition, salt supplementation may be needed for some; recommended doses of a standard ized saline solution are approximately 4–8 mEq/kg/day in divided doses [93, 94]. The saline solution should be made by a pharma cist to assure accurate salt concentration. Frequent monitoring of blood pressure, elec trolytes, and plasma renin activity is essential for subsequent tapering of the fludrocortisone dose to avoid iatrogenic hypertension. Typical fludrocortisone doses for older children and adults range between 0.05 and 0.2 mg daily, divided into one or two oral doses. ### 11.6.1.3 Novel Glucocorticoid ### Therapies Multiparticulate technology was utilized to develop a modified-release capsule prepara tion consisting of an inert microcrystalline core coated with hydrocortisone and covered with an enteric coat layer (Chronocort®, Diurnal Limited, UK) [95, 96]. Although bed time dosing successfully blunted the excessive ACTH surge in the early morning, once-daily dosing was insufficient to prevent excessive androgen secretion during the late afternoon in adults [97]. A phase III multicenter clinical trial involving adults with CAH in which the Chronocort capsules (Efmody®) were taken before bed (11 PM) and upon awakening (7 AM) showed that the capsules were not superior to hydrocortisone when judged by 24-h 17OHP profiling. Nevertheless, individu als taking Chronocort had lower 17OHP and androstenedione concentrations during the morning and early afternoon [98]. In May 2021, the European Medicines Agency (EMA) approved Efmody® for patients with CAH 12 years of age and older. To better mimic HPA axis diurnal varia tion, continuous subcutaneous hydrocorti sone infusion therapy (CSHI) has been attempted. A phase II, open-label clinical trial involving eight adults with classic CAH showed improved androgen concentrations and quality of life compared to oral glucocor ticoid therapy [99, 100]. Yet, despite the attractiveness of CSHI in replicating physio logic glucocorticoid diurnal rhythm, this approach is complicated, labor-intensive, costly, and encumbered with numerous tech nical issues [101]. Corticotropin-releasing hormone type 1 receptor (CRHR1) antagonists are agents that interfere with ACTH secretion. These medications include the CRHR1 antagonists, tildacerfont (SPR001; LY2371712), and crinecerfont (NBI-74788). These medications do not obviate the need for glucocorticoid replacement and, if needed, mineralocorti coid treatment. Themes from these conversations often warrant repeti tion and, ultimately, need to be discussed with the patient using age-appropriate terminol ogy. Teaching parents how to administer daily hydrocortisone and the indications for stress dosing are essential. Parents need to be capa ble of administering parental hydrocortisone sodium succinate (Solu-Cortef®). Kits for parental hydrocortisone administration should be kept at home and wherever the child spends a lot of time, e.g., grandparents’ home. All patients taking glucocorticoids need to wear Medic Alert Identification tags ( www. medicalert.org). Parents need to educate fam ily members and school personnel regarding their child’s medical needs. Children with CAH should participate in all school events and activities. Regular follow-up evaluations to assess general health, linear growth, pubertal status, salt craving, BMI, and blood pressure are essential. Pertinent biochemical monitoring is important to assess hormone replacement therapy. For patients with classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency, regular monitoring of androstenedione, 17-OHP, testosterone, and plasma renin activity is necessary. Bone age X-rays are essential to monitor the rate of bone maturation. The goal is to titrate hor mone replacement to avoid features of Cushing syndrome due to overtreatment and signs of androgen excess due to undertreat ment. In some instances, children develop sec ondary GnRH-dependent precocious puberty. Treatment with a GnRH agonist may be help ful in this situation [104]. ### 11.7 Reproductive Concerns ### 11.7.1 Pregnancy This formidable topic warrants extensive dis cussion with adolescent and young adult women with CAH because many women with CAH have limited knowledge regarding their fertility potential [105]. Typically, women with 21-hydroxylase deficiency encounter difficulty achieving pregnancy and experiencing live births. Factors interfering with reproductive success include elevated progesterone concen trations, variations in urogenital anatomy, and decreased interest in procreation. Importantly, however, women with 21-hydroxylase deficiency need to be informed that they can deliver healthy infants with appropriate medical care before conception, throughout pregnancy, and during delivery. Elevated progesterone concentrations interfere with several aspects of female repro ductive function. Progesterone thickens cervi cal mucus hindering sperm motility, disrupting endometrium maturation, and impairing embryo implantation. At the level of the hypothalamus, a unified explanation for the consequences of increased progesterone and C19 steroid concentrations remains to be clar ified due to apparent opposing effects. Elevated progesterone concentrations disrupt pulsatile GnRH secretion leading to decreased LH pulse frequency and LH pulse amplitude, culminating in anovulation [106]. Yet, andro gens also impair the ability of progesterone to decrease GnRH/LH pulses resulting in increased LH pulse frequency and pulse amplitude, increased ovarian theca cell andro gen secretion, and polycystic ovary morphol ogy [107]. Other factors potentially contributing to the increased GnRH and LH pulsatility include the consequences of prena tal androgen programming on the hypothala mus and interference with neuroendocrine feedback due to persistently elevated postna tal C19 steroids [108, 109]. Vaginal and urogenital sinus anatomy with a smaller vaginal introitus often contributes to dyspareunia and decreased sexual satisfac ## PDF page 325 | printed page 312 tion [110]. Women with more severe genotypes are reported to be less interested in sexual activity and experience less satisfaction with their surgical interventions [111]. Selfperceived body image, self-gender identity, sexual intimacy preferences, and quality of life impact sexual activity. Despite these fac tors, the pregnancy rate in women with classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency who wished to con ceive is over 90% [112]. Most women with classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency are delivered by Caesarian section due to prior urogenital sinus surgery. Women with nonclassic 21-hydroxylase deficiency may benefit from glucocorticoid replacement before conception and during pregnancy to improve the likelihood of con ception and decrease the risk of miscarriage [113]. Using assisted reproductive technology, a limited number of pregnancies have been reported in other forms of adrenal hyperpla sia including 17α-hydroxylase deficiency, iso lated 17,20-lyase deficiency, P450 oxidoreductase deficiency, and congenital lipoid adrenal hyperplasia [114–117]. ### 11 ### 11.7.2 Prenatal Treatment In the 1980s, prenatal high-dose dexametha sone treatment was introduced to decrease virilization of the external genital structures of XX fetuses with virilizing forms of CAH. Dexamethasone was used because it “crosses the placenta” and was not inactivated by placental 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2. The usual dexametha sone dose is comparable to 60 times physio logic cortisol concentrations at that timepoint in gestation [118]. To effectively decrease pre natal virilization, dexamethasone therapy must be initiated by 6–7 weeks of gestation. Hence, all “at-risk” fetuses must be treated until prenatal diagnosis can be performed. At that point, treatment was continued only in affected XX fetuses [119–121]. Nonetheless, eight fetuses are exposed to prenatal dexa methasone early in gestation to treat one affected XX fetus. However, dexamethasone is a potent gene transcription factor that influences many developmental processes in the developing fetus, raising concerns about the safety of pre natal dexamethasone exposure. In humans, early gestation dexamethasone treatment has been associated with a slightly increased risk for cleft palate and lip [122]. In rodent models, prenatal dexamethasone exposure is associ ated with decreased birth weight and aberrant fetal programming effects on brain, thyroid, cardiovascular, metabolic, and reproductive functions [123]. Swedish pediatric endocrinologists and colleagues have provided the most extensive human follow-up data regarding prenatal dexamethasone treatment. Their initial studies showed negative cognitive effects, especially related to working memory in a cohort of exposed unaffected XX fetuses [124]. Adverse effects on pancreatic beta cell function and higher cholesterol and LDL-cholesterol were reported among CAH unaffected dexamethasone-exposed individuals [125]. Structural brain altera tions were observed in dexamethasonetreated unaffected adults; this finding was associated with increased methylation of the promotor region of the FKBP5 gene. Though no apparent cognitive changes were detected, potential explanations included a small sample size and brain plasticity enabling compensatory mechanisms [126]. These researchers also described changes in DNA methylation after prenatal DEX treat ment [127]. During early gestation, neurogenesis is an active complex process with neurons migrat ing to their cortical locations. Prenatal dexa methasone appears to alter this developmental trajectory. In a mouse model, even a single dexamethasone dose-administered midgestation led to changes in brain architecture, neurite complexity in the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus, and anxiety and depressivelike behaviors in the adult mice [128]. Returning to the Swedish experience, based on their findings including a large change in amygdala size, increased size of the superior prefrontal gyrus, widespread alterations in white-matter microstructure, and epigenetic changes, these researchers reinforce ongoing safety concerns regarding first-trimester dexa ## PDF page 326 | printed page 313 methasone treatment in CAH [126]. At pres ent, the Endocrine Society Guidelines state that prenatal dexamethasone treatment should be considered experimental and should only be performed through Institutional Review Board-approved research protocols [30]. ### 11.7.3 Gonadal Function in Boys ### and Men Boys and men with CAH may develop tes ticular adrenal rest tissue (TART) in their testes. TARTs are benign lesions that com press the surrounding testicular tissue. Typically, TARTs are painless, bilateral, and generally detected near the testicular medi astinum on imaging studies such as ultra sound [129]. Reported prevalence is approximately 25% in adolescents and 46% in men [130]. Elevated ACTH concentra tions are believed to contribute to the devel opment of TARTs. However, TARTs have been identified in men with well-controlled CAH and men with nonclassic CAH [131]. TARTs are not restricted to boys and men with 21-hydroxylase deficiency; they have been identified in individuals with CYP11A1, CYP11B2, and HSD3B2 variants [132]. Although this section is focused on TARTS, ovarian adrenal rest tumors can occur in ovaries [133]. TARTs can cause mechanical obstruction of the seminiferous tubules, as well as injury to Sertoli and germ cells. Azoospermia can occur. Treatments include optimization of glucocorticoid treatment. Testis-sparing surgery has been described, but gonadal func tion generally does not improve. Semen analy sis and sperm cryopreservation should be offered. Poorly controlled CAH is character ized by elevated adrenal C19 steroids, which suppress gonadotropin secretion, contribut ing to a secondary hypogonadotropic hypogo nadism. Boys with CAH and their families should be counseled about TARTs and the risks of infertility [134]. Screening for TARTs should begin in early adolescence for boys with CAH and be repeated every other year unless clinical concerns arise. Expression of adrenal-specific genes such as CYP11B1, CYP11B2, CYP21A2, and MC2R within this tissue supports the hypoth esis that TARTs are ectopic adrenal-like cells that migrate to the testes during gestation [135]. Recent detailed transcriptome studies of TARTs showed the greatest similarity to adult adrenal tissue followed by adult testis tissue with little resemblance to fetal adrenal and fetal testis. These findings suggest that TARTs may represent a mature adrenal-like cell exhibiting features of both adrenal and testicular cells [136]. TARTs need to be differentiated from Leydig cell tumors which can become malig nant. Unlike Leydig cell tumors which tend to be unilateral, TARTs are generally bilateral. TARTs tend to decrease in size with increased glucocorticoid dosing. ### 11.7.4 Contraception The discussion regarding pregnancy should be expanded to inform both women and men that CAH is not an effective form of birth control. Hence, contraception needs should be discussed. Effective options for women include combined hormonal contraceptives (pills, patches, or contraceptive rings). Progestin-only methods such as progesterone pills, Depo-Provera, and Nexplanon can be used despite the typically elevated circulating progesterone concentrations [137]. Adolescent and young adult men should be counseled that CAH does not typically cause infertility in men. All should be counseled to use barrier methods (condoms) to prevent pregnancy and STI transmission. ### 11.7.5 Delayed Puberty Defects in sex steroid biosynthesis may pres ent at birth due to atypical genitalia. Other affected individuals present with delayed puberty due to impaired sex steroid biosyn thesis. Laboratory studies typically showed hypergonadotropic hypogonadism due to sex steroid hormone deficiency. Individuals with CYP17A1 variants may have hypertension. ## PDF page 327 | printed page 314 For girls, estrogen replacement therapy can be initiated with transdermal estradiol patches. Commercially available matrix patches may need to be cut into halves or quarters to provide an initial low estradiol dose to mimic physiologic pubertal estrogen secretion. Over 12–24 months, the estradiol dose can be gradually increased. After 12–24 months, cyclic progesterone treatment should be initiated. Regimens for hormone replacement therapy include transdermal estradiol with cyclic oral progesterone, com bined estradiol-progesterone patches, or com bined oral contraceptives [138]. For boys with impaired sex steroid synthe sis and micropenis, low-dose short-term tes tosterone replacement therapy has been used to promote phallic growth [139]. Testosterone can be initiated to induce pubertal develop ment and maintain masculine features. Typically, testosterone esters are used and administered subcutaneously or intramuscu larly. Initially, low testosterone doses are used with a gradual increase in adult male replace ment dosages [140]. ### 11 ### 11.7.6 Urogenital Surgery During the early years of pediatric endocri nology in the 1950s, contemporaneous phi losophy specified that the appearance of the external genital structures needed to be con sistent with the sex of rearing. It was pre sumed that sex/gender identity was fluid at birth and was established by 18 months of age through interactions with the postnatal envi ronment. Thus, sex/gender assignment was typically based on the appearance of the external genital structures regardless of karyotype, gonadal histology, or internal gen ital structures. However, subsequent clinical experiences indicated that many factors such as prenatal hormone exposures and postnatal environment contributed to the development of gender identity obliging reexamination of the medical approach to individuals with atypical genital structures [141]. To address these concerns about the lack of patient/family involvement in medical decision-making, nondisclosure of diagnostic details, repeated medical examinations, and questions about urogenital surgery, the 2005 DSD Consensus Conference was organized. At this conference, DSDs were defined as con genital disorders associated with atypical development of chromosomal, gonadal, and/ or anatomic sex. Specific recommendations included: (1) postponing medically unneces sary interventions until the child is competent to participate in decision-making; (2) promot ing open and ongoing communication with families; and (3) providing holistic openminded multidisciplinary care [142]. In 2016, an expert panel including clinicians and repre sentatives from patient advocacy and support groups reassessed and updated the 2006 rec ommendations [143]. Most girls with classic virilizing CAH are born with virilized external genital structures characterized by an enlarged phallus (clito ris), fused labioscrotal folds, a single perineal opening, and a urogenital sinus. Feminizing genitoplasty involves clitoroplasty, the open ing of the vaginal introitus, and labioplasty. Current surgical techniques attempt to pre serve clitoral sensitivity. In the past, these operations were performed during the first years of life. More recently, the need and tim ing for these operations have been questioned due to the inability of the person to consent to surgery, unfavorable outcomes, and greater acceptance of human variation. Potential sur gical interventions should be discussed with families and affected individuals using a shared decision-making process [144]. ### 11.7.7 Quality of Life Individuals with CAH and other conditions affecting steroidogenesis can impact selfesteem. Parents often experience distress when their child is born with atypical genitalia or other chronic health problems. Parents should be encouraged to share the details of their health situation with children positively to reinforce the message that the child’s DSD is a part of who they are and should not be a source of shame. ## PDF page 328 | printed page 315 ### 11.8 Conclusion 2. paragraphs.text: Cushing syndrome (CS) refers to the constel lation of signs and symptoms resulting from exposure of the body to supraphysiologic lev els of glucocorticoids (GCs). CS was first described in “Minnie G,” a patient evaluated and reported by Dr Harvey Cushing, who presented with the “syndrome of painful obe sity, hypertrichosis, and amenorrhea...” amongst other findings [1]. Since then, CS became more prevalent when exogenous use of supraphysiologic doses of GCs was found to offer therapeutic effects in several disorders and their widespread use continues until today [2–5].
paragraphs.heading: 12.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: 12.1 A circadian rhythm of ACTH and cortisol secretion are necessary to maintain body homeostasis. ACTH usually peaks between 6:00 and 8:00 am while cortisol follows ACTH secretion closely with peak levels between 7:30 and 8:00 am. A nadir level for both hormones is detected around midnight [10, 11]. These time points are taken advantage of in diag nostic testing. An ultradian-like rhythm is also recorded throughout the day for these hormones with pulsatile secretion under the effect of stress and several other factors, which may also be considered upon diagnostic test ing, especially during CRH stimulation [10].

paragraphs.text: Endogenous CS is usually classified based on the level of ACTH, which further suggests different origins of hypercortisolemia. ACTHdependent CS resulting from pituitary ACTHsecreting adenomas is the most common cause of endogenous CS in older children and adolescents, while ectopic ACTH/CRH secre tion or other ACTH-secreting pituitary tumors (such as pituitary blastomas or carci nomas) are much rarer but may present with similar features. In younger children, less than 5–10 years old, endogenous CS is more likely to be ACTH-independent related to autono mous adrenal secretion of cortisol [16–18].
