paragraphs.text: CS caused by an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma (corticotropinoma), also referred to as Cushing disease (CD), is the most common cause of endogenous CS in children and ado lescents. Patients present at a mean age of 10.6–14.9 years, but younger patients with CD (as early as 5 years of age) have been described, especially in the setting of genetic predisposi tion [19]. Gender distribution depends on the pubertal stage, with reports of a higher inci dence in prepubertal males compared to females, which reverses after puberty [20, 21].
paragraphs.heading: Adenomas and Carcinomas

paragraphs.text: Corticotropinomas are monoclonal in nature, most often benign, and commonly small in size with a median diameter of 5 mm [22, 23]. Aggressive pituitary adenomas are rare in the pediatric population, but specific genetic defects and histologic subtypes, such as Crooke’s cell adenomas, may bear a higher risk for more aggressive behavior and resis tance to treatment [24, 25]. Pituitary carcino mas (PCs), defined as pituitary tumors with noncontiguous distal central nervous system (CNS) or other metastases, have only been described in limited case reports in the pediat ric population, with a mean interval of 10 years from first diagnosis to identification of metastatic lesions [25–31].
paragraphs.heading: Adenomas and Carcinomas

paragraphs.text: Pituitary blastomas constitute a separate his tologic type of pituitary tumor—these embry onal tumors are composed of mixed Rathke-type epithelial cells, small folliculostel late cells, and differentiated ACTH-secreting cells [32]. In 2014, de Kock et al. identified that many of the previously reported cases of neo natal “Cushing disease” were pituitary blasto mas, on review of histologic images and shared genetic defects in the DICER1 gene [33]. DICER1 or pleuropulmonary syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder presenting with pleuropulmonary blastomas, cystic nephro
paragraphs.heading: 12.4.2 Pituitary Blastomas

paragraphs.text: mas, Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors, multinodular goiter, and other findings. Pituitary blastomas, although rare even in patients with DICER1 syndrome, are a pathognomonic finding of the disease [33]. This diagnosis should always be considered in young patients (<2 years old) with ACTH-dependent CS and a pituitary tumor, and further screening of patients for other clinical features of DICER1 syndrome and genetic testing should be ordered.
paragraphs.heading: 12.4.2 Pituitary Blastomas

paragraphs.text: Ectopic CS (ECS) results from ACTH and/or CRH secretion from neuroendocrine tumors located outside the HPA axis. Although these tumors are very rare in the pediatric population, case reports and small case series have shown that tumors with the potential of leading to ECS in older children/adolescents may be found in the lungs (bronchial carcinoids), pancreas (pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors), and thy mus (thymic carcinoids) [34, 35]. In younger children (infants and early toddlerhood), ECS has been reported in association with tumors more prevalent in this age group, such as neuro blastomas, Wilm’s tumors, and others [36, 37].
paragraphs.heading: 12.4.3 Ectopic CRH/ACTH Secretion

paragraphs.text: ACTH-independent CS is the main cause of endogenous CS in children <5–10 years of age [16]. In young children, adrenocortical adeno mas (ACAs) and carcinomas (ACCs), com monly referred to as adrenocortical tumors (ACTs) due to the complex distinction of the two entities, are common sources of autono mous cortisol secretion [38]. ACTs are rare, representing 0.2% of all pediatric tumors, though incidence in Southern Brazil is signifi cantly higher [39]. The median age of presen tation of ACTs is 3–4 years old, and most of them exhibit autonomous hormone secretion, commonly involving adrenal androgen excess with or without cortisol excess [38].
paragraphs.heading: Tumors

paragraphs.text: Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia (BAH) may present as adrenocortical dysfunction and autonomous cortisol secretion. In some cases of BAH, ACTH secretion by the adrenals with paracrine effects has been reported, sug gesting that the term “ACTH-independent” may not accurately describe them and instead the term “adrenal CS” should be used [40].
paragraphs.heading: Hyperplasia

paragraphs.text: BAH-related disorders are commonly divided based on the size of the nodules reported, such as macronodular (most nod ules >1 cm) or micronodular (most nodules <1 cm). Primary bilateral macronodular adre nal hyperplasia (PBMAH) can be further classified based on the histologic presence or absence of internodular hyperplasia, as well as the expression pattern of surface receptors [41, 42]. Primary bimorphic adrenocortical disease where histologic evaluation reveals characteristic macronodules surrounded by a distinctive form of cortical atrophy is a term used to describe adrenal disease in neonatal CS seen in McCune Albright syndrome [43].
paragraphs.heading: Hyperplasia

paragraphs.text: Micronodular adrenocortical hyperplasia can be further classified as pigmented, such as pri mary pigmented nodular adrenocortical dis ease (PPNAD, commonly in the context of Carney complex, or isolated) or nonpig mented isolated micronodular adrenocortical disease (iMAD) [41]. Of note, secondary BAH is found in the setting of high ACTH secretion (such as in CD), which acts as a tro phic factor for bilateral adrenals and can even present as macronodular hyperplasia.
paragraphs.heading: Hyperplasia

Somatic genetic defects in pituitary corti cotropinomas are reported more commonly. Pathogenic gene variants in the hot-spot region of the USP8 gene were described origi nally in 2015 [55, 56]. Investigation of the fre quency of USP8 hotspot mutations in the pediatric population suggested that almost 30% of pediatric corticotropinomas bear this defect and may present with more aggressive behavior [57]. Somatic variants in USP48, BRAF, TP53, and other genes, are also reported in the literature [58, 59]. Finally, a subset of these tumors harbors large chromosomal aberrations that may contribute to more aggressive behavior [60].

ECS has a more variable and unclear genetic background mainly associated with the underlying source/tissue of ectopic ACTH/CRH secretion. Genetic defects in MEN1 and RET may be associated with neu roendocrine tumors and ECS. Somatic vari ants in genes such as TP53 and BRAF have also been reported.

ACTs are commonly associated with germline or somatic TP53 gene defects [61]. A founder effect is identified in the South Brazilian population, where the germline vari ant Arg337His is identified in more than 75% of all ACTs [62, 63]. Germline TP53 genetic defects are also linked with Li-Fraumeni syn drome (LFS), an autosomal dominant condi tion presenting with soft tissue sarcomas, osteosarcomas, adrenocortical carcinomas, and other tumors [62].

PPNAD is commonly associated with the Carney complex caused in most cases by PRKAR1A gene defects [64]. Patients with Carney complex also present with skin and cardiac myxomas, pituitary adenomas, thy roid heterogeneity, testicular tumors, and characteristic skin findings. PRKAR1A codes for the regulatory subunit 1-alpha of protein kinase A (PKA) and inactivating mutations of the gene lead to constitute activation of downstream signaling. In the same pathway, BAH and cortisol-producing ACTs have also been associated with genes coding phospho diesterases (PDE8B and PDE11A gene defects), enzymes that catalyze the hydrolysis of cyclic AMP (cAMP) and regulate PKA activation, and PRKACA, which codes for

the catalytic subunit of PKA [65–67]. In 2015, macronodular adrenocortical disease was linked to a new genetic locus, ARMC5, a tumor suppressor gene which explains half of the cases of PBMAH in the adult population [68]. Finally, neonatal adrenal hyperplasia may rarely be associated with McCune- Albright syndrome or Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome [43, 69].

Laboratory findings may include hypoka lemia (most common in patients with ECS), dyslipidemia, and glucose intolerance/diabe tes mellitus [70, 77]. The complete blood
count of patients with CS commonly shows elevated WBC, neutrophil and monocyte counts, and decreased lymphocyte and eosinophil counts [78]. Recently we described

neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) as a biomarker of cortisol effects on the immune system and an indirect marker of CS diagno sis [79]. Hypercoagulability, noted in adults, marked by increased von Willebrand factor and factor VIII and decreased aPTT, is also reported in the pediatric population, sug gesting that risk for venous thromboembolic events should be considered for every patient, though much more rare in children [80, 81].

Elevated midnight salivary cortisol repre sents the loss of the normal circadian rhythm of ACTH/cortisol secretion and is one of the earliest biochemical findings in (and evidence of) CS. Measurement of midnight or bedtime (late night) salivary cortisol should be per formed on two or more days and the cutoff for abnormal levels depends on the specific laboratory assay [84]. Midnight serum corti sol measurements are also very accurate in diagnosing CS, especially when performed under appropriate conditions, but require inpatient admission and are not convenient as a first-line screening test. When performed, a midnight serum cortisol concentration of >4.4 mcg/dL is highly sensitive and specific for the diagnosis of CS in children [85, 86].
paragraphs.heading: 12.8.1 Screening Labs

paragraphs.text: Elevated urinary-free cortisol (UFC) mea surement in a 24-h urine collection represents increased overall production of cortisol. UFC has high sensitivity (88–89%) and specificity (90–100%) for the detection of hypercorti solemia, but at least two or more, preferably consecutive, 24-h urine collections should be performed due to high variation and often inaccurate collection procedures [85].
paragraphs.heading: 12.8.1 Screening Labs

paragraphs.text: Additionally, measurement of serum and urine creatinine should be added and patients with renal disorders should be excluded due to possible falsely low urinary cortisol excre tion [87].
paragraphs.heading: 12.8.1 Screening Labs

paragraphs.text: DST is based on the negative feedback effects of GC at the hypothalamic and pitu itary level and can be completed in the outpa tient setting. The overnight 1 mg (or weight-based equivalent dose of 15 mcg/kg, max 1 mg) DST is not validated in children but the cutoff of 1.8 mcg/dL is widely adopted for the interpretation of the test in this patient population [83]. Dexamethasone is adminis tered orally at 11:00 pm, and serum cortisol is assessed at 8–9 am the following morning. DST is the preferred screening lab when an adrenal lesion is suspected. The low-dose 48-h dexamethasone test (LDDT) can also be used in specific conditions, such as in nonneoplas tic hypercortisolism [83]. During LDDT, 0.5 mg (or weight-based equivalent dose of 7.5 mcg/kg, max 0.5 mg) of dexamethasone is administered every 6 h for 8 doses. Although different versions of this test have been pub lished, a commonly performed protocol is administering the first dose at 9:00 am on day 1 of the test. Serum cortisol is measured at 9:00 am on day 3 and a level of >1.8 mcg/dL is considered abnormal [88]. In any DST, the dexamethasone level should be measured at the time of the cortisol assessment to ensure the serum dexamethasone concentration is within the expected reference range for each test.
paragraphs.heading: 12.8.1 Screening Labs

paragraphs.text: Once the diagnosis of CS is confirmed, an investigation of the source of hypercorti solemia should be pursued. In most cases, an ACTH level can direct further evaluation toward adrenal or nonadrenal-related condi tions. An ACTH level >20–29 pg/mL is usu ally suggestive of ACTH-dependent CS while a low or suppressed ACTH of <5 pg/mL sug
paragraphs.heading: of Hypercortisolemia

paragraphs.text: gests ACTH-independent CS [89, 90]. However, one should be aware of assay per formance, requirements for specimen collec tion, and the possibility of atypical causes of CS (episodic/cyclic) when interpreting the results.
paragraphs.heading: of Hypercortisolemia

paragraphs.text: Biochemical and imaging tests can be used to investigate the source of ACTH-dependent hypercortisolemia. The CRH stimulation test has typically been used in these cases. During this test, ovine CRH (oCRH, 1 mcg/kg, max 100 mcg) is administered through IV, and cor tisol and ACTH concentrations are measured every 15 min for 45 min. Increased concentra tions of ACTH (>35%) and cortisol (>20%) following administration of oCRH suggest a pituitary source of hypercortisolemia, whereas in ectopic tumors low or no response is reported [91]. If CRH is not available, a DDAVP stimulation test can be used. Corticotropinomas express ectopic vasopres sin V1b receptors, and thus stimulation of ACTH and cortisol with DDAVP is reported, with a similar pattern as observed with CRH [92]. Specifically, during the DDAVP stimula tion test, 10 mcg of DDAVP is administered intravenously, and cortisol and ACTH con centrations are measured every 15 min for 2 h. Increased concentration of ACTH (>35–50%) and/or cortisol (>20%) suggests a pituitary source of hypercortisolemia [92, 93].
paragraphs.heading: 12.8.3 ACTH-Dependent CS

paragraphs.text: High-dose DST (HDDST) has also been used to differentiate pituitary adenomas ver sus ectopic tumors [94]. Dexamethasone (120 mcg/kg, max 8 mg) is administered orally at 11:00 pm and serum cortisol is mea sured at baseline (8:00 am on the day of dexa methasone administration) and the following day (8–9 am). Suppression of cortisol by >69% is considered consistent with a pitu itary source. Caution should be used when interpreting the test in patients with hemor rhagic/necrotic adenomas, where suppression to dexamethasone may be lower than the cut off of 69% [95].
paragraphs.heading: 12.8.3 ACTH-Dependent CS

paragraphs.text: 23 When biochemical results are inconclusive or the pituitary MRI does not identify a con vincing adenoma, bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling (BIPSS) is considered the gold standard for the localization of the source of hypercortisolemia. BIPSS should be per formed in centers with experience in the pro cedure because several technical and anatomical factors can lead to inaccurate
paragraphs.heading: 12.8.3 ACTH-Dependent CS

paragraphs.text: results. BIPSS is based on ACTH measure ment before and after stimulation with CRH or DDAVP, and a gradient of central to peripheral ACTH of >2 at baseline and/or >3 after stimulation is considered suggestive of a pituitary source [83]. Although initial reports of BIPSS, suggested that an interpetrosal sinus gradient >1.4 suggested the side of the tumor, later studies reported that BIPSS results are not as accurate in predicting later alization [99, 100].
paragraphs.heading: 12.8.3 ACTH-Dependent CS

paragraphs.text: Recently a noninvasive algorithm avoiding BIPSS has been suggested in the adult popu lation [92]. Based on this approach, if the CRH/DDAVP stimulation test is suggestive of a pituitary source but the pituitary MRI does not clearly identify a pituitary tumor, whole-body CT could be performed and if negative, a presumed diagnosis of CD could be made without the need for BIPSS [92]. This is an option in centers where BIPSS is not available, considering potential risks from radiation exposure and a delay of the final diagnosis due to incidental findings on CT assessment.
paragraphs.heading: 12.8.3 ACTH-Dependent CS

paragraphs.text: When ectopic CS is suspected, neck-topelvis imaging with thin-slices CT (or in cer tain cases MRI) and nuclear imaging preferably with 68Ga-DOTATATE scan should be considered [83].
paragraphs.heading: 12.8.3 ACTH-Dependent CS

paragraphs.text: 101 In the case of ACTH-independent CS with reportedly normal adrenal CT, Liddle’s test should be performed to identify whether par adoxical stimulation of cortisol secretion by dexamethasone is present. This is a pathogno monic finding of PPNAD and could help with further treatment decisions [102].
paragraphs.heading: 12.8.4 ACTH-Independent CS

paragraphs.text: Nonneoplastic CS (previously reported as pseudo-Cushing syndrome) is the main differ ential diagnosis in patients where screening biochemical testing suggests hypercorti solemia but additional factors in the patient’s history increase the suspicion of a nonneo plastic source [103]. Causes of nonneoplastic CS include severe depression and other neuro psychiatric disorders, morbid obesity, uncon trolled diabetes, and alcohol dependence or withdrawal [104]. Screening labs in these cases may be abnormal, although in most cases do not significantly exceed the upper limit of normal, for example, UFC is usually less than 3–4 times the upper limit of the normal range. Additional testing should be considered in these patients. The DST combined with CRH stimulation has been used to evaluate patients. During the DST-CRH test, dexamethasone 0.5 mg (or weight-based equivalent dose of 7.5 mcg/kg, max 0.5 mg) is administered every 6 h for 8 doses starting at 12 pm of day 1. On the morning of day 3, oCRH (1 mcg/kg, max 100 mcg) is administered IV, and cortisol and ACTH concentrations are measured 15 min after administration. A cortisol concentration >1.4 mcg/dL is considered suggestive of endogenous CS. Modification of the cutoff for severe obesity may be appropriate [104, 105]. DDAVP stimulation test has also been studied as an alternative to the DST-CRH test for differentiation of nonneoplastic CS, where an increase of ACTH by >27 pg/mL is consid ered suggestive of endogenous CS [106, 107].
paragraphs.heading: 12.9 Differential Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: If none of these tests are informative, then close monitoring with repeat labs in 3–6 months is reasonable before further thera peutic decisions are made [83].
paragraphs.heading: 12.9 Differential Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Surgical resection of an identified tumor (pituitary, adrenal, or ectopic) is the first line of treatment whenever possible.
paragraphs.heading: 12.10 Management

paragraphs.text: Transsphenoidal microscopic or endo scopic approach of the pituitary is the pre ferred route for resection of pituitary adenomas [108]. A postoperative serum corti sol level <2 mcg/dL is currently accepted as the cutoff criterion for remission, but the tim ing of nadir cortisol is also important with earlier detection (<24 h) being a good prog nostic factor for durable remission [83, 109]. Remission rates depend on neurosurgical experience with rates up to 98% reported in high-volume centers [110, 111].
paragraphs.heading: 12.10 Management

paragraphs.text: Unilateral ACTs should be treated with uni lateral adrenalectomy. ACCs may require addi tional treatment with medical therapy, such as mitotane. BAH is often managed with bilateral adrenalectomy, however unilateral adrenalec tomy has also been studied in selected cases, especially in patients with macronodular disor ders [112, 113]. Bilateral adrenalectomy should also be considered in patients with CD or ECS if the primary tumor cannot be resected, or the patient has failed pituitary surgery and/or radi ation therapy, or when critical clinical deterio ration due to CS without improvement on medical therapy is present [111].
paragraphs.heading: 12.10 Management

paragraphs.text: After successful resection of unilateral ACTs, pituitary adenomas, or ectopic tumors, patients undergo an expected period of adre nal insufficiency. The period may differ based on the diagnosis and ranges from 6 months to more than 2 years [114]. Patients are thus dis charged after surgery on GC replacement, usually hydrocortisone given 2–3 times a day, on slightly supraphysiologic doses (10–12 mg/ m2/day) to manage GC withdrawal (GW) symptoms. We recommend adjusting the GC dose later to more physiologic replacement doses based on weight loss and tolerance of
paragraphs.heading: 12.10 Management

paragraphs.text: GW symptoms, though different tapering schedules may be used. Regular assessment of the HPA axis every 3–6 months with morning cortisol and/or the ACTH stimulation test should be ordered until full recovery of corti sol secretion.
paragraphs.heading: 12.10 Management

paragraphs.text: For patients where complete surgical resection is not possible or not successful, medical treat ment should be considered. Of note, although there are several medical options available, none of them is approved for children with hypercortisolemia at this time and caution should be taken when prescribing these medi cations.
paragraphs.heading: 12.10.1 Medical Therapy

paragraphs.text: If the patient does not achieve remission after surgery or is not a candidate for surgery or presents with recurrent CD, or mass effect from unresectable tumor is a concern, radio therapy should be discussed as an option.
paragraphs.heading: 12.10.2 Radiotherapy

paragraphs.text: Medical treatment in these cases should also be used as a bridge until the effects of radio therapy are evident. Conventional radiother apy (usually delivered in multiple fractions) or stereotactic radiosurgery (usually delivered as a single or few fractions) have been success fully used and up to 80% of patients will even tually achieve remission [115]. Delivery of stereotactic radiosurgery has been reported with various technologies, most commonly linear accelerator or gamma knife [116, 117]. There are fewer reports on the use of proton radiosurgery in CD, but a recent review of the literature and comparison of the various tech niques suggested similar efficacy and side effect profiles [118]. Elaborate follow-up inter vals for patients with CD after radiation have been recently recommended based on the clinical and biochemical control of hypercor tisolemia [119].
Recurrence rates are variable, and although lower in the pediatric population compared to adults, they range from 6% to 11% up to
paragraphs.heading: 12.10.3 Postremission Follow-Up

paragraphs.text: 10 years after remission [114, 120]. After recovery of the HPA axis, annual screening for recurrence should be considered in all patients, preferably with late-night salivary cortisol measurements [111]. In cases or recur rence, repeat TSS, radiation or medical ther apy, or a combination of these options could be considered based on imaging findings.
paragraphs.heading: 12.10.3 Postremission Follow-Up

paragraphs.text: Endogenous CS is a rare diagnosis in children and adolescents. ACTH-secreting pituitary adenomas are the most common cause of CS in older children and adolescents, while adre nal disorders are the main cause of CS in infants and younger children. When suspect ing CS, two or more of the screening labs should be evaluated. Several additional bio chemical tests and imaging studies can help in identifying the source of hypercortisolemia once CS is confirmed. Surgery is usually the first line of therapy for all types of CS, but medical therapy or radiation therapy may be considered in recurrent or persistent disease, or when surgery is not an option.
paragraphs.heading: 12.11 Conclusions

paragraphs.text: After consulting with the pituitary neurosur geon, a decision was made to proceed with transsphenoidal pituitary exploration where the neurosurgeon identified a microadenoma with the characteristic pseudocapsule. Histologic evaluation confirms diffuse ACTH staining with a breakdown of reticulin. The patient is discharged home on hydrocortisone replacement at a total daily dose of 11 mg/m2/ day. The case illustrates that a growth chart showing weight gain and height deceleration should urge physicians to proceed with bio chemical testing for hypercortisolemia.

Children with CS may not present with cen tripetal obesity nor have the characteristic thick dark purple striae described in adults. Most cases of CS in adolescents are due to a pituitary microadenoma, but the pituitary MRI may be negative in 20–30% of patients. Further biochemical testing and discussion in a multidisciplinary team with endocrine, neu rosurgery, and interventional radiology are often needed to decide the best next steps in patients’ management. A neurosurgeon with expertise in pituitary adenomas is recom mended in most cases.

Stratakis ### Contents ### 12.1 Introduction – 327 ### 12.2 The Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Adrenal Axis – 327 ### 12.3 Etiology – 329 ### 12.4 ACTH-Dependent CS – 330 12.4.1 ACTH-Secreting Pituitary Adenomas and Carcinomas – 330 12.4.2 Pituitary Blastomas – 330 12.4.3 Ectopic CRH/ACTH Secretion – 330 ### 12.5 ACTH-Independent CS – 330 12.5.1 Isolated Adrenocortical Tumors – 330 12.5.2 Bilateral Adrenal Hyperplasia – 331 ### 12.6 Genetics of CS – 331 ### 12.7 Presentation – 333 12.7.1 Clinical and Laboratory Findings – 333 ### 12.8 Diagnosis – 335 12.8.1 Screening Labs – 337 12.8.2 Evaluating the Source of Hypercortisolemia – 338 12.8.3 ACTH-Dependent CS – 338 12.8.4 ACTH-Independent CS – 340 ### 12.9 Differential Diagnosis – 340 ### 12.10 Management – 341 12.10.1 Medical Therapy – 341 © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2024 S. Radovick, M. CS was first described in “Minnie G,” a patient evaluated and reported by Dr Harvey Cushing, who presented with the “syndrome of painful obe sity, hypertrichosis, and amenorrhea...” amongst other findings [1]. Since then, CS became more prevalent when exogenous use of supraphysiologic doses of GCs was found to offer therapeutic effects in several disorders and their widespread use continues until today [2–5]. ### 12.2 The Hypothalamic-Pituitary- ### Adrenal Axis 12.1 6 6 7 8 9 12.1 A circadian rhythm of ACTH and cortisol secretion are necessary to maintain body homeostasis. ACTH usually peaks between 6:00 and 8:00 am while cortisol follows ACTH secretion closely with peak levels between 7:30 and 8:00 am. A nadir level for both hormones is detected around midnight [10, 11]. These time points are taken advantage of in diag nostic testing. An ultradian-like rhythm is also recorded throughout the day for these hormones with pulsatile secretion under the effect of stress and several other factors, which may also be considered upon diagnostic test ing, especially during CRH stimulation [10]. ## PDF page 340 | printed page 328 ### 12 ![Source image](../../figures/ch012_p0340_01.jpg) Unmatched source image; PDF page 340. Patients present at a mean age of 10.6–14.9 years, but younger patients with CD (as early as 5 years of age) have been described, especially in the setting of genetic predisposi tion [19]. Gender distribution depends on the pubertal stage, with reports of a higher inci dence in prepubertal males compared to females, which reverses after puberty [20, 21]. Corticotropinomas are monoclonal in nature, most often benign, and commonly small in size with a median diameter of 5 mm [22, 23]. Aggressive pituitary adenomas are rare in the pediatric population, but specific genetic defects and histologic subtypes, such as Crooke’s cell adenomas, may bear a higher risk for more aggressive behavior and resis tance to treatment [24, 25]. Pituitary carcino mas (PCs), defined as pituitary tumors with noncontiguous distal central nervous system (CNS) or other metastases, have only been described in limited case reports in the pediat ric population, with a mean interval of 10 years from first diagnosis to identification of metastatic lesions [25–31]. ### 12 ### 12.4.2 Pituitary Blastomas Pituitary blastomas constitute a separate his tologic type of pituitary tumor—these embry onal tumors are composed of mixed Rathke-type epithelial cells, small folliculostel late cells, and differentiated ACTH-secreting cells [32]. In 2014, de Kock et al. identified that many of the previously reported cases of neo natal “Cushing disease” were pituitary blasto mas, on review of histologic images and shared genetic defects in the DICER1 gene [33]. DICER1 or pleuropulmonary syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder presenting with pleuropulmonary blastomas, cystic nephro mas, Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors, multinodular goiter, and other findings. Pituitary blastomas, although rare even in patients with DICER1 syndrome, are a pathognomonic finding of the disease [33]. This diagnosis should always be considered in young patients (<2 years old) with ACTH-dependent CS and a pituitary tumor, and further screening of patients for other clinical features of DICER1 syndrome and genetic testing should be ordered. ### 12.4.3 Ectopic CRH/ACTH Secretion Ectopic CS (ECS) results from ACTH and/or CRH secretion from neuroendocrine tumors located outside the HPA axis. Although these tumors are very rare in the pediatric population, case reports and small case series have shown that tumors with the potential of leading to ECS in older children/adolescents may be found in the lungs (bronchial carcinoids), pancreas (pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors), and thy mus (thymic carcinoids) [34, 35]. In younger children (infants and early toddlerhood), ECS has been reported in association with tumors more prevalent in this age group, such as neuro blastomas, Wilm’s tumors, and others [36, 37]. ### 12.5 ACTH-Independent CS ### 12.5.1 Isolated Adrenocortical ### Tumors ACTH-independent CS is the main cause of endogenous CS in children <5–10 years of age [16]. In young children, adrenocortical adeno mas (ACAs) and carcinomas (ACCs), com monly referred to as adrenocortical tumors (ACTs) due to the complex distinction of the two entities, are common sources of autono mous cortisol secretion [38]. ACTs are rare, representing 0.2% of all pediatric tumors, though incidence in Southern Brazil is signifi cantly higher [39]. The median age of presen tation of ACTs is 3–4 years old, and most of them exhibit autonomous hormone secretion, commonly involving adrenal androgen excess with or without cortisol excess [38]. ## PDF page 343 | printed page 331 ### 12.5.2 Bilateral Adrenal ### Hyperplasia Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia (BAH) may present as adrenocortical dysfunction and autonomous cortisol secretion. In some cases of BAH, ACTH secretion by the adrenals with paracrine effects has been reported, sug gesting that the term “ACTH-independent” may not accurately describe them and instead the term “adrenal CS” should be used [40]. BAH-related disorders are commonly divided based on the size of the nodules reported, such as macronodular (most nod ules >1 cm) or micronodular (most nodules <1 cm). Primary bilateral macronodular adre nal hyperplasia (PBMAH) can be further classified based on the histologic presence or absence of internodular hyperplasia, as well as the expression pattern of surface receptors [41, 42]. Primary bimorphic adrenocortical disease where histologic evaluation reveals characteristic macronodules surrounded by a distinctive form of cortical atrophy is a term used to describe adrenal disease in neonatal CS seen in McCune Albright syndrome [43]. Pathogenic gene variants in the hot-spot region of the USP8 gene were described origi nally in 2015 [55, 56]. Investigation of the fre quency of USP8 hotspot mutations in the pediatric population suggested that almost 30% of pediatric corticotropinomas bear this defect and may present with more aggressive behavior [57]. Somatic variants in USP48, BRAF, TP53, and other genes, are also reported in the literature [58, 59]. Finally, a subset of these tumors harbors large chromosomal aberrations that may contribute to more aggressive behavior [60]. ECS has a more variable and unclear genetic background mainly associated with the underlying source/tissue of ectopic ACTH/CRH secretion. Genetic defects in MEN1 and RET may be associated with neu roendocrine tumors and ECS. Somatic vari ants in genes such as TP53 and BRAF have also been reported. ACTs are commonly associated with germline or somatic TP53 gene defects [61]. A founder effect is identified in the South Brazilian population, where the germline vari ant Arg337His is identified in more than 75% of all ACTs [62, 63]. Germline TP53 genetic defects are also linked with Li-Fraumeni syn drome (LFS), an autosomal dominant condi tion presenting with soft tissue sarcomas, osteosarcomas, adrenocortical carcinomas, and other tumors [62]. PPNAD is commonly associated with the Carney complex caused in most cases by PRKAR1A gene defects [64]. Patients with Carney complex also present with skin and cardiac myxomas, pituitary adenomas, thy roid heterogeneity, testicular tumors, and characteristic skin findings. PRKAR1A codes for the regulatory subunit 1-alpha of protein kinase A (PKA) and inactivating mutations of the gene lead to constitute activation of downstream signaling. In the same pathway, BAH and cortisol-producing ACTs have also been associated with genes coding phospho diesterases (PDE8B and PDE11A gene defects), enzymes that catalyze the hydrolysis of cyclic AMP (cAMP) and regulate PKA activation, and PRKACA, which codes for the catalytic subunit of PKA [65–67]. In 2015, macronodular adrenocortical disease was linked to a new genetic locus, ARMC5, a tumor suppressor gene which explains half of the cases of PBMAH in the adult population [68]. Finally, neonatal adrenal hyperplasia may rarely be associated with McCune- Albright syndrome or Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome [43, 69]. ### 12.7 Presentation ### 12.7.1 Clinical and Laboratory ### Findings 12.3 70 12.2 71 72 74 75 76 18 ## PDF page 346 | printed page 334 Table 12.3 Clinical and laboratory findings of patients with CS Clinical findings Anthropometric Height deceleration Weight gain Cardiovascular Hypertension Cardiopathy Musculoskeletal Decreased bone mineral density with or without fractures Proximal muscle weakness Skin Striae Facial plethora Easy bruising Acanthosis nigricans Hirsutism Abnormal fat deposition Neuropsychiatric Behavioral changes (compulsive behavior, overachievement tendency, irritability) Psychiatric disorders (depression, anxiety) Changes in cognitive function Sleep disturbance (difficulty falling asleep) Memory problems ### 12 Reproductive system Delayed puberty Irregular menses Immunologic Increased risk for infections Laboratory findings Anthropometric Hyperglycemia Hyperlipidemia Cardiovascular Hypokalemia Hypercalciuria Musculoskeletal Elevated liver enzymes Skin Abnormal WBC findings: – Elevated WBC, neutrophil and monocyte counts – Decreased lymphocyte and eosinophil count – Elevated neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio Abnormal coagulation factors – Increased von Willebrand and factor VIII – Decreased aPTT Laboratory findings may include hypoka lemia (most common in patients with ECS), dyslipidemia, and glucose intolerance/diabe tes mellitus [70, 77]. DST is based on the negative feedback effects of GC at the hypothalamic and pitu itary level and can be completed in the outpa tient setting. The overnight 1 mg (or weight-based equivalent dose of 15 mcg/kg, max 1 mg) DST is not validated in children but the cutoff of 1.8 mcg/dL is widely adopted for the interpretation of the test in this patient population [83]. Dexamethasone is adminis tered orally at 11:00 pm, and serum cortisol is assessed at 8–9 am the following morning. DST is the preferred screening lab when an adrenal lesion is suspected. The low-dose 48-h dexamethasone test (LDDT) can also be used in specific conditions, such as in nonneoplas tic hypercortisolism [83]. During LDDT, 0.5 mg (or weight-based equivalent dose of 7.5 mcg/kg, max 0.5 mg) of dexamethasone is administered every 6 h for 8 doses. Although different versions of this test have been pub lished, a commonly performed protocol is administering the first dose at 9:00 am on day 1 of the test. Serum cortisol is measured at 9:00 am on day 3 and a level of >1.8 mcg/dL is considered abnormal [88]. In any DST, the dexamethasone level should be measured at the time of the cortisol assessment to ensure the serum dexamethasone concentration is within the expected reference range for each test. ### 12 ### 12.8.2 Evaluating the Source ### of Hypercortisolemia Once the diagnosis of CS is confirmed, an investigation of the source of hypercorti solemia should be pursued. In most cases, an ACTH level can direct further evaluation toward adrenal or nonadrenal-related condi tions. An ACTH level >20–29 pg/mL is usu ally suggestive of ACTH-dependent CS while a low or suppressed ACTH of <5 pg/mL sug gests ACTH-independent CS [89, 90]. However, one should be aware of assay per formance, requirements for specimen collec tion, and the possibility of atypical causes of CS (episodic/cyclic) when interpreting the results. ### 12.8.3 ACTH-Dependent CS Biochemical and imaging tests can be used to investigate the source of ACTH-dependent hypercortisolemia. The CRH stimulation test has typically been used in these cases. During this test, ovine CRH (oCRH, 1 mcg/kg, max 100 mcg) is administered through IV, and cor tisol and ACTH concentrations are measured every 15 min for 45 min. Increased concentra tions of ACTH (>35%) and cortisol (>20%) following administration of oCRH suggest a pituitary source of hypercortisolemia, whereas in ectopic tumors low or no response is reported [91]. If CRH is not available, a DDAVP stimulation test can be used. Corticotropinomas express ectopic vasopres sin V1b receptors, and thus stimulation of ACTH and cortisol with DDAVP is reported, with a similar pattern as observed with CRH [92]. Specifically, during the DDAVP stimula tion test, 10 mcg of DDAVP is administered intravenously, and cortisol and ACTH con centrations are measured every 15 min for 2 h. Increased concentration of ACTH (>35–50%) and/or cortisol (>20%) suggests a pituitary source of hypercortisolemia [92, 93]. High-dose DST (HDDST) has also been used to differentiate pituitary adenomas ver sus ectopic tumors [94]. Dexamethasone (120 mcg/kg, max 8 mg) is administered orally at 11:00 pm and serum cortisol is mea sured at baseline (8:00 am on the day of dexa methasone administration) and the following day (8–9 am). Suppression of cortisol by >69% is considered consistent with a pitu itary source. Caution should be used when interpreting the test in patients with hemor rhagic/necrotic adenomas, where suppression to dexamethasone may be lower than the cut off of 69% [95]. ## PDF page 351 | printed page 339 96 83 97 12.4 83 98 23 When biochemical results are inconclusive or the pituitary MRI does not identify a con vincing adenoma, bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling (BIPSS) is considered the gold standard for the localization of the source of hypercortisolemia. Although initial reports of BIPSS, suggested that an interpetrosal sinus gradient >1.4 suggested the side of the tumor, later studies reported that BIPSS results are not as accurate in predicting later alization [99, 100]. Recently a noninvasive algorithm avoiding BIPSS has been suggested in the adult popu lation [92]. Based on this approach, if the CRH/DDAVP stimulation test is suggestive of a pituitary source but the pituitary MRI does not clearly identify a pituitary tumor, whole-body CT could be performed and if negative, a presumed diagnosis of CD could be made without the need for BIPSS [92]. This is an option in centers where BIPSS is not available, considering potential risks from radiation exposure and a delay of the final diagnosis due to incidental findings on CT assessment. When ectopic CS is suspected, neck-topelvis imaging with thin-slices CT (or in cer tain cases MRI) and nuclear imaging preferably with 68Ga-DOTATATE scan should be considered [83]. ### 12 ### 12.8.4 ACTH-Independent CS 12.4 12.4 101 In the case of ACTH-independent CS with reportedly normal adrenal CT, Liddle’s test should be performed to identify whether par adoxical stimulation of cortisol secretion by dexamethasone is present. This is a pathogno monic finding of PPNAD and could help with further treatment decisions [102]. ### 12.9 Differential Diagnosis Nonneoplastic CS (previously reported as pseudo-Cushing syndrome) is the main differ ential diagnosis in patients where screening biochemical testing suggests hypercorti solemia but additional factors in the patient’s history increase the suspicion of a nonneo plastic source [103]. Causes of nonneoplastic CS include severe depression and other neuro psychiatric disorders, morbid obesity, uncon trolled diabetes, and alcohol dependence or withdrawal [104]. Screening labs in these cases may be abnormal, although in most cases do not significantly exceed the upper limit of normal, for example, UFC is usually less than 3–4 times the upper limit of the normal range. Additional testing should be considered in these patients. The DST combined with CRH stimulation has been used to evaluate patients. During the DST-CRH test, dexamethasone 0.5 mg (or weight-based equivalent dose of 7.5 mcg/kg, max 0.5 mg) is administered every 6 h for 8 doses starting at 12 pm of day 1. On the morning of day 3, oCRH (1 mcg/kg, max 100 mcg) is administered IV, and cortisol and ACTH concentrations are measured 15 min after administration. A cortisol concentration >1.4 mcg/dL is considered suggestive of endogenous CS. Modification of the cutoff for severe obesity may be appropriate [104, 105]. DDAVP stimulation test has also been studied as an alternative to the DST-CRH test for differentiation of nonneoplastic CS, where an increase of ACTH by >27 pg/mL is consid ered suggestive of endogenous CS [106, 107]. ## PDF page 353 | printed page 341 If none of these tests are informative, then close monitoring with repeat labs in 3–6 months is reasonable before further thera peutic decisions are made [83]. ### 12.10 Management Surgical resection of an identified tumor (pituitary, adrenal, or ectopic) is the first line of treatment whenever possible. Transsphenoidal microscopic or endo scopic approach of the pituitary is the pre ferred route for resection of pituitary adenomas [108]. A postoperative serum corti sol level <2 mcg/dL is currently accepted as the cutoff criterion for remission, but the tim ing of nadir cortisol is also important with earlier detection (<24 h) being a good prog nostic factor for durable remission [83, 109]. Remission rates depend on neurosurgical experience with rates up to 98% reported in high-volume centers [110, 111]. Unilateral ACTs should be treated with uni lateral adrenalectomy. ACCs may require addi tional treatment with medical therapy, such as mitotane. BAH is often managed with bilateral adrenalectomy, however unilateral adrenalec tomy has also been studied in selected cases, especially in patients with macronodular disor ders [112, 113]. Bilateral adrenalectomy should also be considered in patients with CD or ECS if the primary tumor cannot be resected, or the patient has failed pituitary surgery and/or radi ation therapy, or when critical clinical deterio ration due to CS without improvement on medical therapy is present [111]. After successful resection of unilateral ACTs, pituitary adenomas, or ectopic tumors, patients undergo an expected period of adre nal insufficiency. The period may differ based on the diagnosis and ranges from 6 months to more than 2 years [114]. Patients are thus dis charged after surgery on GC replacement, usually hydrocortisone given 2–3 times a day, on slightly supraphysiologic doses (10–12 mg/ m2/day) to manage GC withdrawal (GW) symptoms. We recommend adjusting the GC dose later to more physiologic replacement doses based on weight loss and tolerance of GW symptoms, though different tapering schedules may be used. Regular assessment of the HPA axis every 3–6 months with morning cortisol and/or the ACTH stimulation test should be ordered until full recovery of corti sol secretion. ### 12.10.1 Medical Therapy For patients where complete surgical resection is not possible or not successful, medical treat ment should be considered. Of note, although there are several medical options available, none of them is approved for children with hypercortisolemia at this time and caution should be taken when prescribing these medi cations. 12.5 ### 12.10.2 Radiotherapy If the patient does not achieve remission after surgery or is not a candidate for surgery or presents with recurrent CD, or mass effect from unresectable tumor is a concern, radio therapy should be discussed as an option. ## PDF page 354 | printed page 342 ### 12 ![Source image](../../figures/ch012_p0354_01.jpg) Unmatched source image; PDF page 354. Consult the original caption. ## PDF page 355 | printed page 343 Medical treatment in these cases should also be used as a bridge until the effects of radio therapy are evident. Conventional radiother apy (usually delivered in multiple fractions) or stereotactic radiosurgery (usually delivered as a single or few fractions) have been success fully used and up to 80% of patients will even tually achieve remission [115]. Delivery of stereotactic radiosurgery has been reported with various technologies, most commonly linear accelerator or gamma knife [116, 117]. There are fewer reports on the use of proton radiosurgery in CD, but a recent review of the literature and comparison of the various tech niques suggested similar efficacy and side effect profiles [118]. Elaborate follow-up inter vals for patients with CD after radiation have been recently recommended based on the clinical and biochemical control of hypercor tisolemia [119]. ### 12.10.3 Postremission Follow-Up Recurrence rates are variable, and although lower in the pediatric population compared to adults, they range from 6% to 11% up to Case Study 12.2 10 years after remission [114, 120]. After recovery of the HPA axis, annual screening for recurrence should be considered in all patients, preferably with late-night salivary cortisol measurements [111]. In cases or recur rence, repeat TSS, radiation or medical ther apy, or a combination of these options could be considered based on imaging findings. ### 12.11 Conclusions Endogenous CS is a rare diagnosis in children and adolescents. ACTH-secreting pituitary adenomas are the most common cause of CS in older children and adolescents, while adre nal disorders are the main cause of CS in infants and younger children. When suspect ing CS, two or more of the screening labs should be evaluated. Several additional bio chemical tests and imaging studies can help in identifying the source of hypercortisolemia once CS is confirmed. Surgery is usually the first line of therapy for all types of CS, but medical therapy or radiation therapy may be considered in recurrent or persistent disease, or when surgery is not an option. ## PDF page 356 | printed page 344 Time (min) Right petrosal (RP) Left petrosal (LP) −5 66.7 455 0 62.3 326 3 251 646 5 106 855 10 168 779 After consulting with the pituitary neurosur geon, a decision was made to proceed with transsphenoidal pituitary exploration where the neurosurgeon identified a microadenoma with the characteristic pseudocapsule. paragraphs.heading: 13.7 Glucocorticoid Remediable Aldosteronism (GRA) – 361

paragraphs.text: Mineralocorticoid production in the adrenal cortex functions within the renin-angiotensinaldosterone (RAA) system. The RAA system acts in concert with antidiuretic hormone (ADH) secretion from the posterior pituitary to maintain normal intravascular volume and normal plasma osmolality, sodium, and potassium concentrations. This control of intravascular volume is necessary to maintain normal blood pressure, while the regulation of plasma sodium and potassium concentra tions is vital for the electrochemical gradients necessary for cell signaling. As discussed in Chap. 35, ADH is predominantly respon sible for controlling plasma osmolality through the regulation of free water excretion in the kidney, although, with significant vol ume loss, the body sacrifices osmolality to maintain extracellular volume. ADH defi ciency, as in diabetes insipidus, can result in hypernatremic/hyperosmolar dehydration, while overaction of ADH, as in the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH), causes hyponatremia/hyposmolal ity. The RAA system, through the regulation of sodium and potassium handling in the kid ney, regulates intravascular volume and the serum potassium level. Derangements of this system can lead to hypertension and hypoka lemia when overactive or to dehydration,
paragraphs.heading: 13.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and metabolic acidosis when underactive. The most common abnormality of the RAA system in children is mineralocorticoid deficiency in the setting of primary adrenal insufficiency. This is dis cussed in Chap. 10. This chapter will dis cuss more specific disorders leading to an underactive RAA system, as well as the disor ders within this system that lead to hyperten sion from an overactive RAA system.
paragraphs.heading: 13.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: In the kidney, the mineralocorticoid recep tor (MR, systematic name NR3C2) is expressed in the cells of the DCT, mediating this regula tion of sodium, potassium, and water handling of the DCT by the RAA system. Aldosterone is the primary ligand activating MR signaling in the DCT. It is produced exclusively in the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex due to the specific expression of aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2) in these cells [1]. Aldosterone syn thase contains enzymatic activity for 11β-hydroxylation, 18-hydroxylation, and 18-methyloxidation and thus metabolizes 11-deoxycorticosterone through corticosterone and 18-OH-corticosterone to produce aldoste
paragraphs.heading: 13.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: rone. (Note that 11β-hydroxylase, the gene product of the CYP11B1 gene, is responsible for the conversion of 11-deoxycortisol to corti sol in the zona fasciculata; 11β-hydroxylase conversion of deoxycorticosterone (DOC) to corticosterone in the zona glomerulosa is medi ated by aldosterone synthase.) The aldosterone precursors 11-deoxycorticosterone and corti costerone can also bind to the MR, albeit with low affinity. Therefore, at the usual physiologic circulating concentrations, these compounds do not activate MR signaling.
paragraphs.heading: 13.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: SGK1, while the genomic actions of the MR increase SGK1 expression (before increasing ENaC expression). In addition to increasing the expression of ENaC, the SGK1 kinase increases the activity of ENaC [7]. The final effect of aldosterone action on the cells of the DCT is an increase in sodium and water reab sorption from urine and an increase in potas sium secretion into urine. Aldosterone also stimulates hydrogen ion secretion into urine through both direct and indirect mechanisms.

Aldosterone production is stimulated by the renin-angiotensin system and by hyperka lemia. The juxtaglomerular cells (JG cells) in the afferent arteriole in the kidney secrete renin into the systemic circulation in response to a fall in renal perfusion pressure. This occurs with a decrease in the systemic blood pressure, with a change to an upright posture, and with a decrease in the serum sodium con centration. Renin is also secreted in response to an increase in the sympathetic nervous sys tem input to the kidney. Renin catalyzes the cleavage of angiotensinogen (produced con stitutively in the liver) into angiotensin I. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), pro duced constitutively in the lung, then cleaves angiotensin I into angiotensin II. Angiotensin II binds to the AT1 receptor in the adrenal cortex, stimulating aldosterone production. An elevated serum potassium level directly stimulates aldosterone production in the adre nal cortex, independent of the RAA system. ACTH also can stimulate aldosterone produc tion. However, since the RAA system is the primary regulator of aldosterone production, ACTH deficiency does not result in mineralo corticoid deficiency.

Newborns have relative insensitivity to aldosterone, thought to be due to either a decreased expression of mineralocorticoid receptors [8] or a decrease in postreceptor sig naling [9]. This, as well as lower sodium intake, leads to higher renin and aldosterone levels in neonates and infants than in older children [10]. Disorders of mineralocorticoid action include disorders of insufficient action and disorders of excess action. These are listed below. The consequences of impaired or excess mineralocorticoid action can be pre

dicted from the known actions of aldosterone. Disorders of impaired mineralocorticoid action typically result in hyponatremia, dehy dration, and hyperkalemia. These patients also typically have metabolic acidosis from impaired acid secretion. Primary adrenal insufficiency, with impaired production of all adrenal steroid hormones, is discussed in Chap. 10. Certain forms of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) result in miner alocorticoid deficiency, as discussed in Chap. 11. Disorders of excess mineralocor ticoid action typically result in hypertension with hypokalemia and can have a metabolic alkalosis. The hypertensive forms of CAH are discussed in Chap. 11.
