paragraphs.heading: ↓TSH ↑TSH

paragraphs.text: Also problematic is the hospital manage ment systems’ implementation of early dis charge. Infants discharged from the hospital before 48 h of life often undergo screening on day of life 1, leading to a high rate of false positives in those infants who have a physiologic postnatal rise in TSH [14]. After birth, as a physiological response to temper ature change, TSH concentration increases in order to stimulate neonatal rise in T4 and T3. TSH values peak between 70 and 100 mIU/L within 1 h of life. Thyrotropin values progressively decline over the follow ing 48 h of life, while T4 and T3 values nor malize by 3–5 days [15]. As noted in the discussion of primary T4 assays, TSH surge is blunted in the preterm and V/LBW infants. In term infants, early hospital dis charge has increased the ratio of false-posi tive TSH elevations from 3:1 to 5:1. Recommendations suggest that NBS be per formed at 48 h of age; however, the optimal time to obtain a primary TSH NBS is around 3–5 days of life [4].
paragraphs.heading: ↓TSH ↑TSH

paragraphs.text: Recent data show that primary TSH screening is more cost-effective in reducing false-positive and false-negative cases for mass screening despite the dual TSH and T4 approach theo retically being the ideal method of screening [16]. Dual TSH and T4 screening is expensive and not practical in most countries. As with any screening, the value of identifying an infant with CH must be balanced against the cost of screening normal newborns. NBS is expensive and not weighed in the costs are the psychosocial burdens created by screening for
paragraphs.heading: Method

paragraphs.text: nondisease [17]. Given recall rates of 0.05%, over 1000 children will undergo further diag nostic testing with negative results for each child with true-positive results. Even more costly are children without true hypothyroid ism who undergo therapeutic intervention. Not limited to monetary disadvantages are the psychosocial burdens associated with non disease, including, but not limited to, parental anxiety, aversion of the child to repeat intrave nous catheters, and risks of therapeutic side effects.
paragraphs.heading: Method

paragraphs.text: NBS test results must be communicated rapidly back to the physician or hospital iden tified on the screening filter paper card. The responsibility for transmission of these results rests with the authority or agency that per formed the test. In general, when an abnormal screening result is found, the responsible phy sician is notified immediately so that he or she can arrange for follow-up testing. Screening test results should be entered into the patient’s record. If the informed physician is no longer caring for or cannot locate the infant, he or she should notify the NBS laboratory imme diately. In such situations, the local health department is often helpful in locating these infants to ensure that they are not lost to fol low-up [14, 18, 19].
paragraphs.heading: 14.1.5 Confirmatory Results

paragraphs.text: Genetic predisposition to thyroid dysgen esis may in part explain the observed higher incidence of CH among certain ethnic groups [21]. Mutations in developmental genes, which play important roles in embryogenesis and developmental cell migrations, contribute to genetic predisposition to thyroid dysgenesis. Mutations in genes (such as TTF-1, TTF-2, and PAX8) have been associated with devel opmental anomalies including thyroid dys genesis and likely account for the higher incidence of CH in Hispanic patients [3].

RTH are rarely diagnosed in the newborn period, given the propensity for normal TSH values and elevated T4 values. The thyrotro pin receptor (TSHR) is also involved in thy roid organogenesis. Thus, mutations in the TSHR gene can cause CH as well.

Except in geographic regions of iodine defi ciency, the diagnosis of CH is rarely made on physical examination. In industrialized coun tries with a high emphasis on prenatal care, signs and symptoms of CH are rarely appar ent. Unfortunately, it is within this newborn period when missing clinical features of hypo thyroidism lend to irreversible brain damage, thus the importance of newborn screening [7, 18, 19].

Infants with CH are often described as “good babies” as they sleep well and cry infre quently. As with any newborn, a complete history, including maternal thyroid status and family history, should be obtained, and careful physical examination must be per formed.

Laboratory assessment of thyroid function provides a sensitive and specific methodology for diagnosing CH. The most significant con founder in the confirmation of CH is its tran sient form. The most common form of transient hypothyroidism worldwide is iodine deficiency. Iodine deficiency must be consid ered in high-risk populations such as those from underdeveloped countries, infants of mothers whose diets are limited in meats (vegans) or iodinated salts (sea salt consum ers), and infants whose condition limits gas tric intake of nutrients (total parenteral nutrition-dependence). Even in infants with transient neonatal hypothyroidism, treat ment is recommended if certain diagnostic criteria are met. If newborns continue to exhibit persistent TSH elevation with normal f/T4 after 4–6 weeks of life, treatment is rec ommended [19].
paragraphs.heading: 14.4 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: A common cause of transient neonatal hypothyroidism in developed countries is pre maturity (gestational age <37 weeks). Temporary thyroid dysfunction also occurs in infants who are born 10% below expected body weight (i.e., V/LBW), ill neonates admit ted to the neonatal intensive care unit, neo nates who are discharged within the first 24 h of life, and cohorts of multiple births, includ ing monozygotic twins. In these special popu lations, a repeat NBS specimen should be
paragraphs.heading: 14.4 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: collected at about 2 weeks of age or 2 weeks after the first screening test was carried out [7], at 4 weeks later [18, 19], and at 36 weeks corrected gestational age [10].
paragraphs.heading: 14.4 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: To confirm the diagnosis of permanent CH, the European Society for Pediatric Endocrinology (ESPE) recommends perform ing imaging studies to determine its specific etiology [7]. The American Academy of Pediatrics denotes that imaging before the age of 3 years is unlikely to change clinical man agement [18, 19]. Diagnostic imaging may be helpful in cases in which CH diagnosis is not clear [18, 19]. Treatment may be altered based on results, especially if clinical evaluation is also consistent with CH. The option to initi ate, hold, and potentially stop treatment may be based on imaging results as well. When the cause of abnormal thyroid studies cannot be determined as either transient or permanent, both scintigraphy and ultrasound can be con sidered in neonates with abnormal TSH val ues. Of course, the time interval to imaging should not delay treatment in any circum stance in which there is a high degree of suspi cion of thyroid disease. Even in circumstances in which differentiation between transient and permanent CH is blurred, imaging can always be deferred until the child reaches the age of 3 years. At 3 years, neuronal migration and myelination are fairly advanced; thus risk of neurocognitive dysfunction as a result of thy roid hormone withdrawal at age 3 years is lower than what would have been expected in the first 3 years of life [9].
paragraphs.heading: 14.4 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: In the era of genetic testing, several muta tions have been discovered which account for some cases of CH. Genetic studies for muta tions in thyroid hormone synthesis can con firm inborn errors of thyroid hormone biosynthesis [28]. Despite the importance of confirming CH in permanent cases, the costs of genetic testing do not yet outweigh the ben efits. The exceptions include families in which multiple siblings are affected. In these cases, genetic counseling is suggested to ensure fam ilies are aware of potential risks in future pregnancies.
paragraphs.heading: 14.4 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Once the diagnosis of CH is confirmed, levo thyroxine replacement is recommended as the treatment of choice. There is no place in pediatric thyroid disease for formularies including T3 treatment or desiccated animal product. Treatment with levothyroxine (crushed tablets or branded liquid) should be started as soon as possible. Goal for initia tion of treatment is within the first 2 weeks of life. However, given that some abnormal screenings require repeated measurements or further diagnostic testing, treatment should begin once testing confirms the disease. Initial treatment is with levothyroxine 10–15 mg/kg/day; however, several factors interfere with thyroid hormone absorption. Severity of the disease also affects the choice of replacement dose. More severe disease, such as athyreosis, indicates the use of doses at the upper end of the treatment scale (15 mg/kg/day), while the same dose in infants affected by defects in thyroid hor mone synthesis may lead to overtreatment. Goal of all therapy is to normalize thyroid hormone function [7, 18, 19].
paragraphs.heading: 14.5 Treatment

paragraphs.text: Based on TSH concentration, the dosage of levothyroxine is adjusted. Use of serum fT4 can be adjunctive in ensuring an appro priate clinical response. In the first 3 years, serum total T4 and/or fT4 values should be in the upper half of the reference range, and serum TSH levels should be between 0.5 and 2.0 mIU/L [14, 18, 19]. Relative pituitary resistance may delay the normalization of serum TSH, resulting in a normal or increased serum T4 concentration with an inappropri ately high TSH level. In these cases, the dose should be titrated based on the TSH value, after first ruling out nonadherence to treat ment.
paragraphs.heading: 14.5 Treatment

paragraphs.text: Normalizing thyroid function may be challenging in the first year of life. Despite tightened Federal Drug Administration regu lations, levothyroxine preparations can vary by up to 12% in the amount of active hor mone, even within the brand [29]. Guidelines
paragraphs.heading: 14.5 Treatment

paragraphs.text: recommend brand name levothyroxine; how ever, the cost can be prohibitive for most fam ilies whose formularies require generic prescriptions [7]. Children initiated on generic formulations should remain on generic, and those started on brand name formulations should remain on brand. If there is any change in the thyroid hormone manufacturer, followup laboratory testing should be ordered to ensure euthyroidism [18, 19].
paragraphs.heading: 14.5 Treatment

paragraphs.text: Other factors affecting thyroid hormone dosing include absorption in the gastrointesti nal tract, ranging from 70% to 80%, hence the pharmaceutical company’s recommendations for consuming levothyroxine on an empty stomach [30]. Practically, however, infants are in a perpetual postprandial state. Adhering to specific preprandial timing of medication administration has been associated with lower medication adherence [31]. Therefore, medica tion can be given with or without food as long as there remains consistency with each dose. Dosing can be adjusted based on the most realistic mode of consumption.
paragraphs.heading: 14.5 Treatment

Rapid normalization of thyroid hormone lev els (within the first 2 weeks after treatment initiation) and maintenance of relatively higher fT4 concentrations during the first year of life lead to better intellectual outcomes. However, overtreatment has also been associ ated with lower intelligence quotients in chil dren with CH [32].

Thyroid function testing should be per formed every 1–2 months for the first 6 months of life, 2–3 months in the latter half of the first year of life, and subsequently every 3–4 months until the age of 3 years. Perform thyroid function testing approximately 4–6 weeks after dose changes or changes in brand or administration route. If clinical symptoms of thyroid disease develop, repeat testing is indicated even if normal previously.

Neurocognitive development and growth are dependent on sufficient serum thyroid hor mone concentration in fetal and early child development. Iodine is essential for thyroid hormone production, and deficiency (hypo thyroidism) can affect maternal, fetal, and postnatal thyroid function. Hypothyroidism remains the leading cause worldwide of treat able intellectual disability. At birth, there may be few signs or symptoms of hypothyroidism, making NBS for thyroid function a critical step in detecting CH. Interpretation of NBS in various clinical settings may alter diagnosis and treatment. Once identified early and treated appropriately. CH becomes a treatable condition with normal or near-normal devel opmental outcomes [3].

Rose Contents 14.1 Introduction and Background Information – 372 14.1.1 Newborn Screening – 372 14.1.2 Primary T4, Secondary TSH NBS Method – 372 14.1.3 Primary TSH with and Without T4 NBS Method – 373 14.1.4 Dual TSH and T4 NBS Method – 374 14.1.5 Confirmatory Results – 374 14.2 Etiology – 375 14.3 Clinical Presentation – 378 14.4 Diagnostic Evaluation – 378 14.5 Treatment – 379 14.6 Case Studies – 380 14.7 Summary – 382 References – 382 © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2024 S. Radovick, M. Misra (eds.), Pediatric Endocrinology, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-66296-6_14 ## PDF page 383 | printed page 372 Key Points 5 Congenital hypothyroidism is a devas tating yet preventable cause of intellec tual disability. 5 Newborn screening for congenital hypothyroidism is crucial for the pre vention of long-term impairments in child development. 5 Interpretation of laboratory results requires an understanding of newborn screening methodologies and the timing of data collection. 5 Optimal treatment of congenital hypo thyroidism requires timely confirmation of diagnosis and adequate medication administration. ### 14.1 Introduction and Background ### Information ### 14.1.1 Newborn Screening Most infants born with CH have no appre ciable physical stigmata of the disease; there fore, screening to detect which newborns are at risk for thyroid disease is paramount. The introduction of NBS in the 1970s has decreased the incidence of untreated CH although prevalence rates have increased [1]. Prevalence of CH ranges from 1:1404 to 1:4149 depending on region and ethnicity [2]. Before screening, only one-third of hypothy roid infants were clinically detected before 3 months of age, leading children to suffer from severe intellectual disability, including language, learning, and coordination delays. With the introduction of screening, the age of detection has steadily declined. In the early phases of NBS, the target was to identify and initiate treatment by 2 months of life. Currently, with rapid specimen transport of newborn specimens collected on average day of life 2, and advances in technology which allow rapid thyroxine (T4) and thyrotropin (TSH) analysis, many screening programs detect and initiate treatment within 1–2 weeks ### 14 of age, allowing more normal developmental outcomes [3]. NBS can be implemented in sev eral ways, some more sensitive than others. In general, an appropriate interpretation of TSH and/or T4 values, be it total T4 or free T4 (fT4), is required to appropriately diagnose CH. ### 14.1.2 Primary T4, Secondary TSH ### NBS Method A common method for screening newborns for CH consists of collecting blood spots on filter paper for the whole blood total T4. Subsequently, TSH screening occurs only in a select group, based on low T4 values, often the lowest 3rd to 10th percentiles [4]. Using this methodology, the specific numeric cutoff may vary from week to week. The benefits of pri mary T4 screening are its sensitivity for the detection of newborns with hypothalamicpituitary hypothyroidism. Known as central hypothyroidism, delayed detection of this form of hypothyroidism also results in devel opmental deficits. In this form of pituitary dysfunction, TSH is not elevated, often nor mal; therefore, primary TSH screening would not detect this abnormality. Even more pro found is the high prevalence of coexistent pituitary hormone deficiencies such as adre nocorticotropic (ACTH) and growth hor mone deficiency. Isolated central hypothyroidism is rare (incidence 1:65,000); therefore, if central hypothyroidism is detected, consequences such as hypoglycemia and adrenal crisis can be averted [5]. Primary T4 assays offer a significant benefit in detect ing a rare but high-risk thyroid disease. Unfortunately, primary T4 NBS is non specific in other high-risk populations such as low and very low birth weight infants (V/ LBW). Prematurity also lowers the efficacy of the primary T4 assay. Low T4 concentrations in V/LBW and premature infants increase the number of TSH assays by 10% [6]. Low total T4 concentrations may result from deficient protein binding of thyroid hormones, the pri mary cause of transient neonatal hypothy roidism in premature infants and in infants ## PDF page 384 | printed page 373 with T4-binding globulin (TBG) deficiency. Transient hypothyroidism also occurs as a result of maternal TSH receptor-blocking antibodies, exposure to antithyroid medica tions during pregnancy, and iodine deficiency or excess [4]. T4 screening in these infants leads to unnecessary testing and possible treatment in children who require no interven tion. ### 14.1.3 Primary TSH ### with and Without T4 NBS Method Used in most developed countries, the pri mary TSH screening is overall a better screen ing test than the T4/TSH screening [7]. TSH is a suitable indicator of iodine deficiency [8] and a sensitive marker of pituitary triiodothy ronine (T3) concentrations. Intraneural con centration of T3 (derived from the intracellular conversion of T4 to T3) is essential for neuro genesis, neuronal migration, neuronal and glial cell differentiation, as well as myelination in the developing fetus [9]. These higher TSH values can mislead clinicians to diagnose thyroid disease in euthyroid patients. In a TSH/T4 program, T4 assays increase by 6% given the higher number of TSH eleva tions [6]. Also problematic is the hospital manage ment systems’ implementation of early dis charge. Infants discharged from the hospital before 48 h of life often undergo screening on day of life 1, leading to a high rate of false positives in those infants who have a physiologic postnatal rise in TSH [14]. After birth, as a physiological response to temper ature change, TSH concentration increases in order to stimulate neonatal rise in T4 and T3. TSH values peak between 70 and 100 mIU/L within 1 h of life. Thyrotropin values progressively decline over the follow ing 48 h of life, while T4 and T3 values nor malize by 3–5 days [15]. As noted in the discussion of primary T4 assays, TSH surge is blunted in the preterm and V/LBW infants. In term infants, early hospital dis charge has increased the ratio of false-posi tive TSH elevations from 3:1 to 5:1. Recommendations suggest that NBS be per formed at 48 h of age; however, the optimal time to obtain a primary TSH NBS is around 3–5 days of life [4]. ### 14 ### 14.1.4 Dual TSH and T4 NBS ### Method Recent data show that primary TSH screening is more cost-effective in reducing false-positive and false-negative cases for mass screening despite the dual TSH and T4 approach theo retically being the ideal method of screening [16]. Dual TSH and T4 screening is expensive and not practical in most countries. As with any screening, the value of identifying an infant with CH must be balanced against the cost of screening normal newborns. NBS is expensive and not weighed in the costs are the psychosocial burdens created by screening for nondisease [17]. Given recall rates of 0.05%, over 1000 children will undergo further diag nostic testing with negative results for each child with true-positive results. Even more costly are children without true hypothyroid ism who undergo therapeutic intervention. Not limited to monetary disadvantages are the psychosocial burdens associated with non disease, including, but not limited to, parental anxiety, aversion of the child to repeat intrave nous catheters, and risks of therapeutic side effects. ### 14.1.5 Confirmatory Results 14.1 NBS test results must be communicated rapidly back to the physician or hospital iden tified on the screening filter paper card. The responsibility for transmission of these results rests with the authority or agency that per formed the test. In general, when an abnormal screening result is found, the responsible phy sician is notified immediately so that he or she can arrange for follow-up testing. Screening test results should be entered into the patient’s record. If the informed physician is no longer caring for or cannot locate the infant, he or she should notify the NBS laboratory imme diately. In such situations, the local health department is often helpful in locating these infants to ensure that they are not lost to fol low-up [14, 18, 19]. ## PDF page 386 | printed page 375 ### 14.2 Etiology 14.2 20 Genetic predisposition to thyroid dysgen esis may in part explain the observed higher incidence of CH among certain ethnic groups [21]. Mutations in developmental genes, which play important roles in embryogenesis and developmental cell migrations, contribute to genetic predisposition to thyroid dysgenesis. Mutations in genes (such as TTF-1, TTF-2, and PAX8) have been associated with devel opmental anomalies including thyroid dys genesis and likely account for the higher incidence of CH in Hispanic patients [3]. 14.2 ![Source image](../../figures/ch014_p0386_01.jpg) Unmatched source image; PDF page 386. In industrialized coun tries with a high emphasis on prenatal care, signs and symptoms of CH are rarely appar ent. Unfortunately, it is within this newborn period when missing clinical features of hypo thyroidism lend to irreversible brain damage, thus the importance of newborn screening [7, 18, 19]. Symptoms and signs suggestive of CH include the following, with additional signs evident as infants become older: 0 days of life 5 Cardiac malformations 5 Delay in skeletal maturation (absence of femoral and tibial epiphyses) 5 Hypothermia 5 Jaundice 5 Lethargy/decreased activity 5 Macroglossia ### 14 5 Macrosomia 5 Mottled and dry skin 5 Open and wide posterior fontanelle (>2 cm) 5 Poor feeding 5 Umbilical hernia 5 Wide anterior fontanelle Early infancy (0–2 months of life) 5 Constipation 5 Decreased muscle tone 5 Failure to thrive 5 Hoarse cry 5 Linear growth deceleration 5 Poor feeding 5 Prolonged jaundice Late infancy (>2 months of life) 5 Delayed tooth eruption 5 Growth failure 5 Pseudomuscular hypertrophy 5 Psychomotor retardation Infants with CH are often described as “good babies” as they sleep well and cry infre quently. As with any newborn, a complete history, including maternal thyroid status and family history, should be obtained, and careful physical examination must be per formed. ### 14.4 Diagnostic Evaluation Laboratory assessment of thyroid function provides a sensitive and specific methodology for diagnosing CH. The most significant con founder in the confirmation of CH is its tran sient form. The most common form of transient hypothyroidism worldwide is iodine deficiency. Iodine deficiency must be consid ered in high-risk populations such as those from underdeveloped countries, infants of mothers whose diets are limited in meats (vegans) or iodinated salts (sea salt consum ers), and infants whose condition limits gas tric intake of nutrients (total parenteral nutrition-dependence). Even in infants with transient neonatal hypothyroidism, treat ment is recommended if certain diagnostic criteria are met. If newborns continue to exhibit persistent TSH elevation with normal f/T4 after 4–6 weeks of life, treatment is rec ommended [19]. A common cause of transient neonatal hypothyroidism in developed countries is pre maturity (gestational age <37 weeks). Temporary thyroid dysfunction also occurs in infants who are born 10% below expected body weight (i.e., V/LBW), ill neonates admit ted to the neonatal intensive care unit, neo nates who are discharged within the first 24 h of life, and cohorts of multiple births, includ ing monozygotic twins. In these special popu lations, a repeat NBS specimen should be ## PDF page 390 | printed page 379 collected at about 2 weeks of age or 2 weeks after the first screening test was carried out [7], at 4 weeks later [18, 19], and at 36 weeks corrected gestational age [10]. To confirm the diagnosis of permanent CH, the European Society for Pediatric Endocrinology (ESPE) recommends perform ing imaging studies to determine its specific etiology [7]. The American Academy of Pediatrics denotes that imaging before the age of 3 years is unlikely to change clinical man agement [18, 19]. Diagnostic imaging may be helpful in cases in which CH diagnosis is not clear [18, 19]. Treatment may be altered based on results, especially if clinical evaluation is also consistent with CH. The option to initi ate, hold, and potentially stop treatment may be based on imaging results as well. When the cause of abnormal thyroid studies cannot be determined as either transient or permanent, both scintigraphy and ultrasound can be con sidered in neonates with abnormal TSH val ues. Of course, the time interval to imaging should not delay treatment in any circum stance in which there is a high degree of suspi cion of thyroid disease. Even in circumstances in which differentiation between transient and permanent CH is blurred, imaging can always be deferred until the child reaches the age of 3 years. At 3 years, neuronal migration and myelination are fairly advanced; thus risk of neurocognitive dysfunction as a result of thy roid hormone withdrawal at age 3 years is lower than what would have been expected in the first 3 years of life [9]. In the era of genetic testing, several muta tions have been discovered which account for some cases of CH. Genetic studies for muta tions in thyroid hormone synthesis can con firm inborn errors of thyroid hormone biosynthesis [28]. Despite the importance of confirming CH in permanent cases, the costs of genetic testing do not yet outweigh the ben efits. The exceptions include families in which multiple siblings are affected. In these cases, genetic counseling is suggested to ensure fam ilies are aware of potential risks in future pregnancies. ### 14.5 Treatment Once the diagnosis of CH is confirmed, levo thyroxine replacement is recommended as the treatment of choice. There is no place in pediatric thyroid disease for formularies including T3 treatment or desiccated animal product. Treatment with levothyroxine (crushed tablets or branded liquid) should be started as soon as possible. Goal for initia tion of treatment is within the first 2 weeks of life. However, given that some abnormal screenings require repeated measurements or further diagnostic testing, treatment should begin once testing confirms the disease. Initial treatment is with levothyroxine 10–15 mg/kg/day; however, several factors interfere with thyroid hormone absorption. Severity of the disease also affects the choice of replacement dose. More severe disease, such as athyreosis, indicates the use of doses at the upper end of the treatment scale (15 mg/kg/day), while the same dose in infants affected by defects in thyroid hor mone synthesis may lead to overtreatment. Goal of all therapy is to normalize thyroid hormone function [7, 18, 19]. Based on TSH concentration, the dosage of levothyroxine is adjusted. Use of serum fT4 can be adjunctive in ensuring an appro priate clinical response. In the first 3 years, serum total T4 and/or fT4 values should be in the upper half of the reference range, and serum TSH levels should be between 0.5 and 2.0 mIU/L [14, 18, 19]. Relative pituitary resistance may delay the normalization of serum TSH, resulting in a normal or increased serum T4 concentration with an inappropri ately high TSH level. In these cases, the dose should be titrated based on the TSH value, after first ruling out nonadherence to treat ment. Normalizing thyroid function may be challenging in the first year of life. Despite tightened Federal Drug Administration regu lations, levothyroxine preparations can vary by up to 12% in the amount of active hor mone, even within the brand [29]. Guidelines ## PDF page 391 | printed page 380 recommend brand name levothyroxine; how ever, the cost can be prohibitive for most fam ilies whose formularies require generic prescriptions [7]. Children initiated on generic formulations should remain on generic, and those started on brand name formulations should remain on brand. If there is any change in the thyroid hormone manufacturer, followup laboratory testing should be ordered to ensure euthyroidism [18, 19]. Other factors affecting thyroid hormone dosing include absorption in the gastrointesti nal tract, ranging from 70% to 80%, hence the pharmaceutical company’s recommendations for consuming levothyroxine on an empty stomach [30]. Practically, however, infants are in a perpetual postprandial state. Adhering to specific preprandial timing of medication administration has been associated with lower medication adherence [31]. Therefore, medica tion can be given with or without food as long as there remains consistency with each dose. Dosing can be adjusted based on the most realistic mode of consumption. paragraphs.text: Autoimmune thyroid disease affects approxi mately 2% of females and 0.2% of males [1]. Although its prevalence peaks in adulthood,
paragraphs.heading: 15.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: it is the most common cause of acquired thy roid dysfunction in children and adolescents [2, 3]. Normal thyroid hormone levels are critical to neurodevelopment and growth, and by maintaining an appropriate index of suspicion, the clinician can often recognize thyroid dysfunction in its early stages. This chapter presents a summary of autoimmune thyroid diseases, discussing chronic autoim mune thyroiditis and Graves’ disease in detail, emphasizing their clinical manage ment.
paragraphs.heading: 15.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: The childhood prevalence of chronic autoim mune thyroiditis peaks in early to midpuberty, and a female preponderance of 2:1 has been reported [4]. Presentation is rare under the age of 3 years, but cases have been described in infancy [5, 6].
paragraphs.heading: Thyroiditis

paragraphs.text: In 1912, Hashimoto described four women with thyromegaly and transformation of the thyroid into lymphoid tissue (“struma lym phomatosa”). These patients comprise the first report of Hashimoto’s disease, which is now recognized as chronic autoimmune thy roiditis. The term thyroiditis is pathologically defined as evidence of “intrathyroidal lym phocytic infiltration” with or without follicu lar damage; clinically, it implies inflammation of the thyroid gland. Improvements in the measurement of circulating autoantibodies have obviated the need for biopsy to diagnose autoimmune thyroid disease. There have been proposals to redefine nomenclature based on pathological and clinical criteria—i.e., based on the presence or absence of goiter and vary ing degrees of thyroid dysfunction in the con text of circulating thyroid autoantibodies ( Box 15.1) [6, 7].
paragraphs.heading: 15.2.1 Terminology and Definitions

paragraphs.text: The first step in the pathogenesis of chronic autoimmune thyroiditis is the activation of CD4 (helper) T lymphocytes specific for thy roid antigens. These activated CD4 T cells recruit cytotoxic CD8 T cells and autoreactive B cells into the thyroid, which leads to the generation of an autoantibody response and intrathyroidal inflammation [8]. The three main targets of thyroid antibodies are thyro globulin (Tg), thyroperoxidase (TPO), and thyrotropin receptor (TSHR). While anti- TPO antibodies have been shown to inhibit the activity of thyroid peroxidase in vitro, the primary mechanism of hypothyroidism in vivo is likely via thyroid follicular cell destruction by the CD8 T cells [8]. Anti-TSH receptor antibodies (TRAbs) may also con tribute to hypothyroidism in a minority of patients with the atrophic form of chronic autoimmune thyroiditis [8–10].
paragraphs.heading: 15.2.2 Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: Histologically, goitrous autoimmune thy roiditis is characterized by diffuse lympho cytic infiltration with occasional germinal centers. Thyroid follicles may be reduced in size and contain sparse colloid. Individual thyroid cells are often enlarged with oxyphilic cytoplasm (Hurthle cells). In contrast, the gland in atrophic autoimmune thyroiditis is small, with lymphocytic infiltration and fibrous replacement of the parenchyma.
paragraphs.heading: 15.2.2 Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: The presentation of chronic autoimmune thyroiditis includes either hypothyroidism, goiter/thyromegaly, or both. A goiter (enlarged thyroid gland) is usually the first physical sign of chronic autoimmune thy roiditis. Thyromegaly is typically diffuse with a “pebbly” or “seedy” surface that evolves into a firm and nodular consistency [11]. As the disease progresses, subclinical and then overt hypothyroidism develops. Subclinical hypothyroidism is defined as a TSH concen tration above the upper limit of the normal range, with a free T4 within the normal range.
paragraphs.heading: 15.2.3 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: In contrast, overt hypothyroidism is defined as an elevated TSH with a low free T4 level. Typically, the TSH concentration in subclini cal hypothyroidism is only mildly elevated, between 5 and 10 μU/mL, though it occa sionally rises higher. In adults, the natural history of subclinical hypothyroidism is fairly well-described, with progression to overt hypothyroidism in up to 20% of cases. Symptoms of hypothyroidism may be subtle, even with significant biochemical derange ment ( Box 15.2).
paragraphs.heading: 15.2.3 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: The initial history should include inquiries into energy level, sleep pattern, menses, cold intolerance, bowel patterns, and school per formance. In addition to palpation of the thy roid, assessment of extraocular movements, fluid status, and deep tendon reflexes are important components of the physical exami nation. Chronic autoimmune thyroiditis may be the initial presentation of an autoimmune polyglandular syndrome, and the possibility of coexisting autoimmune diseases such as type 1 diabetes, Addison’s disease, and perni cious anemia should be addressed in the med ical history.
paragraphs.heading: 15.2.3 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: In the absence of hypothalamic or pituitary disease, the serum TSH concentration is the most sensitive screen for thyroid function. TSH levels are elevated in primary hypothy roidism. If the differential diagnosis includes central hypothyroidism or the overall suspi cion for hypothyroidism is high, a free T4 (or calculated free T4 index) should be included on the initial screen. In mild hypothyroidism, serum T3 concentrations can remain in the normal range due to increased conversion of T4 to T3 by type 2 deiodinase and the prefer ential secretion of T3 by residual thyroid tis sue under the influence of hyperthyrotropinemia [16]. For these reasons, measuring the serum T3 concentration is not useful in diagnosing or monitoring patients with primary hypothyroidism.
paragraphs.heading: 15.2.4 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: The presence of goiter or hyperthyrotro pinemia should prompt the measurement of anti-TPO antibodies. Anti-TPO antibodies are the most sensitive screen for chronic auto immune thyroiditis; up to 90% of patients with hypothyroidism secondary to autoim mune thyroiditis are anti-TPO antibody posi tive [17]. The additional measurement of antithyroglobulin antibodies gains little fur ther benefit, although they may be added if anti-TPO titers are negative. It should be noted that 10–15% of the general population are positive for anti-TPO antibodies and 5–15% for anti-thyroglobulin antibodies, and low titers are not very specific for autoim mune thyroid disease [1]. If anti-TPO anti bodies are absent, less common etiologies of
paragraphs.heading: 15.2.4 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: primary hypothyroidism, such as transient hypothyroidism, subacute thyroiditis, external irradiation, consumptive hypothyroidism, or iodine deficiency should be considered [18–20].
paragraphs.heading: 15.2.4 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: The typical patient with hypothyroidism secondary to chronic autoimmune thyroiditis will have an elevated TSH (over 10 μU/mL), a low free T4, and positive anti-TPO antibodies. In the early stages of the disease (type 1A), anti-TPO antibodies may be positive with goi ter, though TSH may be normal. Later, TSH elevation becomes modest (between 5 and 10 μU/mL) with normal circulating free T4 (sub clinical hypothyroidism).
paragraphs.heading: 15.2.4 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: The log-linear relationship between serum TSH and free T4 explains how small reduc
paragraphs.heading: 15.2.4 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: tions in serum free T4 lead to large deviations in TSH. Most patients with subclinical hypo thyroidism are asymptomatic. However, indi viduals with the combined risk factors of hyperthyrotropinemia and positive thyroid antibodies (anti-thyroglobulin or anti-TPO) are at high risk for progression to overt hypo thyroidism [20]. Therefore, typical recommen dations are for patients with TSH values greater than 10 μU/mL, goiter, and/or thyroid autoantibodies, to be started on thyroid hor mone replacement [21, 22].
paragraphs.heading: 15.2.4 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Given the critical importance of thyroid hormone in neurodevelopment, persistent hyperthyrotropinemia in infancy is often empirically treated, and a trial off therapy or with reduced doses may be considered after the age of 2–3 years. Similarly, the presence of growth failure may lower the threshold to ini tiate replacement therapy in children with per sistent hyperthyrotropinemia. Euthyroid children with autoimmune thyroiditis (type 1A or type 1B) can be observed without treat ment and monitored carefully with TSH mea surements every 6–12 months, as a significant fraction will progress to overt hypothyroidism [23].
paragraphs.heading: 15.2.4 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Levothyroxine (l-T4) is the recommended treatment for children with hypothyroidism. There are minimal adverse reactions, and its long half-life of 5–7 days allows the conve nience of daily administration. Of note, while desiccated thyroid extracts and liothyronine (T3) are commercially available as replace ment options, current consensus guidelines recommend against the routine use of these preparations in children due to the lack of long-term outcome data and their risk of iat rogenic hypertriiodothyronemia [24].
paragraphs.heading: 15.2.5 Therapy

paragraphs.text: 4 TSH normalization (typical range 0.5–5 μU/mL) is the goal of replacement therapy. This will usually be associated with a free T4 concentration in the upper half of the normal range. Thyroid function tests should be obtained 6 weeks after initiating or adjusting the levothyroxine dosage. Growth and sexual development should be followed systemati cally. Most children achieve adequate catchup growth and a normal adult stature after initiating levothyroxine replacement. However, catch-up growth may be compro mised and target height may not be achieved if treatment has been started after a prolonged duration of severe hypothyroidism. Once bio chemical euthyroidism has been achieved, TSH can be monitored every 4–6 months in the growing child and yearly once final height has been attained.

Robert Graves first reported the clinical syn drome of goiter, palpitations, and exophthal mos in 1835 [29]. Graves’ disease is relatively rare, with a yearly incidence of 8–9 per 1,000,000 children less than 15 years old and 1 per 1,000,000 children less than 4 years old [30–32]. Girls are affected four to five times more frequently than boys, although no gen der difference is noted under 4 years of age [31–33]. The term thyrotoxicosis refers to the clinical state resulting from any condition that leads to elevated serum thyroid hormone level; whereas hyperthyroidism refers specifically to increased thyroid hormone production from the gland. Graves’ disease is the most com mon etiology of hyperthyroidism in children [34], and it is important to accurately diag nose this condition as the choice of therapy depends on the etiology of the thyrotoxicosis. For example, antithyroid drugs, which are the mainstay in the management of Graves’ dis ease, play no role in treating thyrotoxicosis secondary to chronic autoimmune thyroiditis or subacute thyroiditis.
paragraphs.heading: 15.3 Graves’ Disease

paragraphs.text: Graves’ hyperthyroidism results from the overproduction of thyroid-stimulating anti bodies that bind to and activate the G-proteincoupled thyrotropin receptor (TSHR), leading to follicular cell hyperplasia and hypersecre tion of thyroid hormone [35]. Graves’ disease shares many features with chronic autoim mune thyroiditis, including autoantibodies directed against thyroglobulin, thyroperoxi dase, and the sodium-iodine symporter. Lymphocytic infiltration of the thyroid paren chyma is present, and germinal centers consti tute a significant source of intrathyroidal autoantibodies. The gland is often highly vas
paragraphs.heading: 15.3.1 Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: cular by ultrasound doppler. For unclear rea sons, lymphocytic infiltration and the accumulation of glycosaminoglycans can also be found in orbital connective tissue and skin, which results in the extrathyroidal manifesta tions of Graves’ ophthalmopathy and der mopathy [36, 37].
paragraphs.heading: 15.3.1 Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: The clinical presentation of Graves’ disease in childhood is variable and can be insidious. A careful history will often reveal a severalmonth history of progressive symptoms. Common signs and symptoms of Graves’ disease are listed in Box 15.3. In contrast to children with hypothyroidism, those with hyperthyroidism can show a linear growth acceleration and advanced skeletal matura tion. Goiter is present in most cases, charac terized by diffuse, nontender, spongiform enlargement of the gland. The pyramidal lobe is often palpable, and a bruit may be audible secondary to increased blood flow through the gland. Extrathyroidal manifesta tions such as ophthalmopathy and dermopa thy are rare and tend to be less severe than in adults [36–38]. While the pediatric literature indicates that 50–70% of children have ocu lar manifestations, the majority of such cases are a consequence of increased sympathetic tone and not true ophthalmopathy. Periorbital edema, proptosis, lid retraction, erythema, and pain are often mild and responsive to improvement in thyroid func tion. Even children with infiltrative disease of the orbital structures typically improve with restoration of euthyroidism. Therefore, conservative management is generally rec ommended, as long as vision is not threat ened [36].
paragraphs.heading: 15.3.2 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Thyrotoxicosis is biochemically defined by an elevation of serum free thyroxine (FT4) with suppressed serum thyrotropin (TSH) concen trations to <0.1 μU/mL. A determination of total triiodothyronine (T3) concentration is warranted if TSH is suppressed and serum FT4 is normal. In patients with early disease or iodine-deficient patients, serum FT4 con centrations may be normal or reduced despite elevated levels of T3. This is due to increased peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 and is the only situation in which a serum T3 measure ment is required to confirm the diagnosis [39]. The triad of thyrotoxicosis, goiter, and orbitopathy is diagnostic for Graves’ disease [39], and no other laboratory tests or imaging studies are typically necessary. However, addi tional diagnostic tools can confirm the diag nosis and distinguish Graves’ disease from other forms of thyrotoxicosis.
paragraphs.heading: 15.3.3 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Most patients with Graves’ disease have measurable serum thyrotropin receptor bind ing antibody titers (TRAbs). TRAbs can be measured by either a bioassay (thyroid stimu lating immunoglobulin, TSI) or competitive binding assay (thyrotropin binding inhibitory immunoglobulin, TBII). In the functional TSI assay, a patient’s serum antibodies directly stimulate the TSH receptor in vitro and increase cAMP production. In the TBII assay, all antibodies that compete with the TSH receptor are measured regardless of their activity (stimulating, blocking, or neu tral to the TSHR). Both assays are highly sen sitive and specific for diagnosing Graves’ disease [40].
paragraphs.heading: 15.3.3 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: In most cases of thyrotoxicosis, the pres ence of TRAbs is a helpful adjunctive test to confirm the diagnosis. However, if antibody titers are equivocal, measurement of radioio dine uptake (RAIU) with 123I or 99Tc can be used [41]. RAI uptake is elevated and diffusely distributed in Graves’ disease. In hyperthy roidism from a toxic nodule(s), there is focal uptake at the site of the nodule(s) with sup pression of the remainder of the gland. RAI uptake is low in other causes of thyrotoxico sis, such as thyroiditis or exogenous thyroid hormone ingestion.
paragraphs.heading: 15.3.3 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: There is a subgroup of patients with sub clinical hyperthyroidism characterized by a low but not overtly suppressed TSH (0.1–0.3 μU/mL) and normal serum concentrations of thyroid hormone [42]. In adults over 60 years, a low serum TSH concentration has been associated with an increased risk of atrial fibrillation [43]. Some studies suggest that postmenopausal women are also at risk of bone loss [44]. However, these risks have not been identified in children. Several studies indicate that a significant fraction of patients with subclinical thyrotoxicosis experience spontaneous remission [44, 45]. Accordingly, the initial detection of a suppressed TSH con centration without elevated thyroid hormone levels or associated symptoms should be man aged conservatively by repeating thyroid func tion tests in 4–8 weeks. Asymptomatic children with subclinical hyperthyroidism and no specific cardiac risk factors can be followed
paragraphs.heading: 15.3.3 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: with the expectation that TSH suppression due to transient thyroiditis will resolve spon taneously, while that due to Graves’ disease or an autonomous nodule will persist.
paragraphs.heading: 15.3.3 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: The duration of symptoms is an important factor to consider in the differential diagnosis of thyrotoxicosis. If thyrotoxicosis has been present for less than 8 weeks, transient thyro toxicosis secondary to thyroiditis (autoim mune, viral, postpartum, drug-induced) should be considered. These forms of thy roiditis are self-limited and refractory to ther apy with thionamides. For thyrotoxicosis present for more than 8 weeks, the diagnosis of Graves’ disease is more likely [34, 46] ( Box 15.4).
paragraphs.heading: of Thyrotoxicosis in Children

paragraphs.text: The treatment of thyrotoxicosis is based on addressing the increased levels of thyroid hor mone from the gland and managing periph eral effects. Beta-adrenergic antagonists, atenolol (0.8–1.0 mg/kg/day divided once or twice daily) or propranolol (10–40 mg every 6–8 h), should be offered in all patients to help control the increased sympathetic tone (tachy cardia, hypertension, anxiety, tremors), pend ing no contraindications (bronchospastic asthma) [46]. Treatment of Graves’ hyperthy roidism is divided into two categories: (1) Antithyroid drugs or (2) Definitive therapy with radioiodine ablation or surgical thyroid ectomy.
paragraphs.heading: 15.4.1 Antithyroid Medications

paragraphs.text: The antithyroid drugs (ATDs, thionamide derivatives), methimazole (MMI), and pro pylthiouracil (PTU) block the organification of iodine and thyroid hormone synthesis. PTU also inhibits the conversion of T4 to T3, and both have some immunosuppressive effects. Methimazole (MMI) is the first-line treatment for children with Graves’ disease and is preferred due to its longer half-life and more favorable safety profile. The recom mended starting dose for methimazole is 0.5–1.0 mg/kg/day administered once or twice daily [34, 45]. PTU is no longer used in chil dren due to the risk of liver failure [47, 48]. However, PTU can be reserved for use in firsttrimester pregnancy (due to concerns of MMI-associated birth defects), lifethreatening thyroid storm (to inhibit T4-to-T3 conversion), and allergic reactions to MMI as a short bridge to definitive therapy.
paragraphs.heading: 15.4.1 Antithyroid Medications

paragraphs.text: After initiation of ATD, thyroid function tests should be monitored every 2 weeks ini tially and then every 4 weeks after any dose adjustment. Once the free T4 concertation has fallen to the upper end of the normal range, the MMI dose should be decreased by 50%. Further dose adjustments are guided by serial thyroid function tests, initially relying upon the FT4 concentration and later the TSH con centration to guide adjustments to the MMI dose. After TSH secretion recovers from its chronic suppression, which can take up to 6

months, the goal of maintenance therapy is TSH normalization [46]. The first clinical response to medications is 2–4 weeks into therapy. Weight loss subsides, and weight gain may occur. Long-term remission rates in chil dren have been reported at 25% after 2 years of ATD and 50% after 4 years [49]. However, based on more recent studies, long-term treat ment with ATDs of up to 120 months is con sidered efficacious and safe [50–52].

Antithyroid drugs are usually well toler ated but can cause side effects. Minor adverse reactions, such as hives, rash, and myalgias/ arthralgias, occur approximately 5–25% of the time and within the first weeks to months of therapy. Hives can be treated with antihis tamines, but they can also be severe enough to require discontinuation of the drug. The more severe adverse effects include agranulocytosis (absolute neutrophil count (ANC) <500) and hepatotoxicity. Agranulocytosis occurs with both methimazole and PTU. It is more com mon with methimazole, dose-dependent, and typically develops within the first 90 days. It can also be idiosyncratic and occur upon reexposure to the drug after several years. Patients should be counseled that if fever, sore throat, or unexplained mouth sores develop, they should discontinue the drug and seek medical attention. Because leukopenia can also be a manifestation of Graves’ disease, a white blood cell count and differential should be performed before starting antithyroid drug therapy and if the patient develops any con cerning symptoms [53, 54].

Methimazole induced hepatotoxicity is typically cholestatic, whereas PTU has been associated with hepatocellular injury. Routine monitoring of liver function tests has not been found to reduce the severity of hepato toxicity. However, ATDs should be avoided when aminotransferases are greater than 3–5 times the upper limit of normal and discon tinued with jaundice, extreme pruritus, anorexia, or acholic stools [53, 54]. In addi tion, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodyassociated vasculitis occurs more frequently with PTU and can present after months to years of therapy.

The options for the definitive treatment of Graves’ disease are radioactive iodine ablation and surgical thyroidectomy; both, if success ful, result in permanent hypothyroidism. Candidates for radioiodine include those who fail to remit on ATD, develop severe side effects of ATDs, are nonadherent, or personal preference [55, 56]. Before radioiodine abla tion, euthyroidism should be restored to mini mize the development of severe radiation induced thyroiditis. Methimazole should be stopped 3–5 days before radioiodine adminis tration. The goal is to administer a sufficient dose of radioiodine to ablate thyroid tissue and develop hypothyroidism [57]. Some cen ters measure radioiodine uptake before treat ment and calculate an 131I dose that delivers an absorbed thyroid dose of >150 μCi/g thy roid. Alternatively, an empiric fixed dose of 131I (usually 10–15 mCi) can be offered [58]. The theoretical advantage of calculated doses is that it defines the lowest administered dose for each patient to achieve the therapeutic effect. This benefit is most important in small children because the absorbed radiation dose to bone marrow and other normal tissues is inversely proportional to body size. Based on this concept and theoretical modeling of radi ation exposure, 131I therapy should be avoided in children younger than 5 years [57]. It may be used cautiously in children between 5 and 10 years of age as long as the administered dose is <10 mCi. Radioiodine ablation has a low failure rate (5–20%), and patients with persistent hyperthyroidism more than 6 months after their first 131I therapy can be offered retreatment [57].
paragraphs.heading: 15.4.2 Definitive Therapy

paragraphs.text: Thyroidectomy is typically used as defini tive therapy for those patients with a massive goiter (>4 times normal), severe orbitopathy, coexisting nodules or carcinoma, children less than 5 years of age, and those with contrain dications for radioactive iodine (pregnancy) [59]. Thyroidectomy is a safe procedure when performed by an experienced surgeon, and a referral to a surgeon with a low complication rate minimizes postoperative risks. Ideally, thyroid surgery should be performed after the
paragraphs.heading: 15.4.2 Definitive Therapy

paragraphs.text: patient has been rendered euthyroid with methimazole and pretreated for 7–14 days with saturated potassium iodide (SSKI; 1–3 drops, 2–3 times per day) [59]. The latter helps decrease the vascularity of the gland. Complications of surgical treatment include hypoparathyroidism (transient or permanent) and paralysis of the vocal cords, but such complications are reduced substantially in a high-volume center [59, 60]. Patients immedi ately become hypothyroid and require lifelong thyroid hormone replacement. Recurrence of hyperthyroidism is rare.
paragraphs.heading: 15.4.2 Definitive Therapy

paragraphs.text: Given the documented risks of surgery and the theoretical risks of radioiodine, a pro longed course of antithyroid medication is now more accepted in treating pediatric Graves’ disease. Monitoring of thyroid func tion tests every 3–4 months in the growing child and 4 weeks after any medication adjust ment to normalize the TSH is recommended [61]. Physical examination should focus on heart rate, blood pressure, pubertal status, lin ear growth, goiter size, and orbitopathy (vision, and ocular movements). The transi tion to adulthood should prompt a rediscussion of therapy. For young adults with persistent hyperthyroidism, 131I is the defini tive treatment of choice [62]. Definitive ther apy allows for a more straightforward regimen of medication and laboratory monitoring. Additionally, prior definitive therapy simpli fies the management of patients during preg nancy.
paragraphs.heading: Disease and the Transition to Adult Care

paragraphs.text: Approximately 0.6% of infants born to moth ers with a history of Graves’ disease will develop neonatal hyperthyroidism due to the transplacental passage of maternal TRAbs. While the development of neonatal Graves’
paragraphs.heading: 15.5 Neonatal Graves’ Disease

paragraphs.text: disease is more common in mothers with active Graves’ disease, it can also occur after those who have previously received definitive therapy with radioiodine or thyroidectomy [63, 64]. These infants are at risk for neonatal Graves’ disease as well as congenital hypothy roidism due to the transplacental passage of TSH receptor blocking (rather than stimulat ing) antibodies. The signs can be immediate or delayed by 3–10 days due to the time required for clearance of maternal antithyroid drugs. Typically, neonatal Graves’ disease spontane ously remits by 12 weeks of life following clearance of maternal TRAbs from the infant’s circulation, but the condition has been reported to persist for as long as 6 months. Prenatal ultrasounds should monitor fetal heart rate, growth, and glandular size. The measurement of TRAbs between 20 and 24 weeks of gestation is recommended as a predictor for the development of fetal and neo natal Graves’ disease. Mothers with TSI >3×, TBII >5 IU/L, or those with a prior infant with neonatal Graves’ disease are at highest risk [65]. In utero, the presence of goiter, tachycardia, and intrauterine growth restric tion suggests fetal hyperthyroidism. In some circumstances, antithyroid drugs can be administered to the mother to control fetal hyperthyroidism. For high-risk infants, such as those born to mothers with high levels of thyrotropin-stimulating antibodies or those with a history of an affected sibling, thyroid function tests and TRAbs should be obtained at birth. Thereafter, thyroid function tests should be monitored at 3–5 days of life, and 10–14 days of life, and clinically followed closely through 3 months [65].
paragraphs.heading: 15.5 Neonatal Graves’ Disease

paragraphs.text: Affected infants with Graves’ disease are often growth restricted, diaphoretic, and hyperkinetic. Goiter can occur and, when severe, can compress the infant’s airway. Diarrhea, vomiting, poor weight gain, exoph thalmos, arrhythmias, and congestive heart failure can develop. Confirmatory thyroid function tests (TSH, free T4, T3) and TRAbs should be obtained, and treatment initiated immediately. In cases of acute neona tal thyrotoxicosis, MMI (0.25–1.0 mg/kg/day) or PTU (5–10 mg/kg/day) may be adminis

tered orally, or through a nasogastric tube in divided doses every 8–12 h. Inorganic iodine will speed the decrease in circulating thyroid hormone, and is administered as SSKI (48 mg iodide/drop) at the dose of one drop per day. Supportive therapy with intravenous flu ids, beta-blockers (propranolol 2 mg/kg/day), and glucocorticoids (prednisone 2 mg/kg/day) may be helpful in severe cases [66]. Thyroid function tests should be monitored weekly, and treatment can be gradually weaned weekly to prevent the development of iatro genic hypothyroidism. After the clearance of TSH-receptor antibodies, therapy can be dis continued. The cumulative mortality of neo natal Graves’ disease is estimated to be as high as 25% [65]. Potential long-term morbidity includes growth restriction, craniosynostosis, impaired intellectual function, and central hypothyroidism [67, 68]. Since the half-life of maternal immunoglobulin is approximately 14 days, most cases of neonatal Graves’ dis ease will resolve after 3–12 weeks. The differ ential diagnosis of neonatal thyrotoxicosis also includes McCune-Albright syndrome and activating mutations of the TSH receptor. These non-autoimmune etiologies are exceed ingly rare but should be considered if thyro toxicosis persists beyond 3 months.

Autoimmune thyroid diseases, both Hashimoto’s thyroiditis and Graves’ disease, are due to dysregulation of the immune sys tem and potential development of overt thy roid dysfunction. In a genetically predisposed individual, activated T cells infiltrate the thy roid gland, leading to B cell dysregulation and antibody production with the loss of toler ance to multiple thyroid antigens, including thyroglobulin, thyroperoxidase, sodiumiodine symporter, and the TSH receptor. In Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, there may be a wax ing and waning of thyroid function with pro longed periods of euthyroidism before progression to hypothyroidism. In general, treating subclinical hypothyroidism is not beneficial in the pediatric population, unless
paragraphs.heading: 15.6 Summary

paragraphs.text: TSH concentrations exceed 10 μU/mL and the patient has goiter and/or anti-TPO or anti-Tg antibodies. In Graves’ disease, TSH receptor antibodies stimulate the gland result ing in excessive thyroid hormone production and development of symptoms of thyrotoxi cosis. It is essential to differentiate between thyroiditis and Graves’ disease because the use of antithyroid drugs is not indicated in the former. Treatment for Graves’ disease is always individualized. Antithyroid drugs are the first line of therapy in children, with defin itive therapy reserved for refractory cases or serious adverse effects. Side effects of antithy roid drugs occur in up to 25% of patients with rash and hives being the most common. Educating families about the risks of serious side effects such as agranulocytosis, hepatitis, arthritis, vasculitis, and Stevens-Johnson syn drome is paramount. While adults have a more favorable remission rate, children often require a more prolonged course of antithy roid drug to achieve remission. For those that do not remit, permanent therapy with either radioiodine ablation or surgical thyroidec tomy in a high-volume center can be pursued. Thyroidectomy is typically reserved for patients with a very large gland, severe orbi topathy, coexisting nodules or carcinoma, children less than 5 years of age, and those with contraindications for radioactive iodine. Finally, neonatal Graves’ disease is a rare dis order that results from the transplacental pas sage of TSH receptor antibodies from a mother with active or a prior history of treated Graves’ disease. It has a high morbid ity rate, so prompt recognition and treatment are critical. Therapy consists of beta-block ade, antithyroid drugs, inorganic iodine, and glucocorticoids depending on the severity of presentation. Fortunately, neonatal Graves’ disease typically resolves within 3 months once maternal TSH receptor antibodies clear the infant’s circulation.

paragraphs.text: 1. B. Treatment options for children and

adolescents with Graves’ disease include antithyroid drugs or definitive therapy with thyroidectomy or radio active iodine. In children, the antithy roid drug is recommended as the initial treatment. Antithyroid drugs inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis by interfering with the thyroperoxidase (TPO) enzyme. Methimazole (MMI) is favorable to propylthiouracil (PTU) in children due to the potentially adverse hepatotoxicity associated with PTU. Indications for definitive treat ment in children (RAI or thyroidec tomy) include relapse after a prolonged trial of antithyroid drug, nonadher

Radioactive iodine ablation (RAI) is effective in children and adolescents with hyper thyroidism caused by Graves’ disease, and most patients can be successfully treated with a single ablative dose. RAI is contraindicated during pregnancy and is generally avoided in chil dren under 5 years because of an increased potential risk of neoplasia. Evidence of reproductive dysfunction or higher frequencies of secondary malignancies in treated patients is con troversial. Surgery is commonly reserved for patients with a large goi ter, nodules, or severe ophthalmopa thy.

In the setting of positive thyroperoxidase antibodies, the most likely etiology of his goiter and abnormal laboratory tests is auto immune thyroiditis. Subclinical hypo thyroidism is defined as a TSH concentration above the upper limit of the normal range, with a normal free T4 concentration. Typically, TSH in subclinical hypothyroidism is only mildly elevated, usually between 5 and 10 μU/mL. Evidence-based data regarding whether to treat subclinical hypothyroidism in children is limited. In most studies, the rate of progression to overt hypothyroidism ranges from 15% to 30%. In addition, the effect of treatment with levothyroxine on growth and thyroid gland size is some what variable. In pediatrics, the general recommendation is observation with TSH levels less than 10 μU/mL with serial monitoring of thyroid function.

Cherella and Jessica R. Smith ### Contents ### 15.1 Introduction – 386 ### 15.2 Chronic Autoimmune Thyroiditis – 386 15.2.1 Terminology and Definitions – 386 15.2.2 Pathophysiology – 387 15.2.3 Clinical Presentation – 387 15.2.4 Diagnosis – 388 15.2.5 Therapy – 390 ### 15.3 Graves’ Disease – 391 15.3.1 Pathophysiology – 391 15.3.2 Clinical Presentation – 392 15.3.3 Diagnosis – 392 ### 15.4 Differential Diagnosis of Thyrotoxicosis in Children – 393 15.4.1 Antithyroid Medications – 394 15.4.2 Definitive Therapy – 395 15.4.3 Monitoring of Graves’ Disease and the Transition to Adult Care – 395 ### 15.5 Neonatal Graves’ Disease – 395 ### 15.6 Summary – 396 ### References – 399 © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2024 S. Radovick, M. Misra (eds.), Pediatric Endocrinology, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-66296-6_15 ## PDF page 397 | printed page 386 Key Points 5 The most common cause of goiter in the pediatric population is autoimmune (Hashimoto’s) thyroiditis. 5 Typical symptoms of thyroid dysfunc tion may be present, and growth and puberty may be deranged. 5 There may be a prolonged period of euthyroidism until overt hypothyroid ism develops; therefore, the decision to treat children with subclinical hypothy roidism remains controversial. 5 Graves’ disease is due to (thyroid- stimulating hormone) TSH receptor binding antibodies that stimulate the thyroid gland and result in production of excess thyroid hormone. 5 Initial treatment includes the use of the antithyroid drug (methimazole); how ever, patients should be monitored for serious side effects of methimazole, which include agranulocytosis, hepati tis, arthritis, vasculitis, and Stevens- Johnson syndrome. 5 More prolonged use of antithyroid medications may be required to achieve remission in children relative to adults. 5 If remission does not occur or an adverse reaction develops, then perma nent therapy with either radioactive iodine or surgical thyroidectomy can be considered. 5 Neonatal Graves’ disease has a high ### 15 morbidity and mortality rate; thus, prompt diagnosis and treatment are necessary. 5 Most cases of neonatal Graves’ disease will spontaneously remit after 3–12 weeks as the maternal TSH receptor binding antibodies clear the infant’s cir culation. ### 15.1 Introduction Autoimmune thyroid disease affects approxi mately 2% of females and 0.2% of males [1]. Although its prevalence peaks in adulthood, it is the most common cause of acquired thy roid dysfunction in children and adolescents [2, 3]. Normal thyroid hormone levels are critical to neurodevelopment and growth, and by maintaining an appropriate index of suspicion, the clinician can often recognize thyroid dysfunction in its early stages. This chapter presents a summary of autoimmune thyroid diseases, discussing chronic autoim mune thyroiditis and Graves’ disease in detail, emphasizing their clinical manage ment. ### 15.2 Chronic Autoimmune ### Thyroiditis The childhood prevalence of chronic autoim mune thyroiditis peaks in early to midpuberty, and a female preponderance of 2:1 has been reported [4]. Presentation is rare under the age of 3 years, but cases have been described in infancy [5, 6]. ### 15.2.1 Terminology and Definitions In 1912, Hashimoto described four women with thyromegaly and transformation of the thyroid into lymphoid tissue (“struma lym phomatosa”). These patients comprise the first report of Hashimoto’s disease, which is now recognized as chronic autoimmune thy roiditis. The term thyroiditis is pathologically defined as evidence of “intrathyroidal lym phocytic infiltration” with or without follicu lar damage; clinically, it implies inflammation of the thyroid gland. Improvements in the measurement of circulating autoantibodies have obviated the need for biopsy to diagnose autoimmune thyroid disease. There have been proposals to redefine nomenclature based on pathological and clinical criteria—i.e., based on the presence or absence of goiter and vary ing degrees of thyroid dysfunction in the con text of circulating thyroid autoantibodies ( Box 15.1) [6, 7]. ## PDF page 398 | printed page 387 Box 15.1 Classification of Autoimmune Thyroiditis 5 Type 1 autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashi moto’s disease type 1) –– 1A Goitrous. –– 1B Nongoitrous. –– Status: Euthyroid with normal thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH); autoantibodies to thyro globulin (Tg) and thyroid peroxi dase (TPO) are typically present. 5 Type 2 autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashi moto’s disease type 2) –– 2A Goitrous (classic Hashimoto’s disease). –– 2B Nongoitrous (primary myx edema, atrophic thyroiditis). –– Status: Persistent hypothyroidism with increased TSH; autoantibod ies to Tg and TPO are typically present. –– 2C Transient thyroiditis (e.g., post partum thyroiditis). –– Status: May start as transient, low radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU) thyrotoxicosis, followed by tran sient hypothyroidism; autoanti bodies to Tg and TPO are typically present. 5 Type 3 autoimmune thyroiditis (Graves’ disease) –– 3A Hyperthyroid Graves’ disease. –– 3B Euthyroid Graves’ disease. –– Status: Hyperthyroid or euthyroid with suppressed TSH. Stimulatory autoantibodies to the TSH recep tor are present (autoantibodies to thyroglobulin (Tg) and TPO are also usually present). –– 3C Hypothyroid Graves’ disease. –– Status: Orbitopathy with hypothy roidism. Diagnostic levels of auto antibodies to the TSH receptor (blocking or stimulating) may be detected (autoantibodies to Tg and TPO are also usually present). Data from Davies [6]. ### 15.2.2 Pathophysiology The first step in the pathogenesis of chronic autoimmune thyroiditis is the activation of CD4 (helper) T lymphocytes specific for thy roid antigens. These activated CD4 T cells recruit cytotoxic CD8 T cells and autoreactive B cells into the thyroid, which leads to the generation of an autoantibody response and intrathyroidal inflammation [8]. The three main targets of thyroid antibodies are thyro globulin (Tg), thyroperoxidase (TPO), and thyrotropin receptor (TSHR). While anti- TPO antibodies have been shown to inhibit the activity of thyroid peroxidase in vitro, the primary mechanism of hypothyroidism in vivo is likely via thyroid follicular cell destruction by the CD8 T cells [8]. Anti-TSH receptor antibodies (TRAbs) may also con tribute to hypothyroidism in a minority of patients with the atrophic form of chronic autoimmune thyroiditis [8–10]. Histologically, goitrous autoimmune thy roiditis is characterized by diffuse lympho cytic infiltration with occasional germinal centers. Thyroid follicles may be reduced in size and contain sparse colloid. Individual thyroid cells are often enlarged with oxyphilic cytoplasm (Hurthle cells). In contrast, the gland in atrophic autoimmune thyroiditis is small, with lymphocytic infiltration and fibrous replacement of the parenchyma. ### 15.2.3 Clinical Presentation The presentation of chronic autoimmune thyroiditis includes either hypothyroidism, goiter/thyromegaly, or both. A goiter (enlarged thyroid gland) is usually the first physical sign of chronic autoimmune thy roiditis. Thyromegaly is typically diffuse with a “pebbly” or “seedy” surface that evolves into a firm and nodular consistency [11]. As the disease progresses, subclinical and then overt hypothyroidism develops. Subclinical hypothyroidism is defined as a TSH concen tration above the upper limit of the normal range, with a free T4 within the normal range. ## PDF page 399 | printed page 388 In contrast, overt hypothyroidism is defined as an elevated TSH with a low free T4 level. Typically, the TSH concentration in subclini cal hypothyroidism is only mildly elevated, between 5 and 10 μU/mL, though it occa sionally rises higher. In adults, the natural history of subclinical hypothyroidism is fairly well-described, with progression to overt hypothyroidism in up to 20% of cases. Symptoms of hypothyroidism may be subtle, even with significant biochemical derange ment ( Box 15.2). The initial history should include inquiries into energy level, sleep pattern, menses, cold intolerance, bowel patterns, and school per formance. In addition to palpation of the thy roid, assessment of extraocular movements, fluid status, and deep tendon reflexes are important components of the physical exami nation. Chronic autoimmune thyroiditis may be the initial presentation of an autoimmune polyglandular syndrome, and the possibility of coexisting autoimmune diseases such as type 1 diabetes, Addison’s disease, and perni cious anemia should be addressed in the med ical history. 15.1 12 13 ### 15 14 15 15.2 Box 15.2 Symptoms and Signs of Hypo thyroidism 5 Goiter/thyromegaly 5 Slowing of linear growth 5 Skeletal maturational delay 5 Pubertal disorders (delay or pseudo precocity) 5 Slowed mentation (lethargy and impaired school performance) 5 Fatigue 5 Constipation 5 Increased cold sensitivity 5 Depression 5 Irregular and/or heavy menstrual peri ods 5 Bradycardia (decreased cardiac out put) 5 Hypothermia 5 Weight gain 5 Dry, sallow, coarse skin 5 Brittle hair 5 Delayed deep tendon reflexes ### 15.2.4 Diagnosis In the absence of hypothalamic or pituitary disease, the serum TSH concentration is the most sensitive screen for thyroid function. TSH levels are elevated in primary hypothy roidism. If the differential diagnosis includes central hypothyroidism or the overall suspi cion for hypothyroidism is high, a free T4 (or calculated free T4 index) should be included on the initial screen. In mild hypothyroidism, serum T3 concentrations can remain in the normal range due to increased conversion of T4 to T3 by type 2 deiodinase and the prefer ential secretion of T3 by residual thyroid tis sue under the influence of hyperthyrotropinemia [16]. For these reasons, measuring the serum T3 concentration is not useful in diagnosing or monitoring patients with primary hypothyroidism. ## PDF page 400 | printed page 389 The presence of goiter or hyperthyrotro pinemia should prompt the measurement of anti-TPO antibodies. Anti-TPO antibodies are the most sensitive screen for chronic auto immune thyroiditis; up to 90% of patients with hypothyroidism secondary to autoim mune thyroiditis are anti-TPO antibody posi tive [17]. The additional measurement of antithyroglobulin antibodies gains little fur ther benefit, although they may be added if anti-TPO titers are negative. It should be noted that 10–15% of the general population are positive for anti-TPO antibodies and 5–15% for anti-thyroglobulin antibodies, and low titers are not very specific for autoim mune thyroid disease [1]. If anti-TPO anti bodies are absent, less common etiologies of primary hypothyroidism, such as transient hypothyroidism, subacute thyroiditis, external irradiation, consumptive hypothyroidism, or iodine deficiency should be considered [18–20]. The typical patient with hypothyroidism secondary to chronic autoimmune thyroiditis will have an elevated TSH (over 10 μU/mL), a low free T4, and positive anti-TPO antibodies. In the early stages of the disease (type 1A), anti-TPO antibodies may be positive with goi ter, though TSH may be normal. Later, TSH elevation becomes modest (between 5 and 10 μU/mL) with normal circulating free T4 (sub clinical hypothyroidism). The log-linear relationship between serum TSH and free T4 explains how small reduc ![Source image](../../figures/ch015_p0400_01.jpg) Unmatched source image; PDF page 400. Consult the original caption. ## PDF page 401 | printed page 390 tions in serum free T4 lead to large deviations in TSH. Most patients with subclinical hypo thyroidism are asymptomatic. However, indi viduals with the combined risk factors of hyperthyrotropinemia and positive thyroid antibodies (anti-thyroglobulin or anti-TPO) are at high risk for progression to overt hypo thyroidism [20]. Therefore, typical recommen dations are for patients with TSH values greater than 10 μU/mL, goiter, and/or thyroid autoantibodies, to be started on thyroid hor mone replacement [21, 22]. Given the critical importance of thyroid hormone in neurodevelopment, persistent hyperthyrotropinemia in infancy is often empirically treated, and a trial off therapy or with reduced doses may be considered after the age of 2–3 years. Similarly, the presence of growth failure may lower the threshold to ini tiate replacement therapy in children with per sistent hyperthyrotropinemia. Euthyroid children with autoimmune thyroiditis (type 1A or type 1B) can be observed without treat ment and monitored carefully with TSH mea surements every 6–12 months, as a significant fraction will progress to overt hypothyroidism [23]. ### 15.2.5 Therapy Levothyroxine (l-T4) is the recommended treatment for children with hypothyroidism. There are minimal adverse reactions, and its long half-life of 5–7 days allows the conve nience of daily administration. Of note, while desiccated thyroid extracts and liothyronine (T3) are commercially available as replace ment options, current consensus guidelines recommend against the routine use of these preparations in children due to the lack of long-term outcome data and their risk of iat rogenic hypertriiodothyronemia [24]. ### 15 25 26 26 15.1 4 4 TSH normalization (typical range 0.5–5 μU/mL) is the goal of replacement therapy. This will usually be associated with a free T4 concentration in the upper half of the normal range. Thyroid function tests should be obtained 6 weeks after initiating or adjusting the levothyroxine dosage. Growth and sexual development should be followed systemati cally. Most children achieve adequate catchup growth and a normal adult stature after initiating levothyroxine replacement. However, catch-up growth may be compro mised and target height may not be achieved if treatment has been started after a prolonged duration of severe hypothyroidism. Once bio chemical euthyroidism has been achieved, TSH can be monitored every 4–6 months in the growing child and yearly once final height has been attained. Graves’ disease is relatively rare, with a yearly incidence of 8–9 per 1,000,000 children less than 15 years old and 1 per 1,000,000 children less than 4 years old [30–32]. Girls are affected four to five times more frequently than boys, although no gen der difference is noted under 4 years of age [31–33]. The term thyrotoxicosis refers to the clinical state resulting from any condition that leads to elevated serum thyroid hormone level; whereas hyperthyroidism refers specifically to increased thyroid hormone production from the gland. Graves’ disease is the most com mon etiology of hyperthyroidism in children [34], and it is important to accurately diag nose this condition as the choice of therapy depends on the etiology of the thyrotoxicosis. For example, antithyroid drugs, which are the mainstay in the management of Graves’ dis ease, play no role in treating thyrotoxicosis secondary to chronic autoimmune thyroiditis or subacute thyroiditis. ### 15.3.1 Pathophysiology Graves’ hyperthyroidism results from the overproduction of thyroid-stimulating anti bodies that bind to and activate the G-proteincoupled thyrotropin receptor (TSHR), leading to follicular cell hyperplasia and hypersecre tion of thyroid hormone [35]. Graves’ disease shares many features with chronic autoim mune thyroiditis, including autoantibodies directed against thyroglobulin, thyroperoxi dase, and the sodium-iodine symporter. Lymphocytic infiltration of the thyroid paren chyma is present, and germinal centers consti tute a significant source of intrathyroidal autoantibodies.
