For unclear rea sons, lymphocytic infiltration and the accumulation of glycosaminoglycans can also be found in orbital connective tissue and skin, which results in the extrathyroidal manifesta tions of Graves’ ophthalmopathy and der mopathy [36, 37]. ### 15.3.2 Clinical Presentation The clinical presentation of Graves’ disease in childhood is variable and can be insidious. A careful history will often reveal a severalmonth history of progressive symptoms. Common signs and symptoms of Graves’ disease are listed in Box 15.3. In contrast to children with hypothyroidism, those with hyperthyroidism can show a linear growth acceleration and advanced skeletal matura tion. Goiter is present in most cases, charac terized by diffuse, nontender, spongiform enlargement of the gland. The pyramidal lobe is often palpable, and a bruit may be audible secondary to increased blood flow through the gland. Extrathyroidal manifesta tions such as ophthalmopathy and dermopa thy are rare and tend to be less severe than in adults [36–38]. While the pediatric literature indicates that 50–70% of children have ocu lar manifestations, the majority of such cases are a consequence of increased sympathetic tone and not true ophthalmopathy. Periorbital edema, proptosis, lid retraction, erythema, and pain are often mild and responsive to improvement in thyroid func tion. Even children with infiltrative disease of the orbital structures typically improve with restoration of euthyroidism. Therefore, conservative management is generally rec ommended, as long as vision is not threat ened [36]. ### 15 Box 15.3 Symptoms and Signs of Hyper thyroidism in Children Signs Symptoms Goiter Exophthalmos Lid lag Stare Accelerated linear growth Advanced bone age Tachycardia Hypertension Widened pulse pressure Tremors Brisk deep tendon reflexes Thyroid bruit Heat intolerance/ diaphoresis Weight loss or gain Polyphagia Fatigue Palpitations Decreased concentra tion/hyperactivity Nervousness/ irritability Insomnia Headaches Increased frequency of bowel movements Polyuria ### 15.3.3 Diagnosis Thyrotoxicosis is biochemically defined by an elevation of serum free thyroxine (FT4) with suppressed serum thyrotropin (TSH) concen trations to <0.1 μU/mL. A determination of total triiodothyronine (T3) concentration is warranted if TSH is suppressed and serum FT4 is normal. In patients with early disease or iodine-deficient patients, serum FT4 con centrations may be normal or reduced despite elevated levels of T3. This is due to increased peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 and is the only situation in which a serum T3 measure ment is required to confirm the diagnosis [39]. The triad of thyrotoxicosis, goiter, and orbitopathy is diagnostic for Graves’ disease [39], and no other laboratory tests or imaging studies are typically necessary. However, addi tional diagnostic tools can confirm the diag nosis and distinguish Graves’ disease from other forms of thyrotoxicosis. ## PDF page 404 | printed page 393 Most patients with Graves’ disease have measurable serum thyrotropin receptor bind ing antibody titers (TRAbs). TRAbs can be measured by either a bioassay (thyroid stimu lating immunoglobulin, TSI) or competitive binding assay (thyrotropin binding inhibitory immunoglobulin, TBII). In the functional TSI assay, a patient’s serum antibodies directly stimulate the TSH receptor in vitro and increase cAMP production. In the TBII assay, all antibodies that compete with the TSH receptor are measured regardless of their activity (stimulating, blocking, or neu tral to the TSHR). Both assays are highly sen sitive and specific for diagnosing Graves’ disease [40]. In most cases of thyrotoxicosis, the pres ence of TRAbs is a helpful adjunctive test to confirm the diagnosis. However, if antibody titers are equivocal, measurement of radioio dine uptake (RAIU) with 123I or 99Tc can be used [41]. RAI uptake is elevated and diffusely distributed in Graves’ disease. In hyperthy roidism from a toxic nodule(s), there is focal uptake at the site of the nodule(s) with sup pression of the remainder of the gland. RAI uptake is low in other causes of thyrotoxico sis, such as thyroiditis or exogenous thyroid hormone ingestion. There is a subgroup of patients with sub clinical hyperthyroidism characterized by a low but not overtly suppressed TSH (0.1–0.3 μU/mL) and normal serum concentrations of thyroid hormone [42]. In adults over 60 years, a low serum TSH concentration has been associated with an increased risk of atrial fibrillation [43]. Some studies suggest that postmenopausal women are also at risk of bone loss [44]. However, these risks have not been identified in children. Several studies indicate that a significant fraction of patients with subclinical thyrotoxicosis experience spontaneous remission [44, 45]. Accordingly, the initial detection of a suppressed TSH con centration without elevated thyroid hormone levels or associated symptoms should be man aged conservatively by repeating thyroid func tion tests in 4–8 weeks. Asymptomatic children with subclinical hyperthyroidism and no specific cardiac risk factors can be followed with the expectation that TSH suppression due to transient thyroiditis will resolve spon taneously, while that due to Graves’ disease or an autonomous nodule will persist. ### 15.4 Differential Diagnosis ### of Thyrotoxicosis in Children The duration of symptoms is an important factor to consider in the differential diagnosis of thyrotoxicosis. If thyrotoxicosis has been present for less than 8 weeks, transient thyro toxicosis secondary to thyroiditis (autoim mune, viral, postpartum, drug-induced) should be considered. These forms of thy roiditis are self-limited and refractory to ther apy with thionamides. For thyrotoxicosis present for more than 8 weeks, the diagnosis of Graves’ disease is more likely [34, 46] ( Box 15.4). Beta-adrenergic antagonists, atenolol (0.8–1.0 mg/kg/day divided once or twice daily) or propranolol (10–40 mg every 6–8 h), should be offered in all patients to help control the increased sympathetic tone (tachy cardia, hypertension, anxiety, tremors), pend ing no contraindications (bronchospastic asthma) [46]. Treatment of Graves’ hyperthy roidism is divided into two categories: (1) Antithyroid drugs or (2) Definitive therapy with radioiodine ablation or surgical thyroid ectomy. The antithyroid drugs (ATDs, thionamide derivatives), methimazole (MMI), and pro pylthiouracil (PTU) block the organification of iodine and thyroid hormone synthesis. PTU also inhibits the conversion of T4 to T3, and both have some immunosuppressive effects. Methimazole (MMI) is the first-line treatment for children with Graves’ disease and is preferred due to its longer half-life and more favorable safety profile. The recom mended starting dose for methimazole is 0.5–1.0 mg/kg/day administered once or twice daily [34, 45]. PTU is no longer used in chil dren due to the risk of liver failure [47, 48]. However, PTU can be reserved for use in firsttrimester pregnancy (due to concerns of MMI-associated birth defects), lifethreatening thyroid storm (to inhibit T4-to-T3 conversion), and allergic reactions to MMI as a short bridge to definitive therapy. ### 15 After initiation of ATD, thyroid function tests should be monitored every 2 weeks ini tially and then every 4 weeks after any dose adjustment. Once the free T4 concertation has fallen to the upper end of the normal range, the MMI dose should be decreased by 50%. Further dose adjustments are guided by serial thyroid function tests, initially relying upon the FT4 concentration and later the TSH con centration to guide adjustments to the MMI dose. After TSH secretion recovers from its chronic suppression, which can take up to 6 months, the goal of maintenance therapy is TSH normalization [46]. The first clinical response to medications is 2–4 weeks into therapy. Weight loss subsides, and weight gain may occur. Long-term remission rates in chil dren have been reported at 25% after 2 years of ATD and 50% after 4 years [49]. However, based on more recent studies, long-term treat ment with ATDs of up to 120 months is con sidered efficacious and safe [50–52]. Antithyroid drugs are usually well toler ated but can cause side effects. Minor adverse reactions, such as hives, rash, and myalgias/ arthralgias, occur approximately 5–25% of the time and within the first weeks to months of therapy. Hives can be treated with antihis tamines, but they can also be severe enough to require discontinuation of the drug. The more severe adverse effects include agranulocytosis (absolute neutrophil count (ANC) <500) and hepatotoxicity. Agranulocytosis occurs with both methimazole and PTU. It is more com mon with methimazole, dose-dependent, and typically develops within the first 90 days. It can also be idiosyncratic and occur upon reexposure to the drug after several years. Patients should be counseled that if fever, sore throat, or unexplained mouth sores develop, they should discontinue the drug and seek medical attention. Because leukopenia can also be a manifestation of Graves’ disease, a white blood cell count and differential should be performed before starting antithyroid drug therapy and if the patient develops any con cerning symptoms [53, 54]. Methimazole induced hepatotoxicity is typically cholestatic, whereas PTU has been associated with hepatocellular injury. Routine monitoring of liver function tests has not been found to reduce the severity of hepato toxicity. However, ATDs should be avoided when aminotransferases are greater than 3–5 times the upper limit of normal and discon tinued with jaundice, extreme pruritus, anorexia, or acholic stools [53, 54]. In addi tion, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodyassociated vasculitis occurs more frequently with PTU and can present after months to years of therapy. ## PDF page 406 | printed page 395 ### 15.4.2 Definitive Therapy The options for the definitive treatment of Graves’ disease are radioactive iodine ablation and surgical thyroidectomy; both, if success ful, result in permanent hypothyroidism. Candidates for radioiodine include those who fail to remit on ATD, develop severe side effects of ATDs, are nonadherent, or personal preference [55, 56]. Before radioiodine abla tion, euthyroidism should be restored to mini mize the development of severe radiation induced thyroiditis. Methimazole should be stopped 3–5 days before radioiodine adminis tration. The goal is to administer a sufficient dose of radioiodine to ablate thyroid tissue and develop hypothyroidism [57]. Some cen ters measure radioiodine uptake before treat ment and calculate an 131I dose that delivers an absorbed thyroid dose of >150 μCi/g thy roid. Alternatively, an empiric fixed dose of 131I (usually 10–15 mCi) can be offered [58]. The theoretical advantage of calculated doses is that it defines the lowest administered dose for each patient to achieve the therapeutic effect. This benefit is most important in small children because the absorbed radiation dose to bone marrow and other normal tissues is inversely proportional to body size. Based on this concept and theoretical modeling of radi ation exposure, 131I therapy should be avoided in children younger than 5 years [57]. It may be used cautiously in children between 5 and 10 years of age as long as the administered dose is <10 mCi. Radioiodine ablation has a low failure rate (5–20%), and patients with persistent hyperthyroidism more than 6 months after their first 131I therapy can be offered retreatment [57]. Thyroidectomy is typically used as defini tive therapy for those patients with a massive goiter (>4 times normal), severe orbitopathy, coexisting nodules or carcinoma, children less than 5 years of age, and those with contrain dications for radioactive iodine (pregnancy) [59]. Thyroidectomy is a safe procedure when performed by an experienced surgeon, and a referral to a surgeon with a low complication rate minimizes postoperative risks. Ideally, thyroid surgery should be performed after the patient has been rendered euthyroid with methimazole and pretreated for 7–14 days with saturated potassium iodide (SSKI; 1–3 drops, 2–3 times per day) [59]. The latter helps decrease the vascularity of the gland. Complications of surgical treatment include hypoparathyroidism (transient or permanent) and paralysis of the vocal cords, but such complications are reduced substantially in a high-volume center [59, 60]. Patients immedi ately become hypothyroid and require lifelong thyroid hormone replacement. Recurrence of hyperthyroidism is rare. ### 15.4.3 Monitoring of Graves’ ### Disease and the Transition to Adult Care Given the documented risks of surgery and the theoretical risks of radioiodine, a pro longed course of antithyroid medication is now more accepted in treating pediatric Graves’ disease. Monitoring of thyroid func tion tests every 3–4 months in the growing child and 4 weeks after any medication adjust ment to normalize the TSH is recommended [61]. Physical examination should focus on heart rate, blood pressure, pubertal status, lin ear growth, goiter size, and orbitopathy (vision, and ocular movements). The transi tion to adulthood should prompt a rediscussion of therapy. For young adults with persistent hyperthyroidism, 131I is the defini tive treatment of choice [62]. Definitive ther apy allows for a more straightforward regimen of medication and laboratory monitoring. Additionally, prior definitive therapy simpli fies the management of patients during preg nancy. ### 15.5 Neonatal Graves’ Disease Approximately 0.6% of infants born to moth ers with a history of Graves’ disease will develop neonatal hyperthyroidism due to the transplacental passage of maternal TRAbs. While the development of neonatal Graves’ ## PDF page 407 | printed page 396 disease is more common in mothers with active Graves’ disease, it can also occur after those who have previously received definitive therapy with radioiodine or thyroidectomy [63, 64]. These infants are at risk for neonatal Graves’ disease as well as congenital hypothy roidism due to the transplacental passage of TSH receptor blocking (rather than stimulat ing) antibodies. The signs can be immediate or delayed by 3–10 days due to the time required for clearance of maternal antithyroid drugs. Typically, neonatal Graves’ disease spontane ously remits by 12 weeks of life following clearance of maternal TRAbs from the infant’s circulation, but the condition has been reported to persist for as long as 6 months. Prenatal ultrasounds should monitor fetal heart rate, growth, and glandular size. The measurement of TRAbs between 20 and 24 weeks of gestation is recommended as a predictor for the development of fetal and neo natal Graves’ disease. Mothers with TSI >3×, TBII >5 IU/L, or those with a prior infant with neonatal Graves’ disease are at highest risk [65]. In utero, the presence of goiter, tachycardia, and intrauterine growth restric tion suggests fetal hyperthyroidism. In some circumstances, antithyroid drugs can be administered to the mother to control fetal hyperthyroidism. For high-risk infants, such as those born to mothers with high levels of thyrotropin-stimulating antibodies or those with a history of an affected sibling, thyroid function tests and TRAbs should be obtained at birth. Thereafter, thyroid function tests should be monitored at 3–5 days of life, and 10–14 days of life, and clinically followed closely through 3 months [65]. ### 15 Affected infants with Graves’ disease are often growth restricted, diaphoretic, and hyperkinetic. Goiter can occur and, when severe, can compress the infant’s airway. Diarrhea, vomiting, poor weight gain, exoph thalmos, arrhythmias, and congestive heart failure can develop. Confirmatory thyroid function tests (TSH, free T4, T3) and TRAbs should be obtained, and treatment initiated immediately. In cases of acute neona tal thyrotoxicosis, MMI (0.25–1.0 mg/kg/day) or PTU (5–10 mg/kg/day) may be adminis tered orally, or through a nasogastric tube in divided doses every 8–12 h. Inorganic iodine will speed the decrease in circulating thyroid hormone, and is administered as SSKI (48 mg iodide/drop) at the dose of one drop per day. Supportive therapy with intravenous flu ids, beta-blockers (propranolol 2 mg/kg/day), and glucocorticoids (prednisone 2 mg/kg/day) may be helpful in severe cases [66]. Thyroid function tests should be monitored weekly, and treatment can be gradually weaned weekly to prevent the development of iatro genic hypothyroidism. After the clearance of TSH-receptor antibodies, therapy can be dis continued. The cumulative mortality of neo natal Graves’ disease is estimated to be as high as 25% [65]. Potential long-term morbidity includes growth restriction, craniosynostosis, impaired intellectual function, and central hypothyroidism [67, 68]. Since the half-life of maternal immunoglobulin is approximately 14 days, most cases of neonatal Graves’ dis ease will resolve after 3–12 weeks. The differ ential diagnosis of neonatal thyrotoxicosis also includes McCune-Albright syndrome and activating mutations of the TSH receptor. These non-autoimmune etiologies are exceed ingly rare but should be considered if thyro toxicosis persists beyond 3 months. ### 15.6 Summary Autoimmune thyroid diseases, both Hashimoto’s thyroiditis and Graves’ disease, are due to dysregulation of the immune sys tem and potential development of overt thy roid dysfunction. In a genetically predisposed individual, activated T cells infiltrate the thy roid gland, leading to B cell dysregulation and antibody production with the loss of toler ance to multiple thyroid antigens, including thyroglobulin, thyroperoxidase, sodiumiodine symporter, and the TSH receptor. In Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, there may be a wax ing and waning of thyroid function with pro longed periods of euthyroidism before progression to hypothyroidism. In general, treating subclinical hypothyroidism is not beneficial in the pediatric population, unless ## PDF page 408 | printed page 397 TSH concentrations exceed 10 μU/mL and the patient has goiter and/or anti-TPO or anti-Tg antibodies. In Graves’ disease, TSH receptor antibodies stimulate the gland result ing in excessive thyroid hormone production and development of symptoms of thyrotoxi cosis. It is essential to differentiate between thyroiditis and Graves’ disease because the use of antithyroid drugs is not indicated in the former. Treatment for Graves’ disease is always individualized. Antithyroid drugs are the first line of therapy in children, with defin itive therapy reserved for refractory cases or serious adverse effects. Side effects of antithy roid drugs occur in up to 25% of patients with rash and hives being the most common. Educating families about the risks of serious side effects such as agranulocytosis, hepatitis, arthritis, vasculitis, and Stevens-Johnson syn drome is paramount. While adults have a more favorable remission rate, children often require a more prolonged course of antithy roid drug to achieve remission. For those that do not remit, permanent therapy with either radioiodine ablation or surgical thyroidec tomy in a high-volume center can be pursued. Thyroidectomy is typically reserved for patients with a very large gland, severe orbi topathy, coexisting nodules or carcinoma, children less than 5 years of age, and those with contraindications for radioactive iodine. Finally, neonatal Graves’ disease is a rare dis order that results from the transplacental pas sage of TSH receptor antibodies from a mother with active or a prior history of treated Graves’ disease. It has a high morbid ity rate, so prompt recognition and treatment are critical. Therapy consists of beta-block ade, antithyroid drugs, inorganic iodine, and glucocorticoids depending on the severity of presentation. title: Non-thyroidal Illness Syndrome

paragraphs.text: Julie Park and Lisa D. Madison
paragraphs.heading: Non-thyroidal Illness Syndrome

paragraphs.text: 16.3.1 Change in the Central Hypothalamic–Pituitary–Thyroid Axis – 406 16.3.2 Changes in Peripheral Thyroid Hormone Metabolism – 406 16.3.3 Changes in Thyroid Hormone-Binding Protein Kinetics – 407 16.3.4 Changes in Thyroid Hormone Transport and Action at the Tissue Level – 407 16.3.5 Summary of Pathogenesis of NTIS–Thyroid Changes ( Fig. 16.2) – 408
paragraphs.heading: 16.3 Pathogenesis of NTIS–Thyroid Changes – 406

paragraphs.text: 16.5.1 Preterm Infants – 409 16.5.2 Critically Ill Children – 412 16.5.3 Cardiac Surgery in Children – 413 16.5.4 Renal Insufficiency (Acute and Chronic) – 415 16.5.5 COVID 19 – 416
paragraphs.heading: 16.5 Clinical Presentation and Diagnostic Evaluation of Pediatric NTIS – 409

paragraphs.text: Non-thyroidal illness is the term used to describe the changes in thyroid hormone and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) with
paragraphs.heading: 16.1 Introduction and Background

paragraphs.text: acute illness not caused by an intrinsic abnor mality of thyroid function [1]. In children, non-thyroidal illness is most commonly seen in acutely ill patients admitted to pediatric or neonatal intensive care units (ICUs). The characteristic decrease in thyroid hormone levels also can be seen with starvation, trauma, or surgical procedures. Nonthyroidal illness probably occurs with any severe illness, and the pattern of changes in thyroid hormones correlates with the severity of illness. Typically, the first changes are a decrease in serum triiodothyronine (T3) and a rise in reverse T3 (rT3) levels [2]. This disor der has been referred to as the low-T3 syn drome or the euthyroid sick syndrome. However, as it is not clear that these patients are clinically “euthyroid,” non-thyroidal ill ness syndrome (NTIS) is the term preferred at present [3, 4].
paragraphs.heading: 16.1 Introduction and Background

paragraphs.text: This chapter will begin with a descrip tion of the changes in thyroid hormones and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels that occur in NTIS. This will be fol lowed by a brief review of what is known about the pathogenesis of NTIS in starva tion and acute illness. This will include a discussion of changes in hypothalamic– pituitary–thyroid (HPT) axis function, changes in peripheral thyroid hormone metabolism (as regulated by the three deio dinase enzymes), changes in thyroid hor mone binding in the circulation, thyroid hormone transport into the cell, and finally changes in thyroid hormone action at the tissue level in NTIS. Next will be a discus sion of some of the most common pediatric clinical disorders associated with NTIS, including “hypothyroxinemia of prematu rity,” acutely ill patients in an ICU setting, renal insufficiency (acute and chronic), car diac surgery, and COVID-19 infection. NTIS is characterized by changes in thyroid hormone levels and TSH consistent with central hypothyroidism. Discussion of the clinical disorders will review evidence that NTIS is either a beneficial “adaptive response” to starvation or acute illness or a “maladaptive response” that might be improved by thyroid hormone treatment.
paragraphs.heading: 16.1 Introduction and Background

paragraphs.text: A fall in serum T3 accompanied by a rise in rT3 levels is the most common change in patients with NTIS (thus, as noted above, in the past, NTIS has been referred to as the “low-T3 syndrome”), but it is now recognized that rT3 may be normal or even low in some cases [4]. Simple fasting pro duces these changes within 24–36 h; refeeding (particularly with glucose) rapidly reverses these changes. Serum T4 levels do not fall with fasting in healthy subjects. Many acute illnesses are asso ciated with “starvation”; reduced caloric intake thus is likely one factor resulting in the initial changes in serum T3 and rT3.
paragraphs.heading: Hormone Changes in NTIS

paragraphs.text: Serum T4 levels tend to be normal in mild acute illness, but with increasing severity of ill ness, serum T4 levels will decrease. The degree of fall in serum T3 and T4 is related to the severity of the acute illness [5]. Changes in serum free T4 and free T3 levels are less cer tain, with results varying with the assay method. When free T4 is measured by most common “analogue” immunoassays, serum free T4 levels appear to decrease with acute ill ness [6]. If free T4 is calculated using a mea sure of total T4 and some measure of serum
paragraphs.heading: Hormone Changes in NTIS

paragraphs.text: protein binding, e.g., T3 resin uptake, serum free T4 levels also appear to decrease. However, if free T4 is measured by methods that involve initial physical separation of free T4 from pro tein-bound T4, e.g., equilibrium dialysis or ultrafiltration, serum free T4 levels are usually normal or even increased in patients with acute illness [7]. A similar pattern is seen with free T3 measurements. If free T3 is measured by the more common commercial assays, the fall in serum free T3 parallels the fall in total T3. However, if free T3 is measured by a dialy sis or filtration method, the decrease in serum free T3 does not match the fall in total T3. One study reported serum free T3 levels only 10% lower than a healthy control group [8].
paragraphs.heading: Hormone Changes in NTIS

paragraphs.text: TSH measurements generally are in the normal range, though serum TSH may decrease below normal in some patients with severe acute illness [9]. Thus, it is not uncommon to find low serum T3 and T4 levels, low free T4 levels (by commonly used assay methods), and normal or low TSH levels, results that are con sistent with central hypothyroidism.
paragraphs.heading: Hormone Changes in NTIS

paragraphs.text: normal range, with recovery it rises back into the normal range and even mildly above the normal range in some patients (e.g., 10–20 mU/L) [10]. Serum T4 rises back to the normal range, followed by a rise in total T3 and a fall in rT3 back into the normal range. Serum free T4, if measured by an analogue immunoassay, will rise back into the normal range; if free T4 is measured by equilibrium dialysis or ultrafiltration, it typically remains normal throughout the NTIS. Serum free T3 follows a similar pattern.
paragraphs.heading: Hormone Changes in NTIS

paragraphs.text: Although serum T3 and T4 levels fall, there is no increase in serum TSH levels, and with increasing severity of illness, there may be a decrease in TSH levels. Frequent sampling studies show a decrease in the nocturnal TSH surge and amplitude [11]; similar changes occur in patients with central hypothyroidism. Evidence points to a decrease in thyrotropinreleasing hormone (TRH) as a cause of diminished TSH secretion, along with direct effects of acute illness on pituitary thyrotroph cell function. Postmortem studies in patients with NTIS show decreased TRH mRNA expression in the paraventricular nucleus (PVN), the main source of TRH [12]. Reduced intake of calories, either as part of an acute illness or with fasting, results in decreased leptin levels. In experimental animal studies, decreased leptin levels result in altered neuro endocrine regulation of TRH secretion [13]. Further, cytokines along with increased corti sol produced with acute illness appear to have a direct inhibitory effect on TSH secretion in the pituitary [14]. If acutely ill patients are treated with dopamine (to maintain cardio
paragraphs.heading: Hypothalamic–Pituitary– Thyroid Axis

paragraphs.text: vascular function) or glucocorticoids, these drugs also inhibit TSH secretion. There is also one other proposed mechanism that may inhibit TSH secretion. Although PVN cells do not appear to directly sense circulating T3 or T4 levels, a unique glial cell with processes that extend into the hypothalamus, the tany cyte, provides a communication between the portal circulation and the hypothalamus. Studies in an animal model of NTIS show an increase in tanycyte deiodinase type 2 (D2) enzyme activity [15]. Increased D2 activity could increase T4 to T3 conversion, resulting in “local tissue hyperthyroidism” in the hypo thalamus, which, by way of negative feedback, would inhibit TRH synthesis. In summary, current evidence supports diminished TRH production and decreased TSH secretion as a major cause of decreased thyroid gland T4 production and secretion and perhaps also decreased T3 levels (see below: since the majority of T3 is produced by peripheral tis sue deiodination of T4, changes in tissue deio dinases also appear to be a cause of lower serum T3 levels). Cytokines produced during illness also exhibit a direct inhibitory effect on the thyroid hormone synthesis pathway. Thyroglobulin production, iodide uptake, and thyroid peroxidase expression, an important regulator of the oxidation of iodide to iodine, are altered in response to cytokines in studies of animal and human thyrocytes [16].

Thyroid hormone metabolism in extrathyroi dal tissue is regulated by three deiodinase enzymes. Type 1 and type 2 deiodinase (D1 and D2) are the main activating enzymes, while type 3 deiodinase (D3) is the inactivat ing enzyme [17]. D1 is present in many extra thyroidal tissues, including the liver and kidney, while D2 is present in the pituitary, brain, and brown adipose tissue. The main action of D1 and D2 is to convert T4 to bio
paragraphs.heading: Thyroid Hormone Metabolism

paragraphs.text: logically active T3; D1, located on the plasma membrane, is the enzyme responsible for pro duction of most of the T3 that enters the cir culation. D3 is present in many extrathyroidal tissues, including the brain; the main action of D3 is to convert T4 to biologically inactive rT3 and, to a lesser extent, T3 to 3,3′-diiodo thyronine (T2). The expression of the deiodin ase enzymes is modified in acute illness and appears to be highly tissue specific. It is gener ally accepted that the fall in serum T3 levels is the result of decreased D1 and increased D3 activity [18]. There is some evidence that these changes in D1 and D3 are mediated by the increased levels of cytokines and glucocorti coids seen in acute illness. More recent evi dence, however, including studies in D1/D2 and D3 knockout mice, find that the changes in serum T3 and T4 with induced acute illness are similar to wild-type animals. These stud ies suggest that the changes noted in deiodin ase enzymes may be a consequence, not the cause of the NTIS [19]. Finally, there is evi dence of increased degradation of T4 and T3 via non-deiodination pathways, manifested by increased levels of T3 sulfate and triiodo thyroacetic acid (TRIAC) and tetraiodothy roacetic acid (TETRAC) in patients with NTIS [1].
paragraphs.heading: Thyroid Hormone Metabolism

paragraphs.text: Thyroid hormone-binding proteins including thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG), trans thyretin (formerly termed thyroxine-binding prealbumin), and albumin are “acute-phase” reactants and tend to fall with acute illnesses [2]. This appears to be the result of both impaired synthesis but also rapid breakdown and movement out of the plasma space. This is particularly true with sepsis and cardiopul monary bypass. As the vast majority of serum T4 (99.97%) and T3 (99.70%) are bound, con centrations of serum total T4 and total T3 may be lower in large part as a result of lower binding protein levels. In addition, there is
paragraphs.heading: Hormone-Binding Protein Kinetics

paragraphs.text: evidence of circulating inhibitors of T4 and T3 binding to their binding proteins in NTIS. Non-esterified fatty acids and certain drugs used to treat patients with NTIS appear to act as inhibitors, including heparin, furosemide, and salicylate. Heparin’s action appears to be in vitro; it activates lipoprotein lipase which then breaks down triglycerides into glycerol and fatty acids, resulting in a dramatic release of bound T4 and false elevation of free T4 measurements [20].
paragraphs.heading: Hormone-Binding Protein Kinetics

paragraphs.text: Entry of thyroid hormone into the cell is car ried out by ATP-dependent transporters, including monocarboxylate transporter 8 (MCT8), monocarboxylate transporter 10 (MCT10), and organic anion transporting polypeptide family 1C1 (OATP1C1). The effect of illness on the expression of these transporters is complex and varied, depend ing on tissue type and on duration of illness. Changes in transporter expression in the hypothalamus, liver, and muscle may all play a role in NTIS, but specific functional conse quences and effect on tissue T3 concentra tions remain unclear [4, 16]. Once thyroid hormone enters the cell, T3 (either from direct entry or via intracellular T4 deiodination to T3) binds to a specific thyroid hormone recep tor (THR). Studies in humans with acute ill ness and animal models of NTIS yield conflicting information on changes in THR, with reports of increased, decreased, or no change in THR expression. THR action is regulated by co-activators and corepressors; there is some evidence that cytokines pro duced with acute illness compete with coactivators or corepressors and so may regulate tissue-specific THR action. It appears that THR expression is downregulated in acute ill ness and upregulated in chronic illness, though again this appears to be tissue specific and likely an overgeneralization [1, 4].
paragraphs.heading: Hormone Transport and Action at the Tissue Level

paragraphs.text: Acute illness results in diminished TRH pro duction and TSH secretion, as well as direct effects on the thyroid gland itself. The charac teristic fall in serum T3 levels appears to be the result of decreased production in the thy roid gland, decreased D1 and D2 activity resulting in decreased extrathyroidal conver sion of T4 to T3, and increased D3 activity with increased conversion of T4 to rT3. Decreased levels of total T3 and total T4 are also the result of decreased thyroid hormonebinding proteins. Levels of free T4 and free T3 are assay dependent; assays using physical separation techniques, such as equilibrium dialysis, tend to show normal serum free T4 and normal or only mildly low free T3 results. Complex changes in thyroid hormone trans port into the cell and in thyroid hormone receptor expression across tissue types also occur in NTIS, with resulting alterations in thyroid hormone metabolism that may play a role in organ function or dysfunction at vary ing stages of illness [4].

It can be difficult to separate the changes in serum thyroid hormone levels seen in patients with NTIS from those who have true thyroid dysfunction. While good data do not exist for children, studies in adult patients admitted to medical services report a low serum T3 level in 50%, low serum T4 level in 15–20%, and an abnormal (low or high) TSH in 10% [2]. If there is a clinical suspicion of hypothyroid ism, we recommend that patients undergo measurement of serum free T4 by equilibrium dialysis and TSH levels. In true primary hypo thyroidism, patients will have a low free T4 level and elevated TSH level. Caution must be used, however, as patients recovering from NTIS may manifest a low free T4 and elevated TSH. Typically, the elevation in TSH concen tration is mild, in the 10–20 mU/L range. A TSH elevation >20 mU/L is suspicious for true hypothyroidism. As autoimmune thy roiditis is the most common cause of acquired hypothyroidism, finding positive antithyroglobulin and/or thyroid peroxidase anti bodies would support a diagnosis of
paragraphs.heading: Thyroid Dysfunction

paragraphs.text: hypothyroidism. Clinicians should be aware that in patients with true hypothyroidism, ele vated TSH levels may decrease, even into the normal range, in situations associated with NTIS, particularly if patients are treated with drugs that inhibit TSH secretion such as dopamine or glucocorticoids. If thyroid hor mone treatment is to be started, patients should undergo evaluation of pituitaryadrenal function first. Thyroid hormone treat ment in the face of unrecognized adrenal insufficiency may precipitate adrenal crisis, certainly undesirable in the face of acute ill ness.
paragraphs.heading: Thyroid Dysfunction

paragraphs.text: If there is a clinical suspicion of hyperthy roidism, we recommend measurement of serum free T4, free T3 (both by equilibrium dialysis), and TSH levels. In true hyperthy roidism, patients will have an elevated free T4 and free T3 level and a TSH suppressed below the normal range. Patients with severe NTIS may manifest a low TSH level, but this usually is not confused with hyperthyroidism as serum free T4 and free T3 are not elevated. Again, in patients with true hyperthyroidism, the con centration of TSH is not just low, but com monly unmeasurable (<0.01 mU/L). A normal TSH level excludes hyperthyroidism. Elevated concentrations of thyrotropin receptorstimulating antibody (e.g., thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin [TSI]) would support the diagnosis of Graves’ disease and hyperthy roidism.
paragraphs.heading: Thyroid Dysfunction

paragraphs.text: As many clinical manifestations of acute illness overlap with thyroid dysfunction, often the best course is to recheck thyroid function tests after resolution of the acute illness.
paragraphs.heading: Thyroid Dysfunction

paragraphs.text: In the next section, we will review common instances of pediatric NTIS. This includes infants admitted to neonatal intensive care units (primarily infants born preterm), chil dren admitted to pediatric intensive care units, children with congenital heart disease under going cardiac surgery, and children with renal
paragraphs.heading: and Diagnostic Evaluation of Pediatric NTIS

paragraphs.text: insufficiency (acute and chronic). We will also discuss NTIS in the setting of COVID-19. For each, we will summarize the clinical manifes tations of these syndromes that may be the result of changes in thyroid function and the evidence that thyroid hormone treatment is beneficial, harmful, or neither.
paragraphs.heading: and Diagnostic Evaluation of Pediatric NTIS

paragraphs.text: The third trimester of pregnancy is an impor tant period in the development of the thyroid gland and the maturation of the HPT axis [21]. Full maturation of the HPT axis does not occur until term gestation or the early neonatal period. Between 24 and 40–42 weeks gestation, the following developmental steps are accomplished: an eight- to tenfold increase in thyroid gland volume, a three- to fourfold increase in thyroid hormone reserve, increas ing TSH secretion leading to increasing thy roxine secretion, as well as maturation of the negative feedback system of control of TSH. In addition, the profile of expression of deiodinase enzymes differs between the fetal and postnatal periods with approximately 75% lower levels of D1 and 10–15-fold higher levels of D3 in the fetus as compared to adults. This altered ratio of D1 to D3 results in a lower concentration of T3 and higher concen tration of rT3 in the circulation of a preterm infant as compared to a term infant. Other manifestations of HPT axis immaturity in preterm infants include a lower neonatal TSH surge, lower thyroid reserve, and persistent production of inactive thyroid hormone metabolites (compared to term infants). Serum T4 levels are reduced in proportion to the degree of prematurity, representing both loss of the maternal contribution and immaturity of the HPT axis [22].
paragraphs.heading: 16.5.1 Preterm Infants

paragraphs.text: Preterm infants with low circulating T4, low circulating T3, high circulating rT3, and inappropriately normal or even frankly low TSH are displaying a phenotype that closely resembles NTIS. This constellation of find ings is also sometimes termed transient hypo thyroxinemia of prematurity (THOP). In addition to developmental immaturity of the HPT axis, there are a number of acute events
paragraphs.heading: 16.5.1 Preterm Infants

paragraphs.text: in the postnatal period as well as drugs used to treat these events that have been associated with lower T4, T3, and TSH levels and/or with higher rT3 and inactive thyroid hormone metabolite levels in preterm infants. Williams et al., as part of the Scottish Preterm Thyroid Group, showed that relevant postnatal events include bacteremia, endotracheal bacterial colonization, persistent patent ductus arterio sus, necrotizing enterocolitis, acute intraven tricular hemorrhage, or the development of periventricular leukomalacia and the develop ment of chronic lung disease as evidenced by oxygen dependency at 28 days of age. Drugs associated with alterations in thyroid function in the same study include aminophylline, caf feine, dexamethasone, diamorphine, and dopamine [23].
paragraphs.heading: 16.5.1 Preterm Infants

paragraphs.text: Before considering the impact of THOP, it is important to understand how common this condition is among preterm infants. The majority of studies categorize infants accord ing only to total T4 levels, and the cutoff val ues for hypothyroxinemia differ considerably among these studies. Hadeed et al., studied 215 preterm infants at 28–36 weeks gesta tional age and found an overall incidence of hypothyroxinemia of 22% relative to term infants, with 52% of the hypothyroxinemic infants falling in the 28–30 weeks gestation cohort, while 33% were within the range of 31–33 weeks gestation and 12% were 34 weeks or greater [24]. A 1996 study by Reuss and col leagues defined mild hypothyroxinemia as a T4 level 1.3–2.6 standard deviations (SD) below the mean for the assay (with each assay including a significant number of normal term newborns) and severe hypothyroxinemia as a T4 level more than 2.6 SD below the mean for the assay. By this definition, 38–61% of infants ≤24–33 weeks gestation exhibited mild hypothyroxinemia (with no clear increase or decrease in prevalence across the range of gestational ages included in the study), while 19–44% of infants ≤24–27 weeks gestation showed severe hypothyroxinemia vs 16–27% of infants 28–30 weeks gestation and only 4–7% of infants >30 weeks gestation [25]. The Scottish Preterm Thyroid Group has addressed this question in several different studies. Delahunty et al. used the group’s
paragraphs.heading: 16.5.1 Preterm Infants

paragraphs.text: dataset to assess neurodevelopmental out comes. For this purpose, they defined hypo thyroxinemia as a T4 value below the 10th percentile of cord serum corrected for gesta tional age, which is an attempt to normalize the value to a similar aged fetus still in utero. As such, 38% of infants at 23–27 weeks gesta tion, 23% of infants at 28–30 weeks gestation, and 10% of infants at 31–34 weeks gestation were classified as hypothyroxinemic [26]. Finally, in a more comprehensive interpreta tion of the Scottish Preterm Thyroid Group’s dataset that takes into account trends in T4, free T4, and T3 in preterm infants as com pared to cord blood of similar gestational age and postnatal values in term infants, it appears that almost all infants <28 weeks gestational age experience hypothyroxinemia as evidenced by total T4 values but may have preservation of free T4 levels [27].

The greatest concern regarding THOP in the preterm infant is its potential impact on neurocognitive development. While this was historically not believed to be a problem, sev eral studies suggested an association between THOP, increased risk of cerebral palsy, and worsened developmental outcome at 2–5 years of age. Delahunty et al. with the Scottish Preterm Thyroid Group showed that hypothyroxinemic preterm infants, defined as infants with a T4 <10th percentile of cord sera of the same gestational age, scored sig nificantly worse on cognitive and verbal scales than euthyroid preterm infants, even after adjusting for confounders of neurodevelop ment such as parental intellect, maternal age, length of breastfeeding, significant postnatal events, and several others. Perceptual perfor mance, memory, and motor scores were also lower in the hypothyroxinemic infants, but these differences fell away with adjustment for confounders [26]. In the 1996 study by Reuss et al., severe hypothyroxinemia was found to increase the risk of disabling cere bral palsy 4.4-fold compared to the risk in preterm infants with normal thyroxine con centrations. The severely hypothyroxinemic group also had mental development scores approximately 7 points lower after adjust ment for confounders than did the euthyroid group [25].

Given the prevalence of hypothyroxinemia in preterm infants, particularly those below 28–30 weeks gestational age, and the apparent association of this finding with neurodevelop mental deficits later in childhood, it is reason able to question whether supplementation of thyroid hormone might be beneficial for this population. Several trials have been under taken without a clear consensus of benefit, but sample sizes and study design have dem onstrated some limitations.

The largest study of thyroid hormone sup plementation in preterm infants <30 weeks gestation was conducted by van Wassenaer et al. This group conducted a prospective, ran domized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of thyroxine supplementation in 200 infants; 100 of whom received treatment and 100 placebo. The study group was not limited to those infants with hypothyroxinemia but included all newborns 25–30 weeks gestation without severe congenital malformations, maternal endocrine disease, or maternal drug use. Follow-up developmental assessments included the Bayley Developmental Index and neurological examinations at 24 months of age as well as a more detailed follow-up at 5.7 years of age. No overall difference in devel opmental outcome was seen; however, those born at <27 weeks gestational age did have an

18-point improvement in developmental quo tient as assessed by the Bayley Index with thy roxine treatment, while those born at 29 weeks gestation or later actually scored worse on all measures of developmental outcome if treated with thyroxine [28, 29]. A Cochrane database systematic review concluded that there is insufficient evidence to determine whether use of thyroid hormones for treatment of preterm infants with transient hypothyroxinemia results in changes in severity of respiratory distress syndrome, neonatal mortality, or reductions in neurodevelopmental impair ments [30]. Uchiyama et al., randomized 70 very low birth weight with THOP at 2 weeks of age to a levothyroxine dose of 5 μg/kg/day vs nontreatment and found LT4 supplementa tion showed no benefit to growth and neuro developmental outcomes at 18 months and 3 years of age [31, 32]..

Despite what we know about fetal and neonatal thyroid physiology more research is needed. LaFranchi points out unresolved questions and areas of controversy in this age group including at what age can the postnatal HPT axis compensate for loss of maternal thyroid hormone, does treatment improves outcome in preterm infants, and should iodine be routinely supplemented in this pop ulation [22].

Critical illness in children admitted to the PICU is associated with substantial neuroen docrine and metabolic changes [33]. In the pediatric population, NTIS has been described mostly in neonates (above), critically ill chil dren after cardiac surgery (below), sepsis or septic shock, diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), or oncological problems [34]. Hebbar et al. from Emory University studied 73 children admit ted to their PICU (ages 3 months to 19 years) [29]. In blood samples obtained in the first 12 h of admission, the children had lower mean serum T3, normal mean T4, normal mean TSH, and elevated rT3 compared to ref erence ranges for healthy subjects. Children with sepsis had lower mean serum T3 and higher rT3 levels compared to non-septic chil dren. As might be expected, thyroid results were influenced by drug therapy (vasopres sors, including dopamine and steroids) and low serum albumin levels. Other iatrogenic factors common in the PICU include antiepi leptic drugs, antiarrhythmic drugs, iodine exposure with contrast or antiseptics, and fasting.
paragraphs.heading: 16.5.2 Critically Ill Children

paragraphs.text: Children with DKA often are admitted to a PICU for management. In a retrospective case-control study from China, Hu et al., reported that the subgroup of children judged to have NTIS, as compared to an euthyroid subgroup, had lower serum free T4 (0.88 vs 1.33 ng/dL), free T3 (171 vs 323 pg/dL), and TSH (1.77 vs 2.56 mIU/L) [35]. Guidelines recommend obtaining screening thyroid func tion tests in children with type 1 diabetes mel litus; however, it may be misleading to assess thyroid function while they are in DKA.
paragraphs.heading: 16.5.2 Critically Ill Children

paragraphs.text: Previous studies have shown adult patients admitted to the ICU who ultimately do not survive critical illness present with

much lower plasma concentrations of T4, T3, and TSH, and with higher plasma con centrations of rT3 than do survivors [36]. This is complicated by patients suffering from prolonged critical illness who present with symptoms and signs that could theoreti cally be explained by a degree of hypothy roidism. Several observational studies have investigated associations of HPT axis hor mone changes in critically ill children with clinical outcome. Like in adults, the severity of NTIS in children has been associated with poor clinical outcomes of critical illnesses. However, causality of this association is not established. Abdelaziz et al. performed a pro spective cohort study examining thyroid function values in mechanically ventilated children to determine extubation outcomes. Their study did not correlate NTIS with extubation outcomes in critically ill children undergoing mechanical ventilation [37]. This highlights the need for randomized con trolled trials (RCTs) to address any causality of changes in thyroid hormones with mor bidity and mortality in these patients.

Our search of the literature did not yield any clinical trials of thyroid hormone treat ment in children admitted to PICUs (other than for cardiac surgery). However there have been two RCT studies investigating the impact of randomized metabolic intervention in the PICU on changes in the thyroid axis in rela tion to acute clinical outcomes [38, 39]. Gielen et al. examined the effect of tight glucose con trol with insulin and found that tight glucose control improved survival and reduced mor bidity with a decrease in T3 and elevation of rT3. They inferred that the preferential periph eral conversion of T4 to inactive rT3 rather than metabolically active T3 during the first days of critical illness is adaptive and benefi cial for recovery. The Early vs Late Parenteral

Nutrition in the Pediatric ICU (PEPaNIC) trial was a multicenter prospective random ized controlled trial that evaluated the impact of early vs late parenteral nutrition [40]. As fasting is related to NTIS, these metabolic interventions were extrapolated to determine the effect of NTIS on clinical outcomes in an acute critical setting. Jacobs et al. performed a secondary analysis of the PEPaNIC trial and assessed the prognostic value of NTIS on admission and its benefit on clinical outcomes [41]. A higher mortality and morbidity were noted in patients with a more pronounced

It is well established that infants and children who undergo cardiac surgery, with or without cardiopulmonary bypass, display significant HPT axis suppression consistent with NTIS. The most profound and consistent changes in this population are reduced total and free T3 levels, with free T3 falling as much as 80% from preoperative levels 12–48 h post operatively [43–45]. TSH and total T4 are also suppressed after cardiac surgery, reaching a nadir within the first 24 h [44, 45]. Free T4 rises initially when bypass is initiated, likely due to displacement of thyroxine from its
paragraphs.heading: 16.5.3 Cardiac Surgery in Children

paragraphs.text: NTIS picture with low T4 and T3, and high rT3. Data suggested a maladaptive role for the central component of NTIS and a beneficial role for the peripheral inactivation of thyroid hormone in NTIS.
paragraphs.heading: 16.5.3 Cardiac Surgery in Children

paragraphs.text: To date, no evidence-based consensus or guideline recommends thyroid hormone replacement in critically ill patients with NTIS. Studies have suggested a potential ben efit of treating the central rather than the peripheral component of NTIS with TRH that will need to be confirmed in further stud ies [42].
paragraphs.heading: 16.5.3 Cardiac Surgery in Children

paragraphs.text: binding globulin as a result of exposure to heparin. Levels then return to baseline in most studies and remain there throughout the post operative period [44]. Reverse T3 rises postop eratively, reaching a peak at about 24 h [44, 45]. All changes in the HPT axis resolve grad ually over the course of 5–7 days [44, 46]. Cantinotti et al. demonstrated that circulating thyroid hormone response after cardiac sur gery differs significantly among age groups with neonates differing substantially from other age groups. Neonates had prolonged impairment in TSH secretion, reaching a nadir at 36 h and remaining depressed up to 108 h, with subsequent slow recovery. In contrast,
paragraphs.heading: 16.5.3 Cardiac Surgery in Children

paragraphs.text: older children reached a nadir earlier at 6–12 h with prompt and progressive recovery [47].
paragraphs.heading: 16.5.3 Cardiac Surgery in Children

paragraphs.text: The etiology of NTIS following cardiac surgery is multifactorial. Fasting and the physiologic stress of surgery contribute to the suppression of the HPT axis. Extent of hypo thermia, duration of cardiac arrest, and hemodilution during cardiopulmonary bypass have also been associated with the develop ment of NTIS. Many medications used in the perioperative management of cardiac surgery patients are also known to have a suppressive effect on thyroid function, including dopa mine, glucocorticoids, anesthetic agents, and iodinated antiseptics [43, 44, 46].
paragraphs.heading: 16.5.3 Cardiac Surgery in Children

paragraphs.text: Reduced circulating thyroid hormone in the postoperative period is associated with unfavorable physiologic changes including decreased cardiac output, left ventricular dys function, increased vascular resistance, and impaired ventilatory drive [43]. Children who have significant thyroid suppression after car diac surgery have been shown to require lon ger periods of mechanical ventilation and intensive care treatment and to have higher requirements for inotropic support [43, 46], all suggesting that NTIS in this setting may be a maladaptive response and may warrant inter vention.
paragraphs.heading: 16.5.3 Cardiac Surgery in Children

paragraphs.text: Given the rapid onset and transient nature of thyroid suppression following cardiac sur gery, intervention studies have focused on the use of T3, which has a half-life of less than 24 h in infants and young children, as opposed to thyroxine, which may take up to 2 weeks to reach steady state. T3 supplementation in adults has been fairly well studied, and there are data to support improved cardiac function postoperatively as well as decreased need for inotropes, decreased rate of arrhythmias, and decreased length of hospital stay with T3 treatment [46]. Previous meta-analysis, how ever, showed no evidence of alteration in post operative mortality in the adult population with T3 supplementation [48]. Studies in chil dren are still somewhat limited and have been less conclusive. Only the results of random ized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials will be summarized below.
paragraphs.heading: 16.5.3 Cardiac Surgery in Children

paragraphs.text: Bettendorf et al. studied 40 children aged 0–10 years. The study intervention was a once-

daily infusion of T3 beginning on postopera tive day 1 and continuing until subjects were weaned off dopamine support or until post operative day 12, whichever came first. Neither thyroid hormone levels nor cardiac function postoperatively was considered in subject selection. Treated subjects had increased plasma T3 levels, improved cardiac index and decreased need for intensive care services. Improved cardiac function was most pronounced in those with longer bypass time and lower cardiac output postoperatively. No adverse events were seen [49]. Portman et al. studied 14 subjects less than 1 year of age. The study intervention was a T3 bolus immedi ately before bypass initiation and with reper fusion. Heart rate was transiently elevated in the treatment group without concomitant decrease in blood pressure. Treated subjects had an increased peak systolic pressure-rate product, suggesting improved cardiac func tion [50]. Chowdhury et al. evaluated 75 sub jects aged 0–18 years and subsequently randomized 29 subjects with significantly reduced postoperative T3 levels and a need for mechanical ventilation to the treatment or placebo arm of the study. The study interven tion was continuous T3 infusion. There were no adverse events. Only subjects less than 1 month of age showed a significant effect of T3 therapy with reduced need for inotropes and lower therapeutic intervention scores indicating a decreased need for intensive care. Neither neonates nor older children showed any difference in need for diuretics, days of mechanical ventilation, or length of hospital stay [51]. Mackie et al. enrolled 42 neonates randomized to continuous T3 infusion vs pla cebo for 72 h postoperatively. Neonates in the study demonstrated negative fluid balance more quickly in the treated group than in the placebo group, but neither clinical outcome scores nor cardiac index values were signifi cantly different. Treatment was discontinued in two subjects due to hypertension and arrhythmia [52]. A Cochrane review encom passing three of the above studies concluded that there was insufficient evidence to support a positive effect of T3 supplementation in infants undergoing cardiac surgery [43]. A larger prospective, multicenter, double-blind,

randomized, placebo-controlled study, called the TRICC trial, evaluated the effects of T3 supplementation after bypass in children younger than 2 years. A total of 193 patients were randomized with 98 receiving T3 and 95 receiving placebo. The study showed that T3 supplementation was safe. Although the pri mary outcome measure of time to extubation did not differ between treatment groups, there was a difference with age stratification. In children younger than 5 months, time to extu bation was significantly shorter than in the placebo group. There was an improvement in cardiac function as well as decrease in inotro pic support in the group younger than 5 months [53]. The largest study by Marwali et al. studied 208 Indonesian children, of whom 104 children were randomized to oral T3 every 6 h for 60 h after induction of anes thesia and 101 children were administered placebo. They also showed an age dependent effect with shorter time to extubation in infants 5 months or younger with higher rates of sepsis in the placebo group [54]. Talwar et al. studied 100 infants; 50 randomized to oral thyroxine 12 h before surgery and once daily during ICU stay and 50 to placebo. The T4 treated group had higher cardiac index at all time points with reduction in inotropic requirement, duration of mechanical ventila tion, ICU, and hospital stay. There was no sig nificant difference in sepsis, arrhythmia, reintubation, need for CPR, and mortality between the two groups [55]. Further random ized large trials looking with age stratification to investigate the timing and route of T3/T4 administration are needed to better under stand outcomes in terms of cardiovascular performance, morbidity, mortality, and neu rological development.

Children with chronic renal insufficiency (CRI) have many, but not all, of the changes in thyroid function tests summarized above for NTIS. They typically have low serum T4 and T3 levels, while TSH levels are not ele
paragraphs.heading: and Chronic)

paragraphs.text: vated [56]. Conversion of T4 to T3 by the kid ney is reduced. However, patients do not have elevated rT3 levels. Serum free T4 and free T3 levels are found to be normal in some reports and low in others, even when determined by equilibrium dialysis technique. Chronic meta bolic acidosis may contribute to decreased peripheral conversion to T3 from T4 [57]. Some children with CRI have reduced binding protein levels, as a result of either malnutri tion or protein-losing nephropathies. In addi tion, some uremic factors appear to inhibit binding of T4 and T3 to their binding pro teins. All these effects contribute to low serum total T4 and T3 concentrations. NTIS is reported in ~20% of adult non-dialysis depen dent chronic renal failure patients and up to 50% of adult dialysis patients [58]. Data on pediatric CRI patients are lacking.
paragraphs.heading: and Chronic)

paragraphs.text: Children with CRI manifest some of the clinical symptoms and signs seen in hypothy roidism, including growth retardation, leth argy, poor appetite, and a puffy appearance. The prevalence of goiter is increased, present in up to 50% of children with CRI in some reports [59]. Studies report increased plasma iodine concentrations, most likely the result of decreased renal iodine clearance with CRI. Increased iodine concentrations likely play a role in goiter formation.
paragraphs.heading: and Chronic)

paragraphs.text: Some children with CRI have thyroid function tests consistent with central hypothy roidism (low free T4, inappropriately “nor mal” TSH). In addition, some studies report a “prolonged” TSH response to TRH stimula tion and a subnormal nocturnal TSH surge [60]. However, given that studies also report that TRH degradation is decreased in chil dren with CRI [61], these results may be an indirect effect of CRI on TRH clearance rather than clear evidence of abnormal hypo thalamic–pituitary–thyroid function. While a low free T4 in the face of a normal TSH level would appear to be consistent with central hypothyroidism, the fact that free T4 levels are reported to normalize immediately after hemodialysis is difficult to reconcile with true hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid dysfunction [60].
paragraphs.heading: and Chronic)

paragraphs.text: Patients with acute renal failure (ARF) have thyroid function tests similar to NTIS
paragraphs.heading: and Chronic)

paragraphs.text: but may not have elevation of rT3 [62]. A trial of thyroid hormone treatment was under taken by Acker et al. in adults to determine whether it might help recovery from ARF [63]. Adult patients received either 150 mcg of L-thyroxine or placebo IV every 12 h for a total of 48 h. Thyroid hormone treatment resulted in a decrease in TSH (vs a rise in the control group), but it had no effect on any measure of ARF. Mortality was higher in the thyroxine-treated vs control group (43% vs 13%). Acker et al. also undertook a random ized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of T3 treatment in adult patients with ARF due to acute tubular necrosis undergoing kidney transplantation to determine whether it might improve “delayed graft function” [64]. Patients received an intravenous bolus of 0.2 mcg/kg of T3, followed by an infusion of 0.2 mcg/kg over 6 h. T3 treatment had no effect on per centage requiring dialysis, time for recovery of renal function, or percentage recovering func tion. At 1-year follow-up, graft function was similar in both groups.
paragraphs.heading: and Chronic)

paragraphs.text: In summary, the changes seen in thyroid function tests in children with CRI are con founded by the effects of decreased metabolic clearance of iodine, thyroid hormone and its metabolites, and TSH and TRH; decreased T4 to T3 conversion in the kidney; uremic fac tors that appear to inhibit binding of T4 and T3 to their binding proteins; and drugs used to treat patients after kidney transplant, including glucocorticoids that lower TSH lev els. Many or most of these changes in thyroid function tests revert to normal after hemodi alysis, arguing against true central hypothy roidism. The few treatment studies of thyroid hormone administration carried out in adult patients with ARF do not show benefit and demonstrate possible harmful effects of such treatment.
paragraphs.heading: and Chronic)

paragraphs.text: Several studies have reported thyroid dysfunc tion in SARS-CoV2 infected adult patients ranging from a silent destructive thyroiditis, Graves’ disease, subclinical hypothyroidism, overt hypothyroidism, and NTIS [65]. The
paragraphs.heading: 16.5.5 COVID 19

paragraphs.text: most consistently observed alteration of thy roid function parameters in hospitalized patients with COVID 19 was NTIS [66]. In a retrospective study of pediatric patients with COVID 19 related multisystem inflammatory syndrome at a single pediatric hospital in Italy, Calcaterra et al. reported that 88.4% of patients presented with NTIS [67]. The SARS- CoV-2 virus binds to the angiotensinconverting-enzyme 2 receptor, which is expressed on many cells including immune cells, and cells in the thyroid and pituitary, for cell entry. SARS-CoV-2 can cause a cytokine storm, an uncontrolled inflammatory response that is derived from the direct cytotoxic effect of the virus on target cells and from the acti vation of host immune cells, which is detri mental to host cells. Lui et al. showed that a higher CRP level was independently associ ated with low FT3 levels as well as worsening clinical severity, suggesting that systemic inflammation led to NTIS [68]. This pattern was also reported in a small sample prospec tive study by Ayranci et al. of 19 COVID-19 positive pediatric patients [69].
paragraphs.heading: 16.5.5 COVID 19

paragraphs.text: Chen et al. studied 50 adult patients with COVID 19 that did not have a history of thy roid disease and were not pregnant, and found the serum TSH and TT3 levels were signifi cantly lower in these patients than in the healthy control group and non-COVID 19 pneumonia patients [70]. The more severe the COVID-19 infection, the lower the TSH and TT3 levels, with the degree of decrease of TSH and TT3 being positively correlated with the severity of the disease.
paragraphs.heading: 16.5.5 COVID 19

paragraphs.text: Treatments used for COVID 19 are known to interfere with the HPT axis as well as labo ratory tests, and can be confounders. These include glucocorticoids and heparin. Of note Khoo et al. showed decreased TSH and increased cortisol levels in their study popula tion of 456 patients diagnosed with COVID 19 compared to 122 COVID negative patients [71]. Their study did not include any patients who received exogenous steroids and con cluded that the marked elevations in cortisol were from endogenous cortisol elevations with COVID infection. Again, studies are lim ited by small sample size as well as the evolv ing nature of the virus, and gaps persist in our
paragraphs.heading: 16.5.5 COVID 19

paragraphs.text: knowledge of the clinical spectrum of thyroid function in patients with COVID 19 infection.
paragraphs.heading: 16.5.5 COVID 19

paragraphs.text: NTIS is a common clinical syndrome affect ing infants and children with a broad spec trum of acute and chronic illnesses. It is characterized by reduced T3 and T4 levels, increased rT3 levels, variable free T3 and free T4 levels, and inappropriately normal TSH. These changes are the result of altera tions in regulation of the HPT axis, and in peripheral thyroid hormone metabolism as regulated by deiodinase enzymes, thyroid hormone-binding proteins, and thyroid hor mone action at the cellular level. The tradi tional view of NTIS is that it is an adaptive mechanism, protecting the body from high metabolic demands in the face of acute illness. There is, however, evidence that in certain clinical situations, the alterations in thyroid hormone secretion and action seen in NTIS may, in fact, be detrimental. Particularly in preterm infants who may have worse neuro logic outcomes if they have experienced sig nificantly reduced thyroid hormone levels in the neonatal period and cardiac surgery patients who may have prolonged intensive care unit stays, prolonged need for mechanical ventilation and inotropic support, and worse cardiac function in the immediate postopera tive period, it is tempting to think that inter vention with thyroid hormone may be warranted in NTIS. Treatment studies to date, however, have not shown clear benefit and in some subgroups (preterm infants older than 27 weeks, adult acute renal failure patients) suggest possible harm resulting from thyroid hormone administration. Significantly more research is needed to understand the true impact of NTIS, and the appropriate inter ventions in this situation, if any.
