Key Points

5 Non-thyroidal illness syndrome (NTIS)

is characterized by decreased serum T3 and to a lesser extent T4 levels, increased reverse T3 (rT3) levels, variable serum free T3 and free T4 levels, and “inap propriately” normal or low TSH levels. 5 There is evidence that acute illness

results in diminished TRH production and TSH secretion, leading to decreased thyroidal T3 and T4 production. Decreased deiodinase type 1 (D1) and type 2 (D2) result in decreased extrathy roidal conversion of T4 to T3, while increased deiodinase type 3 (D3) activ ity increases T4 conversion to rT3. Decreased total T3 and total T4 are also the result of decreased thyroid hor mone binding proteins. 5 While the changes in thyroid function in

NTIS may be “adaptive,” there is some evidence that thyroid hormone treat ment in certain clinical situations may be beneficial, such as preterm infants <27 weeks gestation. 5 Post-operative pediatric cardiac surgery

patients demonstrate marked suppres sion of T3 levels in combination with other findings of NTIS. These labora tory changes are associated with longer periods of mechanical ventilation and intensive care treatment and higher requirements for inotropic support, suggesting that NTIS in this setting may be a maladaptive response and may warrant intervention. Studies of postoperative T3 administration have dem onstrated some improvement in post-operative cardiac function but the evidence remains inadequate to support a recommendation for treatment.

### 16

### 16.1 Introduction and Background

Non-thyroidal illness is the term used to describe the changes in thyroid hormone and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) with

acute illness not caused by an intrinsic abnor mality of thyroid function [1]. In children, non-thyroidal illness is most commonly seen in acutely ill patients admitted to pediatric or neonatal intensive care units (ICUs). The characteristic decrease in thyroid hormone levels also can be seen with starvation, trauma, or surgical procedures. Nonthyroidal illness probably occurs with any severe illness, and the pattern of changes in thyroid hormones correlates with the severity of illness. Typically, the first changes are a decrease in serum triiodothyronine (T3) and a rise in reverse T3 (rT3) levels [2]. This disor der has been referred to as the low-T3 syn drome or the euthyroid sick syndrome. However, as it is not clear that these patients are clinically “euthyroid,” non-thyroidal ill ness syndrome (NTIS) is the term preferred at present [3, 4].

This chapter will begin with a descrip tion of the changes in thyroid hormones and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels that occur in NTIS. This will be fol lowed by a brief review of what is known about the pathogenesis of NTIS in starva tion and acute illness. This will include a discussion of changes in hypothalamic– pituitary–thyroid (HPT) axis function, changes in peripheral thyroid hormone metabolism (as regulated by the three deio dinase enzymes), changes in thyroid hor mone binding in the circulation, thyroid hormone transport into the cell, and finally changes in thyroid hormone action at the tissue level in NTIS. Next will be a discus sion of some of the most common pediatric clinical disorders associated with NTIS, including “hypothyroxinemia of prematu rity,” acutely ill patients in an ICU setting, renal insufficiency (acute and chronic), car diac surgery, and COVID-19 infection. NTIS is characterized by changes in thyroid hormone levels and TSH consistent with central hypothyroidism. Discussion of the clinical disorders will review evidence that NTIS is either a beneficial “adaptive response” to starvation or acute illness or a “maladaptive response” that might be improved by thyroid hormone treatment.


## PDF page 415 | printed page 405

### 16.2 Description of Thyroid

### Hormone Changes in NTIS

A fall in serum T3 accompanied by a rise in rT3 levels is the most common change in patients with NTIS (thus, as noted above, in the past, NTIS has been referred to as the “low-T3 syndrome”), but it is now recognized that rT3 may be normal or even low in some cases [4]. Simple fasting pro duces these changes within 24–36 h; refeeding (particularly with glucose) rapidly reverses these changes. Serum T4 levels do not fall with fasting in healthy subjects. Many acute illnesses are asso ciated with “starvation”; reduced caloric intake thus is likely one factor resulting in the initial changes in serum T3 and rT3.

Serum T4 levels tend to be normal in mild acute illness, but with increasing severity of ill ness, serum T4 levels will decrease. The degree of fall in serum T3 and T4 is related to the severity of the acute illness [5]. Changes in serum free T4 and free T3 levels are less cer tain, with results varying with the assay method. When free T4 is measured by most common “analogue” immunoassays, serum free T4 levels appear to decrease with acute ill ness [6]. If free T4 is calculated using a mea sure of total T4 and some measure of serum



protein binding, e.g., T3 resin uptake, serum free T4 levels also appear to decrease. However, if free T4 is measured by methods that involve initial physical separation of free T4 from pro tein-bound T4, e.g., equilibrium dialysis or ultrafiltration, serum free T4 levels are usually normal or even increased in patients with acute illness [7]. A similar pattern is seen with free T3 measurements. If free T3 is measured by the more common commercial assays, the fall in serum free T3 parallels the fall in total T3. However, if free T3 is measured by a dialy sis or filtration method, the decrease in serum free T3 does not match the fall in total T3. One study reported serum free T3 levels only 10% lower than a healthy control group [8].

TSH measurements generally are in the normal range, though serum TSH may decrease below normal in some patients with severe acute illness [9]. Thus, it is not uncommon to find low serum T3 and T4 levels, low free T4 levels (by commonly used assay methods), and normal or low TSH levels, results that are con sistent with central hypothyroidism.





16.1




## PDF page 416 | printed page 406

normal range, with recovery it rises back into the normal range and even mildly above the normal range in some patients (e.g., 10–20 mU/L) [10]. Serum T4 rises back to the normal range, followed by a rise in total T3 and a fall in rT3 back into the normal range. Serum free T4, if measured by an analogue immunoassay, will rise back into the normal range; if free T4 is measured by equilibrium dialysis or ultrafiltration, it typically remains normal throughout the NTIS. Serum free T3 follows a similar pattern.

### 16.3 Pathogenesis of NTIS–Thyroid

### Changes

### 16.3.1 Change in the Central

### Hypothalamic–Pituitary– Thyroid Axis

Although serum T3 and T4 levels fall, there is no increase in serum TSH levels, and with increasing severity of illness, there may be a decrease in TSH levels. Frequent sampling studies show a decrease in the nocturnal TSH surge and amplitude [11]; similar changes occur in patients with central hypothyroidism. Evidence points to a decrease in thyrotropinreleasing hormone (TRH) as a cause of diminished TSH secretion, along with direct effects of acute illness on pituitary thyrotroph cell function. Postmortem studies in patients with NTIS show decreased TRH mRNA expression in the paraventricular nucleus (PVN), the main source of TRH [12]. Reduced intake of calories, either as part of an acute illness or with fasting, results in decreased leptin levels. In experimental animal studies, decreased leptin levels result in altered neuro endocrine regulation of TRH secretion [13]. Further, cytokines along with increased corti sol produced with acute illness appear to have a direct inhibitory effect on TSH secretion in the pituitary [14]. If acutely ill patients are treated with dopamine (to maintain cardio

### 16

vascular function) or glucocorticoids, these drugs also inhibit TSH secretion. There is also one other proposed mechanism that may inhibit TSH secretion. Although PVN cells do not appear to directly sense circulating T3 or T4 levels, a unique glial cell with processes that extend into the hypothalamus, the tany cyte, provides a communication between the portal circulation and the hypothalamus. Studies in an animal model of NTIS show an increase in tanycyte deiodinase type 2 (D2) enzyme activity [15]. Increased D2 activity could increase T4 to T3 conversion, resulting in “local tissue hyperthyroidism” in the hypo thalamus, which, by way of negative feedback, would inhibit TRH synthesis. In summary, current evidence supports diminished TRH production and decreased TSH secretion as a major cause of decreased thyroid gland T4 production and secretion and perhaps also decreased T3 levels (see below: since the majority of T3 is produced by peripheral tis sue deiodination of T4, changes in tissue deio dinases also appear to be a cause of lower serum T3 levels). Cytokines produced during illness also exhibit a direct inhibitory effect on the thyroid hormone synthesis pathway. Thyroglobulin production, iodide uptake, and thyroid peroxidase expression, an important regulator of the oxidation of iodide to iodine, are altered in response to cytokines in studies of animal and human thyrocytes [16].

### 16.3.2 Changes in Peripheral

### Thyroid Hormone Metabolism

Thyroid hormone metabolism in extrathyroi dal tissue is regulated by three deiodinase enzymes. Type 1 and type 2 deiodinase (D1 and D2) are the main activating enzymes, while type 3 deiodinase (D3) is the inactivat ing enzyme [17]. D1 is present in many extra thyroidal tissues, including the liver and kidney, while D2 is present in the pituitary, brain, and brown adipose tissue. The main action of D1 and D2 is to convert T4 to bio


## PDF page 417 | printed page 407

logically active T3; D1, located on the plasma membrane, is the enzyme responsible for pro duction of most of the T3 that enters the cir culation. D3 is present in many extrathyroidal tissues, including the brain; the main action of D3 is to convert T4 to biologically inactive rT3 and, to a lesser extent, T3 to 3,3′-diiodo thyronine (T2). The expression of the deiodin ase enzymes is modified in acute illness and appears to be highly tissue specific. It is gener ally accepted that the fall in serum T3 levels is the result of decreased D1 and increased D3 activity [18]. There is some evidence that these changes in D1 and D3 are mediated by the increased levels of cytokines and glucocorti coids seen in acute illness. More recent evi dence, however, including studies in D1/D2 and D3 knockout mice, find that the changes in serum T3 and T4 with induced acute illness are similar to wild-type animals. These stud ies suggest that the changes noted in deiodin ase enzymes may be a consequence, not the cause of the NTIS [19]. Finally, there is evi dence of increased degradation of T4 and T3 via non-deiodination pathways, manifested by increased levels of T3 sulfate and triiodo thyroacetic acid (TRIAC) and tetraiodothy roacetic acid (TETRAC) in patients with NTIS [1].

### 16.3.3 Changes in Thyroid

### Hormone-Binding Protein Kinetics

Thyroid hormone-binding proteins including thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG), trans thyretin (formerly termed thyroxine-binding prealbumin), and albumin are “acute-phase” reactants and tend to fall with acute illnesses [2]. This appears to be the result of both impaired synthesis but also rapid breakdown and movement out of the plasma space. This is particularly true with sepsis and cardiopul monary bypass. As the vast majority of serum T4 (99.97%) and T3 (99.70%) are bound, con centrations of serum total T4 and total T3 may be lower in large part as a result of lower binding protein levels. In addition, there is

evidence of circulating inhibitors of T4 and T3 binding to their binding proteins in NTIS. Non-esterified fatty acids and certain drugs used to treat patients with NTIS appear to act as inhibitors, including heparin, furosemide, and salicylate. Heparin’s action appears to be in vitro; it activates lipoprotein lipase which then breaks down triglycerides into glycerol and fatty acids, resulting in a dramatic release of bound T4 and false elevation of free T4 measurements [20].

### 16.3.4 Changes in Thyroid

### Hormone Transport and Action at the Tissue Level

Entry of thyroid hormone into the cell is car ried out by ATP-dependent transporters, including monocarboxylate transporter 8 (MCT8), monocarboxylate transporter 10 (MCT10), and organic anion transporting polypeptide family 1C1 (OATP1C1). The effect of illness on the expression of these transporters is complex and varied, depend ing on tissue type and on duration of illness. Changes in transporter expression in the hypothalamus, liver, and muscle may all play a role in NTIS, but specific functional conse quences and effect on tissue T3 concentra tions remain unclear [4, 16]. Once thyroid hormone enters the cell, T3 (either from direct entry or via intracellular T4 deiodination to T3) binds to a specific thyroid hormone recep tor (THR). Studies in humans with acute ill ness and animal models of NTIS yield conflicting information on changes in THR, with reports of increased, decreased, or no change in THR expression. THR action is regulated by co-activators and corepressors; there is some evidence that cytokines pro duced with acute illness compete with coactivators or corepressors and so may regulate tissue-specific THR action. It appears that THR expression is downregulated in acute ill ness and upregulated in chronic illness, though again this appears to be tissue specific and likely an overgeneralization [1, 4].


## PDF page 418 | printed page 408



### 16.3.5



### 16.2

Acute illness results in diminished TRH pro duction and TSH secretion, as well as direct effects on the thyroid gland itself. The charac teristic fall in serum T3 levels appears to be the result of decreased production in the thy roid gland, decreased D1 and D2 activity resulting in decreased extrathyroidal conver sion of T4 to T3, and increased D3 activity with increased conversion of T4 to rT3. Decreased levels of total T3 and total T4 are also the result of decreased thyroid hormonebinding proteins. Levels of free T4 and free T3 are assay dependent; assays using physical separation techniques, such as equilibrium dialysis, tend to show normal serum free T4 and normal or only mildly low free T3 results. Complex changes in thyroid hormone trans port into the cell and in thyroid hormone receptor expression across tissue types also occur in NTIS, with resulting alterations in thyroid hormone metabolism that may play a role in organ function or dysfunction at vary ing stages of illness [4].

### 16

### 16.4 Separating NTIS from True

### Thyroid Dysfunction

It can be difficult to separate the changes in serum thyroid hormone levels seen in patients with NTIS from those who have true thyroid dysfunction. While good data do not exist for children, studies in adult patients admitted to medical services report a low serum T3 level in 50%, low serum T4 level in 15–20%, and an abnormal (low or high) TSH in 10% [2]. If there is a clinical suspicion of hypothyroid ism, we recommend that patients undergo measurement of serum free T4 by equilibrium dialysis and TSH levels. In true primary hypo thyroidism, patients will have a low free T4 level and elevated TSH level. Caution must be used, however, as patients recovering from NTIS may manifest a low free T4 and elevated TSH. Typically, the elevation in TSH concen tration is mild, in the 10–20 mU/L range. A TSH elevation >20 mU/L is suspicious for true hypothyroidism. As autoimmune thy roiditis is the most common cause of acquired hypothyroidism, finding positive antithyroglobulin and/or thyroid peroxidase anti bodies would support a diagnosis of

![Source image](../../figures/ch016_p0418_01.jpg)

Unmatched source image; PDF page 418. Consult the original caption.


## PDF page 419 | printed page 409

hypothyroidism. Clinicians should be aware that in patients with true hypothyroidism, ele vated TSH levels may decrease, even into the normal range, in situations associated with NTIS, particularly if patients are treated with drugs that inhibit TSH secretion such as dopamine or glucocorticoids. If thyroid hor mone treatment is to be started, patients should undergo evaluation of pituitaryadrenal function first. Thyroid hormone treat ment in the face of unrecognized adrenal insufficiency may precipitate adrenal crisis, certainly undesirable in the face of acute ill ness.

If there is a clinical suspicion of hyperthy roidism, we recommend measurement of serum free T4, free T3 (both by equilibrium dialysis), and TSH levels. In true hyperthy roidism, patients will have an elevated free T4 and free T3 level and a TSH suppressed below the normal range. Patients with severe NTIS may manifest a low TSH level, but this usually is not confused with hyperthyroidism as serum free T4 and free T3 are not elevated. Again, in patients with true hyperthyroidism, the con centration of TSH is not just low, but com monly unmeasurable (<0.01 mU/L). A normal TSH level excludes hyperthyroidism. Elevated concentrations of thyrotropin receptorstimulating antibody (e.g., thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin [TSI]) would support the diagnosis of Graves’ disease and hyperthy roidism.

As many clinical manifestations of acute illness overlap with thyroid dysfunction, often the best course is to recheck thyroid function tests after resolution of the acute illness.

### 16.5 Clinical Presentation

### and Diagnostic Evaluation of Pediatric NTIS

In the next section, we will review common instances of pediatric NTIS. This includes infants admitted to neonatal intensive care units (primarily infants born preterm), chil dren admitted to pediatric intensive care units, children with congenital heart disease under going cardiac surgery, and children with renal

insufficiency (acute and chronic). We will also discuss NTIS in the setting of COVID-19. For each, we will summarize the clinical manifes tations of these syndromes that may be the result of changes in thyroid function and the evidence that thyroid hormone treatment is beneficial, harmful, or neither.

### 16.5.1 Preterm Infants

The third trimester of pregnancy is an impor tant period in the development of the thyroid gland and the maturation of the HPT axis [21]. Full maturation of the HPT axis does not occur until term gestation or the early neonatal period. Between 24 and 40–42 weeks gestation, the following developmental steps are accomplished: an eight- to tenfold increase in thyroid gland volume, a three- to fourfold increase in thyroid hormone reserve, increas ing TSH secretion leading to increasing thy roxine secretion, as well as maturation of the negative feedback system of control of TSH. In addition, the profile of expression of deiodinase enzymes differs between the fetal and postnatal periods with approximately 75% lower levels of D1 and 10–15-fold higher levels of D3 in the fetus as compared to adults. This altered ratio of D1 to D3 results in a lower concentration of T3 and higher concen tration of rT3 in the circulation of a preterm infant as compared to a term infant. Other manifestations of HPT axis immaturity in preterm infants include a lower neonatal TSH surge, lower thyroid reserve, and persistent production of inactive thyroid hormone metabolites (compared to term infants). Serum T4 levels are reduced in proportion to the degree of prematurity, representing both loss of the maternal contribution and immaturity of the HPT axis [22].

Preterm infants with low circulating T4, low circulating T3, high circulating rT3, and inappropriately normal or even frankly low TSH are displaying a phenotype that closely resembles NTIS. This constellation of find ings is also sometimes termed transient hypo thyroxinemia of prematurity (THOP). In addition to developmental immaturity of the HPT axis, there are a number of acute events


## PDF page 420 | printed page 410

in the postnatal period as well as drugs used to treat these events that have been associated with lower T4, T3, and TSH levels and/or with higher rT3 and inactive thyroid hormone metabolite levels in preterm infants. Williams et al., as part of the Scottish Preterm Thyroid Group, showed that relevant postnatal events include bacteremia, endotracheal bacterial colonization, persistent patent ductus arterio sus, necrotizing enterocolitis, acute intraven tricular hemorrhage, or the development of periventricular leukomalacia and the develop ment of chronic lung disease as evidenced by oxygen dependency at 28 days of age. Drugs associated with alterations in thyroid function in the same study include aminophylline, caf feine, dexamethasone, diamorphine, and dopamine [23].

Before considering the impact of THOP, it is important to understand how common this condition is among preterm infants. The majority of studies categorize infants accord ing only to total T4 levels, and the cutoff val ues for hypothyroxinemia differ considerably among these studies. Hadeed et al., studied 215 preterm infants at 28–36 weeks gesta tional age and found an overall incidence of hypothyroxinemia of 22% relative to term infants, with 52% of the hypothyroxinemic infants falling in the 28–30 weeks gestation cohort, while 33% were within the range of 31–33 weeks gestation and 12% were 34 weeks or greater [24]. A 1996 study by Reuss and col leagues defined mild hypothyroxinemia as a T4 level 1.3–2.6 standard deviations (SD) below the mean for the assay (with each assay including a significant number of normal term newborns) and severe hypothyroxinemia as a T4 level more than 2.6 SD below the mean for the assay. By this definition, 38–61% of infants ≤24–33 weeks gestation exhibited mild hypothyroxinemia (with no clear increase or decrease in prevalence across the range of gestational ages included in the study), while 19–44% of infants ≤24–27 weeks gestation showed severe hypothyroxinemia vs 16–27% of infants 28–30 weeks gestation and only 4–7% of infants >30 weeks gestation [25]. The Scottish Preterm Thyroid Group has addressed this question in several different studies. Delahunty et al. used the group’s

### 16

dataset to assess neurodevelopmental out comes. For this purpose, they defined hypo thyroxinemia as a T4 value below the 10th percentile of cord serum corrected for gesta tional age, which is an attempt to normalize the value to a similar aged fetus still in utero. As such, 38% of infants at 23–27 weeks gesta tion, 23% of infants at 28–30 weeks gestation, and 10% of infants at 31–34 weeks gestation were classified as hypothyroxinemic [26]. Finally, in a more comprehensive interpreta tion of the Scottish Preterm Thyroid Group’s dataset that takes into account trends in T4, free T4, and T3 in preterm infants as com pared to cord blood of similar gestational age and postnatal values in term infants, it appears that almost all infants <28 weeks gestational age experience hypothyroxinemia as evidenced by total T4 values but may have preservation of free T4 levels [27].

The greatest concern regarding THOP in the preterm infant is its potential impact on neurocognitive development. While this was historically not believed to be a problem, sev eral studies suggested an association between THOP, increased risk of cerebral palsy, and worsened developmental outcome at 2–5 years of age. Delahunty et al. with the Scottish Preterm Thyroid Group showed that hypothyroxinemic preterm infants, defined as infants with a T4 <10th percentile of cord sera of the same gestational age, scored sig nificantly worse on cognitive and verbal scales than euthyroid preterm infants, even after adjusting for confounders of neurodevelop ment such as parental intellect, maternal age, length of breastfeeding, significant postnatal events, and several others. Perceptual perfor mance, memory, and motor scores were also lower in the hypothyroxinemic infants, but these differences fell away with adjustment for confounders [26]. In the 1996 study by Reuss et al., severe hypothyroxinemia was found to increase the risk of disabling cere bral palsy 4.4-fold compared to the risk in preterm infants with normal thyroxine con centrations. The severely hypothyroxinemic group also had mental development scores approximately 7 points lower after adjust ment for confounders than did the euthyroid group [25].


## PDF page 421 | printed page 411

Given the prevalence of hypothyroxinemia in preterm infants, particularly those below 28–30 weeks gestational age, and the apparent association of this finding with neurodevelop mental deficits later in childhood, it is reason able to question whether supplementation of thyroid hormone might be beneficial for this population. Several trials have been under taken without a clear consensus of benefit, but sample sizes and study design have dem onstrated some limitations.

The largest study of thyroid hormone sup plementation in preterm infants <30 weeks gestation was conducted by van Wassenaer et al. This group conducted a prospective, ran domized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of thyroxine supplementation in 200 infants; 100 of whom received treatment and 100 placebo. The study group was not limited to those infants with hypothyroxinemia but included all newborns 25–30 weeks gestation without severe congenital malformations, maternal endocrine disease, or maternal drug use. Follow-up developmental assessments included the Bayley Developmental Index and neurological examinations at 24 months of age as well as a more detailed follow-up at 5.7 years of age. ### 16.5.2 Critically Ill Children

Critical illness in children admitted to the PICU is associated with substantial neuroen docrine and metabolic changes [33]. In the pediatric population, NTIS has been described mostly in neonates (above), critically ill chil dren after cardiac surgery (below), sepsis or septic shock, diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), or oncological problems [34]. Hebbar et al. from Emory University studied 73 children admit ted to their PICU (ages 3 months to 19 years) [29]. In blood samples obtained in the first 12 h of admission, the children had lower mean serum T3, normal mean T4, normal mean TSH, and elevated rT3 compared to ref erence ranges for healthy subjects. Children with sepsis had lower mean serum T3 and higher rT3 levels compared to non-septic chil dren. As might be expected, thyroid results were influenced by drug therapy (vasopres sors, including dopamine and steroids) and low serum albumin levels. Other iatrogenic factors common in the PICU include antiepi leptic drugs, antiarrhythmic drugs, iodine exposure with contrast or antiseptics, and fasting.

Children with DKA often are admitted to a PICU for management. In a retrospective case-control study from China, Hu et al., reported that the subgroup of children judged to have NTIS, as compared to an euthyroid subgroup, had lower serum free T4 (0.88 vs 1.33 ng/dL), free T3 (171 vs 323 pg/dL), and TSH (1.77 vs 2.56 mIU/L) [35]. Guidelines recommend obtaining screening thyroid func tion tests in children with type 1 diabetes mel litus; however, it may be misleading to assess thyroid function while they are in DKA.

### 16.5.3 Cardiac Surgery in Children

It is well established that infants and children who undergo cardiac surgery, with or without cardiopulmonary bypass, display significant HPT axis suppression consistent with NTIS. The most profound and consistent changes in this population are reduced total and free T3 levels, with free T3 falling as much as 80% from preoperative levels 12–48 h post operatively [43–45]. TSH and total T4 are also suppressed after cardiac surgery, reaching a nadir within the first 24 h [44, 45]. The etiology of NTIS following cardiac surgery is multifactorial. Fasting and the physiologic stress of surgery contribute to the suppression of the HPT axis. Extent of hypo thermia, duration of cardiac arrest, and hemodilution during cardiopulmonary bypass have also been associated with the develop ment of NTIS. Many medications used in the perioperative management of cardiac surgery patients are also known to have a suppressive effect on thyroid function, including dopa mine, glucocorticoids, anesthetic agents, and iodinated antiseptics [43, 44, 46].

Reduced circulating thyroid hormone in the postoperative period is associated with unfavorable physiologic changes including decreased cardiac output, left ventricular dys function, increased vascular resistance, and impaired ventilatory drive [43]. Children who have significant thyroid suppression after car diac surgery have been shown to require lon ger periods of mechanical ventilation and intensive care treatment and to have higher requirements for inotropic support [43, 46], all suggesting that NTIS in this setting may be a maladaptive response and may warrant inter vention.

Given the rapid onset and transient nature of thyroid suppression following cardiac sur gery, intervention studies have focused on the use of T3, which has a half-life of less than 24 h in infants and young children, as opposed to thyroxine, which may take up to 2 weeks to reach steady state. T3 supplementation in adults has been fairly well studied, and there are data to support improved cardiac function postoperatively as well as decreased need for inotropes, decreased rate of arrhythmias, and decreased length of hospital stay with T3 treatment [46]. Previous meta-analysis, how ever, showed no evidence of alteration in post operative mortality in the adult population with T3 supplementation [48]. Studies in chil dren are still somewhat limited and have been less conclusive. Only the results of random ized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials will be summarized below.

### 16.5.4 Renal Insufficiency (Acute

### and Chronic)

Children with chronic renal insufficiency (CRI) have many, but not all, of the changes in thyroid function tests summarized above for NTIS. They typically have low serum T4 and T3 levels, while TSH levels are not ele

vated [56]. Conversion of T4 to T3 by the kid ney is reduced. However, patients do not have elevated rT3 levels. Serum free T4 and free T3 levels are found to be normal in some reports and low in others, even when determined by equilibrium dialysis technique. Chronic meta bolic acidosis may contribute to decreased peripheral conversion to T3 from T4 [57]. Some children with CRI have reduced binding protein levels, as a result of either malnutri tion or protein-losing nephropathies. In addi tion, some uremic factors appear to inhibit binding of T4 and T3 to their binding pro teins. All these effects contribute to low serum total T4 and T3 concentrations. NTIS is reported in ~20% of adult non-dialysis depen dent chronic renal failure patients and up to 50% of adult dialysis patients [58]. Data on pediatric CRI patients are lacking.

Children with CRI manifest some of the clinical symptoms and signs seen in hypothy roidism, including growth retardation, leth argy, poor appetite, and a puffy appearance. The prevalence of goiter is increased, present in up to 50% of children with CRI in some reports [59]. Studies report increased plasma iodine concentrations, most likely the result of decreased renal iodine clearance with CRI. Increased iodine concentrations likely play a role in goiter formation.

Some children with CRI have thyroid function tests consistent with central hypothy roidism (low free T4, inappropriately “nor mal” TSH). In addition, some studies report a “prolonged” TSH response to TRH stimula tion and a subnormal nocturnal TSH surge [60]. However, given that studies also report that TRH degradation is decreased in chil dren with CRI [61], these results may be an indirect effect of CRI on TRH clearance rather than clear evidence of abnormal hypo thalamic–pituitary–thyroid function. While a low free T4 in the face of a normal TSH level would appear to be consistent with central hypothyroidism, the fact that free T4 levels are reported to normalize immediately after hemodialysis is difficult to reconcile with true hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid dysfunction [60].

Patients with acute renal failure (ARF) have thyroid function tests similar to NTIS


## PDF page 426 | printed page 416

but may not have elevation of rT3 [62]. A trial of thyroid hormone treatment was under taken by Acker et al. in adults to determine whether it might help recovery from ARF [63]. Adult patients received either 150 mcg of L-thyroxine or placebo IV every 12 h for a total of 48 h. Thyroid hormone treatment resulted in a decrease in TSH (vs a rise in the control group), but it had no effect on any measure of ARF. Mortality was higher in the thyroxine-treated vs control group (43% vs 13%). Acker et al. also undertook a random ized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of T3 treatment in adult patients with ARF due to acute tubular necrosis undergoing kidney transplantation to determine whether it might improve “delayed graft function” [64]. Patients received an intravenous bolus of 0.2 mcg/kg of T3, followed by an infusion of 0.2 mcg/kg over 6 h. T3 treatment had no effect on per centage requiring dialysis, time for recovery of renal function, or percentage recovering func tion. At 1-year follow-up, graft function was similar in both groups.

In summary, the changes seen in thyroid function tests in children with CRI are con founded by the effects of decreased metabolic clearance of iodine, thyroid hormone and its metabolites, and TSH and TRH; decreased T4 to T3 conversion in the kidney; uremic fac tors that appear to inhibit binding of T4 and T3 to their binding proteins; and drugs used to treat patients after kidney transplant, including glucocorticoids that lower TSH lev els. Many or most of these changes in thyroid function tests revert to normal after hemodi alysis, arguing against true central hypothy roidism. The few treatment studies of thyroid hormone administration carried out in adult patients with ARF do not show benefit and demonstrate possible harmful effects of such treatment.

### 16.5.5 COVID 19

Several studies have reported thyroid dysfunc tion in SARS-CoV2 infected adult patients ranging from a silent destructive thyroiditis, Graves’ disease, subclinical hypothyroidism, overt hypothyroidism, and NTIS [65]. The

most consistently observed alteration of thy roid function parameters in hospitalized patients with COVID 19 was NTIS [66]. In a retrospective study of pediatric patients with COVID 19 related multisystem inflammatory syndrome at a single pediatric hospital in Italy, Calcaterra et al. reported that 88.4% of patients presented with NTIS [67]. The SARS- CoV-2 virus binds to the angiotensinconverting-enzyme 2 receptor, which is expressed on many cells including immune cells, and cells in the thyroid and pituitary, for cell entry. SARS-CoV-2 can cause a cytokine storm, an uncontrolled inflammatory response that is derived from the direct cytotoxic effect of the virus on target cells and from the acti vation of host immune cells, which is detri mental to host cells. Lui et al. showed that a higher CRP level was independently associ ated with low FT3 levels as well as worsening clinical severity, suggesting that systemic inflammation led to NTIS [68]. This pattern was also reported in a small sample prospec tive study by Ayranci et al. of 19 COVID-19 positive pediatric patients [69].

Chen et al. studied 50 adult patients with COVID 19 that did not have a history of thy roid disease and were not pregnant, and found the serum TSH and TT3 levels were signifi cantly lower in these patients than in the healthy control group and non-COVID 19 pneumonia patients [70]. The more severe the COVID-19 infection, the lower the TSH and TT3 levels, with the degree of decrease of TSH and TT3 being positively correlated with the severity of the disease.

Treatments used for COVID 19 are known to interfere with the HPT axis as well as labo ratory tests, and can be confounders. These include glucocorticoids and heparin. Of note Khoo et al. showed decreased TSH and increased cortisol levels in their study popula tion of 456 patients diagnosed with COVID 19 compared to 122 COVID negative patients [71]. Their study did not include any patients who received exogenous steroids and con cluded that the marked elevations in cortisol were from endogenous cortisol elevations with COVID infection. Again, studies are lim ited by small sample size as well as the evolv ing nature of the virus, and gaps persist in our

### 16.6 Summary and Conclusions

NTIS is a common clinical syndrome affect ing infants and children with a broad spec trum of acute and chronic illnesses. It is characterized by reduced T3 and T4 levels, increased rT3 levels, variable free T3 and free T4 levels, and inappropriately normal TSH. These changes are the result of altera tions in regulation of the HPT axis, and in peripheral thyroid hormone metabolism as regulated by deiodinase enzymes, thyroid hormone-binding proteins, and thyroid hor mone action at the cellular level. The tradi tional view of NTIS is that it is an adaptive mechanism, protecting the body from high metabolic demands in the face of acute illness. There is, however, evidence that in certain clinical situations, the alterations in thyroid hormone secretion and action seen in NTIS may, in fact, be detrimental. Particularly in preterm infants who may have worse neuro logic outcomes if they have experienced sig nificantly reduced thyroid hormone levels in the neonatal period and cardiac surgery patients who may have prolonged intensive care unit stays, prolonged need for mechanical ventilation and inotropic support, and worse cardiac function in the immediate postopera tive period, it is tempting to think that inter vention with thyroid hormone may be warranted in NTIS. Treatment studies to date, however, have not shown clear benefit and in some subgroups (preterm infants older than 27 weeks, adult acute renal failure patients) suggest possible harm resulting from thyroid hormone administration. Significantly more research is needed to understand the true impact of NTIS, and the appropriate inter ventions in this situation, if any.

title: Resistance to Thyroid Hormone (RTH) and Resistance to TSH (RTSH)

paragraphs.text: Michelle B. Lemelman and Alexandra M. Dumitrescu

paragraphs.text: Key Points
paragraphs.heading: References – 437

paragraphs.text: 5 Resistance to TH (RTH) refers to a
paragraphs.heading: References – 437

paragraphs.text: group of disorders manifesting as impaired sensitivity to TH.
paragraphs.heading: References – 437

paragraphs.text: –– The classical form of RTH is caused
paragraphs.heading: References – 437

paragraphs.text: in most cases by mutations in the TH receptor β (THRB) gene and is classified as RTH-β. Fifteen percent of patients with this phenotype do not have a detectable mutation in the THRB gene, and this entity is known as non-TR-RTH. –– Mutations in the THRA gene have
paragraphs.heading: References – 437

paragraphs.text: been recently reported to cause RTH-α. Patients with this defect are phenotypically different from the RTH patients with THRB gene mutations in terms of thyroid func tion tests and clinical features. –– Other disease entities reported are
paragraphs.heading: References – 437

paragraphs.text: the TH cell membrane transport defect caused by MCT8 gene muta tions and TH metabolism defect caused by SBP2 and DIO1 gene mutations. These disorders can be distinguished by their characteristic abnormalities of thyroid function. 5 Resistance to TSH (RTSH) manifests
paragraphs.heading: References – 437

paragraphs.text: with high serum TSH of normal bio logical activity in the absence of goiter. Several genetic defects have been reported to present the phenotype of RTSH, including inactivating muta tions in the TSH receptor TSHR gene, mutations in the PAX 8 gene, and a dominantly inherited form without TSHR and PAX8 mutations that is linked to a region on chromosome 15.
paragraphs.heading: References – 437

paragraphs.text: dation, sensorineural deafness, and nystag mus. Clinical features of hyperthyroidism may include tachycardia, hyperactivity, and increased basal metabolic rate. Most patients with the RTH-β phenotype have autosomal dominant mutations of the THRB gene. Patients have been identified from a wide range of races and ethnic groups; the exact geographic distribution of the disorder is unknown but it has been estimated that RTH-β occurs in about 1 case per 50,000 live births [4]. Individuals without an identifiable THRB mutation but with thyroid function tests consistent with RTH-β, may have non- TR-RTH and dynamic testing is required to confirm or exclude the diagnosis. Therapeutic strategies for RTH-β are not well-defined and treatment (if any) must be individualized. Most studies of patients with RTH-β have been performed in adults, and approaches for the pediatric population may need to be deduced in the absence of firm data. In the past several years, additional syndromes of reduced sensitivity to TH, distinct from the classic RTH-β, have been described, and these will be discussed below ( Fig. 17.1).
paragraphs.heading: and Background

paragraphs.text: Until recently, mutations in the THRA have remained elusive. In fact, because THRA mutations were not previously identified, they were believed to be extremely rare, potentially lethal, or sub-clinically expressed [5]. Mouse models of Trα defects (knock outs [6, 7] and knock ins [8]), were investigated in an attempt to infer the phenotype of human THRA mutations. The first patients with THRA mutation were reported in 2012 [9, 10] and their phenotype is now classified as RTH-α. Because TRα is not involved in the feedback regulation of the hypothalamic-pituitarythyroid axis, their TFTs are distinct from RTH-β, namely, they have low serum T4, bor derline high T3, and very low rT3, with nor mal to elevated TSH levels. Some THRA gene mutations affect only the TRα1 subunit and tend to be more severe, while some mutations affect both TRα1 and α2 subunits [11]. Deiodinase 3 (D3) is an inactivating enzyme which degrades active T3 and converts T4 to inactive rT3 and was shown to be controlled by TRα [12]. Thus, patients with impaired
paragraphs.heading: and Background

paragraphs.text: TRα1 have dysregulation of D3, which con tributes to the higher levels of serum T3 and lower levels of rT3 [13]. The clinical manifes tations in this syndrome are variable but con sistent with the manifestations of untreated congenital hypothyroidism in peripheral tis sues expressing predominantly TRα such as bone, gastrointestinal (GI), and central ner vous system (CNS) tissues [5].
paragraphs.heading: and Background

paragraphs.text: The TH receptor (TR) is a member of the nuclear hormone receptor (NHR) family of transcription factors. These proteins directly bind DNA to modulate gene transcription [14, 15]. NHRs contain several important domains: an N-terminal transactivation or AF-1 domain (A/B domain); a central DNAbinding domain (DBD); and a C-terminal ligand-binding domain (LBD) with liganddependent activation (AF-2) function. In addition to ligand binding, the LBD is involved in the recruitment of key nuclear cofactors such as corepressors and coactiva tors.
paragraphs.heading: 17.1.2 Etiology

paragraphs.text: of histone acetylation, modulating interac tions with general transcription factors, and other mechanisms [31–39]. More recently, rapid non-genomic actions of TH have been identified (independent of transcription) [14], although it is currently unclear how these effects relate to syndromes of RTH ( Fig. 17.2).
paragraphs.heading: 17.1.2 Etiology

paragraphs.text: There are two major isoforms of the TR, termed TRα and TRβ, which are encoded by genes on different chromosomes: THRA on chromosome 17 and THRB on chromosome 3 [40, 41]. Additional isoforms of TRα and TRβ are generated by alternative splicing or differential promoter usage. Although TRα1 is a true TH receptor, TRα2 is an alternatively spliced isoform that does not bind TH [42]. In contrast, TRβ1, TRβ2, and the more recently described TRβ3 isoform [43] all bind TH and differ only in their N terminus. The function of TRβ3 in vivo remains unknown.
paragraphs.heading: 17.1.2 Etiology

paragraphs.text: Mutations in the THRB gene have been identified in many patients with RTH and are now classified as RTH-β. In most cases, this
paragraphs.heading: 17.1.2 Etiology

paragraphs.text: syndrome is inherited in an autosomal domi nant fashion. A subset of classical RTH patients, however, does not exhibit THRB mutations [44], and this entity is known as non-TR-RTH. These patients may have defects in other proteins involved in TH action [45], but such mutations have not yet been identified [46]. This is an ongoing area of research, and novel mutations are being sought. A recent search for mutations in the retinoid X receptor gamma (RXRγ) gene was not successful [47]. It has been hypothesized that some non-TR-RTH patients may exhibit mosaicism for de novo THRB mutations [48].

tor recruitment [51, 52]. Interestingly, it has been shown that the mutant TRs interfere with wild-type TR function, an effect has been termed “dominant-negative effect” [53, 54]. Mouse models have clarified the role of the mutant TRs in the pathogenesis of RTH- β. Although complete knockout of TRβ pro duces mice with thyroid function tests consistent with RTH-β [55], modeling “knock-in” of Thrb mutations found in patients with RTH-β yields mice with more severe resistance [56, 57].

RTH-β can be subdivided into (1) general ized resistance to TH (GRTH) and (2) pitu itary resistance to TH (PRTH). In GRTH, the elevated TH levels generated by resistance at the level of the hypothalamus and pituitary have diminished activity in the periphery; thus, there is a variable degree of generalized resistance. In contrast, in PRTH (also called central resistance to TH, or CRTH), there is resistance solely (or at least primarily) at the level of the hypothalamus and pituitary. This resistance leads to elevated levels of TH, but in contrast to GRTH, sensitivity to TH is maintained in peripheral tissues, causing thy rotoxicosis. Patients with GRTH frequently exhibit tachycardia due to the high levels of TH stimulating intact TRα1 receptors in the heart; thus, tachycardia should not be used to differentiate GRTH and PRTH. Some investi gators do not recognize the existence of PRTH as a distinct clinical entity [58], arguing that the same mutations have been reported to cause both GRTH and PRTH [59]. However, a careful evaluation of clinical and biochemi cal indices in a patient with RTH suggested that PRTH may very well exist [60]. In addi tion, experiments have revealed that mutant TRβs of patients with PRTH behave differ ently than TRβs of patients with GRTH, par ticularly with respect to the TRβ2 isoform [61, 62]. A mouse model of the R429Q mutation (which has been reported to cause PRTH) showed that the mutant TRβ selectively inter feres with negative regulation by TH [63]. Another study identified differential recruit ment of nuclear cofactors by a different TRβ defect associated with PRTH [64].

In contrast, knockout of Thra in mice causes a syndrome of hypothyroidism with growth arrest [6, 7]. Mice with heterozygous knock-in Thra1 mutations are viable and have a heterogeneous phenotype, depending on the severity and the location of the mutation [8]. Most adult Thra1 mutant mice have a mildly elevated TSH. Various knock-in mouse mod els manifest other features, such as delayed endochondral ossification resulting in dwarf ism, disturbed behavior, memory impairment, locomotor dysfunction, mild bradycardia, and insulin resistance [8]. Thus, a patient with a dominant-negative THRA mutation was expected to have a different phenotype from the classical RTH-β phenotype. In fact, because THRA mutations were not identified until recently, they were considered to be extremely rare, lethal, or sub-clinically expressed [5].

In 2012, the first patients with THRA mutations were reported [9, 10] and their phe notype was classified as RTH-α. Currently, 38 patients belonging to 24 families and harbor ing 24 different THRA mutations, have been reported in the literature [11]. The cases included de novo and familial mutations which are caused by missense or frameshift mutations affecting the ligand binding domain of the receptor. Eight mutations are frame shifts with early termination located in the part of the gene specific only to the TRα1 iso form. Four are point mutations of TRα1 and 12 are located in the part of the protein com mon between the TRα1 and TRα2 isoforms. As in the case of THRB mutations, this results in three different mechanisms causing func tional impairment: (1) reduced affinity for T3, (2) interference of the normal TRα allele by the mutant TRα, resulting in a dominant neg ative effect; and (3) defective coactivator recruitment to the ligand bound receptor. Interestingly, some of the mutations identified in the THRA gene in cases of RTH-α were also identified in the THRB gene in cases of RTH-β. Comparison of the α and β forms of RTH for equivalent mutations enables the study of the distinctive roles of the different receptors [5].

The clinical presentation of RTH-β is variable ( Box 17.1). The initial family described by Refetoff et al. [1] included an 81⁄2-year-old girl and a 121⁄2-year-old boy, both of whom were overall clinically euthyroid but exhibited goi ter, deaf-mutism, stippled epiphyses on radio logical skeletal survey, and elevated protein-bound iodine (PBI) levels. In contrast to most cases of RTH-β, this family was shown to have an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance, and affected family members were later found to have a complete deletion of the THRB gene [65]. The heterozygous parents were phenotypically normal, suggest ing that a single wild-type TRβ (in the absence of a mutant TR) may be sufficient for TH action. In contrast, most cases of RTH-β are inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion because mutant TRβs exhibit dominantnegative inhibition over wild-type alleles ( Box 17.1).
paragraphs.heading: 17.1.3.1 RTH-β Phenotype

paragraphs.text: Patients with RTH-β come to medical attention for a variety of reasons. Goiter is the presenting sign in about 38% of cases; less common reasons include learning disabilities, developmental delay, tachycardia, suspected thyrotoxicosis, and elevated thyroxine levels at birth [4]. Thyroid function tests reveal elevated TH levels in the setting of a non-suppressed TSH (see “Diagnostic Guidelines” below). Infants with RTH-β may have congenital deafness, congenital nystagmus, neonatal jaundice, and hypotonia [2]. Patients with RTH-β may have an increased risk of develop ing autoimmune thyroid disease [66]. Individuals with RTH-β who inappropriately undergo thyroidectomy or radioactive iodine treatment will exhibit signs and symptoms of hypothyroidism despite TH levels in the nor mal range following replacement therapy. Therefore, higher doses of L-T4 and L-T3 are usually needed to normalize TSH in these patients when endogenous TH production is not available.
paragraphs.heading: 17.1.3.1 RTH-β Phenotype

paragraphs.text: A National Institute of Health study [67] evaluated prospectively a cohort of 42 kin

dreds manifesting the RTH-β phenotype. There was autosomal dominant transmission in 22 kindreds, sporadic transmission in 14, and an unknown transmission in 6. This last group was characterized as non-TR-RTH, as they manifested the classical RTH-β like phe notype without a detectable THRB mutation. A palpable goiter was identified in 74% of females and 53% of males. Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) was present in 72% of the males and 43% of females. IQ was about 13 points lower in patients with the RTH-β phenotype compared to controls, and one-third of patients had an IQ < 85. In con trast, only a few patients had actual mental retardation. Patients with the RTH-β pheno type had a higher incidence of speech delay (24%), stuttering (18%), and hearing loss than controls. Although resting pulse was higher in patients with RTH-β, in this partic ular study, the correlation did not persist after adjustment for age (though it has been noted by other groups). Children with the RTH-β phenotype exhibited delayed bone matura tion. Bone age was delayed in 29% of patients, and 18% had short stature, though another study suggested that the RTH-β phenotype is not associated with decreased final adult height [68].

Investigation of mutations within families have elucidated new findings about the RTH- β. A novel THRB heterozygous missense mutation (c.1033G>T, p.G345C) was discov ered in a nonconsanguineous family. The pro band was clinically and biochemically more affected than her sibling and father harboring the same mutation. The proband was symp tomatic (tachycardia, exercise, and heat intol erant) with significantly higher iodothyronine levels, and a larger thyroid gland suggesting more significant resistance to TH despite an identical mutant genotype [69]. In another case report, an RTH-β missense mutation was found in a “cold region,” a codon region not previously thought to harbor disease causing mutations. This patient’s mutation was only confirmed to be causal after investigation of other family members through phenotypegenotype correlation [70].

Patients have been reported to have RTH-β and thyroid gland dysgenesis. Five cases have been reported with only three cases being studied including one report of a patient with athyreosis complicated by a heterozygous paternally inherited RTH-β mutation [71].

As noted previously, certain tissues dem onstrate increased TH-mediated effects in patients with RTH-β. This is presumably caused by TH stimulation of TRα1 in these (TRα1-predominant) tissues. The classic example of this phenomenon is tachycardia, which has been reported in many patients with GRTH. More recently, Mitchell et al. reported that patients with RTH also exhibit increased energy expenditure, muscle mito chondrial uncoupling, and hyperphagia [72].

Findings of abnormal IQ and ADHD in patients with RTH-β suggest the importance of TH in CNS development and function. Matochik et al. used positron emission tomog raphy (PET) scans to study CNS activity in patients with RTH [73]. This study showed that RTH-β patients have higher cerebral metabolism in certain key areas of the central nervous system (CNS) during a continuous auditory discrimination task, including the anterior cingulate gyrus and the parietal lobe. While PET scanning techniques remain a research tool for RTH-β, these results suggest an important role for TH in these CNS regions. A study of children with ADHD with and without coexisting RTH-β examined the role of TH therapy (in this case, L-T3) in ADHD [74]. Most patients with RTH-β and ADHD improved when placed on T3 therapy, whereas patients with ADHD (in the absence of RTH-β) deteriorated or remained stable. Thus, ADHD in patients with RTH-β appears to be distinct from ADHD in patients without RTH-β [75].

While several unusual coexisting condi tions in patients with RTH-β have been reported, some of these may have occurred by chance. These include a birdlike appearance of the face, various vertebral and other skele tal anomalies, short fourth metacarpals, pat ent ductus arteriosus, and noncommunicating hydrocephalus [2].

The first patient identified with RTH-α pre sented with delayed linear growth, delayed tooth eruption, severe constipation, decreased muscle tone, and impaired gross and fine motor skills [9]. Neurocognitive deficits in patients with RTH-α include reduced nonverbal IQ, motor incoordination, impaired visual motor integration consistent with find ings in untreated congenital hypothyroidism. Structural brain abnormalities include decreased cerebellar volume and decreased white matter tract density [76]. Additional defects in the cardiovascular system, includ ing decreased heart rate and blood pressure, were also reported [9].
paragraphs.heading: 17.1.3.2 RTH-α Phenotype

paragraphs.text: The absence of goiter, which is among the typical manifestations of RTH-β, is particu larly notable. Diagnosis prior to 1 year of age was not reported until recently [11, 13]. A 10-month-old presented with an umbilical hernia, pointed ears, and large fetal size. This young patient was also found to have a nevus of the right cheek at 6 months of age. It has been recently reported that patients with TRα1 and/or TRα2 are more likely to have skin tags and benign melanocytic nevi [13].
paragraphs.heading: 17.1.3.2 RTH-α Phenotype

paragraphs.text: The initial testing of a patient suspected to have RTH-β phenotype should include rou tine thyroid function tests. Patients with RTH-β phenotype have elevated free TH lev els in the setting of non-suppressed (normal or elevated) TSH levels. Other causes of “euthyroid hyperthyroxinemia” should be excluded ( Box 17.2), including method ological laboratory artifacts due to the pres ence of heterophile antibodies [77]. Such patients may in fact be hyperthyroid, with elevated TH levels and (appropriately) sup pressed TSH levels when measured accurately. This problem has decreased, but not elimi nated, with improvements in the TSH assay. Reevaluation of TSH levels after serial dilu tions may be useful. Similarly, patients with autoimmune hypothyroidism occasionally exhibit falsely elevated TH levels due to the presence of antibodies interfering with the measurement of T4 and/or T3 ( Box 17.2).
paragraphs.heading: 17.1.4.1 RTH-β

paragraphs.text: Patients with defects in TH-binding pro teins, such as TBG, transthyretin, and albu min, can also exhibit abnormal levels of total T4 and T3. Euthyroid patients with TBG excess, which can be congenital or acquired (e.g., in pregnancy [78] and liver disease [79]), have elevated total T4 levels in the setting of a non-suppressed TSH. These patients have normal free T4 levels, when measured directly or estimated based on T3 resin uptake, T3RU. Familial dysalbuminemic hyperthyroxinemia (FDH) is a syndrome caused by the produc tion of albumin variants with Arg-His or Arg-
paragraphs.heading: 17.1.4.1 RTH-β

paragraphs.text: Pro mutations at codon 218 [80, 81]. These albumin variants have increased affinity for T4. Therefore, measurement of total serum T4 is elevated; correction of T4 based on T3RU may also yield abnormally high results. Free T4 levels are falsely elevated when mea sured by certain analog measurements, but a free T4 level measured by dialysis will be nor mal. Serum T3 levels are normal in FDH and exclude the diagnosis of RTH.

Certain medications such as amiodarone [82] and propranolol (at high doses) inhibit T4 to T3 conversion. Euthyroid patients with T4 to T3 conversion defects may have elevated T4 levels and inappropriately normal TSH levels; however, these patients have low-normal or low T3 levels, excluding the diagnosis of RTH. Finally, a few other conditions such as acute psychiatric illness [83] can also cause abnormal thyroid function tests that can occa sionally be confused with RTH ( Box 17.2).

Once these various conditions are excluded, the diagnosis is generally one of RTH-β vs thyrotroph adenoma [84]. Differentiation between these two disorders can be difficult. In general, TSH adenomas are associated with hyperthyroidism, whereas patients with RTH-β have variable degrees of compensated TH hyporesponsiveness. In addition, patients with thyrotroph adenomas generally have higher serum levels of the gly coprotein α subunit than patients with RTH-β [84], though there is significant overlap.

In terms of radiology studies, patients with TSH adenomas generally have pituitary findings on MRI scans, but it should be noted that patients with RTH-β may have incidental pituitary adenomas, mimicking a thyrotroph adenoma [85]. In addition, a study used Doppler ultrasonography to determine whether thyroid blood flow distinguishes between RTH-β and thyrotroph adenomas [86]. These investigators showed that parame ters of thyroid blood flow normalized in T3-treated RTH-β patients, but not in those with TSH-secreting adenomas.
An effective method to confirm a diagno sis of RTH-β (at least GRTH) is to administer graded doses of T3 and measure a battery of TH-responsive tests. Although patients with

thyrotroph adenomas have impaired TSH responses to T3, they retain intact peripheral responses to T3. In contrast, patients with GRTH have impaired TSH and peripheral responses to exogenous T3. Patients are gen erally admitted to a clinical research center for the duration of the protocol. A few protocols have been described, during which time exog enous T3 is given in an escalating regimen, and various TH-responsive measurements are taken [2].

Most cases of RTH-β are associated with mutations in the TRβ gene. Ultimately, the most secure way to make a diagnosis of RTH-β is to demonstrate (a) elevated TH lev els in the setting of a non-suppressed TSH, (b) TH hyporesponsiveness, and (c) a THRB gene mutation.

If a child is born to a parent with RTH-β with a known THRB mutation, the most straight forward way to confirm or exclude the diagno sis in the infant is to sequence the known mutation. There are two other ways infants with RTH-β frequently come to medical atten tion: (a) symptoms consistent with RTH-β and (b) abnormal thyroid screening tests. Infants with RTH-β may have congenital deafness, congenital nystagmus, neonatal jaundice, and hypotonia. In addition, screen ing programs that are in place to identify infants with congenital hypothyroidism occa sionally identify RTH-β instead. A fetus with suspected RTH-β can be tested for THRB mutations by chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis and gDNA analysis [87], though the benefits of making the diagnosis at this stage of development have not been clearly established.
paragraphs.heading: 17.1.4.2 Neonatal Considerations

paragraphs.text: As RTH-α patients present primarily with dys morphic features and GI symptoms in the con text of only mild thyroid test abnormalities, they might not present early to the attention of the Endocrinologist. There is no standard test ing recommended for these patients at this point. Astute clinicians who identify the syn dromic features of this defect and review the
paragraphs.heading: 17.1.4.3 RTH-α

paragraphs.text: literature will be able to consider THRA muta tions as a possible diagnosis. The typical pat tern of TFTs includes low or normal T4, high normal T3, and normal or slightly elevated TSH. Identification of more patients will allow further insight into this novel defect.
paragraphs.heading: 17.1.4.3 RTH-α

paragraphs.text: There is no reason to treat patients with RTH- β who have elevated levels of TH that are appropriate for the degree of both thyrotroph and peripheral tissue resistance. In fact, the mainstay of the management of asymptom atic RTH-β patients is to recognize the correct diagnosis and avoid antithyroid treatment. Attempts aimed at decreasing the circulating TH levels, either with antithyroid drugs, or with ablative treatment by surgery or radioio dide, will result in objective findings of TH deprivation and need for supraphysiological doses of TH. In such patients, the dose of TH needs to be uptitrated to normalize the serum TSH levels and high doses of L-T4 will be nec essary, sometimes as high as 500–1000 μg/day.
paragraphs.heading: 17.1.5.1 RTH-β

paragraphs.text: Mutations in THRA gene have been only recently recognized and limited data are cur rently available to accurately assess long term outcomes and possible complications. Based on the few patients known to date, it seems that L-T4 treatment during childhood has some benefits; however, there is the risk of making the TR-β predominant tissues hyper thyroid. Lack of intervention has an overall poor outcome in patients with severe THRA mutations.
paragraphs.heading: 17.1.5.2 RTH-α

paragraphs.text: No specific therapy is available to correct the underlying defect in RTH-β. Frequently, patients with RTH-β are in a clinical state of
paragraphs.heading: 17.1.6.1 RTH-β

paragraphs.text: compensated TH hyporesponsiveness. In these patients, no specific therapy is indicated. In those few patients who have greater peripheral hyporesponsiveness and thus clinical hypothy roidism, treatment with TH (e.g., levothyrox ine) may be considered. If used, the specific dosage must be individualized based on mark ers of TH action (such as sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG), cholesterol, ferritin, basic metabolic rate, and bone density) [59]. The use of TRIAC (3,5,3′-triiodothyroacetic acid), a TH analog with relative specificity toward the TRβ receptor [88, 89], has been advocated for use in patients with RTH. A study reported the use of up to 3.0 mg TRIAC per day, in an RTH-β patient, resulting in reduction in the thyroid volume, resolution of supraventricular arrhythmia, and decrease in TSH and free T4 levels. In addition, attention-deficit hyperactiv ity disorder (ADHD) symptoms improved, with a concomitant decline in the ADHD Rating Scale score [90]. d-Thyroxine has also been used [91], though one study suggested it was less effective than TRIAC [92]. Novel TR analogs hopefully will be developed that acti vate mutant receptors [93]. In sum, therapy (or lack thereof) must be individualized for each patient. Of course, for patients who have had their thyroid glands inappropriately ablated for misdiagnosed hyperthyroidism, treatment with TH will be necessary.
paragraphs.heading: 17.1.6.1 RTH-β

paragraphs.text: In patients with PRTH, beta blockers have been used to control symptoms; the use of anti-thyroid drugs in this situation is contro versial, and these medications are not indi cated in patients with GRTH. Agents that have been used to decrease TSH levels include somatostatin analogs and bromocriptine, but these have had only limited success.
paragraphs.heading: 17.1.6.1 RTH-β

paragraphs.text: The care of RTH-β patients during preg nancy needs to be individualized as well and depends on the genotype of both the fetus and mother [94]. High miscarriage rates, low birth weight, and suppressed TSH of wildtype fetuses of pregnant RTH-β mothers have been suggested to be due to high circulating levels of TH [95].
paragraphs.heading: 17.1.6.1 RTH-β

paragraphs.text: A retrospective review discovered improve ment in neonatal birth weight and TSH sup pression when affected mothers were given
paragraphs.heading: 17.1.6.1 RTH-β

paragraphs.text: anti-thyroid medications. Conclusions from the study support a goal for maternal fT4 lev els to not exceed 50% of the upper limit of normal in RTH-β mothers carrying wild type fetuses [96].
paragraphs.heading: 17.1.6.1 RTH-β

paragraphs.text: A prenatal diagnosis of RTH-β was made [87] in a 29-year-old pregnant woman at 17 weeks gestation. The fetus and mother were both found to harbor the TRβ mutation (T337A), and the pregnant woman was treated with TRIAC with beneficial effects on mater nal symptoms and fetal goiter size. Cordocentesis was performed to evaluate effects of the medication on the fetal thyroid function tests. However, an accompanying editorial to the report [59] points out some potential dangers of this approach, since cor docentesis may lead to the need for emergency C-section.
paragraphs.heading: 17.1.6.1 RTH-β

paragraphs.text: Epigenetic studies have demonstrated how maternal hyperthyroxinemia in utero subse quently decreases thyrotroph sensitivity in adulthood. A transgenerational epigenetic study assessed TH sensitivity in subsequent generations of an Azorean population who harbored a heterozygous THRB mutation. Twenty-six individuals among 17 nuclear fam ilies were studied. Subjects were second or third generation wild type born to wild type mothers (first generation) exposed to elevated intrauterine TH. Subsequent wild type gener ations (second and third) had reduced sensi tivity to TH when born to males but not when born to females with reduced sensitivity to TH [97].
paragraphs.heading: 17.1.6.1 RTH-β

paragraphs.text: In children with RTH-β, special care should be directed toward issues of growth and mental development. Patients with delayed bone age may be candidates for ther apy. One approach is to consider treatment in children with the following signs and symp toms: (a) elevated serum TSH levels, (b) unex plained failure to thrive, (c) unexplained seizures, (d) developmental delay, and (e) his tory of growth or mental retardation in other affected members of the family [59]. As noted above, patients with RTH-β and coexisting ADHD may improve when treated with TH [74]. In any case, patients who require treat ment should be followed closely, with careful
paragraphs.heading: 17.1.6.1 RTH-β

paragraphs.text: evaluation of growth, bone age, and thyroidresponsive biochemical indices.
paragraphs.heading: 17.1.6.1 RTH-β

paragraphs.text: L-T4 therapy has been shown to have benefi cial effects on certain components of the phe notype; however, cognitive and fine motor skill defects do not improve [5]. During L-T4 treat ment, serum T4 increased, rT3 levels normal ized while serum T3 remained elevated, and this resulted in suppressed TSH. However, some peripheral markers of TH action have been reported to respond to L-T4 therapy, and markers of bone turnover rose progressively upon L-T4 treatment, with certain markers, including procollagen type 1 N-propeptide, and C-telopeptide cross-linked collagen type I, becoming frankly elevated. Some patients reported feeling more energetic and showed greater alertness after the initiation of L-T4 therapy, which induced an initial catch-up growth in one patient. Of note, in all patients, L-T4 treatment had a beneficial effect on con stipation. However, L-T4 therapy may be of limited benefit in RTH-α, as the resulting hyperthyroidism in TRβ-expressing tissues may preclude the use of higher doses of L-T4. L-T3 treatment was tried in only one case, and led to a reduction in TSH and consequently T4 levels, with an increase in heart rate, thus L-T3 treatment might be difficult to implement [5]. It is possible that different treatment regimens could be used in children vs adults, considering the important role of TH in growth and devel opment. Thus, judicious supplementation may be necessary in young patients, while the L-T4 doses used in adults could be lower.
paragraphs.heading: 17.1.6.2 RTH-α

paragraphs.text: As only a few patients with RTH-α are known, there is limited information about treatment of this condition. Severe RTH-α is due to silencing of gene transcription at sev eral levels—interactions with corepressors, failure of corepressor release, and failure of coactivator recruitment by ligand binding. Many THRA mutants, however, retain ability to bind T3. Use of synthetic thyroid mimetic ligands in zebrafish models of RTH-α show promise of treatment by releasing the tran scriptional repression by the TRα corepressor complex [98].
paragraphs.heading: 17.1.6.2 RTH-α

paragraphs.text: A 1-year-old baby presents for genetic evalua tion of his thyroid condition. He is the first child born to unrelated parents. He was born premature as the mother developed pre-eclamp sia and C-section was performed at 32 weeks. Apgar score was 9/9, birth weight 1320 g, birth length 46 cm, and he was diagnosed as being of small for gestational age. Heart rate was 130/ min. Due to initial hypoglycemia, growth hor mone, insulin, cortisol, TSH, and fT4 levels were tested. TSH and fT4 were found to be ele vated at 7.1 mIU/L and 51 pmol/L, respectively. Thyroid ultrasound showed a mildly enlarged gland (right lobe 0.76 × 1.05 cm, and left lobe 0.84 × 0.71 cm) with normal structure. He had no signs of hypo- or hyperthyroidism, and heart rate was 134/min even when asleep. He was initially treated with propylthiouracil (PTU) and propranolol; however, a pediatric endocrine consult recommended stopping this regimen. He was seen later in Pediatric
paragraphs.heading: 17.1.6.2 RTH-α

paragraphs.text: RTH is an inherited syndrome characterized by reduced responsiveness of target tissues to TH caused by mutations in the TH receptor genes.
paragraphs.heading: 17.1.7 Summary

paragraphs.text: Mutations in the THRB cause the classical form of RTH known as RTH-β and patients present with elevated TH levels with unsup pressed TSH. The reduced sensitivity to TH at the level of the hypothalamus and pituitary leads to elevated TSH levels, which stimulate the thyroid gland to increase production of TH. Both hyperthyroid and hypothyroid signs or symptoms may be present depending on the relative expression of TRβ and TRα in dif ferent tissues.
paragraphs.heading: 17.1.7 Summary

paragraphs.text: Identification of THRA mutations has led to the characterization of RTH-α. These patients are phenotypically different from the RTH-β patients in both TFTs and clinical fea tures. Typical TFTs include low serum T4, borderline high T3, very low rT3, and with normal to elevated TSH. The resistance to TH

Thyroid gland was easily palpable and TSH was 5.53 mIU/L (0.62–8.05), and fT4 60.10 pmol/L. This case illustrates a case of early diagnosis of RTH-β prompted by abnormal blood tests in perinatal period.
