tioning appropriately, little if any phosphate should escape in the urine and the tubular reabsorption of phosphate should be greater than 95%. These measures differentiate patients with hypophosphatemia due to renal wasting from those with inadequate intake or reduced gastrointestinal absorption of phos phate.

FGF23 can be measured directly to differ entiate between FGF23 mediated and non- FGF23 mediated causes of hypophosphatemia and renal phosphate wasting. However, this assay is not always readily available and other tests can be used as a surrogate for the presence of excess FGF23. Under normal conditions,

hypophosphatemia is a potent stimulus for 1,25(OH)2D3 production. In the absence of excess FGF23, 1,25(OH)2D3 becomes elevated leading to increased gastrointestinal calcium absorption and to high urine calcium excre tion. Therefore, in the context of hypophos phatemia, a low or normal low-normal 1,25(OH)2D3 and relatively low or normal urine calcium are evidence of an underling FGF23 mediated disorder. Conversely, if 1,25(OH)2D3 and urine calcium are elevated, the FGF23 concentration is expected to be low.
Aminoaciduria, glucosuria, along with low serum bicarbonate would indicate gener alized renal proximal tubule dysfunction con sistent with renal Fanconi syndrome.

Treatment of nutritional rickets is aimed at restoring adequate vitamin D and calcium levels to allow appropriate mineralization and healing of bones and to prevent permanent skeletal deformity if left un- or undertreated. As discussed earlier in this chapter, it is criti cal to remember that nutritional rickets is a preventable disease. The American Academy of Pediatrics, Endocrine Society, Institute of Medicine (IOM), and a Global Consensus of experts all endorse 400 IU vitamin D intake daily for infants up to 12 months of age for prevention of rickets. It is uncertain if 400 IU is sufficient for optimal bone health and growth but has been clearly shown to prevent rickets in this age group. IOM and the Global Consensus recommend 600 IU vitamin D for children over 12 months of age. Adequate cal cium intake is also required to prevent rickets. According to the IOM, children up to 6 months of age should receive 200 mg cal cium per day and 260 mg per day for those 6–12 months old. The Global Consensus guideline recommends 500 mg calcium intake per day as sufficient for children after 12 months of age. We and others endorse the
paragraphs.heading: D and Calcium Deficiency)

paragraphs.text: IOM recommendation for progressively increasing calcium intake through childhood from 700 mg per day after 12 months of age up to 1300 mg per day starting at age 9 years up to 17 years old, a time when linear growth and thus skeletal mineral demands are high.
paragraphs.heading: D and Calcium Deficiency)

paragraphs.text: Multiple dosing regimens for vitamin D have been reported as effective in healing nutrition rickets including daily oral dosing and intermittent high dose therapy (as high as 600,000 IU as a single dose) given orally or intramuscularly. As noted above, vitamin D intake of 400 IU per day for all infants is endorsed by several organizations and has been shown to prevent rickets [10, 13, 91–93]. Although this amount may be sufficient to prevent rickets, it is insufficient for treatment of established disease. Global Consensus guidelines recommend oral treatment with 2000 IU vitamin D per day for at least 3 months for all ages [10]. Oral therapy is rec ommended over intramuscular therapy, and “stoss” therapy, where very large doses are administered on one or over several days, due to the risk of vitamin D toxicity leading to hypercalciuria and/or hypercalcemia [94].
paragraphs.heading: D and Calcium Deficiency)

paragraphs.text: Calcium supplementation is recommended during treatment of vitamin D deficiency rickets, even in those without hypocalcemia. Hypocalcemia may occur with vitamin D replacement as mineral is deposited in the skeleton and as PTH levels fall. For those who are eucalcemic or mildly hypocalcemic, oral dosing is sufficient. However, severe symp tomatic hypocalcemia does occur that can cause seizures, tetany, laryngospasm, and car diomyopathy with fatalities being reported. Children with severe, symptomatic hypocalce mia due to nutritional rickets require hospital ization for intravenous calcium administration and monitoring until an oral regimen can be established that maintains serum calcium in a safe range.
paragraphs.heading: D and Calcium Deficiency)

paragraphs.text: Various dosing recommendations exist for calcium including weight-based dosing (35–75 mg elemental calcium per kilogram per day in 2–3 divided doses) or a simple fixed dose of 500 mg per day regardless of age or weight [10, 16]. The recommendation for both vitamin D and calcium supplementation for treatment of nutritional rickets acknowledges
paragraphs.heading: D and Calcium Deficiency)

paragraphs.text: the often-coexisting low calcium intake of those with vitamin D deficiency and that some degree of vitamin D deficiency can be over come by adequate calcium intake. Calcium carbonate should be taken with food to allow appropriate absorption, while calcium citrate can be taken on an empty stomach [95]. It is important to clarify with parents how to assess the dose of calcium provided by vari ous calcium preparations. Calcium carbonate is 40% elemental calcium by weight (i.e., 1000 mg calcium carbonate contains only 400 mg of elemental calcium). Likewise, cal cium citrate contains 21% elemental calcium and calcium glubionate 6.5% elemental cal cium by weight. Confirmation of the elemen tal calcium intake is crucial, primarily to prevent underdosing.
paragraphs.heading: D and Calcium Deficiency)

paragraphs.text: While uncommon in the US, nutritional rickets due to calcium deficiency without vita min D deficiency is well described in other regions and has been successfully treated with calcium alone [96]. A randomized controlled trial conducted in Nigerian children revealed that in children with calcium deficiency rick ets, treatment with calcium alone or calcium plus vitamin D was more effective than treat ment with vitamin D alone [97].
paragraphs.heading: D and Calcium Deficiency)

paragraphs.text: Response to therapy should be monitored not only for efficacy but also for potential tox icity. Vitamin D is a fat-soluble vitamin and as such, excess administration can result in long standing toxicity. The frequency of monitor ing depends on the severity of disease and the presence and severity of hypocalcemia. Even in severe disease, serum calcium, phosphorus, and PTH can normalize in days to weeks. However, alkaline phosphatase and radio graphic changes often take months to normal ize. For most children (excluding those with severe hypocalcemia), we recommend measur ing serum calcium phosphorus, creatinine, PTH, total alkaline phosphatase, and vitamin D 2–3 weeks after initiating therapy and after dose adjustments if required. Less frequent monitoring is required once biochemical parameters are improving. We recommend obtaining radiographs 2–3 months after initi ating therapy to document improvement or resolution of rickets. Treatment doses of vita
paragraphs.heading: D and Calcium Deficiency)

paragraphs.text: min D and calcium are recommended for at least 3 months, but some may require a longer duration to exhibit full healing of rickets. Urine calcium (24 our collection or calcium to creatinine ratio) is helpful in monitoring for efficacy and toxicity. Initially, urine calcium is low due to inadequate absorption and deposi tion into bone. Urine calcium can remain rela tively low until the rickets resolves and the bone reservoir for mineral has been suffi ciently filled.

Once biochemical and radiographic reso lution of rickets has been established, preven tion of recurrence requires maintenance dosing of vitamin D and adequate calcium intake via diet and/or supplementation. Children with malabsorption may require higher doses than is recommended for other wise healthy children and should undergo periodic monitoring of vitamin D concentra tion to assure adequate levels are maintained.

Vitamin D toxicity is well documented in children and adults with overzealous supple mentation. The vitamin D concentration at which toxicity occurs can be highly variable but serum levels greater than 150 ng/mL are generally considered excessive and levels up to 100 ng/mL unlikely to cause toxicity. However, lower vitamin D concentrations may be associated with increased risk of nephrolithiasis. Symptoms of vitamin D tox icity are those of hypercalcemia and hyper calciuria including poor appetite, weight loss, abdominal pain, vomiting, constipation, polyuria, polydipsia, and nephrolithiasis. This can lead to dehydration, nephrocalcino sis and reduced renal function if severe hyper calcemia is present [98].

25-Hydroxylase deficiency is rare and there fore the optimal treatment strategy is not known. Thacher et al. reported that one of the two siblings responded to calcium supplemen tation alone, perhaps due to passive intestinal absorption independent of the effects of vita
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency Rickets

paragraphs.text: min D [99]. However, his older brother did not experience healing of rickets with calcium alone but responded to calcium supplementa tion in addition to two doses of intramuscular vitamin D 600,000 IU each given 3 months apart. Others have reported improvement in vitamin D concentrations and rickets severity with daily vitamin D doses of 5000 and 10,000 IU per day. The efficiency of alternate pathways for 25-hydroxylation of vitamin D likely influences an individual’s ability to gen erate 25-hydroxyvitamin D in the presence of CYP2R1 pathogenic variants.
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency Rickets

paragraphs.text: Molin et al. described seven patients from two families with homozygous inactivating CYP2R1 variants, several of whom experi enced rickets during childhood. Treatment of a 4-year-old with alfacalcidiol (1α-hydroxylated vitamin D) resulted in nor malization of serum calcium and phosphate but persistent elevation of PTH and alkaline phosphatase [17]. After 9 months of therapy, hypercalcemia and hypercalcuria developed and calcium supplementation was discontin ued. After the genetic cause of his rickets was established, therapy was transitioned to cal cifediol (25-hydroxyvitamin D) effectively bypassing the enzyme defect. Calcifediol ther apy led to normalization of all biochemical abnormalities including PTH and alkaline phosphatase.
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency Rickets

paragraphs.text: Treatment of 1α-hydroxylase deficiency is aimed at bypassing the enzymatic defect, which can be achieved with calcitriol or 1α-cholecalciferol, though the latter is not available in the US. Calcitriol has a short halflife and requires twice daily dosing, while 1α-cholecalciferol can be dosed once daily [100]. Suggested dosing of calcitriol is 0.25–2 mcg daily and initial dosing of 1α-cholecalciferol is 0.25–3 mcg daily. Higher doses may be required during initial treatment with a lower dose used for indefinite mainte nance therapy. The goal is to heal rickets, improve (or prevent) limb deformity and keep serum parameters in a safe range. It is recom mended to maintain serum calcium at the low end of normal, serum phosphate in the nor mal range, and PTH at the high end of nor mal. If PTH is pushed to the low normal
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency Rickets

paragraphs.text: range or below, urine calcium will likely be elevated with the risk of nephrocalcinosis and nephrolithiasis.
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency Rickets

paragraphs.text: Similar to those with nutritional rickets, during the initial 3–6 months of treatment, children should also receive 30–50 mg/kg ele mental calcium daily. After healing of rickets, the dose of calcitriol and calcium is tapered to maintain biochemical parameters in goal range.
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency Rickets

paragraphs.text: Response to treatment of rickets caused by VDR variants is dependent on the underlying mutation leading to disease. Medical therapy is challenging and requires careful monitoring of laboratory values to determine responsive ness to therapy. Some infants respond to high dose calcium therapy alone, while others require intravenous calcium to bypass the poor intestinal calcium absorption. Some may respond to high dose vitamin D or calcitriol therapy. Those who fail oral therapy require ongoing intravenous calcium [100]. The goal of treatment is similar to other forms of rick ets, to normalize serum calcium levels, nor malize PTH and alkaline phosphatase, and reverse clinical features of rickets. Cinacalcet has been reported to normalize PTH, phos phate, and alkaline phosphatase levels in patients who failed to have PTH suppression with IV calcium and high dose vitamin D therapy [101]. Given the complex and variable nature of treatment for rickets due to VDR variants, management by a metabolic bone disease specialist is recommended.
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency Rickets

paragraphs.text: All patients with heritable forms of cal cium deficiency rickets require lifelong moni toring. Laboratory assessment may be required every 1–2 weeks during the initial phase of therapy when frequent dose adjust ments may be required. Once rickets heals, lower calcium and vitamin D (or D analog) doses are necessary for maintenance. Children require more frequent monitoring owing to ongoing bone accrual, particularly during rapid pubertal growth. Once linear growth is complete, treatment doses are expected to remain more stable. Monitoring should not only include parameters of efficacy (healing of rickets and normalization of serum cal cium, phosphate, PTH, and alkaline phospha
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency Rickets

paragraphs.text: tase), but also for complications, principally hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria. Periodic urine calcium assessment should be under taken to assess risk of nephrocalcinosis and nephrolithiasis. Renal ultrasound is helpful for monitoring these complications.
paragraphs.heading: Deficiency Rickets

paragraphs.text: Two options are available for treatment of FGF23 medicated hypophosphatemic rickets, conventional therapy with calcitriol and phos phate supplementation, or targeted therapy with anti-FGF23 antibody therapy (buro sumab). Targeted therapy with burosumab was approved by the FDA initially for treat ment of XLH (6 months and older) and sub sequently for select patient with TIO in whom the offending tumor cannot be identified or completely resected. Treatment guidelines are best established for patients with XLH [35, 40, 102]. However, the principles of management with conventional therapy for XLH can be applied to the other FGF23 mediated hypo phosphatemic disorders.
paragraphs.heading: Hypophosphatemic Rickets

paragraphs.text: Early identification and treatment of XLH is crucial. A retrospective study of children with XLH identified better long-term out comes when treatment with conventional therapy was initiated prior to 1 year of age compared to those who initiated treatment after 1 year [36, 103, 104]. This finding likely also applies to early initiation of burosumab which can be used for as young as 6 months of age.
paragraphs.heading: Hypophosphatemic Rickets

paragraphs.text: Conventional therapy consists of supple mentation with activate vitamin-D (calcitriol) and phosphate to supply sufficient mineral to bone to improve or heal rickets. Although the primary deficiency is phosphate, 1,25(OH)2D3 is deficient due to the inhibitory effect of FGF23 on 1α-hydroxylase activity. Calcitriol enhances not only calcium but also phosphate absorption in the intestine and helps prevent secondary hyperparathyroidism that occurs if phosphate supplementation is given alone.
paragraphs.heading: Hypophosphatemic Rickets

paragraphs.text: Treatment requires frequent monitoring to assure the appropriate balance between phos phate and calcitriol are achieved to improve efficacy and, importantly, avoid complica tions.

The principal goals of therapy are to improve linear growth by healing rickets radiographically and biochemically (lowering of alkaline phosphatase) and improvement (or prevent progression) of lower extremity deformity. Importantly, goals of therapy should also include avoidance of treatment complications. As such, normalization of serum phosphate should not be a primary goal with conventional therapy [3, 35]. Excessive phosphate supplementation in an effort to normalize serum phosphate will likely lead to complications including nephro calcinosis and secondary (and sometimes ter tiary) hyperparathyroidism [105].

The recommended initial phosphate dose for children is 20–40 mg/kg/day in 3–5 divided doses [35, 40]. Owing to the rapid excretion of phosphate in the urine, frequent dosing throughout the day is required [106]. Phosphate salts are available in several prepa rations, most containing 250 mg of phosphate per tablet. For infants and children unable to swallow tablets, we prefer to use Neutra-phos powder (250 mg phosphate per packet) that can be dissolved in liquid for easy titration and administration of the dose. Initial dosing may be limited by gastrointestinal side effects but can usually be managed by slow titration over a couple of weeks. Calcitriol is given in two divided doses, typically starting with 20–30 ng/kg/day. Calcitriol is available in cap sules (0.25 mcg or 0.5 mcg each) or a liquid with a concentration of 1 mcg/mL. Given the wide range in clinical severity (even within a single family), phosphate and calcitriol doses may need to be higher or lower than those listed above.

Monitoring of conventional therapy should include clinical assessment of linear growth, monitoring of limb deformities and pain. Lab measurements should include serum phosphate, calcium, PTH, creatinine, and alkaline phosphatase. Urine calcium should be assessed periodically aiming to avoid hypercalciuria (urine calcium to creati

nine ratio varies by age; 24 urine calcium less than 4 mg/kg/day is considered normal). Knee radiographs should be utilized to moni tor healing of rickets [35]. We recommend radiographs 3–6 months after initiation of therapy followed by less frequent imaging (annually) after adequate treatment has been established.

In growing children, monitoring labs should be performed every 3–4 months. We prefer more frequent monitoring (monthly) at initiation and in the early dose titration phase. It is expected that dose adjustments will be required as the child grows. However, after cessation of linear growth, phosphate and cal citriol requirements are lower and the fre quency of phosphate dosing can usually be reduced to 2–3 divided doses per day. Once daily calcitriol is often sufficient in postpubertal children and adults.

Dose adjustment is dictated by response to therapy (improvements in rickets) and by the pattern of monitoring labs. If radiographic and biochemical (elevated alkaline phosphate) abnormalities persist, the dose of calcitriol and/or phosphate can be increased. However, it is important to remember that not all chil dren with heritable forms of rickets will expe rience full radiographic healing and normalization of alkaline phosphatase. The pattern of laboratory tests dictates which of the two medications may need to be adjusted. If PTH is elevated, this suggests the dose of calcitriol is too low and/or the phosphate dose may be excessive. Monitoring laboratory stud ies should be performed fasting before the first daily doses of phosphate and calcitriol. PTH values will increase transiently after a phosphate dose is taken. If hypercalcemia or hypercalciuria is present, the dose of calcitriol should be reduced and/or dose of phosphate increased.

Phosphate and active vitamin-D supple mentation can lead to hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis, with nephrocalcinosis reported in 30–70% of patients with XLH on conventional treatment [29, 103, 107]. Increasing grades of nephrocalcinosis can be seen with higher doses [103, 107]. Although mild nephrocalcinosis is common, renal func tion is usually well preserved. Renal ultra
sound is recommended at 1–3 years intervals to detect the presence and monitor progres sion of nephrocalcinosis.

After initiation and with proper manage ment on conventional therapy, bone pain (if present) can improve within weeks. Serum alkaline phosphatase will improve over the course of months but may not fully normalize in all who have heritable forms of hypophos phatemic rickets. Although linear growth improves with treatment, height potential remains compromised. Bowing deformities can improve with medical therapy but often takes several years to see substantial changes highlighting the importance of early initiation of treatment [108].

Burosumab is approved in the US and other countries to treat XLH in adults and children aged 6 months and older. Burosumab is a recombinant human IgG monoclonal antibody that blocks the activity of FGF23, addressing not only the renal phosphate wast ing, but also the inhibition of active vitamin D production. An early phase, randomized, placebo-controlled study in adults with XLH demonstrated improvements in renal phos phate reabsorption, serum phosphate, and serum 1,25(OH)2D3 with no significant change in serum or urine calcium or PTH [109].

Multiple clinical trials including children ages 1–12 years have shown improvement in radiographic appearance of rickets, normal ization of fasting serum phosphate concentra tions, improved renal tubular phosphate reabsorption, and lower serum alkaline phos phatase levels [110–112]. One study of 52 chil dren 5–12 years of age demonstrated these effects to be durable up to 160 weeks of ther apy with sustained serum phosphate and maintained improvement in the radiographic appearance of rickets [113]. Imel et al. com pared the efficacy of burosumab to continued conventional therapy in 61 children with XLH [111]. Burosumab therapy was superior to conventional treatment in this group with lower alkaline phosphatase levels and lower radiographic rickets severity scores. Despite these findings, many children do quite well with conventional therapy prompting some providers and families to continue calcitriol

and phosphate rather than transition to buro sumab treatment. Although the burden of therapy with burosumab is lower compared to conventional treatment (twice monthly injec tions vs 3–5 daily medication doses), the cost of burosumab is high.

For children receiving conventional ther apy who elect to transition to burosumab, calcitriol and phosphate should be discon tinued for 1 week and serum phosphate level should be below the normal reference range for age prior to the initial dose of burosumab [29]. The starting dose for children under 10 kg body weight is 1 mg/kg (rounded to the nearest 1 mg) administered subcutaneously every 2 weeks. For children over 10 kg, the initial dose is 0.8 mg/kg (rounded to the nearest 10 mg) administered subcutaneously every 2 weeks. The clinical goals of treat ment with burosumab are the same as with conventional therapy. However, in contrast to conventional therapy, serum phosphate concentration is key in dose titration. After initiation of treatment, fasting serum phos phate should be measured every 4 weeks for 3 months, and every 3 months thereafter once on stable dosing. Dose adjustments are based not only on serum phosphate levels, but also improvement (or lack of improve ment) in clinical parameters of rickets. Dose adjustments should be made no more fre quently than every 4 weeks. Goal serum phosphate level is within the reference range for age but below 5 mg/dL. If serum phos phate levels are below reference range for age, the dose should be increased stepwise up to a maximum dose of 2 mg/kg (maximum 90 mg) every 2 weeks in children. If serum phosphate levels become elevated, the next dose should be held, and serum phosphate should be reassessed in 4 weeks. When serum phosphate is no longer elevated, burosumab at a reduced dose can be reintroduced [114].

Adverse events were common among par ticipants in the clinical trials for burosumab but generally mild and well tolerated. The most common side effect is injection site changes, including mild injection site reac tions, erythema, bruising, pruritus, swelling, or pain. These were typically short-lived and did not lead to treatment cessation [110–113].

No significant increase in serum calcium, urine calcium, or parathyroid hormone was observed [113]. Interestingly, vitamin D defi ciency was more common in children treated with burosumab compared to conventional therapy [111]. This may be due to increased conversion of 25-hydroxyvitamin D to its active metabolite (1,25(OH)2D3) as the inhibi tory effect of FGF23 on 1a-hydroxylase activ ity is blunted with anti-FGF23 antibody therapy. It is thus important to assure ade quate vitamin D intake and periodic monitor ing of levels for patients treated with burosumab to avoid deficiency.

An ongoing post-marketing, monitoring study should provide insight into longer-term outcomes with burosumab therapy including effects on nephrocalcinosis over conventional therapy, effect on final adult height, need for orthopedic procedures, frequency of dental abscess, and the impact on disease morbidity in adulthood (early osteoarthritis and enthe sopathy).

Some have reported short-term improve ment of growth with growth hormone in chil dren with XLH. However, there is insufficient evidence to warrant routine use in these chil dren [115]. Growth hormone for patients with XLH may be considered on an individual basis for those with extreme short stature [29, 35].

Orthopedic care for children with XLH (and other forms of rickets) is crucial. Although a main goal of medical manage ment (conventional therapy or burosumab) is to prevent and treat limb deformities, some maintain or develop sufficient deformity to result in gait disturbances, activity limitation, pain, and compromised function that requires surgical correction. Surgical options depend on the type and degree of deformity and if growth plates are fused or remain open. If growth plates remain open, epiphysiodesis or guided growth plates can be used to correct valgus or varus deformities. For those with more severe deformity or when growth plates are closed, corrective osteotomy is required.
Children with XLH should receive regular dental care to minimize the risk of abscess and tooth loss. Conventional therapy improves but does not normalize the dentin mineralization

defect and the larger size of the pulp chamber. However, dental outcomes are improved in those treated with conventional therapy [116]. It is not yet clear if burosumab improves den tal health in children or adults with XLH.

As children reach skeletal maturity, transi tion from a pediatric dosing to an adult regi men should be undertaken. The optimal time and method for doing so is not well studied. Our approach is to start this transition after puberty and closure of growth plates (prefer ably closer to the time of peak bone mass). For those on conventional therapy, we slowly reduce the dose and frequency of dosing to the lowest dose required to mitigate symp toms of hypophosphatemia and osteomala cia. This often is achieved with once daily calcitriol and 2–3 daily doses of phosphate. There are adults who do not clearly benefit symptomatically from ongoing therapy, but it is difficult to predict who fits in this category. Even within the same family, disease manifes tations and need for treatment can vary widely during adulthood requiring an individualized treatment plan. For those treated with buro sumab, dosing is every 2 weeks during child hood and every 4 weeks for adults. Our approach is similar to conventional therapy by transitioning to the adult dosing frequency after cessation of linear growth (preferably closer to the time of peak bone mass). Complicating this transition is the readiness of an adolescent to assume more responsibil ity for their own care as they become young adults and often move away from home for college or work. Guiding principles have been published to assist in this transition for young adults with XLH [117].

Specific guidelines for the treatment of other FGF23 mediated hypophosphatemic disor ders are not as robust as those for XLH. However, the same principles of con ventional therapy with phosphate and cal citriol therapy as noted above can be used [118]. Titration of doses, laboratory monitor ing, and screening for complications, includ ing secondary hyperparathyroidism and
paragraphs.heading: Disorders

paragraphs.text: nephrocalcinosis, are the same as manage ment for XLH.
paragraphs.heading: Disorders

paragraphs.text: ADHR is unique in that the disease course can wax and wane over time, thus not always requiring lifelong treatment [43]. This phe nomenon may be partly related to the interac tion of iron deficiency leading to increased FGF23 production which cannot be efficiently inactivated in patients with ADHR [44]. Kapelari et al. reported a 5-year-old girl with ADHR with clinical features of rickets coex isting with low iron stores but resolution of rickets without need for calcitriol and phos phate therapy after iron deficiency was cor rected [119]. Thus, monitoring and treating iron deficiency may preclude the need for cal citriol and phosphate in some with ADHR.
paragraphs.heading: Disorders

paragraphs.text: Successful treatment of hypophospha temic rickets caused by the various forms of ARHR, fibrous dysplasia of bone, and CSHS with oral phosphate and calcitriol have been reported [50, 56, 59, 62, 120].
paragraphs.heading: Disorders

paragraphs.text: There has been speculation that removal of epidermal nevi causing CSHS might improve hypophosphatemia, but no therapeu tic benefit has been found in patients with excision or ablation of nevi [62, 121]. Successful treatment with off label use of medications targeting the underlying disease mechanism have been reported. One patient had improvement in clinical, biochemical, and radiographic signs of rickets with a mito gen-activated protein kinase (MEK) inhibitor, which acts directly on the RAS/MAPK path way [122].
paragraphs.heading: Disorders

paragraphs.text: Use of burosumab has been explored (off label) for FGF23 mediated conditions other than XLH and TIO. Normalization of serum phosphate and improved clinical outcomes related to rickets in multiple patients with CSHS treated with burosumab has been described [123, 124]. Likewise, use in a 7-yearold boy with severe fibrous dysplasia led to the normalization of serum phosphate, improve ment in alkaline phosphatase, and resolution of radiographic rachitic changes after 17 months of therapy [125]. Successful use of burosumab for autosomal recessive hypo phosphatemic rickets due to DMP1 muta tions has also been reported [126].
paragraphs.heading: Disorders

paragraphs.text: TIO is unique among the FGF23 medi ated disorders in that it can be cured assuming the offending tumor can be localized and removed. It is, therefore, important to con sider this diagnosis in a child with acquired disease in whom an alternate cause of FGF23 mediated rickets is not identified. After com plete resection, FGF23, phosphate, and 1,25(OH)2D3 concentrations normalize over days to weeks. Normalization of alkaline phosphatase and radiographic change of rick ets/osteomalacia can take months. For those with disease that cannot be localized or resected medical therapy (calcitriol and phos phate or burosumab) should be initiated [65, 66]. Burosumab has been approved for treat ment of TIO when surgical cure is not possi ble [127].
paragraphs.heading: Disorders

paragraphs.text: Similar to FGF23 mediated hypophospha temic disorders, hereditary hypophospha temic rickets with hypercalciuria (HHRH) caused by SLC34A3 mutations leads to renal phosphate wasting. However, in contrast to FGF23 mediated disease, 1α-hydroxylase activity is high since FGF23 concentrations are appropriately low. As a result, 1,25(OH)2D3 concentrations can be markedly elevated lead ing to increased intestinal calcium absorption and hypercalciuria. This distinction is impor tant in that treatment consists of phosphate supplementation alone without calcitriol since endogenous 1,25(OH)2D3 production is already high. Additional calcitriol would exacerbate the hypercalciuria and nephrocal cinosis. Phosphate administration also serves to limit intestinal calcium absorption and can reduce endogenous 1,25(OH)2D3 production, both of which lessen the degree of hypercalci uria. With phosphate supplementation, bone pain and muscle strength improve, radio graphic evidence of rickets (if present) can resolve, urine calcium excretion is reduced, and serum alkaline phosphatase levels improve [71, 72].
paragraphs.heading: Hypophosphatemia

paragraphs.text: Renal Fanconi syndrome is a complex col lection of disorders. Hypophosphatemia can be treated with phosphate supplementation.
paragraphs.heading: Hypophosphatemia

paragraphs.text: Bicarbonate replacement therapy may also improve the associated bone disease. When possible, treatment of the underlying disorder causing proximal tubular dysfunction may preclude the need for phosphate replacement therapy. Likewise, for children with nutri tional phosphate deficiency, correction of the underlying malabsorptive disease or the addi tion of phosphate to the diet (or via a supple ment) will resolve the hypophosphatemia and associated rickets.

Rickets constitutes a broad spectrum of dis eases leading to a common clinical disorder of impaired growth plate and skeletal mineral ization. Although entirely preventable and despite campaigns to raise awareness, nutri tional rickets due to vitamin D and/or calcium deficiency remains a frequent cause of mor bidity worldwide. Treatment of nutritional rickets is fairly straightforward but continued public health efforts aimed at prevention remain of utmost importance. Our under standing of the molecular cause of many heri table forms of rickets has expanded in recent years with targeted therapy now available for some. History, exam, and relatively few labo ratory tests can identify the underlying cause of rickets for most which allows use of disease specific treatment strategies in an effort to optimize long-term outcomes.

Misra (eds.), Pediatric Endocrinology, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-66296-6_21 ## PDF page 534 | printed page 528 ### 21.9 Treatment and Monitoring – 545 21.9.1 Nutritional Rickets (Vitamin D and Calcium Deficiency) – 545 21.9.2 Heritable Forms of Calcium Deficiency Rickets – 546 21.9.3 FGF23 Mediated Hypophosphatemic Rickets – 548 ### 21.10 Summary – 552 ### References – 552 ## PDF page 535 | printed page 529 ### 21.1 Introduction Rickets and osteomalacia are terms describ ing the clinical and radiographic findings of a variety of distinct diseases but with the com mon underlying characteristic of impaired mineralization. Rickets results from disorga nized chondrocyte differentiation and abnor mal mineralization of the growth plate and therefore, is only present in patients prior to the closure of growth plates and cessation of growth. Osteomalacia occurs due to impaired mineralization of mature cortical and trabec ular bone undergoing remodeling, and there fore, can occur both prior to and after growth plate closure. Children, therefore, who experi ence insufficient calcium and or phosphate availability prior to growth plate closure will have evidence of rickets at the growth plate and osteomalacia in areas of mature bone. Those affected after growth is complete will present with features of osteomalacia only [1]. Rickets and osteomalacia are clinically distinct from osteopenia and osteoporosis, which are due to an imbalance between osteo blastic bone formation and osteoclastic bone resorption without abnormal bone mineral ization. This imbalance leads to bone archi tecture change, decreased bone density, and increased risk for low trauma fractures. Although the evaluation of management of low bone density is substantially different compared to children with rickets, adequate dietary intake of calcium, phosphate, and vitamin D are important to support optimal bone health. 21.1 2 21.1 ![Source image](../../figures/ch021_p0535_01.jpg) Unmatched source image; PDF page 535. Despite efforts to increase awareness and prevention, reports of nutritional rickets con tinue worldwide. Geographic differences exist in the relative contribution of vitamin D and/ or calcium deficiency. Even in developed countries, the incidence of nutritional rickets has increased in recent years. Distinguishing clinical features Other nutritional deficiencies often present Serum calcium is tightly regulated by parathy roid hormone (PTH) and vitamin D. In the setting of low serum calcium, PTH acts to increase active vitamin D (1,25(OH)2D3) in the kidney which then increases calcium absorption in the small intestine. Bone is the largest calcium reservoir in the body and is released by the indirect action of PTH on osteoclastic bone resorption [3]. The production of biologically active 1,25(OH)2D3 begins in the skin where UV light alters the structure of 7-dehydrocholesterol into vitamin D3. Vitamin D can also be obtained through intake of fatty fish in the diet, or as vitamin D2 from supplements, plants, and fungi. Activation of vitamin D occurs in a stepwise fashion by cytochrome P450 enzymes located in various tissues through the body [4]. In the liver, CYP2R1 is the major 25-hydroxylase enzyme catalyzing conversion of vitamin D to 25-hydroxyvitamin D, though multiple CYP enzymes have some degree of 25-hydroxylase activity [5]. The kidney is the major site of synthesis of active vitamin D (1,25(OH)2D3) via 1α-hydroxylase activity of CYP27B1. 1,25(OH)2D3 binds the vitamin D receptor (VDR), which serves as a transcription factor altering gene expression impacting both cal cium and phosphate homeostasis [6]. In the presence of active vitamin D, protein and mRNA expression of calcium transport pro teins present both in the renal tubule and in the enterocyte is increased [7]. Defects in any of the enzymatic processes leading to vitamin D activation, excessive degradation, or decreased receptor binding/activity can lead to reduced calcium and phosphate and cause rickets in children. ### 21.2.2 Phosphate Homeostasis Phosphate homeostasis is primarily regulated by 1,25(OH)2D3, parathyroid hormone (PTH), and fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23) via actions on the small intestine, skeleton, and kidneys. 1,25(OH)2D3 is primarily produced in renal tubular cells and is regulated by calcium, phosphate, PTH, and FGF23 concentrations. Higher 1,25(OH)2D3 concentrations increase small intestine absorption of phosphate via the vitamin D dependent sodium-phosphate 2b (NaPi-2b) cotransporter. High 1,25(OH)2D3 and/or calcium reduce PTH secretion thereby indirectly increasing phos phate reabsorption in the kidney. In contrast, 1,25(OH)2D3 increases FGF23 production in osteocytes which subsequently enhances renal phosphate excretion [3]. PTH decreases phosphate reabsorption by reducing NaPi-2a and NaPi-2c cotransporters in the renal proximal tubule thereby increas ing phosphate excretion in the urine. PTH is a potent stimulator of 1α-hydroxylase activity thereby increasing 1,25(OH)2D3 production, which indirectly activates osteoclastic bone reabsorption releasing both calcium and phosphate into the extracellular space [3]. FGF23 is produced in osteocytes under the influence of 1,25(OH)2D3 and phosphate concentrations. Like PTH, FGF23 decreases phosphate reabsorption in the kidney by decreasing NaPi-2a and NaPi-2c cotransports in the proximal tubule. In contrast to PTH, FGF23 inhibits the action of 1α-hydroxylase thereby decreasing 1,25(OH)2D3 production [3]. FGF23 production is stimulated by phos ### 21 phate, PTH, and 1,25(OH)2D3, and is down regulated by low extracellular phosphate concentrations [8]. ### 21.3 Etiology ### 21.3.1 Pathophysiology of Rickets ### and Osteomalacia 9 21.2a In osteomalacia, osteoblasts continue to deposit osteoid bone matrix, but the osteoid remains under-mineralized due to deficiencies in calcium and/or phosphate availability. Tetracycline labeled bone biopsy reveals an overall decrease in mineralized bone, increased osteoid thickness, and increased mineraliza tion lag time [9]. Defective mineralization resulting in rick ets and osteomalacia occurs when there is inadequate availability of either calcium and/ or phosphate and may be due to a nutritional deficiency or genetic variant leading to abnor mal mineral homeostasis. Calcium deficiency rickets can be due to nutritional deficiency or abnormalities in the activation or tissue responsiveness to vitamin D. Phosphate defi ## PDF page 539 | printed page 533 ciency rickets is rarely due to nutritional defi ciency and is most often caused by renal phosphate wasting due to disorders causing excess FGF23 production. ### 21.4 Calcium Deficiency Rickets ### 21.4.1 Nutritional Causes Nutritional rickets remains the most common cause of rickets worldwide. Occurring on a spectrum of primarily vitamin D deficiency to primarily calcium deficiency, nutritional rick ets is influenced by a variety of factors includ ing the relative contribution of low vitamin D and calcium availability. Vitamin D deficiency rickets occurs more often in areas where sun exposure is limited by latitude, pollution, body coverings, darker skin pigment, in chil dren born to mothers with vitamin D defi ciency, and those who are exclusively breastfed [10]. Calcium deficiency rickets has been increasingly described in African countries including South Africa and Nigeria, where children have adequate sun exposure yet lack enough dietary calcium, leading to rickets [11]. Although often underrecognized, nutri tional rickets remains problematic in devel oped countries. A population-based study in Olmsted County, Minnesota revealed an increase in nutritional rickets in children under 3 years of age from 2.2 per 100,000 in the decade from 1980 to 1989 to 24.1 per 100,000 in the subsequent decade. Not sur prisingly, children with nutritional rickets were more likely to be black, breastfed, and not receiving vitamin D supplementation [12]. Although breastmilk provides excellent over all nutrition for normal growth and develop ment, vitamin D content is relatively low in the absence of high-dose vitamin D supple mentation by the mother. Because of continued reports of vitamin D deficiency and of rising levels of nutritional rickets, in 2008 the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommended a minimum vitamin D intake of 400 IU/day for all chil dren starting after a few days of life [13]. Whether a child with vitamin D deficiency develops rickets is at least partly dependent on calcium intake. The lower the dietary calcium intake for a given degree of hypovitaminosis D, the risk of developing rickets will increase. Children with malabsorptive disorders, including inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease, cystic fibrosis, or those with increased vitamin D loss or inactivation including nephrotic syndrome and use of anticonvul sant or certain HIV medications, are at increased risk of vitamin D deficiency and rickets due to their underlying medical disease or treatment [10, 15]. ### 21.4.2 Heritable Causes ### 21.4.2.1 25-Hydroxylase Deficiency 25-Hydroxylase catalyzes the formation of 25-hydroxyvitamin D from vitamin D and mainly occurs through the activity of CYP2R1 [5]. Rare individuals have been described with inactivating variants in CYP2R1 causing rick ets with features indistinguishable for nutri tional vitamin D deficiency including hypocalcemia, hypophosphatemia, elevated PTH, elevated alkaline phosphatase, and low 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentrations [17–19]. It is postulated that there is some, albeit insuf ficient, conversion of vitamin D to 25-hydroxyvitamin D by CYP enzymes other than CYP2R1, allowing some substrate for production of 1,25(OH)2D3. The 1,25(OH)2D3 levels observed in two Saudi patients were in the low normal range despite elevated PTH and hypocalcemia, both of which would be expected to raise active vitamin D levels [19]. In a Cyp2r1−/− knockout mice model, greater than 50% reduction in circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D level was observed com pared to wild-type mice [20]. While CYP2R1 may be the major 25-hydroxylase enzyme, other cytochrome P450 enzymes exhibit 25-hydroxylase activity and likely ### 21 contribute to the circulating amount of 25-hydroxyvitamin D allowing some patients to be treated with high-dose vitamin D sup plementation. Although Cyp2r1−/− knockout mice and patients with biallelic mutations exhibit significantly reduced 25-hydroxyvita min D, the levels are not always undetectable. ### 21.4.2.2 1α-Hydroxylase Deficiency ### (CYP27B1 Inactivating Variant) 1α-Hydroxylase deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by the inability to covert 25-hydroxyvitamin D to the active metabolite, 1,25(OH)2D3. Biallelic variants in the CYP27B1 gene renders the kidney unable to produce active vitamin D despite high PTH and low serum calcium thus leading to clinical disease [21–23]. Symptoms often present during the first year of life with hypocalcemic seizures [23]. In older children, typical skeletal and radio graphic findings of rickets, difficulty walking, and poor linear growth are present. Laboratory evaluation reveals hypocalcemia, hypophosphatemia, elevated alkaline phos phatase, and elevated PTH. 25-Hydroxyvitamin D concentrations can be normal or increased, and 1,25(OH)2D3 concentration remains low or undetectable [22, 24, 25]. Unlike nutritional rickets, vitamin D supplementation does not lead to clinical or biochemical improvement. Active vitamin D therapy with calcitriol is required to bypass the absence of endogenous 1α-hydroxylation of 25-hydroxyvitamin D. ### 21.4.2.3 Vitamin D Receptor ### Inactivating Variants Inactivating variants in the vitamin D recep tor (VDR) gene cause end organ resistance to 1,25(OH)2D3. Multiple variants leading to VDR defects have been described and result in reduced or abolished affinity for 1,25(OH)2D3 binding, impaired heterodimer ization of the VDR, or alteration of coactiva tor function [26]. VDR variants are rare and inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Despite elevated 1,25(OH)2D3 intestinal calcium absorption is severely reduced leading to hypocalcemia, sec ## PDF page 541 | printed page 535 ondary hyperparathyroidism, hypophospha temia, and elevated alkaline phosphatase concentrations. Patients typically present with early onset rickets in the first weeks to months of life, poor growth, poor dentition, and, in some, varying degrees of alopecia due to the role of VDR in the hair follicle [27]. Hair loss can be in patches, cause thin, sparse hair, or complete alopecia. When present, alopecia distinguishes disease caused by VDR variants from other forms of rickets. ### 21.4.2.4 Increased Vitamin D ### Inactivation Two unrelated patients have been reported with rickets due to an autosomal dominant, gain-of-function mutation in CYP3A4, lead ing to accelerated inactivation of vitamin D metabolites [28]. These two patients presented with classic signs of rickets at 2 and 4.5 years of age with laboratory values that revealed hypocalcemia, hypophosphatemia, elevated PTH, and low or undetectable 25-hydroxyvitamin D and 1,25(OH)2D3. Both experienced normalization of laboratory abnormalities and improvement in rickets with high dose vitamin D or calcitriol therapy. ### 21.5 Phosphate Deficiency Rickets ### 21.5.1 FGF23 Mediated ### Hypophosphatemic Rickets ### 21.5.1.1 X-Linked ### Hypophosphatemic Rickets (XLH) X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets (XLH) is the most common form of heritable rickets with a prevalence estimated between 1 in 60,000 and 1 in 20,000 [29–31]. XLH is an x-linked dominant disorder that results from loss of function variants in the PHEX gene on chromosome Xp22.1 [32], which encodes a metalloprotease with an as yet unidentified substrate. As in other X-linked dominant dis orders, family history can be helpful in distin guishing it from other heritable forms of hypophosphatemic rickets and identifying children with the condition even prior to genetic testing or clinical features occurring. In X-linked dominant disorders, there is no father to son transmission but all daughters of an affected male will have the disease. Affected women will pass on XLH equally (50% risk) to both sons and daughters. PHEX is expressed in multiple organs, including osteoblasts, odontoblasts, and para thyroid tissue but is not expressed in the kid ney [33]. While the pathogenesis for XLH is not fully understood, loss of function variants in PHEX ultimately result in increased FGF23 production which have an endocrine effect in the proximal tubule leading to reduced sodium-phosphate cotransports causing phos phate wasting and hypophosphatemia [34]. Elevated FGF23 also inhibits 1α-hydroxylase activity in the kidney and increases expression of CYP24A1 (which enhances catabolism of active vitamin D), both of which lead to lower than expected 1,25(OH)2D3 concentration in the face of hypophosphatemia [8]. Hypophosphatemia, high renal fractional excretion of phosphate, and low (or inappro priately normal) 1,25(OH)2D3 are the charac teristic biochemical findings of all FGF23 mediated hypophosphatemic disorders includ ing XLH [3, 34, 35]. 21.1 36 Children with XLH are also at high risk for recurrent dental abscesses due to poor dentin mineralization, allowing bacterial migration resulting in abscesses even in the absence of dental caries or trauma [37]. Although not unique to XLH, craniosynosto sis has been reported in children with a variety ## PDF page 542 | printed page 536 of causes of hypophosphatemic rickets [38]. The underlying mechanism is not known but may be related to activation of fibroblast growth factor receptors (FGFR2 and FGFR3) present in the cranial sutures by the high FGF23 concentration present in patients with XLH. Mutations in these receptors are known to be associated with craniosynostosis syndromes [39]. Although historically, XLH was felt to be a disease of childhood, most adults experi ence some degree of ongoing disease manifes tations including fractures and pseudofractures, hearing loss, dental abscess, early osteoarthritis, and pain and stiffness from enthesopathy that can be debilitating [40]. ### 21.5.1.2 Autosomal Dominant ### Hypophosphatemic Rickets (ADHR) 41 2 3 21.2 Unlike other hereditary forms of rickets, age at presentation is widely variable. In a review of 23 affected individuals within a sin gle family, two general presentation patterns were present: childhood onset and delayed onset. Onset in childhood is characterized by clinical findings of rickets including limb deformities, slow growth, and short stature. Resolution of renal phosphate wasting and normalization of serum phosphate over time ### 21 without intervention were reported in two affected individuals. In those with delayed dis ease manifestation, presentation was after puberty with onset ranging from 14.5 to 45 years old. These adults presented with typ ical features of osteomalacia including bone pain, fatigue, and weakness, but with no his tory of rickets in childhood [42]. The variability in age at onset of symp toms and waxing and waning course for some individuals correlated with fluctuating FGF23 concentrations [43]. One explanation for the variability may be the relationship of iron sta tus and FGF23 production. Iron deficiency increases FGF23 production which can be cleaved to inactive fragments in the healthy state thus maintaining normal intact (biologi cally active) FGF23 and normal phosphate homeostasis. However, individuals with ADHR who produce FGF23 that is resistant to proteolytic cleavage, intact FGF23 can accumulate when production is stimulated, thus bringing about the clinical phenotype when iron deficiency is present [44]. ### 21.5.1.3 Autosomal Recessive ### Hypophosphatemic Rickets (ARHR) Autosomal recessive hypophosphatemic rick ets (ARHR) is caused by biallelic mutations in multiple genes including Dentin Matrix acidic Phosphoprotein 1 (DMP1), Ectonucleotide Pyrophosphatase/Phosphodiesterase 1 (ENPP1), and Family with Sequence Similarity 20, Member C (FAM20C). All may result in elevated (or inappropriately normal) FGF23 concentrations but can be associated with dif ferent extraskeletal manifestation. DMP1 is a member of the Small Integrin Binding Ligand N-linked Glycoprotein (SIBLING) family of non-collagenous extra cellular matrix proteins important in osteo genesis [45, 46]. Studies in DMP1 null mice demonstrate abnormal osteocyte function, and DMP1 appears to be important for osteoblast-osteocyte differentiation and bone mineralization [47]. Children with biallelic loss of function variants in DMP1 (ARHR Type 1) phenotypically present with hypophosphatemic rickets [48, 49]. FD can affect any part of the skel eton with the abnormal bone producing excess FGF23 and hypophosphatemia in some [56–60]. For those with minimal skele tal involvement of FD, hypophosphatemia is uncommon, likely due to increased cleav age of intact FGF23 to inactive fragments [61]. Overt hypophosphatemia with rickets ### 21 or osteomalacia occurs primarily in those with the highest skeletal burden of FD [56–58]. ### 21.5.1.5 Cutaneous Skeletal ### Hypophosphatemia Syndrome Similar to McCune-Albright syndrome, Cutaneous skeletal hypophosphatemia syn drome (CSHS) is due to gain of function mutations leading to a mosaic disorder affect ing both skin and bone. Mutations in RAS lead to disease characterized by FGF23 medi ated hypophosphatemic rickets/osteomalacia in the setting of epidermal or melanocytic nevi, eye, and brain malformations, and skel etal dysplasia with focal dysplastic cortical bone lesions. Patients present with symptoms consistent with rickets including bone pain, limb deformities, and impaired mobility with laboratory findings consistent with FGF23 mediated renal phosphate wasting. Radiographs demonstrate dysplastic bony lesions that are sclerotic or lytic as well as clas sic growth plate abnormalities of rickets [62]. ### 21.5.1.6 Tumor Induced ### Osteomalacia (TIO) Tumor induced osteomalacia (TIO) is a rare paraneoplastic disease caused by phosphatu ric mesenchymal tumors (PMT) that secrete phosphatonins (substances causing renal phosphate wasting), principally FGF23 [63, 64]. Tumors are frequently small and diffi cult to find, and while typically benign, can sometimes become malignant and metasta size. The vast majority of reported cases are of adults, but a few children have been described. Children with TIO typically pres ent with fractures and radiographic and clin ical features of rickets. Laboratory evaluation reveals a serum low phosphate, low or inap propriately normal 1,25(OH)2D3, low renal phosphate reabsorption, normal calcium, and normal PTH, though secondary hyper parathyroidism can occur due to low 1,25(OH)2D3 concentrations [65]. Because TIO is so rare in children, evalua tion should exclude other causes of hypo phosphatemic rickets including heritable ## PDF page 545 | printed page 539 causes such as ADHR that can appear as to be an acquired disease when presenting in adolescence or early adulthood. If TIO is sus pected, tumor localization is of upmost importance since resection will lead to nor malization of FGF23 (or other phosphato nins if present) and resolution of the clinical consequences of chronic hypophosphatemia. Localization begins with a careful physical exam with special attention to the skin. Because offending lesions can be found throughout the body, functional whole-body imaging is obtained first (PET/CT or Octreotide based imaging) [64, 66]. 68Gallium- DOTATATE PET/CT appears to be particu larly sensitive in localizing PMTs [67, 68]. When functional imaging suggests a possible tumor location, cross-sectional imaging with computed tomography (CT) or magnetic res onance imaging (MRI) is helpful to further characterize the lesion and for surgical plan ning [65, 66]. ### 21.5.2 FGF23 Independent ### Hypophosphatemic Rickets ### 21.5.2.1 Hereditary ### Hypophosphatemic Rickets with Hypercalciuria Hereditary hypophosphatemic rickets with hypercalciuria is an autosomal recessive dis ease caused by biallelic loss of function vari ants in the SLC34A3 gene on chromosome 9q34. Inactivating variants result in reduced ability of the sodium phosphate cotransporter NaPi-2c to reabsorb phosphate in the proxi mal tubule leading to hypophosphatemia [69, 70]. In contrast to hypophosphatemic condi tions caused by excess FGF23, 1,25(OH)2D3 is elevated rather than reduced. Because FGF23 is low in this condition, 1α-hydroxylase activ ity is appropriately increased in the face of hypophosphatemia. High 1,25(OH)2D3 leads to increased intestinal calcium absorption and subsequent hypercalciuria with nephrolithia sis and nephrocalcinosis [71]. FGF23 concen tration is reduced, parathyroid hormone levels are low or low-normal, 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels are normal, and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D levels are elevated [70, 72]. Clinical presentation is variable with most exhibiting skeletal disease (rickets/osteomala cia) while others have primarily a renal pheno type (hypercalciuria/nephrocalcinosis) and some with a combination of both [71]. Onset of skeletal symptoms can occur in infancy but much later in childhood for others. Findings include lower limb deformities, bone pain, change in gait, decreased physical activity, short stature, and muscle weakness [72]. Although hereditary hypophosphatemic rickets with hypercalciuria (HHRH) is consid ered an autosomal recessive condition, an attenuated phenotype has been described in some individuals with monoallelic variants [73]. ### 21.5.2.2 Renal Fanconi Syndrome Renal Fanconi syndrome describes a heterog enous group of diseases that ultimately result in generalized dysfunction of the proximal tubule of the kidney. The proximal tubule is responsible for the reabsorption of water, sodium, amino and organic acids, filtered pro teins, glucose, and phosphate. Generalized dysfunction results in inappropriate excretion of these substances in the urine and subse quent clinical sequelae including hypophos phatemic rickets. Fanconi syndrome can result from a variety of disorders including genetic conditions that result in progressive proximal renal tubular damage due to the buildup of renal toxic materials over time (including Wilson disease, galactosemia, cystinosis), exposure to certain drugs, or isolated renal Fanconi syndrome [74]. Lowe syndrome, also known as oculocere brorenal syndrome, is an X-linked recessive disorder characterized by congenital cata racts, intellectual disability, and proximal renal tubular dysfunction. Anywhere from 20% to 50% of patients with untreated Lowe syndrome are reported to have phosphate wasting leading to hypophosphatemic rickets, and usually present after 1 year of age. Lowe syndrome has been linked to variants in the OCRL gene [75]. Variants in the CLCN5 gene, which lead to an inactive voltage-gated chloride transporter ## PDF page 546 | printed page 540 expressed in the renal proximal tubules, com prise a heterogenous group of hereditary tubular disorders referred to as Dent’s disease or X-linked Recessive Nephrolithiasis. This spectrum of disorders is characterized by renal Fanconi syndrome, hypercalcuria with nephrolithiasis and nephrocalcinosis, progres sive renal failure, and hyperphosphaturia with hypophosphatemic rickets [76, 77]. Biallelic loss of function mutations in the SLC34A1 gene, which encodes the NaPi-2a sodium phosphate cotransporter in the proxi mal tubule, have been reported to cause an autosomal recessive proximal tubulopathy including renal phosphate wasting, and hypo phosphatemic rickets [78]. ### 21.5.2.3 Nutritional Phosphate ### Deficiency Nutritional phosphate deficiency is rare, as most diets contain abundant phosphate. However, generalized malnutrition or intesti nal malabsorption can result in chronic hypo phosphatemia and ultimately rickets. This often occurs in combination with vitamin D and other nutritional deficiencies [79]. Antacids containing aluminum, calcium, and magne sium bind dietary phosphorus and prevent its absorption [80]. With excessive use, antacids have been reported to cause hypophosphate mia and osteomalacia [81]. Nutritional rickets with hypophosphatemia was reported in a ret rospective review of 51 children with complex medical histories receiving a specific amino acid-based formula (Neocate) [82]. Laboratory features included markedly low serum phos phate, elevated alkaline phosphatase, normal 25-hydroxyvitamin D, and elevated 1,25(OH)2D3 levels suggestive of decreased intestinal phosphate absorption [82, 83]. Urine phosphate excretion was low as was FGF23 when measured. Serum phosphate levels nor malized, and bone disease improved when phosphate supplementation was added or for mula was changed [82, 84]. Additional cases of hypophosphatemia associated with this for mula have not been reported after the phos phate content was altered by the manufacturer. ### 21 Premature infants are a unique population at risk for hypophosphatemia and rickets. During the final trimester of pregnancy, rapid skeletal growth and mineralization occurs. When born premature, the high mineral requirement to support bone development is not available in breast milk. Breast milk forti fiers contain additional phosphate to mini mize the risk of rickets of prematurity. ### 21.6 Clinical Mimickers of Rickets Some patients with clinical findings suggestive of rickets, such as limb deformities and short stature can be mistaken to have a form of rick ets. However, laboratory and radiographic evaluation is not consistent with mineral defi ciency rickets. Although several skeletal dys plasias demonstrate overlapping features with rickets, Blount disease, Schmid type metaphy seal chondrodysplasia, and hypophosphatasia (HPP) are three important disorders to con sider when evaluating a child with suspected rickets. Blount disease presents with unilateral or bilateral tibial bowing and varus deformity and is due to asymmetric growth at the tibial growth plate. Radiographic findings show varus angulation of the metaphysis and wid ening and irregularity at the medial growth plate of the tibia with breaking of the medial part of the epiphysis [85]. Laboratory evalua tion is normal, and management is surgical correction of the deformity when severe. Schmid type metaphyseal chondrodysplasia caused by autosomal dominant mutations in COL10A1 which encodes type X collagen, presents with short stature, lower limb abnor malities including varus or valgus deformities. Radiographic findings can be difficult to distin guish from rickets and demonstrate growth plate irregularity and flaring [86]. As with Blount disease, laboratory assessment of vita min D and mineral homeostasis are normal. Hypophosphatasia (HPP) is caused by pathogenic variants of the tissue nonspecific alkaline phosphatase gene located on chromo some 1. Clinical severity is broad, ranging from death in the neonatal period to early loss of deciduous teeth with the root fully intact and no detectable skeletal abnormalities [87]. Autosomal recessive inheritance predicts more ## PDF page 547 | printed page 541 severe disease compared to those with a single allele mutation. Radiographs reveal extensive under mineralization of the entire skeleton in the most severely affected. Children with less severe disease have findings localized to the growth plates characterized by radiolucent bands that extend from the physis into the metaphysis of long bones. Although this radiographic appearance helps distinguish HPP from other forms of rickets, the most important difference between HPP and rickets is the presence of low serum alkaline phos phatase activity. All other forms of rickets are characterized by high alkaline phosphatase. ### 21.7 Clinical Presentation ### 21.7.1 History and Physical Exam 21.1 In cases of suspected rickets, a careful his tory should include nutritional intake of cal cium and vitamin D, with attention to any specialized formulas and restrictive diets, sun exposure, medical history of renal, liver, or endocrine dysfunction, and dental history. Family history can identify many with herita ble disease. A thorough exam should include assessment of growth, limb deformities, and coexisting disorders (as detailed above) that may provide insight into the underlying pathology. History and examination are often sufficient to establish the cause of rickets such as in a child with family history of XLH or a breastfed infant with dark skin pigment with no vitamin D supplementation. Although some genetic forms of rickets can be associated with unique clinical fea tures, the general findings of rickets are con sistent regardless of the underlying mechanism leading to disease. Presenting clinical features will depend on severity and duration of rick ets, as well as the patient’s age and develop mental abilities, which alter the mechanical forces applied to the bone. Infants with rickets may have abnormal head shape due to positional changes and pal pable craniotabes (softening of the skull bones) in the setting of undermineralized and thin bone. A prominent forehead (frontal bossing) and delayed closure of fontanelles may be present. The “rachitic rosary” (enlarge ment of the costochondral joints) may be vis ible or palpable on the anterior chest. Although not unique to children with rickets, a horizonal concavity (Harrison’s groove or sulcus) originating from the attachment of the diaphragm at the sixth costal cartilage that is exaggerated with contraction of the dia phragm during inspiration may be present [88]. Similar to the cartilage abnormalities causing enlargement of the costochondral junction, enlargement or widening of the wrists, knees, and ankles with moderate to severe rickets can be visible and palpable. Children able to support their weight with their arms may experience bowing of the humerus, ulna, and radius. Lower extremity abnormalities such as varus and valgus defor mities are more likely to become apparent after children gain the ability to stand and walk. Varus deformity in toddlers may be overlooked as physiological bowing. However, the bowing becomes more pronounced over time in the absence of treatment. Exaggerated anterior bowing of the tibia can occur and is sometimes referred to as the “sabere shin” deformity. Scoliosis is common but certainly not a unique finding in children with rickets [2, 89]. Delayed gross motor milestones may be present. Extraskeletal manifestations vary depend ing on underlying etiology. Muscle weakness, bone pain, fatigue, and gross motor difficul ties are common regardless of etiology. Children with calcium deficiency rickets may present with failure to thrive or hypocalcemic seizures and tetany or, when severe, develop heart failure due to hypocalcemic cardiomy opathy which can be fatal. Individuals with X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets fre quently have dental abscess. Those with vita ## PDF page 548 | printed page 542 min D receptor variants may have various degrees of alopecia. Characteristic skin find ings of epidermal or melanocytic nevi or “coast of Maine” café au lait lesions are pres ent in cutaneous skeletal hypophosphatemia syndrome and fibrous dysplasia associated with McCune-Albright syndrome, respec tively. ### 21.8 Diagnostic Evaluation ### 21.8.1 Imaging Evaluation 21.2 21.2b ### 21 1 In ambulatory children with longstanding rickets (often those with heritable disease such as XLH), a scanogram, which is a single radiograph that includes the entire leg from hip to ankle, can be helpful in determining the degree of bowing and overall joint alignment. As discussed earlier in this chapter, it is criti cal to remember that nutritional rickets is a preventable disease. The American Academy of Pediatrics, Endocrine Society, Institute of Medicine (IOM), and a Global Consensus of experts all endorse 400 IU vitamin D intake daily for infants up to 12 months of age for prevention of rickets. It is uncertain if 400 IU is sufficient for optimal bone health and growth but has been clearly shown to prevent rickets in this age group. IOM and the Global Consensus recommend 600 IU vitamin D for children over 12 months of age. Adequate cal cium intake is also required to prevent rickets. According to the IOM, children up to 6 months of age should receive 200 mg cal cium per day and 260 mg per day for those 6–12 months old. The Global Consensus guideline recommends 500 mg calcium intake per day as sufficient for children after 12 months of age. We and others endorse the IOM recommendation for progressively increasing calcium intake through childhood from 700 mg per day after 12 months of age up to 1300 mg per day starting at age 9 years up to 17 years old, a time when linear growth and thus skeletal mineral demands are high. Multiple dosing regimens for vitamin D have been reported as effective in healing nutrition rickets including daily oral dosing and intermittent high dose therapy (as high as 600,000 IU as a single dose) given orally or intramuscularly. As noted above, vitamin D intake of 400 IU per day for all infants is endorsed by several organizations and has been shown to prevent rickets [10, 13, 91–93]. Although this amount may be sufficient to prevent rickets, it is insufficient for treatment of established disease. Global Consensus guidelines recommend oral treatment with 2000 IU vitamin D per day for at least 3 months for all ages [10]. Oral therapy is rec ommended over intramuscular therapy, and “stoss” therapy, where very large doses are administered on one or over several days, due to the risk of vitamin D toxicity leading to hypercalciuria and/or hypercalcemia [94]. Calcium supplementation is recommended during treatment of vitamin D deficiency rickets, even in those without hypocalcemia. Hypocalcemia may occur with vitamin D replacement as mineral is deposited in the skeleton and as PTH levels fall. For those who are eucalcemic or mildly hypocalcemic, oral dosing is sufficient. However, severe symp tomatic hypocalcemia does occur that can cause seizures, tetany, laryngospasm, and car diomyopathy with fatalities being reported. Children with severe, symptomatic hypocalce mia due to nutritional rickets require hospital ization for intravenous calcium administration and monitoring until an oral regimen can be established that maintains serum calcium in a safe range. Various dosing recommendations exist for calcium including weight-based dosing (35–75 mg elemental calcium per kilogram per day in 2–3 divided doses) or a simple fixed dose of 500 mg per day regardless of age or weight [10, 16]. The recommendation for both vitamin D and calcium supplementation for treatment of nutritional rickets acknowledges ## PDF page 552 | printed page 546 the often-coexisting low calcium intake of those with vitamin D deficiency and that some degree of vitamin D deficiency can be over come by adequate calcium intake. Calcium carbonate should be taken with food to allow appropriate absorption, while calcium citrate can be taken on an empty stomach [95]. It is important to clarify with parents how to assess the dose of calcium provided by vari ous calcium preparations. Calcium carbonate is 40% elemental calcium by weight (i.e., 1000 mg calcium carbonate contains only 400 mg of elemental calcium). Likewise, cal cium citrate contains 21% elemental calcium and calcium glubionate 6.5% elemental cal cium by weight. Confirmation of the elemen tal calcium intake is crucial, primarily to prevent underdosing. While uncommon in the US, nutritional rickets due to calcium deficiency without vita min D deficiency is well described in other regions and has been successfully treated with calcium alone [96]. A randomized controlled trial conducted in Nigerian children revealed that in children with calcium deficiency rick ets, treatment with calcium alone or calcium plus vitamin D was more effective than treat ment with vitamin D alone [97]. Response to therapy should be monitored not only for efficacy but also for potential tox icity. Vitamin D is a fat-soluble vitamin and as such, excess administration can result in long standing toxicity. The frequency of monitor ing depends on the severity of disease and the presence and severity of hypocalcemia. Even in severe disease, serum calcium, phosphorus, and PTH can normalize in days to weeks. However, alkaline phosphatase and radio graphic changes often take months to normal ize. For most children (excluding those with severe hypocalcemia), we recommend measur ing serum calcium phosphorus, creatinine, PTH, total alkaline phosphatase, and vitamin D 2–3 weeks after initiating therapy and after dose adjustments if required. Less frequent monitoring is required once biochemical parameters are improving. We recommend obtaining radiographs 2–3 months after initi ating therapy to document improvement or resolution of rickets. Treatment doses of vita ### 21 min D and calcium are recommended for at least 3 months, but some may require a longer duration to exhibit full healing of rickets. Urine calcium (24 our collection or calcium to creatinine ratio) is helpful in monitoring for efficacy and toxicity. Initially, urine calcium is low due to inadequate absorption and deposi tion into bone. Urine calcium can remain rela tively low until the rickets resolves and the bone reservoir for mineral has been suffi ciently filled. Once biochemical and radiographic reso lution of rickets has been established, preven tion of recurrence requires maintenance dosing of vitamin D and adequate calcium intake via diet and/or supplementation. Children with malabsorption may require higher doses than is recommended for other wise healthy children and should undergo periodic monitoring of vitamin D concentra tion to assure adequate levels are maintained. Vitamin D toxicity is well documented in children and adults with overzealous supple mentation. The vitamin D concentration at which toxicity occurs can be highly variable but serum levels greater than 150 ng/mL are generally considered excessive and levels up to 100 ng/mL unlikely to cause toxicity. However, lower vitamin D concentrations may be associated with increased risk of nephrolithiasis. Symptoms of vitamin D tox icity are those of hypercalcemia and hyper calciuria including poor appetite, weight loss, abdominal pain, vomiting, constipation, polyuria, polydipsia, and nephrolithiasis. This can lead to dehydration, nephrocalcino sis and reduced renal function if severe hyper calcemia is present [98]. ### 21.9.2 Heritable Forms of Calcium ### Deficiency Rickets 25-Hydroxylase deficiency is rare and there fore the optimal treatment strategy is not known. However, his older brother did not experience healing of rickets with calcium alone but responded to calcium supplementa tion in addition to two doses of intramuscular vitamin D 600,000 IU each given 3 months apart. After the genetic cause of his rickets was established, therapy was transitioned to cal cifediol (25-hydroxyvitamin D) effectively bypassing the enzyme defect.
