Treatment of 1α-hydroxylase deficiency is aimed at bypassing the enzymatic defect, which can be achieved with calcitriol or 1α-cholecalciferol, though the latter is not available in the US. Calcitriol has a short halflife and requires twice daily dosing, while 1α-cholecalciferol can be dosed once daily [100]. Suggested dosing of calcitriol is 0.25–2 mcg daily and initial dosing of 1α-cholecalciferol is 0.25–3 mcg daily. Higher doses may be required during initial treatment with a lower dose used for indefinite mainte nance therapy. The goal is to heal rickets, improve (or prevent) limb deformity and keep serum parameters in a safe range. It is recom mended to maintain serum calcium at the low end of normal, serum phosphate in the nor mal range, and PTH at the high end of nor mal. If PTH is pushed to the low normal range or below, urine calcium will likely be elevated with the risk of nephrocalcinosis and nephrolithiasis. Similar to those with nutritional rickets, during the initial 3–6 months of treatment, children should also receive 30–50 mg/kg ele mental calcium daily. After healing of rickets, the dose of calcitriol and calcium is tapered to maintain biochemical parameters in goal range. Response to treatment of rickets caused by VDR variants is dependent on the underlying mutation leading to disease. Medical therapy is challenging and requires careful monitoring of laboratory values to determine responsive ness to therapy. Some infants respond to high dose calcium therapy alone, while others require intravenous calcium to bypass the poor intestinal calcium absorption. Some may respond to high dose vitamin D or calcitriol therapy. Those who fail oral therapy require ongoing intravenous calcium [100]. The goal of treatment is similar to other forms of rick ets, to normalize serum calcium levels, nor malize PTH and alkaline phosphatase, and reverse clinical features of rickets. Cinacalcet has been reported to normalize PTH, phos phate, and alkaline phosphatase levels in patients who failed to have PTH suppression with IV calcium and high dose vitamin D therapy [101]. Given the complex and variable nature of treatment for rickets due to VDR variants, management by a metabolic bone disease specialist is recommended. All patients with heritable forms of cal cium deficiency rickets require lifelong moni toring. Laboratory assessment may be required every 1–2 weeks during the initial phase of therapy when frequent dose adjust ments may be required. Once rickets heals, lower calcium and vitamin D (or D analog) doses are necessary for maintenance. Children require more frequent monitoring owing to ongoing bone accrual, particularly during rapid pubertal growth. Once linear growth is complete, treatment doses are expected to remain more stable. Monitoring should not only include parameters of efficacy (healing of rickets and normalization of serum cal cium, phosphate, PTH, and alkaline phospha ## PDF page 554 | printed page 548 tase), but also for complications, principally hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria. Periodic urine calcium assessment should be under taken to assess risk of nephrocalcinosis and nephrolithiasis. Renal ultrasound is helpful for monitoring these complications. ### 21.9.3 FGF23 Mediated ### Hypophosphatemic Rickets ### 21.9.3.1 X-Linked ### Hypophosphatemic Rickets Two options are available for treatment of FGF23 medicated hypophosphatemic rickets, conventional therapy with calcitriol and phos phate supplementation, or targeted therapy with anti-FGF23 antibody therapy (buro sumab). Targeted therapy with burosumab was approved by the FDA initially for treat ment of XLH (6 months and older) and sub sequently for select patient with TIO in whom the offending tumor cannot be identified or completely resected. Treatment guidelines are best established for patients with XLH [35, 40, 102]. However, the principles of management with conventional therapy for XLH can be applied to the other FGF23 mediated hypo phosphatemic disorders. Early identification and treatment of XLH is crucial. A retrospective study of children with XLH identified better long-term out comes when treatment with conventional therapy was initiated prior to 1 year of age compared to those who initiated treatment after 1 year [36, 103, 104]. This finding likely also applies to early initiation of burosumab which can be used for as young as 6 months of age. Conventional therapy consists of supple mentation with activate vitamin-D (calcitriol) and phosphate to supply sufficient mineral to bone to improve or heal rickets. Although the primary deficiency is phosphate, 1,25(OH)2D3 is deficient due to the inhibitory effect of FGF23 on 1α-hydroxylase activity. Calcitriol enhances not only calcium but also phosphate absorption in the intestine and helps prevent secondary hyperparathyroidism that occurs if phosphate supplementation is given alone. ### 21 Treatment requires frequent monitoring to assure the appropriate balance between phos phate and calcitriol are achieved to improve efficacy and, importantly, avoid complica tions. The principal goals of therapy are to improve linear growth by healing rickets radiographically and biochemically (lowering of alkaline phosphatase) and improvement (or prevent progression) of lower extremity deformity. Importantly, goals of therapy should also include avoidance of treatment complications. As such, normalization of serum phosphate should not be a primary goal with conventional therapy [3, 35]. Excessive phosphate supplementation in an effort to normalize serum phosphate will likely lead to complications including nephro calcinosis and secondary (and sometimes ter tiary) hyperparathyroidism [105]. The recommended initial phosphate dose for children is 20–40 mg/kg/day in 3–5 divided doses [35, 40]. Owing to the rapid excretion of phosphate in the urine, frequent dosing throughout the day is required [106]. Phosphate salts are available in several prepa rations, most containing 250 mg of phosphate per tablet. For infants and children unable to swallow tablets, we prefer to use Neutra-phos powder (250 mg phosphate per packet) that can be dissolved in liquid for easy titration and administration of the dose. Initial dosing may be limited by gastrointestinal side effects but can usually be managed by slow titration over a couple of weeks. Calcitriol is given in two divided doses, typically starting with 20–30 ng/kg/day. Calcitriol is available in cap sules (0.25 mcg or 0.5 mcg each) or a liquid with a concentration of 1 mcg/mL. Given the wide range in clinical severity (even within a single family), phosphate and calcitriol doses may need to be higher or lower than those listed above. Monitoring of conventional therapy should include clinical assessment of linear growth, monitoring of limb deformities and pain. Lab measurements should include serum phosphate, calcium, PTH, creatinine, and alkaline phosphatase. Urine calcium should be assessed periodically aiming to avoid hypercalciuria (urine calcium to creati ## PDF page 555 | printed page 549 nine ratio varies by age; 24 urine calcium less than 4 mg/kg/day is considered normal). Knee radiographs should be utilized to moni tor healing of rickets [35]. We recommend radiographs 3–6 months after initiation of therapy followed by less frequent imaging (annually) after adequate treatment has been established. In growing children, monitoring labs should be performed every 3–4 months. We prefer more frequent monitoring (monthly) at initiation and in the early dose titration phase. It is expected that dose adjustments will be required as the child grows. However, after cessation of linear growth, phosphate and cal citriol requirements are lower and the fre quency of phosphate dosing can usually be reduced to 2–3 divided doses per day. Monitoring laboratory stud ies should be performed fasting before the first daily doses of phosphate and calcitriol. PTH values will increase transiently after a phosphate dose is taken. If hypercalcemia or hypercalciuria is present, the dose of calcitriol should be reduced and/or dose of phosphate increased. Phosphate and active vitamin-D supple mentation can lead to hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis, with nephrocalcinosis reported in 30–70% of patients with XLH on conventional treatment [29, 103, 107]. Increasing grades of nephrocalcinosis can be seen with higher doses [103, 107]. Although mild nephrocalcinosis is common, renal func tion is usually well preserved. Renal ultra sound is recommended at 1–3 years intervals to detect the presence and monitor progres sion of nephrocalcinosis. After initiation and with proper manage ment on conventional therapy, bone pain (if present) can improve within weeks. Serum alkaline phosphatase will improve over the course of months but may not fully normalize in all who have heritable forms of hypophos phatemic rickets. Although linear growth improves with treatment, height potential remains compromised. Bowing deformities can improve with medical therapy but often takes several years to see substantial changes highlighting the importance of early initiation of treatment [108]. Burosumab is approved in the US and other countries to treat XLH in adults and children aged 6 months and older. Burosumab is a recombinant human IgG monoclonal antibody that blocks the activity of FGF23, addressing not only the renal phosphate wast ing, but also the inhibition of active vitamin D production. An early phase, randomized, placebo-controlled study in adults with XLH demonstrated improvements in renal phos phate reabsorption, serum phosphate, and serum 1,25(OH)2D3 with no significant change in serum or urine calcium or PTH [109]. Multiple clinical trials including children ages 1–12 years have shown improvement in radiographic appearance of rickets, normal ization of fasting serum phosphate concentra tions, improved renal tubular phosphate reabsorption, and lower serum alkaline phos phatase levels [110–112]. One study of 52 chil dren 5–12 years of age demonstrated these effects to be durable up to 160 weeks of ther apy with sustained serum phosphate and maintained improvement in the radiographic appearance of rickets [113]. Imel et al. com pared the efficacy of burosumab to continued conventional therapy in 61 children with XLH [111]. Burosumab therapy was superior to conventional treatment in this group with lower alkaline phosphatase levels and lower radiographic rickets severity scores. Despite these findings, many children do quite well with conventional therapy prompting some providers and families to continue calcitriol ## PDF page 556 | printed page 550 and phosphate rather than transition to buro sumab treatment. Although the burden of therapy with burosumab is lower compared to conventional treatment (twice monthly injec tions vs 3–5 daily medication doses), the cost of burosumab is high. For children receiving conventional ther apy who elect to transition to burosumab, calcitriol and phosphate should be discon tinued for 1 week and serum phosphate level should be below the normal reference range for age prior to the initial dose of burosumab [29]. The starting dose for children under 10 kg body weight is 1 mg/kg (rounded to the nearest 1 mg) administered subcutaneously every 2 weeks. For children over 10 kg, the initial dose is 0.8 mg/kg (rounded to the nearest 10 mg) administered subcutaneously every 2 weeks. The clinical goals of treat ment with burosumab are the same as with conventional therapy. However, in contrast to conventional therapy, serum phosphate concentration is key in dose titration. After initiation of treatment, fasting serum phos phate should be measured every 4 weeks for 3 months, and every 3 months thereafter once on stable dosing. Dose adjustments are based not only on serum phosphate levels, but also improvement (or lack of improve ment) in clinical parameters of rickets. Dose adjustments should be made no more fre quently than every 4 weeks. Goal serum phosphate level is within the reference range for age but below 5 mg/dL. If serum phos phate levels are below reference range for age, the dose should be increased stepwise up to a maximum dose of 2 mg/kg (maximum 90 mg) every 2 weeks in children. If serum phosphate levels become elevated, the next dose should be held, and serum phosphate should be reassessed in 4 weeks. When serum phosphate is no longer elevated, burosumab at a reduced dose can be reintroduced [114]. Adverse events were common among par ticipants in the clinical trials for burosumab but generally mild and well tolerated. The most common side effect is injection site changes, including mild injection site reac tions, erythema, bruising, pruritus, swelling, or pain. These were typically short-lived and did not lead to treatment cessation [110–113]. ### 21 No significant increase in serum calcium, urine calcium, or parathyroid hormone was observed [113]. Interestingly, vitamin D defi ciency was more common in children treated with burosumab compared to conventional therapy [111]. This may be due to increased conversion of 25-hydroxyvitamin D to its active metabolite (1,25(OH)2D3) as the inhibi tory effect of FGF23 on 1a-hydroxylase activ ity is blunted with anti-FGF23 antibody therapy. It is thus important to assure ade quate vitamin D intake and periodic monitor ing of levels for patients treated with burosumab to avoid deficiency. An ongoing post-marketing, monitoring study should provide insight into longer-term outcomes with burosumab therapy including effects on nephrocalcinosis over conventional therapy, effect on final adult height, need for orthopedic procedures, frequency of dental abscess, and the impact on disease morbidity in adulthood (early osteoarthritis and enthe sopathy). Some have reported short-term improve ment of growth with growth hormone in chil dren with XLH. However, there is insufficient evidence to warrant routine use in these chil dren [115]. Growth hormone for patients with XLH may be considered on an individual basis for those with extreme short stature [29, 35]. Orthopedic care for children with XLH (and other forms of rickets) is crucial. Although a main goal of medical manage ment (conventional therapy or burosumab) is to prevent and treat limb deformities, some maintain or develop sufficient deformity to result in gait disturbances, activity limitation, pain, and compromised function that requires surgical correction. Surgical options depend on the type and degree of deformity and if growth plates are fused or remain open. If growth plates remain open, epiphysiodesis or guided growth plates can be used to correct valgus or varus deformities. For those with more severe deformity or when growth plates are closed, corrective osteotomy is required. Children with XLH should receive regular dental care to minimize the risk of abscess and tooth loss. Conventional therapy improves but does not normalize the dentin mineralization ## PDF page 557 | printed page 551 defect and the larger size of the pulp chamber. However, dental outcomes are improved in those treated with conventional therapy [116]. It is not yet clear if burosumab improves den tal health in children or adults with XLH. As children reach skeletal maturity, transi tion from a pediatric dosing to an adult regi men should be undertaken. The optimal time and method for doing so is not well studied. Our approach is to start this transition after puberty and closure of growth plates (prefer ably closer to the time of peak bone mass). For those on conventional therapy, we slowly reduce the dose and frequency of dosing to the lowest dose required to mitigate symp toms of hypophosphatemia and osteomala cia. This often is achieved with once daily calcitriol and 2–3 daily doses of phosphate. There are adults who do not clearly benefit symptomatically from ongoing therapy, but it is difficult to predict who fits in this category. Even within the same family, disease manifes tations and need for treatment can vary widely during adulthood requiring an individualized treatment plan. For those treated with buro sumab, dosing is every 2 weeks during child hood and every 4 weeks for adults. Our approach is similar to conventional therapy by transitioning to the adult dosing frequency after cessation of linear growth (preferably closer to the time of peak bone mass). Complicating this transition is the readiness of an adolescent to assume more responsibil ity for their own care as they become young adults and often move away from home for college or work. Guiding principles have been published to assist in this transition for young adults with XLH [117]. ### 21.9.3.2 Other FGF23-Mediated ### Disorders Specific guidelines for the treatment of other FGF23 mediated hypophosphatemic disor ders are not as robust as those for XLH. However, the same principles of con ventional therapy with phosphate and cal citriol therapy as noted above can be used [118]. Titration of doses, laboratory monitor ing, and screening for complications, includ ing secondary hyperparathyroidism and nephrocalcinosis, are the same as manage ment for XLH. ADHR is unique in that the disease course can wax and wane over time, thus not always requiring lifelong treatment [43]. This phe nomenon may be partly related to the interac tion of iron deficiency leading to increased FGF23 production which cannot be efficiently inactivated in patients with ADHR [44]. Kapelari et al. reported a 5-year-old girl with ADHR with clinical features of rickets coex isting with low iron stores but resolution of rickets without need for calcitriol and phos phate therapy after iron deficiency was cor rected [119]. Thus, monitoring and treating iron deficiency may preclude the need for cal citriol and phosphate in some with ADHR. Successful treatment of hypophospha temic rickets caused by the various forms of ARHR, fibrous dysplasia of bone, and CSHS with oral phosphate and calcitriol have been reported [50, 56, 59, 62, 120]. There has been speculation that removal of epidermal nevi causing CSHS might improve hypophosphatemia, but no therapeu tic benefit has been found in patients with excision or ablation of nevi [62, 121]. Successful treatment with off label use of medications targeting the underlying disease mechanism have been reported. One patient had improvement in clinical, biochemical, and radiographic signs of rickets with a mito gen-activated protein kinase (MEK) inhibitor, which acts directly on the RAS/MAPK path way [122]. Use of burosumab has been explored (off label) for FGF23 mediated conditions other than XLH and TIO. Normalization of serum phosphate and improved clinical outcomes related to rickets in multiple patients with CSHS treated with burosumab has been described [123, 124]. Likewise, use in a 7-yearold boy with severe fibrous dysplasia led to the normalization of serum phosphate, improve ment in alkaline phosphatase, and resolution of radiographic rachitic changes after 17 months of therapy [125]. Successful use of burosumab for autosomal recessive hypo phosphatemic rickets due to DMP1 muta tions has also been reported [126]. ## PDF page 558 | printed page 552 TIO is unique among the FGF23 medi ated disorders in that it can be cured assuming the offending tumor can be localized and removed. It is, therefore, important to con sider this diagnosis in a child with acquired disease in whom an alternate cause of FGF23 mediated rickets is not identified. After com plete resection, FGF23, phosphate, and 1,25(OH)2D3 concentrations normalize over days to weeks. Normalization of alkaline phosphatase and radiographic change of rick ets/osteomalacia can take months. For those with disease that cannot be localized or resected medical therapy (calcitriol and phos phate or burosumab) should be initiated [65, 66]. Burosumab has been approved for treat ment of TIO when surgical cure is not possi ble [127]. ### 21.9.3.3 Non-FGF23 Mediated ### Hypophosphatemia Similar to FGF23 mediated hypophospha temic disorders, hereditary hypophospha temic rickets with hypercalciuria (HHRH) caused by SLC34A3 mutations leads to renal phosphate wasting. However, in contrast to FGF23 mediated disease, 1α-hydroxylase activity is high since FGF23 concentrations are appropriately low. As a result, 1,25(OH)2D3 concentrations can be markedly elevated lead ing to increased intestinal calcium absorption and hypercalciuria. This distinction is impor tant in that treatment consists of phosphate supplementation alone without calcitriol since endogenous 1,25(OH)2D3 production is already high. Additional calcitriol would exacerbate the hypercalciuria and nephrocal cinosis. Phosphate administration also serves to limit intestinal calcium absorption and can reduce endogenous 1,25(OH)2D3 production, both of which lessen the degree of hypercalci uria. With phosphate supplementation, bone pain and muscle strength improve, radio graphic evidence of rickets (if present) can resolve, urine calcium excretion is reduced, and serum alkaline phosphatase levels improve [71, 72]. Renal Fanconi syndrome is a complex col lection of disorders. Hypophosphatemia can be treated with phosphate supplementation. ### 21 Bicarbonate replacement therapy may also improve the associated bone disease. When possible, treatment of the underlying disorder causing proximal tubular dysfunction may preclude the need for phosphate replacement therapy. Likewise, for children with nutri tional phosphate deficiency, correction of the underlying malabsorptive disease or the addi tion of phosphate to the diet (or via a supple ment) will resolve the hypophosphatemia and associated rickets. ### 21.10 Summary Rickets constitutes a broad spectrum of dis eases leading to a common clinical disorder of impaired growth plate and skeletal mineral ization. Although entirely preventable and despite campaigns to raise awareness, nutri tional rickets due to vitamin D and/or calcium deficiency remains a frequent cause of mor bidity worldwide. Treatment of nutritional rickets is fairly straightforward but continued public health efforts aimed at prevention remain of utmost importance. Our under standing of the molecular cause of many heri table forms of rickets has expanded in recent years with targeted therapy now available for some. History, exam, and relatively few labo ratory tests can identify the underlying cause of rickets for most which allows use of disease specific treatment strategies in an effort to optimize long-term outcomes. ### References 1. title: Pseudohypoparathyroidism
group: IV: Pediatric Mineral and Bone Disorders

paragraphs.text: Emily L. Germain-Lee and Michael A. Levine
paragraphs.heading: Pseudohypopara thyroidism

paragraphs.text: 22.3.1 Nomenclature for PHP and Related Disorders – 564
paragraphs.heading: 22.3 Etiologies and Mechanisms – 561

paragraphs.text: 22.4.1 Albright Hereditary Osteodystrophy (AHO) – 565 22.4.2 Pseudohypoparathyroidism Type 1A (PHP1A): iPPSD2, OMIM #103580 – 574 22.4.3 Pseudohypoparathyroidism Type 1C (PHP1C): iPPSD2, OMIM #612462 – 585 22.4.4 Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism (PPHP): iPPSD2, OMIM #612463 – 585 22.4.5 Pseudohypoparathyroidism Type 1B (PHP1B): iPPSD3, OMIM # 603233 – 586 22.4.6 Other GNAS Inactivation Disorders with Heterotopic Ossifications (HOs): Progressive Osseous Heteroplasia (POH) and Osteoma Cutis (OC)—iPPSD2, OMIM #166350 – 587 22.4.7 Acrodysostosis Syndromes Affecting cAMP Signaling Downstream of GNAS: Acrodysostosis Type 1 (ACRDYS1)—iPPSD4, OMIM #101800 and Acrodysostosis Type 2 (ACRDYS2)—iPPSD5, OMIM #614613 – 588 22.4.8 Molecular Diagnosis – 589
paragraphs.heading: 22.4 Clinical Diagnosis and Management – 565

paragraphs.text: The term pseudohypoparathyroidism (PHP) describes a group of disorders that have in common renal resistance to parathyroid hor mone (PTH) with consequent hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia despite elevated serum levels of bioactive PTH. PHP was first characterized by Fuller Albright and col leagues in 1942 in a publication that described three unrelated patients with striking physical features who lacked the appropriate phospha turic response to the administration of para thyroid extract “in spite of the fact that larger and larger amounts were given [1].” They demonstrated that although the patients had evidence of biochemical hypoparathyroidism with hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia, these patients failed to respond to exogenous parathyroid extract, leading the investigators to conclude that this was “not lack of para thyroid hormone but a failure of the organism to respond to it.” They hypothesized that these patients had end-organ resistance to PTH, and because they manifested the bio chemical features of hypoparathyroidism, they named this unusual variant “pseudohy poparathyroidism.”
paragraphs.heading: 22.1 Historical Background

paragraphs.text: In addition to the biochemical abnormali ties, Albright and his associates also noted that these patients manifested a unique con stellation of developmental features. The orig inal description revealed specific characteristics that included being “short and rather thick-set” and having a “very round face” with “metacarpal and metatarsal bones [that were] extremely short and stubby.” In addition, examinations of the patients revealed “marked density of the skull” with the “skeleton as a whole [being] abnormally dense,” multiple dental abnormalities, and subcutaneous ectopic ossifications described as “hard, calcified masses in the subcutaneous tissues.” Cognitive impairment was noted at varying levels with one described as “extremely” affected and another as “some what backward mentally.” However, aside from the hormone resistance, not all features were ubiquitously present in each individual patient [1]. Subsequent investigations by
paragraphs.heading: 22.1 Historical Background

paragraphs.text: Albright and his colleagues over the next decade led to the publication in 1952 of a unique patient who presented with similar somatic features to PHP but who displayed normal calcium and phosphate levels and a normal phosphaturic response after adminis tration of parathyroid extract. They empha sized three unique findings in this patient that seemed consistent with PHP patients as well, including “(a) round faces and short, thick-set figures; (b) early epiphyseal closure of some of the metacarpal and metatarsal bones with resulting shortening of the involved fingers and toes; and (c) subcutaneous foci of ectopic ossification.” However, end-organ resistance to parathyroid extract was absent unlike in PHP. Therefore, Albright and his colleagues referred to this new disorder as “pseudopseu dohypoparathyroidism” (PPHP) because the condition resembled PHP in having the same somatic features but lacked evidence of hor monal resistance [2]. These developmental characteristics were later collectively termed “Albright hereditary osteodystrophy” (AHO). Subsequently, other patients were described who had PTH resistance but lacked features of AHO [3, 4], thus further extending the complexity of the disorder.
paragraphs.heading: 22.1 Historical Background

paragraphs.text: In the late 1960s, with the discovery that cyclic AMP (cAMP) produced by adenylyl cyclase was the second messenger for many hormones, Gerald Aurbach and colleagues began studies that would ultimately identify the molecular basis for PTH resistance in PHP [5, 6]. They showed first that cAMP was the second messenger for PTH in the kidney and second that the absent phosphaturic response to PTH in PHP was associated with a markedly blunted increase in urinary excre tion of cAMP. These observations implicated a failure of PTH to stimulate the enzyme ade nylyl cyclase in the kidney as the basis for hor mone resistance. PHP patients with defective cAMP and phosphaturic responses to PTH were termed PHP type 1 (PHP1) to distin guish them from patients with PHP type 2 (PHP2) who lacked features of AHO and in whom PTH administration elicited an appro priate increase in urinary excretion of nephrogenous cAMP but failed to induce a
paragraphs.heading: 22.1 Historical Background

paragraphs.text: phosphaturic response [3, 7]. Key investiga tions published in 1980 by Michael Levine, Henry Bourne, and others revealed that patients with PHP with concomitant features of AHO had a 50% reduction in Gαs bioactiv ity utilizing in vitro assays of extracts from human erythrocyte membranes whereas those without AHO had normal or minimally diminished activity [8, 9]. With that discovery came a revised nosology for PHP1: those with reduced Gαs bioactivity with AHO features were referred to as having PHP1A, whereas those with overall normal Gαs bioactivity but without AHO features were said to have PHP1B. This molecular dichotomy led to a further refinement in the endocrine phenotype of PHP1 such that resistance to multiple hor mones whose receptors required Gαs to acti vate adenylyl cyclase was a feature of PHP1A [10, 11] while isolated PTH resistance was typical of PHP1B [12].
paragraphs.heading: 22.1 Historical Background

paragraphs.text: By the late 1980s, the ability to assay PTH accurately from direct measurements in patients was available [13], and by 1990, the first mutations in GNAS, the gene encoding Gαs, were identified as being the cause of PHP1A and PPHP [14, 15]. Soon after this major discovery, a greater understanding of the complexities of PHP and its related disor ders began to unfold, and a search for the eti ology of PHP1B was underway [16–20] (for review, [21]). Concomitantly over this period of time, the distinction between PHP1A and PPHP was found to be a manifestation of the parental origin of the defective GNAS allele, and with further delineation of the regulation of the highly complex GNAS locus, the basis for this unusual pattern of inheritance was determined to be paternal imprinting of GNAS [22–27]. During this time, investiga tions on mouse models not only demonstrated that the Gnas locus was regulated by a highly complex system of reciprocal imprinting but also showed that hormone resistance in spe cific tissues was related to a tissue-specific pat tern of paternal imprinting for Gαs [28, 29]. In the sections that follow, the further delinea tion of the mode of inheritance as well as the pathophysiologic processes uncovered by investigations in both humans and mice to
paragraphs.heading: 22.1 Historical Background

paragraphs.text: determine the etiologies and mechanisms of PHP and related disorders will be detailed along with their clinical implications (for review [30–43]).
paragraphs.heading: 22.1 Historical Background

paragraphs.text: chapter, these will be referred to as subcutane ous ossifications (SCOs) when discussing AHO.

Since the original description of PHP1A and PPHP, other forms of PHP have been identified, such as PHP1B, that are not due to mutations within the coding exons of GNAS that produce Gαs. PHP1B is characterized pri marily by PTH resistance and occasional TSH resistance (sometimes with calcitonin resis tance) but typically without other hormonal resistances or the complete AHO phenotype. It is due to imprinting errors that impair the transcription of Gαs from the maternal GNAS allele (for review, [21, 30–43]), [19, 45–51]. Mutations in other genes in this pathway, spe cifically PRKAR1A and PDE4D, can lead to acrodysostosis type 1 and type 2 respectively. These conditions are chondrodysplasias and resemble PHP due to the presence of endo crine defects such as resistance to PTH, TSH, and other hormones in addition to brachydac tyly, skeletal abnormalities, short stature, and obesity (for review, [37–43]) [52–56].

Advances are continually being made toward understanding the mechanisms under lying the PHP spectrum and related disorders, and through clinical and laboratory studies, the phenotypes are being more carefully eluci dated as are the etiologies of their clinical issues, such as hormone resistance, short stat ure, skeletal and craniofacial/dental abnor malities, heterotopic ossifications, obesity and metabolic disturbances, and cognitive/behav ioral impairments.

As alluded to above, PHP1A and PPHP with the associated AHO phenotype are caused by heterozygous inactivation of GNAS, the gene that encodes the α-stimulatory subunit (Gαs) of the heterotrimeric G protein, Gs, that cou ples heptahelical receptors (G protein-coupled receptors, GPCRs) for a large variety of hor mones and neurotransmitters to adenylyl cyclase [14, 15, 30–43]. Transmembrane signal transduction is initiated by the binding of agonist ligands to specific GPCRs (e.g., PTH in the case of the type 1 PTH receptor), which
paragraphs.heading: 22.3 Etiologies and Mechanisms

paragraphs.text: leads to the dissociation of Gαs from the het erotrimeric αβγ Gs complex. Free Gαs binds to and activates adenylyl cyclase, while the βγ subunits can stimulate other signaling enzymes as well as some isoforms of adenylyl cyclase. Adenylyl cyclase generates cAMP, which activates a variety of downstream effec tors to produce the physiological responses to hormone stimulation. Levels of intracellular cAMP are regulated by the balance between the activities of adenylyl cyclase and cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterase (PDE). A large number of genes encode a variety of isoforms for these two important enzymes, which vary in their patterns of tissue-specific expression and provide discrete mechanisms for generat ing cell-type and stimulus-specific responses to GPCR activation. The most well-studied of the effector targets of cAMP is protein kinase A (PKA), which regulates a variety of signaling pathways via phosphorylation of many metabolic enzymes and transcription factors. However, cAMP also regulates the activity of EPAC (a guanine-nucleotideexchange factor) and cyclic-nucleotide-gated ion channels.
paragraphs.heading: 22.3 Etiologies and Mechanisms

paragraphs.text: Gαs is encoded by exons 1–13 of GNAS. Mutations can occur in any exon as well as intron/exon boundaries [57] and can be inher ited or occur spontaneously. The GNAS locus is highly complex given that it generates tran scripts for not only Gαs (exons 1–13) but also neuroendocrine secretory protein 55 (NESP55), extra-large alpha-stimulatory sub unit (XLαs), A/B (also called 1A), as well as an antisense transcript (AS). The A/B tran script may encode a truncated form of Gαs that can act in an inhibitory fashion, (for review, [21, 34–43]), [25, 27, 58–64]. The dif ferent transcripts are generated through the use of alternative first exons. The GNAS locus is controlled by genomic imprinting, which is regulated through differentially methylated regions (DMRs) that are within the promoter regions for each exon, except exon 1 of GNAS (which is part of the coding sequence for Gαs). The promoters for XLαs, AB, and AS are methylated on the maternal allele, thus lead ing to transcription predominantly from the paternal allele. Of note is that XLαs can act similarly to Gαs and even augment its action
paragraphs.heading: 22.3 Etiologies and Mechanisms

paragraphs.text: [64, 65]. NESP55, on the other hand, is meth ylated on the paternal allele resulting in expression predominantly from the maternal allele [25, 27]. Imprinting is often partial and leads to transcriptional repression of one allele. In particular, expression of Gαs tran scripts from the paternal allele is suppressed in certain tissues, many of which are endo crine. This is termed “paternal imprinting” because there is inhibition of transcription of the paternal allele. In other tissues, imprinting does not occur, leading to biallelic expression of both the maternal and paternal alleles. The development of PHP1A versus PPHP is dependent on the parent-of-origin of the mutant allele and is due to this mechanism of imprinting, specifically determined to be due to tissue-specific paternal imprinting based on investigations in humans as well as mouse models. In tissues in which imprinting plays a role, the consequences on clinical phenotype can be very different between the two condi tions [28, 29, 66–74], whereas in those tissues in which imprinting does not play a promi nent role, the clinical phenotypes can be simi lar [22–29], (for review, [32, 34–38, 40–43]).
paragraphs.heading: 22.3 Etiologies and Mechanisms

paragraphs.text: The presence or absence of hormonal resistance in association with AHO was first determined through clinical analysis of family pedigrees, which revealed that mothers affected with either PHP1A or PPHP had children with PHP1A, whereas fathers with either PHP1A or PPHP had children with PPHP. It was eventually determined that patients with PHP1A have GNAS mutations on their maternally inherited allele, and those with PPHP carry mutations on their pater nally inherited allele, which led to the discov ery of the mechanisms involved [22–27]. This unique mode of inheritance was confirmed in murine models with a targeted disruption of Gnas, which revealed tissue-specific silencing of Gαs expression from the paternal allele [28, 29, 66].
paragraphs.heading: 22.3 Etiologies and Mechanisms

paragraphs.text: Because the normal paternally inherited GNAS allele in PHP1A patients is suppressed in imprinted tissues (many of which are endocrine-related), the loss of Gαs from the abnormal maternal allele results in a near complete absence of Gαs. The severe defi ciency of Gαs impairs GPCR signal transduc
paragraphs.heading: 22.3 Etiologies and Mechanisms

paragraphs.text: tion in these imprinted tissues and accounts for resistance to multiple hormones and neu rotransmitters. By contrast, hormone respon siveness is normal in cells in which the paternal GNAS allele is active, as the loss of Gαs from the defective maternal allele results in only a 50% reduction in Gαs protein. As demon strated in investigations both in humans and in murine models, the imprinting is partial with only modest expression of Gαs from the paternal GNAS allele in the renal proximal tubules, thyroid follicular epithelial cells, gonad cells, and pituitary somatotropes, thereby causing multihormone resistance to PTH, TSH, LH/FSH, and GHRH, respec tively [28, 29, 66–74]. Calcitonin resistance has also been reported [34–43, 75, 76], and there is suggestive evidence in an AHO mouse model that partial imprinting in osteoclasts may affect bone remodeling due to calcitonin resistance [77, 78]. In contrast to PHP1A, patients with paternally inherited GNAS mutations develop PPHP and do not develop hormone resistance. They are often small-forgestational-age (SGA) at birth. This may be due to decreased XLαs, which is normally expressed from the paternal allele and is thought to be important in fetal growth [34, 79, 80].

In addition to hormone resistance, patients with PHP1A are typically obese, especially characterized by marked early-onset obesity starting soon after birth, whereas those with PPHP are not severely obese [44]. This obser vation changed the classic description of AHO that had previously been thought to include obesity. In addition, this noted differ ence in the obesity phenotype in PHP1A ver sus PPHP raised the possibility of imprinting in the hypothalamus given that the melano cortin-4 receptor (MC4R) is Gαs-coupled. Investigations in mice demonstrated no imprinting in adipose tissue [29, 81], and it was eventually determined through continued work on mouse models that imprinting occurs in the dorsomedial hypothalamus, specifically in MC4R-expressing cells [82, 83]. Human studies have also revealed the lack of imprint ing in adipose [84]. Therefore, the evidence supports hypothalamic imprinting as an underlying cause of the obesity such that
patients with PHP1A have hormone resis tance with severe obesity, whereas patients with PPHP do not have hormone resistance or obesity.

Although tissue-specific imprinting of GNAS leads to differences in the clinical phe notypes seen in PHP1A and PPHP, GNAS is biallelically expressed in other cell types and tissues, such as skin (fibroblasts), renal medulla, renal collecting ducts/ascending limb, adrenal, heart, nasal epithelia, lympho cytes, adipocytes, and chondrocytes, as has been demonstrated through both human and mouse investigations [11, 28, 29, 47, 66, 67, 70, 81, 84–90]. This biallelic expression results in clinical phenotypes that are shared between PHP1A and PPHP, specifically brachydactyly, shortened adult stature, and subcutaneous ossifications. These result from partial loss of Gαs activity in the specific cell types involved in which GNAS is biallelically expressed, such as chondrocytes in the case of brachydactyly and short stature. This would implicate that these phenotypes would be similar between PHP1A and PPHP because GNAS would be expressed equivalently in both.

Disorders besides PHP1A and PPHP can result from mutations in the GNAS locus. PHP1C presents clinically and biochemically in the same manner as PHP1A but is due to mutations that impair receptor coupling activ ity of Gαs but not its basal activity [26, 37–43]. It has been proposed by experts that PHP1C be removed from the nomenclature in the future [41, 42].

Other distinct conditions in the PHP spectrum that result from mutations in GNAS exons encoding Gαs specifically on the pater nal allele have heterotopic ossifications (HOs) as the predominant feature (for review, [34–43, 78]), [91–97]. One of these is progressive osse ous heteroplasia (POH), characterized by penetrating HOs as the main feature, typically without other physical features or hormonal resistance. There is also a very rare condition involving an overlap of both PHP1A and POH [98, 99], in which patients have features of both disorders. Finally, isolated osteoma cutis (OC) can occur, which is the clinical find ing of subcutaneous ossifications in isolation, also typically from mutations on the paternal

allele within the exons encoding Gαs. This can evolve into PPHP or POH over time (and even into PHP1A with hormonal resistance in rare circumstances when the SCOs are the only presenting sign and are inadvertently diag nosed as OC). POH and OC are typically caused by spontaneous mutations (unless the OC is representative of the early phase of PPHP and has been inherited) (for review, [34, 35, 37–43, 78]), [100–102].

Epigenetic defects within the GNAS gene cause PHP1B (for review [21, 30–43]), [19, 45–51]. All patients to date with PHP1B have a loss of methylation (LOM) within the Exon A/B DMR (specifically A/B:TSS-DMR) on the maternal GNAS allele. In most patients with familial PHP1B, the methylation defect is limited to LOM of exon A/B, but some cases of familial PHP1B and nearly all cases of sporadic PHP1B exhibit more extensive methylation defects that include LOM at the DMR for XLαs and gain of methylation (GOM) at the DMRs for NESP55. Approximately 15–20% of PHP1B is familial and due to maternal transmission of heterozy gous microdeletions within the maternal STX16 allele about 220 kb upstream of GNAS that include either STX16 exons 4–6 or exons 2–4, which presumably affect a cis-regulatory element that is important for methylation of the GNAS exon A/B DMR. The sporadic forms of PHP1B make up the majority of cases and tend to have more extensive meth ylation defects involving GNAS exon A/B:TSS-DMR and AS2:DMR in associa tion with methylation changes affecting vari ous alternative transcripts. Deletions within NESP and XL or paternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 20q (patUPD20q) have been identified in some PHP1B patients with global methylation defects (for review, [21, 36–38, 41–43, 103, 104]), [45–50, 105–111].

these disorders that resemble PHP are down stream from GNAS and include PRKAR1A, which leads to acrodysostosis type 1 (ACRDYS1), and PDE4D, which leads to acrodysostosis type 2 (ACRDYS2) (for review, [37–43]), [52–56, 112–115]. Patients with ACRDYS1 can have PTH resistance but have an unusual response to exogenous PTH that easily distinguishes them from patients with PHP1. Specifically, after administration of PTH, patients with ACRDYS1 show a nor mal urinary cAMP response but fail to gener ate a normal phosphaturic response, a pattern that has been attributed to an inability of intracellular cAMP to activate PKA. This response is similar to that of patients with PHP2, who generally lack features of AHO. PHP2 may be due to undiagnosed vita min D deficiency [7, 37, 38, 40–43] and is no longer referred to commonly. In summary, a spectrum of PHP and related disorders with certain shared features can result from muta tions in different components of the G pro tein-coupled signal transduction cascade.

Although the prevalence of PHP overall is not truly known, this group of disorders is quite rare with three reported estimates rang ing from 0.34 to 1.1 per 100,000 [43, 116, 117]. However, the prevalence may be as high as 1:15,000–20,000 in the United States given that many patients with these disorders are misdiagnosed or go completely unrecognized. For example, PPHP is often completely missed until a mother has a child with PHP1A [40].

Each of the PHP and related disorders is cata logued in the Online Mendelian Inheritance of Man (OMIM) with a unique number [118] corresponding to the common terminology utilized for each condition. Because the names are descriptive in nature, the European con sortium for PHP (EuroPHP) proposed the term “inactivating PTH/PTHrP signaling dis order (iPPSD)” several years ago as an alter native to PHP [119, 120]. The motivation for
paragraphs.heading: and Related Disorders

paragraphs.text: this proposed change in nomenclature was to classify these disorders based on the underly ing mechanism rather than on the clinical phenotype, which is often overlapping among the different disorders. Based on this new clas sification, all disorders involving GNAS muta tions affecting the coding sequence, including PHP1A, PPHP, PHP1C, and POH, would instead be designated iPPSD2; PHP1B, which affects methylation of GNAS, would be desig nated iPPSD3; acrodysostosis type 1 (due to mutations in PRKAR1A) and acrodysostosis type 2 (due to mutations in PDE4D) would be designated iPPSD4 and iPPSD5, respectively. There are also two other categories depending on the specific gene affected, including iPPSD1 involving mutations in PTH1R, and iPPSD6 involving mutations in PDE3A.
paragraphs.heading: and Related Disorders

paragraphs.text: After this iPPSD classification system was proposed in 2016, the EuroPHP network assembled international experts in 2017 to develop the first international Consensus Statement on the diagnosis and management of PHP and related disorders. Published in 2018, this Consensus Statement has been a milestone in the field. It presents a detailed and well-organized approach to evaluate PHP and related disorders [38], with an updated practical tool to this Consensus Statement published in 2020 [42]. Before moving on to the clinical diagnosis and management of PHP as well as related disorders, the reader is directed not only to the 2018 international Consensus Statement and its update but also to several recent additional comprehensive reviews and guides that detail the etiologies and mechanisms [21, 36, 37, 39–41, 43].
paragraphs.heading: and Related Disorders

paragraphs.text: 22.1 The second focus of this chapter is to pro vide recommendations for the management of this complex set of disorders. In addition to the international Consensus Statement and its update (of which the authors were a part) [38, 42], as well as comprehensive reviews as previously referenced, management recom mendations within this chapter are also based on the authors’ personal clinical experiences, having evaluated and followed well over a thousand patients with PHP and related con ditions for the past several decades. In many of these cases, the authors have had the opportunity to manage individual patients longitudinally from early childhood through adulthood, ranging from birth through approximately 85 years of age.
paragraphs.heading: and Management

paragraphs.text: The AHO phenotype common to both PHP1A and PPHP is characterized by brachy dactyly, adult short stature, and subcutaneous ossifications, although the presence of all three is not required for the diagnosis. This shared phenotype results from partial loss of Gαs activity in cell types and tissues in which GNAS is biallelically expressed. In other cell types and tissues in which there is imprinting of GNAS with differential expression of the maternal versus paternal alleles, many of which are endocrine tissues, GNAS mutations can have numerous physiological and clinical manifestations that are seen in PHP1A but are absent in PPHP such as hormonal resistance and obesity, given that many hormones require Gαs for signaling. Likewise, the bial lelic expression in skin fibroblasts presumably leads to the development of SCOs in both conditions [11, 78, 90, 100]. paragraphs.heading: PPHP PHP1B OC POH

paragraphs.text: The brachydactyly is thought to occur in approximately 70–80% of patients with this condition [38, 42, 121] and often involves metacarpals/metatarsals III, IV, and V (known as brachydactyly type E when multi ple metacarpals/metatarsals are affected) [122]. However, any metacarpal/metatarsal can be involved ( Fig. 22.3a–e). The distal phalanx of the thumb is affected in up to 75% of cases and is typically short and broad (when isolated this is referred to as brachydac tyly D) [121–123]. This finding is referred to as “potter’s thumb,” “stub thumb,” or “murder er’s thumb” ( Fig. 22.3a and c) [40]. The brachydactyly is usually not apparent in infancy and instead becomes more evident later in childhood, and it can be asymmetric between the two hands and feet ( Fig. 22.3a– e). By contrast, brachydactyly is usually obvi ous at birth in ACRDYS syndromes. Variability of brachydactyly in AHO, includ ing the effect on hand/foot size, can occur even among family members with the condi tion, as well as among nonfamily members with the same genotype, suggesting that there is not a direct genotype-phenotype correla tion [40, 100, 121]. Another skeletal feature present in AHO patients is Archibald’s sign, which is the absence of one or more knuckles upon making a fist and which occurs second ary to the shortened metacarpals. Often a dimple is observed in place of the knuckle ( Figs. 22.1d and 22.3e).
paragraphs.heading: 22.4.1.1 Brachydactyly

paragraphs.text: These physical features are often a key to unlocking the diagnosis, particularly for patients with PPHP, who may have been unaware of these specific abnormalities because they had not been considered to be medically significant or because they had gone unnoticed. Indeed, a common scenario is that a mother brings her child with PHP1A to the clinic, and she is then noticed to have skeletal features of AHO, leading to the diagnosis of PPHP in the mother. The brachydactyly and brachymetacarpia/brachymetatarsia can cause problems with both fine and gross motor activities as well as orthopedic issues [34, 38, 40, 124, 125], and early initiation of occupational and physical therapy can be helpful [40, 42, 125]. Occasionally patients
paragraphs.heading: 22.4.1.1 Brachydactyly

paragraphs.text: have one or two digits that are out of propor tion in length to the others and undergo surgi cal intervention, which is not advised; the irregularity in sizes between the various fin gers and toes seems to be easily adapted to over time with proper management, such as with customized shoes and orthotics. Occupational and physical therapy as well as management by podiatry and specialized shoe stores can be of great benefit. In addition, the hand abnormalities predispose these patients to develop carpal tunnel syndrome, which has been documented as being at an increased prevalence in both children and adults with PHP1A and PPHP; the overall prevalence of carpal tunnel syndrome in AHO for patients of all ages is 67%; in children, the prevalence is 36% [125]. The symptoms of carpal tunnel syndrome can mimic those of paresthesias secondary to hypocalcemia; therefore, it is important to follow up on these symptoms if the patient is normocalcemic, as early inter vention can prevent the need for surgery.
paragraphs.heading: 22.4.1.1 Brachydactyly

paragraphs.text: Another physical feature in AHO is short stat ure at the time that final adult height is attained. The short stature in adulthood (or late adolescence) is thought to be largely due to premature epiphyseal fusion of the long bones as a result of accelerated chondrocyte differentiation, just as described for the brachydactyly [85–88]. This process seems to be accentuated at the onset of puberty. The mean final height of adults with PHP1A with out intervention is more than 2.5 standard deviations below the mean (146.3 +/− 8.0 cm for women and 158.1 cm +/− 6.7 cm for men) [37, 38, 40, 126, 127].
paragraphs.heading: Premature Epiphyseal Fusion and Bone Age Evaluation
Premature Epiphyseal Fusion and Bone Age Evaluation

paragraphs.text: typically does not become apparent until early adolescence (approximately ages 9–13 years), at which time a rapid advance ment in bone age occurs concomitant with the absence of any pubertal growth spurt, even though puberty occurs at a typical age and is not precocious [34, 37, 40, 41, 72, 127] ( Fig. 22.4). The absence of the growth spurt is due not only to premature epiphyseal closure but also, in the case of PHP1A, resistance to gonadotropins. However, even patients with PPHP, who are not resistant to gonadotropins, exhibit a somewhat blunted pubertal growth spurt from the epiphyseal fusion alone [34, 40]. The advanced hand/wrist bone age that is seen in AHO is often misconstrued as earlyonset puberty even without other signs of puberty, and because of this, GnRH ago nists are sometimes started inadvertently and inappropriately [40].

paragraphs.text: itant cause in approximately 2/3 of PHP1A patients is growth hormone (GH) deficiency due to GHRH resistance [34, 38, 40, 72, 73, 127] (69% per authors [40, 72, 127]). Therefore, the short stature in PHP1A is multifactorial due to a combination of premature epiphyseal fusion, absent pubertal growth spurt (par tially from gonadotropin resistance), and GH deficiency secondary to GHRH resistance, as will be discussed in later sections on hormonal resistance.

In both humans and mice, SCOs are uniformly restricted to the dermis and subcutaneous tissue and do not penetrate underlying fascial planes [78, 90, 100]. In the mouse model, extensive imaging could be per formed documenting the restricted formation of the ossifications to the dermis and subcutis
paragraphs.heading: (SCOs)

paragraphs.text: without exception [90]. Clearly, this cannot be done in patients, but for any imaging per formed in this 16-year study [100], as well as in hundreds of AHO patients who have had imaging studies and biopsies performed for clinical reasons, the heterotopic bone forma tion did not extend beyond the dermis and subcutis layers. In addition to being spontane ous, SCOs also frequently occur in areas of trauma and/or pressure, such as the belt area,

heel of the foot, or bridge of the nose in indi viduals who wear glasses. They can also be mistaken for warts ( Fig. 22.6) and discov ered because of their refractoriness to typical wart treatment modalities. In the aforemen tioned cases, these SCOs can form punctate lesions on their surfaces that exude a chalklike white substance. This is another hallmark of the lesions being SCOs ( Fig. 22.5g), although a biopsy can be performed for verifi cation when needed [37, 40, 100].

Males are affected more than females, as has been seen in investigations in both humans and mice [90, 100]. They tend to increase in size and number with age, with a possible increase in adolescence, but both SCO size and number appear to level out by early adult hood, as has been documented in both human and mouse investigations. There is no correla tion between the severity or degree of ossifica tion formation with BMI or the degree of PTH and other hormonal resistances [100]. A greater severity of SCOs is found in patients with frameshift and nonsense mutations, thereby implicating a genotype-phenotype

correlation. In addition, severity within fami lies tends to be similar, and parents with SCOs usually have children with ossifications to the same degree; those parents without SCOs typ ically have children without ossifications, again implicating a genotype-phenotype cor relation [100]. This is in contrast to the brachy dactyly, as previously discussed, in which there is no genotype-phenotype correlation [37, 40, 100, 121].
