Advances are continually being made toward understanding the mechanisms under lying the PHP spectrum and related disorders, and through clinical and laboratory studies, the phenotypes are being more carefully eluci dated as are the etiologies of their clinical issues, such as hormone resistance, short stat ure, skeletal and craniofacial/dental abnor malities, heterotopic ossifications, obesity and metabolic disturbances, and cognitive/behav ioral impairments.

### 22.3 Etiologies and Mechanisms

As alluded to above, PHP1A and PPHP with the associated AHO phenotype are caused by heterozygous inactivation of GNAS, the gene that encodes the α-stimulatory subunit (Gαs) of the heterotrimeric G protein, Gs, that cou ples heptahelical receptors (G protein-coupled receptors, GPCRs) for a large variety of hor mones and neurotransmitters to adenylyl cyclase [14, 15, 30–43]. Transmembrane signal transduction is initiated by the binding of agonist ligands to specific GPCRs (e.g., PTH in the case of the type 1 PTH receptor), which

leads to the dissociation of Gαs from the het erotrimeric αβγ Gs complex. Free Gαs binds to and activates adenylyl cyclase, while the βγ subunits can stimulate other signaling enzymes as well as some isoforms of adenylyl cyclase. Adenylyl cyclase generates cAMP, which activates a variety of downstream effec tors to produce the physiological responses to hormone stimulation. Levels of intracellular cAMP are regulated by the balance between the activities of adenylyl cyclase and cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterase (PDE). A large number of genes encode a variety of isoforms for these two important enzymes, which vary in their patterns of tissue-specific expression and provide discrete mechanisms for generat ing cell-type and stimulus-specific responses to GPCR activation. The most well-studied of the effector targets of cAMP is protein kinase A (PKA), which regulates a variety of signaling pathways via phosphorylation of many metabolic enzymes and transcription factors. However, cAMP also regulates the activity of EPAC (a guanine-nucleotideexchange factor) and cyclic-nucleotide-gated ion channels.

Gαs is encoded by exons 1–13 of GNAS. Mutations can occur in any exon as well as intron/exon boundaries [57] and can be inher ited or occur spontaneously. The GNAS locus is highly complex given that it generates tran scripts for not only Gαs (exons 1–13) but also neuroendocrine secretory protein 55 (NESP55), extra-large alpha-stimulatory sub unit (XLαs), A/B (also called 1A), as well as an antisense transcript (AS). The A/B tran script may encode a truncated form of Gαs that can act in an inhibitory fashion, (for review, [21, 34–43]), [25, 27, 58–64]. The dif ferent transcripts are generated through the use of alternative first exons. The GNAS locus is controlled by genomic imprinting, which is regulated through differentially methylated regions (DMRs) that are within the promoter regions for each exon, except exon 1 of GNAS (which is part of the coding sequence for Gαs). The promoters for XLαs, AB, and AS are methylated on the maternal allele, thus lead ing to transcription predominantly from the paternal allele. Of note is that XLαs can act similarly to Gαs and even augment its action


## PDF page 568 | printed page 562

[64, 65]. NESP55, on the other hand, is meth ylated on the paternal allele resulting in expression predominantly from the maternal allele [25, 27]. Imprinting is often partial and leads to transcriptional repression of one allele. In particular, expression of Gαs tran scripts from the paternal allele is suppressed in certain tissues, many of which are endo crine. This is termed “paternal imprinting” because there is inhibition of transcription of the paternal allele. In other tissues, imprinting does not occur, leading to biallelic expression of both the maternal and paternal alleles. The development of PHP1A versus PPHP is dependent on the parent-of-origin of the mutant allele and is due to this mechanism of imprinting, specifically determined to be due to tissue-specific paternal imprinting based on investigations in humans as well as mouse models. In tissues in which imprinting plays a role, the consequences on clinical phenotype can be very different between the two condi tions [28, 29, 66–74], whereas in those tissues in which imprinting does not play a promi nent role, the clinical phenotypes can be simi lar [22–29], (for review, [32, 34–38, 40–43]).

The presence or absence of hormonal resistance in association with AHO was first determined through clinical analysis of family pedigrees, which revealed that mothers affected with either PHP1A or PPHP had children with PHP1A, whereas fathers with either PHP1A or PPHP had children with PPHP. It was eventually determined that patients with PHP1A have GNAS mutations on their maternally inherited allele, and those with PPHP carry mutations on their pater nally inherited allele, which led to the discov ery of the mechanisms involved [22–27]. This unique mode of inheritance was confirmed in murine models with a targeted disruption of Gnas, which revealed tissue-specific silencing of Gαs expression from the paternal allele [28, 29, 66].

Because the normal paternally inherited GNAS allele in PHP1A patients is suppressed in imprinted tissues (many of which are endocrine-related), the loss of Gαs from the abnormal maternal allele results in a near complete absence of Gαs. The severe defi ciency of Gαs impairs GPCR signal transduc

### 22

tion in these imprinted tissues and accounts for resistance to multiple hormones and neu rotransmitters. By contrast, hormone respon siveness is normal in cells in which the paternal GNAS allele is active, as the loss of Gαs from the defective maternal allele results in only a 50% reduction in Gαs protein. As demon strated in investigations both in humans and in murine models, the imprinting is partial with only modest expression of Gαs from the paternal GNAS allele in the renal proximal tubules, thyroid follicular epithelial cells, gonad cells, and pituitary somatotropes, thereby causing multihormone resistance to PTH, TSH, LH/FSH, and GHRH, respec tively [28, 29, 66–74]. Calcitonin resistance has also been reported [34–43, 75, 76], and there is suggestive evidence in an AHO mouse model that partial imprinting in osteoclasts may affect bone remodeling due to calcitonin resistance [77, 78]. In contrast to PHP1A, patients with paternally inherited GNAS mutations develop PPHP and do not develop hormone resistance. They are often small-forgestational-age (SGA) at birth. This may be due to decreased XLαs, which is normally expressed from the paternal allele and is thought to be important in fetal growth [34, 79, 80].

In addition to hormone resistance, patients with PHP1A are typically obese, especially characterized by marked early-onset obesity starting soon after birth, whereas those with PPHP are not severely obese [44]. This obser vation changed the classic description of AHO that had previously been thought to include obesity. In addition, this noted differ ence in the obesity phenotype in PHP1A ver sus PPHP raised the possibility of imprinting in the hypothalamus given that the melano cortin-4 receptor (MC4R) is Gαs-coupled. Investigations in mice demonstrated no imprinting in adipose tissue [29, 81], and it was eventually determined through continued work on mouse models that imprinting occurs in the dorsomedial hypothalamus, specifically in MC4R-expressing cells [82, 83]. Human studies have also revealed the lack of imprint ing in adipose [84]. Therefore, the evidence supports hypothalamic imprinting as an underlying cause of the obesity such that


## PDF page 569 | printed page 563

patients with PHP1A have hormone resis tance with severe obesity, whereas patients with PPHP do not have hormone resistance or obesity.

Although tissue-specific imprinting of GNAS leads to differences in the clinical phe notypes seen in PHP1A and PPHP, GNAS is biallelically expressed in other cell types and tissues, such as skin (fibroblasts), renal medulla, renal collecting ducts/ascending limb, adrenal, heart, nasal epithelia, lympho cytes, adipocytes, and chondrocytes, as has been demonstrated through both human and mouse investigations [11, 28, 29, 47, 66, 67, 70, 81, 84–90]. This biallelic expression results in clinical phenotypes that are shared between PHP1A and PPHP, specifically brachydactyly, shortened adult stature, and subcutaneous ossifications. These result from partial loss of Gαs activity in the specific cell types involved in which GNAS is biallelically expressed, such as chondrocytes in the case of brachydactyly and short stature. This would implicate that these phenotypes would be similar between PHP1A and PPHP because GNAS would be expressed equivalently in both.

Disorders besides PHP1A and PPHP can result from mutations in the GNAS locus. PHP1C presents clinically and biochemically in the same manner as PHP1A but is due to mutations that impair receptor coupling activ ity of Gαs but not its basal activity [26, 37–43]. It has been proposed by experts that PHP1C be removed from the nomenclature in the future [41, 42].

Other distinct conditions in the PHP spectrum that result from mutations in GNAS exons encoding Gαs specifically on the pater nal allele have heterotopic ossifications (HOs) as the predominant feature (for review, [34–43, 78]), [91–97]. One of these is progressive osse ous heteroplasia (POH), characterized by penetrating HOs as the main feature, typically without other physical features or hormonal resistance. There is also a very rare condition involving an overlap of both PHP1A and POH [98, 99], in which patients have features of both disorders. Finally, isolated osteoma cutis (OC) can occur, which is the clinical find ing of subcutaneous ossifications in isolation, also typically from mutations on the paternal

allele within the exons encoding Gαs. This can evolve into PPHP or POH over time (and even into PHP1A with hormonal resistance in rare circumstances when the SCOs are the only presenting sign and are inadvertently diag nosed as OC). POH and OC are typically caused by spontaneous mutations (unless the OC is representative of the early phase of PPHP and has been inherited) (for review, [34, 35, 37–43, 78]), [100–102].

Epigenetic defects within the GNAS gene cause PHP1B (for review [21, 30–43]), [19, 45–51]. All patients to date with PHP1B have a loss of methylation (LOM) within the Exon A/B DMR (specifically A/B:TSS-DMR) on the maternal GNAS allele. In most patients with familial PHP1B, the methylation defect is limited to LOM of exon A/B, but some cases of familial PHP1B and nearly all cases of sporadic PHP1B exhibit more extensive methylation defects that include LOM at the DMR for XLαs and gain of methylation (GOM) at the DMRs for NESP55. Approximately 15–20% of PHP1B is familial and due to maternal transmission of heterozy gous microdeletions within the maternal STX16 allele about 220 kb upstream of GNAS that include either STX16 exons 4–6 or exons 2–4, which presumably affect a cis-regulatory element that is important for methylation of the GNAS exon A/B DMR. The sporadic forms of PHP1B make up the majority of cases and tend to have more extensive meth ylation defects involving GNAS exon A/B:TSS-DMR and AS2:DMR in associa tion with methylation changes affecting vari ous alternative transcripts. Deletions within NESP and XL or paternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 20q (patUPD20q) have been identified in some PHP1B patients with global methylation defects (for review, [21, 36–38, 41–43, 103, 104]), [45–50, 105–111].

Although the prevalence of PHP overall is not truly known, this group of disorders is quite rare with three reported estimates rang ing from 0.34 to 1.1 per 100,000 [43, 116, 117]. However, the prevalence may be as high as 1:15,000–20,000 in the United States given that many patients with these disorders are misdiagnosed or go completely unrecognized. For example, PPHP is often completely missed until a mother has a child with PHP1A [40].

### 22.3.1 Nomenclature for PHP

### and Related Disorders

Each of the PHP and related disorders is cata logued in the Online Mendelian Inheritance of Man (OMIM) with a unique number [118] corresponding to the common terminology utilized for each condition. Because the names are descriptive in nature, the European con sortium for PHP (EuroPHP) proposed the term “inactivating PTH/PTHrP signaling dis order (iPPSD)” several years ago as an alter native to PHP [119, 120]. Based on this new clas sification, all disorders involving GNAS muta tions affecting the coding sequence, including PHP1A, PPHP, PHP1C, and POH, would instead be designated iPPSD2; PHP1B, which affects methylation of GNAS, would be desig nated iPPSD3; acrodysostosis type 1 (due to mutations in PRKAR1A) and acrodysostosis type 2 (due to mutations in PDE4D) would be designated iPPSD4 and iPPSD5, respectively. After this iPPSD classification system was proposed in 2016, the EuroPHP network assembled international experts in 2017 to develop the first international Consensus Statement on the diagnosis and management of PHP and related disorders. Published in 2018, this Consensus Statement has been a milestone in the field. It presents a detailed and well-organized approach to evaluate PHP and related disorders [38], with an updated practical tool to this Consensus Statement published in 2020 [42]. Before moving on to the clinical diagnosis and management of PHP as well as related disorders, the reader is directed not only to the 2018 international Consensus Statement and its update but also to several recent additional comprehensive reviews and guides that detail the etiologies and mechanisms [21, 36, 37, 39–41, 43].

The brachydactyly is thought to occur in approximately 70–80% of patients with this condition [38, 42, 121] and often involves metacarpals/metatarsals III, IV, and V (known as brachydactyly type E when multi ple metacarpals/metatarsals are affected) [122]. However, any metacarpal/metatarsal can be involved ( Fig. 22.3a–e). The distal phalanx of the thumb is affected in up to 75% of cases and is typically short and broad (when isolated this is referred to as brachydac tyly D) [121–123]. This finding is referred to as “potter’s thumb,” “stub thumb,” or “murder er’s thumb” ( Fig. 22.3a and c) [40]. The brachydactyly is usually not apparent in infancy and instead becomes more evident later in childhood, and it can be asymmetric between the two hands and feet ( Fig. 22.3a– e). By contrast, brachydactyly is usually obvi ous at birth in ACRDYS syndromes. Variability of brachydactyly in AHO, includ ing the effect on hand/foot size, can occur even among family members with the condi tion, as well as among nonfamily members with the same genotype, suggesting that there is not a direct genotype-phenotype correla tion [40, 100, 121]. Another skeletal feature present in AHO patients is Archibald’s sign, which is the absence of one or more knuckles upon making a fist and which occurs second ary to the shortened metacarpals. Often a dimple is observed in place of the knuckle ( Figs. 22.1d and 22.3e).

These physical features are often a key to unlocking the diagnosis, particularly for patients with PPHP, who may have been unaware of these specific abnormalities because they had not been considered to be medically significant or because they had gone unnoticed. Indeed, a common scenario is that a mother brings her child with PHP1A to the clinic, and she is then noticed to have skeletal features of AHO, leading to the diagnosis of PPHP in the mother. The brachydactyly and brachymetacarpia/brachymetatarsia can cause problems with both fine and gross motor activities as well as orthopedic issues [34, 38, 40, 124, 125], and early initiation of occupational and physical therapy can be helpful [40, 42, 125]. Occasionally patients

have one or two digits that are out of propor tion in length to the others and undergo surgi cal intervention, which is not advised; the irregularity in sizes between the various fin gers and toes seems to be easily adapted to over time with proper management, such as with customized shoes and orthotics. Occupational and physical therapy as well as management by podiatry and specialized shoe stores can be of great benefit. In addition, the hand abnormalities predispose these patients to develop carpal tunnel syndrome, which has been documented as being at an increased prevalence in both children and adults with PHP1A and PPHP; the overall prevalence of carpal tunnel syndrome in AHO for patients of all ages is 67%; in children, the prevalence is 36% [125]. The symptoms of carpal tunnel syndrome can mimic those of paresthesias secondary to hypocalcemia; therefore, it is important to follow up on these symptoms if the patient is normocalcemic, as early inter vention can prevent the need for surgery.

### 22.4.1.2 Adult Short Stature:

### Premature Epiphyseal Fusion and Bone Age Evaluation

Another physical feature in AHO is short stat ure at the time that final adult height is attained. The short stature in adulthood (or late adolescence) is thought to be largely due to premature epiphyseal fusion of the long bones as a result of accelerated chondrocyte differentiation, just as described for the brachydactyly [85–88]. This process seems to be accentuated at the onset of puberty. The mean final height of adults with PHP1A with out intervention is more than 2.5 standard deviations below the mean (146.3 +/− 8.0 cm for women and 158.1 cm +/− 6.7 cm for men) [37, 38, 40, 126, 127].

### 22.4.2 Pseudohypoparathyroidism

### Type 1A (PHP1A): iPPSD2, OMIM #103580

Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A is charac terized by multihormone resistance and obe sity with features of the AHO phenotype. The next section will discuss the hormonal resis tances followed by several other important clinical features of PHP1A along with appro priate treatment and management strategies.

### 22.4.2.1 Parathyroid Hormone (PTH)

### Resistance

PTH resistance is the hallmark of pseudohy poparathyroidism and can lead to hypocalce mia and hyperphosphatemia. Because both hypoparathyroidism and pseudohypoparathy roidism are characterized by hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia, it is important to dif ferentiate these two entities. In hypoparathy roidism, there is insufficient production of PTH by the parathyroid glands, leading to low, undetectable, or inappropriately normal PTH levels. There is a normal response to the administration of PTH in terms of increased urinary excretion of cAMP and phosphate. In pseudohypoparathyroidism, on the other hand, there is end-organ resistance to PTH,

### 22

resulting in increased PTH levels, with a lack of response to PTH administration and a blunted or absent urinary excretion of cAMP and phosphate. Although PTH resistance clas sically manifests as the association of elevated PTH levels, hyperphosphatemia, and hypocal cemia, it must be diagnosed in the setting of normal 25-hydroxyvitamin D and magnesium levels, as well as normal renal function. Otherwise, the diagnosis is not definitive.

In PHP1A, the PTH resistance is often not present at birth but develops later in child hood, typically in the elementary school years (approximately 7–8 years of age) [37, 40, 41, 137]. A typical sequence is that the PTH eleva tion is accompanied by hyperphosphatemia initially and is then followed by hypocalcemia. The delay in the onset of PTH resistance in PHP1A is thought to be secondary to the pro gressive loss of GNAS expression in the proxi mal convoluted renal tubules due to paternal imprinting [28, 29, 67, 137, 138]. Because imprinting occurs only in the proximal tubules and not in the collecting ducts or ascending limb based on mouse models [28, 29, 67], it is thought that hypercalciuria is rarely observed in PHP1A since calcium reabsorption in the distal parts of the kidney is unaffected. As a result, nephrocalcinosis and renal stones are rarely seen. Renal ultrasounds are deemed necessary only if there is hypercalciuria or symptoms, although measuring a urine [calcium]:[creatinine] ratio is prudent at least once a year [34, 35, 38, 40, 139].

If PTH resistance is untreated, the PTH will continue to rise along with the phosphate, and hypocalcemia will ensue. Because the pro gression of hypocalcemia can be very gradual with adaptation to symptoms, patients can often present to the outpatient clinic with PTH levels in the 300 pg/mL range and serum calcium levels significantly below 2 mmol/L. In those patients previously undiagnosed, the initial presentation can sometimes be hypo calcemic seizures due to prolonged PTH resis tance leading to a gradual decline in calcium, which may be unnoticed until it reaches criti cally low levels. Therefore, it is of utmost importance that PTH resistance be diagnosed early and treated appropriately upon its pre sentation. In addition, over time, hyperphos

phatemia can lead to ectopic calcifications from an elevated calcium x phosphate prod uct. This entity is distinct from the SCOs typi cal of AHO, and when these calcifications occur, they are most commonly observed in the basal ganglia and/or lens of the eye. Dyskinesia is very rarely reported [34, 37, 38, 41, 42, 140, 141]. Finally, if PTH resistance is undertreated, there can be excessive bone resorption due to persistently elevated PTH levels, and monitoring of bone health is important (discussed in a later section).

It is crucial to start treatment with acti vated vitamin D early as soon as PTH resis tance is detected, such as with calcitriol or alfacalcidol. Calcitriol can be given in a liquid form in order to titrate the dose appropriately since the capsules are in standard increments and cannot be fine-tuned. This is especially important in treating infants and young chil dren who often need doses below the lower limits of the standardized microgram amount per capsule. In addition, the liquid is easier for children to swallow and can be mixed with drinks or food. The goal of therapy with cal citriol should be to keep PTH levels in the high normal range or even slightly above nor mal since over-suppression of PTH can lead to an increased risk of hypercalciuria and the development of renal stones/nephrocalcinosis. Due to its half-life, calcitriol should be given every 12 hours in order to maintain steadystate levels. In the initial phases of treatment when PTH levels may be particularly elevated, doses of calcitriol may need to be increased beyond normal treatment doses to lower the PTH. Once the PTH is near the desired range, the calcitriol can be appropriately lowered. During periods of rapid growth such as dur ing infancy and puberty, the dose often needs to be increased fairly frequently, and it is best to check PTH, calcium, and phosphate levels approximately every 3 months. In later childhood, if laboratory results seem stable, the testing can shift to every 6 months; this is advised for adults as well.

It is also important to maintain serum cal cium in the normal range based on ageappropriate normal values. If there is significant hypocalcemia, calcium supple

mentation should be given appropriately to the degree of deficiency either orally with meals or intravenously in times of crisis. For oral supplementation, calcium carbonate is the preferred formulation for absorption and should be taken at least twice a day with meals. Calcium citrate is another appropriate option. Typically, calcium supplements can be weaned from the initial doses needed at the time of diagnosis and even tapered off totally over time as long as the dietary amounts of calcium are adequate. For base line outpatient management at times of good control, it is ideal that appropriate amounts of calcium be taken in through the diet, and excess dietary phosphate intake should be limited. It is of utmost importance that the calcium, phosphate, and PTH levels be fol lowed at routine intervals (approximately every 3 months) because, in younger children, changes can occur even in a time period of several months. As part of this follow-up, as mentioned previously, it is best to screen urine [calcium]:[creatinine] ratios at least once a year (and more often if any abnormal ity) in spite of the low risk of hypercalciuria.

It is recommended that a maintenance dose of 25-hydroxyvitamin D be provided as cholecalciferol, although ergocalciferol can also be used. In addition to the age of the patient, factors such as skin pigmentation, body mass index, and exposure to sunlight should be taken into account since dark skin, obesity, and staying indoors are all risk fac tors for vitamin D deficiency. Levels of 25-hydroxyvitamin D should be monitored at least twice a year.

### 22.4.2.2 Thyroid-Stimulating

### Hormone (TSH) Resistance

TSH resistance is also very commonly associ ated with PTH resistance in PHP1A—in fact, most of the time. The resistance leads to mildly elevated TSH levels (approximately 14 ± 10 mIU/L [37]) with normal to slightly low thyroxine/free thyroxine levels and with out an associated goiter. Both mouse and human studies have revealed that there is par tial imprinting in the thyroid, with approxi mately 26–40% expression of the paternal


## PDF page 582 | printed page 576

allele, thereby providing a likely explanation as to why the TSH resistance is mild com pared to the PTH resistance that occurs in the renal proximal tubules [29, 68–70].

An elevated TSH is sometimes detected in infants with PHP1A at the time of the new born screen and incorrectly interpreted as congenital hypothyroidism [34, 35, 37–43, 142, 143]. The presence of SCOs in an infant with a “positive” newborn screen for congeni tal hypothyroidism should immediately sug gest an extremely high probability of the diagnosis of PHP1A. In addition, if an infant or child is successfully treated with levothy roxine based on normalization of the thyroid function tests but continues to have excessive weight gain despite adequate treatment, then the possible diagnosis of PHP1A should be considered. In any infant in whom the diagno sis of PHP1A is being suspected, a PTH level should be checked, although there is typically no evidence of PTH resistance in infancy or early childhood, as previously described.

Even with a mild elevation of TSH, thy roxine or free thyroxine levels should be mea sured and treatment started with the goal of achieving hormone levels in the normal range. Because of the developmental and cognitive consequences of hypothyroidism in infancy and early childhood, thyroid function tests should be monitored very closely. In child hood, monitoring should occur at least every 3 months, especially as children are growing, although infants should be checked much more frequently. In adolescence and adult hood, follow-up laboratory tests can be extended to every 6 months–1 year depending on the stability of the laboratory results and length of time on a consistent dose.

### 22.4.2.3 Luteinizing Hormone (LH)

### and Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH) Resistance

Patients with PHP1A, both males and females, have evidence of partial hypogonad ism presumably secondary to the imprinting of GNAS in the gonads [70, 74]. Elevated LH/ FSH levels would be expected in the setting of gonadotropin resistance, but this is not

### 22

consistently observed and therefore not gen erally helpful in the evaluation [34, 40, 74, 144–146]. Physical examination typically reveals evidence of pubertal development at the usual time, but the pubertal progression is incomplete, most notably in females with breast development halting at Tanner Stage III–IV. Early breast development is often hard to detect in females who have severe obesity. Other signs of hypogonadism that are frequently observed in PHP1A females are amenorrhea or oligomenorrhea [34, 37, 38, 40–42, 74]. Low-dose estrogen therapy is often needed; however, one should be aware of the potential risk of DVT formation due to the common predisposing factors of severe obesity and limited physical activity [40]. Severe obesity in females with PHP1A can also be a complicating issue in contributing to amenorrhea/oligomenorrhea. In addition, polycystic ovarian syndrome is evident in a subset of females with PHP1A, which can be accompanied by clinical and laboratory evi dence of insulin resistance as well as meta bolic syndrome (as discussed in the section on obesity).

Although not as recognizable, boys also have evidence of incomplete pubertal progres sion on physical exam by Tanner staging, again halted at Tanner Stage III–IV, and there is sometimes a delay in secondary sexual char acteristics. A greater risk of cryptorchidism in PHP1A has been reported [37, 38, 41, 74], which can also lead to pubertal issues. A urol ogy consult is advisable. In adulthood, symp toms of testosterone insufficiency can occur.

Fertility has been difficult to assess in PHP1A given that there are often associated cognitive and social impairments that limit potential opportunities for having children. Although human studies are lacking, previ ously described mouse studies in an AHO mouse model indicate that fertility is impacted for both males and females [29]. In humans, both males and females with PHP1A have been reported to have children [38, 40, 42, 74, 147]. In specific cases in which pregnancy has been pursued, reproductive endocrinology involvement is helpful and usually necessary.

### 22.4.2.4 Growth Hormone-Releasing

### Hormone (GHRH) Resistance

In addition to premature fusion of the epiphy ses, another contributing factor to adult short stature in PHP1A is GH deficiency as a result of GHRH resistance secondary to partial imprinting of GNAS in the pituitary, specifi cally causing a deficient response in pituitary somatotropes [71]. GH deficiency occurs in approximately 70% of patients with PHP1A [34, 40, 72, 73, 127], and it is usually partial, although severe deficiency can be observed. It is important to reiterate that most children with PHP1A are NOT short. Therefore, GH deficiency needs to be considered even if chil dren are of normal or tall stature. Because GH deficiency is so common, it is standard of care to perform GH stimulation testing in all patients with PHP1A [34, 38, 40, 42, 72, 127, 148]. Treatment with recombinant growth hormone (rGH) is within approved guidelines for those who are found to be GH-deficient [38, 40, 72, 127, 149]. Testing for GH status, as well as rGH treatment for GH-deficient PHP1A patients (provided that there are no risk factors), is also currently supported by the international Consensus Statement, for which experts worldwide established uniform guidelines for management of pseudohypo parathyroidism [38] (also reviewed in [40–42]).

The mean adult height of untreated GH-deficient adults with PHP1A is signifi cantly shorter than for PHP1A adults who are GH-sufficient, consistent with GH deficiency contributing to the short stature. Although GH deficiency contributes to short stature in approximately 2/3 of patients with PHP1A, premature fusion of the epiphyses also has a large impact on final adult height, as previ ously discussed. It is important to note that although rGH treatment can increase growth velocity and height short term [34, 72, 127,

149], the long-term efficacy of rGH treatment with respect to stature can truly only be assessed once the final height has been achieved in a large cohort in the setting of premature epiphyseal closure. The effects of rGH treatment on final height in GH-deficient children with PHP1A are being assessed in a long-term prospective clinical trial that has been ongoing for close to two decades [38, 40, 150]. Given that even without GH deficiency, children with PHP1A still have a short final adult height, a longitudinal prospective study of GH-sufficient PHP1A children treated with rGH is also being analyzed in order to determine the effect on final adult height while increasing growth velocity maximally with rGH before growth plate closure [150]. There are no definitive studies addressing the use of aromatase inhibitors or GnRH analogs in AHO.

### 22.4.2.5 Calcitonin Resistance

### and Bone Mineral Density/ Bone Remodeling

Calcitonin resistance has also been reported in patients with PHP1A, although it typically does not present clinically in a manner requir ing treatment. Calcitonin resistance exhibit ing hypercalcitoninemia, both with and without pentagastrin stimulation, has been reported in isolated cases in the literature [75, 76, 160–164], but its prevalence may be higher based on the experiences of experts who took part in the international Consensus Statement for PHP and related disorders [38]. Although the effects of calcitonin resistance itself do not usually require treatment, it is important to exclude the diagnosis of medullary thyroid carcinoma.

Investigations in both humans and mice have revealed that regulation of bone remod eling is impacted by paternal imprinting and results in effects on bone mineral density (BMD) [77, 78, 165]. Specifically, recent evi dence from studies in an AHO mouse model [77] indicates that the parental origin of a mutant Gnas allele can differentially affect bone remodeling, with data suggesting that this may be due to partial calcitonin resistance in osteoclasts [77, 78]. Based on these studies, it appears that calcitonin resistance may potentially contribute to the bone density phenotype that has been observed in patients with PHP1A [77, 78, 165]. It had been thought in the past that these patients may be more prone to low BMD due to PTH resistance being specific to renal proximal tubules but not bone. However, it became clear based on studies in a large cohort of PHP1A patients evaluated with dual-energy x-ray absorptiom etry (DXA) scans that BMD is instead nor mal or increased and that early osteopenia/ osteoporosis is not of clinical concern [165].

### 22.4.2.6 Other Hormone Resistances

Glucagon resistance has also been reported but does not have the striking features of other hormonal resistances; it is not as com mon and does not have obvious clinical conse quences. ACTH and vasopressin resistance are not seen, presumably as a result of cells that express the receptors for these hormones exhibiting biallelic expression of GNAS [28, 29, 38, 40, 41, 67, 70].

### 22.4.2.7 Obesity

Obesity in AHO had been classically described as being similar in both PHP1A and PPHP according to Fuller Albright’s original description many decades ago [1, 2]. However, approximately 15 years ago, it became clear that severe obesity is a feature solely of PHP1A [44]. Although birthweight is slightly below the mean, early-onset obesity is signifi cant and is often one of the first signs of PHP1A [34, 37–41, 44, 126, 127, 167]. There is a striking increase in BMI through the first two years of life. Severe obesity often contin ues throughout the lifespan, though seem ingly less pronounced in adulthood, with women tending to be heavier than men [34, 37, 40, 41, 44, 126].

Multiple factors have been identified that may contribute to the development of obesity in PHP1A, a major one being hypothalamic imprinting. The observation that severe obe sity is present in PHP1A but not PPHP was the first indication that imprinting may be involved [44]. Investigations in both humans and mice revealed that obesity was not due to imprinting in adipose tissue [29, 81, 84]. Further studies in mice led to the finding that paternal imprinting of Gnas in MC4Rexpressing cells of the dorsomedial hypothal amus plays a major role in the development of

obesity and that imprinting was indeed involved. In addition, these studies revealed that Gαs is necessary to control energy bal ance, thermogenesis, and peripheral glucose metabolism; however, there was no effect on food intake [82, 83]. It had previously been demonstrated that morbid obesity can be seen without evidence of hyperphagia in PHP1A patients. In addition, studies revealed that hyperphagia does not play a significant role in the rapid weight gain seen during childhood which is instead due to a decrease in resting energy expenditure [44, 168–172]. Other con tributing factors toward obesity include peripheral resistance to epinephrine, low sym pathetic nervous system activity, and decreased lipolysis [44, 173–175]. In addition, GH deficiency in approximately 2/3 of patients can contribute to the obesity phenotype in PHP1A [40, 72, 127].

Concomitant with the obesity, adults with PHP1A also exhibit higher rates of type 2 dia betes along with reduced insulin sensitivity, even compared to obese controls. This impli cates that the reduced insulin sensitivity could contribute to the pathogenesis of glucose intolerance and that obesity is not the sole cause [173]. Children with PHP1A are at high risk for dysglycemia but do not appear to have reduced insulin sensitivity; they appear to have lower hemoglobin A1c (HgbA1c) levels compared to controls [172]. Metabolic syn drome also occurs in both children and adults with PHP1A. Lipid profiles are not markedly affected [172, 176], although patients have the classic profiles observed in obesity. Most stud ies have not found an increased risk of hyper tension [169, 172, 173]. Therefore, the relationship between obesity and metabolic effects in patients with PHP1A is complex, and further investigations are clearly needed. In terms of the implications of obesity and type 2 diabetes, patients with PHP1A have a normal life expectancy [116] consistent with findings in the mouse model [29].

Treatment of obesity is one of the most challenging issues for PHP1A patients and families. Dietary management and exercise are helpful, but the decreased resting energy expenditure makes obesity very difficult to control. Exercise needs to be encouraged but


## PDF page 588 | printed page 582

at a pace that will be maintained. Therefore, this should be started slowly from a young age and advanced with routine monitoring. It is also important to monitor fasting glucose lev els and HgbA1c intermittently. In addition, obesity is a common predisposing factor to OSA. If snoring develops, sleep studies and ENT evaluations may be indicated, especially because central apnea can also be present as an additional underlying condition that can compound the risks. Of note, the prevalence of sleep apnea in PHP1A (including both OSA and central apnea) seems to be increased disproportionately compared to what might be expected due to obesity alone, which may result from craniofacial issues along with an increased prevalence of hypotonia and asthma [40, 124, 151, 152].

### 22.4.2.8 Craniofacial and Dental

### Abnormalities

Craniofacial abnormalities are common in patients with PHP1A [38, 40, 153, 177]. These may make them more prone to otitis media in addition to OSA, perhaps secondary to the mid-face hypoplasia, a relatively common finding [124, 151]. In fact, the “very round face” noted in the initial description of PHP by Fuller Albright [1] could be related to cra niofacial abnormalities; the face appears fuller and flatter in the setting of a smaller cranial vault and midface hypoplasia. Recent studies in a mouse model of AHO revealed a smaller cranial vault, increased cranial dome angle, and premature closure of the sphenooccipital synchondrosis (SOS), all of which are independent of the parental origin of the mutant allele [153]. It is known that prema ture SOS closure can lead to midface hypopla sia in a variety of syndromes and that it correlates directly with the severity [178–181]; this could also be a factor in the craniofacial findings in AHO. Craniosynostosis can also be a complication in PHP1A [37, 38, 40, 41, 153], and it is known to be associated with premature SOS fusion [179, 181].

In addition, Chiari malformation type 1 (CM1) is observed in PHP1A and can be an issue that leads to significant neurologic sequelae [37, 38, 40–42, 153]. Specifically, a

### 22

recent investigation revealed that CM1 (including low-lying cerebellar tonsils) occurs at a prevalence at least 20-fold higher in patients with PHP1A compared to the general population [153]. The abnormal cranial devel opment in the AHO mouse model as previ ously described provides a potential etiology for this increased prevalence of CM1/lowlying cerebellar tonsils [153]. Specifically, cra nial hyperostosis is a prominent feature in PHP1A, even commented on extensively in Albright’s first description in which the authors noted “marked density of the skull.” [1, 38, 40, 129, 153] This cranial hyperostosis, which had been demonstrated to be second ary to increased osteogenesis in the AHO mouse model, was observed only when the Gnas mutation was inherited maternally, con sistent with imprinting [153]. Thus, cranial thickening could potentially be an added factor impacting CM1 development in PHP1A and is also consistent with the increased BMD identified in the condition [77, 153, 165]. Of note is that investigations of cranial synchondroses of Pthlh/Pthrp-deletion mice revealed chondrocyte differentiation that is significantly accelerated compared to chon drocytes in long bones, which provides an eti ology for the greater impact on cranial development compared to the long bones in those mice [181–184]. This is consistent with what is observed phenotypically in both the AHO mouse model and patients with PHP1A, perhaps explaining the significant craniofacial abnormalities compared to the lesser impact on long bones.

Given the increased prevalence of CM1, it is important to monitor patients with PHP1A for potential neurological signs and symp toms, especially because early interventions can improve outcomes greatly. In addition, because approximately 2/3 of patients with PHP1A develop GH deficiency and are poten tially treated with rGH, it is important to dis tinguish headaches caused by benign intracranial hypertension from those caused by CM1 if a patient is on rGH therapy. Careful examination for the possible presence of CM1 and low-lying cerebellar tonsils is encouraged when brain imaging is performed

### 22.4.2.10 CNS: Cognitive/Behavioral

### and Neurodevelopmental Abnormalities

Cognitive issues were noted within the initial description of patients with PHP1A (then referred to as PHP) by Albright and col leagues in 1942. In 1986, Farfel and Friedman reported that cognitive impairment was asso ciated with reductions in Gαs levels in patients with PHP1A affected with intellectual disabil ity [201]. Over the ensuing years, further stud ies demonstrated that as many as 79% of patients with PHP1A have cognitive impair ment [38, 202]. In general, it is now estimated that at least 1/2 to 2/3 of patients with PHP1A are affected, ranging from minimal to severe learning disabilities [34, 37, 38, 40, 43, 203–205] often requiring early interventions and therapies in grade school and beyond [34, 40, 204, 205]. Studies of children with PHP1A have revealed lower IQ scores (full scale, non verbal, and verbal) and impaired behavioral, adaptive, attention, and/or executive function, along with both verbal and nonverbal com promise; in addition, ADHD and autism spectrum disorders are common in PHP1A and can compromise learning and social func

### 22

tion [34, 40, 204, 205]. There can often be fre quent episodes of anxiety and emotional outbursts. In general, patients with PHP1A have a wide range of functioning in school during childhood, affected by both the cogni tive and behavioral issues. Various levels of education are completed depending on the degree of dysfunction, and individualized educational plans are very common [40, 205].

Patients with PPHP appear to have overall higher educational and social functioning as adults than those with PHP1A [40]. Cognitive testing in a single kindred with AHO showed that PHP1A family members were more affected than those with PPHP [202], although this study was limited by a small cohort and by the use of a single measure for cognitive function. Specific CNS abnormalities, such as with olfaction, hearing, and taste, have also been reported in PHP1A patients and are not present in PPHP patients [206–209], thereby raising the possibility that imprinting could be involved. In addition, mothering behavior has been shown to be impaired in mice carry ing a Gnas deletion on their maternally inher ited allele (PHP1A) but not in mice carrying a paternally inherited mutant Gnas allele (PPHP) [29, 34]. All of these studies suggest an important role for paternal imprinting in the CNS for which further investigation is needed comparing cognitive and behavioral function in PHP1A versus PPHP [150].

The impact on cognition and behavior in PHP1A can be one of the most difficult aspects of this disorder for both the patients and their families. Early intervention pro grams are extremely important, as are appro priate developmental evaluations and rehabilitation involvement, such as with occupational, physical, and speech therapies [205]. This is especially the case in light of underlying issues with fine and gross motor delay as well as speech apraxia [40, 125, 204, 205]. Hypotonia is noted in some children and can lead to gross motor delay. Once in school, it is important to have educational support with individual educational and learning plans as needed. It is best if these plans are based on neurocognitive and psy

chosocial testing by a professional with exper tise in the area in order to have the most appropriate interventions and school place ments. Issues of self-esteem often arise during the elementary school years due to develop mental and educational delays as well as the phenotypic stigmata that can be visually apparent. Psychological counseling as well as family support are crucial [38, 40, 210]. The cognitive, behavioral, and social issues can lead to difficulty with living independently as an adult, as will be discussed next.

### 22.4.2.11 Transition to Adult Care

Transition to adult care is an especially diffi cult time for patients with PHP1A. It is hard to find specialists in the field, and work should be done ahead of time so that there is a smooth transition. Some clinics allow the pediatric specialist to follow the patient into adulthood, but plans need to be made well ahead if this will not be possible in order to transition to another healthcare provider. In PHP1A, part of the provider’s role is to advo cate for help with disability issues and support of activities of daily living when no longer under their parents’ care. In fact, the concern about independent living is one of the greatest that families have on a daily basis [40]. Many patients with the disorder live with their fami lies long-term or transition to group homes. They can have difficulty completing high school and only occasionally attend college depending on the level of learning disability. There can also be difficulty in maintaining jobs. The medical provider can provide sup port in laying out appropriate guidelines for educational choices and part-time job place ments that can help to achieve gradual inde pendence along with the help of the school, employer, and social work. Over the past decade, there have been an increasing number of colleges and jobs that provide a great deal of support to help patients with cognitive and social challenges, typically requiring a letter from the provider on the specific disabilities involved. In this regard, advocacy is a very important part of the clinical management of

PHP1A in order to maximize the quality of life for these patients [38, 40, 210].

### 22.4.3 Pseudohypoparathyroidism

### Type 1C (PHP1C): iPPSD2, OMIM #612462

Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1C (PHP1C) presents identically to PHP1A, but the AHO features are generally milder. PHP1C is due to mutations that affect receptor coupling of Gαs, specifically thought to be due to mutations in exon 13 (last exon) of the maternally derived GNAS allele [26, 38, 40–43]. Testing to separate PHP1C from PHP1A is impractical, and it has been proposed that PHP1C be removed from the nomenclature [37, 38, 40–42]. The manage ment is the same as for PHP1A.

### 22.4.4 Pseudopseudohypoparathy

### roidism (PPHP): iPPSD2, OMIM #612463

PPHP patients have the clinical phenotype of AHO involving brachydactyly, adult short stature, and SCOs, although all three of these features do not need to be present in order to make the diagnosis. This condition has been discussed in detail in the previous sections. An important feature to note is that infants with PPHP are often born SGA [80], which can be a helpful sign in overall clinical diagnosis. Recombinant GH treatment can be consid ered for the FDA-approved indication of SGA if the patient meets the appropriate cri teria, but there are no published data at pres ent in terms of the impact on height.

Because hormonal resistance and brachy dactyly are often absent clinically in infants and young children with PHP1A, it is difficult to discriminate PPHP from PHP1A at these early ages. For example, this is the case if the diagno sis is based on the finding of SCOs. The defini tive diagnosis of PPHP can only be made if there is known inheritance of either PHP1A or PPHP in the family or if the mutation is deter

mined to be on the paternal GNAS allele (see section on “Molecular Diagnosis”). If the diag nosis is not fully determined, the child should be monitored closely for signs of PHP1A devel oping, such as hormone resistance or signifi cant cognitive impairment; if the child has SCOs, it is also important to monitor because POH can emerge.

Patients with PPHP have shorter final adult heights than what is genetically predicted [34, 37, 38, 40–44, 127] due to the premature epiph yseal fusion, as previously described. (This genetically predicted height applies only to those with a spontaneous mutation, as this clearly cannot be estimated if the father has PPHP or PHP1A.) A blunted pubertal growth spurt also contributes to the adult short stat ure even though there are no associated hor monal abnormalities [40, 126]. Hand/wrist bone ages are often advanced and not indica tive of early puberty, and height predictions cannot be performed due to the variability in tempo of the premature fusion of the growth plates as in PHP1A [40]. In general, the adult short stature in PPHP ranges from approxi mately −1.9 to −2.26 standard deviations below the mean based on various investiga tions [38, 44, 126]. The data for longitudinal growth in children and adolescents with PPHP are lacking in comparison to the data for PHP1A [126] since the diagnosis of PPHP often goes unrecognized until adulthood, most notably at the time that a mother with unno ticed PPHP has a child with PHP1A [40].

### 22.4.5 Pseudohypoparathyroidism

### Type 1B (PHP1B): iPPSD3, OMIM # 603233

As previously discussed, PHP1B is also due to a GNAS defect, specifically due to loss of meth ylation (detailed in “Etiology and Mechanisms”). PHP1B patients do not have the associated AHO physical features or cognitive abnormalities observed in PHP1A, although they can occasionally have subtle brachydactyly on clinical examination. As in PHP1A, patients with PHP1B exhibit PTH resistance, and there is occasional mild TSH resistance with normal

### 22

Symptoms of hypocalcemia such as pares thesias, tetany, or a Chvostek sign in an other wise normal child or adolescent who is found to have an elevated PTH (with normal 25-hydroxyvitamin D and magnesium levels) are likely due to PHP1B. In addition, hypocal cemic seizures can be the first presentation simply because there are often no suspicious physical features, and the symptoms of hypo calcemia can be subtle and/or gradual. The biochemical features can develop very slowly over time, and because of this prolonged slow decline in serum calcium and acclimation to these levels, the hypocalcemia can often be very pronounced by the time of clinical pre sentation. As a result, these patients can pres ent in the teenage years. In addition, patients with PHP1B tend to present with hypocalce mic seizures more commonly than in PHP1A, specifically because there are no clinical fea tures to trigger a workup.

Patients with PHP1B have been found to have early-onset obesity similar to PHP1A [38, 40, 41, 126, 211]. However, they often have macrosomia at birth, whereas infants with PHP1A have birthweights that are slightly below the mean [37, 38, 40–44, 126, 211]. Therefore, a diagnosis of PHP1B should be considered in the setting of early-onset obesity. Patients with PHP1B also have an increased BMI in childhood, and they are overweight/obese as adults but not as severe as for PHP1A. Dietary control is important, as obesity can be an issue from infancy through adulthood.

There is typically no evidence of GHRH resistance in PHP1B [38, 42, 51]. There can be an increased growth velocity in childhood associated with the increased weight. Final height does not seem to be compromised (and if so, minimally), although there can be a shortened or absent pubertal growth spurt [126, 212]. Early in life, when obesity seems to be more obvious, an advanced bone age can be seen [38, 42, 126, 212] (approximately

Gonadal develop ment, fertility, cognition, and social function ing all appear to be unaffected [38, 40–43], although there are rare case reports of neuro cognitive issues [38, 213]. Mild brachydactyly is seen in some cases of PHP1B as previously described and is estimated to be present in approximately 15–33% of patients [42]. SCOs are not thought to be part of this condition [37, 40, 41, 100]. Although micronodular ossi fications have been reported on rare occasions [41, 47], none have been seen by the authors.

A close examination of a large cohort of patients with PHP1B evaluating bone mark ers and DXA scan data revealed the impor tance of maintaining normal PTH levels in order to avoid adverse effects on bone [214]. Because of the prolonged periods that can occur before diagnosis, PHP1B patients can suffer from bone pain as well as skeletal defor mities, which can even resemble rickets. Brown tumors and tertiary hyperparathyroidism can also occur [37, 38, 41, 42]. Teeth can be affected [192, 194], and routine dental followup is important.

Treatment for PTH and TSH resistance in PHP1B is the same as outlined for PHP1A. There should be routine monitoring of laboratory tests for PTH, calcium, phos phorous, and thyroid function as well as appropriate follow-up of bone health markers.

Additionally, it will be important to determine the true preva lence of GHRH resistance in these acrodysos tosis syndromes, as this remains unclear [217].

Finally, a separate condition resulting from mutations in PDE3A is characterized by brachydactyly type E concomitant with hyper tension [219]. PDE3A catalyzes the hydrolysis of cAMP and cGMP.

### 22.4.8 Molecular Diagnosis

As described in the preceding sections, the spectrum of pseudohypoparathyroidism and related disorders comprises a group of condi tions that have a unique yet overlapping set of clinical phenotypes. Additionally, many of these disorders have clinical signs, symptoms, and biochemical/hormonal profiles that change over the lifespan. In many cases, the diagnosis of these disorders can be narrowed down significantly based on family history, physical examination, laboratory testing, and imaging even before performing mutation analysis. However, as is evident throughout this chapter, patients with PHP and related disorders can have findings consistent with more than one condition. Therefore, genetic testing can be quite helpful in several respects.

First, in some cases, the clinical diagnosis can be inconclusive. This especially pertains to PHP and related disorders since the range


## PDF page 596 | printed page 590

of phenotypes can be variable, both in terms of the age of onset of clinical and laboratory features as well as the severity of signs and symptoms. As discussed earlier, patients can sometimes be given a diagnosis consistent with one disorder, which is subsequently amended as additional clinical features develop or become apparent over time. Therefore, identification of the specific genetic alteration is important in order to confirm the diagnosis of the patient. Second, knowing the specific mutation can provide information for current and future family members since tar geted testing for the specific region of the affected gene can be performed if needed for their own evaluations or future evaluations; this saves both time and money as well. In this respect, prenatal diagnosis is also possible, and collaborations with geneticists and genetic counselors can be very helpful. Third, and important going forward into the future, genetic testing can reveal the severity of the mutation, which can be useful in a general sense in anticipating the severity of certain clinical features based on genotype-phenotype correlations, such as the correlation observed with subcutaneous ossifications [100]. Although genotype-phenotype correlations are not available for many of the clinical issues observed in PHP and related disorders, more of these correlations may evolve with the greater availability and sophistication of molecular testing over the past decade and with scientific investigations continually advancing.

Genetic testing for diagnostic purposes is available for most of the PHP and related dis orders in multiple commercial CLIAapproved laboratories through targeted testing and sequencing of key genes, such as GNAS, PRKAR1A, PDE4D, and PDE3A, that are discussed in this chapter (for review, [38–43]). Methylation analysis, as well as test ing for STX16 deletions to confirm the diag nosis of PHP1B, can also be performed in CLIA-approved laboratories, although meth ylation testing is not always routinely avail able. A small percentage of sporadic PHP1B is due to patUPD20q, which can also be assessed. If determination of the parental ori

### 22

gin of the mutant allele is important for diag nostic purposes, a simple approach is to perform genetic testing on the parents or other family members. In cases in which this is not possible due to adoption or spontaneous mutations, analysis of the parental origin of the mutation from patient RNA can be per formed in a research laboratory for investiga tional purposes. Finally, although there are instances in which the diagnosis of these dis orders is identified by whole exome (or genome) sequencing, these tests are not typi cally needed for diagnostic purposes if a thor ough clinical workup has been completed, including a detailed history, physical examina tion, and laboratory/radiologic evaluation. However, on occasion, these more extensive analyses are truly necessary and can prove to be quite helpful.

### 22.5 Summary

Remarkable advances have been made toward understanding the mechanisms underlying the PHP spectrum ever since its initial descrip tion by Fuller Albright and colleagues approximately eight decades ago. Through both clinical and laboratory investigations, the phenotypes have been elucidated in more detail, and the mechanisms of the multiple clinical issues have been unfolding, such as for the multihormone resistance, adult short stat ure, brachydactyly, subcutaneous ossifica tions, obesity and metabolic disturbances, craniofacial and dental abnormalities, aber rant bone regulation, and cognitive/behav ioral impairments that are often a part of these conditions. As more knowledge has continually been gained from clinical and lab oratory investigations, the diagnosis, treat ment, and management for these patients have improved immensely, as has the aware ness of these conditions overall. Due to the evolving nature of the clinical issues in PHP and related disorders as well as their complex ities, constant attention to early intervention, close follow-up, and long-term management is key to the overall health and quality of life for patients with these conditions.

The congeni tal hypothyroidism is an important piece of information; it is often a misdiagno sis and instead represents TSH resistance in an infant with PHP1A. paragraphs.text: While many principles from the adult osteoporosis literature can be adapted to chil dren, the development of the mature skeleton is nevertheless a complex, multi-decade pro cess that gives rise to unique considerations. Some of these differences have been unearthed through long-term natural history studies using standard, widely available evaluative tools, while others have been demonstrated through more recent developments such as peripheral quantitative computed tomogra phy (pQCT) and trans-iliac bone histomor phometry. Knowledge of paediatric-specific principles and their biological basis is essen tial when developing logical management decisions in the young.

The purpose of this chapter is to review evidence that shapes the current approach to diagnosis, monitoring and treatment of osteoporosis in childhood, with particular emphasis on the key biological principles that are pivotal to the overall approach, and on the main questions that clinicians face during routine care. The scope of this article spans a review of the specific disorders and risk factors associated with osteoporosis in childhood, the clinical manifestations of osteoporosis, issues in the definition and diagnosis, and the recommendations for monitoring and prevention in at-risk chil dren. As well, this article discusses when a child is a candidate for osteoporosis drug therapy, which agents and doses should be prescribed, the length of therapy, how the response to therapy should be evaluated, and steps to mitigate the side effects of treatment. With this information, the bone health clini cian will be poised to diagnose osteoporosis in children, to identify when children need osteoporosis therapy and for how long, the safe administration of osteoporosis treat ment, and the clinical outcomes that gauge treatment efficacy.

paragraphs.heading: 23.2.1 Primary Osteoporosis

paragraphs.text: such as Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) [13–15]. With enhanced care for such children ( Fig. 23.2), there is increasing focus on long-term sequelae and quality of life. Despite advances in chemotherapy and disease-modifying interventions, GC therapy remains the mainstay of treatment for many serious illnesses, both in the first few years of the illness for disorders such as leukaemia and rheumatic conditions [16, 17], and for decades in boys with DMD [14]. The use of GC-

sparing biological agents has led to improved health outcomes for children with Crohn’s disease [18] and juvenile arthritis [19, 20]; not surprisingly, evidence for a positive effect of these agents on skeletal health has been dem onstrated in several studies [19, 21–23]. Therefore, a key principle of osteoporosis management in children is to seek a therapeu tic approach that is as GC-sparing as possible, given the potent adverse effect of GC therapy on the developing skeleton [24].

Low-trauma vertebral fractures, both symp tomatic and asymptomatic, are a radiographic signature of osteoporosis in both children and adults. To this point, the International Society for Clinical Densitometry (ISCD) endorses that ≥1 vertebral fracture, defined as >20% loss of vertebral height ratio according to the Genant semi-quantitative method [25], is con sistent with a diagnosis of osteoporosis in children [26]. Paediatric vertebral fractures are extremely rare in the absence of trauma
paragraphs.heading: 23.3.1 Vertebral Fractures

paragraphs.text: [27], but occur in 75% of children with even mild OI [28], in one-third of children with leu kaemia [29], in >50% of boys with GC-treated DMD [30] and in 16% of otherwise healthy fracture-prone children [31]. In a study of children with leukaemia, the positive relation ship between Genant-defined vertebral frac tures at diagnosis and subsequent new vertebral and long bone fractures provided validity for the use of the Genant method to define vertebral fractures in children [29]. The fact that vertebral fractures can be a present ing sign of serious systemic diseases like leu kaemia and inflammatory disorders underscores the importance of the 2013 ISCD recommendation that even a single lowtrauma vertebral fracture can be a manifesta tion of osteoporosis in children [32–34].
paragraphs.heading: 23.3.1 Vertebral Fractures

paragraphs.text: Despite advances in genetic testing and diag nostic imaging, the history and physical examination still provide most of the informa tion required to decide the extent to which a comprehensive skeletal evaluation is neces sary and/or to formally diagnose a child with osteoporosis. The history is particularly important to understand the mechanisms of injury resulting in fracture; to this end, some basic ‘paediatric fracture statistics’ are neces sary to contextualize the child’s fracture phe notype, as discussed next.

The risk of fracture between birth and 16 years ranges from 42 to 64% for boys and from 27 to 40% for girls [35]. A consistent finding across all epidemiological studies is that the most frequent site of fracture is the forearm, which accounts for nearly half of all paediatric fractures [35, 36]. Sixty-five percent of long bone fractures in childhood involve the upper extremity and 7–28% the lower extremity [35]. The fracture rate during child hood is higher than during adult life, hypoth esized to result from the constant lag during the growing years between the mechanical challenges that induce bone tissue strain (muscle forces and longitudinal growth), and the necessary adaptive changes in bone struc ture that foster bone strength in response to tissue strain [37].

23.3 Recognizing that long bone fractures are extremely common in childhood, the ISCD 2013 Position Statement defined a significant fracture history as ≥2 long bone fractures by age 10 years, or ≥3 long bone fractures by age 19 years [39]. These numbers are reasonable for a child without physical stigmata or risk factors for fractures, to avoid over-diagnosis of osteoporosis in a child who has been unlucky during sports or play. However, other factors should also be considered in the deci sion to initiate a comprehensive bone health evaluation and/or to diagnose a child with osteoporosis: the clinical context in which the child presents with fractures, the degree of trauma and the location + radiographic fea tures of the fracture(s).

The importance of the clinical contexts in which children present with fractures (or asso ciated risk factors) cannot be underestimated. Even a single long bone fracture can represent a major osteoporotic event in children with first presentations of OI or other skeletal dys plasias associated with bone fragility [40], and in children with significant risk factors for osteoporosis such as neuromuscular disor ders, leukaemia, and other GC-treated condi tions [32, 41, 42]. In settings without a known fracture risk, the degree of trauma associated with the fracture is particularly important in adjudicating the fracture’s significance. The ISCD [39] has defined low-trauma fractures as those occurring outside of motor vehicle accidents or falling from 10 ft (3 m) or less. With respect to falls in the high-risk chronic illness setting, a more conservative definition has been used—falling from a standing height or less, at no more than walking speed [29]. This latter definition has proven valid in the paediatric chronic illness setting since verte bral fractures predicted incident low-trauma long bone fractures defined in this way [29].
At the same time, it is important to rec ognize that children with high-trauma frac

tures may also have a bone fragility condition, a reminder that screening for tell tale stigmata, even at the time of first pre sentation for fracture management in the orthopaedic clinic, is important. While femur fractures are particularly concerning, even a single tibia or humerus fracture can represent an osteoporotic event in those at risk and should therefore trigger careful evaluation of the injury’s mechanism. Forearm fractures are so common in chil dren that usually recurrent fractures at this site are needed to instigate a more compre hensive bone health evaluation, unless the clinical context and/or physical examination findings (i.e. blue sclerae) suggest otherwise. Comminuted fractures and those with atypi cal displacement are also significant regard less of the long bone site, especially when they occur in the absence of trauma.

In children with GC-treated rheumatic disorders, other dis crete clinical features in the first year were also independent predictors of future VF, includ ing increases in disease activity scores in the first 12 months of GC therapy as well as increases in body mass index and decreases in lumbar spine (LS) BMD Z-scores, both in the first 6 months of GC therapy [17]. In children with solid organ transplantation, older age was another consistent predictor of increased VF risk [53, 59, 61, 62].
