paragraphs.heading: 26.6.3 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: 26.3 The most common cause of DSD in a 46, XX genetic female with the diagnosis of CAH is a 21-hydroxylase deficiency; 75% are salt losers who develop low sodium, high potas sium, and significant weight loss during the second week of life. High renin levels can identify the asymptomatic salt loser before developing clinical dehydration. 46, XY males with CAH are at increased risk for shock because their genitalia is entirely normal. In the United States, screening newborns for CAH by measuring 17-hydroxyprogesterone has protected infants from high morbidity and death.
paragraphs.heading: and Treatment of DSD

paragraphs.text: Female gender assignment is relatively straightforward in virilized CAH genetic females because the infants have a uterus and ovaries [45]. Many 46, XX CAH individuals with a penile urethra are being raised as girls following clitoral reduction and genital recon structive surgery. In contrast, others have been raised as males and have undergone gonadec tomy and hysterectomy. There is an ongoing debate about the best choice for these females who have unambiguously male external geni talia with female internal sex structures. The International Consensus Conference on Intersex 2006 on CAH recommends that all 46, XX CAH patients be raised, female. The CAH consensus statement indicated that “there is insufficient evidence to support rear ing a 46, XX infant at Prader 5 as a male” [56]. However, in one report, the majority (10 of the 12) 46, XX individuals diagnosed with CAH, born with Prader 4 or 5 genitalia, and assigned the male gender at birth, always lived as a male [57]. Two were reassigned to the female gender in childhood but eventually self-reassigned themselves as male. At the time of the study, the age range of the men was between 35 and 69 years. Houk and Lee proposed “consideration of male assignment for 46, XX patients who have fully developed male genitalia” [57, 58]. In a third paper, Lee and Houk [44] report rare cases of individuals
paragraphs.heading: and Treatment of DSD

paragraphs.text: assigned the male gender at birth. These indi viduals were established as males in adult hood. Given this new evidence, e best standard of care requires that parents be fully informed of the most current information when the ini tial gender assignment is considered.
paragraphs.heading: and Treatment of DSD

paragraphs.text: Female gender assignment is also straight forward in 46, XY individuals with Complete Androgen Insensitivity (CAIS). On the other hand, gender assignment may be challenging in 46, XY infants with either isolated micro penis or associated hypospadias. Further, these individuals may have an average size or hypoplastic testes. Partial androgen insensitiv ity is a concern because male genital growth is permanently compromised. In the past, 46, XY infants with micropenis, with or without hypospadias, were reassigned as female [59, 60]. This recommendation was based on the belief that it was easier to make a functional
paragraphs.heading: and Treatment of DSD

paragraphs.text: vagina than a functioning penis. Thus, a female gender assignment was believed to result in a more favorable psychosexual out come. The proponents of this recommenda tion appreciated the influences of intrinsic genetic forces (nature) as well as the impact of environmental factors (nurture). Still, they reasoned that the environmental factors within the family were more dominant than the genetic forces if the gender reassignment was done within the first year of life [61]. With this strategy, genital reconstruction was done in infancy without a prior trial of testosterone to enlarge the micropenis. The presumption was that the penile response to treatment would not accurately predict the size of the penis in adulthood. Also, it was believed that a micropenis at birth was synonymous with micropenis in adulthood. Unfortunately, there is virtually no long-term follow-up of adult
paragraphs.heading: and Treatment of DSD

paragraphs.text: individuals with micropenis assigned and reared females. One study reported on ten such individuals, but all were prepubertal [62]. In addition, there is a case report of an indi vidual born with a micropenis due to growth hormone deficiency who underwent femi ninizing surgery in infancy but reported a male gender identity and self-gender changed to male as an adult [63].
paragraphs.heading: and Treatment of DSD

paragraphs.text: Multiple observations have challenged this approach. 46, XY infants with micropenis reared as males have reported satisfactory sexual function as adults, even though they have expressed concerns about their penile size [64–66]. Many pediatric endocrinologists believe that 46, XY infants with isolated micropenis and a fused scrotum should receive a short course of depot testosterone (25 mg IM once a month for three injections) in infancy and be reared as males. They believe that rapid increases in the length and width of the phallus are good prognosticators of future penile growth. Penile enlargement following testosterone treatment facilitates reconstruc tive surgery to correct hypospadias in 46, XY infants with micropenis and hypospadias. The outcome of these infants in adult life appears to be reasonably good, even though penis size may not be in the normal range [64–66]. In the most severely affected 46, XY males with neg ligible phallic tissue, the urologists often advise the team and parents that penile recon struction is not advisable in childhood or ado lescence due to ongoing tissue growth. However, it may be possible in adulthood if requested.

Gender assignment is an “imperfect art” [50]. In the past, it was based solely on anec dotal evidence and “the medical team’s fear of the worst outcome”. It was also based on the notion that feminizing surgery has better long-term outcomes, a belief that is being challenged. Early feminizing genitoplasty has been criticized by some women who com plained of genital discomfort and the loss of arousability in adult life [67]. We now know that female sexual arousal and functioning are more complicated than previously assumed. It requires the preservation of erec tile tissue and neurovascular anatomy. A con structed vagina lacking intravaginal sensory

responses or the ability to lubricate will likely not result in satisfactory adult female sexual function. The reconstructive vaginoplasty may be associated with scarring of the introi tus, further affecting sexual satisfaction. Additionally, it may carry the risk of neopla sia [68]. However, it must be mentioned that female sexual arousal is even more compli cated because psychosocial factors also influ ence female sexual responses [69].

Early genital surgery may be medically indicated for infants with a urogenital sinus connecting to the upper vagina. Although some centers advocate early correction for all genital differences, vaginal reconstructive or cosmetic constructive surgery is usually done in late adolescence by an experienced surgeon. In the past, early surgery (i.e., clitoral reduc tion; hypospadias) was promoted to maximize psychosexual adjustment [70, 71]. The timing of various elective surgical procedures has become a point of great debate since they are not medically essential. One view favors the postponement of genital surgery until adoles cence [50, 67] when the person’s level of matu rity and commitment to postsurgical self-care (e.g., dilation) are crucial variables to the like lihood of a fully functional vagina. In addi tion, “nerve-sparing” clitoral surgery focusing on functional rather than cosmetic outcomes is being promoted [50].

However, the issue of no surgery, delay of surgery, or early surgery is highly controver sial. There is evidence that adverse effects of such surgery have occurred [67]. Consequently, there are proponents of performing only med ically necessary surgery for an individual’s health [50], while delaying surgery that is med ically unnecessary until adolescence, when the individual can participate in the decisionmaking along with parents and medical care takers. This position has created debate and divided the medical community with no clear consensus. Two major US children’s hospitals, Lurie Children’s Hospital in Chicago and Boston Children’s Hospital, suspended unnec essary genital surgery, especially clitoral reduction [72, 73].
There is no consensus among professionals, as shown in the recently published World Professional Association for Transgender

Health (WPATH) Standard of Care (SOC) eighth edition [74]. Those responsible for Chapter ten (Intersex) could not come to a consensus on recommendation nine, suggest ing that early genital surgery be delayed if not medically indicated. Chapter ten provides rea sons for and against this recommendation as well as published research supporting both sides. Currently, there is no long-term pro spective follow-up on individuals with a DSD diagnosis reared female who have not under gone genital surgery (e.g., clitoral reduction) or delayed surgery for the atypical external genitalia. A report summarizes ten surveys of DSD individuals (CAH 46, XX, and 47, XY reared female) who had early genital surgery [75]. The salient finding of this review is that a clear majority of patients with somatic inter sexuality favor genital surgery before the age of consent, particularly in infancy or early childhood.

Measuring outcome parameters such as vaginal width, depth, and comfort during intercourse may help resolve the early vs. later vaginal surgery debate. The variability of postsurgical and psychosexual outcomes appears to tip the balance in favor of waiting until the patient can actively participate in the decision-making process and give full consent. However, without long-term pro spective follow-up and the fact that sexual dysfunction is common in the general popu lation, it is counterintuitive that the outcome would be better if not performed in early childhood [72].

Legally, the parents decide about accept ing a female gender of rearing for a 46, XY individual and the possible need for gonadec tomy and later vaginal construction. However, religious and social beliefs may influence par ents’ decisions regarding rearing 46, XY indi viduals as males regardless of penile size or future function. Therefore, giving parents all the options regarding gender assignment, including the pros and cons of each choice, is essential. If language barriers exist, an inter preter must assist in communication. In some cultures, a male gender of rearing is consid ered an advantage regardless of genital defor mities. Parents must be comfortable with the gender assignment decision since they are

responsible for rearing their children. They should not feel pressured by the medical team to make decisions they are uncomfortable with or do not want. The level of parental understanding may require prolonged discus sions and great patience by the medical team. The trained psychologist is particularly help ful in this situation.

DSD may be present in infants with nor mal or nearly normal external genitalia [53, 76] and may be a diagnostic challenge in these infants. These include 46, XY males who have complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (CAIS) or the 17α (alpha)-hydroxylase (P450C17 or CYP17) deficiency and are born with normal female genitalia. 46, XY females with CAIS present either in childhood with a hernia containing a testis or in late adoles cence or adulthood with primary amenorrhea or absence of sexual hair. Conversely, 46, XY females with the 17α-hydroxylase deficiency may also present with primary amenorrhea. However, these individuals are hypertensive due to ACTH-mediated excess of mineralo corticoids. The latter condition is autosomal recessive, and consanguinity may be present in the parents. These patients fail to make all sex steroids because this enzyme plays a piv otal steroidogenic role in the testes and adre nal glands. Therefore, they lack sexual hair and may be misdiagnosed as having CAIS. The Sertoli cells of the testes usually function appropriately. Thus, Müllerian structures are absent, similar to individuals with CAIS. A 46, XX female with the same genetic defect lacks sex hormones and is hypertensive, but will menstruate when given estrogen replace ment because the uterus is structurally nor mal. Androgen replacement in 46, XY individuals with the 17α-hydroxylase defi ciency will result in sexual hair growth, distin guishing them clinically from individuals with CAIS.
Gender change from initial gender assignment does occur in congenital adrenal hyperplasia [77], 5-α (alpha)-reductase deficiency, 17-β
paragraphs.heading: Dysphoria

paragraphs.text: (beta)-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency [78], partial androgen insensitivity syndrome [62], and 46, XY persons with penile agenesis, cloacal exstrophy of the bladder, or penile abla tion raised as female [79, 80]. While most indi viduals diagnosed with CAIS remain in their initial female gender assignment [70], there are rare reports of individuals changing gender from female to male [51, 81]. There are also reports of gender change from male to female in a 46, XY individual diagnosed with CAH due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency [82]. Gender change has been reported in one case of a 46, XY indi vidual with CAH due to 21-hydroxylase defi ciency from male to female. No gender change has been reported in Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster- Hauser (MRKH) syndrome.
paragraphs.heading: Dysphoria

paragraphs.text: Summarizing the data on gender change in 46, XY individuals, it is clear that gender change occurs in various frequencies in various condi tions [80]. Second, gender change from femaleto-male occurs more often than from male to female; the only condition where gender change occurs in both directions is partial androgen insensitivity syndrome. Third, gender change is not 100% in any situation (even in persons reared female with a history of prenatal andro gen exposure). These data do not support bio logical factors determining adult gender identity. However, it may suggest an indirect influence of androgens on such development as gender change appears more common in conditions with relatively high androgen exposure [79].

These data also suggest that the best pre dictor, although not perfect, of what the established adult gender identity will be is the initial gender assignment. In cases of isolated micropenis, the extant literature showed only one case report of a person with documented micropenis initially assigned and reared female who changed from female to male [63]. However, the number of individuals with micropenis assigned and reared female is small, and many were young at the time of the review, ranging from 1 week to 29 years of age. Consequently, we do not know their established adult gender identity. Until fur ther evidence proves otherwise, we recom mend an initial male gender assignment in individuals with isolated micropenis [62].

A person who desires to change gender has a Gender Identity Disorder (GID) (diagnosed by mental health professionals) using the cri teria found in the fourth version of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manuel of Mental Disorders (DSM-IV-TR). The fifth version (DSM-5) replaced the term GID with Gender Dysphoria (GD) and allowed this diagnosis to include persons with a DSD diagnosis. DSD was an exclusionary criterion for GID in DSM-IV-TR. The main reason for the change in the DSM-5 was the evidence mentioned above that self-gender change occurs in many different DSD. Perhaps another finding that was also influential but not mentioned by the DSM-5 working group was surveyed data showing that 40% of professionals working with adult transgender persons provided ser vices for people with a DSD diagnosis [83]. These professionals were members of the World Professional Association for Transgendered Health (WPATH). At the time of the survey, WPATH was the Harry Benjamin International Gender Dysphoria Association (HBIGDA). Everyone does not accept this change [84, 85] primarily because there are historical, medical, and manage ment differences between those who have Gender Dysphoria and a DSD condition and those who do not [86]. In addition to the above changes, the World Health Organization (2019) 11th edition (ICD-11) replaced older terms “Transsexualism for Adults and Adolescents and Gender Identity Disorder for Children with Gender Incongruence. Also, in ICD-11, Gender Incongruence was moved out of the “Mental and behavioral disorders” chapter and into the new “Conditions related to sexual health” chapter. This reflects current knowledge that trans-related and genderdiverse identities are not conditions of mental illness and that classifying them as such can cause enormous stigma. Unfortunately, ICD- 11 has yet to be adopted for use in the US which is using ICD-10.
paragraphs.heading: and DSD

paragraphs.text: Diagnosis of patients with a DSD has tradi tionally been through assessing the patient’s phenotype, including a physical examination of the external genitalia, imaging of the inter nal reproductive structures, endocrine assess ment in basal and stimulated states, and molecular analysis of a small number of genes known to cause DSD. Modern technology, increasingly wide availability, and decreasing prices of genetic testing have allowed the genetic investigation to be utilized earlier in the diagnostic process. Potential benefits of new genetic diagnostic tools include a shorter diagnostic time, improved genetic counseling, an understanding of the family’s reproductive options, and improved monitoring [87].
paragraphs.heading: 26.6.7 Genetics and DSD

paragraphs.text: The scientific and medical communities rapidly adopted the term DSD, formulated at the Consensus meeting in Chicago and published in 2006. However, some vocal elements of the patient community strongly opposed the word “disorder”. They contend that the term “disor der” leads to an unnecessary pathologizing of atypical bodies that contribute to potentially harmful surgical “normalization” procedures [4]. Some affected individuals prefer “differ ences” to “disorders”, i.e., “differences of sex development”. Others reject DSD entirely and choose the term “intersex’ as it refers to an identity rather than a diagnosable medical con dition. The Consensus meeting was based on a global initiative to address several issues, including the nomenclature [88]. Perhaps it is not surprising that there was no resolution. Therefore, DSD can mean “disorder of sexual development” or “differences of sexual devel opment.” Then there are those who choose the descriptor intersex. There also remains dis agreement on whether conditions like Turner Syndrome, Klinefelter, and hypospadias con stitute a DSD. The CARES Foundation sup
paragraphs.heading: Nomenclature and Who Is Considered to Have a DSD Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: ports individuals diagnosed with Congenital Adrenal Hypoplasia and their families, but do not consider CAH a DSD.
paragraphs.heading: Nomenclature and Who Is Considered to Have a DSD Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: National registries provide an extensive data base for research and clinical purposes. Categorization and standardization of infor mation allow for improved clinical care, research, and general understanding. While there have been registries for several medical conditions for years (e.g., cancer), national registries for DSD were created only recently. There are currently two such registries; the International DSD (I-DSD) in Europe and the National Institutes of Health-funded Disorders of Sex Development-Translational Research Network (DSD-TRN) in the United States [89]. Additionally, in Europe, the “dsd- LIFE” consortium consists of 16 participat ing institutions based in six different EU member states: Germany, France, UK, Sweden, The Netherlands, and Poland [90]. These registries, plus “dsd-Life”, create vast databases for research purposes. The DSD- TRN delineates the clinical care process to provide a more standardized noncategorical approach to patient and family care, thus improving outcomes [91].
paragraphs.heading: 26.6.9 DSD National Registries

paragraphs.text: A new data base has been recently estab lished in the US using electronic health records (HER) from three large Kaiser Permanente health systems to identify with high confidence that the diagnosis is correct systematically [92]. Currently, this project has identified CAH and CAIS individuals. Other DSD conditions will be added. The goal is to be able to track this large number of individu als to ascertain the type of care they are receiving.
paragraphs.heading: 26.6.9 DSD National Registries

paragraphs.text: In the United States, Short-Term Outcomes of Genitoplasty is a prospective study of the short-term outcomes of feminizing or mascu linizing surgeries for children under the age of two. There are three aims of this investigation: [1] the cosmetic outcomes of current surgical techniques to feminize or masculinize external genitalia in young children with ambiguous genitalia, [2] the incidence of urinary tract
paragraphs.heading: 26.6.9 DSD National Registries

paragraphs.text: infections and surgical complications associ ated with different types of feminizing and masculinizing genitoplasty currently in use for young children with ambiguous genitalia, and [3] psychological outcomes following parents’ decisions to proceed with genitoplasty for their child (or not), including parents’ depressive, anxious, and posttraumatic stress symptoms, parents’ quality of life, uncertainty about their child’s illness, and decisional regret regarding their choices at the time of surgical decisionmaking. The first publications focused on the aims of this project and addressed factors that influence shared decision-making regarding early genital surgery [93], adjustment of par ents to such surgery [94], and surgical outcomes [94].
paragraphs.heading: 26.6.9 DSD National Registries

paragraphs.text: Familial and extrafamilial experiences shape children and adolescents’ social and emotional development, especially with peers. Developing friendships and involvement in group interaction requires specific skills. The concept of “similarity” and self-perception of typicality in normative development repre sents a challenge faced by individuals with a DSD. Children and adolescents with DSD may not benefit to the same degree as other children and adolescents from experiences with peers [95]. The little evidence that exists is mixed, leading to the conclusion that the effects of DSD on psychosocial well-being and adjustment in individuals vary as a func tion of a large number of person and contextrelated variables and conditions. More multisite collaborative research is needed.

The European study (Comprehensive European Clinical Outcome Study) focuses on the long-term outcomes of adults and adoles cents with various DSD diagnoses. Another developmental task associated with enveloping positive emotional self-concept and body image is experiencing age-appropriate psychosexual milestones, including intercourse [96]. Individuals with DSD were less likely to reach each of the romantic and sexual milestones compared to their peers without a DSD and were significantly older when reaching these milestones. Additionally, differences were found based on DSD diagnosis [97]. Mental health has been shown to be a challenge for some, but it varies based on the DSD diagnosis [98, 99].

Legislatures in several countries have passed laws accommodating those born with a DSD and identifying as other than male or female [100]. For example, in 2012, Argentina passed the Gender Identity Law, which allows for name and sex changes on official documents without proof of surgical reconstruction or other medical or psychiatric treatment. This law was the first to allow gender reassignment based solely on an individual proclamation and applies to both DSD and transsexual cases [100]. In 2013, the Australian Senate passed the Sex Discrimination Amendment Bill [101], introducing legislation prohibiting discrimination based on DSD status. The new guidelines on gender recognition state that individuals should be given the option of selecting male, female, or intersex on their documents. In the same year, Germany intro duced an “indeterminate” sex option on birth certificates. Also, in 2013, the Council of Europe [102] adopted a resolution on the pro tection of children’s rights to physical integ rity, demanding no one be “subjected to unnecessary medical or surgical treatment that is cosmetic rather than vital for health during infancy or childhood.” In 2021, The United States issued its first U.S. passport with an “X” gender marker, acknowledging the rights of people who do not identify as male or female,
paragraphs.heading: 26.6.10 Global Legislation

paragraphs.text: Greater emphasis on “patientcenteredness” in health care delivery and increased awareness of DSD have been accompanied by controversy, especially about the utility of elective genital surgery in infancy or early childhood. In addition, legal ques tions have been raised, and there was a lawsuit regarding the legality of surgical intervention in managing a child with a DSD [103].
paragraphs.heading: 26.6.10 Global Legislation

paragraphs.text: Individuals with a DSD, or their parents, have brought lawsuits regarding unnecessary medi cal surgery that were primarily settled out of the public’s eye [104]. In the United States, the first public lawsuit challenging early sex assignment surgery on a child with a DSD
paragraphs.heading: 26.6.11 Lawsuits and DSD

paragraphs.text: involved a child diagnosed with ovotesticular DSD. After obtaining parental consent, this child was assigned a female gender and received feminizing genital surgery at 16 months of age. Shortly after that, the biological parents abandoned their child, who came under the South Carolina Department of Social Services’ care and was later adopted. Despite the feminizing surgery, the child even tually identified as male. The adoptive parents alleged that the medically unnecessary early genital surgery performed without the child’s consent violated the child’s constitutional rights. This case was eventually settled out of court [73]. In Germany, a woman with 46, XX CAH successfully sued the surgeon who removed her fully intact female internal organs when she was 18. She had previously been reared as a male and undergone surgery to correct hypospadias in childhood. Her diagnosis of CAH occurred following an appendectomy in which a uterus and ovaries were discovered. She sought 100,000 euros in damages for pain and suffering, claiming the surgeon failed to fully inform her about the consequences of the operation or possible alternatives [88]. In both cases, the issue of informed consent concerning elective surgery appears to lie at the heart of the matter.
paragraphs.heading: 26.6.11 Lawsuits and DSD

paragraphs.text: For years, the clinical research and manage ment of persons with DSD focused on the relationship between gender identity, gender role, sexual orientation, sexual functioning, and pre- and postnatal hormones because there was evidence from animal research that hormones, primarily androgens, affected sex ual behavior. The reviews above mirror that focus. They do not report the quality of life for individuals regardless of gender assign ment and rearing or even in those who changed gender. If such data are available, they are insufficient to draw meaningful con clusions. They also do not focus on the influ ence of genes on brain sexual differentiation and development, an area that is only begin ning to be explored [105].
paragraphs.heading: and Clinical Care

paragraphs.text: This approach was categorical, meaning that the focus was on investigating and managing psychosexual development and hormones to exclude other variables of human development (i.e., quality-of-life variables, in addition to psy chosexual status and hormones). Later, Sandberg and Mazur outlined an approach encompassing psychosexual development in persons with a DSD in a broader, noncategori cal approach to clinical care [91]. This noncate gorical approach guides clinical care by considering a growing body of evidence. It sup ports the notion that the successful developmen tal trajectories of persons with chronic medical conditions are influenced by the psychosocial environment, support systems, and healthcare delivery organization, in addition to the specific nature of the person’s medical condition [106, 107]. Such an approach holds the potential to systematically account for variability in DSD patient quality-of-life outcomes and translate clinical interventions, proven effective in manag ing other chronic conditions, to the circum stances faced by those affected by DSD.
paragraphs.heading: and Clinical Care

paragraphs.text: While the investigation of basic biological mechanisms will continue, so will the quality of life studies in individuals with various DSD syn dromes. Examples of this work include those by Wisniewski et al. [108], and Stout et al. [109] on CAH, and Schonbucker et al. [110] on sexual quality of life in 46, XY individuals with a DSD diagnosis, Mazur on a small sample of five 46, XY individuals assigned and reared female [111], and Bean’s review of MRKH [112]. Additionally, others have focused on the effects of having a child with a DSD on parenting char acteristics [113–115] and peer relations [95].
paragraphs.heading: and Clinical Care

paragraphs.text: Since Hermaphrodites with Attitude, the first advocacy group in North America, numerous advocacy organizations have formed to advo cate for individuals with DSD and their fami lies. Advocacy and peer support groups have grown internationally [116]. These different advocacy organizations hold meetings to pro vide support and allow individuals to meet oth ers, voice concerns, and educate themselves and others on their conditions. The link
paragraphs.heading: 26.6.13 Advocacy

paragraphs.text: http://www.accordalliance.org/ is a portal to access many of these advocacy/support groups.
paragraphs.heading: 26.6.13 Advocacy

paragraphs.text: The Consensus Statement not only created a new nomenclature (DSD) to replace old stigma tizing and confusing terminology, but also emphasized the importance of a “multidisci plinary team” to provide the best possible care for individuals with a DSD diagnosis and their families. The focus of this team is patient-cen tered care. Such care requires that the team of professionals has experience with DSD condi tions and pays attention to the patient’s and family’s needs, preferences, and beliefs, which
paragraphs.heading: Emphasized

paragraphs.text: Birth history: A full-term infant, born vagi nally with normal APGAR scores, was trans ferred from an outlining hospital soon after delivery because of “ambiguous genitalia”. At birth, the parents were expecting a girl based on prenatal ultrasound findings and were told that they had a little girl at delivery. Shortly after the delivery, they were informed that the female gender assignment might not be correct based on further inspection of the external genitalia. The parents were upset. A member of the DSD team (TM) was informed, and the DSD proto col (see: DSD Protocol above) was immediately initiated. TM contacted all other team mem bers and immediately went to meet the parents. TM informed parents that their child would be cared for by a multidisciplinary team with extensive experience in helping parents whose infant was born with features such as those present in their infant. TM explained the proto col to parents, which included referring to their baby as “baby” with no name until a possible diagnosis could be established. Further, TM informed parents that they would be part of a discussion of all findings once all results were reported. They would be informed about the current and future management. TM reassured parents that the multidisciplinary team would discuss the recommendation gender assign ment but would support parental decisions.

the traditional hierarchal medical model typi cally overlooks. Within this context, support groups and other “interested parties” caring for patients diagnosed with a DSD can be helpful as long as their approach is constructive [117]. In essence, the patient (when old enough) and fam ily become part of the team interacting in open communication. A nonprofit organization (Accord Alliance) was created to assist institu tions in establishing successful interdisciplinary teams [118]. This organization also maintains a web-based clearinghouse ( http://www. accordalliance.org/) that includes educational tools and information about living with and car ing for those with DSD. It also includes ‘Handbook for Parents’ [49] and ‘Guidelines for the Management of Disorder of Sex Development in Childhood’ [50].

TM also identified each member of the team and their respective specialty. He also began to demystify why the gender of assignment was in question by educating them on how the inter nal and external sexual/reproductive systems develop and differentiate. TM further focused on their child’s future care, including medical and psychological needs.

Physical examination: healthy infant with no dysmorphology other than the external gen itals; enlarged phallic structure (longitudinal length = 2 cm) with an opening at the base, fused labioscrotal folds with hyperpigmenta tion, giving the appearance of a bifid scrotum, no gonads palpated.

Test results: Laboratory tests were done as per the hospital protocol outlined. Serum LH, FSH, testosterone (18 ng/dL (normal for female: 20–64)), and DHT (10 ng/dL (normal for female <2–15)) concentrations were drawn within 24 h of life and were normal. The child’s karyotype was 46, XX. At 72 h of life, blood tests were done at a reference laboratory: serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone: 571 ng/dL ((high); normal range: day 3 < 78), 17-hydroxypregnenolone: 887 ng/dL (normal: 10–829), Androstenedione: 210 ng/dL (normal <10–279) and DHEAS: 166 μg/dL (normal: 88–356). Serum electrolyte concentrations and plasma renin activity were normal. Pelvic ultra

The current understanding of DSD and how to care for children with these conditions result from years of basic scientific investiga tion on the sexual reproductive system. This work elucidated this system’s complex sequen tial signaling networks, which involve multiple interacting molecular signals, hormone influ ences, and cross-talk between these signaling pathways.
paragraphs.heading: 26.7 Summary

paragraphs.text: There has been little change in the endo crine treatment of DSD over the last few decades. The advances are primarily in the domain of genetics. On the other hand, there have been evolving dynamics in many differ ent aspects of patient care. These included (1) debates about the efficiency and timing of medically and nonmedically necessary genital surgery: should this wait until the child can consent or not, its effects on sexual arousal, and even whether it should or should not be performed; (2) the creation of laws regarding unnecessary surgery and gender; (3) more transparency from physicians and other health professionals with family and patients
paragraphs.heading: 26.7 Summary

paragraphs.text: about the condition and what options are available to them—in brief patient and fam ily-centered care; (4) the creation of decisionmaking tools which become the vehicle for “shared decision making” on issues such as genital surgery, meaning that the physician or health professional enters into a dialog with the family and patient about the risks and benefits of various treatments such as genital surgery [120]. Such an approach is client- or patient-centered and follows the recommen dation of the Consensus Report [5].
paragraphs.heading: 26.7 Summary

paragraphs.text: The rise of advocacy in this area has dra matically influenced this approach. As a result, there has been an evolving shift to a ‘patient, family first’ approach and attention to the quality of life. Gender assignment decisions are no longer hurried or thought of as medical emergencies, with parents given incomplete information for fear of increasing their level of anxiety. Instead, current recommendations promote full disclosure with the active involve ment of the families in the gender assignment process. While urgency is still present, informed parents are willing to accept long waiting times to obtain all the data from molecular studies,
paragraphs.heading: 26.7 Summary

paragraphs.text: other diagnostic tests, and information about treatment. Patients with micropenis are no lon ger assigned female at birth with associated genital surgery. Clitoral reduction is no longer considered a “preferred therapy”. In time there has been extensive discussion about what is known and not known about both short and long-term quality of life, including functioning in the common domains of living: school, friends, romance, sexual functioning, fertility, and general overall mental health.
paragraphs.heading: 26.7 Summary

paragraphs.text: Furthermore, recent evidence underscores that gender assignment in the newborn period is still imperfect. Self-gender change may occur later in the child’s life despite the best intentions of the parents and the DSD team. Full disclosure demands that parents be made aware of this possibility.

Gender identity development and differen tiation remain complex and incompletely understood phenomena. Despite our incom plete knowledge, we know that having a DSD has physical, social, psychological, and mental health consequences for individuals and their families. The fact that a DSD is invisible to oth ers cannot be underestimated and might be the biggest consequence experienced by a person. This means that while endocrine care needs to continue regularly, so does psychological care and social support to track developmental milestones and offer counseling and support if there is a challenge to meeting the developmen tal tasks. Maintaining open, honest communi cation on the part of all practitioners and parents creates a foundation of trust which can only result in the best care possible for the child and their family. All of these changes and the awareness they bring will produce a better stan dard of care in the years ahead.

Misra (eds.), Pediatric Endocrinology, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-66296-6_26 ## PDF page 725 | printed page 722 26.6.5 Gender Change and Gender Dysphoria – 735 26.6.6 Gender Dysphoria Diagnosis and DSD – 736 26.6.7 Genetics and DSD – 737 26.6.8 Disagreements over Nomenclature and Who Is Considered to Have a DSD Diagnosis – 737 26.6.9 DSD National Registries – 737 26.6.10 Global Legislation – 738 26.6.11 Lawsuits and DSD – 738 26.6.12 A Shift in Research Focus and Clinical Care – 739 26.6.13 Advocacy – 739 26.6.14 Patient-Centered Care Emphasized – 740 ### 26.7 Summary – 741 ### References – 742 ## PDF page 726 | printed page 723 Key Points 5 Disorders of Sex Development/Differ ences of Sex Development 5 Medical management of DSD 5 Gender Change 5 Gender dysphoria ### 26.1 Introduction and Background The European Society for Pediatric Endocrinol ogy (ESPE) and the Pediatric Endocrine Society (PES) replaced the terms intersex, hermaphro ditism, pseudohermaphroditism, sex errors of the body, and ambiguous genitalia with an umbrella term, disorders of sex development (DSD) in 2006. DSD is defined as “congenital conditions in which development of chromo somal, gonadal, or anatomical sex is atypical” [1]. Most patients and professionals supported the nomenclature change as the prevailing ter minologies were confusing to patients and their medical providers and considered derogatory by some. DSDs are rare conditions, and the lack of specific medical codes precludes the collection of accurate population statistics for DSD. How ever, the estimated incidence is 0.1–0.5% of live births [2]. Approximately one in 4000 infants are born with atypical external genitalia and will receive a DSD diagnosis [1]. The current genetic-based classification system of DSD highlights the importance of chromosomal analysis in diagnosing and managing individuals with DSD. Since its inception, the term DSD has been accepted and used widely by the medical profession; however, critics have raised concerns because of the negative connotations associated with the words “disorder” and “sex” [3, 4]. Some professionals and organizations define “DSD” as Differences of Sexual Development, hence the two terms used in the title of this chapter. ### 26.2 Purpose The aims of this chapter are to (1) provide a concise update on the mechanisms controlling normal and abnormal sexual differentiation; (2) share a protocol used for the practical management of infants born with DSD; (3) provide information to guide the physician when making a DSD diagnosis and designing its medical management; (4) provide new behavioral information on DSD; and (5) high light current differences of opinions about the care of infants born with DSD. ### 26.3 Etiology ### 26.3.1 Mechanisms Involved ### in Sexual Differentiation: Tissues, Genes, and Hormones ### 26.3.1.1 The Bipotential Gonad 26.1 The bipotential gonads arise from the coe lomic epithelium’s somatic precursor cells that form the urogenital ridge. The midportion of the urogenital ridge consists of multiplying undifferentiated cells to form the genital ridge between 4 and 6 weeks of gestation. Then, the primordial germ cells translocate into the mass of multiplying cells that develop into the primitive gonads [5]. The fetus’s genetic sex (XX or XY) is determined when an X or Y-bearing sperm fertilizes the ovum at conception and is cru cial for somatic sex development. On the other hand, germ cells develop in the allantoin. They migrate from their point of origin in the endoderm of the yolk sac wall to their final destination within the primitive gonad and develop into spermatogonia or oogonia [6]. Unlike somatic sex development, germ cell differentiation into oogonia and spermatogo nia depends on the gonadal environment and autosomal genes. This pathway is better defined in mice, where high retinoic acid con centration activates the stimulation by reti ## PDF page 727 | printed page 724 Table 26.1 Genes controlling sexual differentiation Gene/chromosome Family/function SRY, Yp11.3 HMG protein, transcription factor WT1, 11p13 Zinc finger protein transcription factor ### 26 SF1, 9q33 Orphan nuclear receptor transcription factor DAX1, Xp21.3 Orphan nuclear receptor transcription factor SOX9, 17q24.3 HMG protein transcription factor WNT4, 1p32–36 Growth factor Reprinted with permission from Springer noic acid 8 (STRA8) gene. It encodes for a protein involved in the differentiation of germ cells to oogonia and the initiation of meiosis in fetal ovaries [7]. However, unlike mouse models, STRA8 and retinoic acid may play only a partial role in human ovaries [8]. A crucial step of germ cell development is meiosis which results in the halving of chro mosomes in the gametes. However, germ cells enter meiosis at differing times in the ovaries and the testes. In ovaries, germ cells enter mei osis in fetal life. In the testes, mitotic expan sion of spermatogonia continues till puberty, when germ cells enter the meiotic halving of chromosomes [8]. STRA8 also appears to play a role in developing testes. In male mice lack ing STRA8, the early mitotic activity of germ cells is preserved; however, later meiotic acti vation and differentiation into spermatogonia are affected [7]. ### 26.3.1.2 Testicular Differentiation Testicular differentiation depends primarily on the Sex determining Region Y (SRY) gene located on the short arm of the Y chromo Clinical phenotype XY gonadal dysgenesis Denys-Drash syndrome Frasier syndrome XY gonadal dysgenesis Adrenal insufficiency Duplication causes: – XY sex reversal Mutation causes – XY adrenal hypoplasia Congenita (AHC) and Gonadotropin deficiency Mutation causes: – XY sex reversal – Campomelic dysplasia Duplication causes: – 46, XY sex reversal Deletion causes – Masculinization of 46, XX female some. SRY induces bipotential cells of the genital ridge to differentiate into Sertoli cells and form the seminiferous tubules by the sixth week of gestation. Additionally, steroidogenic precursors differentiate into Leydig cells [6]. The SRY gene codes for a 204 amino acid transcription factor that binds to and bends the DNA strands and allows access by other tran scription factors. However, the mechanism by which SRY determines gonadal sex is not fully understood. There are two proposed mecha nisms: (1) SRY activates a cascade of genes needed for male development, or (2) SRY inhibits a repressor of the male-determining genes. In the activator model, the male pathway is dominant, and the female path is the default. In contrast, the repressor model suggests an active female development pathway, which a male gene must suppress. In humans, SRY is expressed in the testes and various brain struc tures. However, it is unclear if the expression of SRY in the brain influences sexual behav ior. SRY expression is tightly regulated. It is seen early during testicular development and is transient. ### Automatic table extraction — verify rendered original |Gene/chromosome|Family/function|Clinical phenotype| |---|---|---| |_SRY_, Yp11.3|HMG protein, transcription factor|XY gonadal dysgenesis| |_WT1_, 11p13|Zinc fnger protein transcription factor|Denys-Drash syndrome

The importance of the HMG region of the SRY in testicular development is highlighted by mutations within the HMG region of the SRY gene that result in the failure of testicu lar development and sex reversal with a female phenotype or genital ambiguity [9–11]. SRY mutations are not responsible for all cases of sex reversal in 46, XY females, nor do they explain the presence of testes in 46, XX males with genital ambiguity. Only 25% of 46, XY females with gonadal dysgenesis (streak gonads) and female phenotype have an SRY mutation. Further, SRY is present in only 10% of individuals with 46, XX ovotesticular DSD and 10% of those with 46, XX DSD. In con trast, most 46, XX males with typical male geni talia and testes are SRY positive. The role of SRY may be underestimated in individuals with sex reversal if it is present only in the gonads and not in peripheral blood lymphocytes [9]. 26.2 Table 26.2 Causes of 46, XY disorders of sex development (DSD) 1. XY gonadal dysgenesis 2. Denys-Drash syndrome; WT1 mutation, also nephropathy, Wilms’ tumor 3. Frasier syndrome; WT1 mutation, also nephropathy, Gonadoblastoma 4. XO/XY mosaicism-mixed gonadal dysgenesis 5. Campomelic dysplasia-SOX 9 mutation 6. DAX1 duplication (DSS syndrome) 7. WNT4 duplication 8. SF1 (NR5A1 gene) mutation 9. Deletion of 9p-, 10 q- 10. Duplication: X p + Reprinted with permission from Springer 10 12 13 14 12 15 26.1 16 17 Two additional genes, steroidogenic factor 1 (SF1) and Wilms’ tumor 1 (WT1), have a synergistic role in testicular development [18]. SRY is transactivated by the WT1 gene prod uct [19]. In the testis, SRY and SF1 coopera tively upregulate SOX9 [20]. The role of DAX1 (Dosage-sensitive sex reversal-Adrenal hypoplasia congenita critical region on the X chromosome, gene 1) in testic ular development needs special mention. Duplication of DAX1 inhibits SRY [21, 22] and inhibits the synergy between WT1 and SF1 [18], blocking subsequent testicular develop ment. Mouse models also demonstrated a “pro-testis” effect of DAX1 [23]. The animal models indicate that a precise dose of DAX1 is vital for testicular development, “too much or too little can prevent cord formation” [24]. ### 26.3.1.3 Ovarian Differentiation Ovarian differentiation is poorly understood, but recent evidence suggests that a network of genes and transcription factors regulates the process. Contrary to previous belief, ovarian development is not a passive or default pro cess. Ovarian development appears to depend on the suppression of testis-inducing genes and activation of ovary-inducing genes. The probable candidate genes for suppression of testes differentiation include DAX1 and ## PDF page 729 | printed page 726 ### 26 WNT4. The DAX1 gene is located on the X chromosome and inherited from the mother in males. DAX1 duplication inactivates SRY [21, 22] and SOX9 function, thereby blocking testicular development and AMH expression [15]. DAX1 is an essential anti-testis gene in the ovary. 46, XY individuals with a duplica tion of DAX1 have a female phenotype (sex reversal) and gonadal dysgenesis [25, 26]. The duplicated DAX1 gene may be located on the X-chromosome. Alternatively, one DAX1 gene can be normally located on the X chro mosome, and a second translocated DAX1 gene on the Y chromosome. Autosomal genes also play a significant role in ovarian development in the differentiating ovary. R-Spondin-1(RSPO-1) affects WNT4 signaling [27, 28], which in turn appears to inhibit testicular vascular growth, stabilize oocytes, and induce Müllerian development [29]. Deletion of WNT4 leads to masculiniza tion in 46, XX individuals and degeneration of Müllerian duct derivatives [30]. WNT4 appears upstream of and in concert with DAX1. In 46, XY individuals, duplication of WNT4 causes upregulation of DAX1 in the testes, suppress ing SOX9, resulting in a female phenotype [31]. Hence, duplication of either DAX1 or WNT4 ## PDF page 730 | printed page 727 causes dosage-sensitive 46, XY sex reversal. WNT4 is complemented by forkhead box L2 (FOXL2) which may play an independent role in ovarian development [17, 32]. In mice mod els, loss of WNT4 and FOXL2 is associated with female-to-male sex reversal and upregula tion of SOX9 [32]. Genes that support ovarian development have not been completely identified. However, they are probably located on the X-chromosome and may have dosage-sensitive functions. Women with Turner syndrome, a condition associated with a partial or total absence of one X chromosome, have a loss of ovarian germ cell development. The sequence of genetic events in ovarian development is depicted in the following theo retical model: 1. Activation of DAX1 antagonizes SF1and SOX9; 2. Granulosa cells develop from the support ing cells while Sertoli cell differentiation is blocked; 3. WNT4 and FOXL2 induce differentiation of Müllerian structures into the uterus, fallopian tubes, and upper third of the vagina; and 26.1 Specific mechanisms have been shown to cause sex reversal. For example, duplication of SOX9 is an autosomal cause of sex reversal in 46, XX individuals [33]. In addition, the mutations in the SF1 gene and other sex-determining genes are also known to cause 46, XY gonadal dys genesis and a female phenotype. ### 26.4 The Paired Internal Ducts: ### Wolffian and Müllerian Ducts ### 26.4.1 Wolffian Ducts In 46, XY males, local testosterone produc tion by the Leydig cells helps the differentia tion of the Wolffian duct into the epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, and ejaculatory ducts [34, 35]. Human chorionic gonadotro pin (hCG) initially regulates testosterone pro duction [36]. Additionally, AMH plays a vital role in developing internal ducts. The function of AMH is highlighted in agonadal genetic males, where Müllerian ducts persist because AMH is not produced [34, 37]. Typically, AMH is produced by the Sertoli cells. Hence, AMH is a marker of Sertoli cell function in patients with DSDs [38]. ### 26.4.2 Müllerian Ducts Müllerian duct differentiation progresses without AMH and develops the fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and upper third of the vagina. The transcription factor WNT4 plays an essential role in Müllerian duct differentia tion and ovarian function during fetal life. Female WNT4 knock-out mice fail to develop Müllerian structures and lose oocytes [30]. Further, they manifest hypersecretion of ovar ian androgens derived from Leydig cell pre cursors in the interstitium [39]. Thus, it appears that WNT4 suppresses androgen pro duction by Leydig cells’ precursors in the ova ry’s interstitium and is a regulator of Müllerian duct development. ### 26.4.3 The Bipotential External ### Genitalia The primordial structures of the male and female external genitalia are homologous, and the external genitalia of genetic males cannot be distinguished from genetic females at 8 weeks of life. The genital tubercle becomes either the clitoris or the penis. The urethral folds become the labia minora, the clitoral hood, the skin covering the penis, and the foreskin. Finally, the labioscrotal folds or gen ital swellings become the labia majora or fuse together to become the scrotum. The future development and differentiation of the bipo tential external genitalia from this homolo gous state into male structures depend on the presence of androgens. Female-appearing ## PDF page 731 | printed page 728 external genitalia will differentiate and develop if androgens are absent, as seen in the fetus with no gonads, streak gonads, and non functional testes, or if androgen function is defective, as in androgen insensitivity due to genetic defects. ### 26 ### 26.4.4 Male External Genitalia The development of male external genitalia depends on the adequacy of testosterone (T) and 5-α (alpha)—dihydrotestosterone (5α (alpha)-DHT) production, as well as func tional androgen receptors (AR). The testes form by 6–7 weeks of fetal life. The Leydig cells are stimulated by placental hCG in the first trimester [36] and fetal pituitary LH in the second trimester [40]. Male external geni tal differentiation is complete by 12 weeks; additional penile enlargement in the second trimester depends on Leydig cell stimulation by LH from the fetal pituitary gland. Complete masculinization of external male genitalia requires the conversion of T to 5α (alpha) DHT; the enzyme responsible for this conversion is 5α (alpha)-reductase, which is present in genital tissue. 46, XY infants with 5α (alpha)-reductase deficiency have normally functioning testes; the predominantly female phenotype in early childhood is due to the defec tive conversion of T to 5α (alpha) DHT during early fetal life. However, 5-α (alpha) DHT is critical for normal external male genital differ entiation in fetal life and the virilization of males during puberty [41–43]. Therefore, gender reas signment to males usually occurs in puberty in many societies where rates of 5α (alpha)-reduc tase deficiency are high. Cultural practices and preferences play another important role in gen der reassignment. In many of these cultures, male identity is valued over female identity. Historically, these cultures expect a change from female to male and have even codified such expectations in their language [44]. ### 26.4.5 Female External Genitalia Female external genitalia will be normal except when exposed to androgens in early fetal life. Androgens may be derived from (1) the mother (ingested or endogenously pro duced); (2) the fetus (Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH)); (3) due to homozygous or heterozygous mutations in the placental aromatase gene, which leads to a failure to convert maternal androgens to estrogens, with virilization of both the mother and the fetus during the pregnancy; (4) ovotesticular DSD; (5) mixed gonadal dysgenesis [45–47]. The vir ilization degree depends on the quantity, tim ing, and actions of androgens to which the 46, XX fetus is exposed. Virilization ranges from clitoromegaly to severe posterior fusion of labia majora, absence of the labia minora and vaginal orifice, or a urogenital sinus with a large phallic-appearing clitoris that resembles hypospadias. Rarely, extreme virilization causes complete labioscrotal fusion and a “penile urethra” (Prader stage 5). In the last example, the external genitalia appears typical male. Therefore, the only clue to the possibility of a genetic female is the absence of palpable gonads in an individual with cryptorchidism. ### 26.5 Clinical Approach to Care ### of Infants with DSD The care of a baby born with DSD starts with recognizing the presence of a genital abnor mality. Is the infant a genetic female (46, XX) exposed to fetal androgens (i.e., 46, XX DSD)? 2. Is the infant an undervirilized genetic male (46, XY) due to underproduction or decreased action of androgens (i.e., 46, XY DSD)? 3. In nearly all cases, an external gonad is a testis. In the absence of an external gonad, the genetic sex of the infant cannot be identified by inspection if the infant has (1) 46, XY DSD with incomplete virilization, (2) 46, XX DSD with excess virilization, (3) ovotes ticular DSD, or (4) mixed gonadal dysgenesis. It is best to avoid using absolute terms such as penis or scrotum until the diagnostic studies are completed. Instead, the phallic structure (clitoris or penis) is measured and examined for the presence of chordee, a downward curving phallus due to a shortened ventral surface. The phallic measurement may not be easy because an erectile mass is sometimes buried in pubic fat and is curved. A tape measure placed on the point of origin on the pubic ramus along the dorsum to the “erectile mass” gives a reason able estimate of length [53, 54]. If the stretched length is less than 2.0 cm, microphallus diagno sis is made [55]. The width of the erectile tissue and its consistency should also be recorded. Hypospadias is defined by the location of a single urethral opening and classified as first degree (asymmetric on “glans”), second degree (mid-phallic shaft), third degree (junction of the phallus with scrotum), or fourth degree (perineal, closer to anus). They resemble male infants with cryptorchidism. The presence of a vaginal dimple or introi tus should be recorded. Babies with complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (CAIS) have typical female-appearing external genitalia with a normally positioned urethra and a blind vaginal pouch. In most infants with DSD, the labioscrotal folds look like two separate sacs separated by an indentation, giving a “bifid scrotum,” either flat or rounded. High renin levels can identify the asymptomatic salt loser before developing clinical dehydration. 46, XY males with CAH are at increased risk for shock because their genitalia is entirely normal. In the United States, screening newborns for CAH by measuring 17-hydroxyprogesterone has protected infants from high morbidity and death. Female gender assignment is relatively straightforward in virilized CAH genetic females because the infants have a uterus and ovaries [45]. Many 46, XX CAH individuals with a penile urethra are being raised as girls following clitoral reduction and genital recon structive surgery. In contrast, others have been raised as males and have undergone gonadec tomy and hysterectomy. There is an ongoing debate about the best choice for these females who have unambiguously male external geni talia with female internal sex structures. The International Consensus Conference on Intersex 2006 on CAH recommends that all 46, XX CAH patients be raised, female. The CAH consensus statement indicated that “there is insufficient evidence to support rear ing a 46, XX infant at Prader 5 as a male” [56]. However, in one report, the majority (10 of the 12) 46, XX individuals diagnosed with CAH, born with Prader 4 or 5 genitalia, and assigned the male gender at birth, always lived as a male [57]. Two were reassigned to the female gender in childhood but eventually self-reassigned themselves as male. At the time of the study, the age range of the men was between 35 and 69 years. Houk and Lee proposed “consideration of male assignment for 46, XX patients who have fully developed male genitalia” [57, 58]. Female gender assignment is also straight forward in 46, XY individuals with Complete Androgen Insensitivity (CAIS). On the other hand, gender assignment may be challenging in 46, XY infants with either isolated micro penis or associated hypospadias. Further, these individuals may have an average size or hypoplastic testes. Partial androgen insensitiv ity is a concern because male genital growth is permanently compromised. In the past, 46, XY infants with micropenis, with or without hypospadias, were reassigned as female [59, 60]. This recommendation was based on the belief that it was easier to make a functional vagina than a functioning penis. Thus, a female gender assignment was believed to result in a more favorable psychosexual out come. The proponents of this recommenda tion appreciated the influences of intrinsic genetic forces (nature) as well as the impact of environmental factors (nurture). Still, they reasoned that the environmental factors within the family were more dominant than the genetic forces if the gender reassignment was done within the first year of life [61]. With this strategy, genital reconstruction was done in infancy without a prior trial of testosterone to enlarge the micropenis. The presumption was that the penile response to treatment would not accurately predict the size of the penis in adulthood. Also, it was believed that a micropenis at birth was synonymous with micropenis in adulthood. The little evidence that exists is mixed, leading to the conclusion that the effects of DSD on psychosocial well-being and adjustment in individuals vary as a func tion of a large number of person and contextrelated variables and conditions. More multisite collaborative research is needed. The European study (Comprehensive European Clinical Outcome Study) focuses on the long-term outcomes of adults and adoles cents with various DSD diagnoses. Another developmental task associated with enveloping positive emotional self-concept and body image is experiencing age-appropriate psychosexual milestones, including intercourse [96]. Individuals with DSD were less likely to reach each of the romantic and sexual milestones compared to their peers without a DSD and were significantly older when reaching these milestones. Additionally, differences were found based on DSD diagnosis [97]. Mental health has been shown to be a challenge for some, but it varies based on the DSD diagnosis [98, 99]. ### 26.6.10 Global Legislation Legislatures in several countries have passed laws accommodating those born with a DSD and identifying as other than male or female [100]. For example, in 2012, Argentina passed the Gender Identity Law, which allows for name and sex changes on official documents without proof of surgical reconstruction or other medical or psychiatric treatment. This law was the first to allow gender reassignment based solely on an individual proclamation and applies to both DSD and transsexual cases [100]. In 2013, the Australian Senate passed the Sex Discrimination Amendment Bill [101], introducing legislation prohibiting discrimination based on DSD status. The new guidelines on gender recognition state that individuals should be given the option of selecting male, female, or intersex on their documents. In the same year, Germany intro duced an “indeterminate” sex option on birth certificates. Also, in 2013, the Council of Europe [102] adopted a resolution on the pro tection of children’s rights to physical integ rity, demanding no one be “subjected to unnecessary medical or surgical treatment that is cosmetic rather than vital for health during infancy or childhood.” In 2021, The United States issued its first U.S. passport with an “X” gender marker, acknowledging the rights of people who do not identify as male or female, Greater emphasis on “patientcenteredness” in health care delivery and increased awareness of DSD have been accompanied by controversy, especially about the utility of elective genital surgery in infancy or early childhood. In addition, legal ques tions have been raised, and there was a lawsuit regarding the legality of surgical intervention in managing a child with a DSD [103]. ### 26.6.11 Lawsuits and DSD Individuals with a DSD, or their parents, have brought lawsuits regarding unnecessary medi cal surgery that were primarily settled out of the public’s eye [104]. In the United States, the first public lawsuit challenging early sex assignment surgery on a child with a DSD ## PDF page 742 | printed page 739 involved a child diagnosed with ovotesticular DSD. After obtaining parental consent, this child was assigned a female gender and received feminizing genital surgery at 16 months of age. Shortly after that, the biological parents abandoned their child, who came under the South Carolina Department of Social Services’ care and was later adopted. Despite the feminizing surgery, the child even tually identified as male. The adoptive parents alleged that the medically unnecessary early genital surgery performed without the child’s consent violated the child’s constitutional rights. This case was eventually settled out of court [73]. In Germany, a woman with 46, XX CAH successfully sued the surgeon who removed her fully intact female internal organs when she was 18. She had previously been reared as a male and undergone surgery to correct hypospadias in childhood. Her diagnosis of CAH occurred following an appendectomy in which a uterus and ovaries were discovered. She sought 100,000 euros in damages for pain and suffering, claiming the surgeon failed to fully inform her about the consequences of the operation or possible alternatives [88]. In both cases, the issue of informed consent concerning elective surgery appears to lie at the heart of the matter. ### 26.6.12 A Shift in Research Focus ### and Clinical Care For years, the clinical research and manage ment of persons with DSD focused on the relationship between gender identity, gender role, sexual orientation, sexual functioning, and pre- and postnatal hormones because there was evidence from animal research that hormones, primarily androgens, affected sex ual behavior. The reviews above mirror that focus. They do not report the quality of life for individuals regardless of gender assign ment and rearing or even in those who changed gender. If such data are available, they are insufficient to draw meaningful con clusions. They also do not focus on the influ ence of genes on brain sexual differentiation and development, an area that is only begin ning to be explored [105]. This approach was categorical, meaning that the focus was on investigating and managing psychosexual development and hormones to exclude other variables of human development (i.e., quality-of-life variables, in addition to psy chosexual status and hormones). Later, Sandberg and Mazur outlined an approach encompassing psychosexual development in persons with a DSD in a broader, noncategori cal approach to clinical care [91]. This noncate gorical approach guides clinical care by considering a growing body of evidence. It sup ports the notion that the successful developmen tal trajectories of persons with chronic medical conditions are influenced by the psychosocial environment, support systems, and healthcare delivery organization, in addition to the specific nature of the person’s medical condition [106, 107]. Such an approach holds the potential to systematically account for variability in DSD patient quality-of-life outcomes and translate clinical interventions, proven effective in manag ing other chronic conditions, to the circum stances faced by those affected by DSD. While the investigation of basic biological mechanisms will continue, so will the quality of life studies in individuals with various DSD syn dromes. Examples of this work include those by Wisniewski et al. [108], and Stout et al. [109] on CAH, and Schonbucker et al. [110] on sexual quality of life in 46, XY individuals with a DSD diagnosis, Mazur on a small sample of five 46, XY individuals assigned and reared female [111], and Bean’s review of MRKH [112]. Additionally, others have focused on the effects of having a child with a DSD on parenting char acteristics [113–115] and peer relations [95]. ### 26.6.13 Advocacy Since Hermaphrodites with Attitude, the first advocacy group in North America, numerous advocacy organizations have formed to advo cate for individuals with DSD and their fami lies. Advocacy and peer support groups have grown internationally [116]. These different advocacy organizations hold meetings to pro vide support and allow individuals to meet oth ers, voice concerns, and educate themselves and others on their conditions. This work elucidated this system’s complex sequen tial signaling networks, which involve multiple interacting molecular signals, hormone influ ences, and cross-talk between these signaling pathways. There has been little change in the endo crine treatment of DSD over the last few decades. The advances are primarily in the domain of genetics. On the other hand, there have been evolving dynamics in many differ ent aspects of patient care. These included (1) debates about the efficiency and timing of medically and nonmedically necessary genital surgery: should this wait until the child can consent or not, its effects on sexual arousal, and even whether it should or should not be performed; (2) the creation of laws regarding unnecessary surgery and gender; (3) more transparency from physicians and other health professionals with family and patients ing adolescence if there was scarring or if it was not adequate for intercourse. paragraphs.text: The evaluation of menstrual disorders in ado lescents requires special consideration. Adolescents are in the midst of developing physically and physiologically to achieve adult reproductive function. Thus, the normal varia tion in the age of onset of puberty and subse quent menarche should be taken into account when evaluating adolescent girls. Menarche will be delayed if puberty is delayed in onset. The average age of menarche is 12.6 years in the normal-weight general American popula tion, with the normal range being 10.0–14.1 years [1]. Normally, cyclic menstrual bleeding usually occurs at 21–45-day intervals even during the first post-menarcheal year, and cycles outside 19–90 days are always abnormal. Because these menstrual patterns are statis tically abnormal, even within the first year after menarche (occurring in less than 5% of adolescents), these patterns represent “symptomatic” rather than the usual “physi ologic” adolescent anovulation, and evalua tion is suggested if they persist. The risk of persistent menstrual irregularity is slightly over 50% if symptoms persist for 1 year beyond menarche and nearly two-thirds if symptoms persist 2 years beyond menarche; thus, evaluation is indicated if symptoms persist for 1–2 years after menarche [10].
