Obstruction of the genital outflow tract— most commonly due to imperforate hymen— causes hydrocolpos, which results in a fullness and bluish appearance at the vaginal introitus from the bulging imperforate hymen, or hydrometrocolpos when the uterus is involved, which may present as an abdominal mass. Uterine aplasia may also result from differences in sexual differentiation (DSD) in which anti-Müllerian hormone secretion by testicular tissue has occurred. For this rea son, primary amenorrhea may be the present ing symptom of phenotypic girls with complete androgen resistance (formally known as testicular feminization syndrome), congenital deficiency in one of the enzymes necessary for testicular testosterone secre tion, or in patients with ambiguous genitalia due to partial versions of these disorders or due to 5α-reductase deficiency.
Intrauterine adhesions (Asherman’s syn drome) may result from trauma, such as postcurettage or as a complication of radiation
therapy of pelvic disease or chronic inflamma tory disease [13].
Abnormal bleeding, on the other hand, can result from genital tract trauma or infec tion such as from sexual abuse or a foreign body. Bleeding may also result from genital tract tumors.

gonadism may cause either secondary amen orrhea or oligomenorrhea. At its mildest, hypogonadism may present with abnormal menstrual bleeding. Hypogonadism can be categorized according to whether or not gonadotropins, particularly serum follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) levels, are ele vated ( Table 27.1).
paragraphs.heading: 27.2.2 Anovulatory Disorders

paragraphs.text: Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism: Hypoestrogenism with elevated FSH (hypergo nadotropic hypergonadism) indicates primary ovarian insufficiency (POI). The causes include both hereditary and acquired disor ders [14] . Acquired ovarian insufficiency may result from irradiation, chemotherapy, trauma to the ovary, galactosemia, or autoimmune disease. Gonadal dysgenesis due to deficiency of genes on the X chromosome causing Turner syndrome is the most common cause of POI, with an incidence of about 1 in 2500 live-born girls. About one-third of girls with Turner syndrome enter puberty spontane ously, and about 5% progress to complete it, with most developing secondary amenorrhea [15]. In women and adolescents with sponta neous POI not due to gonadal agenesis, a cause is identified in ~15% [16]. Fragile X chromosome premutation causes some cases of X-linked POI. Genetic causes of POI include hereditary gonadotropin resistance due to mutations in the LH or FSH receptor or along their signaling pathway, as in the context of Albright hereditary osteodystro phy, or to steroidogenic blocks in estradiol biosynthesis [14]. Genes involved in ovarian development, meiosis, and germ cell mainte nance have been identified as single gene causes of POI [14].
paragraphs.heading: 27.2.2 Anovulatory Disorders

paragraphs.text: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism: Frank hypoestrogenemia without elevated FSH lev els usually indicates secondary ovarian insuf ficiency (gonadotropin deficiency, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism). FSH lev els are not necessarily low because a normal gonadotropin level is inappropriate in the set ting of hypoestrogenism. Gonadotropin defi ciency can be congenital or acquired.
Congenital gonadotropin deficiency can arise from diverse cerebral, hypothalamic, or pituitary disorders, single gene mutations in the pituitary development cascade [17], or a

chromosomal disorder (such as Prader-Willi syndrome). Congenital isolated gonadotropin deficiency may result from autosomal domi nant or recessive disorders [18], of which GnRH receptor deficiency is more common in women than the anosmia-associated Kallmann syndrome. These and other specific gene defects that cause congenital isolated gonadotropin deficiency are discussed in Chap. 25. These disorders are typically associated with absent puberty but primary or secondary amenorrhea may manifest.

Acquired gonadotropin deficiency may be organic or functional. Organic acquired gonadotropin deficiency can be a consequence of tumors, trauma, autoimmune hypophysitis [19], irradiation [20], or chronic illness of vir tually any organ system [21]. Functional hypogonadotropinism (referred to as func tional hypothalamic amenorrhea in sexually mature girls) is commonly caused by energydeficit states such as eating disorders and excessive exercise (associated with low or nor mal weight) and emotional or psychological stress [22].

In some situations, it can be difficult to dif ferentiate between gonadotropin deficiency and POI as a cause of low estrogen. The most common situation is in children who are too young to have undergone neuroendocrine puberty, as indicated by a bone age less than about 11 years. The other situation occurs in incomplete or early POI because gonadotro pin levels are often normal in the early stages as ovarian function is declining progressively yet intermittently, as during the menopausal transition [16]. Suppression of gonadotropins and estrogens also occurs in frankly virilizing disorders.

Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea occurs in sexually mature (e.g., feminized) adolescents. It occurs in patients who secrete sufficient gonadotropin to feminize normally but have functional disorders which interfere with normal GnRH pulsatility. These disor ders arise from disturbances of cyclic or pul satile GnRH release that interfere with LH pulse frequency and the positive feedback mechanism necessary for ovulation. If the dis turbance of GnRH release affects baseline LH pulse frequency, then a hypogonadotropic

hypogonadism clinical picture results with hypoestrogenemia. If disturbance of GnRH pulsatile release primarily affects the positive feedback mechanism for ovulation, then amenorrhea with normal serum estradiol will occur. Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea is commonly caused by disorders of energy imbalance or psychological stress [22].

Anorexia nervosa is the prototypic eating disorder, but bulimia nervosa, the bingeeating/purging variant, is easily overlooked because the weight is often normal and vomit ing surreptitious. Energy imbalance due to excessive exercise and disorganized eating may occur in adolescents with normal weight who are muscular without appropriate fat stores; insight can be provided by a careful exercise history. It is also seen in the setting of psychological stress. Implicit with its categori zation as “functional,” return of menses occurs with amelioration of energy imbalance or psychological stress. Even when these fac tors are not obvious, similar mechanisms seem to underlie idiopathic functional hypo thalamic amenorrhea [23]. Post-pill amenor rhea may be suspected after the long-term use of hormonal contraceptives. However, this entity usually results from an undetected ante cedent anovulatory disturbance or an inter current illness, so a diagnostic evaluation is required.

Hyperprolactinemia requires special con sideration because it varies greatly in its pre sentation, depending to a great extent on the degree of gonadotropin deficiency. Prime among the multiple mechanisms of functional hypothalamic anovulation is disruption of GnRH pulsatility [24]. Galactorrhea is pres ent in about half of the patients, occurring among those with sufficient gonadotropin secretion to maintain residual estrogen pro duction; these girls may also have adrenal hyperandrogenism. The causes of hyperpro lactinemia are diverse and include hypotha lamic or pituitary disorders, medications, hypothyroidism, renal or liver failure, periph eral neuropathy, stress, or idiopathic [25]. Hyperprolactinemia is not only in the differ ential diagnosis of hypogonadotropic hypo gonadism and hypothalamic amenorrhea; it may cause short luteal phase (characterized
by menstrual cycles less than 22 days), exces sive uterine bleeding, or hyperandrogenic symptoms.

Chronic disease of virtually any organ sys tem can mimic gonadotropin deficiency or functional hypothalamic amenorrhea. Obesity may cause amenorrhea via suppression of LH levels, distinct from its roles in polycystic ovary syndrome, discussed below [26]. The main mechanism involves in part accelerated LH turnover [26, 27] and possibly in part gonadotropin suppression by inflammatory cytokines [28]. Glucocorticoid excess (organic or iatrogenic) causes amenorrhea by multiple mechanisms, prime among which is interfer ence with gonadotropin responsiveness to GnRH [29]. Thyroid disorders are well-known causes of menstrual irregularity.

PCOS accounts for over 80% of cases of androgen excess presenting at or after the onset of puberty. The classic syndrome origi nally described by Stein and Leventhal includes various combinations of amenor rhea, hirsutism (defined as excessive malepattern hair growth), and polycystic ovaries and is frequently associated with obesity and insulin resistance. The etiology of PCOS is not fully understood, and the manifestations differ widely among affected females. Consequently, there is no single test to diag nose PCOS. Diagnostic criteria for PCOS in adult women are encompassed in the “Rotterdam criteria” as various combinations of hyperandrogenism, oligo-anovulation, and polycystic ovary morphology (PCOM) that are otherwise unexplained [30]. If adult crite ria are applied to adolescents, the criteria will result in overdiagnosis of PCOS because nor mal physiologic events of adolescence may

Polycystic ovaries are a physiologic variant in normal adolescent girls, and there is a paucity of nor mative data in adolescents; thus, use of ovarian morphology or size parameters in adolescents as diagnostic criteria is not recommended [31, 32, 34]. To avoid mislabeling physiologic anovulation as PCOS, it is recommended that the menstrual abnormality and hyperandro genemia persist for 2 years [31, 32]. This recom mendation should not preclude earlier diagnostic evaluation for causes other than PCOS if hyperandrogenic anovulation occurs in this timeframe (see ‘other causes of hyperan drogenic anovulation’).

The manifestations of PCOS are quite variable. Only about a third of cases have the classic Stein-Leventhal syndrome. Anovula tory symptoms vary from oligomenorrhea to excessive anovulatory bleeding to otherwise asymptomatic infertility. Hirsutism or inflam matory acne may not be evident at presenta tion. Over half of PCOS adolescents have an abnormal degree of hirsutism or acne, but hyperandrogenemia does not always have a cutaneous manifestation. Obesity and acan thosis nigricans, a sign of insulin resistance, are common presenting features [35]. Obesity is present in about half of cases. Females with PCOS have a high prevalence of the metabolic syndrome and are predisposed to type 2 dia betes mellitus [26]. In adolescents, there may be an antecedent history of premature adre narche or early childhood obesity with a Cushingoid fat distribution or overgrowth (i.e., pseudo-Cushing’s syndrome or pseudoacromegaly) [36]. Congenital virilizing disor ders, such as congenital adrenal hyperplasia, are a risk factor for PCOS at puberty.

PCOS was initially thought to be a fundamen tally neuroendocrine disorder. This concept was rooted in the early observation that base line LH levels and responses to GnRH are elevated in PCOS. Compared to control women, women with PCOS have increased LH pulse frequency and amplitude. In addi tion, LH stimulates the expression of thecal

steroidogenic enzymes and steroidogenesis; conversely, LH suppression inhibits them. Therefore, the increased LH of PCOS was ini tially considered the cause of the androgen excess. However, this theory does not account for the subsequent finding that half of women with PCOS do not have elevated LH levels because LH levels are inversely correlated with the degree of obesity [27]. Furthermore, normally the ovarian response to excessive LH stimulation is downregulation of andro gen secretion. The mechanism involves down regulation of LH receptor expression (“homologous desensitization”), which is fol lowed by specific downregulation of androgen secretion that is exerted by intraovarian fac tors inhibiting the rate-limiting step in andro gen formation, the 17,20-lyase activity of cytochrome P450c17, which has both 17-hydroxylase and 17,20-lyase activities. As a consequence, increased LH levels normally cause downregulation of LH receptor sites, downregulation of 17,20-lyase activity with a rise in 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels, but the downstream androgenic response to LH is limited [26]. In PCOS, there is partial escape from these normal downregulation processes, so ovarian androgen excess occurs [26].

Excessive LH levels in some women with PCOS may be the result of hyperandrogenism inhibit ing estrogen-progestin negative feedback [26, 37, 38]. The LH pulse frequency of women with PCOS is less sensitive than that of controls to sex steroid suppression. Antiandrogen therapy restores the inhibitory effect of estrogen-proges tin on LH pulse frequency [39].

Eighty-seven percent of individuals with PCOS have functional ovarian hyperan drogenism (FOH) according to tests of ovar ian androgenic function [26]. Two-thirds of cases have functionally typical PCOS, which is characterized by steroidogenic hyperrespon siveness, particularly at the level of 17-hydroxyprogesterone, to LH (as deter mined by a GnRH agonist or hCG test); most of these cases also have an elevated free tes tosterone after suppression of adrenocortical function with dexamethasone [40]. One-third of cases have only the latter abnormality (functionally atypical FOH) [41].

An abnormal degree of insulin resistance, obesity, or luteinizing hormone (LH) excess is each found in approximately one-half of cases. The common denominator in most PCOS then is ovarian hyperandrogenism, with insulin-resistant hyperinsulinism being a nonessential but common aggravating factor in the pathophysiology. LH excess and the propensity to obesity seem to usually be sec ondary to the underlying ovarian hyperan drogenism and hyperinsulinism, respectively. However, the heterogeneity in the syndrome leaves open the possibility that in some cases LH excess or severe insulin resistance may be the inciting factor.

In vitro studies indicate that PCOS theca cells in culture have a steroidogeneic pheno type similar to women with PCOS in response to GnRH agonist testing [42, 43]. This results from an overexpression of enzymes on the ste roidogenic pathway from cytochrome P450scc (cholesterol side chain cleavage) through P450c17. The abnormal steroidogenesis is due to an intrinsic defect in the theca cells of PCOS patients that persists through passage [42, 43]. Recently, genome-wide association screening (GWAS) has led to the discovery of involvement of a previously unsuspected pro tein modulating steroidogenesis: DENND (differentially expressed in normal and neo plastic differentiation). The expression of the DENND1A.V2 isoform is increased in PCOS theca cells and accounts for the PCOS theca cell steroidogenic phenotype in culture [44].

A related steroidogenic defect some times seems to involve the adrenal gland. About a quarter of women with FOH have a related steroidogenic defect in adrenal formation of DHEA and its precursor, 17-hydroxypregnenolone, without evidence of a steroidogenic block in response to ACTH stimulation, as would occur in viril izing congenital adrenal hyperplasia. This dysfunction is termed primary functional adrenal hyperandrogenism (FAH). FAH had earlier been mistaken for “exaggerated adrenarche” or nonclassical 3ß-hydroxys teroid dehydrogenase deficiency, which is now known to be a rare disorder. Notably, DENND1A is also highly expressed in the adrenal androgen-forming zone [44].

Insulin-resistance is a common feature of PCOS [26, 45]. This insulin resistance is intrin sic: it is abnormal for the degree of obesity in about half of cases. The insulin resistance affects the glucose metabolic effects of insulin and is tissue-selective, primarily affecting skel etal muscle and hepatic cells, but it spares the ovaries and adipose tissue. Consequently, the hyperinsulinemia that is compensatory for the glucose-metabolic defect in insulin resistance acts on the ovary, causing “insulin-resistant hyperinsulinism”. An important effect of this hyperinsulinism is that it counteracts normal homologous desensitization/downregulation of LH receptors, thereby sensitizing the ovary to LH [46]. Insulin also stimulates formation of testosterone by 17ß-hydroxysteroid dehy drogenase. It does so by stimulating expres sion of KLF15, a Kruppel-like transcription factor that is part of the gene’s proximal pro moter coactivator complex and that also stim ulates adipogenesis in adipocytes [47]. Thus, the insulin-resistant hyperinsulinism of PCOS seems to contribute to both androgen and fat excess.

Another aggravating factor in hyperan drogenism is the pro-inflammatory nature of obesity, which occurs because monocytes accumulate in adipose tissue and the gastroin testinal microbiome changes. These mono cytes elaborate that increased inro-inflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor-alpha and lipopolysaccharide directly upregulate insulin resistance and ste roidogenesis [26, 48–51]. Glucose or saturated fat ingestion aggravates insulin resistance and FOH by triggering increased serum levels of several of these proinflammatory factors, often more so in PCOS than in obesity [50, 51].

The arrest of follicular matura tion that causes anovulation may in part be related to the high AMH levels and in part related to the premature luteinization of gran ulosa cells, which seems to result from thecal androgen excess when accompanied by insulin excess [52]; however, an independent folliculo genesis defect cannot be ruled out [26, 41, 53].

Similar to type 2 diabetes mellitus, PCOS is a complex trait that seems to arise because of an interaction between congenital predispos ing factors and environmental factors [26]. These complex interactions generally mimic an autosomal dominant pattern of inheri tance with variable penetrance. Heritability of PCOS has been estimated at over 70%, based on studies in identical twin sisters [54].

Highly heritable traits include elevated tes tosterone levels, PCOM, maternal PCOS, parental metabolic syndrome, and type 2 dia betes mellitus [26]. Ongoing research aims to identify specific genes that underlie PCOS pathogenesis. A wide variety of genetic vari

ants with linkage to and/or association with PCOS have been identified by candidate gene and molecular genetic studies. The candidate gene approach led to the discovery of coding and regulatory variants in the AMH and AMH receptor gene (AMHR2) in 6.7% of PCOS patients who have decreased signaling and may have pathologic significance [55]. Deleterious androgen receptor splice variants may underlie about 1% of PCOS [56, 57]. Several important investigations utilizing GWAS identified multiple genes linked to PCOS [58]. One of the most striking findings from GWAS studies in diverse PCOS cohorts has been the discovery of the DENND1A splice variant DENND1A.V2, which, as dis cussed above, encodes a previously unrecog nized protein that accounts for the PCOS biochemical phenotype in cultured theca cells [44]. A whole-genome sequencing study of 261 individuals from 62 PCOS families showed that half of these PCOS families had one or more of 30 rare DENND1A variants [59]. The vast majority of these were noncod ing variants, most of which were predicted to alter V2 expression via altered binding of transcription factors or RNA-binding pro teins. Cluster analysis based on anthropomet ric, reproductive, and metabolic traits in a population of nearly 1000 women with PCOS showed two distinct clusters of cases: a rela tively nonobese group (21–23% of cases) with

higher LH and higher sex hormone-binding globulin levels (termed “reproductive” group) and a relatively obese group (37–39%) with higher glucose and insulin levels (“metabolic” group) [60]. DENND1A variants were present in two-thirds of the reproductive phenotype group, which differed significantly from those with the intermediate (35%) or metabolic (27%) phenotype. Micro-RNAs (miRNAs) have been found to be differentially expressed in ovarian cells from PCOS and normal; these molecules inhibit gene expression via post transcriptional mechanisms. Pathway and network analysis suggested that miR-130b-3p was at the hub of a network that links DENND1A to upregulation of LH receptor expression and to the insulin signaling path way [61]). DENND1A.V2 may also directly stimulate steroidogenic transcription [62].

Epigenetic change may be important to the pathogenesis of PCOS. Abnormal epigen etic methylation of cytosine-guanine (CpG) has been identified in multiple tissues from adult women with PCOS [26] reflecting envi

ronmental exposures and altered expression of diverse genes. Epigenetic changes have var iously been found to reflect dietary distur bances in the intrauterine [63] or postnatal [64] environment. Perhaps the best known of the intrauterine perturbations is that indi cated by low birth weight, which has a delete rious effect on cardiovascular outcome [65] and which may be a risk factor for PCOS [26, 66].

Early prenatal virilization of the female fetus is well-established to cause PCOS in humans [26] and a PCOS-like state in all species studied [67]. The mechanism likely involves epigenetic changes [68]. The patho physiology may involve reduction of hypotha lamic progesterone receptor expression by prenatal androgen excess, with consequent hypersecretion of LH [69]. Although ordinary PCOS seems unlikely to be attributable to pre natal virilization in humans [26], the prenatal effect of virilization is transgenerational in mice and related to PCOS-related epigenetic changes [70]: common gene expression signa
tures were found in oocytes of prenatally androgenized mice and in blood cells of PCOS daughters and unrelated women with PCOS.

Postnatal risk factors in the internal or external environment can be viewed as a sec ond “hit,” which cause a latent heritable or congenitally programmed susceptibility trait to manifest as PCOS. These include obesity, syndromes of severe insulin resistance, and poorly controlled congenital virilizing con genital adrenal hyperplasia [26]. Premature adrenarche may sometimes be an early mani festation of the steroidogenic dysregulation that underlies PCOS.

81 Dexamethasone-resistant forms of hyper androgenism such as Cushing’s syndrome and cortisol resistance are even less prevalent than nonclassical congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Prolactin excess causes adrenal hyperan drogenism; Cushing’s disease and hyperpro lactinemia are sometimes associated with polycystic ovaries [82, 83].

paragraphs.heading: Ovarian Hyperandrogenism

paragraphs.text: Dependable testosterone assays may not be available to all practitioners, but are becom ing more widely available. The most available, reliable methods to assay total testosterone in women and children involve preliminary chro matography followed by either specific radio immunoassay or tandem mass spectrometry (abbreviated LC-MS) [75, 84, 90]. Most com mercial specialty laboratories now use tandem mass spectrometry. Some direct total testos terone radioimmunoassays give comparable results to LC/MS, but many do not [84, 91]. The automated assays of total testosterone, available in multichannel immunometric pan els, and direct free testosterone assays are very inaccurate at the relatively low testosterone levels of women and children; thus they give misleading information about androgen sta tus in women and girls.

The calculated serum-free testosterone (aka bioavailable testosterone) is also useful to detect androgen excess [75]. The most reliable method to detect free testosterone is to calculate it as the product of the total testosterone and the frac tion that is free from sex hormone-binding glob ulin (SHBG) binding (free testosterone = total testosterone X percent free testosterone). Percent-free testosterone is calculated from the SHBG concentration or directly determined by dialysis methods. The main problem with inter preting calculated serum-free testosterone levels is that the absolute values are method-depen dent, so it is important to use a specialty labora tory that has well-established normal ranges.

An early morn ing blood sample for total testosterone by LC/ MS, steroid intermediates, and cortisol is obtained, followed by a dexamethasone andro gen suppression test [84]. We reserve ACTH testing for a comprehensive panel of steroid intermediates, for the subset of patients in whom dexamethasone-suppressible androgen excess is present. Mutation-confirmed nonclas sical congenital adrenal hyperplasia is present if one of the steroid intermediates rises over 10
SD above average in response to ACTH [93–95]. Rare steroid metabolic defects are in the differential diagnosis [79, 96–98].

If the source of androgen excess cannot be localized by these tests, one may be able to definitively demonstrate an ovarian source by a GnRH agonist challenge test [84]. If no source for the androgen excess can be found, one is dealing with idiopathic hyperandrogenism; such patients should be followed to ensure that their course is as benign as expected.

Appropriate therapy of menstrual disorders depends upon the diagnosis. Amenorrhea due to genital tract outflow obstruction often requires surgical treatment, as in the case of vaginal aplasia or imperforate hymen. Some cases of intrauterine adhesions respond to hysteroscopic lysis. If a DSD is diagnosed, utmost sensitivity must be used when discuss ing the diagnosis with the patient and family. The gender identity and wishes of the patient must be considered when recommending hor monal therapy. Persons with ovotesticular gonadal dysgenesis are at risk for gonadal malignancy; close follow-up to monitor for gonadoblastoma is mandatory. In some cases, prophylactic surgical removal of dysgenetic gonadal tissue is advisable.
paragraphs.heading: 27.4 Management

paragraphs.text: For some underlying causes, treatment of hypogonadism is achieved without hormone replacement. The treatment of choice for a prolactinoma is dopaminergic agents. Hyperprolactinemia will be maximally sup pressed within 1 month, and the menstrual cycle will normalize within 3 months with an effective regimen. Cabergoline 0.25–1.0 mg once or twice weekly will usually control galactorrhea and shrink prolactinomas [25]. To minimize nausea, it is best to start with a low dose at bedtime. Two years of treatment will minimize recurrence. Transsphenoidal resection of prolactinomas is considered if the patient’s condition or eyesight is critical and for the rare treatment failures. A link between cabergoline treatment and mild-moderate tri cuspid valve regurgitation has been suggested in elderly patients with Parkinson’s disease who often take large doses of the drug. It appears that younger persons without preex isting cardiac findings are at low risk for devel opment of valve problems with the doses of cabergoline commonly used for prolactino mas; it is currently recommended to screen for valvulopathy if doses exceed 3 mg/week or a murmur is present [99].

Hypogonadism due to chronic diseases such as cystic fibrosis, heart failure, cirrhosis, chronic renal failure, regional enteritis, or sys temic lupus erythematosus is best treated by controlling the underlying illness. Anorexia

nervosa is best managed by an experienced multidisciplinary team. Refeeding is the first priority, accompanied by long-term manage ment of the psychodynamic disorders [100]. Menses resume when psychotherapy is effec tive and body fat is restored to normal. Estrogen treatment of patients with an eating disorder may mask the psychopathology that underlies the menstrual disturbance by induc ing regular menses, and oral estrogenprogesterone combination therapy does not yield the recovery of bone loss that occurs with weight gain [101], although more promis ing results have been reported with physio logic transdermal estradiol replacement [102].

Hormone replacement is the treatment of choice in hypergonadotropic hypogonadism and organic causes of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, such as congenital or acquired hypopituitarism. Stature is an important consideration in sexually imma ture teenagers, especially those with Turner syndrome. The dose of estrogen in standard oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) will inhibit growth and lead to premature fusion of the epiphyses in sexually immature patients. Panhypopituitary patients require replace ment of growth hormone, thyroid hormone, and cortisol deficits. Further discussion of full pituitary hormone replacement is beyond the scope of this chapter.

Optimal estrogen replacement therapy in the sexually immature girl requires the induc tion of puberty in a physiologic manner with extremely low doses of estrogen to maximize growth. Gradual, physiologic replacement of estrogen can be started at a peer-appropriate age without compromising height potential. This technique has been validated using intra muscular depot estradiol [103]. The low doses of intramuscular estradiol required for this effect are only available at compounding pharmacies, so transdermal E2 is the usual alternative [15]. There are various techniques to initiate therapy at an appropriate age at the very low doses required [104]. The recom mended starting dose averages 3–6 mcg daily. Although data are limited, the most widely used regimen begins with one-quarter of a 25 mcg patch applied twice weekly [104, 105]. The dose is increased every 6 months over a

span of 2 years to adult replacement doses of transdermal estradiol 75–100 mcg daily or 2 mg micronized E2 by mouth daily. Conjugated equine estrogens are not advised since doses as low as 0.325 mg daily inhibit growth [106]. Progestin should be added to estrogenic regimens after 2 years of estrogen replacement or after bleeding occurs: the most physiologic replacement regimen is with micronized progesterone (Prometrium®) 100 mg daily for 7 days monthly and advance to a full maintenance dose of 200 mg daily for 10–12 days monthly as tolerated [105]. In the setting of estrogen replacement at adult doses, the addition of progesterone is necessary to lower the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial carcinoma [107].

Hypoestrogenism in sexually mature girls may be managed by administration of an oral contraceptive (OCP) or transdermal patches with a progestin component. The currently available OCPs carry very little risk of venous thromboembolic disease (VTE) [108], and the progestational component protects against endometrial hyperplasia, but evidence in post menopausal women suggests that transder mal estradiol is slightly safer [109, 110]. VTE risk is related to the dose of estrogen (combi nation OCPs have ethinyl estradiol doses that range from 10 to 35 mcg) and the type of pro gestin (with norethindrone and norgestimate having the lowest risk and antiandrogenic progestins, e.g., drospirenone, with a higher risk). Obese patients may require higher doses of estrogen to achieve menstrual regularity. However, patients at risk of VTE or sensitive to estrogen because of conditions such as hypertension, migraine, or lymphedema are best advised to use a more physiologic form of therapy, such as 17β-estradiol delivered trans dermally. When using an estradiol patch, a progestin is administered for 7–12 days to induce menstrual shedding (e.g., micronized progesterone 100–200 mg orally daily); the more progestin administered, the less the risk of endometrial hyperplasia, but the greater the risk of premenstrual symptoms.

An acute episode of excessive vaginal bleeding typically responds to the adminis tration of a combination estrogen-progestin, low-dose OCP, one tablet four times daily for 7 days. Treatment is then stopped for 5 days, and the patient is warned that heavy with drawal bleeding with cramps may occur. Thereafter, therapy with a low-dose OCP, given as for contraception, is begun to pre vent recurrence of bleeding and is continued for about three cycles. Cyclic progesterone is an alternative treatment to oral contracep tive pills.

A patient who is hypovolemic because of rapid, heavy bleeding should be hospitalized and treated with intravenous fluids, an antifi brinolytic agent (e.g., aminocaproic acid or transenamic acid), and blood products as nec essary [111, 112]. Conjugated equine estro gens in a dose of 25 mg intravenously every 3–4 h for three to four doses are customary to reduce the bleeding, although other oral estro gens are sometimes used. In cases of bleeding of this severity, a bleeding diathesis or uterine structural abnormality should be considered. If heavy bleeding persists, curettage should be performed by a gynecologist.

The management of hyperandrogenic states is individualized according to symp toms and patient goals—hirsutism, acne, and alopecia, menstrual irregularity, obesity, and insulin resistance—and the source of andro gen excess. The hyperandrogenism associated with Cushing’s syndrome, virilizing tumors, DSD, hyperprolactinemia, or acromegaly improves with appropriate treatment of the underlying cause. Undesirable side effects of glucocorticoid treatment of congenital adre nal hyperplasia can be minimized by using a

modest bedtime dose (about 5–7.5 mg predni sone); however, adrenal suppression may still occur and stress dose precautions may still be needed. Monitoring 17-hydroxyprogesterone and testosterone while on treatment is neces sary for dose adjustment [113]. Control of androgens in congenital adrenal hyperplasia may not suffice for menstrual control unless nocturnal progesterone excess is also con trolled [114]. This treatment will typically nor malize the menstrual pattern in nonclassical congenital adrenal hyperplasia, but PCOS complicates many of these cases as a result of congenital or perinatal masculinization [26].

The management of PCOS is directed toward treating symptoms and monitoring for associated disorders. Treatment of menstrual irregularities in PCOS is recommended to pre vent amenorrhea and the associated risk of endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma. A combination OCP containing estrogen and progestin is the first-line treatment to induce regular menstrual cycles, especially in those with hirsutism or its cutaneous equivalents. OCPs containing non-androgenic progestins such as norgestimate generally have favorable risk-benefit ratios and optimize lipid profiles. Those on drospirenone may benefit from its weak antiandrogenic and moderate antimin eralocorticoid effects, though it poses slightly more risk for thromboembolic events: drospi renone is available in the USA with 20 or 30 mcg ethinyl estradiol. Obese patients may require a higher dose of estradiol to provide menstrual regularity.

Progestin-only regimens can be used to induce menstrual regularity as detailed above, especially if hirsutism and its cutaneous equivalents are not a concern. Progestin-only regimens are also useful in patients in whom OCPs are contraindicated or in patients with objections to the use of contraceptive therapy.

The hyperandrogenic manifestations of hirsutism and acne are treated by topical der matologic and cosmetic measures and/or endocrinologic treatment. The choice between the treatment options depends upon symptoms and patient preference. Mild hir sutism can be treated by hair removal tech niques such as shaving, bleaching, or waxing. Eflornithine hydrochloride cream (Vaniqa®)

is a topical agent that is FDA-approved for the removal of unwanted facial hair. Six to eight weeks of use is required before effects are seen, and it must be used indefinitely to prevent regrowth. It is often not covered by third-party payers. Laser therapy and elec trolysis are techniques of permanent hair reduction. Because of expense, discomfort, and occasional scarring, these techniques may be most appropriate for limited areas in patients who do not respond to other means of treating hirsutism.

OCPs are useful to treat hyperandrogenic symptoms as an adjunct to cosmetic treat ments. The estrogen component decreases bioactive testosterone by suppressing LH secretion and ovarian androgen production while increasing serum SHBG. The decrease in bioactive testosterone, assessed 3–6 months after start of therapy, is associated with an improvement in hyperandrogenic cutaneous symptoms; acne can improve within 3 months and progression of hirsutism may arrest within 9–12 months in most PCOS patients. Endocrinologic treatment reduces the androgen-induced transformation of vellus to terminal hairs, and the effects of these agents are maximal at 9–12 months because of the long growth cycles of sexual hair follicles. Thus, a minimum of 6 months is required to determine improvement. OCPs are recom mended as a first-line treatment of hirsutism [33, 75]. Many OCPs contain progestins that may have a mild androgenic component. It is logical, therefore, to treat hirsute women with OCPs that contain non-androgenic or antian drogenic progestins, as detailed above. If after 6 months of treatment no substantial improve ment in hirsutism occurs, antiandrogen ther apy is suggested [75]. Spironolactone has been shown to be effective to the extent of lowering hirsutism score by about one third [115], with considerable individual variation, and is prob ably the most potent and safe antiandrogen available in the USA. We recommend starting with 100 mg twice daily and then reducing the dosage to 50 mg twice daily for maintenance therapy after the maximal effect has been achieved. This dosage is usually well-tolerated; however, polyuria, fatigue, and hyperkalemia at higher doses may limit its usefulness. It is

potentially teratogenic to fetal male genital development and may cause menstrual distur bance in the patient; therefore, it should be prescribed with an oral contraceptive. Flutamide is another antiandrogen of similar efficacy, but is not recommended because of potential hepatotoxicity and expense [75].

menstrual disorders. Girls with delayed puberty, whether it has an organic or func tional basis, can almost always be assured that they will feminize and, if a uterus is present, that they will experience menses. Girls can be reassured that menstrual abnormalities will be regulated. In addition, patients with Turner syndrome or similar primary hypogonadism disorders have the ability to carry a pregnancy, and patients with hypogonadotropic hypogo nadism and chronic anovulatory disorders have the ability to conceive, though in both situations this may require special care by a reproductive endocrinologist.

The risk of metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes mellitus is increased in PCOS; thus a fasting lipid panel and oral glucose tolerance test or other screening methods for type 2 dia betes are recommended in patients with central obesity, hypertension, or family history of type 2 diabetes mellitus [116]. The 2-h blood sugar during an oral glucose tolerance test deterio rated at an average rate of 9 mg/dL/year over about a 3-year period in one study [45]. Women with obesity and PCOS are at risk for obstruc tive sleep apnea; thus, questioning about sleep patterns with appropriate referral to a sleep clinic may be necessary [117]. Screening for fatty liver disease with serum AST and ALT may also be necessary with appropriate referral to a liver specialist as needed.

Weight loss improves ovulation, acanthosis nigricans, androgen excess, and cardiovascular risk in PCOS patients [118, 119], while antian drogens have only a modest effect on metabolic abnormalities [120]. This observation lends promise to the idea that insulin-lowering agents could be useful in the treatment of PCOS. The biguanide metformin is the most studied of the insulin-lowering agents in the treatment of PCOS. Metformin suppresses appetite and enhances weight loss, which is critical to its effect [121]. Randomized trials in adolescents demonstrate that metformin increases the fre quency of menses and ovulation and modestly lowers testosterone levels [122–124]. The decrease in testosterone is not sufficient to improve hirsutism in most adolescents. It is rec ommended that metformin be considered as an adjunct to weight-control measures in women with impaired glucose tolerance, especially if weight-loss measures fail [125]. The new potent generation of glucagon-like peptide agonists shows promise as a means of inducing weight loss beyond that attainable with metformin [126, 127].

DiVall and Robert L. Rosenfield ### Contents ### 27.1 Introduction and Background – 748 ### 27.2 Etiology – 749 27.2.1 Genital Tract Disorders – 749 27.2.2 Anovulatory Disorders – 751 27.2.3 Polycystic Ovary Syndrome – 753 ### 27.3 Differential Diagnosis – 760 ### 27.4 Management – 768 ### References – 771 © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2024 S. Radovick, M. Misra (eds.), Pediatric Endocrinology, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-66296-6_27 ## PDF page 751 | printed page 748 Key Points 5 Anovulatory disorders that feature a low estradiol level are caused by hypo gonadism (hypergonadotropic or hypo gonadotropic). 5 Anovulatory disorders that feature nor mal estradiol may be due to pregnancy, hyperandrogenism, hyperprolactinemia, or hypogonadism in its early phases. 5 Tandem mass spectroscopy after prelim ### 27 inary chromatography is the most accu rate and reliable method to accurately measure estradiol and testosterone. ### 27.1 Introduction and Background The evaluation of menstrual disorders in ado lescents requires special consideration. Adolescents are in the midst of developing physically and physiologically to achieve adult reproductive function. Thus, the normal varia tion in the age of onset of puberty and subse quent menarche should be taken into account when evaluating adolescent girls. Menarche will be delayed if puberty is delayed in onset. The average age of menarche is 12.6 years in the normal-weight general American popula tion, with the normal range being 10.0–14.1 years [1]. The age of menarche is 12.6 years in White girls, 12.7 years in Asian girls, 11.8 years in Hispanic girls, and 12.0 years in Black girls [1]. Although breast development is gradually beginning earlier since the 1970s associated with the obesity epidemic and pos sibly environmental chemicals, this has had only a small impact on age of menarche [1–4]. 5 7 27.1 8 5 7 9 8 ![Source image](../../figures/ch027_p0751_01.jpg) Unmatched source image; PDF page 751. Consult the original caption. ## PDF page 752 | printed page 749 menstruating), oligomenorrhea (fewer than normal menstrual periods a year), and exces sive anovulatory bleeding (formerly termed “dysfunctional uterine bleeding”: bleeding that occurs more often than at 19–21-day intervals or is excessive) ( Table 27.1) [6]. Normally, cyclic menstrual bleeding usually occurs at 21–45-day intervals even during the first post-menarcheal year, and cycles outside 19–90 days are always abnormal. Because these menstrual patterns are statis tically abnormal, even within the first year after menarche (occurring in less than 5% of adolescents), these patterns represent “symptomatic” rather than the usual “physi ologic” adolescent anovulation, and evalua tion is suggested if they persist. The risk of persistent menstrual irregularity is slightly over 50% if symptoms persist for 1 year beyond menarche and nearly two-thirds if symptoms persist 2 years beyond menarche; thus, evaluation is indicated if symptoms persist for 1–2 years after menarche [10]. About one-third of girls with Turner syndrome enter puberty spontane ously, and about 5% progress to complete it, with most developing secondary amenorrhea [15]. Congenital gonadotropin deficiency can arise from diverse cerebral, hypothalamic, or pituitary disorders, single gene mutations in the pituitary development cascade [17], or a chromosomal disorder (such as Prader-Willi syndrome). Congenital isolated gonadotropin deficiency may result from autosomal domi nant or recessive disorders [18], of which GnRH receptor deficiency is more common in women than the anosmia-associated Kallmann syndrome. These and other specific gene defects that cause congenital isolated gonadotropin deficiency are discussed in Chap. 25. These disorders are typically associated with absent puberty but primary or secondary amenorrhea may manifest. Acquired gonadotropin deficiency may be organic or functional. Organic acquired gonadotropin deficiency can be a consequence of tumors, trauma, autoimmune hypophysitis [19], irradiation [20], or chronic illness of vir tually any organ system [21]. The other situation occurs in incomplete or early POI because gonadotro pin levels are often normal in the early stages as ovarian function is declining progressively yet intermittently, as during the menopausal transition [16]. It occurs in patients who secrete sufficient gonadotropin to feminize normally but have functional disorders which interfere with normal GnRH pulsatility. These disor ders arise from disturbances of cyclic or pul satile GnRH release that interfere with LH pulse frequency and the positive feedback mechanism necessary for ovulation. Anovula tory symptoms vary from oligomenorrhea to excessive anovulatory bleeding to otherwise asymptomatic infertility. Hirsutism or inflam matory acne may not be evident at presenta tion. Pathophysiology PCOS was initially thought to be a fundamen tally neuroendocrine disorder. This concept was rooted in the early observation that base line LH levels and responses to GnRH are elevated in PCOS. Compared to control women, women with PCOS have increased LH pulse frequency and amplitude. In addi tion, LH stimulates the expression of thecal steroidogenic enzymes and steroidogenesis; conversely, LH suppression inhibits them. Therefore, the increased LH of PCOS was ini tially considered the cause of the androgen excess. However, this theory does not account for the subsequent finding that half of women with PCOS do not have elevated LH levels because LH levels are inversely correlated with the degree of obesity [27]. Furthermore, normally the ovarian response to excessive LH stimulation is downregulation of andro gen secretion. The mechanism involves down regulation of LH receptor expression (“homologous desensitization”), which is fol lowed by specific downregulation of androgen secretion that is exerted by intraovarian fac tors inhibiting the rate-limiting step in andro gen formation, the 17,20-lyase activity of cytochrome P450c17, which has both 17-hydroxylase and 17,20-lyase activities. As a consequence, increased LH levels normally cause downregulation of LH receptor sites, downregulation of 17,20-lyase activity with a rise in 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels, but the downstream androgenic response to LH is limited [26]. In PCOS, there is partial escape from these normal downregulation processes, so ovarian androgen excess occurs [26]. Excessive LH levels in some women with PCOS may be the result of hyperandrogenism inhibit ing estrogen-progestin negative feedback [26, 37, 38]. The LH pulse frequency of women with PCOS is less sensitive than that of controls to sex steroid suppression. Antiandrogen therapy restores the inhibitory effect of estrogen-proges tin on LH pulse frequency [39]. Eighty-seven percent of individuals with PCOS have functional ovarian hyperan drogenism (FOH) according to tests of ovar ian androgenic function [26]. Two-thirds of cases have functionally typical PCOS, which is characterized by steroidogenic hyperrespon siveness, particularly at the level of 17-hydroxyprogesterone, to LH (as deter mined by a GnRH agonist or hCG test); most of these cases also have an elevated free tes tosterone after suppression of adrenocortical function with dexamethasone [40]. One-third of cases have only the latter abnormality (functionally atypical FOH) [41]. ## PDF page 759 | printed page 756 An abnormal degree of insulin resistance, obesity, or luteinizing hormone (LH) excess is each found in approximately one-half of cases. LH excess and the propensity to obesity seem to usually be sec ondary to the underlying ovarian hyperan drogenism and hyperinsulinism, respectively. These complex interactions generally mimic an autosomal dominant pattern of inheri tance with variable penetrance. Heritability of PCOS has been estimated at over 70%, based on studies in identical twin sisters [54]. Highly heritable traits include elevated tes tosterone levels, PCOM, maternal PCOS, parental metabolic syndrome, and type 2 dia betes mellitus [26]. Ongoing research aims to identify specific genes that underlie PCOS pathogenesis. A wide variety of genetic vari ants with linkage to and/or association with PCOS have been identified by candidate gene and molecular genetic studies. Amenorrhea due to genital tract outflow obstruction often requires surgical treatment, as in the case of vaginal aplasia or imperforate hymen. In some cases, prophylactic surgical removal of dysgenetic gonadal tissue is advisable. ### 27 For some underlying causes, treatment of hypogonadism is achieved without hormone replacement. The treatment of choice for a prolactinoma is dopaminergic agents. Hyperprolactinemia will be maximally sup pressed within 1 month, and the menstrual cycle will normalize within 3 months with an effective regimen. Cabergoline 0.25–1.0 mg once or twice weekly will usually control galactorrhea and shrink prolactinomas [25]. To minimize nausea, it is best to start with a low dose at bedtime. Two years of treatment will minimize recurrence. Transsphenoidal resection of prolactinomas is considered if the patient’s condition or eyesight is critical and for the rare treatment failures. A link between cabergoline treatment and mild-moderate tri cuspid valve regurgitation has been suggested in elderly patients with Parkinson’s disease who often take large doses of the drug. It appears that younger persons without preex isting cardiac findings are at low risk for devel opment of valve problems with the doses of cabergoline commonly used for prolactino mas; it is currently recommended to screen for valvulopathy if doses exceed 3 mg/week or a murmur is present [99]. Hypogonadism due to chronic diseases such as cystic fibrosis, heart failure, cirrhosis, chronic renal failure, regional enteritis, or sys temic lupus erythematosus is best treated by controlling the underlying illness. Anorexia nervosa is best managed by an experienced multidisciplinary team. Refeeding is the first priority, accompanied by long-term manage ment of the psychodynamic disorders [100]. Menses resume when psychotherapy is effec tive and body fat is restored to normal. Estrogen treatment of patients with an eating disorder may mask the psychopathology that underlies the menstrual disturbance by induc ing regular menses, and oral estrogenprogesterone combination therapy does not yield the recovery of bone loss that occurs with weight gain [101], although more promis ing results have been reported with physio logic transdermal estradiol replacement [102]. Hormone replacement is the treatment of choice in hypergonadotropic hypogonadism and organic causes of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, such as congenital or acquired hypopituitarism. Stature is an important consideration in sexually imma ture teenagers, especially those with Turner syndrome. The dose of estrogen in standard oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) will inhibit growth and lead to premature fusion of the epiphyses in sexually immature patients. Panhypopituitary patients require replace ment of growth hormone, thyroid hormone, and cortisol deficits. Further discussion of full pituitary hormone replacement is beyond the scope of this chapter. Optimal estrogen replacement therapy in the sexually immature girl requires the induc tion of puberty in a physiologic manner with extremely low doses of estrogen to maximize growth. Gradual, physiologic replacement of estrogen can be started at a peer-appropriate age without compromising height potential. This technique has been validated using intra muscular depot estradiol [103]. The low doses of intramuscular estradiol required for this effect are only available at compounding pharmacies, so transdermal E2 is the usual alternative [15]. There are various techniques to initiate therapy at an appropriate age at the very low doses required [104]. The recom mended starting dose averages 3–6 mcg daily. Although data are limited, the most widely used regimen begins with one-quarter of a 25 mcg patch applied twice weekly [104, 105]. The dose is increased every 6 months over a ## PDF page 772 | printed page 769 span of 2 years to adult replacement doses of transdermal estradiol 75–100 mcg daily or 2 mg micronized E2 by mouth daily. Conjugated equine estrogens are not advised since doses as low as 0.325 mg daily inhibit growth [106]. Progestin should be added to estrogenic regimens after 2 years of estrogen replacement or after bleeding occurs: the most physiologic replacement regimen is with micronized progesterone (Prometrium®) 100 mg daily for 7 days monthly and advance to a full maintenance dose of 200 mg daily for 10–12 days monthly as tolerated [105]. In the setting of estrogen replacement at adult doses, the addition of progesterone is necessary to lower the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial carcinoma [107]. Hypoestrogenism in sexually mature girls may be managed by administration of an oral contraceptive (OCP) or transdermal patches with a progestin component. The currently available OCPs carry very little risk of venous thromboembolic disease (VTE) [108], and the progestational component protects against endometrial hyperplasia, but evidence in post menopausal women suggests that transder mal estradiol is slightly safer [109, 110]. VTE risk is related to the dose of estrogen (combi nation OCPs have ethinyl estradiol doses that range from 10 to 35 mcg) and the type of pro gestin (with norethindrone and norgestimate having the lowest risk and antiandrogenic progestins, e.g., drospirenone, with a higher risk). Obese patients may require higher doses of estrogen to achieve menstrual regularity. However, patients at risk of VTE or sensitive to estrogen because of conditions such as hypertension, migraine, or lymphedema are best advised to use a more physiologic form of therapy, such as 17β-estradiol delivered trans dermally. When using an estradiol patch, a progestin is administered for 7–12 days to induce menstrual shedding (e.g., micronized progesterone 100–200 mg orally daily); the more progestin administered, the less the risk of endometrial hyperplasia, but the greater the risk of premenstrual symptoms. 27.4 An acute episode of excessive vaginal bleeding typically responds to the adminis tration of a combination estrogen-progestin, low-dose OCP, one tablet four times daily for 7 days. Treatment is then stopped for 5 days, and the patient is warned that heavy with drawal bleeding with cramps may occur. Thereafter, therapy with a low-dose OCP, given as for contraception, is begun to pre vent recurrence of bleeding and is continued for about three cycles. Cyclic progesterone is an alternative treatment to oral contracep tive pills. A patient who is hypovolemic because of rapid, heavy bleeding should be hospitalized and treated with intravenous fluids, an antifi brinolytic agent (e.g., aminocaproic acid or transenamic acid), and blood products as nec essary [111, 112]. Conjugated equine estro gens in a dose of 25 mg intravenously every 3–4 h for three to four doses are customary to reduce the bleeding, although other oral estro gens are sometimes used. In cases of bleeding of this severity, a bleeding diathesis or uterine structural abnormality should be considered. If heavy bleeding persists, curettage should be performed by a gynecologist. The management of hyperandrogenic states is individualized according to symp toms and patient goals—hirsutism, acne, and alopecia, menstrual irregularity, obesity, and insulin resistance—and the source of andro gen excess. The hyperandrogenism associated with Cushing’s syndrome, virilizing tumors, DSD, hyperprolactinemia, or acromegaly improves with appropriate treatment of the underlying cause. Undesirable side effects of glucocorticoid treatment of congenital adre nal hyperplasia can be minimized by using a ## PDF page 773 | printed page 770 modest bedtime dose (about 5–7.5 mg predni sone); however, adrenal suppression may still occur and stress dose precautions may still be needed. Monitoring 17-hydroxyprogesterone and testosterone while on treatment is neces sary for dose adjustment [113]. Control of androgens in congenital adrenal hyperplasia may not suffice for menstrual control unless nocturnal progesterone excess is also con trolled [114]. This treatment will typically nor malize the menstrual pattern in nonclassical congenital adrenal hyperplasia, but PCOS complicates many of these cases as a result of congenital or perinatal masculinization [26]. ### 27 The management of PCOS is directed toward treating symptoms and monitoring for associated disorders. Treatment of menstrual irregularities in PCOS is recommended to pre vent amenorrhea and the associated risk of endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma. A combination OCP containing estrogen and progestin is the first-line treatment to induce regular menstrual cycles, especially in those with hirsutism or its cutaneous equivalents. OCPs containing non-androgenic progestins such as norgestimate generally have favorable risk-benefit ratios and optimize lipid profiles. Those on drospirenone may benefit from its weak antiandrogenic and moderate antimin eralocorticoid effects, though it poses slightly more risk for thromboembolic events: drospi renone is available in the USA with 20 or 30 mcg ethinyl estradiol. Obese patients may require a higher dose of estradiol to provide menstrual regularity. Progestin-only regimens can be used to induce menstrual regularity as detailed above, especially if hirsutism and its cutaneous equivalents are not a concern. Progestin-only regimens are also useful in patients in whom OCPs are contraindicated or in patients with objections to the use of contraceptive therapy. The hyperandrogenic manifestations of hirsutism and acne are treated by topical der matologic and cosmetic measures and/or endocrinologic treatment. The choice between the treatment options depends upon symptoms and patient preference. Mild hir sutism can be treated by hair removal tech niques such as shaving, bleaching, or waxing. Eflornithine hydrochloride cream (Vaniqa®) is a topical agent that is FDA-approved for the removal of unwanted facial hair. Six to eight weeks of use is required before effects are seen, and it must be used indefinitely to prevent regrowth. It is often not covered by third-party payers. Laser therapy and elec trolysis are techniques of permanent hair reduction. Because of expense, discomfort, and occasional scarring, these techniques may be most appropriate for limited areas in patients who do not respond to other means of treating hirsutism. OCPs are useful to treat hyperandrogenic symptoms as an adjunct to cosmetic treat ments. The estrogen component decreases bioactive testosterone by suppressing LH secretion and ovarian androgen production while increasing serum SHBG. The decrease in bioactive testosterone, assessed 3–6 months after start of therapy, is associated with an improvement in hyperandrogenic cutaneous symptoms; acne can improve within 3 months and progression of hirsutism may arrest within 9–12 months in most PCOS patients. Endocrinologic treatment reduces the androgen-induced transformation of vellus to terminal hairs, and the effects of these agents are maximal at 9–12 months because of the long growth cycles of sexual hair follicles. Thus, a minimum of 6 months is required to determine improvement. OCPs are recom mended as a first-line treatment of hirsutism [33, 75]. Many OCPs contain progestins that may have a mild androgenic component. It is logical, therefore, to treat hirsute women with OCPs that contain non-androgenic or antian drogenic progestins, as detailed above. If after 6 months of treatment no substantial improve ment in hirsutism occurs, antiandrogen ther apy is suggested [75]. Spironolactone has been shown to be effective to the extent of lowering hirsutism score by about one third [115], with considerable individual variation, and is prob ably the most potent and safe antiandrogen available in the USA. We recommend starting with 100 mg twice daily and then reducing the dosage to 50 mg twice daily for maintenance therapy after the maximal effect has been achieved. This dosage is usually well-tolerated; however, polyuria, fatigue, and hyperkalemia at higher doses may limit its usefulness. It is ## PDF page 774 | printed page 771 potentially teratogenic to fetal male genital development and may cause menstrual distur bance in the patient; therefore, it should be prescribed with an oral contraceptive. Flutamide is another antiandrogen of similar efficacy, but is not recommended because of potential hepatotoxicity and expense [75]. menstrual disorders. Girls with delayed puberty, whether it has an organic or func tional basis, can almost always be assured that they will feminize and, if a uterus is present, that they will experience menses. Girls can be reassured that menstrual abnormalities will be regulated. In addition, patients with Turner syndrome or similar primary hypogonadism disorders have the ability to carry a pregnancy, and patients with hypogonadotropic hypogo nadism and chronic anovulatory disorders have the ability to conceive, though in both situations this may require special care by a reproductive endocrinologist. The risk of metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes mellitus is increased in PCOS; thus a fasting lipid panel and oral glucose tolerance test or other screening methods for type 2 dia betes are recommended in patients with central obesity, hypertension, or family history of type 2 diabetes mellitus [116]. Women with obesity and PCOS are at risk for obstruc tive sleep apnea; thus, questioning about sleep patterns with appropriate referral to a sleep clinic may be necessary [117]. paragraphs.heading: 28.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: Prolactin is a 23-kilodalton (kDa) protein secreted by lactotrophs (also called mammot rophs) that comprise approximately 15–25% of the cells of the anterior pituitary gland [1]. Whereas secretion of other anterior pituitary hormones requires stimulation from the hypo
paragraphs.heading: and Secretion

paragraphs.text: thalamus, lactotrophs exhibit spontaneous prolactin secretion [2]. Prolactin secretion is thus primarily regulated by the inhibitory effect of dopamine neurons in the medial basal hypothalamus, which secrete dopamine at the median eminence of the pituitary into the pituitary portal vessels [2–4]. Factors that either stimulate or inhibit dopamine neurons also inhibit or stimulate prolactin secretion,
paragraphs.heading: and Secretion

paragraphs.text: respectively. Factors that increase prolactin secretion include thyrotropin releasing hor mone (TRH), oxytocin, vasoactive intestinal peptide, estradiol, vasopressin, angiotensin II, serotonin, opioids, and histamine [2]. Alongside dopamine, other factors that decrease prolactin secretion include GABA, acetylcholine, and somatostatin [2]. Prolactin also stimulates dopamine neurons in a “shortloop” feedback mechanism that inhibits fur ther prolactin secretion [2, 3].
paragraphs.heading: and Secretion

paragraphs.text: Prolactin has both tonic and pulsatile secre tion and exhibits a circadian rhythm, with levels highest during sleep and in the early morning hours and lowest a few hours after awakening [2, 5]. Levels also rise slightly after eating [5]. With regard to prolactin levels across the life course, newborns have high prolactin levels at birth, decreasing to within the normal child hood range by 3 months of age [5]. Childhood prolactin levels are similar between males and females before puberty; during puberty, prolac tin levels rise in females, accounting for the higher normal ranges in female adolescents and adults than males [5]. Levels also increase sig nificantly during pregnancy, due at least in part to stimulation by estradiol. By the same mecha nism, prolactin levels may also increase slightly during the preovulatory phase of the menstrual cycle [4]. Suckling and/or nipple stimulation raises prolactin within 1–3 min, with elevations lasting 20–30 min [2], and prolactin levels are elevated during lactation.
paragraphs.heading: and Secretion

paragraphs.text: There are multiple forms of prolactin in circulation: 23 kDa monomeric prolactin; dimeric prolactin, also called “big prolactin;” and macroprolactin, also called “big big pro lactin,” which is over 150 kDa in size and rep resents some combination of prolactin multimers joined by glycosylation and/or immunoglobulin A or immunoglobulin G [3]. Typically, monomeric prolactin comprises approximately 85% of total circulating pro lactin, but some individuals have a predomi nance of big prolactin or macroprolactin [6]. Importantly, dimeric prolactin and macropro lactin have minimal biological activity, but all forms may be measured in immunoassay.
Key actions of prolactin include promoting the differentiation and proliferation of mam mary cells and, during lactation, increasing

milk production [1]. Additionally, prolactin suppresses gonadotropins (luteinizing hormone [LH] and follicle-stimulating hormone [FSH]) with a putative mechanism of inhibitory prolac tin signaling at kisspeptin (KNDy) neurons resulting in reduced GnRH [1, 4]. Metabolic effects of prolactin, beyond the scope of this chapter, are also increasingly appreciated [1].

Prolactin levels rise with sleep, exercise, coitus, and both physical and psychological stress. Stress—including the stress of venipunc ture—is a common cause of benign elevations in prolactin. To assess the effect of venipunc ture on prolactin levels, multiple studies have assessed “cannulated prolactin levels,” achieved via intravenous catheter (IV) place ment and serial measurement of prolactin at baseline and periodic intervals over the next two or more hours. These studies report two important findings: (1) on average, prolactin levels decline as time from venipuncture increases, and (2) a large percentage of indi viduals with elevated baseline prolactin levels have normal prolactin after 2 h [7, 8]. For example, in a large cohort of adult women referred for infertility and found to have ele vated prolactin levels on two occasions, 61% had normal 2-h prolactin values, including 5 of 11 women with initial prolactin values above 47 ng/mL (1000 mIU/L) [8]. In a differ ent cohort of 235 men and women referred for hyperprolactinemia with initial values up to 260 ng/mL (5500 mIU/L), 17% of adults had a normal baseline repeat sample, and an addi tional 9% had a normal 2-h “resting” prolac tin [7]. In this cohort, the reduction in prolactin between baseline and 2-h ranged from 2.1 to 35.3 ng/mL (44–749 mIU/L), and, among the female participants, an initial referral prolactin value of 96.2 ng/mL (2040 mU/L) had 97% specificity to detect true hyperprolactinemia [7]. Although similar studies in children are not present in the litera ture, children may also have elevated prolactin due to stress of venipuncture, and placing an
paragraphs.heading: of Hyperprolactinemia

paragraphs.text: IV to draw prolactin after 90–120 min may be a helpful step in the diagnostic process.
paragraphs.heading: of Hyperprolactinemia

paragraphs.text: Another important physiologic cause of apparent hyperprolactinemia is “macropro lactinemia,” or an overabundance of circulat ing macroprolactin, which has little biological effect but raises measured prolactin. Assays can differentiate between macroprolactin and monomeric prolactin using either size exclu sion gel filtration chromatography (GFC, the gold standard) or the quicker method of poly ethylene glycol (PEG) precipitation, which precipitates out the macroprolactin along with a small percentage of monomeric prolac tin [9]. If ≤40% of total prolactin remains as monomeric prolactin following PEG precipi tation, macroprolactinemia is confirmed [9]. Macroprolactinemia can coexist with patho logic elevations in monomeric prolactin, such that the diagnosis of benign macroprolac tinemia requires both precipitation of ≥60% immunoreactive prolactin and normalization of remaining monomeric prolactin levels fol lowing PEG precipitation [9]. Additionally, the presence of macroprolactin varies over time within individuals [10], so measurement of macroprolactin may need to be repeated in patients with changing clinical circumstances, such as an individual who previously had macroprolactinemia and newly presents with increasing prolactin elevation and/or new symptoms consistent with hyperprolac tinemia. The 2011 Endocrine Society guide lines recommend checking for macroprolactin in those who are asymptomatic [6]. Individuals with benign macroprolactinemia may also have nonspecific symptoms that could be attributed to hyperprolactinemia, such that clinicians may also want to assess for macrop rolactin if symptoms are nonspecific. Because of the substantial overlap between symptoms in those with true monomeric hyperprolac tinemia and benign macroprolactinemia, the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists recommends consideration of macroprolactin measurement in any clini cal situation with possible inconsistencies between labs, symptoms, imaging findings, and/or response to treatment [9]. At present, there are insufficient data in the pediatric pop ulation to guide a specific pediatric recom
paragraphs.heading: of Hyperprolactinemia

paragraphs.text: mendation regarding testing for macroprolactin, and we typically send it in asymptomatic cases and also in those cases with inconsistencies or nonspecific symptoms.
paragraphs.heading: of Hyperprolactinemia

paragraphs.text: Several medications antagonize dopamine and thereby increase serum prolactin. Medication-induced hyperprolactinemia is most common with certain atypical antipsy chotics, with risperidone causing the largest elevations, up to 200–250 ng/mL (4255–5319 mIU/L), and paliperidone and olanzapine potentially causing more modest elevations [11]. Among the other atypical anti psychotics, aripiprazole tends to lower prolac tin, whereas quetiapine and lurasidone have minimal effect on prolactin levels [11]. Typical antipsychotics such as haloperidol and chlor promazine can also raise prolactin, although not typically to the degree that risperidone does [12, 13]. The antiemetic metoclopramide also raises prolactin, potentially up to 200–250 ng/mL (4225–5319 mIU/L) [14].
paragraphs.heading: Prolactin

paragraphs.text: Several other medications may increase prolactin modestly, as described below, but patients with significant prolactin elevations who also happen to be receiving these medica tions should undergo full evaluation for alter native causes of hyperprolactinemia. There are suggestions in the literature that tricyclic anti depressants and monoamine oxidase inhibi tors may cause modest elevations in serum prolactin, but evidence is scant and conflicting [12]. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) may also increase prolactin slightly, although these effects are not clinically rele vant in most patients. SSRIs have been reported to cause frank hyperprolactinemia in some individuals, although routine monitoring of prolactin levels is not necessary with SSRI administration [12, 15]. Other medications that may cause mild elevations in prolactin include antihypertensives (verapamil, methyl dopa, and reserpine), opiates, cocaine, and estrogens [12]. Oral contraceptives with rela tively higher doses of ethinyl estradiol could potentially cause mild elevations in prolactin,
paragraphs.heading: Prolactin

paragraphs.text: although there is no definitive evidence that this occurs. A study of transgender women suggests no effect of estradiol treatment on serum prolactin [16], and studies of physio logic hormone replacement with estrogens also do not support an effect on prolactin [12].
paragraphs.heading: Prolactin

paragraphs.text: The most common cause of hyperprolac tinemia in children is prolactinoma [17]. A prolactinoma is an adenoma comprised of pituitary lactotrophs that excessively synthe size and secrete prolactin. Prolactinomas are divided by size into microadenomas (<10 mm) and macroadenomas (≥10 mm). Females are more likely to present with prolactinoma than males, and the most common time of pediatric presentation is adolescence [18, 19]. Other sel lar or suprasellar lesions can also cause hyper prolactinemia through compression of the pituitary stalk. Hyperprolactinemia due to “stalk effect” most commonly occurs in chil dren with craniopharyngiomas, germinomas, or large pituitary macroadenomas, although this effect can be seen with any mass or infil trative process that compromises the pituitary stalk. Of note, serum prolactin in children with stalk compression from a mass that is not a prolactinoma typically has prolactin levels below 100 ng/mL (2128 mIU/L), in contrast to the much higher levels seen in prolactinomas. Hyperprolactinemia can also be seen in rapidonset obesity with hypothalamic dysfunction, hypoventilation, autonomic dysfunction syn drome (ROHHAD), septo-optic dysplasia, or pituitary stalk interruption [20].
paragraphs.heading: of Hyperprolactinemia

paragraphs.text: Another pathological cause of hyperpro lactinemia is severe primary hypothyroidism, in which elevated TRH stimulates prolactin secretion. Chronic kidney disease may also cause hyperprolactinemia through both increased prolactin secretion and reduced pro lactin clearance [21]. Serum prolactin is also elevated in patients with advanced liver disease, presumably due to multifactorial etiology, although substantial elevations in prolactin in patients with liver disease still require evalua

tion for other causes [22, 23]. Chest wall trau mas, including burns, other chest injuries, and mastectomy, also raise serum prolactin, pre sumably through the same neural stimulation by which suckling increases prolactin [24]. There is discussion in the literature regarding whether mild elevations in prolactin occur in polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) [25]. Given the risks of missing primary hyperprolac tinemia as a cause of oligomenorrhea in this population, the presence of PCOS should not preclude full evaluation of patients for other causes of prolactin elevation.
