paragraphs.text: hyperprolactinemia could be decreased related to pubertal stalling or concomitant GH defi ciency from a pituitary mass, or it could be accelerated in the less common case of an adenoma co-secreting growth hormone and prolactin. Physical examination in children with hyperprolactinemia should be thorough and include specific focus on the visual field exam and pubertal staging. Clinicians may want to defer physical assessment of galactor
paragraphs.heading: with Hyperprolactinemia

paragraphs.text: rhea during the examination if they are repeating laboratory evaluation at the visit, as the nipple stimulation may raise serum pro lactin.
paragraphs.heading: with Hyperprolactinemia

paragraphs.text: For children who present with one elevated prolactin value, the first step is usually to con firm prolactin elevation with repeat testing. Although guidelines in adults recommend that a single elevated value is enough to con firm hyperprolactinemia [6], our practice is
paragraphs.heading: with Hyperprolactinemia

paragraphs.text: nearly always to repeat the level in children given the possible effects of stress as well as numerous assay considerations including tim ing of the blood draw, possibility of macrop rolactinemia, and need to assess for “hook effect”. Drawing prolactin in the morning, fasting, avoids the mild elevations in prolactin that may occur with eating and standardizes timing at a nadir of the circadian rhythm of prolactin. It is also good practice to request serial dilutions to exclude the “hook effect,” which is an artifact related to the prolactin immunoassay process by which very high serum prolactin actually causes lower assay results. We find it helpful to assess for hook effect on initial evaluation, and in most cases, it is not present and is not required in further prolactin testing. In children with mild eleva tions in prolactin and/or no signs or symp toms related to hyperprolactinemia, sending a macroprolactin level is also helpful. Additionally, clinicians should consider the possibility of a cannulated prolactin, for which an IV is placed and the prolactin level is drawn 90–120 min after placement to exclude possible elevations due to phlebotomy-related stress.
paragraphs.heading: with Hyperprolactinemia

paragraphs.text: Additional laboratory evaluation should include assessment of TSH, creatinine, and liver function tests, to exclude primary hypo thyroidism, renal disease, and liver disease as causes, respectfully. When clinically applica ble, urine or serum HCG should be sent to assess for pregnancy. Gonadotropins (LH and FSH) and relevant gonadal steroids should be sent to assess for hypogonadism caused by hyperprolactinemia. IGF-1 level may also be useful to assess for the possibility of a GH and prolactin co-secreting tumor. Evaluation of other pituitary axes can also be performed at this time in patients with significant prolac tin elevations, although such testing may not be necessary for those with mild elevations until after MRI results are known.

Once hyperprolactinemia is confirmed on repeat testing, subsequent evaluation depends on the degree of prolactin elevation and the clinical context. For example, children taking a medication that could explain their degree of prolactin elevation can be followed conser vatively if they have a normal pretreatment

prolactin value and are not having any signs or symptoms related to hyperprolactinemia. In the absence of a documented pretreatment prolactin that was normal, clinicians may want to consider the possibility of withdraw ing or substituting the offending drug, if pos sible, versus proceeding with an evaluation to exclude other causes of hyperprolactinemia. Asymptomatic children with minimally ele vated prolactin levels can also be followed conservatively, with consideration of cannu lated prolactin versus serial clinical and labo ratory follow-ups. Beyond these two scenarios, most children with persistently elevated pro lactin generally require magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain using pituitary protocol, with 1 mm cuts and use of a gadolinium-based contrast agent. MRI results will typically guide further evaluation and management, as those without lesions can be followed conservatively and those with sellar or suprasellar lesions will be managed accord ingly. Patients whose MRIs show macroade nomas that may be abutting or compromising the optic chiasm should be referred for visual field testing, as neurosurgical involvement and potentially more aggressive treatment are warranted in cases with visual field impair ment.

Goals of therapy in patients with prolacti noma include (1) reduction of prolactin to a level that alleviates symptoms and permits normal functioning of the hypothalamicpituitary-gonadal axis and (2) stability or reduction of tumor size. Dopamine agonists are the first-line treatment for most prolacti nomas. Appropriate treatment differs depend ing on the size of the prolactinoma and the degree of symptomatology. Patients with microprolactinomas, modest prolactin eleva tions, and few or no symptoms may benefit most from observation, gonadal steroid replacement, or dopamine agonist therapy [6]. Patients with more significant elevations in prolactin and/or larger tumors will require
paragraphs.heading: with Prolactinoma

paragraphs.text: dopamine agonist therapy, and patients with aggressive tumors and/or visual field compro mise may also require surgery or radiotherapy. At the time of this writing, pediatric-specific guidelines for the management of prolacti noma are not published, and adult guidelines are cited as relevant below [6].
paragraphs.heading: with Prolactinoma

paragraphs.text: Patients with microprolactinoma, modest prolactin elevations, and no or minimal symp toms may not require medical therapy. Although the natural history of untreated macroprolactinoma is not well-described in children, adult data suggest that microprolac tinomas have a relatively benign course, some times resolving without treatment and rarely progressing [6, 26]. For this reason, children with asymptomatic microprolactinomas can be observed without therapy, with serial pro lactin measurements and MRI. Similarly, for those with microprolactinoma complicated only by hypogonadism, gonadal steroid replacement can be used instead of dopamine agonists as long as immediate fertility is not desired [6]. Of note, these strategies are evidence-based in adults [6], but are not welldescribed in the pediatric literature, nor are there head-to-head comparisons of dopamine agonist therapy versus more conservative treatments in children.
paragraphs.heading: with Prolactinoma

paragraphs.text: Dopamine agonists used for the treatment of prolactinomas include cabergoline, bro mocriptine, and, where available, quinagolide. At the time of this writing, the first-line dopa mine agonist is generally cabergoline, which has proven both more effective and better tol erated than bromocriptine in adults [6, 27–33]. Although cabergoline does not have regula tory approval by the United States Food and Drug Administration for the pediatric age group (<18y), we and others routinely use cabergoline as first-line therapy in children, and multiple reports in the literature support use and efficacy in this age group [18–20]. Starting doses of cabergoline are 0.25–0.5 mg/ week, given once or twice weekly, and the majority of patients will achieve normaliza tion of prolactin on these doses [20]. Cabergoline doses are titrated to achieve nor mal prolactin and can be increased up to 3 mg/week, with doses higher than 3 mg potentially effective in select cases [18, 19, 34,
paragraphs.heading: with Prolactinoma

paragraphs.text: 35]. Dopamine agonists at high doses can cause valvular abnormalities, and echocar diography at baseline and follow-up may be warranted for patients requiring higher doses of cabergoline [6].
paragraphs.heading: with Prolactinoma

paragraphs.text: Prolactin levels should be repeated within 1 month after starting dopamine agonist ther apy and serially thereafter based on clinical context [6]. Patients with macroprolactinomas should have a repeat MRI within 3 months, whereas an initial interval of 6–12 months is likely appropriate for those with microprolac tinomas [6]. Clinicians should titrate dopa mine agonist therapy to normalize prolactin and perform serial MRIs at intervals of 3–12 months as needed to ensure stability or shrinkage of the prolactinoma. In patients with microprolactinomas for whom prolactin normalizes and the adenoma decreases or resolves over time, tapering and eventual dis continuation of dopamine agonist may be appropriate [6], although, again, data are scant in the pediatric age group. Patients with macroadenomas also typically achieve longterm biochemical and tumor control with dopamine agonists, and the dosage can be titrated to maintain normal prolactin and control of adenoma size.
paragraphs.heading: with Prolactinoma

paragraphs.text: Patients who have visual field compromise and/or who do not achieve control with maxi mal doses of dopamine agonist require man agement by a multidisciplinary team that includes neurosurgery and neuroophthalmol ogy. Cabergoline may still be the appropriate first-line therapy for those presenting with visual field compromise, although we recom mend involvement of neurosurgery and neur oophthalmology from diagnosis for close monitoring and, if the visual field defect does not resolve with dopamine agonists, timely TSS. TSS is the appropriate second-line ther apy for those who cannot tolerate required doses of dopamine agonist or those whose tumor is refractory to treatment [6]. Adjunctive radiotherapy and/or temozolamide may also be necessary in rare cases of aggressive pro lactinoma [33].
paragraphs.heading: with Prolactinoma

paragraphs.text: Other important considerations in the management of prolactinomas in children include evaluating the possibility of a genetic etiology and screening for bone health. Given
paragraphs.heading: with Prolactinoma

paragraphs.text: the possibility of multiple endocrine neopla sia 1 (MEN1), our practice is to follow inter val calcium levels in children with prolactinoma. Genetic testing for MEN1 should be considered in those with a family history of hyperparathyroidism or pituitary adenoma, and children with family history of pituitary adenomas should also be tested for AIP mutations [36]. Finally, in children with macroadenomas, genetic testing for MENIN or AIP mutations is advisable even in the absence of family history, as genetic testing in cohorts of children and young adults with apparently sporadic macroprolactinomas has detected mutations in approximately 10–15% of cases [19, 37].

The etiology of hyperprolactinemia in the pediatric age group ranges from benign physi ologic elevations to aggressive macroadeno mas, with medication-related elevations also relatively common. Timely evaluation of chil dren with hyperprolactinemia is critical in determining the etiology and proceeding with necessary management. Prolactinoma is the most common etiology of prolactin elevation in children and usually can be managed suc cessfully with relatively low doses of cabergo line. Less commonly, macroadenomas may require neurosurgery and, less commonly, additional radiotherapy and/or temozol amide.

Mild hyperprolactinemia in indi viduals on these classes of antidepressant requires full evaluation for other possible etiologies ### 28.2 Prolactin Regulation ### and Secretion Prolactin is a 23-kilodalton (kDa) protein secreted by lactotrophs (also called mammot rophs) that comprise approximately 15–25% of the cells of the anterior pituitary gland [1]. Whereas secretion of other anterior pituitary hormones requires stimulation from the hypo thalamus, lactotrophs exhibit spontaneous prolactin secretion [2]. Prolactin secretion is thus primarily regulated by the inhibitory effect of dopamine neurons in the medial basal hypothalamus, which secrete dopamine at the median eminence of the pituitary into the pituitary portal vessels [2–4]. Factors that either stimulate or inhibit dopamine neurons also inhibit or stimulate prolactin secretion, ### Automatic table extraction — verify rendered original |Etiology|Approximate range of expected elevations| |---|---| |Labetolol, verapamil|Generally <50ng/mL| |Estradiola|Generally <50ng/mL| |SSRIsb|Generally <50ng/mL| |Tricyclic antidepressantsc|Generally <50ng/mL| |MAO inhibitorsc|Generally <50ng/mL| [Original table](../../tables/ch028_p0782_1.jpg) ### Automatic table extraction — verify rendered original |Pathologic|Col2| |---|---| |Prolactinoma|Any range, up to 1000s (ng/mL). Factors that increase prolactin secretion include thyrotropin releasing hor mone (TRH), oxytocin, vasoactive intestinal peptide, estradiol, vasopressin, angiotensin II, serotonin, opioids, and histamine [2]. Alongside dopamine, other factors that decrease prolactin secretion include GABA, acetylcholine, and somatostatin [2]. Prolactin also stimulates dopamine neurons in a “shortloop” feedback mechanism that inhibits fur ther prolactin secretion [2, 3]. Prolactin has both tonic and pulsatile secre tion and exhibits a circadian rhythm, with levels highest during sleep and in the early morning hours and lowest a few hours after awakening [2, 5]. Levels also rise slightly after eating [5]. With regard to prolactin levels across the life course, newborns have high prolactin levels at birth, decreasing to within the normal child hood range by 3 months of age [5]. Childhood prolactin levels are similar between males and females before puberty; during puberty, prolac tin levels rise in females, accounting for the higher normal ranges in female adolescents and adults than males [5]. Levels also increase sig nificantly during pregnancy, due at least in part to stimulation by estradiol. By the same mecha nism, prolactin levels may also increase slightly during the preovulatory phase of the menstrual cycle [4]. Suckling and/or nipple stimulation raises prolactin within 1–3 min, with elevations lasting 20–30 min [2], and prolactin levels are elevated during lactation. ### 28 There are multiple forms of prolactin in circulation: 23 kDa monomeric prolactin; dimeric prolactin, also called “big prolactin;” and macroprolactin, also called “big big pro lactin,” which is over 150 kDa in size and rep resents some combination of prolactin multimers joined by glycosylation and/or immunoglobulin A or immunoglobulin G [3]. Typically, monomeric prolactin comprises approximately 85% of total circulating pro lactin, but some individuals have a predomi nance of big prolactin or macroprolactin [6]. Importantly, dimeric prolactin and macropro lactin have minimal biological activity, but all forms may be measured in immunoassay. Key actions of prolactin include promoting the differentiation and proliferation of mam mary cells and, during lactation, increasing milk production [1]. Additionally, prolactin suppresses gonadotropins (luteinizing hormone [LH] and follicle-stimulating hormone [FSH]) with a putative mechanism of inhibitory prolac tin signaling at kisspeptin (KNDy) neurons resulting in reduced GnRH [1, 4]. Metabolic effects of prolactin, beyond the scope of this chapter, are also increasingly appreciated [1]. ### 28.3 Physiologic Causes ### of Hyperprolactinemia Prolactin levels rise with sleep, exercise, coitus, and both physical and psychological stress. Stress—including the stress of venipunc ture—is a common cause of benign elevations in prolactin. To assess the effect of venipunc ture on prolactin levels, multiple studies have assessed “cannulated prolactin levels,” achieved via intravenous catheter (IV) place ment and serial measurement of prolactin at baseline and periodic intervals over the next two or more hours. These studies report two important findings: (1) on average, prolactin levels decline as time from venipuncture increases, and (2) a large percentage of indi viduals with elevated baseline prolactin levels have normal prolactin after 2 h [7, 8]. For example, in a large cohort of adult women referred for infertility and found to have ele vated prolactin levels on two occasions, 61% had normal 2-h prolactin values, including 5 of 11 women with initial prolactin values above 47 ng/mL (1000 mIU/L) [8]. In a differ ent cohort of 235 men and women referred for hyperprolactinemia with initial values up to 260 ng/mL (5500 mIU/L), 17% of adults had a normal baseline repeat sample, and an addi tional 9% had a normal 2-h “resting” prolac tin [7]. In this cohort, the reduction in prolactin between baseline and 2-h ranged from 2.1 to 35.3 ng/mL (44–749 mIU/L), and, among the female participants, an initial referral prolactin value of 96.2 ng/mL (2040 mU/L) had 97% specificity to detect true hyperprolactinemia [7]. Although similar studies in children are not present in the litera ture, children may also have elevated prolactin due to stress of venipuncture, and placing an ## PDF page 784 | printed page 781 IV to draw prolactin after 90–120 min may be a helpful step in the diagnostic process. Another important physiologic cause of apparent hyperprolactinemia is “macropro lactinemia,” or an overabundance of circulat ing macroprolactin, which has little biological effect but raises measured prolactin. Assays can differentiate between macroprolactin and monomeric prolactin using either size exclu sion gel filtration chromatography (GFC, the gold standard) or the quicker method of poly ethylene glycol (PEG) precipitation, which precipitates out the macroprolactin along with a small percentage of monomeric prolac tin [9]. If ≤40% of total prolactin remains as monomeric prolactin following PEG precipi tation, macroprolactinemia is confirmed [9]. Macroprolactinemia can coexist with patho logic elevations in monomeric prolactin, such that the diagnosis of benign macroprolac tinemia requires both precipitation of ≥60% immunoreactive prolactin and normalization of remaining monomeric prolactin levels fol lowing PEG precipitation [9]. Additionally, the presence of macroprolactin varies over time within individuals [10], so measurement of macroprolactin may need to be repeated in patients with changing clinical circumstances, such as an individual who previously had macroprolactinemia and newly presents with increasing prolactin elevation and/or new symptoms consistent with hyperprolac tinemia. The 2011 Endocrine Society guide lines recommend checking for macroprolactin in those who are asymptomatic [6]. Individuals with benign macroprolactinemia may also have nonspecific symptoms that could be attributed to hyperprolactinemia, such that clinicians may also want to assess for macrop rolactin if symptoms are nonspecific. Because of the substantial overlap between symptoms in those with true monomeric hyperprolac tinemia and benign macroprolactinemia, the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists recommends consideration of macroprolactin measurement in any clini cal situation with possible inconsistencies between labs, symptoms, imaging findings, and/or response to treatment [9]. At present, there are insufficient data in the pediatric pop ulation to guide a specific pediatric recom mendation regarding testing for macroprolactin, and we typically send it in asymptomatic cases and also in those cases with inconsistencies or nonspecific symptoms. ### 28.4 Medications that Raise ### Prolactin Several medications antagonize dopamine and thereby increase serum prolactin. Medication-induced hyperprolactinemia is most common with certain atypical antipsy chotics, with risperidone causing the largest elevations, up to 200–250 ng/mL (4255–5319 mIU/L), and paliperidone and olanzapine potentially causing more modest elevations [11]. Among the other atypical anti psychotics, aripiprazole tends to lower prolac tin, whereas quetiapine and lurasidone have minimal effect on prolactin levels [11]. Typical antipsychotics such as haloperidol and chlor promazine can also raise prolactin, although not typically to the degree that risperidone does [12, 13]. The antiemetic metoclopramide also raises prolactin, potentially up to 200–250 ng/mL (4225–5319 mIU/L) [14]. Several other medications may increase prolactin modestly, as described below, but patients with significant prolactin elevations who also happen to be receiving these medica tions should undergo full evaluation for alter native causes of hyperprolactinemia. There are suggestions in the literature that tricyclic anti depressants and monoamine oxidase inhibi tors may cause modest elevations in serum prolactin, but evidence is scant and conflicting [12]. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) may also increase prolactin slightly, although these effects are not clinically rele vant in most patients. SSRIs have been reported to cause frank hyperprolactinemia in some individuals, although routine monitoring of prolactin levels is not necessary with SSRI administration [12, 15]. Other medications that may cause mild elevations in prolactin include antihypertensives (verapamil, methyl dopa, and reserpine), opiates, cocaine, and estrogens [12]. Oral contraceptives with rela tively higher doses of ethinyl estradiol could potentially cause mild elevations in prolactin, ## PDF page 785 | printed page 782 although there is no definitive evidence that this occurs. A study of transgender women suggests no effect of estradiol treatment on serum prolactin [16], and studies of physio logic hormone replacement with estrogens also do not support an effect on prolactin [12]. ### 28.5 Pathologic Causes ### of Hyperprolactinemia The most common cause of hyperprolac tinemia in children is prolactinoma [17]. A prolactinoma is an adenoma comprised of pituitary lactotrophs that excessively synthe size and secrete prolactin. Prolactinomas are divided by size into microadenomas (<10 mm) and macroadenomas (≥10 mm). Females are more likely to present with prolactinoma than males, and the most common time of pediatric presentation is adolescence [18, 19]. Other sel lar or suprasellar lesions can also cause hyper prolactinemia through compression of the pituitary stalk. Hyperprolactinemia due to “stalk effect” most commonly occurs in chil dren with craniopharyngiomas, germinomas, or large pituitary macroadenomas, although this effect can be seen with any mass or infil trative process that compromises the pituitary stalk. Of note, serum prolactin in children with stalk compression from a mass that is not a prolactinoma typically has prolactin levels below 100 ng/mL (2128 mIU/L), in contrast to the much higher levels seen in prolactinomas. Hyperprolactinemia can also be seen in rapidonset obesity with hypothalamic dysfunction, hypoventilation, autonomic dysfunction syn drome (ROHHAD), septo-optic dysplasia, or pituitary stalk interruption [20]. ### 28 Another pathological cause of hyperpro lactinemia is severe primary hypothyroidism, in which elevated TRH stimulates prolactin secretion. Chronic kidney disease may also cause hyperprolactinemia through both increased prolactin secretion and reduced pro lactin clearance [21]. Serum prolactin is also elevated in patients with advanced liver disease, presumably due to multifactorial etiology, although substantial elevations in prolactin in patients with liver disease still require evalua tion for other causes [22, 23]. Chest wall trau mas, including burns, other chest injuries, and mastectomy, also raise serum prolactin, pre sumably through the same neural stimulation by which suckling increases prolactin [24]. There is discussion in the literature regarding whether mild elevations in prolactin occur in polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) [25]. Given the risks of missing primary hyperprolac tinemia as a cause of oligomenorrhea in this population, the presence of PCOS should not preclude full evaluation of patients for other causes of prolactin elevation. ### 28.6 Evaluation of Patients ### with Hyperprolactinemia 28.2 ## PDF page 786 | printed page 783 Table 28.2 Evaluation of hyperprolactinemia History – Review of medications – Assessment for signs/symptoms of pubertal delay or altered growth and galactorrhea – Menstrual history and assessment of libido and sexual function when applicable – Assessment for signs/symptoms of mass effect including headaches, visual changes, vomiting – Family history of hyperparathyroidism or pituitary adenomas Physical Examination – Thorough and with special attention to visual field exam, assessment of gynecomastia in males, careful pubertal staging. Physical assessment of galactorrhea if warranted, although nipple stimulation precludes accurate prolactin measurement immediately afterward Laboratory Evaluation: – Consider repeat in the morning, fasting, with serial dilution to assess for hook effect – Consider measurement of macroprolactinoma to assess for macroprolactinemia – Consider cannulated prolactin (IV placement with measurement of prolactin after 90–120 min to exclude physiologic elevations due to phlebotomy stress) – LH, FSH, estradiol, or testosterone to assess for hypogonadism – Urine or serum HCG to exclude pregnancy when applicable – TSH to assess for primary hypothyroidism as a cause – Creatinine and liver function tests to assess for advanced renal and liver disease, respectively Magnetic Resonance Imaging of the brain using pituitary protocol pre- and post-contrast with 1 mm cuts Additional Evaluation for Patients with Prolactinoma or Sellar/Suprasellar Pathology on MRI – In patients with any adenoma, IGF-1 to assess for co-secretion of GH – In patients with any prolactinoma, DXA – In patients with macroprolactinoma or other large sellar/suprasellar mass, assessment of morning cortisol or other test of adrenal sufficiency; assessment of IGF-1 to assess for GH deficiency; if symptoms warrant, assessment for diabetes insipidus – Consider monitoring calcium in all patients with prolactinoma given possibility of MEN1 – Consider genetic testing for MEN1 for all patients with prolactinoma and family history of pituitary adenoma or hyperparathyroidism – Consider genetic testing for AIP mutations for all patients with prolactinoma and family history of pituitary adenoma – Consider genetic testing for MEN1 and API mutation in all children with macroadenoma, regardless of family history – Visual field testing in patients with macroadenomas or other sellar masses that may abut or compress the optic chiasm Abbreviations: AIP aryl hydrocarbon receptor interacting protein; DXA dual energy x-ray absorptiometry; FSH follicle-stimulating hormone; GH growth hormone; HCG human chorionic gonadotropin; IGF-1 insu lin-like growth factor 1; LH luteinizing hormone; MEN1 multiple endocrine neoplasia 1; TSH thyroidstimulating hormone hyperprolactinemia could be decreased related to pubertal stalling or concomitant GH defi ciency from a pituitary mass, or it could be accelerated in the less common case of an adenoma co-secreting growth hormone and prolactin. Physical examination in children with hyperprolactinemia should be thorough and include specific focus on the visual field exam and pubertal staging. Clinicians may want to defer physical assessment of galactor rhea during the examination if they are repeating laboratory evaluation at the visit, as the nipple stimulation may raise serum pro lactin. For children who present with one elevated prolactin value, the first step is usually to con firm prolactin elevation with repeat testing. Although guidelines in adults recommend that a single elevated value is enough to con firm hyperprolactinemia [6], our practice is ## PDF page 787 | printed page 784 nearly always to repeat the level in children given the possible effects of stress as well as numerous assay considerations including tim ing of the blood draw, possibility of macrop rolactinemia, and need to assess for “hook effect”. Drawing prolactin in the morning, fasting, avoids the mild elevations in prolactin that may occur with eating and standardizes timing at a nadir of the circadian rhythm of prolactin. It is also good practice to request serial dilutions to exclude the “hook effect,” which is an artifact related to the prolactin immunoassay process by which very high serum prolactin actually causes lower assay results. We find it helpful to assess for hook effect on initial evaluation, and in most cases, it is not present and is not required in further prolactin testing. In children with mild eleva tions in prolactin and/or no signs or symp toms related to hyperprolactinemia, sending a macroprolactin level is also helpful. Additionally, clinicians should consider the possibility of a cannulated prolactin, for which an IV is placed and the prolactin level is drawn 90–120 min after placement to exclude possible elevations due to phlebotomy-related stress. ### 28 Additional laboratory evaluation should include assessment of TSH, creatinine, and liver function tests, to exclude primary hypo thyroidism, renal disease, and liver disease as causes, respectfully. When clinically applica ble, urine or serum HCG should be sent to assess for pregnancy. Gonadotropins (LH and FSH) and relevant gonadal steroids should be sent to assess for hypogonadism caused by hyperprolactinemia. IGF-1 level may also be useful to assess for the possibility of a GH and prolactin co-secreting tumor. Evaluation of other pituitary axes can also be performed at this time in patients with significant prolac tin elevations, although such testing may not be necessary for those with mild elevations until after MRI results are known. Once hyperprolactinemia is confirmed on repeat testing, subsequent evaluation depends on the degree of prolactin elevation and the clinical context. For example, children taking a medication that could explain their degree of prolactin elevation can be followed conser vatively if they have a normal pretreatment prolactin value and are not having any signs or symptoms related to hyperprolactinemia. In the absence of a documented pretreatment prolactin that was normal, clinicians may want to consider the possibility of withdraw ing or substituting the offending drug, if pos sible, versus proceeding with an evaluation to exclude other causes of hyperprolactinemia. Asymptomatic children with minimally ele vated prolactin levels can also be followed conservatively, with consideration of cannu lated prolactin versus serial clinical and labo ratory follow-ups. Beyond these two scenarios, most children with persistently elevated pro lactin generally require magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain using pituitary protocol, with 1 mm cuts and use of a gadolinium-based contrast agent. MRI results will typically guide further evaluation and management, as those without lesions can be followed conservatively and those with sellar or suprasellar lesions will be managed accord ingly. Patients whose MRIs show macroade nomas that may be abutting or compromising the optic chiasm should be referred for visual field testing, as neurosurgical involvement and potentially more aggressive treatment are warranted in cases with visual field impair ment. ### 28.7 Management of Patients ### with Prolactinoma Goals of therapy in patients with prolacti noma include (1) reduction of prolactin to a level that alleviates symptoms and permits normal functioning of the hypothalamicpituitary-gonadal axis and (2) stability or reduction of tumor size. Dopamine agonists are the first-line treatment for most prolacti nomas. Appropriate treatment differs depend ing on the size of the prolactinoma and the degree of symptomatology. Patients with microprolactinomas, modest prolactin eleva tions, and few or no symptoms may benefit most from observation, gonadal steroid replacement, or dopamine agonist therapy [6]. Patients with more significant elevations in prolactin and/or larger tumors will require ## PDF page 788 | printed page 785 dopamine agonist therapy, and patients with aggressive tumors and/or visual field compro mise may also require surgery or radiotherapy. At the time of this writing, pediatric-specific guidelines for the management of prolacti noma are not published, and adult guidelines are cited as relevant below [6]. Patients with microprolactinoma, modest prolactin elevations, and no or minimal symp toms may not require medical therapy. Although the natural history of untreated macroprolactinoma is not well-described in children, adult data suggest that microprolac tinomas have a relatively benign course, some times resolving without treatment and rarely progressing [6, 26]. For this reason, children with asymptomatic microprolactinomas can be observed without therapy, with serial pro lactin measurements and MRI. Similarly, for those with microprolactinoma complicated only by hypogonadism, gonadal steroid replacement can be used instead of dopamine agonists as long as immediate fertility is not desired [6]. Of note, these strategies are evidence-based in adults [6], but are not welldescribed in the pediatric literature, nor are there head-to-head comparisons of dopamine agonist therapy versus more conservative treatments in children. Dopamine agonists used for the treatment of prolactinomas include cabergoline, bro mocriptine, and, where available, quinagolide. At the time of this writing, the first-line dopa mine agonist is generally cabergoline, which has proven both more effective and better tol erated than bromocriptine in adults [6, 27–33]. Although cabergoline does not have regula tory approval by the United States Food and Drug Administration for the pediatric age group (<18y), we and others routinely use cabergoline as first-line therapy in children, and multiple reports in the literature support use and efficacy in this age group [18–20]. Starting doses of cabergoline are 0.25–0.5 mg/ week, given once or twice weekly, and the majority of patients will achieve normaliza tion of prolactin on these doses [20]. Cabergoline doses are titrated to achieve nor mal prolactin and can be increased up to 3 mg/week, with doses higher than 3 mg potentially effective in select cases [18, 19, 34, 35]. Dopamine agonists at high doses can cause valvular abnormalities, and echocar diography at baseline and follow-up may be warranted for patients requiring higher doses of cabergoline [6]. Prolactin levels should be repeated within 1 month after starting dopamine agonist ther apy and serially thereafter based on clinical context [6]. Patients with macroprolactinomas should have a repeat MRI within 3 months, whereas an initial interval of 6–12 months is likely appropriate for those with microprolac tinomas [6]. Clinicians should titrate dopa mine agonist therapy to normalize prolactin and perform serial MRIs at intervals of 3–12 months as needed to ensure stability or shrinkage of the prolactinoma. In patients with microprolactinomas for whom prolactin normalizes and the adenoma decreases or resolves over time, tapering and eventual dis continuation of dopamine agonist may be appropriate [6], although, again, data are scant in the pediatric age group. Patients with macroadenomas also typically achieve longterm biochemical and tumor control with dopamine agonists, and the dosage can be titrated to maintain normal prolactin and control of adenoma size. Patients who have visual field compromise and/or who do not achieve control with maxi mal doses of dopamine agonist require man agement by a multidisciplinary team that includes neurosurgery and neuroophthalmol ogy. Cabergoline may still be the appropriate first-line therapy for those presenting with visual field compromise, although we recom mend involvement of neurosurgery and neur oophthalmology from diagnosis for close monitoring and, if the visual field defect does not resolve with dopamine agonists, timely TSS. TSS is the appropriate second-line ther apy for those who cannot tolerate required doses of dopamine agonist or those whose tumor is refractory to treatment [6]. Adjunctive radiotherapy and/or temozolamide may also be necessary in rare cases of aggressive pro lactinoma [33]. Other important considerations in the management of prolactinomas in children include evaluating the possibility of a genetic etiology and screening for bone health. Given ## PDF page 789 | printed page 786 ### References the possibility of multiple endocrine neopla sia 1 (MEN1), our practice is to follow inter val calcium levels in children with prolactinoma. Genetic testing for MEN1 should be considered in those with a family history of hyperparathyroidism or pituitary adenoma, and children with family history of pituitary adenomas should also be tested for AIP mutations [36]. Finally, in children with macroadenomas, genetic testing for MENIN or AIP mutations is advisable even in the absence of family history, as genetic testing in cohorts of children and young adults with apparently sporadic macroprolactinomas has detected mutations in approximately 10–15% of cases [19, 37]. 1. paragraphs.text: Katherine Lord, Diva D. De León, and Charles A. Stanley
paragraphs.heading: Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: 29.3.1 Insulin-Mediated Hypoglycemia – 794 29.3.2 Hormone Deficiencies (Isolated Cortisol and Growth Hormone Deficiencies) and Panhypopituitarism – 797 29.3.3 Disorders of Gluconeogenesis – 797 29.3.4 Glycogen Storage Disorders (GSD) – 797 29.3.5 Fatty Acid Oxidation Defects – 798 29.3.6 Ketotic Hypoglycemia – 798 29.3.7 Post-fundoplication Hyperinsulinemic Hypoglycemia – 799

paragraphs.heading: 29.7 Treatment – 802

paragraphs.text: Hypoglycemia is a medical emergency that may result in seizures, permanent brain dam age, or even sudden death. Hypoglycemia can be the presenting sign of a large list of pathol ogies, and therefore, it is necessary to have a comprehensive and systematic strategy for diagnosis and therapy. This chapter presents an approach to disorders of hypoglycemia based on the metabolic and endocrine systems involved in successful adaptation to fasting. This “fasting systems” approach takes advan tage of the fact that almost all of the hypogly cemia problems in infants and children involve fasting. Since the integrity of these fasting systems is reflected in plasma levels of major fuels and counter-regulatory hormones at the time of hypoglycemia, the most important specimens for diagnosis are the ones obtained at the time of hypoglycemia, which is known as the “critical sample.”
paragraphs.heading: 29.1 Introduction and Background

paragraphs.text: Within 1–2 h after birth, plasma glucose concentrations in newborns decrease to a nadir of 55–60 mg/dL [1]. A study of healthy newborns found a mean glucose of 59 +/− 11 mg/dL during the 48 h of life. However, by 72–96 h of life, the mean glucose was 82 +/− 12 mg/dL [2, 3]. Thus, the physiological plasma glucose range in neonates after the first 3–4 days of life is not different than that for older children and adults (70–100 mg/dL). When plasma glucose decreases below this threshold, the glucose counter-regulatory sys tems are activated. A critical sample obtained when plasma glucose is <50 mg/dL reflects the metabolic response to hypoglycemia and allows the determination of the underlying cause of hypoglycemia.
paragraphs.heading: 29.1 Introduction and Background

paragraphs.text: In infants and children, hypoglycemia, with few exceptions, is almost always fasting hypo glycemia. The physiology of normal success ful fasting adaptation provides a useful framework that encompasses the diagnosis and treatment of potential hypoglycemia dis orders [2].
paragraphs.heading: 29.2 Etiology

paragraphs.text: cogenolysis, supplemented by hepatic gluco neogenesis utilizing amino acids released by muscle protein turnover. After 12–16 h in nor mal infants (24–36 h in adults), glucose pro duction declines, since the supply of liver glycogen is limited and the rate of gluconeo genesis from amino acids remains constant. At this time, a transition to fat as the major fuel for the body begins, with accelerated adi pose tissue lipolysis and increased fatty acid oxidation in muscle and ketogenesis in liver. The brain cannot utilize fatty acids directly; therefore, ketones (β-hydroxybutyrate and
paragraphs.heading: 29.2 Etiology

paragraphs.text: acetoacetate) provide an alternative fatderived fuel for the brain and permit a reduc tion of brain glucose consumption and the drain on essential muscle proteins. In late stages of fasting adaptation, fatty acid oxida tion and ketone utilization account for 90% of total oxygen consumption.
paragraphs.heading: 29.2 Etiology

paragraphs.text: Insulin is the most important regulatory hor mone, and dysregulated insulin secretion with failure to suppress insulin during fasting is the most common cause of persistent hypoglyce mia in infants and children. This can be due to a genetic defect affecting the various steps involved in fuel-stimulated insulin secretion, or in the high-risk neonate precipitated by perinatal stress (IUGR, infants of mothers with preeclampsia, etc.), or an insulinproducing tumor in older children and adoles cents. The possibility of exogenous insulin administration or hypoglycemic agents should also be considered.
paragraphs.heading: Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: Recessive loss-of-function mutations of K
paragraphs.heading: Hyperinsulinism (HI) [5, 6]

paragraphs.text: ATP-channel genes (ABCC8, encoding SUR1, sulfonylurea receptor; KCNJ11, encoding Kir6.2, potassium ion pore) [7, 8]. KATP-HI features include severe neonatal onset, LGA birthweight, protein-induced hypoglycemia, diazoxide unresponsiveness, and very high glucose requirement (up to 20–30 mg/kg/min).
paragraphs.heading: Hyperinsulinism (HI) [5, 6]

paragraphs.text: Dominant loss-of-function mutations of ABCC8 and KCNJ11 [9]. Unlike the severe disease often associated with recessive muta tions in the KATP-channel, some dominant cases have milder hypoglycemia and are diazoxide-responsive. However, those patients who do not respond to diazoxide are clinically indistinguishable from those with recessive forms. Dominant ABCC8 and KCNJ11 muta tions are also associated with protein-induced hypoglycemia [10].
paragraphs.heading: Hyperinsulinism (HI) [5, 6]

paragraphs.text: Focal hyperinsulinism [11, 12]. This is a consequence of somatic loss of heterozygosity for maternal 11p and expression of a pater nally transmitted recessive KATP-channel mutation (either ABCC8 or KCNJ11). The phenotype is very similar to recessive diffuse KATP-channel HI, and focal HI accounts for 40–60% of cases of severe diazoxideunresponsive HI [13]. Preoperative localiza tion of the lesion by 18F-fluoro-L-DOPA PET scan and resection of the lesion can result in cure of the hyperinsulinism [14–16].
paragraphs.heading: Hyperinsulinism (HI) [5, 6]

paragraphs.text: Dominant gain-of-function mutations of glutamate dehydrogenase (GLUD1) :hyperin sulinism/hyperammonemia (HI/HA) syn drome [17–19]. Children with HI/HA typically present within the first year of life
paragraphs.heading: Hyperinsulinism (HI) [5, 6]

paragraphs.text: but may not be diagnosed in the neonatal period as they have normal weight at birth and can fast longer than neonates with KATP-HI. HI/HA is characterized by fasting and protein-induced hypoglycemia which is diazoxide-responsive and a persistent mild hyperammonemia (plasma ammonium, 50–200 micromols/L). They also have increased rates of seizures (typically absence) and learning disabilities, which are thought to be unrelated to the hypoglycemia or the elevated ammonia levels [20].
paragraphs.heading: Hyperinsulinism (HI) [5, 6]

paragraphs.text: Dominant gain-of-function mutations of glucokinase (GCK) [21]. Gain-of-function mutations in GCK result in a lower glucose threshold for insulin release. Children with GCK-HI have hypoglycemia of variable
paragraphs.heading: Hyperinsulinism (HI) [5, 6]

paragraphs.text: degrees of severity and are only partially responsive to diazoxide [22].
paragraphs.heading: Hyperinsulinism (HI) [5, 6]

paragraphs.text: Aberrant expression of Hexokinase (HK1). HK1 is a high affinity glycolytic enzyme which is silenced in the pancreatic beta cell. Mutations in noncoding regions of HK1 lead to its expression in beta cells, resulting in excessive insulin secretion. Individuals with HK1-HI typically present at birth and have hypoglycemia which persists into adulthood. The majority of patients respond to diazox ide, although some have required pancreatec tomy [23].
paragraphs.heading: Hyperinsulinism (HI) [5, 6]

paragraphs.text: Recessive loss-of-function mutations of HADH (encoding SCHAD, the mitochon drial enzyme short-chain 3-hydroxyaxyl-CoA dehydrogenase) [22, 24]. In addition to its function in fatty acid oxidation, in the pancre atic beta cell, SCHAD functions as a negative regulator of glutamate dehydrogenase. Thus, similar to HI/HA, SCHAD-HI presents with fasting and protein-induced hypoglycemia, which is responsive to diazoxide therapy, but without the hyperammonemia. The biochemi cal hallmark, in addition to markers of increased insulin action, is increased levels of 3-hydroxybutyryl-carnitine in plasma and increased levels of 3-hydroxyglutarate in urine.
paragraphs.heading: Hyperinsulinism (HI) [5, 6]

paragraphs.text: Dominant loss-of-function mutations of hepatocyte nuclear factor 4 (HNF4A) and hepatocyte nuclear factor 1 (HNF1A) [25–27]. These transcription factors are well-known causes of familial monogenic diabetes (MODY1 and MODY3, respectively). More recently, it has been recognized that the phe notype in individuals with these mutations is biphasic with neonatal hypoglycemia due to hyperinsulinism and diabetes later in life. The hyperinsulinism phase can last from a few weeks to up to 8 years. Children with these forms of HI respond well to diazoxide.

Dominant mutations of monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1, encoded by SLC16A1) [28, 29]. Mutations in the promoter region of SLC16A1 result in aberrant expression of MCT1 in the beta cells and cause a rare form of HI, which is triggered by exercise. Characterized by episodes of hypoglycemia at the time of anaerobic exercise, MCT1-HI has been primarily identified in the Finnish popu
lation. The degree of hypoglycemia in response to exercise is variable.
Dominant mutations of uncoupling protein 2 (UCP2) [30]. Loss-of-function mutations in UCP2, which encodes an inner mitochondrial membrane carrier, result in a diazoxideresponsive form of HI.

Infant of a diabetic mother. Maternal hyper glycemia {XE “Maternal hyperglycemia”} triggers insulin hypersecretion by the fetal pancreatic beta cells, resulting in larger birth weight and hypoglycemia that typically resolves in 2–3 days. However, in cases com plicated by other perinatal stressors, i.e., pla cental insufficiency, the hyperinsulinism may last longer (see below).
paragraphs.heading: Hyperinsulinism

paragraphs.text: Perinatal stress-induced hyperinsulinism [31, 32]. It is associated with SGA birth weight, birth asphyxia, and maternal toxemia, and other perinatal stressors. Recent studies show that fetal hypoxia results in reduced KATP channel surface expression. Therefore, the glucose threshold for insulin release is decreased, resulting in a reduction in basal levels of plasma glucose. The hypoxic envi ronment during fetal life explains the low glu cose threshold for insulin release and transitional hypoglycemia in normal new borns, while perinatal hypoxic insults explain the more severe and prolonged hypoglycemia seen in perinatal stress-induced hyperinsulin ism (PNSHI) [33]. PNSHI can be clinically indistinguishable from the genetic forms of HI, apart from a history of perinatal insults. PNSHI typically resolves within a few weeks and rarely persists beyond the first 2–3 months of life. Most cases are responsive to treatment with diazoxide, although severe cases may require more intensive treatments [34].
paragraphs.heading: Hyperinsulinism

paragraphs.text: Hypoglycemia due to HI can be the present ing symptom in children with Beckwith- Wiedemann syndrome (BWS), an overgrowth syndrome due to genetic or epigenetic abnor malities in the imprinted region of chromo some 11p which is close to the KATP-channel loci. The severity of the HI in BWS is vari
paragraphs.heading: 29.3.1.3 Syndromic Hyperinsulinism

paragraphs.text: able; infants with paternal UPD11passociated HI have a persistent and severe HI phenotype compared to the transient hypo glycemia of BWS patients caused by other eti ologies [35]. Many other syndromes can be associated with HI including Turner syn drome, Kabuki syndrome, and congenital dis orders of glycosylation (CDG).
paragraphs.heading: 29.3.1.3 Syndromic Hyperinsulinism

paragraphs.text: Insulinomas are typically benign islet cell tumors, which are rarer in the pediatric popula tion than in adults. After diagnostic testing con firms evidence of insulin excess, imaging should be performed to localize the lesion. Multiple modalities (MRI, endoscopic ultrasound) may be necessary given the difficulty in localization. Resection is curative. Genetic testing for multi ple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) should be done in any child with an insulinoma.
paragraphs.heading: 29.3.1.4 Insulinoma

paragraphs.text: Induced hypoglycemia by administration of either insulin or hypoglycemic agents should be considered in the differential of insulinmediated hypoglycemia. The clinical presen tation can be undistinguishable from endogenous forms of hyperinsulinism ; how ever, the abrupt onset of hypoglycemia of unpredictable pattern in an otherwise healthy child may trigger further investigation.
paragraphs.heading: 29.3.1.5 Factitous Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: Hypoglycemia from growth hormone and cortisol deficiency occurs primarily during infancy and presents as ketotic hypoglycemia. However, in the neonate, features may mimic hyperinsulinism, including high glucose requirement, low FFA and BOHB, and a gly cemic response to glucagon. This diagnosis should be suspected in neonates with the phe notype of HI, but who also have midline mal formations, microphthalmia, micropenis, or cholestatic liver disease. Low growth hormone
paragraphs.heading: (Isolated Cortisol and Growth Hormone Deficiencies) and Panhypopituitarism

paragraphs.text: and cortisol levels obtained at the time of hypoglycemia are not diagnostic and prior to starting hormone replacement, appropriate stimulation tests should be performed to con firm the diagnosis [36], in addition to a brain MRI. In infants with midline defects, evidence of other pituitary abnormalities, and/or pitu itary defects on imaging, a low random growth hormone may be sufficient to make the diag nosis without the need for provocative testing. The hypoglycemia resolves with replacement of the missing hormones.
paragraphs.heading: (Isolated Cortisol and Growth Hormone Deficiencies) and Panhypopituitarism

paragraphs.text: myopathy. In contrast, GSD types VI and IX present with hypoglycemia following over night fasting, milder hepatomegaly and growth retardation, and minimal metabolic and hepatic abnormalities. Liver biopsy as the gold standard for diagnosis has been replaced by genetic mutation testing.

These are children, usually 1–4 years of age, with episodes of symptomatic fasting hypo glycemia, but do not have any identifiable metabolic or endocrine defect. In most instances, this can be thought of as merely a quantitative rather than a specific, qualitative abnormality of fasting adaptation. These children may simply represent the lower end
paragraphs.heading: 29.3.6 Ketotic Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: of the normal distribution of fasting toler ance. Note, however, that the features of abbreviated but otherwise normal fasting response are shared by the milder glycogeno ses. Some cases of “ketotic hypoglycemia” have been found to have a mild GSD or inac tivating mutations of monocarboxylate trans porter 1 (MCT1) [42, 43].
paragraphs.heading: 29.3.6 Ketotic Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: Postprandial hypoglycemia may occur in infants following fundoplication surgery for gastroesophageal reflux and may be severe enough to cause seizures and brain damage [44]. The mechanism involves rapid emptying of a meal into the small intestine, with early hyperglycemia followed by an exaggerated insulin surge and subsequent hypoglycemia, usually 1–2 h after the feed or meal. Increased secretion of the potent insulinotropic hor mone, glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), by intestinal enteroendocrine cells after a meal may, at least in part, be responsible for the postprandial hyperinsulinemia [45]. The diag nosis is made by demonstration of the typical plasma glucose and insulin patterns in response to a mixed meal or formula tolerance test. Treatment includes feeds of longer dura tion, reduced high glycemic index foods, and
paragraphs.heading: Hyperinsulinemic Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: inhibitors of gastric motility; the alpha gluco sidase inhibitor, acarbose, may be useful as a means to delay digestion and absorption of complex carbohydrates [46].
paragraphs.heading: Hyperinsulinemic Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: Older children and adults manifest Whipple’s classic triad: neurogenic and neuroglycopenic symptoms/signs of hypoglycemia, a con firmed low plasma glucose value, and resolu tion of the symptoms/signs when the glucose level is restored to normal. However, neo nates, infants, and younger children may not reliably demonstrate and/or lack the ability to communicate such symptoms and are fre quently asymptomatic, even with significant hypoglycemia. Hypoglycemic symptoms may be subtle and difficult to recognize in these age groups and include poor feeding, sweating, somnolence, apnea, and irritability. Myoclonic jerks and seizures may occur with severe hypo glycemia.
paragraphs.heading: 29.4 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Guidelines published by the Pediatric Endocrine Society detail which infants and children require evaluation for hypoglycemia disorders [47]. High-risk neonates (LGA, SGA, perinatal stress, maternal diabetes,
paragraphs.heading: 29.5 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: those with congenital syndromes and family history of genetic hypoglycemia disorders) with plasma glucoses <60 mg/dL after the first 48 h of life should undergo additional evaluation prior to discharge. Evaluation should also occur in infants and young chil dren if plasma glucose concentrations are documented to be <60 mg/dL on laboratory quality assays and in older children only if Whipple’s triad is documented.

The success of the fasting test requires an experienced team of nurses and physicians, a blood-drawing IV, and rapid and accurate plasma glucose monitoring (N.B. Standard bedside glucose meters are not accurate enough). The fast usually begins with an eve ning meal or feed, but may be adjusted later if very short fasting tolerance is suspected (con sider monitoring for 24 h on usual diet before starting the fasting test to assess glucose sta bility). From the beginning of the fast, moni tor plasma glucose and BOHB closely (e.g., every 3 h until <70 mg/dL, every 1 h until <60 mg/dL, then every 30 min to end). End the test at plasma glucose <50 mg/dL or when
paragraphs.heading: 29.5.1 Formal Fasting Test Protocol

paragraphs.text: bedside measurement of BOHB indicates val ues >2.5 mmol/L or a specific duration has been reached (18 h if <1 month; 24 h if 1–12 months; 36 h if >1 year; 48 h for adoles cents) or in case of any worrisome symptoms. At the end of the fast, obtain “critical sample” labs, which should include the basic metabolic panel, lactate, ammonia, insulin, c-peptide, BOHB, FFA, GH, cortisol, plasma acylcarnitine profile, plasma total and free carni tine, and urinary organic acid profile. If considering hyperinsulinism (low BOHB dur ing the fast), perform the glucagon stimula tion test, 1 mg IV, to test liver glycogen reserve (at plasma glucose <50 mg/dL, appropriate glycemic response is <30 mg/dL within 15–30 min after glucagon administration; gly cemic response above 30 mg/dL is consistent with hyperinsulinism) [4]. Caution: fasting tests are potentially hazardous provocative tests that, like the water deprivation test, must be closely monitored for patient safety. Sudden deaths during fasting tests have been reported in patients with fatty acid oxidation defects. Patients with fatty acid oxidation defects may develop life-threatening symp toms before plasma glucose levels fall below 60–65 mg/dL, including progressive lethargy, nausea, vomiting, or unexplained tachycar dia; fasts should be terminated in these cases without waiting for plasma glucose to reach 50 mg/dL.

paragraphs.text: with and without acidemia (HCO3 <16–18 vs. >16–18 mEq/L). The groups are then further divided based on the presence or absence of ketones and lactate: 1. Acidemia due to lactate accumulation typ

paragraphs.text: ifies defects in hepatic gluconeogenesis: glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (GSD type I), GLUT2 deficiency, fructose-1,6diphosphatase deficiency, hereditary fruc tose intolerance, and ethanol ingestion. 2. Acidemia due to ketone accumulation typ
paragraphs.heading: 29.5.1 Formal Fasting Test Protocol

paragraphs.text: ifies normal children, ketotic hypoglyce mia (likely normal, but with shortened fasting tolerance), defects in glycogenoly sis (GSD types 0, III, VI, IX), growth hor mone and/or cortisol deficiencies, and ketone utilization defects. 3. No acidemia with ketones and free fatty
paragraphs.heading: 29.5.1 Formal Fasting Test Protocol

paragraphs.text: acids both suppressed: congenital, perina tal stress or syndromic hyperinsulinism, insulinoma, exogenous administration of insulin or oral hypoglycemic agents, and neonatal hypopituitarism. 4. No acidemia with suppressed ketones but
paragraphs.heading: 29.5.1 Formal Fasting Test Protocol

paragraphs.text: elevated free fatty acids: genetic defects in fatty acid oxidation and ketogenesis.
paragraphs.heading: 29.5.1 Formal Fasting Test Protocol

paragraphs.text: This test using tandem mass spectrometry measures the different fatty acids bound to carnitine to detect many (but not all) of the genetic defects in fatty acid oxidation. The method is now employed in most newborn screening programs using filter paper blood spots to screen for 20 or more inborn errors of metabolism. Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehy drogenase (MCAD) deficiency is particularly common (1/5000) and easily detected by this method [41].
paragraphs.heading: Profile

paragraphs.text: Genetic testing for the most common forms of hyperinsulinism is available in commercial laboratories and should be obtained as soon as the diagnosis is confirmed. This is particu
paragraphs.heading: 29.5.2.2 Genetic Testing

paragraphs.text: larly important for infants with diazoxideunresponsive hyperinsulinism as >90% of these cases will have a KATP channel defect and, therefore, an approximately 50% likeli hood of having focal hyperinsulinism. Mutation screening is useful for glucose- 6-phosphatase deficiency, since 80% of patients have one of five common mutations. Ninety percent of MCAD patients have the common A985G mutation. In addition, for children with repeated episodes of “ketotic hypoglycemia,” genetic testing may identify those with an underlying defect in glycoge nolysis or ketone utilization.
paragraphs.heading: 29.5.2.2 Genetic Testing

paragraphs.text: Lymphoblasts or fibroblasts are useful for diagnosis of some inborn errors of metabo lism (such as fatty acid oxidation disorders) and as sources of DNA for mutation analysis for other genetic defects.
paragraphs.heading: 29.5.2.3 Cultured Cells

paragraphs.text: Severe or recurrent hypoglycemia results in neurologic dysfunction and, in rare cases, death. Therefore, early recognition and treat ment are essential to avoid neurologic damage and later risk of learning disabilities and epi lepsy. Long-term studies of HI patients have found rates of neurodevelopmental abnor malities between 26% and 48% and epilepsy between 13% and 43% [48–50]. Despite a bet ter understanding and recognition of the dis ease, individuals diagnosed with HI in the last 20 years have not demonstrated substantially improved outcomes compared to older indi viduals with HI [51]. This suggests that the neurologic insult from hypoglycemia occurs in the first several days of life and speaks about the importance of screening high-risk infants for hypoglycemia. Given the high risk of neu rocognitive dysfunction, children with HI, regardless of etiology or treatment, require periodic developmental testing.
paragraphs.heading: 29.6 Outcomes

paragraphs.text: Children with HI who undergo pancre atectomy are at increased risk of developing diabetes. By age 14 years, over 90% of indi viduals who have undergone 98% pancreatec
paragraphs.heading: 29.6 Outcomes

paragraphs.text: tomy develop insulin-dependent diabetes [52]. The risk of diabetes is significantly higher in those with surgically treated diffuse disease compared to those with focal form, because of the limited pancreatic resection required for focal lesions [51]. Additionally, children with HI due to HNF4A and HNF1A muta tions require screening for diabetes given the risk of beta cell failure and subsequent diabe tes.

paragraphs.heading: 29.7 Treatment

paragraphs.text: The management of children with hypoglyce mia should be guided by the following goals: (1) prevention of brain damage from recur rent hypoglycemia, (2) establishment of a spe cific diagnosis and therapy, and (3) encouragement of normal feeding behavior while assuring safe fasting tolerance.

paragraphs.text: Hypoglycemia disorders are rare but have potentially severe consequences for children if unrecognized. An understanding of normal fasting adaption and a systematic approach to the interpretation of the critical sample allow for narrowing of the differential diagnosis and making an accurate diagnosis.. Children with hypoglycemic disorders, particularly those with hyperinsulinism, are at risk of neurologic damage, so early detection and initiation of the appropriate disease-specific treatment is critical to improve neurocognitive outcomes.

### 29.1 Introduction and Background

Hypoglycemia is a medical emergency that may result in seizures, permanent brain dam age, or even sudden death. Hypoglycemia can be the presenting sign of a large list of pathol ogies, and therefore, it is necessary to have a comprehensive and systematic strategy for diagnosis and therapy. This chapter presents an approach to disorders of hypoglycemia based on the metabolic and endocrine systems involved in successful adaptation to fasting. This “fasting systems” approach takes advan tage of the fact that almost all of the hypogly cemia problems in infants and children involve fasting. Since the integrity of these fasting systems is reflected in plasma levels of major fuels and counter-regulatory hormones at the time of hypoglycemia, the most important specimens for diagnosis are the ones obtained at the time of hypoglycemia, which is known as the “critical sample.”

Within 1–2 h after birth, plasma glucose concentrations in newborns decrease to a nadir of 55–60 mg/dL [1]. A study of healthy newborns found a mean glucose of 59 +/− 11 mg/dL during the 48 h of life. However, by 72–96 h of life, the mean glucose was 82 +/− 12 mg/dL [2, 3]. Thus, the physiological plasma glucose range in neonates after the first 3–4 days of life is not different than that for older children and adults (70–100 mg/dL). When plasma glucose decreases below this threshold, the glucose counter-regulatory sys tems are activated. A critical sample obtained when plasma glucose is <50 mg/dL reflects the metabolic response to hypoglycemia and allows the determination of the underlying cause of hypoglycemia.

### 29.2 Etiology

In infants and children, hypoglycemia, with few exceptions, is almost always fasting hypo glycemia. The physiology of normal success ful fasting adaptation provides a useful framework that encompasses the diagnosis and treatment of potential hypoglycemia dis orders [2].

After 12–16 h in nor mal infants (24–36 h in adults), glucose pro duction declines, since the supply of liver glycogen is limited and the rate of gluconeo genesis from amino acids remains constant. ### 29.3.1 Insulin-Mediated

### Hypoglycemia

Insulin is the most important regulatory hor mone, and dysregulated insulin secretion with failure to suppress insulin during fasting is the most common cause of persistent hypoglyce mia in infants and children. This can be due to a genetic defect affecting the various steps involved in fuel-stimulated insulin secretion, or in the high-risk neonate precipitated by perinatal stress (IUGR, infants of mothers with preeclampsia, etc.), or an insulinproducing tumor in older children and adoles cents. The possibility of exogenous insulin administration or hypoglycemic agents should also be considered.

### 29.3.1.2 Transient Neonatal

### Hyperinsulinism

Infant of a diabetic mother. Maternal hyper glycemia {XE “Maternal hyperglycemia”} triggers insulin hypersecretion by the fetal pancreatic beta cells, resulting in larger birth weight and hypoglycemia that typically resolves in 2–3 days. However, in cases com plicated by other perinatal stressors, i.e., pla cental insufficiency, the hyperinsulinism may last longer (see below).

Perinatal stress-induced hyperinsulinism [31, 32]. It is associated with SGA birth weight, birth asphyxia, and maternal toxemia, and other perinatal stressors. Recent studies show that fetal hypoxia results in reduced KATP channel surface expression. Therefore, the glucose threshold for insulin release is decreased, resulting in a reduction in basal levels of plasma glucose. The hypoxic envi ronment during fetal life explains the low glu cose threshold for insulin release and transitional hypoglycemia in normal new borns, while perinatal hypoxic insults explain the more severe and prolonged hypoglycemia seen in perinatal stress-induced hyperinsulin ism (PNSHI) [33]. PNSHI can be clinically indistinguishable from the genetic forms of HI, apart from a history of perinatal insults. PNSHI typically resolves within a few weeks and rarely persists beyond the first 2–3 months of life. Most cases are responsive to treatment with diazoxide, although severe cases may require more intensive treatments [34].

### 29.3.1.3 Syndromic Hyperinsulinism

Hypoglycemia due to HI can be the present ing symptom in children with Beckwith- Wiedemann syndrome (BWS), an overgrowth syndrome due to genetic or epigenetic abnor malities in the imprinted region of chromo some 11p which is close to the KATP-channel loci. The severity of the HI in BWS is vari

Many other syndromes can be associated with HI including Turner syn drome, Kabuki syndrome, and congenital dis orders of glycosylation (CDG).

### 29.3.1.4 Insulinoma

Insulinomas are typically benign islet cell tumors, which are rarer in the pediatric popula tion than in adults. After diagnostic testing con firms evidence of insulin excess, imaging should be performed to localize the lesion. Multiple modalities (MRI, endoscopic ultrasound) may be necessary given the difficulty in localization. Resection is curative. Genetic testing for multi ple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) should be done in any child with an insulinoma.

### 29.3.1.5 Factitous Hypoglycemia

Induced hypoglycemia by administration of either insulin or hypoglycemic agents should be considered in the differential of insulinmediated hypoglycemia. The clinical presen tation can be undistinguishable from endogenous forms of hyperinsulinism ; how ever, the abrupt onset of hypoglycemia of unpredictable pattern in an otherwise healthy child may trigger further investigation.

### 29.3.2 Hormone Deficiencies

### (Isolated Cortisol and Growth Hormone Deficiencies) and Panhypopituitarism

Hypoglycemia from growth hormone and cortisol deficiency occurs primarily during infancy and presents as ketotic hypoglycemia. However, in the neonate, features may mimic hyperinsulinism, including high glucose requirement, low FFA and BOHB, and a gly cemic response to glucagon. This diagnosis should be suspected in neonates with the phe notype of HI, but who also have midline mal formations, microphthalmia, micropenis, or cholestatic liver disease. Low growth hormone

and cortisol levels obtained at the time of hypoglycemia are not diagnostic and prior to starting hormone replacement, appropriate stimulation tests should be performed to con firm the diagnosis [36], in addition to a brain MRI. In infants with midline defects, evidence of other pituitary abnormalities, and/or pitu itary defects on imaging, a low random growth hormone may be sufficient to make the diag nosis without the need for provocative testing. The hypoglycemia resolves with replacement of the missing hormones.

### 29.3.7 Post-fundoplication

### Hyperinsulinemic Hypoglycemia

Postprandial hypoglycemia may occur in infants following fundoplication surgery for gastroesophageal reflux and may be severe enough to cause seizures and brain damage [44]. The mechanism involves rapid emptying of a meal into the small intestine, with early hyperglycemia followed by an exaggerated insulin surge and subsequent hypoglycemia, usually 1–2 h after the feed or meal. Increased secretion of the potent insulinotropic hor mone, glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), by intestinal enteroendocrine cells after a meal may, at least in part, be responsible for the postprandial hyperinsulinemia [45]. The diag nosis is made by demonstration of the typical plasma glucose and insulin patterns in response to a mixed meal or formula tolerance test. Treatment includes feeds of longer dura tion, reduced high glycemic index foods, and

inhibitors of gastric motility; the alpha gluco sidase inhibitor, acarbose, may be useful as a means to delay digestion and absorption of complex carbohydrates [46].

### 29.4 Clinical Presentation

Older children and adults manifest Whipple’s classic triad: neurogenic and neuroglycopenic symptoms/signs of hypoglycemia, a con firmed low plasma glucose value, and resolu tion of the symptoms/signs when the glucose level is restored to normal. However, neo nates, infants, and younger children may not reliably demonstrate and/or lack the ability to communicate such symptoms and are fre quently asymptomatic, even with significant hypoglycemia. Hypoglycemic symptoms may be subtle and difficult to recognize in these age groups and include poor feeding, sweating, somnolence, apnea, and irritability. Myoclonic jerks and seizures may occur with severe hypo glycemia.

### 29.5 Diagnostic Evaluation

Guidelines published by the Pediatric Endocrine Society detail which infants and children require evaluation for hypoglycemia disorders [47]. High-risk neonates (LGA, SGA, perinatal stress, maternal diabetes,

### 29.5.1 Formal Fasting Test Protocol

The success of the fasting test requires an experienced team of nurses and physicians, a blood-drawing IV, and rapid and accurate plasma glucose monitoring (N.B. Standard bedside glucose meters are not accurate enough). The fast usually begins with an eve ning meal or feed, but may be adjusted later if very short fasting tolerance is suspected (con sider monitoring for 24 h on usual diet before starting the fasting test to assess glucose sta bility). From the beginning of the fast, moni tor plasma glucose and BOHB closely (e.g., every 3 h until <70 mg/dL, every 1 h until <60 mg/dL, then every 30 min to end). End the test at plasma glucose <50 mg/dL or when

bedside measurement of BOHB indicates val ues >2.5 mmol/L or a specific duration has been reached (18 h if <1 month; 24 h if 1–12 months; 36 h if >1 year; 48 h for adoles cents) or in case of any worrisome symptoms. At the end of the fast, obtain “critical sample” labs, which should include the basic metabolic panel, lactate, ammonia, insulin, c-peptide, BOHB, FFA, GH, cortisol, plasma acylcarnitine profile, plasma total and free carni tine, and urinary organic acid profile. If considering hyperinsulinism (low BOHB dur ing the fast), perform the glucagon stimula tion test, 1 mg IV, to test liver glycogen reserve (at plasma glucose <50 mg/dL, appropriate glycemic response is <30 mg/dL within 15–30 min after glucagon administration; gly cemic response above 30 mg/dL is consistent with hyperinsulinism) [4]. Caution: fasting tests are potentially hazardous provocative tests that, like the water deprivation test, must be closely monitored for patient safety. Sudden deaths during fasting tests have been reported in patients with fatty acid oxidation defects. Patients with fatty acid oxidation defects may develop life-threatening symp toms before plasma glucose levels fall below 60–65 mg/dL, including progressive lethargy, nausea, vomiting, or unexplained tachycar dia; fasts should be terminated in these cases without waiting for plasma glucose to reach 50 mg/dL.

### 29.5.2 Other Tests

### 29.5.2.1 Plasma Acyl-Carnitine

### Profile

This test using tandem mass spectrometry measures the different fatty acids bound to carnitine to detect many (but not all) of the genetic defects in fatty acid oxidation. The method is now employed in most newborn screening programs using filter paper blood spots to screen for 20 or more inborn errors of metabolism. Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehy drogenase (MCAD) deficiency is particularly common (1/5000) and easily detected by this method [41].

### 29.5.2.2 Genetic Testing

Genetic testing for the most common forms of hyperinsulinism is available in commercial laboratories and should be obtained as soon as the diagnosis is confirmed. This is particu

larly important for infants with diazoxideunresponsive hyperinsulinism as >90% of these cases will have a KATP channel defect and, therefore, an approximately 50% likeli hood of having focal hyperinsulinism. Mutation screening is useful for glucose- 6-phosphatase deficiency, since 80% of patients have one of five common mutations. Ninety percent of MCAD patients have the common A985G mutation. In addition, for children with repeated episodes of “ketotic hypoglycemia,” genetic testing may identify those with an underlying defect in glycoge nolysis or ketone utilization.

### 29.5.2.3 Cultured Cells

Lymphoblasts or fibroblasts are useful for diagnosis of some inborn errors of metabo lism (such as fatty acid oxidation disorders) and as sources of DNA for mutation analysis for other genetic defects.

### 29.6 Outcomes

Severe or recurrent hypoglycemia results in neurologic dysfunction and, in rare cases, death. Therefore, early recognition and treat ment are essential to avoid neurologic damage and later risk of learning disabilities and epi lepsy. Long-term studies of HI patients have found rates of neurodevelopmental abnor malities between 26% and 48% and epilepsy between 13% and 43% [48–50]. Despite a bet ter understanding and recognition of the dis ease, individuals diagnosed with HI in the last 20 years have not demonstrated substantially improved outcomes compared to older indi viduals with HI [51]. This suggests that the neurologic insult from hypoglycemia occurs in the first several days of life and speaks about the importance of screening high-risk infants for hypoglycemia. Given the high risk of neu rocognitive dysfunction, children with HI, regardless of etiology or treatment, require periodic developmental testing.

Children with HI who undergo pancre atectomy are at increased risk of developing diabetes. By age 14 years, over 90% of indi viduals who have undergone 98% pancreatec

The risk of diabetes is significantly higher in those with surgically treated diffuse disease compared to those with focal form, because of the limited pancreatic resection required for focal lesions [51]. Additionally, children with HI due to HNF4A and HNF1A muta tions require screening for diabetes given the risk of beta cell failure and subsequent diabe tes.

### 29.8 Summary

Hypoglycemia disorders are rare but have potentially severe consequences for children if unrecognized. An understanding of normal fasting adaption and a systematic approach to the interpretation of the critical sample allow for narrowing of the differential diagnosis and making an accurate diagnosis.. Children with hypoglycemic disorders, particularly those with hyperinsulinism, are at risk of neurologic damage, so early detection and initiation of the appropriate disease-specific treatment is critical to improve neurocognitive outcomes.

title: Type 1 Diabetes in Children and Adolescents

paragraphs.text: Pamela P. Hu, Michelle A. Van Name, Kerry Stephenson, Kristin Sikes, and William V. Tamborlane
paragraphs.heading: Type 1 Diabetes in Children and Adolescents

paragraphs.text: 30.3.1 Goals – 812 30.3.2 Insulin Management – 813 30.3.3 Regimens – 815 30.3.4 Insulin Pumps – 816 30.3.5 Integrated Continuous Glucose Monitors (CGM) and Pump Therapy – 819 30.3.6 Hypoglycemia – 822 30.3.7 Medical Nutrition Therapy – 823 30.3.8 Exercise – 825 30.3.9 Sick Day Management – 825 30.3.10 Psychosocial Considerations – 826 30.3.11 Associated Autoimmune Conditions – 828
paragraphs.heading: 30.3 Treatment of T1D – 812

paragraphs.text: Diabetes mellitus is a lifelong disorder charac terized by alteration in the metabolism of glu cose and other energy-yielding fuels due to an absolute or relative insufficiency of insulin. This lack of insulin plays a primary role in the hyperglycemia and other metabolic derange ments linked to diabetes. Hyperglycemia, in turn, plays a key role in the microvascular and macrovascular complications of diabetes.
paragraphs.heading: 30.1 Introduction and Background

paragraphs.text: Diabetes mellitus can be classified into at least three subclasses: type 1 diabetes (T1D), once known as insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus; type 2 diabetes (T2D), once known as non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus; and secondary diabetes that is linked to another identifiable condition or syndrome. Currently, the majority of children diagnosed with diabetes have T1D, but the rates of T2D in the pediatric population are increasing dramatically. The prevalence of T2D increased by 95.3% from 2001 to 2017, with the highest prevalence noted in African American youth [1]. Risk factors for the development of T2D include a strong family history of T2D, overweight (BMI >85th per centile for age and sex), sedentary lifestyle, and having an African-American, Hispanic, Asian/Pacific Islander, or American Indian background.
paragraphs.heading: 30.1 Introduction and Background

paragraphs.text: T1D occurs when pancreatic β-cells are destroyed in an autoimmune process that is currently the focus of many research studies. Autoimmune-mediated destruction of β-cells ultimately leads to nearly complete absence of endogenous insulin secretion in most patients. Four anti-islet autoantibodies have been described as highly sensitive markers for the diagnosis of T1D: anti-insulin, anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase, anti-insulinomaassociated antigen 2, and anti-zinc transporter 8 antibodies. Two or more positive antibodies are pathognomic for development of T1D [2]. In addition to the presence of islet-cell anti bodies, many genetic and environmental fac tors are known and hypothesized to impact a person’s likelihood of developing T1D.
paragraphs.heading: 30.1 Introduction and Background

paragraphs.text: T1D usually has a prolonged asymptom atic stage in which pancreatic β-cells are pro gressively destroyed.
