Once the critical mass of β-cells falls below a given threshold, children with T1D typically present with acute symp toms of polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, and weight loss and, if these symptoms go unrec ognized, diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).
paragraphs.heading: 30.1 Introduction and Background

paragraphs.text: The pathophysiology of T2D differs from T1D in that insulin resistance (IR) and the inability of β-cells to fully compensate by increasing insulin secretion are at the core of T2D in children. Resistance to insulin places a heavy burden on β-cells, forcing them to increase insulin production, but in youth with prediabetes and T2D, their β-cells are unable to meet the demand for increased insulin secretion. The insulin resistance that develops in lean, healthy children during puberty fur ther exacerbates the insulin demands [3]. Overburdened β-cells can lead to beta cell burnout, further reducing insulin supply rela tive to demand. This complicated pathogene sis results in hyperglycemia despite considerable retention of endogenous insulin secretion. In fact, it is not uncommon for ado lescents with T2D to present acutely ill, with marked hyperglycemia and even ketosis, espe cially in the context of a stressful intercurrent illness.
paragraphs.heading: 30.1 Introduction and Background

paragraphs.text: There is a strong genetic component to the development of T2D, as exemplified by the high concordance rate among identical twins
paragraphs.heading: 30.1 Introduction and Background

paragraphs.text: and a much stronger family history of T2D in affected individuals. It has been reported that anywhere from 74 to 100% of patients with T2D have a first- or second-degree relative with the disease, compared to 5% of patients with T1D. The development of insulin resis tance and β-cell dysfunction is a complex interaction between genetic and environmen tal factors that is still under investigation.
paragraphs.heading: 30.1 Introduction and Background

paragraphs.text: Regardless of the type of diabetes, the current guidelines from the American Diabetes Association for the diagnosis of diabetes are shown in Box 30.1 [4].
paragraphs.heading: 30.2 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: T1D remains the most common type of diabetes in youth; however, in some circum stances, differentiating the type of diabetes may not be straightforward. When insulin is indicated, differentiating the type of diabetes need not affect management decisions. However, understanding the etiology is help ful in future treatment decisions and counsel ing.
paragraphs.heading: 30.2 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: T2D should be considered in youth with a personal history of obesity, insulin resistance, prediabetes, or a family history of T2D. Each case must be considered carefully, given that T1D can occur in those with a phenotype sug gestive of T2D. Autoimmune antibody testing can help the clinician differentiate these two types of diabetes; however, cases of antibodynegative T1D and antibody-positive T2D cloud this as an absolute diagnostic indicator. In youth with new-onset diabetes who have overweight or obesity and clinical suspicion of T2D, metformin should be initiated. For those patients with A1c ≥8.5%, basal insulin should be started. The decision to continue metformin can be made when autoantibody testing results become available [5].
paragraphs.heading: 30.2 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY) is a monogenic, dominantly inher
paragraphs.heading: 30.2 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: ited form of diabetes, which often presents in youth or early adulthood. MODY should be considered in patients with atypical presenta tions or courses of diabetes, family history of similar cases, negative diabetes-associated autoantibodies, and lack of a phenotype con cerning for T2D. Diabetes diagnosed prior to 6 months of age is also usually a monogenic form of diabetes. Genetic testing for mono genic diabetes is available, and results can guide treatment decisions and counseling.
paragraphs.heading: 30.2 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: The treatment of T1D in children and adoles cents presents unique challenges to pediatric health-care providers. The combination of almost complete reliance on exogenous insulin and the physical and psychosocial changes that accompany normal growth and development makes day-to-day management of pediatric patients especially difficult. Indeed, recent data from the T1D Exchange indicate that <30% of pediatric patients have hemoglobin A1c (A1c) levels <7.5% and that mean A1c values often exceed 9.0% in teenagers with T1D [6]. In pedi atric patients, successful diabetes management is best accomplished with a multidisciplinary team of clinicians, including pediatric endocri nologists, nurse practitioners, certified diabetes educators, nutritionists, social workers, and/or psychologists, to provide ongoing education and support of self-management efforts on the part of caregivers and patients.
paragraphs.heading: 30.3 Treatment of T1D

paragraphs.text: In newly diagnosed patients, the first few weeks are critically important in the process of teaching self-management skills to the caregiver and child. Initiation of diabetes management can be accomplished either in the inpatient or outpatient setting. Many chil dren require initial hospitalization for vomit ing, dehydration, and/or moderate-to-severe DKA. In patients who are not ill at presenta tion, admission to the hospital may also pro vide the child and parent with a safe and supportive environment in which to adjust to the shock of the diagnosis and learn the sur vival skills of diabetes management. On the other hand, some parents may prefer initial outpatient management, especially if there are no interfering social issues that would complicate initial treatment. Frequent phone follow-up is an important aspect in the care of all newly diagnosed patients, and members of our staff speak with newly diagnosed families on a daily basis for the first 2–3 weeks after diagnosis. In addition, we routinely schedule follow-up outpatient visits 1–2 weeks and again 6 weeks after diagnosis.
Once out of the newly diagnosed phase, regular follow-up visits approximately every 3 months are recommended [7]. These visits provide the opportunity to evaluate whether the

patient has met treatment goals (see next sec tion), to review diabetes management princi ples, and to assess child and family functioning. During these visits, measurements of A1c pro vide a means of evaluating the impact of overall glycemic control. A point of care method (such as the Afinion or DCA Vantage) is strongly rec ommended since it allows clinicians to incorpo rate A1c results into the clinic visit. Children and teenagers are familiar with the concepts of “progress reports” or “report cards” in the con text of their schooling, and the A1c can stand as a diabetes “report card” to provide feedback on the effectiveness of efforts to maintain or improve glycemic control. Evaluation of con tinuous monitoring data provides critical infor mation on how to adjust management to optimize the A1c. Patients and their families should also have access, via telephone, e-mail, or other communication methods, to clinicians in between visits for adjustments in the treat ment regimen or for advice/counseling on issues that arise between clinic visits.

The traditional goals of treatment in children and adolescents with diabetes were to balance insulin, diet, and exercise to promote optimal growth and development while minimizing episodes of hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia. The result from the landmark Diabetes Control and Complications Trial (DCCT) raised the bar with respect to these traditional treatment goals by demonstrating that inten sive treatment leading to near-normal glucose and A1c levels significantly reduces the risk for retinopathy and the development of microalbuminuria [8–10]. These findings were supported and extended by the follow-up of the DCCT cohort in the Epidemiology of Diabetes Interventions and Complications (EDIC) study. Current standards of care for both the American Diabetes Association (ADA) and the International Society for Pediatric and Adolescent Diabetes (ISPAD) now identify an A1c of <7.0% as the glycemic target for children and adolescents under 19 years of age [11]. Clinically, Time in Range (TIR), a measure of glycemic control defined
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.1 Goals

paragraphs.text: as 70–180 mg/dL measured with the use of continuous glucose monitoring, is gaining traction as it has been correlated with A1c, diabetes complications, and frequency of hypo- and hyperglycemia episodes [12]. TIR has the advantage of providing actionable data as CGM data are collected in real time and TIR >70% strongly corresponds to an A1c of approximately 7% [13, 14]. It contin ues to be important to individualize the treat ment plan to meet the specific needs of each child. For instance, some children with fre quent episodes of hypoglycemia may need a higher glycemic target. Additionally, intensive treatment places an extra burden on patients and their families, and practical consider ations such as acceptability of and compli ance with the treatment regimens must be balanced appropriately in order to achieve treatment goals for that patient.
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.1 Goals

paragraphs.text: Once so simple, the choice of insulin has become ever more complicated. Current insu lin options include standard human regular, neutral protamine Hagedorn (NPH), rapidand long-acting insulin analogs, premixed combinations of these insulins, and newer ultra-long-acting analogs. Most insulin ana logs are available in a standard concentration of 100 U/mL (U-100). A rapid-acting analog is available in a concentration of 200 U/mL (U-200), and long-acting analog is available in a concentration of 300 U/mL (U-300). Regular insulin is also available in a U-500 concentration for patients (usually adults with T2D) who require very large doses of insulin because they have severe insulin resistance. Certain insulins can also be diluted to lower concentrations. Diluted insulin is typically used in the very young child who requires very small doses. Since today’s insulin pumps can deliver very small, incremental doses of insu lin, use of diluted insulin has become less common.
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.2 Insulin Management

paragraphs.text: The three rapid-acting analogs in common use are the following: aspart (NovoLogR), lis pro (HumalogR), and glulisine (ApidraR). Insulin lispro-aabc (LyumjevR) is the newest
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.2 Insulin Management

paragraphs.text: rapid-acting insulin, and was approved for children in 2022. These rapid-acting insulin analogs have amino acid substitutions on the β-chain, which result in more rapid absorp tion following subcutaneous injection, with a sharper peak and shorter duration of action when compared to regular insulin. When compared to regular insulin, rapid-acting insulin analogs give better control of post prandial glucose surges and lower rates of late, post-meal hypoglycemia [15]. An ultrarapid acting insulin was FDA-approved for use in adults and children with type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Fiasp is insulin aspart that has been reformulated with the addition of nia cinamide (vitamin B3) and arginine to decrease absorption time. With this addition, Fiasp enters the blood stream within 2.5 min and can thus be given either immediately prior to a meal or up to 20 min after eating begins [16]. Randomized controlled trials have looked at Fiasp in both adults with T1D on injection and pump therapy and T2D on injection and metformin therapy. In the T1D studies, Fiasp was found to be similar to insu lin aspart in terms of risk of hypoglycemia while improving postprandial glucose levels in pump patients [16, 17]. In T2D, Fiasp was again noninferior to insulin aspart, but did have a slight increase in rates of hypoglycemia in the first 2 h after a meal [18]. Fiasp is cur rently available in U-100 concentration in an insulin pen or vial. Lyumjev is lispro with two additives: Treprostinil which dilates blood vessels for faster absorption and sodium citrate to enhance insulin’s action time. Studies have shown Lyumjev to improve daytime TIR when compared to Lispro [19].
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.2 Insulin Management

paragraphs.text: U-200 lispro is more commonly known as the HumalogR U-200 Kwikpen. The Kwikpen signifies that this insulin is only available in a pen format. The pen has been designed to deliver the same dose of insulin as U-100 but in half the volume. This is especially helpful for patients who require a larger dose of pre prandial insulin. Both U-100 and U-200 lis pro have been shown to have similar pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic actions when compared to each other [20].
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.2 Insulin Management

paragraphs.text: There are now four long-acting analog preparations: glargine U-100 (LantusR,
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.2 Insulin Management

paragraphs.text: BasaglarR), glargine U-300 (ToujeoR), detemir (LevemirR), and degludec (TresibaR). Insulin glargine is engineered to be soluble in the acid pH solution in which it is packaged, but rela tively insoluble in the neutral pH of subcuta neous interstitial fluid. This leads to precipitation of glargine following subcutane ous injection which delays its absorption into the circulation, creating the first long-acting insulin [15]. Glargine U-300 (ToujeoR) has been shown to have a flatter insulin action profile and a longer duration of action when compared to glargine U-100 [21]. Blood glu cose levels should be monitored closely when making the transition between glargine U-100 and glargine U-300 as some patients may need to have their doses increased by 10–15% [22]. Currently, glargine U-300 is approved by the Food & Drug Administration (FDA) for use in adults, and glargine U-100 is FDAapproved for use in children >6 years old.
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.2 Insulin Management

paragraphs.text: The fatty acid side chain in insulin detemir causes it to bind to albumin in the circulation and interstitial fluid, resulting in a prolonged duration of insulin action. Studies show that it too has a flat time-action profile and lower dose-to-dose variability than either NPH or glargine U-100 [23]. Although controversial, insulin detemir may have a shorter duration of action than glargine U100. To date, there are no studies comparing insulin detemir to insulin glargine U-300. Insulin detemir is FDA-approved for use in children (ages 2–17 years) and adults.

Insulin degludec is the first ultra-longacting insulin. It initially forms multihexam ers in subcutaneous tissue in order to delay absorption, and like insulin detemir, it also binds to albumin to delay elimination [24]. Because of this design, insulin degludec has been shown to have a half-life of 24 h and a duration of action that exceeds 42 h [25]. In children and adolescents with T1D, insulin degludec has been shown to be equivalent to insulin detemir in terms of its glucoselowering ability, and it has the ability to do so in a single daily injection [26]. Furthermore, insulin degludec appears to significantly reduce the risk of developing hyperglycemia with ketosis [26]. Two additional features of

insulin degludec that make it very appealing as a basal insulin are that (1) mixing is possi ble with rapid-acting insulin and (2) its ultralong-acting profile can allow for less stringent timing of daily administration [27]. It should be noted that insulin degludec is only available in an insulin pen format, and that there are two available concentrations, U-100 and U-200. The U-200 insulin degludec pen allows for a single dose of insulin up to 160 units and may be most appropriate for those who may have significantly increased insulin needs.

NPH is the only intermediate-acting insu lin in the market today. As an insulin suspen sion, it is imperative that adequate mixing of the components occurs before injection. There is significant dose-to-dose variability in the peak effect of NPH, making it less satisfac tory for basal insulin replacement, particu larly during the overnight period [28].

There are also premixed combinations of both human regular and NPH (e.g., Humulin 70/30R) and of insulin aspart protamine and insulin aspart (NovoLog 70/30R) and insulin lispro protamine and insulin lispro (Humalog 50/50R). These types of premixed insulins may not be as effective in the treatment of T1D as it is difficult to achieve the necessary 24-h insu lin coverage with these fixed ratios of insulin. However, we have used these insulins when faced with a challenging patient who cannot or will not take more than 2–3 injections/day.

Finally, inhaled insulin is now available, although currently only approved for use in adults with diabetes. Insulin human inhala tion powder (AfrezzaR) is a prandial insulin that comes in 4, 8, and 12 unit cartridges. Larger doses of prandial insulin would require a combination of individual cartridges. The dry powdered formulation of insulin is deliv ered from the cartridges to the deep lung through the use of a small, breath-powered inhaler [29]. Although this product has not been shown to significantly reduce hemoglo bin A1c levels, it is associated with improved fasting blood glucose along with a reduction in hypoglycemia and weight gain [29]. Thus, this insulin could be used in young adult patients for whom multiple injections of insu lin are not an option.

With so many types of insulin available, the choice of regimen has also become more com plicated. The findings of the DCCT estab lished that intensive basal-bolus therapy with multiple daily injections or an insulin pump could be used to optimize blood glucose con trol [8, 10]. However, insulin only works if the patient takes it, so other factors such as ability to take four or more injections per day, count carbohydrates, and test blood glucose (BG) levels must be assessed in order to determine the regimen that will provide the best outcomes. Regardless of the regimen that is chosen, no insulin regimen will precisely duplicate normal insulin secretion due to a number of factors including subcutaneous injection affecting absorption rates and a lack of precision in empiric dosing of insulin. Thus, periods of hypoglycemia resulting from excessive plasma insulin concentrations, along with periods of hyperglycemia from inade quate insulin concentrations, will occur even in the most conscientious patients.
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.3 Regimens

paragraphs.text: In the individual without diabetes, basal plasma insulin levels are overlaid by mealrelated spikes in circulating insulin concentra tions. Current intensive insulin regimens attempt to simulate this pattern of insulin secretion by employing a basal-bolus approach to insulin replacement, typically with each component being covered by a par ticular type of insulin. Basal insulin, given once or twice daily with glargine or detemir, or once a day with the newer longer-acting insulins, is paired with food-related boluses of rapid-acting insulin, such as lispro, aspart, or glulisine. Not only is this regimen close to the physiologic model, but it has also been associ ated with lower rates of nocturnal hypoglyce mia compared to NPH-based regimens [28]. Further, this intensive regimen is associated with lower rates of retinopathy in adolescents
paragraphs.heading: with Multiple Daily Injections (MDI, 4+ Injections per Day)

paragraphs.text: when compared to more traditional regimens consisting of one to two injections of insulin per day [30]. A drawback to this type of regi men is that the flat time-action profile of basal insulin makes it imperative that patients take their premeal boluses. In this type of regimen, hungry adolescents can expect to take upward of six to eight injections per day for basal and meal/snack bolus coverage. This can quickly become a problem as the difficulty of daily administration of premeal injections accounted for the findings in a study in which adolescents who were randomized to a glargine-based basal-bolus regimen had a higher A1c than those randomized to the insulin pump [31].
paragraphs.heading: with Multiple Daily Injections (MDI, 4+ Injections per Day)

paragraphs.text: It should also be noted that fixed doses of long-acting insulin analogs, in combination with changes in insulin sensitivity due to antecedent exercise in the afternoon and sup pressed catecholamine responses during sleep, put patients with type 1 diabetes at “tri ple jeopardy” for severe nocturnal hypoglyce mia [32].
paragraphs.heading: with Multiple Daily Injections (MDI, 4+ Injections per Day)

paragraphs.text: Although many clinicians start the newly diagnosed patient on an intensive basal-bolus regimen with four or more daily injections, our patients are started on 3 injections/day using a combination of NPH and aspart with breakfast and separate injections of aspart and glargine with dinner. The initial morning dose is divided into 2/3 NPH and 1/3 aspart, and the evening dose is 1/2 aspart and 1/2 glargine. The rationale for using this regimen is that the relatively flat and consistent insulin profile of the pre-dinner glargine would lower the risk of nocturnal hypoglycemia compared to predinner NPH or even predinner or bed time glargine. Moreover, the prebreakfast injection of NPH insulin (in combination with the patient’s residual endogenous insulin secretion) obviates the need for extra insulin to cover lunch and afternoon snacks. It is our experience that utilizing this regimen at the onset of diabetes to obtain aggressive control of blood glucose levels supports most children
paragraphs.heading: Regimen

paragraphs.text: as they enter a “honeymoon” or partial remis sion period. This partial remission is a result of increased insulin secretion by residual β-cells and improved insulin sensitivity with normalization of blood glucose levels [33].
paragraphs.heading: Regimen

paragraphs.text: To achieve rapid improvements in glucose control, most patients are started on a total daily dose of 0.5–1 unit/kg body weight per day. During the 2–3 weeks following dis charge, insulin doses are titrated toward target premeal glucose values of 80–130 mg/dL dur ing daily telephone calls. The patients are ini tially maintained on an age and weight appropriate, fixed carbohydrate intake with each meal. Follow-up clinic visits are sched uled at approximately 2, 6, 13, 26, 39, and 52 weeks following diagnosis. During these follow-up clinic visits, glycemic control is assessed by review of self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG) records and by pointof-service A1c measurements; episodes of severe hypoglycemia, readmissions for DKA, and changes in insulin regimens are also recorded. It is noteworthy that an increasing proportion of our patients have started to use continuous glucose monitors (CGM) to replace blood glucose meter monitoring very early in the course of their diabetes. Indeed, CGM is typically ordered at the initial followup office visit, approximately 2 weeks after discharge from the hospital. The concepts of correction doses and insulin to carbohydrate ratios that enable more flexible carbohydrate intake are introduced during the second or third follow-up clinic visits.
paragraphs.heading: Regimen

paragraphs.text: A major reason why this 3-injection/day regimen is so effective during the honeymoon phase is that endogenous insulin secretion provides much of the overnight basal insulin requirement, leading to normal fasting blood glucose levels, as well as “smoothing out” blood glucose variations throughout the day. During the “honeymoon” period, insulin requirements drop sharply. Commonly, the doses of rapid-acting insulin are markedly reduced or even discontinued, and some can even be well managed on an injection of intermediate-acting NPH in the morning and long-acting insulin glargine at dinner. In rare cases, young children recover enough beta cell

function to be managed only on basal insulin. As β-cell function declines during the second half of the first year of treatment, blood glu cose levels become more labile, and HbA1c levels begin to rise. It is at this point that the limitations of the three-injection regimen become apparent. These include high presupper and much more variable fasting blood glucose levels. High pre-supper glucose values begin to occur despite normal prelunch and mid-afternoon values, most commonly caused by the consumption of an afternoon snack at the same time as waning effects of the pre breakfast NPH dose. Fasting blood glucose levels become more unpredictable because relatively small dose-to-dose variations in the time-action profile of detemir or glargine can lead to hyper- and hypoglycemia due to the small margin of error in regulating overnight hepatic glucose production. As noted previ ously, patients are more vulnerable to hypo glycemia in the middle of the night because the normal plasma epinephrine response to low blood glucose levels is markedly blunted during sleep [34], and extra physical activity during the day contributes to low glucose con centrations on the following night.

Educational materials regarding continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion (CSII) pump therapy are provided during initial diabetes education, and approximately 30% or more of families in our practice switch to pump ther apy after less than 3 months of injection ther apy. Our youngest patients are especially encouraged to switch to a pump as they often require small total daily doses of insulin, as well as very small correction doses. Early use of CSII pump therapy in the very young infant and toddler has demonstrated durable improvement in both A1c and risk of severe hypoglycemia [35]. In other patients, the deci sion to switch to CSII occurs later, commonly due to increasing difficulties in maintaining adequate glycemic control during the second half of the first year of treatment of T1D. It is often challenging to receive insurance cover
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.4 Insulin Pumps

paragraphs.text: age for insulin pump therapy in patients whose duration of diabetes is less than 6 months.
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.4 Insulin Pumps

paragraphs.text: Insulin pumps emerged as an ideal tool to intensify insulin treatment while minimizing hypoglycemia in the 1980s. However, very few pediatric patients initially used these devices because they were cumbersome to use, few pediatric providers had experience in the use of pumps, and there was uncertainty about the long-term benefits of intensive treatment. The results of the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial (DCCT) indicating that the long-term benefits of strict diabetes con trol outweigh the risks of severe hypoglycemia showed a major paradigm shift in diabetes treatment. This trial, which included youth ages 13–17 years old, dramatically demon strated the benefit of aggressive glycemic control in mitigating the development and progression of complications [9, 36, 37]. As a result, intensive diabetes management rapidly became the gold standard, and insulin pump therapy was promoted by expert diabetes care providers as an effective means of achieving strict metabolic control of T1D.
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.4 Insulin Pumps

paragraphs.text: As we reported more than 10 years ago, approximately half of our patients were using basal/bolus treatment for their diabetes by the end of the first year of treatment [38]. In those patients, the median total daily insulin doses at 3, 6, and 12 months were 0.6, 0.7, and 0.8 U/kg/day, respectively, and nadir A1c lev els were observed at ~6 months (i.e., 6.8 to 6.9%). By 12 months, patients who had switched to pump therapy had a median A1c of 6.9% compared to 7.2% in injection patients. There were severe hypoglycemic events in only 5% of patients during the first year of treatment; all occurred with injection therapy during daytime, and all but one of the patients were younger than 7 years of age. None of the patients had an episode of DKA during the first year of treatment.
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.4 Insulin Pumps

paragraphs.text: CSII via an insulin pump provides what is perhaps the most physiological option for insulin replacement. The proof of concept for CSII was established in the late 1970s, but it is only within the last 20 years that there has been a substantial increase in pump use in pediatrics. Indeed, nearly half of the children
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.4 Insulin Pumps

paragraphs.text: and adolescents in the USA and German/ Austrian type 1 diabetes registries are cur rently receiving insulin pump therapy [39]. Insulin pumps use only one type of insulin, most commonly rapid-acting analogs as they have been associated with better blood glu cose control, particularly postprandially, and fewer episodes of hypoglycemia than human regular insulin [40]. Current technology allows for the delivery of doses as small as 0.025 U of insulin in some models.
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.4 Insulin Pumps

paragraphs.text: Most of today’s insulin pumps are com posed of an insulin reservoir that is incorpo rated into a programmable insulin delivery device. In traditional pumps, plastic tubing connects the insulin reservoir to a catheter that is inserted subcutaneously into either the abdomen or hip. Tubeless insulin pumps (AKA patch pumps) have slightly different structures that are directly connected to the subcutaneous tissue through a catheter with out any tubing. Patch pumps require a hand held device that communicates wirelessly with the pump to adjust insulin doses.
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.4 Insulin Pumps

paragraphs.text: The pump is programmed to deliver “basal rates” of rapid-acting insulin throughout the day. Basal, or background, insulin is designed to keep blood glucose levels steady in between meals and overnight. Multiple basal rates can be programmed throughout a 24-h period which allows for variation in insulin delivery to match the daily variations in insulin need. Additionally, use of temporary basal rates (temporary increases or decreases of the pro grammed basal rates by a percentage or an absolute amount for a specified period of time) is very helpful in modifying doses for ill ness and exercise. Variations in basal rate can be particularly beneficial overnight, since basal rates can be programmed to be lower in the early part of the night to prevent hypogly cemia and higher in the hours before dawn to keep glucose from rising. Basal rates also eliminate the need for the use of intermediate or long-acting insulins, and meal planning does not have to center around peak insulin action, as recommended with multiple daily injection therapies.
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.4 Insulin Pumps

paragraphs.text: The pump is also programmed to deliver “bolus” doses of insulin, or an immediate
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.4 Insulin Pumps

paragraphs.text: burst of insulin that the patient delivers at mealtimes to limit meal-related glucose excur sions and to correct hyperglycemia. During the day, the patient “dials up” a bolus of rapid-acting insulin in accordance with the carbohydrate content of the meal or to cor rect hyperglycemia.
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.4 Insulin Pumps

paragraphs.text: When the pump dose calculator is used for meal boluses, the child or caregiver enters the number of carbohydrates that will be con sumed in the upcoming meal or snack, and the pump’s computer calculates the amount of insulin to be given based on the pro grammed insulin to carbohydrate ratio (e.g., often 1 U/10 g of carbohydrates in adoles cents) for that time of day. Timing of bolus doses is also important. Research has shown that there is significant reduction in postpran dial blood glucose levels when the meal bolus is delivered 10–15 min before the meal [41]. However, delivery of the bolus after or during the meal is acceptable and may be particularly useful for very young children, the “picky” eater, or those in the school setting where there is less oversight to ensure that a child actually eats the amount of carbohydrates entered into the pump [42]. Bolusing for car bohydrate intake allows more flexibility in the quantity and content of food intake. Unfortunately, many patients and parents are not particularly skilled in calculating the car bohydrate content of meals. This observation points to the importance of continued educa tion from both the registered dietitian and the diabetes provider.
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.4 Insulin Pumps

paragraphs.text: For a correction bolus, the pump’s com puter is programmed with a correction or sen sitivity factor (e.g., 1 U drops blood glucose levels by 50 mg/dL) to correct for blood glu cose levels that are outside the target range. The pump is also programmed with a target blood glucose which acts as the mathematical goal for the correction equation. The blood glucose value is entered into the pump either

manually or by wireless transmission from the glucose meter into the pump. In the case of a value that is above target, additional insulin can be given to lower the high reading based on the preset correction factor. In the case of a value that is below target, insulin is sub tracted from a meal or snack bolus in order to compensate for the low reading.

In today’s world of “smart” pump technol ogy, the insulin pump’s computer is able to calculate a recommended dose of insulin for both the meal and correction bolus, which can be combined at mealtime. Bolus calculators only suggest the dose of insulin based on the estimated carbohydrate content of the meal and premeal blood glucose values; it is then up to the patient or caregiver to determine whether this amount of insulin should be adjusted based on previous or anticipated exercise or on overall blood glucose trends.

Some of the limitations of insulin pumps are possible encumbrance during exercise or contact sports. While the pumps with tubing can be removed for a short period of time dur ing sports, it takes careful planning and close monitoring before, during, and after the exer cise period. Additionally, because only rapidacting insulin is used, any interruption in flow (catheter occlusion or disconnection) can lead to relatively rapid deterioration of metabolic control, especially during sleeping hours. Although uncommon, local infections at the site of catheter insertion can occur.

While insulin pump therapy has been dem onstrated to be effective in the management of T1D, not all pediatric patients make good pump candidates. When considering whether or not to initiate insulin pump therapy, it is essential that care providers select candidates and families in whom pump therapy would be both safe and effective. Indications for pump therapy in pediatrics include persistently ele vated A1c levels on injection regimens, wide fluctuations in glucose levels, recurrent and

significant hypoglycemic events, very young children requiring small amounts of insulin, or when lifestyle issues render an injection regimen especially difficult to manage. In short, virtually every youth with T1D has at least one of these indications. Consequently, caregivers should have an extensive conversa tion with both the child (if age appropriate) and family to explore the use of an insulin pump.

It is essential that school-aged children and adolescents themselves want to use an insulin pump. Our young patients need to understand that regardless of the type of pump they select, they will continuously have hardware attached to their body. Even if the parent desires the therapy, if the child is “forced” to use an insulin pump, the outcomes may not be as successful. Similarly, parents must agree with pursuing this therapy, as their support will be crucial to its success.

The family also needs to have appropriate expectations for insulin pump therapy. They have to understand that the therapy is going to require significant effort on their part; perhaps even more than an insulin injection regimen. Moreover, using an insulin pump does not “cure” their diabetes, but it is a device to help them better manage their diabetes. Frequent glucose monitoring or use of a continuous glu cose monitor is also important, and understand ing carbohydrate counting is a necessity. As with patients on injection therapy, they need to know how to manage illnesses with diabetes, the signs and symptoms of ketoacidosis, and when to call their diabetes provider for assistance.
Feedback control of insulin delivery based on real-time changes in sensor glucose levels has advanced management of diabetes. This
paragraphs.heading: Glucose Monitors (CGM) and Pump Therapy

paragraphs.text: is especially true during the overnight period, in which every night is an adventure. Einstein defined insanity as doing the same thing over and over again and always expecting a differ ent result. In contrast, we define insanity for type 1 diabetes as using the same nighttime basal infusion doses over and over and always getting a different result. A major par adigm shift occurred with the introduction of commercially available real-time continu ous glucose monitors (CGMs). Indeed, the current generation CGMs are sufficiently accurate that they have replaced the need to use blood glucose meter testing to guide insulin therapy. The integration of current CGMs with insulin pumps has enabled infor mation on sensor glucose levels to guide insulin dosing.
paragraphs.heading: Glucose Monitors (CGM) and Pump Therapy

paragraphs.text: Recent advances in pump therapy have led to the first commercially available hybrid closed-loop insulin pump system. This sys tem integrates a continuous glucose moni tor (see Sect. 30.3.5.2) with an insulin pump to create a device in which the system dynamically adjusts the basal component of insulin delivery in response to data from an indwelling subcutaneous glucose sensor [18]. This automated insulin delivery is combined with manual delivery of prandial boluses to meet total daily insulin require ments. The results of the pivotal trial in adolescents and adults with type 1 diabetes demonstrated that with this system, not only is there an improvement in A1c and the amount of time patients remain with their glucose levels in the target zone of 70–180 mg/dL, but the percentage of time with sensor glucose values below 70 mg/dL (in the hypoglycemic range) was cut nearly in half [43, 44]. There are multiple compa nies and institutions that are working on closed-loop systems, with three systems FDA-approved at the time of writing. The next several years will likely bring about many further advances in this domain.
paragraphs.heading: Glucose Monitors (CGM) and Pump Therapy

paragraphs.text: It is important to remember that inter ruption of delivery of rapid-acting insulin analogs from a pump can rapidly lead to increases in blood ketone levels (within hours) with progression to ketoacidosis if unrecognized [45]. Training and reinforce ment of diabetes prevention protocols for parents of children treated with insulin pumps can reduce the risk of DKA. Para doxically, the risk of DKA was lower in youth with type 1 diabetes treated with pumps than insulin injections in the T1D Exchange Registry [46], an observation that likely reflects closer monitoring and better overall control in this population.
paragraphs.heading: Glucose Monitors (CGM) and Pump Therapy

paragraphs.text: An important point that is common to most of the closed-loop systems currently available is that they are all “hybrid” closedloop systems; namely, they require manual input of insulin at meal times. Hybrid closedloop systems also adjust basal insulin deliv ery in between meals and overnight. The HCL concept has changed over time in two major ways: (1) Current systems employ manual administration of large pre- meal doses of insulin to fully cover the carbohy drate content of the meal. The aim here is to mitigate the risk of over-delivery of insulin due to a system malfunction by severely restricting the amount of insulin that can be delivered automatically. (2) The system cleans up the back end by automatically adjusting basal insulin infusion rates after meals and during the night. Specifically, the sensor algo rithm often completely suspends insulin delivery due to falling sensor glucose levels in the late, post-meal period.
paragraphs.heading: Glucose Monitors (CGM) and Pump Therapy

paragraphs.text: Clinical trials of the Medtronic 670G have demonstrated excellent safety and control results. In a longitudinal study in 124 adults and adolescents with T1D, mean A1c levels decreased from 7.4% at baseline to 6.9% after 3 months [47]. Time in glucose target, defined

as time spent in 70–180 mg/dL range, increased significantly, from 60 to 69% in the adolescent cohort and from 67 to 74% in the adult cohort [43], with significant decreases in time spent in hyperglycemia and hypoglyce mia. A subsequent study in children 7–13 years old showed similarly significant improvements from baseline to 3 months in A1c level (7.9–7.5%), time in target (56–65%), and reduced time spent in hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia [48].

The second system to become available in the United States is the Tandem t:slim X2 with Control-IQ Technology, which is also a hybrid closed-loop system, with the sensor sending glucose readings directly to the pump. However, there are important differ ences between this system and the Medtronic system, most notably in the sensor and tog gling between auto and manual settings; moreover, the Tandem system incorporates the Dexcom G6 continuous glucose sensor, which does not require blood glucose entries or calibration and it allows users to “share” glucose values in real time remotely with des ignated caregivers. Clinical trials of the Tan dem Control-IQ system have demonstrated similar levels of achieved time in target and HbA1c levels as in the Medtronic 670G trials [49].

A third hybrid closed-loop system has been developed by Insulet. This device differs from the Medtronic and Tandem systems in that as an “untethered” patch pump, the sys tem is controlled through a smartphone device, which relays communications between the glucose sensor (in this case, the Dexcom G6) and the “pod.” The Omnipod 5 is now approved and initial trial data including in children and adolescents have demonstrated its ease of use, safety, and improvements in time in range (TIR) under free-living condi tions [50].

SMBG allows families and clinicians to regu larly evaluate the efficacy of the current insu lin regimen. Today’s glucose meters are small, accurate, and relatively inexpensive. There are many different brands currently commer cially available, and most have reliability and accuracy of 5–8% of laboratory measure ments [51, 52]. Many will display a result within 5 s and require small amounts of blood. Traditionally, SMBG blood samples are obtained from finger stick, but the smaller blood volume that is now needed for today’s meters has allowed the use of alternate sites such as the forearm. However, alternate sites are associated with a lag time effect, espe cially during times of rapidly changing glu cose levels such as with exercise or after meals [53].
paragraphs.heading: Glucose (SMBG)

paragraphs.text: We recommend that children test their blood glucose levels at least four times daily, before meals and at bedtime. However, most patients on either insulin pump therapy or basal-bolus therapy test six to ten times daily: premeals, intermittently postprandially, before exercise or driving, at bedtime, and fol lowing episodes of hyper- or hypoglycemia [54]. In fact, evidence suggests that “more is better” as the T1D Exchange Registry found a strong inverse correlation between increased frequency of SMBG and improved glycemic control as evidenced by lower hemoglobin A1c levels [55]. Nevertheless, SMBG measure ments only provided brief snapshots of glu cose levels before and occasionally 2–3 h after meals and rarely during the night. It also became apparent that treatment of T1D would never be perfect until there was feed back control of insulin administration based on frequent, real-time measurements of changes in glucose con- centrations.
paragraphs.heading: Glucose (SMBG)

paragraphs.text: Even when performed correctly, four or more blood tests a day give only a small glimpse of the wide blood glucose fluctuations that occur over a 24-h period in children with diabetes [56]. Consequently, the introduction of con tinuous glucose monitoring (CGM) has the potential to be the most influential advance ment in the management of diabetes in the last 20 years. Numerous studies highlighted the limitations of the first CGMs, which led to their rapid disappearance from commer cial sales. With further improvements in CGM devices, the JDRF CGM Study Group demonstrated that CGM could provide a bet ter means to achieve optimal control of glu cose than using blood glucose meter monitoring [57].
paragraphs.heading: Monitoring (CGM)

paragraphs.text: Most recently, CGM has become a critical tool in the management of diabetes in chil dren and adolescents. The newest generation CGM sensors are inserted into subcutaneous tissue. The electrochemical reaction between glucose oxidase in the sensor and interstitial glucose in subcutaneous tissue produces an electric current that is directly proportional to the ambient glucose concentration that is read by the sensor and transmitted to a receiver. Key features of the newer CGMs include accuracy, continued use for 10–14 days, and serving as replacement for fingerstick blood glucose monitoring. Additionally, sensor glu cose trend arrows indicate the rate of glucose rise and fall, and some systems provide cus tomizable alerts for high and low glucose thresholds. Web-based data-management software for real-time data upload to the cloud and real-time remote monitoring are features that are very attractive to parents of young children with T1D. Additional features include integration of pumps and sensors into
paragraphs.heading: Monitoring (CGM)

paragraphs.text: sensor-augmented insulin pump systems that can automatically shut off basal infusions in the face of low sensor glucose levels [44] and the availability of programs that allow for the data from the CGM device to be “shared” with other users via cloud interface. These advances in CGM technology have driven the increased uptake of CGM in pediatrics. In the care of pediatric patients, the latter advance allows parents/guardians and other caregivers to monitor CGM data independent of the location of the child. The data from a CGM can be used in many different ways. See Box 30.2 for possible uses of CGM in day-to-day management of T1D.
paragraphs.heading: Monitoring (CGM)

paragraphs.text: Several studies including the JDRF CGM randomized control trial (CGM RCT), the Guard Control study, and others indicated that adults with T1D who had an A1c ≥7.0% had a better improvement in their A1c with the use of CGM than with SMBG alone [58, 59]. Even more importantly, this improvement in A1c was not associated with any increase in hypoglycemia. The JDRF CGM Study Group also showed that adult patients with T1D who use CGM and have baseline A1c levels <7.0% are better able to maintain their A1c at this target level than those patients who only used SMBG [60]. The JDRF CGM RCT showed that youth who wore the sensor almost every day achieved the same benefits as adults with respect to changes in A1c [58, 60]. More recent trials also support the need for continuous use of the CGM in order to see an impact on HbA1c and quality of life, specifically a reduc tion in the number of school days missed due to diabetes [61, 62]. Unfortunately, few pediat ric patients were able to use these early, rela tively inaccurate, and difficult to use CGM devices consistently enough to receive these benefits over the long run [58]. Patient and family education is another cornerstone of the successful use of these devices in pediat rics. Families must understand the strengths and limitations of CGM and must be part of a comprehensive training program to learn the ins and outs of both the mechanics of CGM and the successful interpretation of both real-time and retrospective data. Smaller, more accurate, and easier to use systems are needed for children with T1D.
paragraphs.heading: Monitoring (CGM)

paragraphs.text: Severe hypoglycemia is a significant risk for patients attempting to achieve tight glycemic control. In the DCCT, the risk of severe hypo glycemia was threefold higher in the inten sively managed cohort than it was in the conventionally managed one [8]. Although advances in diabetes technology over the past 20 years have not eliminated the risk of hypo glycemia, they have allowed patients to lower HbA1c into the target range without increas ing the risk of severe hypoglycemia [63–65]. Most severe hypoglycemic events occur in the overnight hours, likely due in part to sleepinduced defects in counter-regulatory hor mone responses to hypoglycemia [34]. Hypoglycemia represents a significant barrier to successful obtainment of tight glycemic control in people with diabetes, and thus, effective management of hypoglycemia has to be at the forefront of any diabetes regimen for children and adolescents.
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.6 Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: Regular SMBG in combination with tar geted SMBG is the mainstay to detecting hypoglycemia and preventing its progression
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.6 Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: to severe hypoglycemia. It is important to note that unawareness of hypoglycemic symp toms can be “developmentally appropriate” in the very young child, making it more chal lenging for caregivers to know when the blood glucose level is low. The normal response to falling plasma glucose levels in nondiabetic individuals includes rapid suppression of insulin secretion followed by release of gluca gon and epinephrine if the plasma glucose level does not stabilize following the decrease in insulin release alone. Children with diabetes suffer from defective counter-regulation because the action of exogenously supplied insulin cannot be adjusted in response to fall ing glucose levels, and they additionally lose the ability to secrete glucagon in response to hypoglycemia. Thus, patients with T1D are dependent upon increases in circulating plasma catecholamines to signal the presence of hypoglycemia. Unfortunately, recurrent episodes of even mild hypoglycemia that occur with intensive treatment lead to blunt ing of catecholamine response leading to epi sodes of hypoglycemia unawareness or hypoglycemia-associated autonomic failure.
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.6 Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: The American Diabetes Association defines hypoglycemia in the setting of diabetes as any plasma glucose of 70 mg/dL or less [54], whether accompanied by symptoms or not. The severity of hypoglycemic events is defined by their impact on function. Mild-tomoderate events are those where patients are able to treat themselves. Severe events are those in which patients have sufficient cogni tive impairment as to be unable to treat them selves and must rely upon the assistance of others.
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.6 Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: Typical treatment for mild-to-moderate hypoglycemia is 15 g of fast-acting carbohy drate such as four ounces of regular juice or soda or three to four glucose tablets. For those children using automated insulin delivery (AID) systems, fewer carbohydrates are needed to correct. Generally, 5–10 g of fastacting carbohydrates are recommended if the blood glucose if 54–70 mg/dl. More carbohy drates may result in rebound hyperglycemia. Regardless of insulin delivery system, ideally, the low blood glucose level is confirmed via SMBG; however, children should be advised
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.6 Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: that if they have symptoms of hypoglycemia, they should treat these right away, even if unable to test their blood glucose level. In the case of severe events, seizure or loss of con sciousness may preclude the safe use of oral carbohydrate sources and an intramuscular, subcutaneous, or nasal injection of glucagon (0.5–1 mg), or IV glucose infusion may be required. Recent studies evaluating intranasal administration of glucagon powder are prom ising as a treatment alternative to glucagon injections for hypoglycemia [66], and this is now commercially available.
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.6 Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: Once an episode of hypoglycemia has been resolved, it is important for children and their families to review the event for precipi tating factors such as changes in eating habits and exercise or activity levels. If this review does not yield a clear cause, the blood glucose records for the last few days should be reviewed to determine whether a change in the insulin regimen is needed. Prevention of hypoglycemia should be the goal, and many options exist to aid in the attainment of this goal. In clinical practice, we consider decreas ing insulin dosage 24–48 h after a severe hypoglycemic episode in efforts to prevent repeat severe hypoglycemia. Although uncommon, recurrent hypoglycemia in the face of reductions in total daily insulin doses may be presenting symptoms of celiac dis ease, adrenal insufficiency, or growth hor mone deficiency.
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.6 Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: Dietary guidance for children with diabetes is a key component in the diabetes regimen and ideally best provided by a registered dietician who is a member of the multidisciplinary dia betes team and is comfortable working with children. In addition to achieving optimal gly cemic control and maximizing growth and development, medical nutrition therapy is also aimed at reducing the risk for other dis eases such as obesity, dyslipidemia, and hyper tension. Underlying all of these goals is the establishment of sound eating patterns incor porating healthy food choices [67]. Current guidelines for healthy eating for youth with
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.7 Medical Nutrition Therapy

paragraphs.text: T1D are the same as for children without dia betes. The main difference being that children with T1D must take insulin. Current guide lines specify that the goal of a proper diet is to provide sufficient energy for appropriate growth and weight maintenance, to amelio rate long-term complications, and to prevent acute complications such as severe hypoglyce mia and diabetic ketoacidosis [68]. Energy intake should be distributed as 45–55% carbo hydrate with less than 10% added sugars, 10–20% protein, and 30–35% fat. Saturated fat should be limited to <10% and polyunsat urated, monounsaturated, and Omega 3 s fatty acids should be encouraged [69].
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.7 Medical Nutrition Therapy

paragraphs.text: Recently, these dietary recommendations have been challenged as some studies have shown that lower carbohydrate intake results in reduced postprandial hyperglycemia, while other observational studies have reported lower HbA1c levels associated with a lower carbohydrate intake [68, 70, 71]. However, there is general agreement that carbohydrates should not be restricted in children and ado lescents with T1D, as it may adversely affect growth and development. Moreover, very low-carbohydrate diets restrict or eliminate many foods that are important sources of micronutrients; therefore, dietary recommen dations must be individualized and be flexible rather than rigid and dogmatic [72].
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.7 Medical Nutrition Therapy

paragraphs.text: A balanced diet that emphasizes nutrientdense foods is recommended for the entire family, not only for the child with diabetes. Families should be educated on macronutri ent composition of the diet; the effects of macronutrients on blood glucose; carbohy drate counting or estimation; hypoglycemia treatment and prevention; timing of insulin action and meals; handling special or festive occasions; weight management; and preven tion of disordered eating. Additionally, barri ers to healthy eating should be addressed during nutrition education, including parent’s perception that healthy eating is costlier, more time is spent preparing healthy meals, con cerns related to social influences on eating, and feelings that their child with T1D might be seen as different. For those patients with coexisting celiac disease, this can be an even greater challenge as many gluten-free foods

have higher glycemic indices [73]. Nutritional advice should also take into consideration cultural, ethnic, and family traditions [74]. It is important that the whole family be involved in making dietary changes based on healthy eating. It is also noteworthy that youth with T1D are no longer “thin.” In fact, approxi mately 36–39% of youth with T1D have BMI z-scores in the overweight to obese ranges. The type of insulin regimen prescribed will determine the nutrition care plan or vice versa; mainly, carbohydrate intake and insulin should be balanced against each other. Fixed doses of insulin will require that a meal plan with fixed carbohydrate intake be established and maintained consistently from day to day. The exception to this rule is during the honey moon phase of T1D. During that period, residual endogenous insulin secretion can often make up for modest increases in carbo hydrate intake.

Injections of rapid-acting insulin analogs before meals in combination with long-acting insulin analogs to cover the overnight period or use of an insulin pump allow for more flex ibility in food intake as insulin doses are matched to the planned carbohydrate intake for each meal (AKA basal-bolus therapy). We initially treat patients with a standard intake of carbohydrate for each main meal, so that we will be better able to establish the insulin to carbohydrate ratio. Subsequently, patients and caregivers will be able to calculate pre meal insulin doses based on the amount of carbohydrate to be consumed with each meal. The latter approach of adjusting insulin doses based on variations in appetite works best in the long run.

Carbohydrate counting is by far the most popular way to introduce flexibility into the dietary plan. In patients using basal-bolus insulin therapy with an insulin pump or mul tiple injections of insulin, bolus doses of insu lin are based on the grams of carbohydrates that will be consumed in the meal. Specifically, patients use a ratio that represents the amount of carbohydrates (in grams) that 1 U of insu lin will cover. This ratio is very individualized; determined and adjusted by trial and error, and often varies throughout the day; more insulin is usually needed for breakfast than

other meals. For this method of insulin cover age to work properly, reasonable accuracy at counting carbohydrates is essential. Patients and their families must be comfortable with reading food labels and quantifying the size of servings, either through measurement or weight. Protein and fat content, while impor tant to an overall healthy meal plan, are not counted as a general rule. However, they can impact the absorption of carbohydrates, and foods such as pizza may thus require an indi vidualized approach. Ultimately, the patient and family determine the size of the meal and its carbohydrate content and then determine an insulin dose to match food intake.

Carbohydrate counting can also be used in a more traditional approach to diabetes ther apy in which set insulin doses are matched with consistent carbohydrate targets for meals and snacks. In fact, we use this approach, stressing consistency in the timing and size of meals, as a starting point for newly diagnosed families who are too overwhelmed to learn more advanced nutritional concepts at the very beginning of treating their child’s diabe tes.

Regular exercise and active participation in organized activities have positive implications for both the psychosocial and physical wellbeing of all children and are especially impor tant for children with diabetes. Exercise and being physically fit are associated with increased sensitivity to insulin and better glu cose utilization. Despite its many benefits, exercise in children with diabetes can make it more challenging to regulate glucose levels. Hypoglycemia is a common occurrence which can then result in excessive carbohydrate intake leading to hyperglycemia. This effect is only compounded by the intermittent and spontaneous nature of physical activity in children, especially those not involved in orga nized sports or activities. Children with T1D who participate in any type of exercise should test their blood glucose values before and after the exercise and potentially during the exercise as well, depending on whether the
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.8 Exercise

paragraphs.text: duration is more than an hour or so. It is also important to test blood glucose for the delayed effects of exercise, since hypoglycemia can occur up to 7–11 h later [75]. As many chil dren participate in late afternoon or evening activities, this delayed hypoglycemic response puts them at risk for nocturnal hypoglycemia.
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.8 Exercise

paragraphs.text: When working with children and their families, it is important to discuss the triad of exercise, food intake, and insulin. When exer cise is increased, one of the others must be adjusted in order to minimize the risk of hypoglycemia. For patients on injections of insulin, the dose of insulin can be adjusted when activities are planned; otherwise, addi tional snacks may need to be eaten. Both additional carbohydrates and reductions in insulin may be necessary if the activity is to last longer than an hour [76]. In patients who use insulin pump therapy, suspension of the basal infusion rate (or simply disconnecting the pump) during exercise can reduce rates of hypoglycemia [77]. Use of lower temporary basal rates during and after exercise can help to prevent hypoglycemia during the activity and later that day or night. Serious athletes may need to reload on carbohydrates follow ing intense and/or prolonged activity in addi tion to adjusting their insulin doses. Some patients find that raw corn starch can slow the digestion of sugar, providing a more sustained fast-acting carbohydrate effect in combatting exercise-induced hypoglycemia.
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.8 Exercise

paragraphs.text: Many studies closely looking at methods to combat the impact of exercise on glycemic control have shown that there is an almost infinite number of factors that need to be con sidered when designing the diabetes manage ment plan. Thus, trial and error are still a key component in the management of exercise and glucose levels in children with diabetes.
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.8 Exercise

paragraphs.text: The T1D Exchange Registry has shown that DKA remains a serious threat to youth with T1D, especially those in poor metabolic con trol [46]. It is imperative that parents of chil dren with T1D who develop acute symptoms of nausea, abdominal discomfort, and vomit
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.9 Sick Day Management

paragraphs.text: ing remember that they need to closely moni tor their child for elevations in blood glucose and blood or urine ketone levels that signal the development of ketosis or DKA, with or without the presence of another acute illness like a viral infection. Not recognizing the threat of DKA until dehydration and acidosis occur can result in a hospital admission in the pediatric intensive care unit.
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.9 Sick Day Management

paragraphs.text: On sick days, blood glucose levels should be checked every 2 h, and urine or blood tested for increases in ketone levels frequently. It should be stressed to all families from the outset that insulin should never be held; adjustments in the doses are necessary during intercurrent illness, but a complete cessation of all insulin replacement will quickly lead to diabetic ketoacidosis.
paragraphs.heading: 30.3.9 Sick Day Management

paragraphs.text: It is important to maintain adequate fluid intake during serious illness in order to pre vent dehydration and to improve excretion of ketones, if present. Families should keep on hand at all times a variety of different fluids including regular soda, juice, sports drinks, sugar-free drinks, clear soups, popsicles, and gelatin as well as water. In the child tolerating oral rehydration, a fluid “dose” of 1 ounce per year of age per hour serves as a rough guide line; the sugar content of which depends on the serum glucose. For blood glucose values >180–200 mg/dL, sugar-free fluids should be given, and for blood sugar <180 mg/dL, sugar-containing fluids should be used.

Insulin doses will likely need to be adjusted depending on blood glucose levels, ketone lev els, and the presence of emesis impairing nor mal oral intake. In the presence of emesis or significant alteration to appetite, it is recom mended that families reduce the dose of inter mediate- or long-acting insulin by 20–50% [78] and may also need to temporarily discon tinue it and instead give small doses of rapidacting insulin every 2–3 h. Small doses of glucagon can be used to treat mild-tomoderate hypoglycemia in the setting of nau sea or vomiting, when the child is unable to ingest fast-acting carbohydrates. Once the ketones have cleared and the child is tolerat ing an oral diet, the family may resume the normal routine. If vomiting is persistent and
ketones remain moderate or large after several supplemental insulin doses, arrangements should be made for hydration and evaluation in the emergency department.

In pump-treated patients, it is critically important that infusion site problems leading to interruption of insulin delivery and ketosis be differentiated from an intercurrent gastro enteritis or other acute infection. Any eleva tion of glucose and ketone levels is an indication for changing the infusion site, whereas, with hyperglycemia alone, the effec tiveness of a correction bolus in lowering blood glucose levels can be checked before changing the infusion site. For those patients on automated insulin delivery (AID) systems, an additional step to consider is to take the pump out of auto mode and start a tempo rary increased basal rate to allow for a more aggressive approach to clear ketones.

Diabetes is an insidious condition; it requires patients and their families to be “on” 24 h a day, 7 days a week. Consequently, it can have a pro found negative impact on lifestyle and interper sonal relationships. All of the burdens of diabetes and its care are superimposed on the already challenging transitions through child hood, adolescence, and into early adulthood.
paragraphs.heading: Considerations

paragraphs.text: Successful adaptation to diabetes was tra ditionally measured by the degree to which patients achieved and maintained blood glu cose and HbA1c as close to target as possible. Increasingly, however, optimizing quality of life has become another important measure of successful adaptation [79]. It is important to remember that in pediatrics, successful man agement of a chronic illness not only involves the child with the illness but the family as well. Factors such as socioeconomic status, family structure and coping styles, the presence of maternal depression, and age can all impact a family’s ability to cope with diabetes and to achieve successful outcomes [79]. In fact, increased psychological stress is directly cor related with reduced self-efficacy regarding
paragraphs.heading: Considerations

paragraphs.text: diabetes management and with poor glucose control [80]. Professionals with expertise in the psychosocial challenges of diabetes care, such as psychologists and social workers, are essen tial members of the multidisciplinary diabetes care team. Regular interaction with these pro fessionals should be encouraged on at least an annual basis, and more formal assessment should be provided for those patients and their families who exhibit psychosocial risk factors and/or have been unable to achieve diabetes care goals. Additionally, it is important to involve these professionals from the time of diagnosis as the actual diagnosis itself causes significant psychological distress in both the child who is diagnosed and the parents and family system [81].
paragraphs.heading: Considerations

paragraphs.text: Depression is the most common psycho logical disorder in children and adolescents with diabetes. Research has shown that symp toms can wax and wane throughout the course of time with diabetes, being higher in the first few years then settling only to rise again after 10 years [82]. The SEARCH for Diabetes in Youth study found that rates of mild depres sion were 14% in youth with diabetes, and 8.6% of study participants exhibited moder ate or severe symptoms [83]. Comprehensive diabetes management should include evalua tion for signs of depression both informally during routine clinic visits and more formally with a standardized screening tool. Managing problems of depression will improve the qual ity of life and can also have an impact on gly cemic control, whereas untreated depression and poor glycemic control can create a vicious cycle of one negatively reinforcing the other.
paragraphs.heading: Considerations

paragraphs.text: Research indicates that disordered eating is more common in adolescent girls and young adult women with T1D [84], in association with poor glycemic control [85]. In addition, with holding insulin is a way of purging excess calo ries that is unique to people with diabetes, hence the name diabulimia. This chronic state of hyperglycemia can lead to dehydration and loss of both body fat and lean muscle mass. It is reported that more than 30% of women with T1D report using insulin restriction for weight control [86]. Patients who chronically use this method of purging are at risk for both the acute complication of diabetic ketoacidosis and more
paragraphs.heading: Considerations

paragraphs.text: chronic complications associated with longstanding poor glycemic control. The first step in the treatment of this condition is to identify it. Warning signs can include persistently poor glycemic control, especially in combination with extreme focus on body shape and weight, strict and/or low-calorie meal plans, strict exer cise regimens, and potentially repeated prob lems with ketonuria and/or ketoacidosis [84]. Treatment is complex and should involve a multidisciplinary team. Initially, glycemic goals should be aimed at promoting the safety of the individual as they begin to address the more complicated psychological issues, with a grad ual return to more intensive glycemic targets as the individual situation warrants.
paragraphs.heading: Considerations

paragraphs.text: Diabetes distress, in the setting of diabetes technologies, is another important psychoso cial factor to consider. Continuous glucose monitors (CGMs) and insulin pumps have improved dramatically over the last two decades, providing individuals with T1D many different options for self-care. Not sur prisingly, some patients who use these devices may find them anxiety provoking and the vol ume of information can be overwhelming. Without a clear sense of how to use the data to guide treatment, the anxiety produced by CGM data can outweigh the benefits of this information. On the other hand, use of CGMs by children with T1D may be associated with a reduction in parental anxiety by both detect ing and alerting the child and parents to low blood glucose numbers, particularly over night, and decreasing the frequency of severe lows and lows at night when used in conjunc tion with a newer insulin pump which shuts off insulin delivery at such times. Insulin pumps, which have been around for nearly 40 years, have more commonly been used than CGMs. The reasons cited for not using pumps include costs, hassles of the device, pain or discomfort with infusion site insertions, lack of trust in the technology, and a sense that the device leads the diabetes to “become visible.” Nevertheless, for many patients and parents, the benefits of insulin pumps far exceed the burdens of using an insulin pump.
paragraphs.heading: Considerations

paragraphs.text: Strategies to address the psychosocial implications of diabetes include familyfocused interventions, behavioral contracting,
paragraphs.heading: Considerations

paragraphs.text: stress management/coping skills, and motiva tional interviewing [81]. These strategies can be utilized in one-on-one situations, peer groups, or with family systems. It cannot be stressed enough that providers with expertise in the psychosocial domain should be a part of every comprehensive diabetes team.
paragraphs.heading: Considerations

paragraphs.text: When treating a child with T1D, care should also include screening for several other auto immune disorders. Autoimmune thyroiditis is the most common comorbid condition associ ated with T1D. According to the International Society for Pediatric and Adolescent Diabetes, up to 29% of children with diabetes will exhibit antithyroid antibodies [87]. It is rec ommended that providers consider obtaining both the antithyroid peroxidase and antithyroglobulin antibodies at the time of diag nosis with type 1 diabetes [88]. Current recommendations for evaluation in all chil dren with T1D include measurement of thyroid-stimulating hormone levels every 1–2 years or whenever there is a change in a child’s growth and development, an unex plained increase in hypoglycemia or signs and symptoms of thyroid disease [88].
paragraphs.heading: Conditions

paragraphs.text: According to various sources, celiac dis ease is found in about 1–15% of children with T1D. Although children may present with classic gastrointestinal symptoms and poor growth [87], most youngsters do not have any symptoms. For some children with T1D, the only signs of celiac disease may be an increase in the frequency of hypoglycemia as well as a persistent reduction in insulin needs in the months leading up to the diagnosis [87]. Current guidelines recommend screening for celiac shortly after diagnosis with either deamidated gliadin antibodies or tissue trans glutaminase antibodies [88]. A total IgA should be a part of the assessment in children, as low circulating levels of IgA will give falsenegative screening results. In this case, tissue transglutaminase IgG or deamidated gliadin IgG should be measured. Children with a pos

itive screening test for celiac should be referred to a pediatric gastroenterologist, ideally one with expertise in the management of celiac disease, for a confirmatory small bowel biopsy. Once a diagnosis is made, the child must be placed on a gluten-free diet of lifelong dura tion. Gluten-free foods and resources have become more plentiful in recent years, and children and their families can benefit from nutrition counseling from a health-care pro fessional that is well versed in today’s options.

T1D patients are also at risk for Addison’s disease, but this is uncommon enough that we do not routinely screen for it. However, when diabetes and thyroid disease coexist, the pos sibility of adrenal insufficiency should be con sidered. This may be heralded by decreasing insulin requirements, increasing pigmentation of the skin and buccal mucosa, salt craving, weakness, and postural hypotension. Rarely, frank Addisonian crisis is the first evidence of adrenal failure. This syndrome generally occurs in the second decade of life or later. The astute clinician should also consider that frequent, unexplained hypoglycemia or a reduction in insulin requirements in the absence of exercise or activity may be a subtle indicator of hypothyroidism, adrenal insuffi ciency, or celiac disease.

Screening for complications and comorbidi ties should be incorporated into diabetes care on an annual basis. The American Diabetes Association provides recommendations for screening pediatric patients for hypertension, dyslipidemia, retinopathy, and nephropathy [88].
paragraphs.heading: 30.4 Screening for Complications

paragraphs.text: Currently, hypertension is defined as three consecutive blood pressures higher than the 95th percentile based on age, gender, and height, and high-normal blood pressure is defined at a blood pressure above the 90th percentile for age, gender, and height. Treatment options include dietary changes to eliminate salt, regular and sustained physical activity, and ultimately, if warranted, initia tion of pharmacological interventions, with
paragraphs.heading: 30.4 Screening for Complications

paragraphs.text: angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibi tors being the first-line agent. When using an ACE inhibitor, it is important to remember to provide preconception counseling as this class of medication is considered a teratogen.
paragraphs.heading: 30.4 Screening for Complications

paragraphs.text: Children with T1D should be evaluated for a familial history of early cardiovascular disease (cardiac event at <55 years old). Children with a positive history should have a fasting lipid panel completed shortly after diagnosis, once glucose levels have normal ized. For those children without a family his tory of early cardiovascular disease, cholesterol screening should begin at puberty or age 10, whichever comes first. Lifestyle changes and maintaining/achieving optimal glucose control are the first-line therapies for dyslipidemia. Specifically, it is recommended that the Step 2 American Heart Association diet be followed for lipid management as this diet has been shown to allow for normal growth and development in children as young as 7 months of age [88]. If after these treat ments there is still evidence of dyslipidemia, pharmacological treatment with a statin in children older than 10 years should be strongly considered. For the younger age group, it is acceptable to consider referral to a pediatric lipid disorder specialist for further treatment. It should be noted that a recent report from the T1D Exchange Clinic Registry suggests that hypertension and dyslipidemia are often underdiagnosed and undertreated in youth with T1D [89].
paragraphs.heading: 30.4 Screening for Complications

paragraphs.text: In general, retinopathy is not seen in pre pubertal children and in those who have had diabetes for less than 5–10 years. Consequently, current guidelines recommend that retinopa thy screening with an eye care professional with diabetes experience does not need to begin until the child is at least 10 years old and has had diabetes for more than 3–5 years. Annual follow-up is recommended after this, unless the eye care professional feels that less frequent exams (every 2 years) are acceptable. Eye exams should encompass both an exam through dilated pupils and retinal photogra phy [90]. It should be noted that the frequency of screening eye exams in youth with T1D is controversial, since improvements in meta bolic control during the intensive treatment
paragraphs.heading: 30.4 Screening for Complications

paragraphs.text: era have made identification of treatable reti nal lesions very uncommon in pediatric patients [91].
paragraphs.heading: 30.4 Screening for Complications

paragraphs.text: Screening for renal disease is an essential component of comorbidity management. In fact, the Pittsburgh Epidemiology of Diabetes Complications study showed that in the absence of renal disease, people with T1D had similar mortality risk to that of the general population [92]. Evaluation for microalbu minuria, a potential early indication of nephropathic changes, does not need to begin until a child has had T1D for at least 5 years.
