paragraphs.text: There are multiple classifications of hyper triglyceridemia based on etiology and risk of pancreatitis [3, 8]. The Endocrine Society clas sifies hypertriglyceridemia into mild (150–199 mg/dl), moderate (200–999 mg/dl), severe (1000–1999 mg/dl), and very severe (≥2000 mg/dl) forms. The American Academy of Pediatrics suggests criteria based on age, with hypertriglyceridemia defined as TG levels >100 mg/dl in children under 10 years of age and >130 mg/dl in children 10–18 years of age.
paragraphs.heading: and Background

paragraphs.text: The most severe cause of primary hypertri glyceridemia is familial chylomicronemia (also known as hyperlipoproteinemia type 1 by the Frederickson classification), which is a deficiency of LPL, the enzyme that catalyzes the hydrolysis of TG. The disease is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern with 100% penetrance. The gene for LPL is located on chromosome 8p22, and to date, over 163 mutations have been identified, 90% of which are loss of function mutations. The disease is rare, with an occurrence of one in
paragraphs.heading: 32.4.2.1 Primary Causes

paragraphs.text: 500,000–1,000,000 for homozygous LPL defi ciency, which is associated with severe hyper triglyceridemia (typically TG > 5000 mg/dl). Heterozygous forms have wide variability in TG levels and are more prevalent, likely occur ring in one of every 500 individuals [9].

LPL binds glycosylphosphatidylinositolanchored high-density lipoprotein-binding protein 1 (GPIHBP1), which serves as a plat form for lipolysis. The gene for GPIHBP1 is located on chromosome 8q24.3, and defi ciency is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. Homozygous mutations in GPIHBP1 lead to TG levels similar to those found in LPL deficiency (>1000 mg/dl), while heterozy gous mutations have not been shown to cause abnormalities in TG levels [10].

Apolipoprotein C-II is a component of CM, VLDL, LDL, and HDL and is required for the activation of LPL. A deficiency in ApoC-II leads to hypertriglyceridemia due to elevated CM and VLDL, as well as decreased LDL and HDL [11]. The gene for ApoC-II is located on chromosome 19q13.32. Deficiency is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern; heterozygotes have normal TG levels despite low levels of ApoC-II. Interestingly, elevated concentrations of ApoC-II also hinder LPL activity and result in hypertriglyceridemia [11].

ApoA-V, via interaction with GPIHBP1 and LPL, stimulates the LPL activity [12]. A deficiency in ApoA-V caused by genetic mutations in the Apo A5 gene located on chromosome 11q23 leads to hypertriglyceri demia.

Type III hyperlipoproteinemia or dysbet alipoproteinemia, also known as CM remnant disease, is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by a mutation in the Apo E gene, located on chromosome 19q13.32, lead ing to impaired uptake of Apo E-containing lipoproteins (CM remnant, VLDL/IDL rem nants) by the liver. ApoE is expressed in three isoforms (ApoE2, ApoE3, and ApoE4), which have variable binding affinity to the remnant receptor and the LDL receptor. Some of these isoforms, in the presence of another genetic defect or cause of altered lipid metabolism, lead to reduced clearance of remnants [3] and hypertriglyceridemia, hypercholesterolemia,
and low HDL. These patients are at high risk for pancreatitis and possible early CVD.

Mutations in lipase maturation factor 1 (LMF1), which is required for transport and activation of LPL, cause hypertriglyceridemia [3]. The gene encoding LMF1 is on chromo some 16p13.3, and deficiencies are inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.

A more common etiology of hypertriglyc eridemia is familial hypertriglyceridemia, with a prevalence of 5–10%. It has an autosomal dominant pattern and is thought to be poly genic in origin, with some cases displaying heterozygous mutations in LPL or overpro duction of VLDL [6]. TG tend to be moder ately elevated, and a positive family history of hypertriglyceridemia and/or pancreatitis tends to be present.

The most common secondary cause of mildmoderate (200–500 mg/dl) hypertriglyceride mia is obesity-associated insulin resistance. The prevalence of obesity in the pediatric population has increased parallel to the increase in obesity rates in adults. The most recent data from the CDC (2017) indicate that the prevalence of obesity is 19.7% in children aged 2–19 years. The COVID 19 pandemic led to dramatic changes in lifestyle habits for most people, with decreased physical activity and increased consumption of nutrient poor, calo rie dense foods. This led to a spike in child hood obesity rates and its related comorbidities.
paragraphs.heading: Hypertriglyceridemia

paragraphs.text: Higher consumption of simple sugars and starches along with foods high in saturated fat raise TG levels. The consumption of excessive amounts of sucrose and fructose has been linked to elevated triglycerides as fructose metabolism bypasses a key rate-determining step in glycolysis and produces glycerol-3phosphate, which is the backbone of triacylg lycerol [13]. Insulin is a powerful regulator of LPL activity. Therefore, in insulin resistance associated with obesity, decreased stimulation of LPL can lead to elevated TG.
paragraphs.heading: Hypertriglyceridemia

paragraphs.text: In cases of insulin deficiency, as in uncon trolled type 1 diabetes or a combination of insulin deficiency and resistance, as in type 2
paragraphs.heading: Hypertriglyceridemia

paragraphs.text: diabetes, an increase in TG can be seen as well [3]. Thyroid hormone has been shown to increase LPL activity via upregulation of ApoA-V activity [14]; thus, hypothyroidism is associated with elevated TG.
paragraphs.heading: Hypertriglyceridemia

paragraphs.text: Hypertriglyceridemia is the most common dyslipidemia in patients with chronic kidney disease, thought to be secondary to defective clearance of TG from the circulation in addi tion to a decrease in LPL activity, although the reason for the latter is not understood.
paragraphs.heading: Hypertriglyceridemia

paragraphs.text: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease is heralded by the accumulation of TG in hepatocytes. This is associated with obesity-related insulin resistance, and the mechanism is similar to that observed in states of type 2 diabetes, met abolic syndrome, and obesity [15]. Alcohol consumption has been found to decrease LPL activity and induce TG accumulation through increased fatty acid synthesis and decreased oxidation in the liver, resulting in alcoholic fatty liver disease [16].
paragraphs.heading: Hypertriglyceridemia

paragraphs.text: Lipodystrophy syndromes are common causes of hypertriglyceridemia, with over 70% of people with congenital lipodystrophy exhibiting elevated TG [3]. Lipodystrophy syndromes are a wide spectrum of congenital and acquired disorders that are characterized by a complete or partial lack of adipose tis sue. The most common form of lipodystrophy is seen in HIV patients and is caused by anti retroviral therapy. The mechanism of hyper triglyceridemia is thought to be a decrease in adipose tissue, leading to increased VLDL synthesis and decreased clearance.
paragraphs.heading: Hypertriglyceridemia

paragraphs.text: Symptoms and signs of LPL deficiency tend to occur in infancy or early childhood, while those of ApoC-II deficiency tend to occur in adolescence or adulthood [17]. Other genetic causes of hypertriglyceridemia, such as famil ial hypertriglyceridemia, manifest themselves in youth, while secondary causes can arise at any age, depending on the underlying disease.
paragraphs.heading: 32.4.3 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: diameter that appear diffusely on extensor surfaces of the limbs, buttocks, and shoulders ( Fig. 32.2). These are generally present when triglyceride levels are >2000 mg/dl. Xanthomas occur secondary to phagocytosis of CM by macrophages. They are generally single lesions and are not painful [17]. Lipemia retinalis is the milky appearance of retinal vessels observed generally at TG > 3000 mg/dl ( Fig. 32.3) [8, 9]. This is reversible and
paragraphs.heading: 32.4.3 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: tends not to impact vision. Hepatomegaly and splenomegaly can occur due to infiltra tion of macrophage foam cells. Infants may present with poor feeding and GI bleeding, in addition to eruptive xanthomas.

The most serious clinical consequence of severe hypertriglyceridemia is pancreatitis, the risk of which increases with TG > 1000 mg/dl. Of note, marked increases in TG can impair accurate measurement of amylase, hemoglo bin, and electrolyte levels, so one must not rule out pancreatitis in the setting of abdomi nal pain and high TG when lipase and amy lase levels are low [9]. The reason for the development of pancreatitis is still unclear but is thought to be in part due to TG hydrolysis within the pancreas, leading to toxic accumu lation of free fatty acids, as well as CMinduced ischemia [3].
paragraphs.heading: Complications

paragraphs.text: CVD is also a concerning outcome of hypertriglyceridemia [18]. Excess TG block the endothelium-dependent relaxation factor through inhibition of nitric oxide and larginine synthesis and promote endothelin 1 secretion, a vasoconstrictor [19].
paragraphs.heading: Complications

paragraphs.text: The presence of lipemic plasma should prompt one to order fasting lipids, including a TG and ApoB level. When presented with a case of hypertriglyceridemia, confirmation with a fasting level is imperative. A careful his tory of medical problems, medication use, and family history are important to diagnose both primary and secondary causes of hypertri glyceridemia. Thyroid function tests, fasting glucose, hemoglobin A1C, and liver function tests are useful to rule out common secondary causes.
paragraphs.heading: 32.4.5 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Diagnosis of genetic causes of hypertri glyceridemia can be made via analysis for LPL and/or GHIBP1 mutations as well as mutations in ApoE and ApoC-II. Lab results suggesting LPL deficiency include
paragraphs.heading: 32.4.5 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: TG > 1000 mg/dl, elevated VLDL with TC that is 1/10th of the triglyceride levels, and a low HDL. While LDL levels tend to be within normal limits or even low, they cannot be cal culated using the Friedewald equation if TG ≥ 400 mg/dl, as the assumptions about VLDL are no longer valid. Direct measure ment by ultracentrifugation or LDL immuno precipitation can be performed. Assays that measure LPL activity, through treatment of plasma with heparin, can also assist in the diagnosis of LPL deficiency, but [17] these assays are no longer commonly performed. The level of ApoB-100 can help distinguish the hypertriglyceridemia-only variant of familial combined hyperlipidemia (elevated ApoB-100) and some cases of familial hyper triglyceridemia from LPL deficiency (normal ApoB-100). Labs suggestive of ApoC-II defi ciency include markedly elevated TG in addi tion to low levels of LDL and HDL. Dysbetalipoproteinemia typically has elevated levels of TG and often LDL due to impaired remnant binding and interference with LDL binding to its receptor. Familial hypertriglyc eridemia tends to exhibit moderate elevations in TG with elevated VLDL.
paragraphs.heading: 32.4.5 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Restriction of long-chain fatty acids from the diet (e.g., breast milk and regular formu las) and substituting medium-chain triglycer ide formula for infants with primary hypertriglyceridemia such as LPL deficiency is very effective, as medium-chain fats enter the circulation without being incorporated into CM [9]. This has been used successfully in cases of both LPL [21] and GPIHBP1 defi ciencies [22].
paragraphs.heading: TG

paragraphs.text: Pharmacologic therapy is added when TG cannot be reduced as much as necessary through dietary restriction to keep pancreati tis risk low (levels <1000 mg/dl). Fibrates such as fenofibrate or gemfibrozil work via stimula tion of PPARα in the liver, which leads to a reduction in VLDL secretion. In addition, through stimulation of LPL gene expression and inhibition of Apo C-III gene expression, fibrates increase TG lipolysis [8]. Fibrates
paragraphs.heading: TG

paragraphs.text: have been shown to reduce TG levels by 30–50% in adults [6]. They are generally well tolerated without major side effects; however, minor side effects such as GI discomfort have been reported. In rare cases, severe side effects such as liver dysfunction and myopathy may occur [7]. There are limited studies on the use of fibrates in children [20].
paragraphs.heading: TG

paragraphs.text: High doses of statins such as atorvastatin or rosuvastatin as a second-line therapy have been shown to improve TG in adults when lev els are <500 mg/dl [6, 8]. The VOYAGER study assessed the impact of statins on TG levels in adults and found that rosuvastatin led to a greater reduction in TG than simvas tatin and low-dose atorvastatin [23]. At higher but equal doses, the reduction was similar between rosuvastatin and atorvastatin but still greater than with simvastatin. Reductions amounted to 15–31%. Statins have not been found to be effective for primary hypertriglyc eridemia secondary to LPL deficiency and are, therefore, not recommended [17].
paragraphs.heading: TG

paragraphs.text: Niacin has been shown to reduce plasma TG levels in adults by 30–45% via inhibition of hepatic TG synthesis. Doses to achieve this result approach 3 g daily and are associated with adverse effects such as flushing, gastroin testinal discomfort, pruritus, or lightheaded ness [6, 8], so they are not used in children.

Orlistat has been used in some pediatric cases of hypertriglyceridemia in conjunction with a low-fat diet with some success [22, 24]. Orlistat is a pancreatic lipase inhibitor that reduces intestinal dietary fat absorption. Side effects of the medication include steatorrhea, fecal incontinence, flatulence, and abdominal pain. While side effects are not severe, they can interfere with patient compliance.

Omega-3 fatty acids have been shown to reduce TG by up to 45% at doses of up to 4 g daily in adult studies by inhibiting hepatic TG and VLDL synthesis [20]. Studies in children and adolescents with hypertriglyceridemia found that doses of 500–1000 mg of omega-3 fatty acids led to a clinically but not statisti cally significant decrease in TG levels when combined with dietary modification [18, 25, 26], suggesting that higher doses of omega-3 fatty acids may be needed in children. The mechanism by which omega-3 fatty acids

leads to an improvement in TG levels is still unclear but may involve impairment of its synthesis through enzyme inhibition and/or a decrease in substrate availability by increasing fatty acid oxidation in the liver [20, 27, 28]. Side effects of omega-3 fatty acids include diarrhea, nausea, eructation, and abdominal pain. Omega-3 fatty acids are ineffective in the treatment of LPL deficiency and are not rec ommended, although cases have been reported of successful treatment, one of which was in an 8-year-old female [29]. Caution should be used when treating patients with hypercholes terolemia and hypertriglyceridemia, as omega-3 fatty acids have been shown to increase LDL levels [20, 28]. If omega 3 fatty acids are offered, prescription products should be used instead of over-the-counter ones, as the latter are not as rigorously regulated and the amount of omega 3 fatty acids in the product will not be consistent [30]. In cases of hypertriglyceridemia-induced pancreatitis, fasting in addition to insulin and dextrose via continuous IV infusion can reduce TG within 48 h. During episodes of hypertriglyceridemiainduced pancreatitis and in those with homo zygous forms of LPL deficiency only, plasmapheresis has been used with success, although TG levels quickly rise without more long-term therapy [28]. A study assessing plasmapheresis versus medical apheresis with insulin in children with LPL deficiencyinduced pancreatitis found no difference in resolution of hypertriglyceridemia, but noted lower rate of adverse effects and decreased cost in the medical apheresis group [31].

LPL gene therapy has been studied in phase I and II clinical trials, where it led to increased LPL activity and decreased TG lev els with no treatment-related adverse events [32]. This treatment is currently being studied in those with homozygous LPL deficiency.

Volanesorsen is an antisense APO C1 mRNA inhibitor, which leads to increased TG clearance and a reduced TG through LDLindependent pathways [33]. Studies showed up to a 80% reduction in TG levels. Unfortunately, due to concerns of thrombo cytopenia, the FDA has denied approval of the medication in the USA. However, it is conditionally approved in Europe [34]. ApoC-

III inhibition by an antisense inhibitor ISI304801 was shown to reduce TG levels in patients with mild to severe hypertriglyceride mia by up to 80% in phase 2 trials [35]. The medication is currently undergoing phase 3 studies in adults.

An angiopoietin 3 synthesis inhibitor led to a 36–56% reduction in TG levels in phase 2 adult studies. Evinacumab is an Angiopoietin L3 blocking monoclonal antibody that reduces LDL and TG levels. It has been approved to treat homozygous FH in children over 12 years old but has not been approved to treat hypertriglyceridemia in youth or adults. Lomitapide is an inhibitor of micro somal transfer protein, which is required for assembly and secretion of CM and VLDL. It is being studied in youth with homozygous FH and has been shown to reduce TG levels in these patients.

If secondary causes of hypertriglyceride mia are present, treatment of the underlying cause generally improves TG levels. Good dia betes management with proper insulin admin istration can improve TG in patients with type 1 diabetes, while weight loss and medical man agement to improve insulin sensitivity are effective in type 2 diabetes. Replacement with levothyroxine restores normal metabolism and reverses hyperlipidemia in cases of hypo thyroidism.

Hypercholesterolemia is a heterogeneous group of lipid disorders that are characterized by abnormalities in LDL and, in some cases, HDL and TG. Polygenic hypercholesterol emia is the most common etiology of geneti cally inherited hyperlipidemia; however, actual estimates of prevalence are difficult to ascertain given the wide range of mutations and severity of lipid abnormalities that are included in the diagnosis. Heterozygous FH is
paragraphs.heading: and Background

paragraphs.text: one of the most common types of genetic dys lipidemias with gene frequency estimated at 1 in 250 in the general population [36]. Heterozygous FH is inherited in an autoso mal dominant pattern. Certain populations, including Afrikaners, French Canadians, Lebanese, and Finns, have been shown to have an increased risk for FH [37]. In contrast to heterozygous FH, homozygous FH is extremely rare, with estimates of 1:1,000,000 in the general population [38]. It is inherited in an autosomal codominant pattern. Familial combined hyperlipidemia (FCHL) is a hetero geneous group of lipid abnormalities that has been linked to multiple loci including 1q21–23, a gene which encodes for a transcription fac tor critical in lipid and glucose metabolism, USF1 [39, 40]. While sometimes difficult to distinguish FCHL from metabolic syndrome, epidemiological data estimate a prevalence of 0.5–2% in the adult population with a higher prevalence in families with a history of pre mature CVD [39]. Familial defective ApoB- 100, an autosomal dominant condition, is due to a missense mutation in the LDL receptorbinding domain of ApoB-100. This results in elevated serum LDL due to reduced hepatic LDL removal and catabolism [41]. The preva lence of familial defective ApoB-100 is esti mated at one in 500 individuals [41].
paragraphs.heading: and Background

paragraphs.text: FH is a primary dyslipidemia caused by genetic anomalies that affect the LDL recep tor (LDL-R) pathway. It is typically charac terized by mutations in the LDL-R gene (LDLR), that are estimated to account for >80% of heterozygous FH. Over 1500 muta tions in LDLR have been described [42]. LDL-R are responsible for binding LDL through ApoB-100, leading to endocytosis of the LDL particle. Mutations in LDLR can
paragraphs.heading: Hypercholesterolemia

paragraphs.text: decrease the production of LDL-R, affect the expression of LDL-R on cell surfaces or the ability of the receptor to bind LDL, and acti vate endocytosis. PCSK9, the gene encoded on chromosome 1, aids in the degradation of the LDL-R [41]. A gain of function mutation in PCSK9 reduces LDL-R recycling to the cell membrane, causing an increase in LDL levels, which phenotypically is similar to mutations in LDLR. Mutations in ApoB-100 gene (APOB), as seen in familial defective ApoB- 100, impair the binding of LDL to the LDL- R, resulting in elevation of serum LDL levels.
paragraphs.heading: Hypercholesterolemia

paragraphs.text: In homozygous FH, the severity of the lipid abnormality is related to the genetic mutation involved. Most commonly, muta tions of two different alleles for the gene cod ing the LDL-R are involved; however, occasionally familial homozygotes can have two mutations of the same allele (a true homozygote). The type of mutation dictates the degree of LDL elevation; typically in homozygous FH, the LDL elevation is >300 mg/dl (often 450–850 mg/dl) and HDL is low.
The proposed mechanism of polygenic hypercholesterolemia is that multiple minor mutations or polymorphisms in the genes encoding LDL-R, ApoB, and/or PCSK9

cumulatively result in abnormalities of lipid metabolism [43]. Typically, the mutations result in mild to moderate cholesterol abnor malities (LDL 130–160 mg/dl) without frank early CVD compared to more moderate to severe LDL elevations (180–300 mg/dl) in het erozygous FH.

FCHL is thought to be due to a number of gene mutations (oligogenic) that result in a variety of abnormalities in TG, LDL, and HDL levels, sometimes within the same fam ily [44]. Type IIa is characterized by isolated LDL elevation, whereas elevated VLDL and TG with low HDL is described in type IV. Type IIB is characterized by an elevated TG, VLDL, and LDL with low HDL. Unlike FH, FCHL may not be associated with an elevation in LDL until adulthood, so it can be missed during pediatric screening. FCHL has been shown to be associated with increased levels of ApoB as a result of overproduction of VLDL. Therefore, measuring ApoB levels may be a better screening test in pediatric patients with a family history of early CVD and moderate hypertriglyceridemia with or without elevated LDL.

Perhaps, the least well-understood risk factor for CVD is lipoprotein (a) (Lp(a)). Lp(a) is an atherogenic and heterogeneous lipoprotein that is linked to CVD and stroke. Lp(a) excess is inherited as an autosomal codominant trait and is expressed in children. Lp(a) particles are modified, newly synthe sized LDL with an extra lipoprotein named ApoA covalently linked to ApoB-100. ApoA has significant homology to plasminogen, so this likely explains the thrombosis risk associ ated with elevated Lp(a) levels. Lp(a) has been shown to be expressed in children who are greater than 13 months old at levels equiva lent to those found in their parents [45]. Furthermore, pediatric studies have shown that elevation in Lp(a) in pediatric patients correlates with increased rates of CVE in their parents [46]. Furthermore, a study in children revealed elevated LP(a) levels was associated with increased thromboembolism risk [47, 48]. While routine screening of Lp(a) is not recommended at this time by current consen sus guidelines, Lp(a) levels may add addi
tional information in assessing risk for patients for future CVE with levels generally over 30 mg/dl being associated with increased risk for CVE.

Secondary hypercholesterolemia needs to be ruled out, so that potential causes can be appropriately treated. Multiple etiologies exist, including medication side effects, renal disease, endocrine and metabolic issues, inflammatory processes, or hepatic dysfunc tion. Medications such as cyclosporines have been shown to increase LDL and lipoproteins; retinoids have been shown to increase the LDL to HDL ratio; and short-term use of thiazide diuretics has been shown to increase LDL and TG, although these findings have not been substantiated by long-term studies. Antiretroviral regimens, especially protease inhibitors, have also been associated with abnormalities in lipid and glucose metabo lism, often as part of a lipodystrophy syn drome. Renal diseases can result in lipid abnormalities, with nephrotic syndrome typi cally being the most profound. It is postulated that elevations in TC and, more specifically, LDL, occur as a compensatory response to low oncotic pressure in patients with nephrotic syndrome [41]. Chronic kidney disease can also result in elevated TC and LDL; however, this is less common than in nephrotic syn drome. Untreated or inadequately treated hypothyroidism can result in elevations in LDL and/or TG; therefore, thyroid function tests should routinely be performed in patients with clinically significant hyperlipidemia.
paragraphs.heading: Hypercholesterolemia

paragraphs.text: The effects of the genetic mutations in hetero zygous FH are completely expressed in infancy, as demonstrated by Kwiterovich et al. who showed elevated LDL levels in cord blood samples of infants that remained elevated on follow-up assessment unless dietary modifica tion occurred [49]. Subclinical early athero sclerotic lesions have been demonstrated in
paragraphs.heading: 32.5.3 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: children by the age of 5 years. Endothelial function is impaired, as has been shown by decreased dilatation of the brachial artery in children with hyperlipidemia after intense postischemic flow of arterial blood [50]. In addition, children with hyperlipidemia due to FH may have increased carotid intima-media thickness [37]. Physical exam is typically nor mal in children except in homozygous FH, in which physical exam may reveal xanthomas, which are cholesterol deposits found in ten dons—most commonly in the Achilles tendon or finger extensor tendons. Xanthelasmas, cholesterol deposits found around the eyes, and corneal arcus, a white ring around the cornea due to lipid deposition, are classic find ings in severe heterozygous FH and homozy gous FH associated with LDL levels >300 mg/ dl. Homozygous FH is also often associated with supravalvar aortic stenosis with estimates of 41% of patients being affected [49].
paragraphs.heading: 32.5.3 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Given that most children are clinically asymp tomatic and most types of FH are inherited, family history is an essential component in screening, but relying on family history has failed to identify many children with FH. Screening questions should ascertain whether there is a family history of premature CVD (including myocardial infarction, percutane ous catheter interventional procedure, coro nary artery bypass grafting, or stroke in men <55 years old or women <65 years old) in par ents, siblings, uncles, aunts, and grandparents; elevated cholesterol in mother, father, and/or siblings; and/or known genetic or suspected inheritable hyperlipidemia. However, given that family history screening is inadequate, the 2011 guidelines recommend universal screening by measuring TC and HDL levels in order to identify those children with no known family history. Cholesterol screening should be considered as early as age 2 years in fami lies with early CVD associated with hypercho lesterolemia. LDL ≥ 190 mg/dl in patients under 20 years old confers an approximately 80% risk of FH [51].
paragraphs.heading: 32.5.4 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Lp(a) can be associated with abnormali ties in lipid profiles (specifically elevations in LDL); however, in some cases, the lipid profile may be normal. Therefore, in the patient with a family history of extensive premature CVE and a normal lipid profile, it is reasonable to measure the Lp(a) level, although no formal recommendations have been made for such screening. Multiple assays are available for screening for Lp(a) levels. It is important to understand the assay that is ordered as this can affect interpretation. Assays include mea surements of only the cholesterol carried by the Lp(a) protein (analogous to the LDL), Lp(a) protein mass, and Lp(a) particle mass, the latter of which is comprised of the pro tein, lipid, and carbohydrate components. Most commonly, Lp(a) particle mass is mea sured with abnormal levels being >30 mg/dl [45].
paragraphs.heading: 32.5.4 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Genetic testing in general is not needed for diagnostic or clinical management but may be useful if the diagnosis is uncertain. Negative testing of common mutations does not rule out FH, as approximately 20–40% of clini cally definite heterozygous FH have had nega tive genetic testing [52].
paragraphs.heading: 32.5.4 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Labs to rule out secondary causes of hypercholesterolemia include thyroid func tion tests, BUN, and creatinine. Mild eleva tions in LDL (130–150 mg/dl) are typically due to a diet very rich in fat and cholesterol or polygenic hypercholesterolemia.

Patients with heterozygous FH have an increased risk for CVE before the age of 50 years, with estimates of 25% of untreated women and 50% of untreated men having an event. Individuals with homozygous FH typi cally have CVE in the first two decades of life due to rapidly accelerated atherosclerosis. Estimates of mortality are higher in patients that have supravalvar aortic stenosis (SVAS) with an ~5-fold increase over a 4 year followup period (32.5% mortality rate of SVAS group vs. 7.0% in non-SVAS group in a study
paragraphs.heading: Complications

paragraphs.text: of 94 patients) [49]. FCHL is associated with type 2 diabetes and the development of meta bolic syndrome in adults [53], and there is a moderate risk for early CVD. FCHL, which may be more difficult to diagnose in child hood, has a significant risk for future CVE, with approximately 11.3% of acute myocar dial infarction survivors <60 years old meet ing diagnostic criteria for FCHL [43]. One study estimates that 40% of all myocardial infarct survivors are diagnosed with FCHL if no age limits are used [54]. Multiple pediatric studies have also shown an increased risk for acute ischemic strokes with elevations in Lp(a) [55].
paragraphs.heading: Complications

paragraphs.text: Nutritionist/dietitian consultation is neces sary in initiation and maintenance of a dietary plan to successfully treat familial hyperlipid emia. The Cardiovascular Health Integrated Lifestyle Diet (CHILD)-1, which emphasizes restricting dietary fat and cholesterol, should be initial therapy. The CHILD-1 diet involves restriction of total fat to <30% of daily caloric intake, saturated fat to 8–10% of daily intake, and modest restriction of cholesterol intake to <300 mg per day. It also recommends the avoidance of trans fat. The CHILD-1 diet can be advanced to the CHILD-2 diet after 3–6 months. Goals of CHILD-2 are to restrict fat intake to 25–30% of daily caloric intake, saturated fat intake to ≤7% of daily intake, and monounsaturated fat to ~10% of total intake and to avoid all trans saturated fat. Total cholesterol intake should be kept to <200 mg/day [56]. This level of restriction will invariably decrease TC levels by up to 10%. Patients with moderate to severe hypercholes terolemia (LDL > 160 mg/dl) begin with the CHILD-2 diet because the cholesterol restric tion in CHILD-1 is minimal. Plant stanol or sterol esters can be considered for adjunctive therapy. Plant sterols work by inhibiting incorporation of cholesterol into the lipid micelles and by preventing intestinal resorp tion of cholesterol by blocking cholesterol receptors. Limited data about the efficacy of plant sterols as a spread have suggested a modest decrease in LDL by about 7.5% [6].
paragraphs.heading: CHILD-1 CHILD-2

paragraphs.text: 64 While data are limited for long-term side effects of statins in children, short-term side effects have been minimal. The major con cerning side effects of statins are hepatic dys function and myopathy. Given the lack of long-term data on the safety of statins in pedi atric patients, statins should be initiated at the lowest dose, and baseline liver function tests and muscle enzyme levels should be measured (AST, ALT, and CK) prior to initiation. During treatment, ALT, AST, and CK should be followed at least every 6 months to ensure no serious adverse effects are developing. Complaints of myalgia should be taken seri ously; serum CK should be measured, and the statin should be stopped until myositis is ruled out. Although rare, if severe myositis occurs, individuals can develop myoglobinuria and renal failure. Concerns have also been raised about effects on sexual development in pediat ric patients as steroid hormones are derived from cholesterol. Studies have shown both
paragraphs.heading: CHILD-1 CHILD-2

paragraphs.text: increases and decreases in dehydroepiandros terone sulfate in boys and girls; however, there has not been any association of abnormal sexual development in multiple studies [60, 61].
paragraphs.heading: CHILD-1 CHILD-2

paragraphs.text: Another class of medication that was fre quently used in children for elevated LDL is bile acid sequestrants. Bile acid sequestrants bind to intestinal bile and prevent its resorp tion, thereby interrupting enterohepatic recir culation. With less bile acid resorption, more cholesterol is converted into bile acids, thus decreasing the hepatic cholesterol pool. This causes an upregulation of LDL-R and thus decreased plasma LDL. Today, bile acid sequestrants are often used as adjunctive ther apy to statins if dietary restriction and statins do not result in target LDL. Bile acid seques trants typically have a more modest effect in decreasing plasma LDL (10–20%) [65]. Cholestyramine and colestipol are two agents not commonly used any more due to signifi cant gastrointestinal side effects [66]. Colesevelam is a newer bile acid sequestrant with fewer side effects and is approved for children aged 10 years and older. It is well tol erated and has been shown to decrease LDL levels by 10–15% [67]. It can be used as mono therapy or in combination with statins. Achieving goal LDL levels can be especially challenging in homozygous FH. Complete
restriction of cholesterol-containing foods and adjunctive therapy to statins with cole sevelam is necessary and even then may not result in achievement of goal levels of LDL.

Ezetimibe is another medication that his torically has been a second-line agent for ele vated cholesterol, in particular for elevated LDL. Ezetimibe inhibits cholesterol absorp tion by targeting the cholesterol transport protein Niemann-Pick C1 like 1 protein at the jejunal enterocyte brush border. Ezetimibe is an effective LDL lowering agent with esti mates of an additional decrease of 10–25% when used as an adjunct to statin and ~25–40% when used as monotherapy [68–70]. However, controversy of its efficacy in prevention of CVE arose after an adult study showed no dif ference in carotid intima-media thickness in patients with heterozygous FH who were treated with simvastatin plus ezetimibe when compared to simvastatin plus placebo despite a statistically significant decrease in the LDL (~25%) [68]. Data in the pediatric population regarding its efficacy and use as a primary or secondary agent are sparse, with relatively short-term follow-up. These studies have shown similar reductions in LDL to adult studies [69, 70]. Ezetimibe is generally a welltolerated medication, and no significant side effects have been reported in pediatric studies, although adult studies have noted occasional occurrence of musculoskeletal symptoms sim ilar to what can occur with use of statins. One study showed an increased risk for cancer; however, subsequent studies have not sup ported these findings [71].

Propotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) inhibitors are a new potent class of medication being used for cholesterol man agement typically in conjunction with statins. PCSK9 is an enzyme that recycles LDL-R on the surface of cells. By inhibition of PCSK9, LDL-R are upregulated on the cell surface resulting in increased uptake of circulating LDL. Medications are given subcutaneously every 2 weeks or month. Two commercially available agents are alirocumab and evo locumab, both which have adult studies show ing a reduction in CVE in patients with prior CVD [72, 73]. Studies have shown reductions

of 36–68% of LDL when added to a statin in the adult population [74]. These medications have not been shown to be effective in patients with homozygous FH with receptor negative mutations [75]. Side effects of PCSK9 have been relatively low with most common being muscle pain (~25%) and less commonly (<15%) back pain, nasopharyngitis, head ache, upper respiratory tract infections, flulike symptoms, joint pain or an increase in ALT or AST levels three times above the upper limit of normal [75].
paragraphs.heading: LDL

paragraphs.text: 32.8 Another target to reduce CVE has been Lp(a). Interestingly, adult studies have not yet shown a conclusive effect of reducing Lp(a) levels on reduction in CVE, which is one rea son that adult and pediatric guidelines do not recommend routine Lp(a) screening. Given that Lp(a) levels are dominated by genetic influences, dietary modification does not lower levels but may decrease the particle mass by lowering the amount of linked LDL [45]. Niacin, which has been shown to down regulate the Lp(a) promoter, is a treatment option that has shown ≤30% decrease in levels in adults [77]. The side effect profile of niacin makes compliance difficult in the pediatric and adolescent population. Statins have a variable effect on reduction of Lp(a) in adults that may be isoform-dependent, however gen erally is not thought to lower Lp(a) levels [78]. PCSK9 inhibitors can decrease Lp(a) levels by directly affecting the hepatic secretion of apoB-containing lipoproteins. Adult studies have begun to show promise as well with anti sense oligonucleotides (ASOs) that inhibit apo(a) mRNA translation with estimates of decrease in Lp(a) levels of ≤90% [79]. Aspirin has also been shown to decrease Lp(a) levels
paragraphs.heading: LDL

paragraphs.text: as well in adults; however, for both ASO inhibitors and Aspirin, data in the pediatric population are lacking.
paragraphs.heading: LDL

paragraphs.text: Family history of CVD: family history of a first-degree relative with MI, CVA, angina, or coronary artery bypass or sudden cardiac death before the age of 55 years in a male and 65 years in a female.
paragraphs.heading: LDL

paragraphs.text: High-risk conditions include type 1 and 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic renal disease, heart transplant, and Kawasaki disease with aneu rysms. High-level risk factors include hyper tension requiring medication, smoking, and morbid obesity.
paragraphs.heading: LDL

paragraphs.text: Moderate-risk conditions include chronic inflammatory disease, systemic lupus erythe matosus, juvenile inflammatory arthritis, nephrotic syndrome, HIV, and Kawasaki dis ease with resolved aneurysms. Moderate-level risk factors include hypertension not on medi cation, obesity, and low HDL.
paragraphs.heading: LDL

paragraphs.text: Abetalipoproteinemia is an extremely rare autosomal recessive condition due to a muta tion in the gene encoding microsomal triglyc eride transfer protein (MTTP) [80]. MTTP is a chaperone protein required for the forma tion of both VLDL and CM through transfer of lipids onto ApoB. The MTTP gene is located on chromosome 4q22–24. Lack of
paragraphs.heading: 32.6.2 Etiology

paragraphs.text: formation of VLDL and CM causes a defi ciency of both IDL and LDL production.
paragraphs.heading: 32.6.2 Etiology

paragraphs.text: Familial hypobetalipoproteinemia (FHBL) is a rare autosomal codominant dis order caused by a mutation in the gene encod ing ApoB (APOB), which is located on chromosome 2p23–24. This causes a trun cated ApoB and therefore reduced lipoprotein lipid content [81]. ApoB cofactors are neces sary for proper LDL, VLDL, and CM forma tion. Heterozygous single mutations, heterozygous compound mutations, and homozygous mutations have been described, with the latter two clinically mimicking abet alipoproteinemia. FHBL is also caused by loss of function mutations in PCSK9, the gene product of which targets the LDL recep tor for degradation. The PCSK9 gene is located on chromosome 1p32.2. Loss of func tion yields a larger number of LDL receptors on the hepatocyte cell surface, resulting in more LDL being taken up by the liver, thus lowering plasma LDL levels [80, 82]. PCSK9 inhibitors were recently approved as a treat ment for FH to due to its LDL-lowering capa bilities [81, 82].
paragraphs.heading: 32.6.2 Etiology

paragraphs.text: CM retention disease is caused by muta tions in SAR1B, which codes for GTPases that are important for allowing CM to travel through the secretory pathways and fuse to the Golgi apparatus. Mutations of this gene, located on chromosome 5q31.3, lead to an inability to secrete CM, resulting in their accumulation within intestinal
paragraphs.heading: 32.6.2 Etiology

paragraphs.text: enterocytes [81]. Familial combined hypo lipidemia (FHBL2) is due to mutations in the gene encoding angiopoietin-like 3, whose role is partial inhibition of LPL and endothelial lipase, both of which are involved in degradation of VLDL and HDL. The ANGPTL3 gene is located on chromosome 1p31, and both compound heterozygous and homozygous mutations have been described [81, 82].
paragraphs.heading: 32.6.2 Etiology

paragraphs.text: Secondary causes of hypobetalipoprotein emias are chronic pancreatitis, malabsorptive states, and profound hyperthyroidism. Hyperthyroidism leads to excessive LPL activ ity through its activation by thyroid hormone, resulting in low levels of VLDL, LDL, and TC. Chronic pancreatitis and malabsorptive states can lead to poor absorption of fat, lead ing to low TC and LDL levels.
paragraphs.heading: 32.6.2 Etiology

paragraphs.text: The clinical presentation of hypobetalipopro teinemia depends on the etiology of the dis ease. The most observed feature of abetalipoproteinemia and CM retention dis ease is fat malabsorption shortly after birth that leads to failure to thrive. Symptoms of malabsorption include steatorrhea, vomiting, and abdominal distention. With the lack of absorption of fat-soluble vitamins, neurologi cal sequelae ensue in the first to second decades of life [81]. Neurologic findings include ataxia and muscle weakness, as well as loss of proprioception, vibration, and deep tendon reflexes. Loss of night and/or color vision can also occur, which may lead to blind ness.
paragraphs.heading: 32.6.3 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Compound heterozygotes and homozy gotes for FHBL have presenting features simi lar to those with MTTP mutations. Heterozygous FHBL is characterized by the development of fatty liver disease secondary to reduced TG export from the liver, but no symptoms of malabsorption or neurologic sequelae are present. FHBL2 cases have not been associated with fatty liver, neurologic findings, or symptoms of malabsorption.
paragraphs.heading: 32.6.3 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Diagnosis of hypobetalipoproteinemia is made with a lipid panel that shows a markedly low LDL level (<50 mg/dl). This is generally found on routine lipid screening or during evaluation of clinical features concerning for lipid disorders. People with abetalipoprotein emia and heterozygous compound or homo zygous FHBL will have low levels of LDL, TC, TG, and ApoB. Those with heterozygous FHBL will have 1/3–1/4 of normal levels of LDL and ApoB. Those with CM retention disease will have low levels of LDL, TC, and HDL, but TG will be normal. FHBL2 is con sidered in cases of low LDL, TG, and HDL. Genetic testing for mutations in MTTP, ANGPTL3, SAR1B, APOB, and PCSK9 can be performed for complete diagnosis. Western blots can be used to assess for truncated ApoB proteins if the ApoB protein is more than 30% of the size of the normal protein.
paragraphs.heading: 32.6.4 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Low levels of LDL and TC are associated with a reduced risk of CVD. However, in some cases of primary hypolipoproteinemia, liver and neurologic dysfunction can be pres ent. Heterozygous FHBL has been associated with hepatocellular carcinoma and cirrhosis; given this risk it is recommended liver func tion tests be monitored and if abnormal, imaging should be pursued [81].
paragraphs.heading: Complications

paragraphs.text: Low levels of LDL and TC have been linked to a reduced risk of CVD, and in cases of het erozygous states of hypolipoproteinemia, no treatment is needed. However, in more severe cases where hepatic steatosis and neurologic sequelae are present, supplementation with fat-soluble vitamins is needed to improve neu rologic findings, and a low-fat diet is required to reduce the fatty deposition in the liver [81].
paragraphs.heading: 32.6.6 Treatment

paragraphs.text: Primary causes of low HDL include genetic mutations leading to a deficiency of any of the apolipoproteins associated with HDL or the enzymes involved in producing it. ApoA1 deficiency is secondary to mutations of the Apo AI gene, located on chromosome 11q23.3. Lack of ApoA1 impacts the structure of the HDL molecule and does not allow for proper HDL assembly. Deficiency of ApoA1 has also been found in conjunction with deficiencies of other apolipoproteins involved in HDL metabolism, such as ApoA-III, ApoC-II, and ApoE [83].
Tangier disease is a rare but severe form of HDL deficiency, named after the island in

Chesapeake Bay, Virginia, where the first few patients were described. It has an autosomal recessive clinical phenotype and is caused by a mutation in the ATP-binding cassette trans porter 1 (ABCA1) gene located on chromosome 9q22–3 [84]. The ABCA1 protein is involved in the transport of cholesterol and phospholipids to ApoA1 to form nascent HDL (HDL3); thus, a defect resulting in low or absent ABCA1 leads to a lack of HDL production.

Lecithin-cholesterol acyl transferase (LCAT) is the enzyme that catalyzes the con version of free cholesterol and lecithin to CE that help form HDL2. The LCAT gene is located on chromosome 16 q21–22. A defi ciency of LCAT is seen in two disease states, both of which are autosomal recessive and result in markedly low levels of HDL. The first, familial LCAT deficiency, involves total loss of the LCAT enzyme, and the second, fish eye disease, is characterized by decreased LCAT enzyme production. LCAT deficiency leads to altered concentrations of both CE and lecithin, leading to abnormal structure of the HDL particles. There are about 50 patients with LCAT deficiency described in the litera ture to date.

Secondary causes of low HDL levels include obesity, smoking [85], states of insulin deficiency such as type 1 diabetes, and states of insulin resistance such as type 2 diabetes. Insulin is a potent activator of LCAT and inhibits hepatic lipase, which hydrolyzes HDL phospholipids to form smaller HDL particles. Thus, in states of insulin resistance or defi ciency, the conformation of the HDL particle is altered, and CE content is decreased, thus predisposing the HDL particle to renal catab olism and excretion, resulting in lower HDL levels [86].

Cholesterol ester transfer protein (CETP) is involved in the transfer of CE from HDL particles onto VLDL, IDL, and LDL in exchange for TG [83, 87]. The gene for CETP is located on chromosome 16q21, and genetic mutations have been found that cause a defi ciency of CETP, which is heralded by marked elevations in HDL, as well as elevated ApoA1, low LDL, and low ApoB.

ApoA1 deficiency manifests as tendinous xanthomas caused by lipid-laden macro phages that usually present on the Achilles tendon and extensor tendons of the hands. Cerebellar ataxia due to decreased fat-soluble vitamin absorption can occur as well. Premature CVD [83] may occur, although there are a number of cases reported where no premature CVD was observed. Clinical mani festations of Tangier disease are secondary to lipid deposition in various tissues, leading to orange tonsils, hepatosplenomegaly, corneal opacities, neuropathy, anemia, and thrombo cytopenia [84]. Clinical features of LCAT deficiency include corneal opacification sec ondary to accumulation of cholesterol and phospholipids, anemia, and proteinuria, with kidney failure being the most common cause of death [88]. There are no clinical features specific to CETP deficiency.
paragraphs.heading: 32.7.3 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Diagnosis of disorders of HDL metabolism generally begins upon finding a markedly low HDL level (<20 mg/dl) on routine lipid testing in childhood or upon workup for some of the secondary manifestations of low HDL in adulthood. The differential of low HDL should be divided into primary and secondary causes, with secondary causes ruled out through a careful history and laboratory eval uation when indicated. Primary causes can be ruled out with genetic testing looking for mutations in genes coding for ApoA1, LCAT, and ABCA1. CETP deficiency is considered in cases of a markedly elevated HDL (>70 mg/ dl) and genetic testing can be done to confirm this.
paragraphs.heading: 32.7.4 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: The risk of heart disease increases in second ary and primary causes of low HDL. No increased risk of premature CVD has been
paragraphs.heading: Complications

paragraphs.text: observed in cases of LCAT deficiency [83]. Studies have suggested that there is a U shaped curve with respect to HDL levels and CVD such that very low levels (<40 mg/dl) and high levels (>80 mg/dl) confer an increased risk [87, 89].
paragraphs.heading: Complications

paragraphs.text: Treatment of low HDL involves, in cases of secondary causes, smoking cessation, and/or treatment of the underlying disease. Insulin administration in cases of type 1 diabetes can restore HDL levels to within the normal range. Dietary modification, weight loss, and especially exercise improve HDL levels in obe sity. Lifestyle modification in addition to blood sugar control in cases of type 2 diabetes improves HDL levels.
paragraphs.heading: 32.7.6 Treatment

paragraphs.text: In cases of primary causes, dietary modifi cation with or without statin therapy to achieve LDL levels below 70 mg/dl is war ranted to reduce cardiovascular morbidity and mortality [90]. Statin therapy improves HDL levels but by only 5–10% in most trials. Niacin can improve HDL levels by 15–35% and fibrates by up to 20%. The benefits of using these medications are that they not only improve HDL levels but also have positive effects on LDL and TG levels and therefore have a beneficial effect on lowering cardiovas cular risk [91].
paragraphs.heading: 32.7.6 Treatment

paragraphs.text: Treatment of LCAT deficiency is focused on preservation of renal function by pharma cologic management using angiotensin recep tor blockers, ACE inhibitors, and/or possibly steroid therapy. Lifestyle modification is also important to reduce LDL levels and cardio vascular morbidity.
paragraphs.heading: 32.7.6 Treatment

paragraphs.text: To date, the neurologic sequelae of Tangier’s disease have not responded to medi cation, but hepatomegaly has been treated successfully with a low-fat diet. CETP inhibi tors such as anacetrapib, evacetrapib, and dal cetrapib have been used in a number of trials in adults to increase HDL levels. CETP inhib itors block the transfer of CE from HDL to other molecules resulting in HDL levels remaining elevated. Studies have shown vari able results with most showing an increase in
paragraphs.heading: 32.7.6 Treatment

paragraphs.text: HDL by up to 25% when used alone and an increase in 60–130% when used in conjunc tion with statin therapy. Results are mixed with respect to cardiovascular outcomes in adults [91–93]. No studies to date have assessed the impact of CETP inhibitors in children or adolescents.

KF is a 17-year-old girl referred to pediatric endocrinology for evaluation of hyperlipid emia. She has no complaints and denies head aches, polyuria, excessive fatigue, snoring, or waking suddenly in her sleep. She has had no recent changes in her weight. She takes no med ications and has no medication allergies. The PCP recently ordered a fasting lipid profile that revealed the following: TC 344 mg/dl, TG 63 mg/dl, HDL 64 mg/dl, and LDL 267 mg/dl. Her family history is notable for the father hav ing hyperlipidemia, for which he had been treated with a statin since his 30s. Paternal grandfather also has hyperlipidemia that was noted “later in life,” for which he was also treated with pharmacologic therapy. There are no first-degree relatives with CVE before the age of 55 years old. Physical examination revealed a well-appearing talkative athletic adolescent in no apparent distress. Lipemic serum should always alert one to hypertriglyceridemia, and lipids should be obtained immediately IV fluids and NPO status will improve the pancreatic inflammation and fasting will lower TG. In cases where TG > 1000 mg/dl, the use of insulin to increase LPL activity and lower TG may be needed. Insulin should always be given with glucose to avoid hypoglycemia. Long-term management of this baby involves a specialized formula that contains mostly medium-chain TG, as these will bypass the steps toward CM formation and reduce post-prandial TG levels. As the baby starts to add other foods to the diet, counseling the family to maintain a low-saturated fat, lowsimple sugar diet, as well as restrict long-chain fat to keep TG < 1000 mg/dl is critical to reduce the risk of pancreatitis. Fibrates can be added much later in childhood or adulthood for fur ther TG reduction.

Discussion/Management

KF has heterozygous FH, given the elevated LDL (>190 mg/dl), normal HDL and TG, and family history of hyperlipidemia. There is no history of early CVD, but this is not terribly unusual. Heterozygous FH is an autosomal dominant disorder that she has inherited from

her father. Initial intervention of dietary modi fication via cholesterol restriction was very suc cessful, reducing her LDL levels by 30%. The expected decrease in LDL with dietary intake <200 mg cholesterol per day is 10–20%, so her cholesterol intake was likely even lower. The success of dietary restriction on her LDL levels was emphasized with her and her family. PDF page 860 | printed page 861 Key Points 5 Screening for abnormal lipids with a nonfasting lipid panel should occur as part of universal screening at ages 9–11 and 17–21 years in order to identify children and adolescents with primary lipid disorders at risk for early CVD. 5 Lipemic serum should alert one to severe hyperlipidemia, most commonly hypertriglyceridemia. 5 Secondary causes of hyperlipidemia, such as obesity, are the most common etiology of hyperlipidemia, especially when the lipid abnormality is mild to moderate. 5 Frequently, more severe lipid abnormal ities are from either a primary cause (i.e., polygenic or heterozygous FH) or a mix of a primary with a secondary condition such as obesity. 5 Homozygous primary causes of hyper lipidemia are exceedingly rare. 5 Heterozygous FH should be suspected if LDL is >190 mg/dl or >160 mg/dl with a family history of early CVD. 5 Lifestyle modification is the first line of treatment for all abnormal lipid states, with the focus on dietary restriction of total and saturated fat as well as TC. 5 Reducing high glycemic index foods in cases of hypertriglyceridemia and regu lar exercise to maintain normal insulin sensitivity and cardiovascular fitness are also recommended. 5 FH often requires pharmacologic man agement, generally in the form of statin therapy for patients >10 years old in addition to lifestyle modification. 5 Medication, including fibrates or omega-3 fatty acids, is often needed in cases of hypertriglyceridemia to avoid pancreatitis. ### 32.1 Introduction Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is typically thought of as an adult disorder; however, its predecessor, atherosclerosis, typically begins during childhood. An abnormal lipid profile is one contributing factor to atherosclerosis that may increase the risk of future premature cardiovascular events (CVE). Normal lipid physiology is based on lipid production and metabolism. Lipid metabolism occurs by three interconnected pathways: exogenous, endoge nous, and reverse cholesterol transport. Abnormalities in these processes result in lipid disorders, which can be acquired or genetic. Acquired lipid disorders are second ary to etiologies such as obesity, type 1 and 2 diabetes, metabolic syndrome, or chronic renal failure. Genetic mutations are inherited abnormalities that in some cases, such as het erozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (FH), have been shown to cause abnormal changes in lipid profiles, endothelial dysfunc tion, and carotid intima-media thickness as early as infancy. In 2014, the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) released new screen ing guidelines for nonfasting cholesterol levels in all children at 9–11 years of age and again at 17–21 years of age in order to identify genetic and acquired causes of lipid disorders. With an estimate of 21% of children and ado lescents in the United States having high TC, low HDL cholesterol, or high non-HDL cho lesterol [1], screening allows for the identifica tion of both mild abnormalities treated with lifestyle modification as well as more severe hyperlipidemia requiring both dietary and pharmacologic management. This chapter reviews the diagnosis, presentation, and man agement of disorders of HDL, LDL, and tri glyceride metabolism. ## PDF page 861 | printed page 862 ### 32.2 Normal Physiology 32.1 ### 32 32.1 ![Source image](../../figures/ch032_p0861_01.jpg) Unmatched source image; PDF page 861. Consult the original caption. ## PDF page 862 | printed page 863 by lipoprotein lipase (LPL) with its cofactor ApoC-II, resulting in the release of free fatty acids. The free fatty acids are taken up by tis sues, including adipose tissue. The resulting CM remnant has acquired ApoE, which binds both remnant receptors and LDL receptors to deliver TG and cholesterol to the liver. LPL activity and clearance of remnants by ApoEbound liver receptors are the major regulators of postprandial TG levels. Endogenous cholesterol is produced in a number of tissues including the gonads, adre nals, brain, and intestine, with about 20% of cholesterol production occurring in the liver. Cholesterol synthesis begins with three mole cules of acetate that form 3-hydroxy-3methylglutaryl-coenzyme A (HMG-CoA), and then, via HMG-CoA reductase, meva lonic acid is synthesized. The formation of mevalonic acid is the rate-limiting step in the cholesterol synthesis. Through a series of steps involving conversion of mevalonic acid to farnesyl pyrophosphate and lanosterol, cholesterol is formed. Cholesterol can be used to synthesize bile acids and is secreted into the intestine or excreted as free cholesterol in the bile. About half of the cholesterol that enters the intestine is reabsorbed and recirculated to the liver, while the other half is excreted in feces. 32.1 2 3 32.1 ### 32.3 General Cholesterol Screening 4 5 ## PDF page 863 | printed page 864 ≥145 mg/dl, a repeat fasting lipid profile should be drawn [4, 5]. The Endocrine Society clas sifies hypertriglyceridemia into mild (150–199 mg/dl), moderate (200–999 mg/dl), severe (1000–1999 mg/dl), and very severe (≥2000 mg/dl) forms. The American Academy of Pediatrics suggests criteria based on age, with hypertriglyceridemia defined as TG levels >100 mg/dl in children under 10 years of age and >130 mg/dl in children 10–18 years of age. ### 32.4.2 Etiology 32.3 ### 32.4.2.1 Primary Causes The most severe cause of primary hypertri glyceridemia is familial chylomicronemia (also known as hyperlipoproteinemia type 1 by the Frederickson classification), which is a deficiency of LPL, the enzyme that catalyzes the hydrolysis of TG. The disease is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern with 100% penetrance. The gene for LPL is located on chromosome 8p22, and to date, over 163 mutations have been identified, 90% of which are loss of function mutations. The disease is rare, with an occurrence of one in ### 32 Table 32.3 Causes of hypertriglyceridemia Primary Secondary LPL deficiency Obesity Apo C-II deficiency Type 1 diabetes Apo A-V deficiency Type 2 diabetes GPIHBP1 deficiency Uncontrolled hypothyroidism Apo E deficiency Lipodystrophy Lipase maturation factor 1 deficiency Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease 500,000–1,000,000 for homozygous LPL defi ciency, which is associated with severe hyper triglyceridemia (typically TG > 5000 mg/dl). Heterozygous forms have wide variability in TG levels and are more prevalent, likely occur ring in one of every 500 individuals [9]. LPL binds glycosylphosphatidylinositolanchored high-density lipoprotein-binding protein 1 (GPIHBP1), which serves as a plat form for lipolysis. The gene for GPIHBP1 is located on chromosome 8q24.3, and defi ciency is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. Homozygous mutations in GPIHBP1 lead to TG levels similar to those found in LPL deficiency (>1000 mg/dl), while heterozy gous mutations have not been shown to cause abnormalities in TG levels [10]. Apolipoprotein C-II is a component of CM, VLDL, LDL, and HDL and is required for the activation of LPL. A deficiency in ApoC-II leads to hypertriglyceridemia due to elevated CM and VLDL, as well as decreased LDL and HDL [11]. The gene for ApoC-II is located on chromosome 19q13.32. Deficiency is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern; heterozygotes have normal TG levels despite low levels of ApoC-II. Interestingly, elevated concentrations of ApoC-II also hinder LPL activity and result in hypertriglyceridemia [11]. ApoA-V, via interaction with GPIHBP1 and LPL, stimulates the LPL activity [12]. A deficiency in ApoA-V caused by genetic mutations in the Apo A5 gene located on chromosome 11q23 leads to hypertriglyceri demia. ApoE is expressed in three isoforms (ApoE2, ApoE3, and ApoE4), which have variable binding affinity to the remnant receptor and the LDL receptor. Mutations in lipase maturation factor 1 (LMF1), which is required for transport and activation of LPL, cause hypertriglyceridemia [3]. The gene encoding LMF1 is on chromo some 16p13.3, and deficiencies are inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. A more common etiology of hypertriglyc eridemia is familial hypertriglyceridemia, with a prevalence of 5–10%. It has an autosomal dominant pattern and is thought to be poly genic in origin, with some cases displaying heterozygous mutations in LPL or overpro duction of VLDL [6]. TG tend to be moder ately elevated, and a positive family history of hypertriglyceridemia and/or pancreatitis tends to be present. ### 32.4.2.2 Secondary ### Hypertriglyceridemia The most common secondary cause of mildmoderate (200–500 mg/dl) hypertriglyceride mia is obesity-associated insulin resistance. The prevalence of obesity in the pediatric population has increased parallel to the increase in obesity rates in adults. The most recent data from the CDC (2017) indicate that the prevalence of obesity is 19.7% in children aged 2–19 years. The COVID 19 pandemic led to dramatic changes in lifestyle habits for most people, with decreased physical activity and increased consumption of nutrient poor, calo rie dense foods. This led to a spike in child hood obesity rates and its related comorbidities. Higher consumption of simple sugars and starches along with foods high in saturated fat raise TG levels. The consumption of excessive amounts of sucrose and fructose has been linked to elevated triglycerides as fructose metabolism bypasses a key rate-determining step in glycolysis and produces glycerol-3phosphate, which is the backbone of triacylg lycerol [13]. Insulin is a powerful regulator of LPL activity. Therefore, in insulin resistance associated with obesity, decreased stimulation of LPL can lead to elevated TG. In cases of insulin deficiency, as in uncon trolled type 1 diabetes or a combination of insulin deficiency and resistance, as in type 2 diabetes, an increase in TG can be seen as well [3]. Thyroid hormone has been shown to increase LPL activity via upregulation of ApoA-V activity [14]; thus, hypothyroidism is associated with elevated TG. Hypertriglyceridemia is the most common dyslipidemia in patients with chronic kidney disease, thought to be secondary to defective clearance of TG from the circulation in addi tion to a decrease in LPL activity, although the reason for the latter is not understood. Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease is heralded by the accumulation of TG in hepatocytes. This is associated with obesity-related insulin resistance, and the mechanism is similar to that observed in states of type 2 diabetes, met abolic syndrome, and obesity [15]. Alcohol consumption has been found to decrease LPL activity and induce TG accumulation through increased fatty acid synthesis and decreased oxidation in the liver, resulting in alcoholic fatty liver disease [16]. Lipodystrophy syndromes are common causes of hypertriglyceridemia, with over 70% of people with congenital lipodystrophy exhibiting elevated TG [3]. Lipodystrophy syndromes are a wide spectrum of congenital and acquired disorders that are characterized by a complete or partial lack of adipose tis sue. The most common form of lipodystrophy is seen in HIV patients and is caused by anti retroviral therapy. The mechanism of hyper triglyceridemia is thought to be a decrease in adipose tissue, leading to increased VLDL synthesis and decreased clearance. ### 32.4.3 Clinical Presentation Symptoms and signs of LPL deficiency tend to occur in infancy or early childhood, while those of ApoC-II deficiency tend to occur in adolescence or adulthood [17]. Other genetic causes of hypertriglyceridemia, such as famil ial hypertriglyceridemia, manifest themselves in youth, while secondary causes can arise at any age, depending on the underlying disease. ## PDF page 867 | printed page 868 diameter that appear diffusely on extensor surfaces of the limbs, buttocks, and shoulders ( Fig. 32.2). These are generally present when triglyceride levels are >2000 mg/dl. Xanthomas occur secondary to phagocytosis of CM by macrophages. They are generally single lesions and are not painful [17]. Lipemia retinalis is the milky appearance of retinal vessels observed generally at TG > 3000 mg/dl ( Fig. 32.3) [8, 9]. This is reversible and ### 32 http://cnx.org/contents/11786e68-a0c1-4675-a4fa- 3437db52ae69@3 tends not to impact vision. Hepatomegaly and splenomegaly can occur due to infiltra tion of macrophage foam cells. Infants may present with poor feeding and GI bleeding, in addition to eruptive xanthomas. ### 32.4.4 Outcomes and Possible ### Complications The most serious clinical consequence of severe hypertriglyceridemia is pancreatitis, the risk of which increases with TG > 1000 mg/dl. Of note, marked increases in TG can impair accurate measurement of amylase, hemoglo bin, and electrolyte levels, so one must not rule out pancreatitis in the setting of abdomi nal pain and high TG when lipase and amy lase levels are low [9]. The reason for the development of pancreatitis is still unclear but is thought to be in part due to TG hydrolysis within the pancreas, leading to toxic accumu lation of free fatty acids, as well as CMinduced ischemia [3]. CVD is also a concerning outcome of hypertriglyceridemia [18]. Excess TG block the endothelium-dependent relaxation factor through inhibition of nitric oxide and larginine synthesis and promote endothelin 1 secretion, a vasoconstrictor [19]. ### 32.4.5 Diagnosis The presence of lipemic plasma should prompt one to order fasting lipids, including a TG and ApoB level. When presented with a case of hypertriglyceridemia, confirmation with a fasting level is imperative. A careful his tory of medical problems, medication use, and family history are important to diagnose both primary and secondary causes of hypertri glyceridemia. Thyroid function tests, fasting glucose, hemoglobin A1C, and liver function tests are useful to rule out common secondary causes. Diagnosis of genetic causes of hypertri glyceridemia can be made via analysis for LPL and/or GHIBP1 mutations as well as mutations in ApoE and ApoC-II. While LDL levels tend to be within normal limits or even low, they cannot be cal culated using the Friedewald equation if TG ≥ 400 mg/dl, as the assumptions about VLDL are no longer valid. Direct measure ment by ultracentrifugation or LDL immuno precipitation can be performed. Assays that measure LPL activity, through treatment of plasma with heparin, can also assist in the diagnosis of LPL deficiency, but [17] these assays are no longer commonly performed. The level of ApoB-100 can help distinguish the hypertriglyceridemia-only variant of familial combined hyperlipidemia (elevated ApoB-100) and some cases of familial hyper triglyceridemia from LPL deficiency (normal ApoB-100). Replacement with levothyroxine restores normal metabolism and reverses hyperlipidemia in cases of hypo thyroidism. ### 32.5 Hypercholesterolemia ### 32.5.1 Introduction ### and Background Hypercholesterolemia is a heterogeneous group of lipid disorders that are characterized by abnormalities in LDL and, in some cases, HDL and TG. Polygenic hypercholesterol emia is the most common etiology of geneti cally inherited hyperlipidemia; however, actual estimates of prevalence are difficult to ascertain given the wide range of mutations and severity of lipid abnormalities that are included in the diagnosis. Heterozygous FH is one of the most common types of genetic dys lipidemias with gene frequency estimated at 1 in 250 in the general population [36]. Heterozygous FH is inherited in an autoso mal dominant pattern. Certain populations, including Afrikaners, French Canadians, Lebanese, and Finns, have been shown to have an increased risk for FH [37]. In contrast to heterozygous FH, homozygous FH is extremely rare, with estimates of 1:1,000,000 in the general population [38]. It is inherited in an autosomal codominant pattern. Familial combined hyperlipidemia (FCHL) is a hetero geneous group of lipid abnormalities that has been linked to multiple loci including 1q21–23, a gene which encodes for a transcription fac tor critical in lipid and glucose metabolism, USF1 [39, 40]. While sometimes difficult to distinguish FCHL from metabolic syndrome, epidemiological data estimate a prevalence of 0.5–2% in the adult population with a higher prevalence in families with a history of pre mature CVD [39]. Familial defective ApoB- 100, an autosomal dominant condition, is due to a missense mutation in the LDL receptorbinding domain of ApoB-100. This results in elevated serum LDL due to reduced hepatic LDL removal and catabolism [41]. The preva lence of familial defective ApoB-100 is esti mated at one in 500 individuals [41]. ### 32.5.2 Etiology 32.5 ### 32.5.2.1 Primary ### Hypercholesterolemia FH is a primary dyslipidemia caused by genetic anomalies that affect the LDL recep tor (LDL-R) pathway. It is typically charac terized by mutations in the LDL-R gene (LDLR), that are estimated to account for >80% of heterozygous FH. Over 1500 muta tions in LDLR have been described [42]. LDL-R are responsible for binding LDL through ApoB-100, leading to endocytosis of the LDL particle. PCSK9, the gene encoded on chromosome 1, aids in the degradation of the LDL-R [41]. A gain of function mutation in PCSK9 reduces LDL-R recycling to the cell membrane, causing an increase in LDL levels, which phenotypically is similar to mutations in LDLR. Mutations in ApoB-100 gene (APOB), as seen in familial defective ApoB- 100, impair the binding of LDL to the LDL- R, resulting in elevation of serum LDL levels. ### 32 In homozygous FH, the severity of the lipid abnormality is related to the genetic mutation involved. Most commonly, muta tions of two different alleles for the gene cod ing the LDL-R are involved; however, occasionally familial homozygotes can have two mutations of the same allele (a true homozygote). The type of mutation dictates the degree of LDL elevation; typically in homozygous FH, the LDL elevation is >300 mg/dl (often 450–850 mg/dl) and HDL is low. The proposed mechanism of polygenic hypercholesterolemia is that multiple minor mutations or polymorphisms in the genes encoding LDL-R, ApoB, and/or PCSK9 cumulatively result in abnormalities of lipid metabolism [43]. Typically, the mutations result in mild to moderate cholesterol abnor malities (LDL 130–160 mg/dl) without frank early CVD compared to more moderate to severe LDL elevations (180–300 mg/dl) in het erozygous FH. FCHL is thought to be due to a number of gene mutations (oligogenic) that result in a variety of abnormalities in TG, LDL, and HDL levels, sometimes within the same fam ily [44]. Type IIa is characterized by isolated LDL elevation, whereas elevated VLDL and TG with low HDL is described in type IV. Type IIB is characterized by an elevated TG, VLDL, and LDL with low HDL. Unlike FH, FCHL may not be associated with an elevation in LDL until adulthood, so it can be missed during pediatric screening. FCHL has been shown to be associated with increased levels of ApoB as a result of overproduction of VLDL. Therefore, measuring ApoB levels may be a better screening test in pediatric patients with a family history of early CVD and moderate hypertriglyceridemia with or without elevated LDL. Perhaps, the least well-understood risk factor for CVD is lipoprotein (a) (Lp(a)). Lp(a) is an atherogenic and heterogeneous lipoprotein that is linked to CVD and stroke. Lp(a) excess is inherited as an autosomal codominant trait and is expressed in children. Lp(a) particles are modified, newly synthe sized LDL with an extra lipoprotein named ApoA covalently linked to ApoB-100. ApoA has significant homology to plasminogen, so this likely explains the thrombosis risk associ ated with elevated Lp(a) levels. Lp(a) has been shown to be expressed in children who are greater than 13 months old at levels equiva lent to those found in their parents [45]. Furthermore, pediatric studies have shown that elevation in Lp(a) in pediatric patients correlates with increased rates of CVE in their parents [46]. Furthermore, a study in children revealed elevated LP(a) levels was associated with increased thromboembolism risk [47, 48].
