### 33.2.8 Hypothalamic-Pituitary-

### Ovarian/Testicular Axis in Obesity

Precocious puberty is more prevalent in girls with obesity compared to those of normal weight. This point had been controversial in earlier studies due to the criteria used to eval uate thelarche and concerns that adipose tis sue deposition may have been mistaken for evidence of early puberty. However, welldesigned studies [201–203] have documented earlier onset of both thelarche and menarche in girls with obesity. A more recent study has shown that the increased risk of central preco cious puberty in children with obesity is significant only when obesity has been present for over 2 years [204].

The impact of obesity on pubertal devel opment in boys has been less well-studied. However, a large investigation of over 4000 boys demonstrated a correlation between age of pubertal onset by testicular size and BMI. Boys with overweight and obesity were found to begin puberty and progress through puberty at an earlier age [205]. Despite some evidence supporting earlier pubertal progres sion in boys, obesity has also been associated with reductions in testosterone level and increased risk of gynecomastia, both lipomas tia and true breast development. This is thought to be due to the aromatization of androgens to estrogens in adipose tissue. Thus, some degree of hypogonadism may be present in some adolescent males with obesity.

Mechanisms underlying earlier pubertal onset in children with obesity remain an area of active investigation. Leptin is known to be permissive in pubertal initiation and leptin deficiency results in a lack of pubertal changes. Leptin is also elevated in obesity. However, while leptin is permissive for puberty, it is not a causative factor. Additional mechanistic possibilities include hyperinsulinism leading to a suppression in sex hormone-binding globulin and thus increased bioavailability of sex steroids. The impact of androgens being aromatized to estrogens by adipose tissue has

also been postulated to play an important role in early pubertal changes in girls and may have variable impact on pubertal changes in boys.

Early hyperandrogenism and premature adrenarche are also more common in girls with obesity and have been linked in some populations to an increased risk of progres sion to PCOS in adolescence and adulthood [206].

Obesity also impacts conception and preg nancy/birth complications. High BMI is asso ciated with reduced semen quality [207]. PCOS can impact female fertility and is asso ciated with obesity and insulin resistance (dis cussed in depth in Chap. 28). Obesity during pregnancy increases risks of pre eclampsia, miscarriage, and congenital abnor malities [208].

### 33.2.9 Other Pituitary Hormone

### Abnormalities in Obesity

Prolactin, a hormone crucial for lactation, may also regulate energy metabolism [209]. Prolactin levels are increased in adults with overweight or obesity and higher levels are associated with metabolically beneficial pro files [210]. This may be in part due to eleva tions of prolactin being associated with visceral fat mass, a more metabolically detri mental fat depot [211].

Oxytocin, another hormone important for lactation but also for normal birth processes, is synthesized in both the brain and the gas trointestinal tract and has important meta bolic actions [212]. Genetic polymorphisms in the oxytocin gene have been linked to obesity in adolescents [213]. Additionally, low oxyto cin levels in adolescents are correlated with higher hyperphagia scores [213], indicating a possible association between satiety and oxy tocin. This association is supported by animal studies which show oxytocin signals through receptors in the brain to activate the POMC pathway and induce satiation [214]; however, it is notable that animal models lacking oxyto


## PDF page 906 | printed page 908

cin action develop obesity without hyperpha gia [215]. On the other hand, oxytocin can impact muscle development [216], inhibit the development of adipocytes [217], stimulate lipolysis [218], and promote increased energy expenditure [219]. Small clinical trials have shown that intranasal oxytocin may signifi cantly reduce hunger and/or food intake [220] and possibly reduce BMI [221], which has led to additional clinical trials underway to deter mine the therapeutic usefulness of oxytocin in obese states.

### 33.2.10 Skeletal Impact of Obesity

As described in detail above, AN, a condition of extreme underweight and nutritional defi ciency, results in a reduction in bone mineral density. However, the opposite extreme, ele vated weight in obesity also leads to changes in bone density and structure [222]. Most studies, including metaanalyses, show increased bone mineral density in individuals with obesity [223–225]. Despite the reassur ing trends in bone density, children with obe sity may be at increased risk for reduced bone strength [226] and fractures [227, 228]. Increased adiposity may cause alterations at the level of the bone through inflammatory markers and mediators. Furthermore, as adi pocytes and osteoblasts are both derived from a common progenitor mesenchymal stem cell, an alteration in one cell type may contribute to alterations in the other [229]. It is well-documented that 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels are lower in individuals with obesity, attributable to both reduced dietary intake and increased distribution in adipose tissue. However, whether or not lower vitamin D levels in children with obesity are associated with fracture risk remains controversial [230, 231].

### 33

Visceral adiposity, the more metabolically active and detrimental fat depot compared to subcutaneous adiposity, appears to be detri mental to bone health. Higher levels of vis ceral fat have been found to correlate with lower bone density in both adolescent girls [232] and women [233] with obesity.

### 33.2.11 Patient Evaluation

The evaluation of a child with obesity starts with an analysis of the weight/BMI trajectory over the patient’s life. Physicians should iden tify whether obesity was severe prior to age 5 years, a marker of possible genetic forms of obesity, or whether there were any inflection points marking a significant change that exac erbated weight gain. In general, the medical history evaluation focuses on determining whether or not there are red flags for genetic forms of obesity or undiagnosed comorbidi ties that need to be addressed. Further, the family history should elucidate any strong family history of severe obesity, bariatric sur gery, or other familial disorders (i.e., vision problems, developmental delays, or pregnancy losses). Additionally, a history of consanguin ity in the family increases the risk for genetic disorders. Current medical problems and past medical history may reveal other hints for syndromic features associated with obesity, such as developmental or cognitive delays, learning disabilities, vision difficulties, or organ abnormalities. The review of systems screens for comorbidities such as headaches for pseudotumor cerebri, joint pain for ortho paedic problems, fatigue for obstructive sleep apnea, or polyuria/polydipsia for diabetes. In the physical exam, care is taken to identify signs of comorbidities such as elevated blood pressure, acanthosis, abnormal optic discs, or hepatomegaly. There are several excellent guidelines which give additional detail for the work-up of childhood obesity [234–237].

Guidelines differ regarding laboratory rec ommendations for childhood obesity. In gen eral, guidelines point to starting screening for obesity comorbidities at age six with an ALT, lipid panel, and haemoglobin A1c, although the recent American Academy of Pediatrics obesity guidelines recommend screening only in those 10 years and older for ALT and abnormal glucose metabolism [238]. However, there is evidence that individuals less than age 6 years can have evidence of obesity-related diseases [239]. Thus, physicians may want to consider testing earlier than the current rec ommendations depending on the specific sce


## PDF page 907 | printed page 909

nario. Referrals to specialists may be necessary based on the history, physical and laboratory findings to further evaluate obesity-related comorbidities or possible genetic causes of obesity.

Treatment of pediatric obesity is based on lifestyle modifications. Unfortunately, there is little to date to help physicians tailor their advice to specific individuals.

### 33.2.12 Management

First-line treatment for obesity and related metabolic factors is behavioral change sup ported by family-centered, multidisciplinary treatment in individual and/or group settings. The goal of behavioral change is to imple ment an improved diet, targeting reducing the glycemic index in foods, increasing intake of fruits, vegetables, lean proteins and healthy fats while eliminating sugar containing bever ages and significantly reducing intake of pro cessed carbohydrates. Physical activity with a goal of 60 min daily, including 30 min three times per week of moderate to vigorous activ ity, can improve insulin resistance and the inflammatory profile even without inducing weight loss. The most recent US Preventative Task Force analysis on obesity in children and adolescents states that only comprehensive, intensive behavioral interventions with at least 26 contact hours were successful for weight loss [236]. Thus, multi-component and multi-specialty/disciplinary programs are instrumental in the treatment of childhood obesity.

Second-line therapies can include medica tions and, in some cases, bariatric surgery. Pharmacotherapy in childhood obesity is underutilized [240], especially given the failure of lifestyle modifications to effectively cause changes at the population level. Expert opin

ion suggests pharmacotherapy initiation could be considered in individuals with obe sity who have not had success with lifestyle interventions and who agree to long-term therapy if efficacy outcomes are met (≥5% BMI reduction from baseline after 12 weeks on optimal dose) [241]. Unfortunately, there are only a small number of pharmacotherapy options available for those at least 12 years of age. The currently approved medications (as of 2023) include orlistat (a lipase inhibitor), liraglutide (a GLP-1 receptor agonist), sema glutide (a weekly GLP-1 receptor agonist), and phentermine/topiramate (a combination stimulant and anticonvulsant). Orlistat, along with behavioral modification, can induce 19% of subjects to have a 5% or greater weight loss, with 9.5% of subjects losing more than 10% of body weight in clinical trials [242]. Liraglutide resulted in 43% of adolescents attaining a ≥5% BMI change with 26% achiev ing at least 10% BMI loss [243]. At the highest dose, 46% of adolescents taking phentermine/ topiramate achieved at least 5% BMI reduc tion and 42% achieved 10% or more BMI loss [244]. Semaglutide resulted in a 5% or more BMI reduction in 76% of adolescents with obesity, with 63% of subjects experiencing a 10% or more BMI loss [245]. Bariatric surgery is also being performed in adolescents, and in recent published data, the results and side effects appear to be similar to those docu mented in adults when performed at experi enced centers [246]. At 5 years, patients had an average weight reduction of 26%, and over 75% had more than a 20% weight loss. The large majority of patients had resolution of diabetes (86%), hypertension (68%), and hypertriglyceridemia (81%). The most com mon complications were micronutrient defi ciencies with potential implications for bone health, and 20% of patients needed an addi tional abdominal surgical procedure.

Case Study and Diagnostic Evaluation

A 14-year-old girl presents to the endocrinol ogy clinic with the complaints of weight gain and irregular menses. She and her mother report that she has always been “heavy” but that over the last 2 years, she has gained over 20 pounds per year, without any linear growth change. They have noticed darkening of the skin on her neck. She has had worsening facial acne and progressive hirsutism on the face and chest. Her weight has recently stabilized after reducing some of her daily intake of soda and processed snacks. Review of systems is negative except for intermittent headaches (1 per month, typically after school).

She was born at term after a pregnancy complicated by gestational diabetes, and has intermittent asthma not requiring daily medi cal therapy. She reached menarche at age 10 years but has never had regular menstrual cycles; menses occur every 3–4 months. She is receiving no medications currently, but has required oral glucocorticoid therapy in the past for acute asthma exacerbations. A review of her medical chart shows her BMI was at 121% of the 95th percentile at age 4 and she has tracked between 120–135% of the 95th percentile for most of her life. Her height has been consis tently between the 90th–95th percentile.

Her family history is significant for obesity in her mother, 12-year-old sister, and maternal grandfather. A maternal aunt had bariatric sur gery. Her father has normal weight and no medical problems. Her 10-year-old brother has ADHD and has normal weight. There is no his tory of consanguinity, pregnancy losses, or other disorders in the family.

Her primary care provider noted a BMI of 35 kg/m2 (127% of the 95th percentile) at her 14-year annual physical and was concerned about her elevated BMI and rapid weight gain. She obtained screening laboratory studies to evaluate causative factors and to screen for potential comorbidities. The results are as fol lows:

5 HbA1C 6.2%.

The labs include impaired fasting glucose (>100 mg/dL), HbA1C (5.7–6.5%) in the pre diabetes range, and mildly elevated liver enzymes concerning for nonalcoholic steato hepatitis. Her lipid panel demonstrated an elevated total cholesterol, LDL, and triglycer ides and a low HDL. Her TSH was mildly ele vated. Her free testosterone and DHEAS were also elevated. The abnormalities were all con sistent with obesity associated metabolic changes and the related syndrome of polycys tic ovary syndrome. Specifically, she has insu lin resistance as noted by her physical findings of acanthosis nigricans and elevated fasting insulin. She has dysglycemia, as indicated by her impaired fasting glucose and a prediabetes range HbA1C. This along with her history of being the result of a pregnancy complicated by gestational diabetes and her family history increases her risk for progression to diabetes. She has lipids and liver function studies con sistent with a dysmetabolic state. Her clinical and biochemical hyperandrogenism along with her irregular menses are consistent with a clinical diagnosis of PCOS. Her strong family history of obesity and history of severe obe sity from an early age is suspicious for a pos sible genetic form of obesity, such as an MC4R variant. Thus, genetic testing should be dis cussed with the family. All metabolic abnor malities will likely improve with weight loss and a reduction in inflammation and insulin resistance. She should be offered an intensive behavior and lifestyle treatment program and obesity pharmacotherapy should be discussed as an adjunct treatment..

In summary, obesity is a common problem in childhood and results in multiple endocrino logic manifestations. These include changes in glycemia, lipids, and other cardiovascular risk factors. In addition, alterations in cortisol production, thyroid function studies, and growth hormone occur. Bone health and reproductive health are also impacted by adi posity. Primary treatment includes treating the individual with intensive lifestyle manage ment and pharmacotherapy when necessary. Metabolic and bariatric surgery is increas ingly being used in adolescents with moderate to severe obesity.

paragraphs.text: Diabetes insipidus is a syndrome of dysregu lated free water balance that may result from a deficiency of arginine vasopressin or from insensitivity (resistance) of the kidney to the action of arginine vasopressin. In the absence of vasopressin-mediated urinary concentra
paragraphs.heading: 34.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: tion, there is increased excretion (polyuria) of dilute urine. The loss of free water leads to increased thirst and water intake (polydipsia). If the thirst is not quenched, the progressive free water deficit leads to a hyperosmolar state characterized by plasma hypernatremia. Diabetes insipidus may be categorized as cen tral (or neurogenic), when due to vasopressin deficiency, or nephrogenic, when the result of diminished renal responsiveness to the antidi uretic action of vasopressin. Central diabetes insipidus can be treated by administration of vasopressin or vasopressin analogs such as desmopressin. Treatment of nephrogenic dia betes insipidus typically depends upon rever sal of the underlying cause, but pharmacological treatment may be partly suc cessful.
paragraphs.heading: 34.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: During the past decade there have been proposals to change the name of diabetes insipidus and to refer routinely to the clinical diagnoses of arginine vasopressin deficiency (AVP-D) and arginine vasopressin resistance (AVP-R) [1]. The most compelling reason for this proposed change is the frequent confu sion between the conditions diabetes insipidus and diabetes mellitus on the part of patients, families, first responders, and others. The terms insipidus (watery) and mellitus (honeylike) serve to distinguish the two forms of dia betes (polyuria). Although polyuria is the first and foremost presentation of diabetes insipi dus, in popular usage, diabetes seems almost always to be associated with disorders of glu cose regulation. This potential confusion and many reported cases of resulting inappropri ate management have led to the proposals to change the nomenclature to reflect the under lying pathophysiology of the disorders and to refer to arginine vasopressin deficiency (AVP- D) for central diabetes insipidus and arginine vasopressin resistance (AVP-R) for nephro genic diabetes insipidus [1]. However, similar to many other hormone deficiency syndromes, patients with either vasopressin deficiency or vasopressin resistance will present with simi lar symptoms of polyuria, polydipsia, and hyperosmolarity, the hallmarks of the clinical syndrome of diabetes insipidus.
paragraphs.heading: 34.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: Arginine-vasopressin (referred to as vasopres sin) is the mammalian antidiuretic hormone and regulator of free water balance and plasma osmolality. Vasopressin regulates plasma sodium concentration but does not control total body sodium content and thus has little effect on total body volume. Vasopressin is synthesized as a prohormone in neurons of the hypothalamus and then undergoes postprocessing during axonal transport through the pituitary stalk to the nerve endings that form the posterior pitu itary gland. Regulated vasopressin secretion from the posterior pituitary occurs in response to physiological stimuli, such as hyperosmo lality and volume depletion [2]. In the kidney, circulating vasopressin can bind to V2 vaso pressin receptors located on the basolateral surface of epithelial cells in the distal tubule and collecting duct of the nephron. V2 vaso pressin receptor activation drives synthesis and translocation of water channels (aquapo rin 2) to the luminal surface of the epithelial cells. These channels facilitate reabsorption of water from luminal fluid into the tubular cell [3]. Other water channels (aquaporin 3 and aquaporin 4) that are constitutively present in the basolateral membrane transport water from within the tubular cell to the circulation [4]. The overall effect of the tubular reabsorp tion of water is to concentrate the urine and conserve total body water. Under normal con ditions, plasma osmolality is regulated within a narrow range of approximately 280–295 mosm/kg [2, 5]. In the setting of water depri vation, increased plasma osmolality stimu lates release of vasopressin from the posterior pituitary. Vasopressin-mediated urine concen tration can increase urine osmolality to greater than plasma osmolality, and, with maximal urinary concentration, urinary osmolality can be as high as 1000 mosm/kg. If the action of circulating vasopressin is not sufficient to maintain appropriate free water balance, a further increase in plasma osmolal ity stimulates thirst, which is the behavioral drive for the intake of additional free water.
paragraphs.heading: Balance

paragraphs.text: With sufficient free water intake, plasma osmolality can be maintained in the normal range [6]. However, if thirst is impaired or water is not available, continued dehydration will result in the development of hyperosmo larity despite high circulating levels of vaso pressin.
paragraphs.heading: Balance

paragraphs.text: The clinical hallmarks of diabetes insipidus are polyuria of inappropriately dilute urine and hyperosmolarity. In general, polyuria can be defined as urine output >2 L/m2 per day, or approximately 40 ml/kg/day [7] and may be due to either a solute diuresis or a water diure sis [8]. A solute diuresis can result from an excess excretion of either inorganic or organic solute. For example, after the intravenous administration of a large volume of saline, glomerular filtration of the excess sodium will produce a solute diuresis as the excess sodium is excreted in the urine. Most pharmacologic diuretics produce a diuresis in this way, by increasing distal delivery of isotonic tubular filtrate to increase the volume of urine output. Excess delivery of other inorganic solutes, such as ammonia or bicarbonate, also can induce a solute diuresis. Glucose will produce polyuria if plasma levels are sufficiently high (typically >180 mg/dl), so that the rate of glo merular filtration overwhelms the tubular reabsorption of glucose. Other organic sol utes, such as mannitol, are filtered at the glomerulus, but do not undergo tubular reab sorption and will produce a solute diuresis [8]. Therefore, a solute diuresis will result in copi ous production of urine, but the presence of solute typically results in a nondilute urine with urine osmolality greater than or equal to plasma osmolality.
paragraphs.heading: 34.3 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: A water diuresis is characterized by pro duction of large volume of dilute urine with an osmolality that is less than plasma osmo lality and typically <200 mosm/kg. A water diuresis can occur in response to a large water load, such as the intentional oral intake of excess free water (polydipsia) [8]. Primary polydipsia may be related to a pathophysio
paragraphs.heading: 34.3 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: logical disorder of thirst secondary to disruption of thirst regulation in the hypo thalamus (dipsogenic polydipsia) [9]. More typically, primary polydipsia is a volitional act with water drunk in a volume in excess of the needs of the body to maintain a normoosmolar state. Primary polydipsia may occur from habit or in response to social cues, as can occur, for example, with frequent drinking from a hand-carried water bottle [10]. When severe, polydipsia usually is related to a psy chiatric disturbance (psychogenic polydipsia). Patients with nondipsogenic polydipsia do not have increased thirst per se, but patients with psychogenic polydipsia have compulsive drinking that typically remits with resolution of psychiatric symptoms [6]. In contrast to primary polydipsia, patients with diabetes insipidus excrete dilute, hypoosmolar urine due to impaired urinary concentrating ability, and the resulting increased thirst and second ary polydipsia are an appropriate physiologi cal response to the loss of free water.
paragraphs.heading: 34.3 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Hypernatremia is the most commonly measured manifestation of a hyperosmolar state. Sodium in combination with an equi molar amount of anions accounts for most of the measurable and effective osmotic load of plasma. A free water deficit that results in a hyperosmolar state will produce hypernatre mia, and therefore, the plasma sodium level frequently serves as a clinical surrogate for osmolality. Hypernatremia can result from either sodium excess or free water deficit [11]. Most circumstances of excess sodium intake occur in situations where the individual has little control of intake. Examples of clinical situations with sodium overload include excess administration of hypertonic intrave nous fluids in a hospitalized patient or exces sive oral ingestion of hypertonic fluids such as seawater or hypertonic infant formula [12]. Hypernatremia more commonly is the result of a free water deficit. Water deprivation with persistent insensible losses leads to a free water deficit that will cause a progressive increase in plasma osmolality. The normal response to hyperosmolality is increased secretion of vasopressin that acts on the kid neys to concentrate the urine and facilitate free water conservation. After loss of both
paragraphs.heading: 34.3 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: salt and water, impaired access to water or a relatively greater loss of water can lead to hypernatremia even if total body sodium is also depleted. Thus, a diuresis can produce both hypernatremia and a decrease in blood volume. Diabetes insipidus is characterized by a defect in renal free water conservation. Patients with diabetes insipidus develop increased thirst and polydipsia to prevent development of hyperosmolality, but if free water intake is limited, hyperosmolality and hypernatremia will develop.

Diabetes insipidus may occur acutely or may present as a more chronic condition. Nontraumatic central diabetes insipidus (vasopressin deficiency) and most cases of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (vasopressin resistance) typically present as chronic condi tions. Less commonly, hypothalamic or pitu itary damage can lead to the acute onset of vasopressin deficient central diabetes insipi dus. A classic triphasic response has been described after injury to the pituitary or neu rohypophysis [13]. This is of particular note when managing the postoperative care of patients after surgery involving the pituitary or hypothalamus. After acute neurohypophy seal injury, vasopressin secretion may be severely impaired and result in the onset of vasopressin-deficient diabetes insipidus within hours of injury (first phase). If the damage is severe enough to produce axonal degenera tion of vasopressin-secreting neurons, there can be subsequent unregulated release of vasopressin into the peripheral circulation. This can result in inappropriate antidiuresis (SIADH) and may lead to development of hyponatremia between 5 and 12 days after pituitary damage (second phase). If the trauma is so severe as to cause death and per manent loss of vasopressinergic neurons, then prolonged vasopressin-deficient diabetes insipidus may ensue (third phase). Some phases of this response may be subclinical and not clinically evident after acute injury to the pituitary or pituitary stalk, with no more than 10% of patients clearly exhibiting all three phases of the classic triphasic response [13].
The effect of diabetes insipidus on growth and development of children depends upon

the age at which the disease becomes clinically apparent. With untreated diabetes insipidus, increased fluid intake will alter caloric intake. Children who drink water in preference to food or who have anorexia related to hyperna tremia may show growth delay due to chronic derangement of water balance and caloric malnutrition [14]. Conversely, intake of large quantities of sweetened beverages in response to the increased thirst of diabetes insipidus can markedly increase caloric intake and lead to obesity. Nursing infants can receive both caloric and free water intake from breast milk or formula. Chronic water deprivation in infants can lead to failure to thrive, irritability, constipation, and even fever [15]. However, increased formula intake in response to increased thirst will provide calories in excess of needs and may result in the development of obesity in infants with diabetes insipidus [16].

Vasopressin deficiency can occur with many congenital disorders of the central ner vous system, such as septo-optic dysplasia and holoprosencephaly, which disrupt the normal development of the pituitary gland and other midline structures [18–20]. Diabetes insipidus is part of Wolfram’s (DIDMOAD) syndrome, which is characterized by central diabetes insipidus, diabetes mellitus, optic atrophy, and sensorineural deafness associ ated with mutation of the wolframin gene [21].
paragraphs.heading: 34.4 Causes of Diabetes Insipidus

paragraphs.text: Familial diabetes insipidus is inherited as an autosomal dominant syndrome of arginine vasopressin deficiency [22]. Infants are nor mal at birth, but between ages 2 and 10 years, they develop vasopressin deficiency and dia betes insipidus. The few reported autopsies in individuals with this disorder have suggested that there may be degeneration of vasopressinsecreting neurons [23] but this has not been confirmed. More than 60 different mutations have been identified within the vasopressin pre-prohormone [24–26]. Most of these are autosomal dominant mutations located in regions of the vasopressin prohormone that encode the signal peptide or the vasopressinassociated neurophysin. Less commonly, vasopressin deficiency is inherited as an auto

somal recessive disorder, with one identified point mutation within the vasopressin peptide sequence that results in leucine-vasopressin, which has a limited ability to activate the vasopressin receptor in the kidney [27].

Destruction of the pituitary gland, pitu itary stalk, or hypothalamus can cause diabe tes insipidus due to vasopressin deficiency [15, 17, 18, 28, 29]. For example, head trauma can transect the pituitary stalk and result in deficiency in vasopressin secretion. In chil dren with severe head trauma, the incidence of central diabetes insipidus may approach 20% [30]. However, the more common causes of pituitary destruction are tumors of the pituitary, hypothalamus, or surrounding structures. Suprasellar tumors such as cra niopharyngioma and germinoma may pres ent with diabetes insipidus. Surgical resection of pituitary or hypothalamic masses can cause temporary or permanent impairment of vasopressin secretion if there is damage to the pituitary gland or stalk. Radiation of the hypothalamus or pituitary can disrupt ante rior pituitary function, but only rarely has radiation been reported to affect the poste rior pituitary and cause vasopressin defi ciency.

A wide variety of infiltrative and infec tious disorders have been associated with the development of central diabetes insipidus [15, 17, 28–33]. Infiltration of the pituitary stalk can disrupt transport of arginine vasopressin from the hypothalamus to the posterior pitu itary. Germinomas, sarcoidosis, and Langerhans cell histiocytosis are the most commonly reported causes of diabetes insipi dus due to infiltration of the pituitary gland or stalk. Acute bacterial meningitis and sub acute meningeal processes such as tuberculo sis and CNS lymphoma also can lead to central diabetes insipidus. Development of “idiopathic” central diabetes insipidus may reflect a stalk lesion that is too small to visual ize with imaging studies, such as MRI. Although more common in adults, lym phocytic hypophysitis with involvement of the pituitary stalk has been reported in children [34, 35]. One report has suggested a relation ship between a prior viral infection and the onset of idiopathic diabetes insipidus [17].

Diabetes insipidus occasionally may pres ent during pregnancy, particularly in individ uals with a pre-existing partial defect of vasopressin secretion. Circulating peptidases, synthesized in the placenta, can participate in the degradation of arginine vasopressin [17]. If the pituitary is unable to respond with an appropriate increase in vasopressin synthesis and secretion, the patient may develop diabe tes insipidus. This syndrome should resolve after delivery, but occurrence of diabetes insipidus during pregnancy may be evidence of an underlying partial diabetes insipidus and can indicate a need for further evaluation of water balance regulation and vasopressin action in the postpartum period [36].

When the renal response to vasopressin is impaired (vasopressin resistance), an individ ual develops nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Inherited defects associated with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus have been identified in the V2 vasopressin receptor and in aquaporin 2, the water channel regulated by vasopressin [37]. Most mutations associated with abnor mal V2 receptor function are inherited as X-linked recessive disorders and impair the receptor response to vasopressin [38] by

decreasing vasopressin binding or down stream signaling [39]. Interestingly, gain of function mutations at the same codon have been associated with the chronic nephrogenic syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hor mone action [40]. Reported mutations of aquaporin 2 that are associated with nephro genic diabetes insipidus are autosomal reces sive. Most functional studies of these mutations have shown them to impair intra cellular transport and subsequent vasopressinmediated translocation of the aquaporin into the apical membrane of the renal tubular cell [41, 42]. Some of these mutations may impair the water channel function of the aquaporin [43] or prevent formation of aquaporin tetra mers in the cell membrane [44].

Acquired arginine vasopressin resistance (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus) typically is not as severe as inherited forms and usually is related to underlying renal tubular or intersti tial damage. Medullary or interstitial damage may affect water balance, not by inhibiting vasopressin action, per se, but by disruption of the normal medullary gradient, which can prevent development of urinary concentra tion greater than plasma osmolality. Thus, interstitial kidney disease can produce a rela tive vasopressin resistance [45]. A wide variety of agents and processes have been associated with development of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Drugs inhibit vasopressin action and exert their effect through a variety of mechanisms [46]. For example, some antibiot ics, including demeclocycline, blunt the renal response to vasopressin by impairing postre ceptor signaling of the V2 receptor [46].

Up to half of all cases of drug-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus are related to the long-term use of lithium salts [47], which may inhibit postreceptor activation and thereby decrease transcription of aquaporin mRNA, aquaporin synthesis, and transloca tion of aquaporin into the apical membrane of tubular cells. In individuals receiving chronic lithium therapy, the reported preva lence of lithium-induced diabetes insipidus varies between 20% and 70% and may depend upon the dose and duration of therapy. The differentiation of acute and chronic lithium

injury remains unclear. Short-term exposure to lithium may impair urine concentrating ability in more than one-half of individuals. With discontinuation of lithium, renal func tion returns to normal. However, with pro longed exposure to lithium, irreversible changes occur with permanent renal tubule insensitivity to vasopressin and resulting impairment of urine concentration and free water preservation [48].

The hallmarks of diabetes insipidus, polyuria and hyperosmolality, can present with varying degrees of severity, and each can be caused by a wide variety of other conditions. Thus, the diagnosis of diabetes insipidus requires suffi cient evaluation to characterize the polyuria and hyperosmolarity and to exclude other conditions that could present with similar findings. It is important to confirm the clinical diagnosis of diabetes insipidus before pursu ing an extensive evaluation to determine the etiology or initiating therapy in an individual patient.
paragraphs.heading: 34.5 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: The diagnosis of diabetes insipidus depends upon confirmation of disrupted free water balance by characterizing the polyuria and the potential hyperosmolar state. Other causes of polyuria, such as primary polydip sia or an osmotic diuresis, must be excluded by clinical evaluation and laboratory analysis. For example, the hyperglycemia of diabetes mellitus can produce polyuria and eventually result in hypernatremia. In many cases, the plasma sodium level may be sufficient to develop a diagnosis. An individual with poly dipsia and plasma sodium level that is low or low normal (and not near the upper range of normal) more likely has primary polydipsia and does not have diabetes insipidus. Conversely, in an individual with diabetes insipidus, polydipsia is driven by the free water deficit and resulting hyperosmolality, and it is unlikely that plasma sodium levels will be low.
The approach to diagnosing diabetes insipidus depends upon the presentation and

clinical setting. A patient that slowly develops diabetes insipidus as an outpatient may be able to sufficiently increase oral intake of free water to maintain a normal plasma osmolal ity. This individual may present with com plaints of excessive thirst and frequent urination. One clinical clue that these symp toms are not due to primary polydipsia may be bed-wetting or frequent nocturia with high levels of urine output persisting during peri ods of decreased water intake. Patients with well-compensated diabetes insipidus are at risk for decompensation if they develop an acute medical illness or are otherwise limited in free water intake. In the same way, an indi vidual developing acute diabetes insipidus after pituitary surgery or head trauma may not be able to respond to the need for increased free water intake and quickly will develop a hyperosmolar state.

The diagnosis of diabetes insipidus can be confirmed by observing the response to water deprivation. The normal response to a free water deficit and mild increase in plasma osmolality is increased vasopressin secretion, which acts on the renal tubules to conserve free water and maintain plasma osmolality in the normal range. By contrast, in an individ ual with diabetes insipidus, impaired free water conservation is accompanied by persis tent excretion of an inappropriate volume of dilute urine. In the absence of increased water intake, this leads to a free water deficit and the development of hypernatremia.

The possibility of diabetes insipidus due to arginine vasopressin deficiency should be con sidered if a patient has a marked polyuria after head trauma or a surgical procedure in which the neurohypophysis and pituitary could be damaged. If access to ad-lib water intake is limited, excretion of inappropriately dilute urine (urine osmolality less than plasma osmolality) will lead to continued free water loss and development of hypernatremia. Careful assessment of documented fluid bal ance (I + O’s) in the operating room and post operative period and measurement of plasma and urine concentration will help in determin ing if persistent polyuria is driven by prior fluid overload or is due to the development of

diabetes insipidus. Development of hyperna tremia with inappropriately dilute urine should be confirmed with laboratory mea surement of plasma and urine osmolality. In the absence of hypernatremia, postoperative polyuria is more likely to represent an appro priate diuresis in response to intravenous fluid administered during or after surgery. Management of individuals with postopera tive diuresis and possible diabetes insipidus should include serial measurement of plasma sodium and urine-specific gravity every few hours until the diuresis resolves or the patient develops hyperosmolality.

In an individual with a likely cause for vasopressin deficiency and acute develop ment of dilute polyuria and hypernatremia, a clinical diagnosis of diabetes insipidus may be made. If this patient has hypernatremia in the presence of dilute urine, then a formal water deprivation may not be required for the diagnosis of diabetes insipidus. In subjects with a clinical diagnosis of acute central dia betes insipidus (arginine vasopressin defi ciency), a therapeutic trial of desmopressin may be an appropriate diagnostic maneuver. However, pitfalls to this approach include the presence of a concurrent cause of polyuria and hypernatremia. For example, an osmotic diuresis following administration of manni tol during a neurosurgical procedure may produce polyuria and possibly mild hyperna tremia if water access if impaired. Other medical problems may obscure the diagnosis of diabetes insipidus. For example, in patients with severe hypothalamic or pituitary destruction, centrally mediated cortisol or thyroid hormone deficiency may impair free water clearance [13].

Once the diagnosis of diabetes insipidus is confirmed, the response to administration of vasopressin (or preferably, a vasopressin analog such as desmopressin) can demon strate whether the diabetes insipidus is due to vasopressin deficiency or vasopressin resis tance resulting in an impaired renal response to vasopressin [7, 15, 31, 49]. After adminis tration of vasopressin or a vasopressin ana log, patients with complete central diabetes insipidus typically have a >50% increase in urinary osmolality. However, a urine osmolal ity >600 mosm/kg is also an appropriate response and may be seen in cases of partial diabetes insipidus. Individuals with primary polydipsia should retain the ability to concen trate urine to >600 mosm/kg and may demon strate little additional response after

In cases of long-standing central diabetes insipidus, the response to exogenous vasopressin adminis tration may be impaired due to washout of the renal medullary gradient. Patients without diabetes insipidus, including those with pri mary polydipsia, should maximally concen trate urine with adequate water deprivation and thus may not have a significant additional

response to exogenous vasopressin. Therefore, endpoints need to be set for concluding a water deprivation study [7, 15, 31, 49]. There are three such as (1) persistent inappropriately low urinary osmolality despite a 3% loss of body weight, (2) plasma hyperosmolarity and hypernatremia with an inappropriately low urinary osmolality, or (3) appropriate urinary concentration (>600 mosm/kg). Urine osmo lality may appear to plateau at a submaximal concentration (<600 mosm/kg) without devel opment of plasma hyperosmolarity. However, if the patient has not shown signs of volume deficiency, then the water deprivation should be continued to determine if further concen tration of urine to >600 mosm/kg can be achieved. A common error that leads to an inconclusive test is ending the test after the patient has lost a certain percentage of body weight without regard for the clinical circum stances. In patients who are fluid replete or overloaded before the test (as in patients with primary polydipsia), the serum osmolality may not have risen enough to reach the thresh old for vasopressin secretion at the end of the test. It is thus useful to also use increase in heart rate and other clinical criteria to assess the fluid status to decide when to end the test. In occasional cases, it may be appropriate to use a therapeutic trial of desmopressin for a week. If the patient responds to therapy, this may confirm the diagnosis of vasopressin deficiency (central diabetes insipidus). Alternatively, if further diagnostic testing is desired, the week of pharmacologic antidi uretic therapy should facilitate recovery of the concentrating gradient in the kidney, which can normalize the response to a test dose of desmopressin.

Other diagnostic tests may be needed to confirm the diagnosis of diabetes insipidus. Typically, urine or plasma vasopressin levels are not readily available. They usually are not required for the diagnosis of diabetes insipi dus, but, in selected clinical circumstances, a vasopressin level may be helpful [6, 49, 50]. A plasma vasopressin level assayed after water deprivation can distinguish between arginine vasopressin deficiency (central diabetes insipi dus) and arginine vasopressin resistance (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus) [50], particu

larly in cases where there is only a partial defect in vasopressin secretion or action [6, 49]. To be most informative, the plasma vaso pressin level must be evaluated as a function of plasma osmolality [49]. Plasma vasopressin levels can be increased by hypotension, smok ing, and nausea, and these stimuli should be avoided during testing of diabetes insipidus [17, 49]. Concurrent plasma osmolality and vasopressin levels obtained during a saline infusion also may help identify a partial defect in vasopressin secretion or may be useful when trying to study a patient that has a high likelihood of both central and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

In some patients, the water deprivation cannot be performed because of hemody namic instability or difficulty in getting coop eration with water deprivation [51]. For example, infants may not tolerate an extended fast. In these circumstances, the saline infu sion test can be used to evaluate for possible diabetes insipidus [6, 49, 50]. A solution of 3% sodium chloride infused intravenously over 2–3 h at a dose of 0.1 cm3/kg/h will provide a hyperosmolar stimulus to arginine vasopressin secretion [6, 51]. When the plasma osmolality threshold for vasopressin secretion is reached, plasma and urinary vasopressin levels will increase, and urinary osmolality will increase abruptly in response to increased vasopressin action on the kidney. Some authors suggest a water load (20 ml/kg of 5% dextrose intrave nous over 2 h) prior to the saline infusion to ensure that vasopressin levels are suppressed at the beginning of the saline infusion test [51]. Comparison of plasma vasopressin levels with corresponding plasma osmolality mea surements can be used to determine if there is an appropriate relationship in the regulation of vasopressin secretion [6, 31, 51]. The saline infusion test also is useful in identifying patients with normal vasopressin secretory ability, but an elevated osmotic threshold for the secretion of vasopressin [31].

Interpretation of the saline infusion test may be confounded by a number of issues. Clinical laboratories typically do not measure plasma osmolality with high precision, and this may complicate the interpretation of the saline infusion test [6]. Arginine vasopressin is

a highly labile peptide and can degrade if the blood sample is not collected, processed, and stored correctly. Blood samples should be kept on ice and carefully processed immedi ately after the blood is obtained, and the plasma kept frozen until assayed [52]. Vasopressin levels rarely are assayed in hospi tal labs, and samples must be sent to a refer ence laboratory, prolonging the turnaround time for receiving test results.

Recently, measurement of copeptin levels has been used as an alternative to measuring vasopressin levels during provocative testing [53]. Copeptin (also called C-terminal provasopressin) is synthesized as part of the vasopressin prohormone, is released during post-translational processing of the prohor mone, and is co-secreted with vasopressin. Copeptin has substantially greater in vivo and in vitro stability than vasopressin, and is less likely to degrade during blood sample han dling and processing. Thus, less fastidious handling of blood samples is required when assaying copeptin [53]. Although experience is limited, copeptin is promising as a more stable and reliable surrogate for assessing vasopres sin secretion.

Once the diagnosis of diabetes insipidus is made, then efforts can be made to further identify the underlying cause if it is not clear from the clinical presentation. Patients with central diabetes insipidus (arginine vasopres sin deficiency) should undergo imaging of the pituitary and hypothalamus. Unless a large intracranial mass is suspected, computed tomography (CT) is of little use in determin ing the cause of diabetes insipidus. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) allows a more detailed study of the neurohypophysis, includ ing the pituitary and the pituitary stalk, espe cially when performed as a study focused on the hypothalamus and pituitary gland [54]. An anterior pituitary microadenoma will not cause vasopressin deficiency. Early studies reported a relationship between intact neuro
paragraphs.heading: of Diabetes Insipidus

paragraphs.text: hypophyseal function and posterior pituitary hyperintensity on T1-weighted MRI [55, 56]. Loss of this pituitary “bright spot” suggested loss of vasopressin-secreting neurons or defi cient vasopressin production and became to be considered diagnostic of diabetes insipidus [17]. Typically, the posterior pituitary bright spot is diminished or absent in both forms of diabetes insipidus, presumably because of decreased vasopressin synthesis in central dis ease and as a result of increased vasopressin release in nephrogenic disease [56–58]. However, loss of the pituitary bright spot is not a specific finding of diabetes insipidus, as a bright spot may not be seen in up to onefifth of normal individuals [59], and a bright spot may persist even in cases of arginine vasopressin deficiency [60, 61].
paragraphs.heading: of Diabetes Insipidus

paragraphs.text: Careful attention to MR images of the pituitary stalk may reveal a lesion that is dis rupting vasopressin transport and secretion [61]. Further evaluation of such a lesion will depend upon the clinical history of the patient. An established diagnosis, such as sar coidosis, that can cause pituitary stalk infiltra tion may indicate that watchful observation, while treating the underlying disease, is appro priate. In the absence of a known diagnosis, additional testing may be needed to identify a systemic illness that may explain the infiltra tive process. In rare circumstances, biopsy of the stalk lesion may be needed to exclude a diagnosis such as central nervous system lym phoma. However, this step should be under taken with due consideration and guidance from experienced endocrinology and neuro surgery consultants, as the biopsy is likely to cause permanent damage to the pituitary stalk, and the reason for biopsy should be diagnosis of a possible systemic disorder. If no lesion can be identified, then other causes, such as an inherited disorder or hypophysitis, should be considered. If no cause for vaso pressin deficiency can be identified, then the patient should be followed and reassessed regularly. For example, germinomas may dis rupt pituitary function and cause diabetes insipidus many years before they are apparent on MRI of the pituitary [29, 32]. Follow-up should include periodic imaging for evidence of a growing mass and repeat assessment of
paragraphs.heading: of Diabetes Insipidus

paragraphs.text: anterior pituitary function, as pituitary stalk lesions also may disrupt anterior pituitary function [17, 31].
paragraphs.heading: of Diabetes Insipidus

paragraphs.text: Patients with nephrogenic diabetes insipi dus should be evaluated to exclude an electro lyte disorder, such as hypercalcemia or hypokalemia, which may contribute to renal resistance to vasopressin. Even in the absence of mechanical urinary outlet obstruction, diagnostic imaging such as renal/bladder ultrasound or CT may reveal urinary tract dilation as a result of the high flow of urine, due to diabetes insipidus or even primary polydipsia [62]. Urinary tract dilation seems to be more common in children and may rep resent functional urinary obstruction as result of the high urinary flow rate compared to the relative size of the urinary outflow system [63]. Treatment of the diabetes insipidus should help to reverse this urinary tract dilation.
paragraphs.heading: of Diabetes Insipidus

paragraphs.text: If there is a family history of diabetes insipidus, genetic studies may be appropriate to confirm the cause of diabetes insipidus in an individual patient [24, 26]. Genetic studies also should be performed in an individual in whom there is no other apparent mechanism to cause diabetes insipidus. Identification of a genetic cause will eliminate the need for more invasive diagnostic evaluation and may be important if symptoms of diabetes insipidus appear in other family members.
paragraphs.heading: of Diabetes Insipidus

paragraphs.text: Adequate free water intake is the first line of therapy for all patients with diabetes insipi dus. Patients with an intact thirst mechanism will appropriately regulate plasma osmolality if allowed free access to water. If the patient is unable to drink by mouth, then intravenous administration of free water in the form of hypotonic fluids should be used to prevent development of a hyperosmolar state. If the patient has severe hypernatremia, intravenous administration of hypotonic fluid should be used to replenish the free water deficit.

paragraphs.text: in the past few years there have been supply chain problems with many of the prepara tions of dDAVP. Desmopressin has two molecular alterations compared to the native nine amino acid peptide hormone arginine vasopressin: deamidation of the amino termi nal cysteine-9 and replacement of arginine-8 with d-arginine, an amino acid isomer of argi nine. These two alterations result in a com pound with a prolonged half-life of antidiuretic activity and elimination of the pressor activity characteristic of native argi nine vasopressin. Desmopressin can be administered parenterally but also can be given by the nasal or oral route. Because of diminished delivery through the nasal or gas tric mucosa and proteolysis by mucosal and gastric enzymes, these non-parenteral routes require higher administered doses of desmo pressin than required with intravenous or sub cutaneous administration ( Table 34.4).
paragraphs.heading: of Central Diabetes Insipidus/ Arginine Vasopressin Deficiency

paragraphs.text: Nasal administration of desmopressin can be accomplished using a rhinal tube or nasal spray, although recent supply chain disrup tions have limited availability of desmopressin in either form. To use the rhinal tube, the patient draws the dose of desmopressin into the flexible plastic rhinal tube, places one end of the tube into the nose, and uses the mouth to blow through the tube to puff the medicine into the nose. Use of the rhinal tube requires that the patient has the dexterity and under standing to follow this technique, although parents can assist children with tube place ment and providing the puff of air. Some authors suggest diluting the desmopressin 1:10 with saline to facilitate administration of small doses by rhinal tube [28, 33]. Nasal administration of desmopressin also can be performed with a spray pump that adminis ters a premeasured dose of 10 mcg desmo pressin per spray. However, utility of this form of nasal desmopressin can be limited in pedi atrics, as the fixed dose of the spray precludes small adjustments of dose, and children may require doses smaller than 10 mcg. Nasal absorption of desmopressin can be affected by upper respiratory congestion. It is, how ever, useful as an alternative to oral desmo pressin in patients with diabetes insipidus who have nausea and vomiting due to illnesses
paragraphs.heading: of Central Diabetes Insipidus/ Arginine Vasopressin Deficiency

paragraphs.text: such as gastroenteritis or in those patients who are unable to take fluids/food orally before anesthesia for a minor procedure.

Most patients with chronic central diabe tes insipidus (arginine vasopressin deficiency) are treated with an oral formulation of des mopressin. As most of an orally administered desmopressin dose is degraded before it can be absorbed, the oral dose is 10–20 fold greater than an equivalent nasal dose. Dosing of sublingual dissolvable tablets is somewhat similar to the oral tablets, although the small est sublingual tablets (if available) contain smaller doses of dDAVP than the oral tablets, which may be advantageous in younger patients with smaller dose needs. Because of variation among individuals in the duration of action of desmopressin, the appropriate dose and frequency of administration must be determined for each individual patient. Although some patients may require only one dose per day, most find management of poly uria and polydipsia easier when taking oral desmopressin two to three times a day. When initiating desmopressin therapy, it may be useful to start with one bedtime dose and then titrate the size and frequency of dosage based on the patient’s response to therapy. In many patients, it be helpful for the bedtime dose to be the largest dose of the day as a way to limit sleep disturbance or enuresis due to nighttime polyuria.

Administration of vasopressin or desmopressin requires careful attention to free water intake to avoid over-drinking and to prevent the development of hyponatremia. Oral intake of fluids may be driven by stimuli other than thirst, such as social cues or habit ual drinking ingrained during a period of untreated diabetes insipidus. At the same time, it is important to avoid excess restriction in urine output [33]. Providing a daily period of “breakthrough” with mild polyuria as the effect of the exogenous vasopressin wanes may be a convenient way to ensure that there is not excessive antidiuresis with an accumula tion of excess free water and progressive development of hyponatremia [67].
In patients treated with desmopressin, oral intake of fluids should be driven by and regu lated by thirst. Some patients with hypotha

lamic injury sufficient to cause clinical diabetes insipidus, for example from suprasellar tumors such as craniopharyngioma, also may have an impaired thirst mechanism. Management of diabetes insipidus in a patient with impaired thirst requires special attention to fluid balance. Daily measurement of fluid intake and output as well as body weight may be needed to maintain optimal fluid balance. Frequent monitoring of plasma sodium levels should be used to provide early identification of problems with water balance. Management of diabetes insipidus in individuals with impairment in both vasopressin secretion and thirst regulation requires special vigilance by the patient, family, and physician.

Management of perioperative and periprocedural diabetes insipidis may involve care of a patient with known diabetes insipidus or expectant post-operative care of a patient without a prior diagnosis who is at risk for post-operative central diabetes insipidus related to hypothalamic or pituitary surgery. In either circumstance, perioperative manage ment requires careful attention to fluid bal ance as assessed by documentation of intake and output, frequent assessment of intravas cular volume status, and laboratory tests including serum sodium and serum and urine osmolality [13, 64]. In patients undergoing major surgery, careful measurement of urine volume and concentration may be facilitated by continuing the use of an indwelling urinary catheter for the first 1–2 days after major sur gery, and in some cases, an intra-arterial cath eter placed during surgery may be maintained for careful post-operative monitoring of intra vascular volume.
paragraphs.heading: and Peri-Procedural Management of Central Diabetes Insipidus

paragraphs.text: Different approaches have been suggested for the management of pre-existing diabetes insipidus in patients undergoing surgery or any other procedure with the potential to dis rupt free water balance, such as endoscopy, an
paragraphs.heading: and Peri-Procedural Management of Central Diabetes Insipidus

paragraphs.text: interventional radiology procedure, or admin istration of chemotherapy [68]. The first line of treatment remains administration of ade quate, but not excess free water to prevent large perturbations in serum osmolality. In patients with central diabetes insipidus, some clinicians prefer to use only fluids, while oth ers continue desmopressin therapy to help to maintain fluid balance and to improve patient comfort by decreasing thirst and decreasing the need to void. For example, in many patients undergoing minor surgery or a brief procedure, it may be appropriate to adminis ter the usual morning dose of desmopressin and to take care not to administer large vol umes of fluid. If the procedure will necessitate oral or intravenous administration of a large fluid volume, the patient will be at an increased risk of hyponatremia and it may be appropri ate to hold pre-operative desmopressin to per mit diuresis and to use hypotonic intravenous fluids or desmopressin only when necessary to maintain free water balance. In patients undergoing major or prolonged surgical pro cedures, careful and frequent monitoring is necessary. Short-acting formulations of vaso pressin or desmopressin are preferred as the risk of hyponatremia is less than with longer acting formulations. If desmopressin is used, patient care must be coordinated with other members of the healthcare team to ensure that fluid balance is carefully managed to pre vent hyponatremia due to excess intravenous fluid administration.
paragraphs.heading: and Peri-Procedural Management of Central Diabetes Insipidus

paragraphs.text: Patients undergoing surgery involving the hypothalamus or pituitary gland are at risk for acute onset of peri-operative central dia betes insipidus from hours up to 2 days after surgical injury and will require careful moni toring during surgery and during the postoperative period. Immediately after transsphenoidal pituitary surgery, desmopres sin or aqueous vasopressin must be adminis tered parenterally because of the difficulty of nasal administration of desmopressin and unpredictable response to oral desmopressin. Another advantage of parenterally adminis tered desmopressin is its shorter duration of action, which decreases the likelihood of hyponatremia developing in response to excess fluid intake. Once a postoperative
paragraphs.heading: and Peri-Procedural Management of Central Diabetes Insipidus

paragraphs.text: patient is taking oral fluids, fluid balance may be regulated by thirst. Depending upon the likely extent of pituitary and hypothalamic damage, the clinician must be sure that thirst is intact and that the patient is not responding to other cues, such as mouth dryness. Acute pituitary damage is likely to be accompanied by some or all of the classic triphasic response as described in Sect. 34.3 [13]. Patients will be at risk for development of severe hypona tremia if desmopressin is continued into the possible second phase of the triphasic response or if a patient drinks to excess while receiving anti-diuretic therapy. Therefore, the decision as to whether to use desmopressin in the immediate postoperative period may depend upon the clinician’s assessment as to the severity of polyuria, the likelihood that the patient will have permanent diabetes insipidus, the presence or the absence of an intact thirst drive, other medical conditions that may be affected by hypernatremia (or hyponatremia), and patient comfort and con venience. Although symptoms may resolve, there still should be close monitoring of urine output volume, urinary osmolality (or specific gravity, which can be performed at the bed side), and plasma sodium levels to ensure that there is adequate, but not excessive, therapy. When patients are receiving intermittent des mopressin therapy, the onset of polyuria of dilute urine indicates the need for the next dose of desmopressin. Each subsequent dose of desmopressin should not be delayed until the patient again develops hypernatremia. However, patients should not be treated on an arbitrary fixed schedule, as breakthrough pre vents the development of hyponatremia that may result with accumulation of excess free water [64]. Continued monitoring may be nec essary for up to 2 weeks to determine if diabe tes will be transient or permanent.
paragraphs.heading: and Peri-Procedural Management of Central Diabetes Insipidus

paragraphs.text: An alternative therapy for management of peri-operative diabetes insipidus is a continu ous intravenous infusion of vasopressin at a low dose (0.08–1.10 mU/kg) during surgery and the immediate post-operative period. This may be useful both for patients with preexisting central diabetes insipidus undergoing major surgery and for patients undergoing surgical procedures at high risk for acute cen

tral diabetes insipidus. Introduction of a stan dard protocol for the multi-disciplinary management of peri-operative diabetes insipi dus has been associated with smaller altera tions in serum sodium levels and a lower incidence of hyponatremia [69]. With this published protocol, the only intravenous fluid routinely administered during surgery is nor mal saline infused at two-thirds of the calcu lated maintenance rate, with additional normal saline administered for blood loss or if needed to maintain hemodynamic stability. With the onset of diabetes insipidus, an aque ous vasopressin infusion is started, and the infusion rate is titrated to result in a urine vol ume of <2 ml/kg/h. The intravenous infusions of vasopressin and normal saline are then continued while the patient is monitored dur ing the post-operative period, until oral intake is resumed.

Infants are a special situation in the manage ment of diabetes insipidus, as fluid intake is linked to caloric intake and usually is regu lated by parents or other caregivers. In infants, an obligatory high oral fluid requirement combined with vasopressin treatment easily can cause free water accumulation and hypo natremia. For this reason, infants with central diabetes insipidus are often managed with fluid therapy alone. The use of breast milk or a low-solute formula (e.g., Similac 60/40) pro vides a lower renal solute load, which can reduce the urine volume by 20–30%. Some infants may benefit from the addition of a thiazide diuretic that can increase urine osmo lality and decrease urine output [20]. Chlorothiazide is available as an oral suspen sion and can be given to infants with central and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus at a dose of 5–10 mg/kg per day, usually divided into doses administered two or three times a day. As an alternative, hydrochlorothiazide (start ing dose of 1–2 mg/kg/day) may be more widely available but will require a pharmacy to compound as an oral suspension. The com bination of low solute formula and a thiazide diuretic can significantly reduce the amount
paragraphs.heading: 34.9 Diabetes Insipidus in Infants

paragraphs.text: of free water supplementation needed in infants with either form of diabetes insipidus to about 20–30 ml for every 120–160 ml of formula [70]. Serum calcium should be moni toring in infants being treated with a thiazide diuretic [20]. In some circumstances, infants with central diabetes insipidus can be treated successfully with once-daily subcutaneous injections of desmopressin (initial dose 0.002–0.1 pg/kg once daily; the dose can be increased and given twice daily if necessary) until they have transitioned to solid food. Desmopressin therapy in infants through the subcutaneous route has been associated with far fewer episodes of hyponatremia and hypernatremia than the intranasal and the oral routes [71]. In general, however, many infants with central diabetes insipidus can be treated successfully with a combination of low-solute formula (or breast milk) and suffi cient free water to maintain a normo-osmolar state. This can be accomplished by careful attention to intake and output and calculation of the volume of formula needed to meet the infant’s caloric needs. If an infant is breast feeding, it may be easier to have the mother use a breast pump so that the volume of milk can be measured accurately. Additional free water then is given to maintain water balance and normal plasma osmolality.
paragraphs.heading: 34.9 Diabetes Insipidus in Infants

paragraphs.text: Treatment of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus can be challenging. Discontinuing or using a decreased dose of the causative drug may lead to improvement or remission of symptoms. However, this must be done in consultation with appropriate specialists who can help in management of the underlying disease and in identification of other agents that may be used without the development of diabetes insipidus. For example, the use of other neu ropsychiatric agents, such as valproic acid or carbamazepine, may permit a dose reduction or discontinuation of lithium. However, some clinical circumstances require continuation of the causative agent and subsequent manage ment of the resulting diabetes insipidus.
paragraphs.heading: Diabetes Insipidus

paragraphs.text: Decreasing the solute load to the kidney with a low-salt and low-protein diet will decrease the total urine volume and limit the degree of polyuria in patients with arginine vasopressin resistance resulting in nephro genic diabetes insipidus. Some patients with partial nephrogenic diabetes insipidus may respond to high doses of desmopressin [6]. A variety of agents, including nonsteroidal anti inflammatory agents and diuretics, have been reported to improve the symptoms of diabetes insipidus. Indomethacin can decrease poly uria and polydipsia, while other nonsteroidal antiinflammatory agents, such as ibuprofen, seem to be much less effective [72]. Diuretics, such as hydrochlorothiazide and amiloride (Midamor), probably ameliorate the polyuria of vasopressin resistance by producing mild chronic volume depletion. This leads to increased volume reabsorption in the proxi mal tubule of the kidney, which results in decreased distal tubule delivery of filtrate and an overall decrease in urine volume. Combined therapy with hydrochlorothiazide and amiloride has been reported to be successful [73]. In patients with lithium-induced diabetes insipidus, amiloride may decrease entry of lithium into tubular cells and thereby decrease the effect of lithium on vasopressin action. In some patients, amiloride therapy may provide complete resolution of lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus [48]. Amiloride may not be available in many community pharmacies but should be available from a hospital pharmacy. Individuals with nephro genic diabetes insipidus can be managed with a combination of hydrochlorothiazide, a non steroidal agent such as indomethacin, and high-dose desmopressin, but most patients have only partial remission of symptoms and require increased free water replacement to maintain normo-osmolality.
paragraphs.heading: Diabetes Insipidus

paragraphs.text: The use of diuretics for the treatment of diabetes insipidus is not risk-free. The persis tent decrease in extracellular volume caused by diuretic therapy puts the patient at risk of hypovolemia and severe dehydration, particu larly during an episode of febrile illness or water deprivation. Thiazide diuretics may cause hypokalemia, which can further impair renal responsiveness to vasopressin. Subjects
paragraphs.heading: Diabetes Insipidus

paragraphs.text: with concurrent lithium-induced diabetes insipidus and hyperparathyroidism are par ticularly susceptible to water deprivation, as dehydration can precipitate hypercalcemia and, in turn, hypercalcemia can further exac erbate vasopressin insensitivity. In patients treated with diuretics for lithium-induced dia betes insipidus, the resulting volume depletion and the effects on tubular function can decrease lithium clearance and may lead to increased plasma lithium levels.
paragraphs.heading: Diabetes Insipidus

paragraphs.text: Management of possible drug-induced vasopressin resistance should begin prior to the development of symptoms such as poly uria and polydipsia. When teenagers and young adults start lithium therapy, they should be informed of the possible develop ment of vasopressin resistance and instructed to monitor urine volume. Progressive develop ment of polyuria may be one indication to reevaluate the need for chronic lithium ther apy and reconsideration of substituting other therapies for lithium.
paragraphs.heading: Diabetes Insipidus

paragraphs.text: With attention to water balance and appropri ate pharmacologic therapy, diabetes insipidus, whether from arginine vasopressin deficiency or arginine vasopressin resistance can be well controlled and should have minimal impact on quality of life. Treatment of diabetes insipidus decreases sleep disruption and facilitates full participation in school and daily activities. Treatment of diabetes insipidus has been reported to improve school performance and behavior and to allow normal growth [8, 14]. Thus, with appropriate treatment, diabetes insipidus should not impair physical or mental development [74]. Patients, families, and school personnel should understand that even short periods of noncompliance with therapy could lead to serious medical complications. However, intercurrent illness or stress can dis rupt management of diabetes insipidus even in a well-controlled patient. Patients and caregiv ers should be instructed to closely follow water intake and urine output and to obtain daily

weights during febrile or gastrointestinal ill ness. Evaluation of any change in mental sta tus should include measurement of serum sodium to exclude hypernatremia due to exac erbation of the diabetes insipidus or hypona tremia secondary to water intoxication. In emergency situations, if a patient or family is unable to communicate the history of diabetes insipidus, severe derangement in water balance could occur before the diagnosis of diabetes insipidus is recognized by emergency personnel or health providers unfamiliar with the patient. Thus, patients should be encouraged to wear a medical alert bracelet or other form of identifi cation that provides a clear indication that they have diabetes insipidus, with an indication of whether they have arginine vasopressin defi ciency or arginine vasopressin resistance.

Diabetes insipidus is a clinical syndrome of dysregulated free water balance that may result from arginine vasopressin deficiency (central diabetes insipidus) or arginine vasopressin resistance (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus). Its clinical hallmarks are polyuria of inappropri ately dilute urine and hyperosmolarity. Making an accurate diagnosis of diabetes insipidus requires a thorough understanding of the physiologic mechanisms that regulate free water balance. Once the diagnosis of either central diabetes insipidus or nephrogenic dia betes insipidus is made, most patients will require further evaluation to determine the eti ology of the disease. Adequate free water intake is the first line of therapy for all cases of diabetes insipidus. Vasopressin and analogs such as desmopressin are the specific therapy for central diabetes insipidus resulting from vasopressin deficiency. The treatment of neph rogenic diabetes insipidus due to vasopressin resistance typically depends upon reversal of the underlying cause, although pharmacologi cal treatment may be partly successful. Treating infants and postoperative patients with either form of diabetes insipidus can be particularly challenging and will require addi tional management strategies and special care.
