The candidiasis associated with APS-1 is usually limited to the skin and mucosa. The candidiasis can be difficult to control, and treatment with antifungals may be required on a continuous basis. Patients may present with candidal esophagitis, which requires endoscopy to diagnose. Additionally, candida that is poorly responsive to treatment is a risk

factor for carcinoma of the esophagus with a high morbidity and mortality. Therefore, aggressive control of candidal infections is recommended [36]. Candidiasis is associated with impaired T helper 17 cell response, which is thought to increase the local production of antifungal chemokines and antimicrobial peptides [37]. This may be related to autoanti bodies against key cytokines.

Patients with APS-1 may also manifest with ocular disease. Approximately 20% of patients develop keratoconjunctivitis. Keratoconjunctivitis often presents in child hood and puts the patient at risk for blind ness. Ectodermal dystrophies include enamel hypoplasia, nail dystrophy, and calcium salt deposits in the tympanic membrane. The underlying cause of these abnormalities is not known.

Successful treatment of APS-1 requires close attention to detail and is dependent upon the underlying disorders that are present. Diseases such as autoimmune hepatitis and autoim mune pulmonary disease are associated with a particularly poor prognosis.
paragraphs.heading: Complications

paragraphs.text: Given the chronic nature of their condi tion, the multiple organ systems that can be involved, and the need for frequent hospital ization and intensive treatment, subjects with APS-1 are at a considerable risk for associated psychiatric disease including depression and anxiety. Screening for such disorders is a vital component of the care of patients with APS- 1.
paragraphs.heading: Complications

paragraphs.text: The treatment of APS-1 is dictated by the clinical features for each patient. Autoimmune endocrine disorders are treated by replacing the missing hormone. Chronic candidal infec tion may require treatment with systemic anti fungals. Patients identified with asplenia require immunization and antibiotics to pre vent overwhelming pneumococcal infection. Additional disease components are treated as they are identified. Diseases such as autoim mune hepatitis and autoimmune pulmonary disease may require treatment with systemic immunosuppressive medications.
paragraphs.heading: 35.2.5 Treatment

paragraphs.text: The association of multiple autoimmune endocrine disorders was initially described by Schmidt as the coexistence of Addison’s dis ease with type 1 diabetes and/or autoimmune hypothyroidism. Other autoimmune associa tions have been described including APS-3 (autoimmune hypothyroidism and another autoimmune disease not including type 1 diabetes or Addison’s disease) and APS-4 (two or more organ-specific autoimmune dis eases). These distinctions do not have clinical significance, and therefore, for the purposes of this discussion, we will use APS-2 to refer to any two organ-specific autoimmune dis eases in one individual. Diseases both within and outside the endocrine system are associ ated with APS-2 including autoimmune thy roid disease (hypo- and hyperthyroidism), type 1 diabetes, Addison’s disease, celiac dis ease, alopecia, vitiligo, autoimmune hypo parathyroidism, primary hypogonadism, myasthenia gravis, and pernicious anemia. Therefore, with the presence of one autoim mune endocrine disorder, practitioners need to be aware of the increased risk for addi tional diseases and screen with comprehen sive history and physical and laboratory testing when indicated.
paragraphs.heading: 35.3.1 Etiology

paragraphs.text: Patients with type 1 diabetes are at an ele vated risk for the development of thyroid autoimmunity (20%) and disease (5–20%), depending upon duration of follow-up. Hypothyroidism is more common than hyper thyroidism. The presence of thyroid-related autoantibodies is associated with progression to thyroid disease [21]. Autoimmunity associ ated with celiac disease is seen in approxi mately 10% of patients with type 1 diabetes. However, 30–50% of these patients have abnormalities on small intestinal biopsies that are consistent with celiac disease [40]. Specific HLA genotypes are associated with an increased risk for celiac disease in the popula

tion with type 1 diabetes [41]. Genes outside the MHC such as CTLA4 and IL2RA have been found in higher proportion of patients with celiac disease and type 1 diabetes than with either disease alone [42]. Adrenal auto immunity is increased in patients with type 1 diabetes, such that approximately 1.5% of patients with type 1 diabetes are positive for 21-hydroxylase autoantibodies. Followed over time, 30–40% of these patients go on to become adrenally insufficient [27, 43]. In this population, the risk for adrenal insufficiency is influenced by genes outside of the MHC, level of 21-hydroxylase autoantibody, gender, and presence of associated autoimmune con ditions [27]. Patients with celiac disease are at an increased risk for the development of auto immune thyroid disease, most commonly hypothyroidism [44, 45]. Patients with auto immune thyroid disease are also at risk for the development of celiac disease [46].

Patients with APS-2 typically present with symptoms of an autoimmune endocrine dis order (type 1 diabetes, Addison’s disease, or autoimmune thyroid disease) and are then found to have an additional autoimmune dis ease based on more subtle symptoms on rou tine screening tests (e.g., testing TSH in a patient with type 1 diabetes). Clues to the development of additional autoimmune dis eases can be identified on careful history, physical examination, and evaluation of the growth chart. Patients with type 1 diabetes developing adrenal insufficiency may present with decreasing insulin requirement, decreas ing A1c, and increasing hypoglycemia. Patients developing hypothyroidism may have a decreased linear growth velocity. Celiac dis ease may manifest with weight loss and decreasing insulin requirements.
paragraphs.heading: 35.3.2 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Given the increased rate of autoimmune dis eases in patients with one autoimmune endo
paragraphs.heading: 35.3.3 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: crine disease, careful screening is required for additional diseases. Current recommenda tions in patients with type 1 diabetes suggest annual screening for thyroid disease with at least measurement of a thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level. Screening for celiac dis ease is recommended at onset of type 1 diabe tes, at 2 and 5 years after diagnosis of diabetes, and with the presence of symptoms of celiac disease. Individuals with a relative with celiac disease should be monitored more frequently for celiac disease than those without a relative. There are no current recommendations for laboratory screening for Addison’s disease in the populations with type 1 diabetes [47]. Practice guidelines acknowledge the relation ship between celiac disease and thyroid dis ease and suggest screening for celiac disease in patients with other autoimmune conditions that are associated with celiac disease such as hypothyroidism or a family history of celiac disease. Practitioners should also consider screening for thyroid disease in patients with celiac disease.
paragraphs.heading: 35.3.3 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Screening for autoimmune diseases includes a careful history and physical exami nation to identify symptoms or signs of the underlying autoimmune condition. In pediat rics, we have the advantage of monitoring growth and development. Any abnormalities of growth or pubertal development in groups at risk for the development of underlying autoimmune disease should serve as a red flag and warrant further evaluation including lab oratory testing. Patients at substantial risk for the development of autoimmune disease include those with a previously diagnosed autoimmune disease such as type 1 diabetes, celiac disease, or thyroid disease and patients with chromosomal disorders associated with autoimmunity including Down and Turner’s syndromes. The specific testing undertaken depends upon the underlying autoimmune disease and can include measurement of auto antibody levels, chemistry, and hormone lev els. Depending upon these tests, additional testing including small intestinal biopsy (for celiac disease) and stimulation testing (for Addison’s disease) may be necessary.
paragraphs.heading: 35.3.3 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Successful treatment of APS-2 requires close attention to detail and is dependent upon the underlying disorders that are present.
paragraphs.heading: Complications

paragraphs.text: Treatment focuses on treating the underlying autoimmune disease identified. Knowing the associations of these diseases allows for care ful assessment for additional underlying auto immune diseases, which has important clinical implications. For example, treatment of patients with undiagnosed adrenal insuffi ciency and hypothyroidism with levothyroxine may unmask the adrenal insufficiency and precipitate an adrenal crisis.
paragraphs.heading: 35.3.5 Treatment

paragraphs.text: Treating the underlying autoimmune pro cess to prevent the development of active dis ease is an area of active research in the setting of type 1 diabetes [48, 49]. Treatment has been targeted at each of the stages of autoimmune disease development, including genetic risk, presence of autoimmunity prior to develop ment abnormalities of glucose metabolism, and presence of autoimmunity, impaired fast ing glucose or impaired glucose tolerance, and early type 1 diabetes. The goals for the treat ment vary depending upon the stage of pro gression to diabetes [50]. Treatment consortiums such as the TrialNet for type 1 diabetes conduct clinical trials in prevention of type 1 diabetes or preservation of C-peptide in patients newly diagnosed with type 1 diabe tes [51].
paragraphs.heading: 35.3.5 Treatment

paragraphs.text: The very earliest stages of disease are found in infants and young children. Therefore, a primary consideration is the safety of the treatment. Treatment trials include the use of hydrolyzed formulas at dis continuation of breast feeding [52], treatment with docosahexaenoic acid (and other com ponents of fish oil), and treatment with oral insulin [53]. These trials are difficult to imple ment and monitor because most people at high genetic risk for disease will never go on
paragraphs.heading: 35.3.5 Treatment

paragraphs.text: to develop disease. Therefore, many patients will be treated who will never develop disease. Additionally, disease develops over months to years. For this reason, many of these trials use markers of the autoimmune process as treat ment end points.
paragraphs.heading: 35.3.5 Treatment

paragraphs.text: People who have diabetes-related autoan tibodies are already at an increased risk for the development of disease. Fewer subjects are needed to see treatment effect, and treat ments can be slightly more toxic compared with interventions directed at antibody nega tive subjects. Large-scale trials have suggested that treatment with oral insulin in subjects who are first-degree relatives of patients with type 1 diabetes and have elevated levels of insulin autoantibodies may be effective in delaying the development of diabetes by approximately 4 years [54]. Follow-up confirmatory studies are underway. Additionally, treatment with glutamic acid decarboxylase 65 (GAD65) has been sug gested to preserve C-peptide production in patients with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes, without significant side effects [55]. Current trials are underway in patients with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes and patients with positive GAD65 autoantibodies identified and followed through the TrialNet study.
paragraphs.heading: 35.3.5 Treatment

paragraphs.text: Patients who are newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes have been treated with immune-modulating drugs with the intent to preserve C-peptide function. Long-term stud ies of patients with type 1 diabetes have shown that persistent production of C-peptide is associated with decreased risk for long-term complications of type 1 diabetes. Patients stand to directly benefit from the sustained production of C-peptide. Taken together, treatments that have a higher toxicity are tol erated in patients newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes compared with treatment directed at antibody-positive subjects without diabetes. At this stage, treatments are targeted toward the immune system with the goal preservation of C-peptide production. Anti-CD3 is a shortterm T-cell-depleting therapy. Its use in humans was suggested by studies in animal models of type 1 diabetes. It has been used in clinical trials of patients with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes and has demonstrated preser

vation of C-peptide production for up to 18 months. These results have led to the FDA approval of teplizumab, a nonactivating, Fcmodified, anti-CD3 monoclonal antibody for treatment of newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes. However, after the initial preservation of C-peptide production, the autoimmune pro cess re-emerges, and C-peptide production begins to decline again [56]. Similarly, treat ment with anti-CD 20 (a B-cell-specific anti body) has shown preservation of C-peptide production for approximately 1 year after treatment [57]. The treatments likely tempo rarily halt the autoimmune process, but do not alter the underlying autoimmunity. It is possible that multiple or combination treat ments will be required over a lifetime to per manently maintain C-peptide production.

IPEX is a rare autoimmune endocrine disor der inherited in an X-linked fashion and asso ciated with autoimmunity and immunodeficiency [58, 59]. The underlying genetic defect is in the FOXp3 gene. FOXp3 is important for the development of regulatory T-cells. Without this gene, CD25+/CD4+ genes do not develop. These cells are regula tors of CD4 effector T-cells in the periphery. Without these cells, fulminant autoimmunity can develop. Boys present as neonates with early onset type 1 diabetes and severe enter opathy resulting in diarrhea and profound failure to thrive. Patients are also at risk for severe dermatitis, hypo- or hyperthyroidism, anemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, hepatitis, and kidney disease. As the genetic cause of the disease has been identified, it is now clear that the clinical phenotype is wider than previously appreciated and includes later onset of disease (into childhood) with a less fulminant presentation [60]. FOXp3 has been reported to be associated with recurrent intra uterine fetal demise of male infants [61]. As

paragraphs.text: Autoimmune endocrine disorders are com mon disorders in pediatric endocrinology and can coexist in recognized syndromes. Classification of subjects into specific syn dromes allows for patient education related to disease and genetic risk, and providers can appropriately monitor their patients for dis ease. APS-1 is an autoimmune endocrine dis order that is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Patients are at risk for the development of multiple autoimmune dis eases, and the disease is characterized by the presence of mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and adrenal insuffi ciency. The disease has a high morbidity and mortality, and multiple organ systems may be involved in the autoimmune process. APS-2 is inherited in a polygenic manner. It is more common in women than man and has a strong HLA association. Other rarer autoimmune endocrine syndromes include the IPEX syn drome. Prompt recognition of this syndrome

Misra (eds.), Pediatric Endocrinology, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-66296-6_35 ## PDF page 944 | printed page 948 Key Points 5 Type 1 diabetes serves as a model for autoimmune endocrine disorders. 5 Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1 (APS-1) also known as autoim mune polyendocrinopathy candidiasis and ectodermal dystrophy (APECED) is an autosomal recessively inherited disorder caused by mutations of the AIRE gene resulting in multiple auto immune diseases. 5 Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 2 (APS-2) is a common disorder associated with type 1 diabetes, primary adrenal insufficiency, and hypothyroid ism. ### 35.1 Introduction and Background ### Information ### 35 1 2 35.1 3 3 ### 35.1.1 Genetic Risk There are multiple genes that have been asso ciated with the risk for autoimmune disease [4]. Genes may influence the risk for the devel opment of autoimmunity and/or the risk for the progression from autoimmunity to glan dular dysfunction. Data derived from pro spective follow-up of high-risk individuals are beginning to tease out these relationships. The most consistent risk has been shown with the genes that make up the human leukocyte anti gens (HLA) found on chromosome 6. In sub jects followed for type 1 diabetes, HLA alleles have been differentially associated with the first positive diabetes-related autoantibody. HLA DR4-DQ 8 has been associated with insulin autoantibodies as the first antibody, and HLA-DR3-DQ 2 has been associated with GAD autoantibodies. These data suggest that these HLA alleles may be important for the initiation of the autoimmune process. HLA may also influence the progression from autoimmunity to disease. For example, HLA- DRB1*15:01-DQA1*01:02-DQB1*06:02 has been shown to be protective for the progres sion of autoimmunity from a single positive autoantibody to multiple positive autoanti bodies and dysglycemia [5]. Subjects that are HLA identical for the DR3/4 locus as their sibling with diabetes have a risk for develop ing diabetes-related autoimmunity of approx imately 75% and diabetes risk of approximately 50% after 5 years of follow-up [6]. Thus, the risk for development of autoimmune disease can be additive. HLA alleles partially explain the disease associations observed in APS-2. DR3-DQ2 and DR4-DQ8 are also associated with auto immune hypothyroidism and celiac disease. Genes outside of the HLA region have been implicated in the risk for autoimmune diseases. Some of these genes increase an individual’s likelihood of developing any autoimmune disease, while other genes are ## PDF page 945 | printed page 949 associated with specific autoimmune condi tions (e.g., the variable number of tandem repeats VNTR of the insulin gene). Specific genes may be associated with progression from autoimmunity to β-cell dysfunction (e.g., PTPN22) [7]. ### 35.1.2 Environmental Factors Despite the strong genetic influence in devel opment of autoimmune diseases, not all with genetic risk develop disease. Environmental triggers have been hypothesized to be impor tant in the development of autoimmune dis ease. The classic example of this is celiac disease, where the environmental trigger, glu ten, is known. In type 1 diabetes, multiple environmental triggers have been proposed [8]. Environmental triggers may influence both steps of the process: initial development of autoimmunity and progression from auto immunity to glandular dysfunction [8]. Earlier introduction of cereals and gluten (<4 months) has been associated with risk for type 1 diabe 2 tes [9, 10] and celiac disease [11]. Increased weight at 12 months has been associated with risk for diabetes-related autoimmunity but not progression from autoimmunity to type 1 diabetes [12]. Emerging data suggest that enteroviral infections may be associated with progression to type 1 diabetes [13]. There may be protective environmental factors as well, such as breast feeding [14]. Other active areas of research include the influence of the intes tinal microbiota and development of autoim munity and disease [15]. It is likely that extensive genetic-genetic and geneticenvironmental interactions disease. ### 35.1.3 Markers of Autoimmunity 35.1 ![Source image](../../figures/ch035_p0945_01.jpg) Unmatched source image; PDF page 945. Consult the original caption. ## PDF page 946 | printed page 950 Table 35.1 Autoimmune endocrine disorders Disease Autoimmune markers Type 1 diabetes Insulin autoantibodies (IAA) GAD65 autoantibodies IA-2 autoantibodies ZnT8 autoantibodies Hypothyroidism Thyroid peroxidase Thyroglobulin autoantibodies Hyperthyroidism Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin Adrenal insufficiency 21-hydroxylase autoantibodies Gonadal failure 21-hydroxylase autoantibodies Celiac disease Tissue transglutaminase autoantibodies Pernicious anemia Intrinsic factor autoantibodies Parietal cell antibodies These autoantibodies are used in the research and clinical setting to identify patients at an increased risk for an autoimmune disease and to confirm autoimmunity as the underlying cause of the disease in an individual with dia betes. Autoantibodies can be detected in serum prior to the development of clinical disease. Studies in subjects with diabetesrelated autoantibodies show that the risk for development of diabetes increases with increasing number of diabetes-related auto antibodies [16], the persistence of the autoan tibodies on multiple tests [17], autoantibody level and affinity of autoantibodies for anti gens [18, 19]. Long-term follow-up of subjects at risk for type 1 diabetes suggests that some of those with single autoantibodies can prog ress to multiple autoantibodies and diabetes [20]. ### 35 The presence of disease-related autoanti bodies can precede the development of overt disease by many years. For example, in patients with type 1 diabetes and antibodies associated with thyroid disease, thyroid dis ease developed over 10–20 years in 80% of the subjects with positive antibodies [21]. The established predictive efficacy of the presence of diabetes related autoantibodies for type 1 diabetes is so strong that programs to screen the general population have been proposed [22]. Regulatory T-cells are thought to be important in the pathogenesis of disease, and regulatory T-cell gene signatures are associ ated with type 1 diabetes [23]. Hemoglobin A1c tends to rise within the normal range as diabetes develops in subjects with diabetes-related autoimmunity [25]. When followed with serial oral glucose toler ance tests, subjects are often noted to demon strate progression from impaired glucose tolerance, to diabetes diagnosed based on the 2-h glucose concentration alone, to overt fast ing hyperglycemia. Some will have a normal hemoglobin A1c at the time of diabetes diag nosis (based on oral glucose tolerance testing) [26]. In subjects with 21-hydroxylase autoanti bodies, progressive deterioration in adrenal secretion of cortisol and aldosterone is noted [27]. In thyroid disease, patients may initially present with compensated hypothyroidism and be relatively asymptomatic (elevated TSH but normal thyroid hormone levels) and even tually progress to overt hypothyroidism. Once sufficient tissue is destroyed, patients present with overt disease. At times, the pre sentation can be catastrophic and lifethreatening such as with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) as the initial presentation for type 1 diabetes and adrenal crisis as the initial pre sentation of Addison’s disease. The decline in C-peptide concentration continues after diag nosis of diabetes in a biphasic fashion [28]. However, some patients with long-standing diabetes continue to secrete C-peptide, open ing the door to treatment options long after onset of overt disease. ### 35.2 Autoimmune Polyendocrine ### Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1)/ Autoimmune Polyendocrinopathy Candidiasis and Ectodermal Dystrophy (APECED) ### 35.2.1 Etiology APS-1 is an (mostly) autosomal recessive dis order historically defined by the presence of two of the following three conditions: hypo parathyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, and candidiasis [29, 30]. The disorder is rare but has an increased frequency in certain popula tions such as Iranian Jews (1:9000), Sardinians (1:14,000), and the Finns (1:25,000). Mutations in the gene (located at 21q22.3) that encodes the AIRE protein are responsible for APS-1. It is inherited in a mostly autoso mal recessive manner. However, a dominant negative mutation has been identified and associated with an atypical presentation of APS-1 [31]. The gene is a transcription factor which influences transcription by interacting with chromatin, not directly the DNA. It is expressed to a high degree in medullary thy mic epithelial cells. These cells play an impor tant role in T-cell maturation. It is hypothesized that the AIRE is important for the expression of self-antigens within the thymus and that this expression is important for the deletion of autoreactive T-cells (negative selection). Therefore, autoreactive T-cells are released into the periphery and can precipitate the autoimmune destruction of the organ to which the T-cells respond [32]. ### 35.2.2 Clinical Presentation 33 35 35.2 30 The autoimmunity associated with APS-1 is not limited to endocrine disorders. Diseases such as autoimmune hepatitis and autoim mune pulmonary disease are associated with a particularly poor prognosis. Given the chronic nature of their condi tion, the multiple organ systems that can be involved, and the need for frequent hospital ization and intensive treatment, subjects with APS-1 are at a considerable risk for associated psychiatric disease including depression and anxiety. Screening for such disorders is a vital component of the care of patients with APS- 1. ### 35.2.5 Treatment The treatment of APS-1 is dictated by the clinical features for each patient. Autoimmune endocrine disorders are treated by replacing the missing hormone. Chronic candidal infec tion may require treatment with systemic anti fungals. Patients identified with asplenia require immunization and antibiotics to pre vent overwhelming pneumococcal infection. Additional disease components are treated as they are identified. Diseases such as autoim mune hepatitis and autoimmune pulmonary disease may require treatment with systemic immunosuppressive medications. ## PDF page 950 | printed page 954 ### 35.3 Autoimmune Polyendocrine ### Syndrome Type 2 (APS2) ### 35.3.1 Etiology The association of multiple autoimmune endocrine disorders was initially described by Schmidt as the coexistence of Addison’s dis ease with type 1 diabetes and/or autoimmune hypothyroidism. Other autoimmune associa tions have been described including APS-3 (autoimmune hypothyroidism and another autoimmune disease not including type 1 diabetes or Addison’s disease) and APS-4 (two or more organ-specific autoimmune dis eases). These distinctions do not have clinical significance, and therefore, for the purposes of this discussion, we will use APS-2 to refer to any two organ-specific autoimmune dis eases in one individual. Diseases both within and outside the endocrine system are associ ated with APS-2 including autoimmune thy roid disease (hypo- and hyperthyroidism), type 1 diabetes, Addison’s disease, celiac dis ease, alopecia, vitiligo, autoimmune hypo parathyroidism, primary hypogonadism, myasthenia gravis, and pernicious anemia. Therefore, with the presence of one autoim mune endocrine disorder, practitioners need to be aware of the increased risk for addi tional diseases and screen with comprehen sive history and physical and laboratory testing when indicated. ### 35 Patients with type 1 diabetes are at an ele vated risk for the development of thyroid autoimmunity (20%) and disease (5–20%), depending upon duration of follow-up. Hypothyroidism is more common than hyper thyroidism. The presence of thyroid-related autoantibodies is associated with progression to thyroid disease [21]. Autoimmunity associ ated with celiac disease is seen in approxi mately 10% of patients with type 1 diabetes. However, 30–50% of these patients have abnormalities on small intestinal biopsies that are consistent with celiac disease [40]. Specific HLA genotypes are associated with an increased risk for celiac disease in the popula tion with type 1 diabetes [41]. Genes outside the MHC such as CTLA4 and IL2RA have been found in higher proportion of patients with celiac disease and type 1 diabetes than with either disease alone [42]. Adrenal auto immunity is increased in patients with type 1 diabetes, such that approximately 1.5% of patients with type 1 diabetes are positive for 21-hydroxylase autoantibodies. Followed over time, 30–40% of these patients go on to become adrenally insufficient [27, 43]. In this population, the risk for adrenal insufficiency is influenced by genes outside of the MHC, level of 21-hydroxylase autoantibody, gender, and presence of associated autoimmune con ditions [27]. Patients with celiac disease are at an increased risk for the development of auto immune thyroid disease, most commonly hypothyroidism [44, 45]. Patients with auto immune thyroid disease are also at risk for the development of celiac disease [46]. ### 35.3.2 Clinical Presentation Patients with APS-2 typically present with symptoms of an autoimmune endocrine dis order (type 1 diabetes, Addison’s disease, or autoimmune thyroid disease) and are then found to have an additional autoimmune dis ease based on more subtle symptoms on rou tine screening tests (e.g., testing TSH in a patient with type 1 diabetes). Clues to the development of additional autoimmune dis eases can be identified on careful history, physical examination, and evaluation of the growth chart. Patients with type 1 diabetes developing adrenal insufficiency may present with decreasing insulin requirement, decreas ing A1c, and increasing hypoglycemia. Patients developing hypothyroidism may have a decreased linear growth velocity. Celiac dis ease may manifest with weight loss and decreasing insulin requirements. ### 35.3.3 Diagnostic Evaluation Given the increased rate of autoimmune dis eases in patients with one autoimmune endo ## PDF page 951 | printed page 955 crine disease, careful screening is required for additional diseases. Current recommenda tions in patients with type 1 diabetes suggest annual screening for thyroid disease with at least measurement of a thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level. Screening for celiac dis ease is recommended at onset of type 1 diabe tes, at 2 and 5 years after diagnosis of diabetes, and with the presence of symptoms of celiac disease. Individuals with a relative with celiac disease should be monitored more frequently for celiac disease than those without a relative. There are no current recommendations for laboratory screening for Addison’s disease in the populations with type 1 diabetes [47]. Practice guidelines acknowledge the relation ship between celiac disease and thyroid dis ease and suggest screening for celiac disease in patients with other autoimmune conditions that are associated with celiac disease such as hypothyroidism or a family history of celiac disease. Practitioners should also consider screening for thyroid disease in patients with celiac disease. Screening for autoimmune diseases includes a careful history and physical exami nation to identify symptoms or signs of the underlying autoimmune condition. In pediat rics, we have the advantage of monitoring growth and development. Any abnormalities of growth or pubertal development in groups at risk for the development of underlying autoimmune disease should serve as a red flag and warrant further evaluation including lab oratory testing. Patients at substantial risk for the development of autoimmune disease include those with a previously diagnosed autoimmune disease such as type 1 diabetes, celiac disease, or thyroid disease and patients with chromosomal disorders associated with autoimmunity including Down and Turner’s syndromes. The specific testing undertaken depends upon the underlying autoimmune disease and can include measurement of auto antibody levels, chemistry, and hormone lev els. Depending upon these tests, additional testing including small intestinal biopsy (for celiac disease) and stimulation testing (for Addison’s disease) may be necessary. ### 35.3.4 Outcomes and Possible ### Complications Successful treatment of APS-2 requires close attention to detail and is dependent upon the underlying disorders that are present. ### 35.3.5 Treatment Treatment focuses on treating the underlying autoimmune disease identified. Knowing the associations of these diseases allows for care ful assessment for additional underlying auto immune diseases, which has important clinical implications. For example, treatment of patients with undiagnosed adrenal insuffi ciency and hypothyroidism with levothyroxine may unmask the adrenal insufficiency and precipitate an adrenal crisis. Treating the underlying autoimmune pro cess to prevent the development of active dis ease is an area of active research in the setting of type 1 diabetes [48, 49]. Treatment has been targeted at each of the stages of autoimmune disease development, including genetic risk, presence of autoimmunity prior to develop ment abnormalities of glucose metabolism, and presence of autoimmunity, impaired fast ing glucose or impaired glucose tolerance, and early type 1 diabetes. The goals for the treat ment vary depending upon the stage of pro gression to diabetes [50]. Treatment consortiums such as the TrialNet for type 1 diabetes conduct clinical trials in prevention of type 1 diabetes or preservation of C-peptide in patients newly diagnosed with type 1 diabe tes [51]. The very earliest stages of disease are found in infants and young children. Therefore, a primary consideration is the safety of the treatment. Treatment trials include the use of hydrolyzed formulas at dis continuation of breast feeding [52], treatment with docosahexaenoic acid (and other com ponents of fish oil), and treatment with oral insulin [53]. These trials are difficult to imple ment and monitor because most people at high genetic risk for disease will never go on ## PDF page 952 | printed page 956 to develop disease. Therefore, many patients will be treated who will never develop disease. Additionally, disease develops over months to years. For this reason, many of these trials use markers of the autoimmune process as treat ment end points. People who have diabetes-related autoan tibodies are already at an increased risk for the development of disease. Fewer subjects are needed to see treatment effect, and treat ments can be slightly more toxic compared with interventions directed at antibody nega tive subjects. Large-scale trials have suggested that treatment with oral insulin in subjects who are first-degree relatives of patients with type 1 diabetes and have elevated levels of insulin autoantibodies may be effective in delaying the development of diabetes by approximately 4 years [54]. Follow-up confirmatory studies are underway. Additionally, treatment with glutamic acid decarboxylase 65 (GAD65) has been sug gested to preserve C-peptide production in patients with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes, without significant side effects [55]. Current trials are underway in patients with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes and patients with positive GAD65 autoantibodies identified and followed through the TrialNet study. ### 35 Patients who are newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes have been treated with immune-modulating drugs with the intent to preserve C-peptide function. Long-term stud ies of patients with type 1 diabetes have shown that persistent production of C-peptide is associated with decreased risk for long-term complications of type 1 diabetes. Patients stand to directly benefit from the sustained production of C-peptide. Taken together, treatments that have a higher toxicity are tol erated in patients newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes compared with treatment directed at antibody-positive subjects without diabetes. At this stage, treatments are targeted toward the immune system with the goal preservation of C-peptide production. Anti-CD3 is a shortterm T-cell-depleting therapy. Its use in humans was suggested by studies in animal models of type 1 diabetes. It has been used in clinical trials of patients with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes and has demonstrated preser vation of C-peptide production for up to 18 months. These results have led to the FDA approval of teplizumab, a nonactivating, Fcmodified, anti-CD3 monoclonal antibody for treatment of newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes. However, after the initial preservation of C-peptide production, the autoimmune pro cess re-emerges, and C-peptide production begins to decline again [56]. Similarly, treat ment with anti-CD 20 (a B-cell-specific anti body) has shown preservation of C-peptide production for approximately 1 year after treatment [57]. The treatments likely tempo rarily halt the autoimmune process, but do not alter the underlying autoimmunity. It is possible that multiple or combination treat ments will be required over a lifetime to per manently maintain C-peptide production. ### 35.4 Immunodysregulation ### Polyendocrinopathy Enteropathy X-Linked Syndrome (IPEX): A Brief Review IPEX is a rare autoimmune endocrine disor der inherited in an X-linked fashion and asso ciated with autoimmunity and immunodeficiency [58, 59]. The underlying genetic defect is in the FOXp3 gene. FOXp3 is important for the development of regulatory T-cells. Without this gene, CD25+/CD4+ genes do not develop. These cells are regula tors of CD4 effector T-cells in the periphery. Without these cells, fulminant autoimmunity can develop. Boys present as neonates with early onset type 1 diabetes and severe enter opathy resulting in diarrhea and profound failure to thrive. Patients are also at risk for severe dermatitis, hypo- or hyperthyroidism, anemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, hepatitis, and kidney disease. As the genetic cause of the disease has been identified, it is now clear that the clinical phenotype is wider than previously appreciated and includes later onset of disease (into childhood) with a less fulminant presentation [60]. FOXp3 has been reported to be associated with recurrent intra uterine fetal demise of male infants [61]. paragraphs.heading: 36.11 Familial Isolated Pituitary Adenoma – 986

paragraphs.text: MEN1 is a rare endocrine tumour predisposi tion syndrome with an approximate preva lence of 1 in 30,000 individuals. The clinical signs of MEN1—including the main manifes tations of pituitary, parathyroid and neuroen docrine tumours—were first described as early as 1903 by Erdheim and was defined by Underdahl and Werner five decades later [1–3]. Wermer proposed that the cause of the disease—first named Wermer-syndrome—is due to a single genetic defect with autosomal inheritance; later, it was renamed as multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 [3].
paragraphs.heading: 36.2.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: MEN1 syndrome is autosomal domi nantly inherited with an overall close to 100% penetrance. In the vast majority of the cases, heterozygous loss-of-function mutations can be identified in the MEN1 gene. Development of different tumours in MEN1 follow the “two-hit” theory suggested by Knudson for retinoblastoma [4]. Affected individuals inherit one mutated copy of the MEN1 gene from one parent (first hit) and one normal copy from the other parent. During tumori genesis in susceptible tissues, there is a somatic mutational event, representing the second hit, affecting the inherited normal copy of the gene MEN1 gene (such as a loss-of-function point mutation, loss of part of chromosome 11q13, or a change affecting the promoter of the gene or a change in regulatory microR NAs miR-24-1) and tumours develop in those somatic cells which are left with no normal copy/normal expression of the gene [5]. In some 10% of MEN1 syndrome patients the germline mutations develop de novo.
paragraphs.heading: 36.2.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: Data from five retrospective paediatric cohorts have been reviewed recently regarding MEN1 [6–11]. The two largest cohorts are the French database (Groupe d’étude des Tumeurs Endocrine, GTE) and an international cohort study with participating centres in the United Kingdom, Austria and USA [7, 11]. In the GTE study, clinical data of 160 MEN1
paragraphs.heading: 36.2.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: patients below the age of 21 years were pre sented having at least one manifestation of the syndrome. Age at manifestation, descrip tion of the first symptoms (clinical symptoms, biological or imaging abnormalities) and data on surgical outcomes, were analysed [7]. The international study describes data of 80 MEN1 carriers before the age of <18 years. Fifty-six patients (70%) developed a MEN1related endocrine tumour, and they gave information on the clinical characteristics of these tumours [11]. Here, we summarised pae diatric MEN1 data mainly from these two cohorts.
paragraphs.heading: 36.2.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: Diagnosis of MEN1 is a clinical diagnosis having two out of the three main MEN1 man ifestations. Pathogenic alteration in the MEN1 gene is not necessary for the diagnosis. For familial diagnosis, patient should have one MEN1-related tumour plus first degree rela tive with MEN1. For genetic diagnosis, a germline mutation of MEN1 has to be detected, but more recently, other genes have also been identified with an MEN1-like phe notype, including MEN4 and MEN5.
paragraphs.heading: 36.2.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: The three main manifestations of MEN1 are parathyroid adenomas, duodenopancre atic neuroendocrine tumours and anterior pituitary adenomas (pituitary neuroendocrine tumours, PitNETs). The most important manifestations of MEN1 in childhood are primary hyperparathyroidism (pHPT), pro lactinomas, non-functioning pituitary adeno mas (NFPAs), functioning (insulinoma, GHRH) or non-functioning pancreas neuro endocrine tumours (NF-PANNETs), and rarely thymic tumours. MEN1-related endo crine tumours have a different clinical course from sporadic tumours in manifesting earlier and having a multifocal presentation of the same organ [6, 12, 13].
paragraphs.heading: 36.2.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: The first symptoms in the GTE cohort were related to pHPT in 75%, pituitary ade nomas in 34%, non-secreting pancreatic tumours in 9%, insulinomas in 12%, gastrino mas in 2%, malignant adrenal tumours in 1%, and a malignant thymic-NET in one case (1%). Hyperparathyroidism was not always the first lesion; it developed first in 56% of the patients. The first symptoms occurred before the age of 10 years in 14% and before 5 years
paragraphs.heading: 36.2.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: in 3% [7]. In the international cohort, 30% of patients with MEN1 did not present clinical signs of the disease by the age of 18 years. Fifty-six patients (70%) developed an endo crine tumour by the age of 18 years (median age 14 years, range 6–18 years). Primary hyperparathyroidism occurred in >80% of patients, Pancreaticoduodenal neuroendo crine tumours developed in ~35% of patients, of whom 70% had non-functioning tumours, 35% had insulinomas, and 5% had gastrino mas, with ~15% having metastases and 55% undergoing surgery. Pituitary tumours devel oped in 30% of patients, and ~35% of these tumours were macroprolactinomas. Tumour occurrence in male and female patients was not significantly different [11]. There are no clear genotype-phenotype correlations, and within the same family, tumour type and age of manifestation are highly different. Malignant presentations of tumours are rare in the paediatric age, but presented in a few cases.
paragraphs.heading: 36.2.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: Thymic NETs are one of the most aggres sive MEN1-related tumours. Thymus NETs are rare in childhood (1 of the 160 cases in GTE study with manifestation at the age of 16 years, this is the earliest case in the litera ture) and none presented in the series of the international study group [7].
paragraphs.heading: 36.2.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: Adrenal tumours are also rare in children, two patients were reported in the GTE cohort (age 4 and 16 years, both adrenocortical carci nomas) and one in the international cohort. The earliest patient reported suffering from adrenocortical tumour was 3 years old [14]. There are only few MEN1-related cases of bronchial tumours in childhood the youngest patient being 15 years. Patients with MEN1 have a decreased life-expectancy mainly due to development of malignant duodenopan creatic and thymus.
paragraphs.heading: 36.2.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: It has been reported that MEN1 mutation negative patients have less aggressive disease, often with a smaller number of organs affected. The median age of first and second tumours development has been reported approximately 10 years later compared to MEN1 mutation–positive patients [15, 16].

Primary hyperthyroidism is the most common (56% of cases) and often the earliest manifes tation of MEN1 in children. In most cases, it is diagnosed as a result of hypercalcaemia on routine or surveillance-driven biochemical screening in asymptomatic patients. The earli est age of manifestation in the literature is 4 years. In contrast to isolated non-MEN1related hyperparathyroidism, it is usually caused by multifocal gland hyperplasia or multiple adenomas of the four main parathy roid glands, and also of some ‘supernumer ary’ and ectopic glands. No malignant parathyroid tumour has been described in children. The male-female ratio is equal. In the GTE study, the mean age at manifestation of hyperparathyroidism was 16 years: 90% of the pHPT cases occurred after 10 years of age. In patients younger than 21 years of age, 17% of the symptomatic cases presented with uro lithiasis, fatigue and bone pain. In ~80% of cases, pHPT was discovered by biochemical screening [7]. The mean age of manifestation was 15 years (ranged 6–18 years) and 20% of the cases were symptomatic [11].
paragraphs.heading: Hyperparathyroidism

paragraphs.text: Screening for hyperparathyroidism always needs parallel measurements of serum cal cium and parathormone while patient has normal vitamin D levels. Chronic renal failure and tertiary hyperparathyroidism have to be excluded. Elevated serum calcium levels can be seen with normal or elevated parathor mone levels, and in mild forms of pHPT, nor mal serum total calcium levels can be detected with elevated serum parathormone levels; 24-h urinary calcium collection could be chal lenge in smaller children, this spot urine cal cium concentration is often used.
paragraphs.heading: 36.2.2.1 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Definitive treatment is surgical removal of the parathyroid glands, but there is debate on the optimal time and type of surgical approach. Subtotal parathyroidectomy (one half gland
paragraphs.heading: 36.2.2.2 Therapy

paragraphs.text: left in situ) or total parathyroidectomy (4 glands and supernumerary and ectopic gland resection) with implantation of parathyroid autograft to the non-dominant forearm) are the different surgical approaches, with trans cervical (partial) thymectomy in an attempt to remove ectopic parathyroid glands from the chest and reduce chances of malignant thymus tumour in MEN1 patients. In cases of subto tal parathyroidectomy, the recurrence rate of hyperparathyroidism is high, but it is also seen with total parathyroidectomy. There needs to be a careful balance of reducing tissue burden, and weighing up the risks to surrounding organs. The use of calcimimetic agents (e.g., cinacalcet) could a form of treatment to diminish hypercalcaemia. Data from 18 paedi atric patients with pHPT have shown that the use of cinacalcet at a dose of 0.6–1.4 mg/kg/ day has a good effect on controlling hypercal caemia and elevated parathormone levels without significant side effects [17].
paragraphs.heading: 36.2.2.2 Therapy

paragraphs.text: MEN1-related pituitary manifestations include pituitary adenomas (pituitary neuro endocrine tumours, PitNETs), which could be the first manifestation (21%) of disease. These tumours are the second in frequency in chil dren, but rarely develop before the age of 10 years. The known earliest age of manifesta tion is 5 years [18]. Pituitary adenomas are usually prolactinomas and non-functioning microadenomas, but all subtypes of pituitary adenomas have been reported in the literature. Most of the pituitary adenomas are microad enomas, but macroprolactinomas are seen most often in boys. Growth-hormone secret ing tumours are rare in children, and they are usually macroadenomas, but we need to be aware of acromegaly due to GHRH-secreting pancreatic NETs [19]. In the GTE study, the mean age of presentation was 17 years, rang ing from 10 years to 21 years. Half of the patients were symptomatic (55%) [7]. In the international cohort, the median age of pre
paragraphs.heading: Pituitary

paragraphs.text: sentation was 14 years, ranging from 10 to 18 years [11]. According to tumour types, the two studies showed 62% (GTE) or 80% (inter national study) of the pituitary adenoma cases being prolactinomas, and 25% and 20% non-functioning-pituitary adenomas, with single corticotropinoma and somatotropi noma in the GTE study [7]. The clinical mani festations depend on the type of hormone secretion, such as growth and pubertal abnor malities, galactorrhoea, Cushingoid signs, headache and vision problems. MEN1-related pituitary adenomas are often multihormonal and also double adenomas have been described.
paragraphs.heading: Pituitary

paragraphs.text: In asymptomatic MEN1 children, annual bio chemical screening should start at the age of 5 years and pituitary imaging at the age of 15 years followed by every 3 years [20]. Screening protocols recommend measuring serum prolactin and serum IGF-1 levels to detect prolactin and growth hormonesecreting tumours. In case of an elevated pro lactin level, macroprolactinemia (the presence of so-called biological inactive big-big prolac tin) has to be excluded. Serial dilution can detect the ‘hook effect’ (extreme hyperprolac tinaemia causing false low results through interference of antibody-antigen complex for mation), although this is now rarely a prob lem. In the presence of MRI-identifiable tumours with elevated serum IGF-1 levels (use age- and sex-matched reference ranges), a GH suppression test with glucose load has to be performed. In the case of failure to supress serum GH levels below 1 μg/L during the diagnostic test, a diagnosis of GH is be estab lished. The cut-off level in adults is 0.4 μg/L, but especially in otherwise healthy teenagers, sometimes, higher levels have been described. Pituitary adenomas are demonstrated on ded icated contrast-enhanced pituitary MRI. Routine biochemical screening for hypercortisolism when clinical suspicion is not present is not recommended. In case of clinical signs of hypercortisolism, biochemi cal evidence of cortisol excess must be con
paragraphs.heading: 36.2.3.1 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: firmed by abnormal results of two different first-line tests (e.g., urinary excretion of free cortisol in a 24-h collection, late-night sali vary cortisol and low-dose dexamethasone suppression test and plasma ACTH measure ment). About 9–22% of paediatric pituitary adenomas are associated with genetic tumourpredisposing syndromes such as MEN1. Screening for both MEN1 and AIP germline mutations in all paediatric patients with pro lactin and GH-secreting adenomas has been suggested. Algorithms for genetic screening in pituitary adenomas presenting in childhood depending on the family history, pituitary tumour type and age at onset are already available [21, 22].
paragraphs.heading: 36.2.3.1 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Therapeutic approaches in MEN1-related pituitary tumours do not differ from treat ment of sporadic forms. Prolactinomas usu ally show a good response to medical therapy with dopamine agonists as first-line therapy and prognosis is good in the majority of the cases. In some cases, after an initial good response, escape has been observed [23, 24]. Cabergoline is the choice of drug in children as well as adults due to its higher efficacy and less side effects. Dose of cabergoline varies between 0.25 and 2 mg per week, but higher doses have been described in severe cases. For all macroprolactinomas before the age of 20 years, dopamine agonist resistance was reported up to 16% of patients, but at this stage, it is unclear if an MEN1 mutation would be an independent predictor of dopa mine agonist resistance [25]. Side effects of dopamine agonists may include cardiac valvu lar fibrosis, especially at prolonged high doses and mood or impulse control problems have also been seen in children. The mechanism for drug-resistance is not clear, it may relate to dopamine receptor down-regulation. In case of intracranial pressure or neuroophthalmological emergencies with worsen ing visual field defect caused by optic chiasma compression, a debulking procedure is needed. In therapy resistant cases, radiotherapy, pos sibly proton beam therapy, can be used. Longterm tumour and treatment-related
paragraphs.heading: 36.2.3.2 Therapy

paragraphs.text: morbidities include hypopituitarism, visual disturbance, obesity, dyslipidaemia and osteo penia or in severe cases osteoporosis.

DpNETs are the primary life-threatening manifestations of MEN1. Clinical screening (imaging and biochemistry) reveals evidence of enteropancreatic tumours in up to 80% of patients with MEN1 throughout life [13]. These tumours are either associated with clin ical signs of excess hormonal production (gas trin, insulin, glucagon, somatostatin, GHRH, calcitonin and vasoactive intestinal peptide) or are clinically non-functioning (may still stain for some of these hormones) [7, 26]. Manifestations of all duodenopancreatic NETs were 23% in the GTE and 38% in the international study. According to these two databases, non-functioning pancreatic NETs were detected in 9% (mean age 16 years) and 27% (mean age 15) with the youngest patient 10 years old [7, 11]. According to the interna tional cohort data among the dpNETs before the age of 18 years, more than 70% were nonfunctioning tumours, >35% were insulinomas, and <5% were gastrinomas, with 15% having metastases [11].
paragraphs.heading: Neuroendocrine Tumours (dpNETs)

paragraphs.text: MEN1-related pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours often synthesise multiple hormones, but hormone synthesis does not always have clinical consequences.
paragraphs.heading: 36.2.4.1 Clinical Manifestations

paragraphs.text: Insulinomas manifest at a younger age than gastrinomas and symptoms of hyperin sulinemia can be the first clinical sign of MEN1 in childhood (10% of paediatric cases), although they typically manifest in the second to fourth decade. MEN1-related insulinomas present earlier than sporadic insulinomas. The mean age of presentation is 15 years, the youngest patient being 5 [7]. Insulinomas are symptomatic in all cases and need interven tion [11]. Patients with insulinomas present signs and symptoms of hypoglycaemia, weak
paragraphs.heading: 36.2.4.1 Clinical Manifestations

paragraphs.text: ness, neuroglycopenia (loss of consciousness and seizures) and autonomic symptoms. It is crucial for children and adolescents and their families to be educated as to the signs of hypoglycaemia and neuroglycopaenic syn dromes.
paragraphs.heading: 36.2.4.1 Clinical Manifestations

paragraphs.text: Gastrinomas are rare in childhood (2%), the youngest being 6 years old. Gastrinomas cause Zollinger-Ellison syndrome presenting with abdominal pain, diarrhoea and steator rhoea associated with elevated gastric acid production and recurrent peptic ulcers.
paragraphs.heading: 36.2.4.1 Clinical Manifestations

paragraphs.text: Glucagonomas have been described only in a single childhood case, where it was a silent glucagonoma [9].
paragraphs.heading: 36.2.4.1 Clinical Manifestations

paragraphs.text: Non-functioning pancreatic tumours usu ally require one of the several imaging tech niques. Blood-based tumour markers as chromogranin A and B, gastric inhibitory polypeptide-GIP, pancreatic polypeptide-PP, somatostatin, vasoactive intestinal peptide- VIP, and GHRH provide important informa tion regarding the presence of tumour, but the only available in specialist laboratories. They may be malignant and metastasise, usually to the liver [11]. Non-functioning pancreatic NETs have been detected as early as 12–14 years in asymptomatic children with MEN1 [27].
paragraphs.heading: 36.2.4.1 Clinical Manifestations

paragraphs.text: Other manifestations include bronchopulmo nary and thymic neuroendocrine tumours and adrenal adenomas or carcinomas. Nonendocrine MEN1-associated tumours are lesions of the skin (e.g., lipomas, angiofibro mas, collagenomas and hibernomas), of the meninges (meningiomas) and of the epen dyma (ependymomas), leiomyomas and Barrett’s oesophagus. In females, breast can cers were shown in the Dutch MEN1 cohort to have a 2.8 times increased risk compared to the general population, but regular screening is needed in adulthood only from the age of 40 years. Thymic NETs occur in 2.0–8.2% and bronchopulmonary NETs in 5–13% of MEN1 patients, with a median age at diagnosis of 43 and 45 years, respectively. The youngest patient with a thymic NET was 16 years old,
paragraphs.heading: in Children

paragraphs.text: the youngest with a bronchopulmonary NET was 20 years old. These tumours are mostly asymptomatic and discovered incidentally or via screening. Various cutaneous lesions such as multiple facial angiofibromas, collageno mas and lipomas are also common and may be useful in identifying the disease. In general, skin lesions need therapy only in the case of local symptoms. Adrenal tumours, uni- or bilateral, are present in approximately 20% of patients with a median age at diagnosis of 46 years. They may be. The majority of MEN1-associated adrenal tumours are hor monally inactive, but ~15% secrete cortisol, androgens or aldosterone. The youngest MEN1 child with adrenal cancer was 3 years old [11, 12, 20]. In two large series of MEN1 patients, hyperandrogenism was the clinical feature of all adrenal tumours before the age of 20 years and was classified as an adrenal carcinoma [7, 20, 28].
paragraphs.heading: in Children

paragraphs.text: For the diagnosis of insulinoma, the gold standard diagnostic test is a 72-h fast with careful monitoring over the whole period. The diagnosis is confirmed if the serum glucose is <3 mmol/L with a parallel finding of serum insulin level of 3 mU/L or higher by immuno chemiluminescent assay and C-peptide of 0.2 nmol/L or higher [20]. If the tumour can not be localised by conventional imaging, arterial calcium stimulation with venous sam pling may be helpful [29]. Benign insulinomas express glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor at high density. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor-based imaging Ga-Exendin-4 PET-CT is very promising in identifying insu linomas [6, 30].
paragraphs.heading: 36.2.4.3 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Serum biomarkers, such as chromogranin A, pancreatic polypeptide, somatostatin or glucagon measurements are of low diagnostic value and imaging screening forms the basis for the diagnosis of non-functioning pancreas NETs. The diagnosis of a gastrinoma can be established by an elevated fasting serum gas trin level (often more than 1000 ng/L) with a gastric pH below 2. The use of proton-pump inhibitors should be stopped for at least 4 weeks before measuring gastrin secretion, and
paragraphs.heading: 36.2.4.3 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: the use of antacids, presence of chronic renal insufficiency or atrophic gastritis with achlor hydria could give false result for the test. In the case of a borderline gastrin level elevation, a gastrin level of more than 120 ng/L above baseline after administration of secretin (2 μg/ kg intravenously) confirm the diagnosis [20]. Gastrin levels may also be elevated in hyper calcaemia caused by hyperparathyroidism [31].
paragraphs.heading: 36.2.4.3 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: The treatment of insulinomas is surgical. The extent of surgery depends on the localisation of tumour and preoperative localisation is crucial. The surgical treatment of other hormone-secreting types or non-functioning tumours can be considered; a size above 4 cm increases the chance of developing metasta ses. Medical treatment is the primary therapy for gastrinomas with proton pump inhibitors and in some cases the addition of an H2 receptor antagonist is needed.
paragraphs.heading: 36.2.4.4 Therapy

paragraphs.text: In 1997, Chandrasekharappa et al. identified the MEN1 gene on chromosome 11q13 and determined that the 9 kb MEN1 gene contains 10 exons coding for a 610 amino-acid protein, named menin [4]. Menin is a nuclear scaffold protein with regulating transcription, genome stability, cell division, and proliferation inter acting several protein partners. MEN1 is con sidered to act as a tumour suppressor gene. Most of the mutations result in a predicted loss of function of the protein, with a second hit at the somatic level resulting in no func tional protein in the tumour tissues, consis tent with a tumour suppressor mechanism [32, 33]. More than 1000 mutations have been reported, mainly frame-shift deletions and insertions, but nonsense, missense, splice-site alterations in-frame deletions and rarely large deletions are also known in the MEN1 gene [32]. No germline promoter mutations have been reported to date. There is no true muta
paragraphs.heading: 36.2.5 Genetics

paragraphs.text: tion hotspots, although some changes were repeatedly reported in independent popula tions. Mutations are dispersed over the entire coding region.

Based on the Dutch MEN1 cohort, de Laat et al. developed a prediction rule predict ing the risk of MEN1 for patients with MEN1-related endocrine tumours with a family history and age at DNA testing also included in the model [34].

It is estimated that approximately 5–10% of patients with a clinical diagnosis of MEN1 are MEN1 gene-mutation negative because (i) mutations are located in MEN1 but not detected by the current genetic testing meth ods, (ii) other hereditary syndromes are pres ent (e.g., MEN4 due to CDKN1B mutations representing 3% of MEN1-like patients [12]) or (iii) the patient has a chance coexistence of two solid sporadic tumour (most frequently pituitary tumours and primary hyperparathy roidism) [35].

According to the guideline from 2012, genetic testing is advised in every patient with a clini cal diagnosis of MEN1, and also in patients at any age without fulfilling the diagnosis if MEN1 but with pHPT <30 years, having mul tinodular pHPT, gastrinomas or multiple pancreatic NETs [36]. Early diagnosis of MEN1 is obligatory to improve patient outcome, but the psychological and medical burden of screening at a young age should be considered. Current practice guidelines rec ommend DNA testing for the familial MEN1 mutation in children before the age of 5 years to establish an early diagnosis and periodic screening is recommended beginning in early childhood at the age of 5 years [37].
paragraphs.heading: Screening

paragraphs.text: MEN1 mutation-positive children and adults need a life-long surveillance program including clinical visits to detect signs and symptoms of the disease, associated with reg ular biochemical and radiological screening in centres with experts and multidisciplinary teams. In the absence of signs and symptoms,
paragraphs.heading: Screening

paragraphs.text: the optimal age to initiate screening for nonfunctioning pNETs is debated. Screening pro tocols advise initiating radiological surveillance around 10–16 years [20, 26, 36]. MRI, computed tomography and endoscopic ultrasound are options for the initial imaging modality for diagnosis. CT surveillance neces sitates a high radiation exposure. Endoscopic ultrasound is the most sensitive method to detect non-functioning pancreas NETs, but because of its disadvantages (being invasive, the need for an expert, cannot easily visualise tumours in the tail), MRI may be preferred.
paragraphs.heading: Screening

paragraphs.text: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 2 (MEN2) is an autosomal dominant heredi tary cancer syndrome caused by germline mutations in the REarranged during Transfection (RET) gene. MEN2 is divided into two entities such as MEN2A and MEN2B. MEN2A is subclassified into four subtypes such as classical MEN2A, MEN2A associated with cutaneous lichen amyloidosis (CLA), MEN2A associated with Hirschsprung’s disease, and familial medul lary thyroid cancer (FMTC). MEN2A repre sents approximately 95% of MEN2 syndromes.
paragraphs.heading: 36.3.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: In 1959, working as a medical resident, Sipple was asked to consult a 33-year-old man suffering from high blood pressure after undergoing stroke surgery for a cerebral arte riovenous malformation. At that time, he believed that hypertension of this patient was
paragraphs.heading: 36.3.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: due to increased intracranial pressure. At autopsy, a large bilateral phaeochromocy toma and a pale mass of 2 cm in both lobes of the thyroid gland were found, as well as nodu lar enlargement of the parathyroid gland. The thyroid tumour was histologically diagnosed as an adenocarcinoma, but later revised to medullary carcinoma. His case was published in 1961, and Sipple’s name had been associ ated with the syndrome (it seems that cerebral arteriovenous malformation is not part of MEN2A syndrome) [39, 40]. Four years later, Williams reported two patients presenting with a phaeochromocytoma, medullary thy roid carcinoma and coexistence with mucosal neuromas [41]. In 1975, Chong and his coworkers suggested the divide patients with MEN2 into MEN2A without mucosal neuro mas and MEN2B with this feature [42].
paragraphs.heading: 36.3.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: The prevalence of MEN2A is 13–24 per million and of MEN2B 1–2 per million, while the incidence ranges between 8 and 28 per mil lion live births per year for MEN2A and 0.9 and 1.6 per million for MEN2B [43–49].
paragraphs.heading: 36.3.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: MEN2A is associated with medullary thyroid carcinoma, phaeochromocytoma and pri mary hyperparathyroidism. In the classical MEN2A syndrome, the prevalence of differ ent disorders includes medullary thyroid car cinoma 90%, phaeochromocytoma 30% and primary hyperparathyroidism 10% [48].
paragraphs.heading: 36.3.2 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: The clinical diagnosis of MEN2A can be established, when MTC and phaeochromocy toma with or without pHPT is present in the same patient or two or more tumours in mul tiple members of the same family. MTC is prevalent in almost all MEN2A patients and is usually the first clinical manifestation of the disease, preceded by C-cell hyperplasia. Depending on the exact location of the RET mutation within the gene, the mean age at diagnosis of the transition from normal thy roid morphology to C-cell hyperplasia ranges from 5 to 11 years. MTC in MEN2A is char acterised by multifocal, bilateral tumours typ ically located in the middle to upper part of the thyroid gland. The youngest patient with
MEN2A-related MTC reported in the litera ture was 10 months old [50].

Data from a nationwide retrospective cohort of MTC from Denmark showed that 15% of MEN2A patients were symptomatic at the age of diagnosis, while 85% were asymp tomatic. Their data highlighted the fact that patients with hereditary MTC diagnosed by screening without regional metastases, and with stage I, II or III disease, may have similar survival as the general population [51]. Disease-specific survival of MTC patients is strongly dependent on the age and stage at diagnosis. C-cell hyperplasia is a precursor of MTC, and in MEN2A and MEN2B, there is a progression from normal histology to C-cell hyperplasia and then to MTC. There is sig nificant phenotypic variability in the timing of MTC, onset and aggressiveness between carriers of MEN2 mutations in the same fam ily, especially in the moderate risk group. There is no real explanation for this phenom enon, and no marker to predict it at the indi vidual level.

The typical clinical features of phaeochro mocytoma are usually absent in MEN2associated adrenal tumours, as half of the patients are asymptomatic and only about one-third are hypertensive [52]. The majority of phaeochromocytomas in MEN2A patients are benign, bilateral, and contralateral phaeo chromocytomas usually develop within 10 years of the unilateral tumour [53].

Primary hyperparathyroidism is caused by parathyroid adenoma or hyperplasia. pHPT is usually diagnosed in the fourth decade of life. Carriers of codon 634 mutations are regarded as having the highest penetrance of pHPT. The youngest child reported in the literature was 5 years old, but it is rare for the disease to develop in childhood [54].

In MEN2A-CLA patients, dermatological lesions are typically located in the scapular region. They may be the first sign of the dis ease before the onset of MTC at an early age. In the subtype of MEN2A and CLA, the fre quency of phaeochromocytoma and pHPT appears to be the same as in classical MEN2A. In MEN2A with cutaneous lichen amyloidosis, the prevalence of different mani festations is medullary thyroid carcinoma
95%, phaeochromocytoma 50% and primary hyperparathyroidism 15% [48]. The earliest age of onset reported in the literature is 3 years [55].

In MEN2A with Hirschsprung’s disease, medullary thyroid carcinoma occurs in 80%, phaeochromocytoma in 20% and primary hyperparathyroidism in 5% [48]. Almost all patients with MEN2A and Hirschsprung’s disease show signs of the abnormality soon after birth. Hirschsprung’s disease occurs in approximately 7% of MEN2A patients, and of patients with Hirschsprung’s disease, 2–5% have MEN2A [56–58].

FMTC is viewed as a milder phenotypic variant of MEN2A with medullary thyroid carcinoma alone, presenting with lower pene trance, later age of onset, and with less aggres sive disease than in classical MEN2A.

MEN2B is associated with medullary thy roid carcinoma, phaeochromocytoma and extra-endocrine manifestations, such as gan glioneuromas of the digestive tract (100% of cases) as well as musculoskeletal and ophthal mological abnormalities. Medullary thyroid carcinoma in MEN2B is the most prominent disease, and the tumour manifests an average 10 years earlier than in MEN2A [20]. It is pre ceded by C-cell hyperplasia followed by devel opment metastasises quickly to lymph nodes and to different organs (liver, lungs and bone brain). Clinical signs of gastrointestinal involvement include intermittent constipation and diarrhoea and, in some cases, urgent sur gery is required for bowel obstruction. Skeletal malformations are present in marfanoid body habitus (70% of cases), narrow long facies, pes cavus, pes excavatum, high-arched palate, sco liosis and slipped capital femoral epiphysis. Ocular abnormalities include inability to pro duce tears in infancy (alacrimia, 40% of cases), thickened and everted eyelids, mild ptosis and corneal nerve hypertrophy (45%) [48]. In the international cohort, median age at first diagnosis of phaeochromocytoma in MEN2B patients was 24 years. Adrenalsparing surgery was done in 31 patients, three (10%) of 31 patients had long-term recur rence, while normal adrenal function was obtained in 16 (61%) of patients [49].

The C-cells of the thyroid gland secrete calci tonin. The serum level of calcitonin indicates the size of the C-cell mass, and it is used as an important tumour marker for MTC. Serum calcitonin levels may be elevated in the absence of MTC in patients with various conditions, such as chronic renal failure, autoimmune thyroiditis, hyperparathyroidism or various neuroendocrine tumours, and in the presence of heterophilic antibodies. If there is a dis crepancy between the clinical signs and the low serum calcitonin levels found, a hook effect (an assay problem seen with sandwich immunoassays) must be ruled out. The paral lel measurement of the prohormone of calci tonin, procalcitonin and calcitonin resulting in a high ratio of procalcitonin to calcitonin suggests a worse outcome of the disease. The interpretation of calcitonin levels must be assay specific. In children, the reference range for calcitonin levels depends on age, and assay method data are available in different paediat ric age groups [59, 60]: <6 months of age < 40 ng/L, between 6 months and 3 years of age < 15 ng/L and over 3 years of age, the adult reference range is acceptable, for girls <5 ng/L, for boys <10 ng/L is acceptable for normal values. In individual cases, an increase in the calcitonin level after calcium or penta gastrin stimulation testing may help to deter mine the timing of prophylactic thyroidectomy in children with MEN2A, to diagnose or exclude the presence of MTC in thyroid nod ules or, for example, to detect progression after thyroidectomy. The production of carci noembryonic antigen is not specific for MTC, and no data for children are available [61]. In some cases, MTC can secrete other hormones in addition to calcitonin, e.g., ectopic ACTH production, leading to hypercortisolism, asso ciated with a poor outcome [62].
paragraphs.heading: 36.3.3 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: MEN2B is often caused by de novo muta tions; in these cases, the initial diagnosis is based on clinical features. In a study of 35 MEN2B children with de novo mutations, 22 presented with endocrine manifestations (phaeochromocytoma or space-occupying symptoms due to MTC) with a mean age of
paragraphs.heading: 36.3.3 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: diagnosis of 11.8 years, while 13 presented with nonendocrine manifestations (oral neu romas, corneal nerve abnormalities, persistent diarrhoea, failure to thrive or skeletal abnor malities) at a mean age of 9.9. It is crucially important to recognise the distinctive pheno type of MEN2B, as early diagnosis can help for early detection of elevated calcitonin and MTC, as well as parathyroid and adrenal dis ease [49].
paragraphs.heading: 36.3.3 Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: The RET proto-oncogene is located on chro mosome 10q11.2 and contains 21 exons. RET encodes a tyrosine kinase receptor with key roles in cells growth, differentiation and survival. This gene is widely expressed in var ious endocrine tissues, such as the C-cells of thyroid gland, adrenal medulla and pituitary as well as in neurons. The gene was discov ered to be an oncogene in 1985 [63]. The germline RET mutations associated with MEN2 result in a gain-of-function. In MEN2A, mutations are located mostly in exon 10 (codons 609, 611, 618, 620) or exon 11 (codon 630, 631, 634, 666), but mutations can also locate in the intracellular tyrosinekinase domain 1, exon 13 (codon 768, 790), exon 14 (codon 804), exon 15 (codon 891) and exon 16 (codon 912) [64]. A germline mutation at codon 634 of the RET gene can be detected in almost all patients of MEN2A and CLA. The most common RET muta tions in MEN2A and Hirschprung’s disease are at codons 620 and 618 [49, 65]. In typical clinical manifestations of MEN2A, the absence of a pathogenic germline mutation in RET gene is very rare. MEN2B is mainly caused by the germline M918T RET muta tion (>95% of cases) or by the A883F variant (<5%). An atypical form of MEN2B is known to present clinical signs of the disease only at the age of 20 to 30 years, and genetic analyses have shown duplicated and tandem RET germline mutations in these patients [64]. Duplicated or multiple RET germline
paragraphs.heading: 36.3.4 Genetics

paragraphs.text: mutations have also been identified in atypi cal FMTC and MEN2A families. The M918V variant was described with an FMTC phenotype, and it is suggested this variant to be classified as moderate risk [66].

Clinical aggressiveness of the MTC associa tion with mutations in RET genes are divided into three groups such as highest risk, high risk and moderate risk, according to the 2015 American Thyroid Association (ATA) guide line for the management of medullary thyroid carcinoma [67]. The highest risk includes patients with MEN2B and RET codon M918T mutation, high risk includes patients with MEN2A and RET codon A883F and C634F/G/R/S/W/Y mutations, and MEN2B patients with RET codon A883F mutation. Moderate risk includes patients with muta tions other than the highest and high risk ones [67].
paragraphs.heading: Mutations and Screening

paragraphs.text: Screening for phaeochromocytoma should begin at the age of 11 years according to the ATA highest and ATA high groups, and at the age of 16 years in the ATA moderate group. To detect adrenal tumour hormone secretion, plasma metanephrines and normetanephrines or urine metanephrines and normetaneph rines from 24-h urine samples are required. Imaging procedures of the adrenal glands are necessary in the case of hormonal activity (ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging of the adrenal gland regions are preferred).
paragraphs.heading: Mutations and Screening

paragraphs.text: Hyperparathyroidism in children is often mild and asymptomatic in MEN2A. Enlarged parathyroid glands have been found in nor mocalcaemic patients at the time of thyroidec tomy. Hyperparathyroidism is most common in patients with the RET codon 634 mutation. Screening for hyperparathyroidism is recom mended from 11 years of age in the ATA high risk category and from 16 years of age in the ATA moderate category, using serum ionised calcium or albumin-corrected calcium with parallel measurement of serum intact para thyroid hormone levels.
paragraphs.heading: Mutations and Screening

paragraphs.text: When the preoperative basal serum calcitonin is <40 ng/L, a total thyroidectomy and cervi cal lymph node dissection is the treatment of choice for patients with MTC; locally advanced or metastatic disease requires more surgical intervention.
