paragraphs.heading: Abbreviations

paragraphs.text: McCune-Albright Syndrome (MAS) is a rare genetic disorder that was first described in 1936 by Dr. Donavan McCune who reported a 9-year-old girl with precious puberty (PP), skin hyperpigmentation and hyperthyroidism [1]. Then in 1937 Dr. Fuller Albright pub lished a case series of 5 patients [2]. The first was a 23-year-old female with skin hyperpig mentation, PP, and osteitis fibrosa cystica with a fracture of the right femur. The second patient was a 39-year-old female with a frac ture of the right femur with osteitis fibrosis, history of PP, irregular menses, hyperpig mented skin, and hyperparathyroidism. The third patient was a 31⁄2 year old female with fractures, PP, rickets, skin hyperpigmentation, intellectual disability, hypophosphatemia, hydrocephalus, and bilateral fibrous dysplasia (FD) of bone. The fourth patient was an 8-year-old female with PP, skin hyperpigmen tation, FD of bone and hypercalcemia. The last was a 10-year-old boy with hyperparathy roidism who had multiple fractures, FD of bone, frontal bossing and skin hyperpigmen tation. It was on the basis of these early cases
paragraphs.heading: 37.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: that MAS was characterized as a classic triad of FD of bone, PP, and café-au-lait (CAL) skin pigmentation. However, as is clear from these original reports, the disease exists within a broad spectrum of additional manifesta tions including other associated endocrinopa thies besides PP.

37.1 With this mutation, there is dysregulation of production of cyclic AMP leading to unregulated ligand-independent signal trans duction affecting multiple receptors including those for LH, FSH, TSH, GHRH, and ACTH [5].
paragraphs.heading: 37.2 Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: The mutations causing MAS arise de novo in an early embryologic cell line and are thus postzygotic and present in a mosaic distribu tion. The most common is the substitution of arginine at codon 201 with cystine or histidine but mutations at codon 227 have also been noted [3, 6]. The presence of mosaicism was first discovered by Dr. Happle in 1986 who found that there was an intermingling of nor mal cells with mutated cells, which presum ably allowed for their survival [7]. The inherent variability in the number of cells and cells lines affected leads to extreme phenotypic heterogeneity among patients with MAS.
paragraphs.heading: 37.2 Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: Early pubertal development in children with MAS is independent of the HPG axis and is thus a form of peripheral PP.
paragraphs.heading: 37.3.2 Gonads

paragraphs.text: PP occurs in up to about 85% of affected girls. This is due to autonomously functioning unilateral ovarian cysts which intermittently produce extreme elevations in serum estra diol. This phenomenon has been termed “constitutive activation”. The PP in MAS is manifested clinically as a sudden onset of painless vaginal bleeding (which can be pro fuse) most commonly beginning between the ages of 1 and 5 years with minimal breast development. The frequency of vaginal bleed ing in girls with MAS is extremely variable. Some girls experience rare episodes separated by long intervals of quiescence whereas others may have frequent vaginal bleeding accompa nied by growth acceleration, advanced skele tal maturation, and a poor prognosis for adult height. If girls with MAS are not identified appropriately, unnecessary oophorectomies can occur due to concerns for ovarian granu losa cell tumors. On ultrasound, the ovaries of girls with MAS typically demonstrate a uni lateral cystic mass which cannot be differenti ated from an ovarian tumor [9]. Once central puberty starts, it generally overrides the autonomous ovarian activation and normal ovulatory cycles (with the potential for nor mal fertility) occur. However, intermittent epi sodes of autonomous ovarian function leading to irregular menses have been reported in adolescent girls and women with MAS. Rarely, these episodes can lead to large and persistent ovarian cysts with risk of tor sion [10, 11].
paragraphs.heading: 37.3.2 Gonads

paragraphs.text: In boys, PP is much less common but when present is characterized by autonomous tes tosterone production due to Leydig cells har boring the mutation. About 85% of males have abnormal testes with unilateral or bilat eral macroorchidism [12]. In cases of Sertoli cell only involvement, there have been elevated levels of inhibin B and anti-Müllerian hor mone with enlarged testes but prepubertal tes tosterone and gonadotropin concentrations. Testicular microlithiasis has also been reported in 30–62% of boys with MAS. On testicular ultrasound, focal hyper- and hypoechoic lesions are seen as well as diffuse heterogeneity and focal calcifications, which tend to not progress [12, 13]. Current recom mendations are to monitor these with repeat
ultrasound, although the exact interval for repeat imaging has not been established [12].

About half of all individuals with MAS have thyroid involvement. Ultrasound findings of mixed cystic and solid lesions interspersed with areas of normal-appearing tissue are common. Hyperthyroidism is present in 10–30% of individuals and is caused by both increased hormone production and increased conversion of thyroxine (T4) to triiodothyro nine (T3) [11]. If undetected this can lead to thyroid storm during anesthetic induction for surgery. Uncontrolled hyperthyroidism can cause accelerated skeletal maturation, ele vated bone turnover and increased susceptibility to fracture [14].
paragraphs.heading: 37.3.3 Thyroid

paragraphs.text: Growth hormone (GH) excess with or with out concurrent hyperprolactinemia can occur if the anterior pituitary is involved. If GH
paragraphs.heading: 37.3.4 Pituitary

paragraphs.text: excess is present, individuals may develop gigantism as well as acromegalic features including jaw and tongue enlargement [15]. GH hypersecretion can lead to the expansion of craniofacial FD, which increases the risk of vision loss and can lead to macrocephaly [11, 16]. Therefore, early diagnosis and treat ment are essential.
paragraphs.heading: 37.3.4 Pituitary

paragraphs.text: Cushing syndrome due to hypercortisolism is a very rare manifestation of MAS. When it occurs, it is typically in the neonatal period and is caused by excess cortisol production from the fetal adrenal gland. Cortisol excess is caused by tonic activation of the G-protein coupled ACTH receptor within the adrenal cortex leading to unregulated overproduction of cAMP [17]. These infants can present as small for gestational age with failure to thrive, hypertension, feeding difficulties, Cushingoid features or respiratory illness [11]. Spontaneous regression from involution of the adrenal gland has been reported in approximately half of survivors of neonatal Cushing syndrome and MAS [17, 18]. Monitoring is needed for late onset develop ment of adrenal insufficiency after the neona tal period [19].
paragraphs.heading: 37.3.5 Adrenal

paragraphs.text: FD occurs early in life and expands during childhood. Increases in the RANKL and IL-6 messaging pathways leads to the formation of abnormal bone and increased osteoclast activ ity. On a cellular level, this appears as poorly mineralized woven bone that replaces the marrow. There is unregulated osteoclast acti vation with increased bone turnover/resorp tion. This can be seen on CT scan as a characteristic ground glass appearance or increased uptake on bone scintigraphy. It is helpful to obtain a Tc99m or 18F-NaF PET/ CT scan to assess the extent of the skeletal burden [20]. It is recommended to obtain the first bone scan at age 5 years as the majority (90% or more) of the clinically significant
paragraphs.heading: 37.3.6 Bone

paragraphs.text: skeletal lesions can be identified by that time [10, 11, 21, 22].
paragraphs.heading: 37.3.6 Bone

paragraphs.text: Due to the increase in osteoclastic activity, there is also an increase in FGF23, which can lead to renal tubulopathy with some degree of phosphate wasting [23, 24]. Hypophosphatemia, though infrequent, is due to alterations in FGF23 processing result ing in abnormal cleavage patterns leading to increased intact serum FGF23 [25]. This can increase during periods of rapid skeletal growth. Hypophosphatemia may contribute to rickets/osteomalacia, increased fractures, and bone pain. Hypophosphatemia and hyperthyroidism are both risk factors for sco liosis [14, 26].
paragraphs.heading: 37.3.6 Bone

paragraphs.text: Skeletal manifestations can occur in a sin gle bone (classified as monostotic), multiple bones (polyostotic) or all bones (panostotic). Patchy bone disease occurs throughout the body leading to pain, deformities, and/or frac tures. Skull invasion can lead to deformities, hydrocephalus and nerve compression leading to hearing loss or blindness. There can also be some nasal obstruction and malocclusion along with facial asymmetry. Vertebral involvement can lead to scoliosis. Appendicular skeletal abnormalities that are commonly seen include “wind-swept” defor mity and “shepherd’s crook” deformity. Windswept deformities are those in which it appears that both legs have been swept to one side by a gust of wind. Shepard’s crook deformity refers to abnormal curvature of the femur or humerus. Fragility fractures are common. As treatment options are extremely limited, bone disease is typically the greatest source of mor bidity in individuals with MAS [5, 27].
paragraphs.heading: 37.3.6 Bone

paragraphs.text: Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMNs) have been described in patients with MAS. These are pancreatic mucin-producing cysts. IPMNs have also been associated with hepatic adenomas, hemangiomas, hamarto mas, focal nodular hyperplasia, biliary cysts and fatty liver in MAS [28]. These findings
paragraphs.heading: 37.3.7.1 Gastrointestinal

paragraphs.text: can also occur independent of IPMNs. IPMNs are thought to form because of increased signaling in the JAK/STAT pathway [29].
paragraphs.heading: 37.3.7.1 Gastrointestinal

paragraphs.text: Upper gastrointestinal polyps have also been described. Gastroesophageal reflux may manifest in childhood. When present, hepati tis and neonatal cholestasis generally wane with age in severity but are persistent [30]. Pancreatitis and diabetes mellitus have also been reported. Diabetes is thought to be caused by a combination of decreased insulin secretion secondary to recurrent pancreatitis and insulin resistance in overweight and obese individuals [10].
paragraphs.heading: 37.3.7.1 Gastrointestinal

paragraphs.text: Patients with MAS may have an increased risk of anaphylaxis, the exact etiology of which is poorly understood. The histamine 1 (H1) and histamine 2 (H2) receptors are coupled with G proteins [31]. The H2 receptor works with Gsα and cAMP for signaling [32–34], which has been associated with increased gastric his taminic activity and a predisposition for reflux. The H1 receptor, which is associated with allergy and urticaria, is coupled with a different G-protein (Gqα) pathway but there is known crosstalk between Gsα and Gq/11α. This may explain the increased wheal and flare responses to histamine observed in MAS patients [35].
paragraphs.heading: 37.3.7.2 Mass Cell Hypersensitivity

paragraphs.text: Rare cases of MAS have been described in which there is involvement of the heart, liver, kidneys, and other vital tissues. In all such cases, the condition has been lethal [36].
paragraphs.heading: 37.3.7.3 Multisystemic Involvement

paragraphs.text: There have been some rare cases of malignant transformation of areas of FD associated with previous radiation therapy and GH excess in adults with MAS. Therefore, radia tion therapy should be avoided in these patients as they are at increased risk of osteo sarcoma [37].
paragraphs.heading: 37.3.7.4 Malignancy

paragraphs.text: There have also been case reports of papil lary thyroid carcinoma in children with MAS in the setting of hyperthyroidism [38]. There is
paragraphs.heading: 37.3.7.4 Malignancy

paragraphs.text: one report of a clear cell thyroid carcinoma in an adult patient [38]. Breast cancer risk is increased in women with MAS especially in those with thoracic FD lesions. Therefore, it is recommended to start screening mammo grams in the third and fourth decades of life [39].
paragraphs.heading: 37.3.7.4 Malignancy

paragraphs.text: Testicular carcinoma has been described at a very low incidence. Abnormal testicular ultrasound findings should be monitored closely [12].
paragraphs.heading: 37.3.7.4 Malignancy

paragraphs.text: IPMNs can be high grade or have worri some features on imaging that should be mon itored as it is not known whether or when malignant transformation will occur or when resection would be optimal [28]. Pancreatic adenocarcinoma has only been described in one patient in the literature [40]. GI and liver tumors have been rarely described [40].
paragraphs.heading: 37.3.7.4 Malignancy

paragraphs.text: MAS is a clinical diagnosis. The criteria include having two or more classic clinical fea tures including CAL macules, FD and endo crinopathies (PP, hyperthyroidism, GH excess, hypophosphatemia or neonatal hypercorti solism). However, it has long been recognized that some patients with MAS have a forme fruste of the disease with only a single mani festation such as isolated FD or isolated peripheral PP. Patients previously thought to have isolated FD have also been found to have other features of MAS on careful review of history and physical exam [41].
paragraphs.heading: 37.4 Diagnostic Criteria

paragraphs.text: There is low yield in identification of a somatic activating pathogenic variant in GNAS1 in peripheral blood lymphocytes. In contrast, genetic analysis of tissue with a suspected mutation has significantly increased accuracy and sensitivity [42]. Biopsies with fresh or fresh frozen samples are ideal but may need to be repeated if they contain more normal tis sue than tissue with the mutation. When undertaken, targeted analysis of exons 8 and
paragraphs.heading: 37.5 Genetic Testing

paragraphs.text: 9 in lesional tissue using PCR sequencing based methods is recommended [43].
paragraphs.heading: 37.5 Genetic Testing

paragraphs.text: The initial evaluation in children with sus pected MAS should include a bone age x-ray and serum IGF-1, prolactin, GH, thyroid function tests, LH/FSH, and testosterone/ estradiol levels, as indicated. An elevated IGF1 or growth acceleration should prompt an oral glucose tolerance test to look for GH excess. Thyroid ultrasound should also be obtained periodically after age 3 years. For concerns of neonatal hypercortisolism, a chemical metabolic panel, 24-h urinary free cortisol, serum cortisol, and/or low dose dexa methasone suppression test may be employed [17]. As mentioned earlier, first bone scans should be performed by age 5 years as most FD lesions will be apparent and additional studies are not necessary after age 15 years [10, 11].
paragraphs.heading: 37.6 Surveillance

paragraphs.text: Patients with PP should have ongoing clinic follow-up and annual bone ages [11]. Annual evaluations by an ophthalmologist and audiologist are important for patients with craniofacial FD [10]. GI surveillance with imagining should be considered in those with a history of pancreatitis [29].
paragraphs.heading: 37.6 Surveillance

paragraphs.text: No single therapy has been found to be supe rior for the treatment of PP in girls with MAS. In addition, clinical trials are hampered by the extreme rarity of the disease and the remarkable phenotypic heterogeneity among affected patients. In the studies that have been conducted, girls typically serve as their own controls. Given the unpredictable nature of vaginal bleeding episodes, a period of obser vation is recommended following an initial diagnosis of MAS. If therapy is deemed nec essary, the goal is to block the effects of estro
paragraphs.heading: 37.7.1 Precocious Puberty

paragraphs.text: gen or to decrease its synthesis. Tamoxifen, a selective estrogen receptor modulator, has been shown to cause cessation of vaginal bleeding and a significant increase in predicted adult height in girls with MAS [44]. While an increase in uterine size was noted after treat ment for 1 year, long term follow-up of tamox ifen treated patients failed to identify any safety signals associated with its use [45]. The third-generation aromatase inhibitor (AI), letrozole, has also been shown to decrease rates of skeletal maturation, growth velocity, and improve predicted adult height, although ovarian torsion has also been reported with the use of this medication [46]. First- and sec ond-generation AIs have not been found to be efficacious in MAS, nor has the thirdgeneration AI, anastrozole [47]. Fulvestrant, a pure estrogen receptor antagonist, has been shown to decrease vaginal bleeding and rate of skeletal maturation [48]. However, the need for weekly injections is a significant drawback of this medication. Surgical intervention for ovarian cysts is typically discouraged as these almost always resolve on their own [9].
paragraphs.heading: 37.7.1 Precocious Puberty

paragraphs.text: In boys, a combination of an androgen receptor blocker such as bicalutamide with a third-generation AI such as letrozole or anas trozole represents state of the art treatment [12]. In both boys and girls, surveillance for the onset of central puberty through periodic measurement of ultrasensitive LH or GnRHa stimulation testing is imperative. If secondary central PP ensues, a GnRH analog is added as adjunctive therapy.
paragraphs.heading: 37.7.1 Precocious Puberty

paragraphs.text: Methimazole is effective for the medical man agement of hyperthyroidism. Propylthiouracil is not recommended because of an increased risk of hepatotoxicity in children. Thyroidectomy is definitive treatment [21]. Radioablation is not recommended due to the potential for increased uptake by tissues bear ing a somatic activating GNAS mutation, which could theoretically increase the risk of malignancy [11, 14].

Medical treatment with bisphosphonates has been used in patients with MAS. It is also important to ensure that Vitamin D and cal cium supplementation are adequate in these patients. Denosumab, a RANKL inhibitor, has also been used to treat FD, but there is a rebound increase in fracture risk when this medication is discontinued in addition to a risk of hypercalcemia and increased bone resorption [21].
paragraphs.heading: 37.7.4 Bone Disease

paragraphs.text: Surgery may be needed for management or prevention of fracture or deformities but is extremely problematic as it can worsen FD. Surgery may also be needed for manage ment of scoliosis as complications of restric tive lung disease can be life threatening. Lower
paragraphs.heading: 37.7.4 Bone Disease

paragraphs.text: extremity surgery may be indicated for weight bearing pain and deformities that impair gait. Craniofacial surgery is needed for facial defor mities, nerve compression and aneurysmal cysts. As mentioned earlier, skull lesions can lead to narrowing of the optic canals, which can lead to blindness if not treated with surgi cal intervention [27, 50].

paragraphs.text: Despite significant advances in diagnosis and treatment, lingering questions remain regard ing many aspects of MAS. The physiologic trigger for the intermittent episodes of gonadal activation in children with MAS and PP is unknown. Whether newer medications will result in improved outcomes of bone dis ease and various endocrinopathies in MAS remains to be seen. Continued multidisci plinary collaboration and multicenter studies are key in order to enhance knowledge and optimize quality of life in patients with MAS.

# 37. McCune-Albright Syndrome > Source attribution: [Source credits](../../SOURCE_CREDITS.md). ## PDF page 993 | printed page 997 ### McCune-Albright Syndrome Sarah A. Ackah and Erica A. Radovick, M. Misra (eds.), Pediatric Endocrinology, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-66296-6_37 ## PDF page 994 | printed page 998 ### Abbreviations AI – Aromatase inhibitor CAL – Café-au-lait FD – Fibrous dysplasia FGF23 – Fibroblast growth factor 23 GH – Growth hormone GPCR – G-protein coupled receptor Gsα – G protein alpha subunit HPG – Hypothalamic pituitary gonadal IPMNs – Intraductal papillary mucinous neo plasms MAS – McCune-Albright syndrome PP – Precocious puberty ### 37.1 Introduction McCune-Albright Syndrome (MAS) is a rare genetic disorder that was first described in 1936 by Dr. Donavan McCune who reported a 9-year-old girl with precious puberty (PP), skin hyperpigmentation and hyperthyroidism [1]. Then in 1937 Dr. Fuller Albright pub lished a case series of 5 patients [2]. The first was a 23-year-old female with skin hyperpig mentation, PP, and osteitis fibrosa cystica with a fracture of the right femur. The second patient was a 39-year-old female with a frac ture of the right femur with osteitis fibrosis, history of PP, irregular menses, hyperpig mented skin, and hyperparathyroidism. The third patient was a 31⁄2 year old female with fractures, PP, rickets, skin hyperpigmentation, intellectual disability, hypophosphatemia, hydrocephalus, and bilateral fibrous dysplasia (FD) of bone. The fourth patient was an 8-year-old female with PP, skin hyperpigmen tation, FD of bone and hypercalcemia. The last was a 10-year-old boy with hyperparathy roidism who had multiple fractures, FD of bone, frontal bossing and skin hyperpigmen tation. It was on the basis of these early cases ### 37 that MAS was characterized as a classic triad of FD of bone, PP, and café-au-lait (CAL) skin pigmentation. However, as is clear from these original reports, the disease exists within a broad spectrum of additional manifesta tions including other associated endocrinopa thies besides PP. ### 37.2 Pathophysiology 3 4 37.1 With this mutation, there is dysregulation of production of cyclic AMP leading to unregulated ligand-independent signal trans duction affecting multiple receptors including those for LH, FSH, TSH, GHRH, and ACTH [5]. The mutations causing MAS arise de novo in an early embryologic cell line and are thus postzygotic and present in a mosaic distribu tion. The most common is the substitution of arginine at codon 201 with cystine or histidine but mutations at codon 227 have also been noted [3, 6]. The presence of mosaicism was first discovered by Dr. Happle in 1986 who found that there was an intermingling of nor mal cells with mutated cells, which presum ably allowed for their survival [7]. The inherent variability in the number of cells and cells lines affected leads to extreme phenotypic heterogeneity among patients with MAS. ## PDF page 995 | printed page 999 ### 37.3 Phenotype/Clinical Features ### 37.3.1 Skin 8 37.2a 37.2b ### 37.3.2 Gonads Early pubertal development in children with MAS is independent of the HPG axis and is thus a form of peripheral PP. ![Source image](../../figures/ch037_p0995_01.jpg) Unmatched source image; PDF page 995. Consult the original caption. ![Source image](../../figures/ch037_p0995_02.jpg) Unmatched source image; PDF page 995. Consult the original caption. ## PDF page 996 | printed page 1000 PP occurs in up to about 85% of affected girls. This is due to autonomously functioning unilateral ovarian cysts which intermittently produce extreme elevations in serum estra diol. This phenomenon has been termed “constitutive activation”. The PP in MAS is manifested clinically as a sudden onset of painless vaginal bleeding (which can be pro fuse) most commonly beginning between the ages of 1 and 5 years with minimal breast development. The frequency of vaginal bleed ing in girls with MAS is extremely variable. Some girls experience rare episodes separated by long intervals of quiescence whereas others may have frequent vaginal bleeding accompa nied by growth acceleration, advanced skele tal maturation, and a poor prognosis for adult height. If girls with MAS are not identified appropriately, unnecessary oophorectomies can occur due to concerns for ovarian granu losa cell tumors. On ultrasound, the ovaries of girls with MAS typically demonstrate a uni lateral cystic mass which cannot be differenti ated from an ovarian tumor [9]. Once central puberty starts, it generally overrides the autonomous ovarian activation and normal ovulatory cycles (with the potential for nor mal fertility) occur. However, intermittent epi sodes of autonomous ovarian function leading to irregular menses have been reported in adolescent girls and women with MAS. Rarely, these episodes can lead to large and persistent ovarian cysts with risk of tor sion [10, 11]. ### 37 In boys, PP is much less common but when present is characterized by autonomous tes tosterone production due to Leydig cells har boring the mutation. About 85% of males have abnormal testes with unilateral or bilat eral macroorchidism [12]. In cases of Sertoli cell only involvement, there have been elevated levels of inhibin B and anti-Müllerian hor mone with enlarged testes but prepubertal tes tosterone and gonadotropin concentrations. Testicular microlithiasis has also been reported in 30–62% of boys with MAS. On testicular ultrasound, focal hyper- and hypoechoic lesions are seen as well as diffuse heterogeneity and focal calcifications, which tend to not progress [12, 13]. Current recom mendations are to monitor these with repeat Table 37.1 Potential clinical features of gonadal involvement in boys vs girls with MAS Boys Girls PP: Testicular enlargement Penile enlargement Pubic hair Growth acceleration Secondary central PP Sertoli cell only involvement: Macroorchidism (unilateral or bilateral) Testicular microlithiasis Calcification on testicular US PP: Vaginal bleeding Breast development Pubic hair Growth acceleration Unilateral ovarian cyst/mass on US Secondary central PP ultrasound, although the exact interval for repeat imaging has not been established [12]. 37.1 ### 37.3.3 Thyroid About half of all individuals with MAS have thyroid involvement. Ultrasound findings of mixed cystic and solid lesions interspersed with areas of normal-appearing tissue are common. Hyperthyroidism is present in 10–30% of individuals and is caused by both increased hormone production and increased conversion of thyroxine (T4) to triiodothyro nine (T3) [11]. If undetected this can lead to thyroid storm during anesthetic induction for surgery. Uncontrolled hyperthyroidism can cause accelerated skeletal maturation, ele vated bone turnover and increased susceptibility to fracture [14]. ### 37.3.4 Pituitary Growth hormone (GH) excess with or with out concurrent hyperprolactinemia can occur if the anterior pituitary is involved. GH hypersecretion can lead to the expansion of craniofacial FD, which increases the risk of vision loss and can lead to macrocephaly [11, 16]. Therefore, early diagnosis and treat ment are essential. ### 37.3.5 Adrenal Cushing syndrome due to hypercortisolism is a very rare manifestation of MAS. When it occurs, it is typically in the neonatal period and is caused by excess cortisol production from the fetal adrenal gland. Cortisol excess is caused by tonic activation of the G-protein coupled ACTH receptor within the adrenal cortex leading to unregulated overproduction of cAMP [17]. These infants can present as small for gestational age with failure to thrive, hypertension, feeding difficulties, Cushingoid features or respiratory illness [11]. Spontaneous regression from involution of the adrenal gland has been reported in approximately half of survivors of neonatal Cushing syndrome and MAS [17, 18]. Monitoring is needed for late onset develop ment of adrenal insufficiency after the neona tal period [19]. ### 37.3.6 Bone FD occurs early in life and expands during childhood. Increases in the RANKL and IL-6 messaging pathways leads to the formation of abnormal bone and increased osteoclast activ ity. On a cellular level, this appears as poorly mineralized woven bone that replaces the marrow. There is unregulated osteoclast acti vation with increased bone turnover/resorp tion. This can be seen on CT scan as a characteristic ground glass appearance or increased uptake on bone scintigraphy. It is helpful to obtain a Tc99m or 18F-NaF PET/ CT scan to assess the extent of the skeletal burden [20]. It is recommended to obtain the first bone scan at age 5 years as the majority (90% or more) of the clinically significant skeletal lesions can be identified by that time [10, 11, 21, 22]. Due to the increase in osteoclastic activity, there is also an increase in FGF23, which can lead to renal tubulopathy with some degree of phosphate wasting [23, 24]. Hypophosphatemia, though infrequent, is due to alterations in FGF23 processing result ing in abnormal cleavage patterns leading to increased intact serum FGF23 [25]. This can increase during periods of rapid skeletal growth. Hypophosphatemia may contribute to rickets/osteomalacia, increased fractures, and bone pain. Hypophosphatemia and hyperthyroidism are both risk factors for sco liosis [14, 26]. Skeletal manifestations can occur in a sin gle bone (classified as monostotic), multiple bones (polyostotic) or all bones (panostotic). Patchy bone disease occurs throughout the body leading to pain, deformities, and/or frac tures. Skull invasion can lead to deformities, hydrocephalus and nerve compression leading to hearing loss or blindness. There can also be some nasal obstruction and malocclusion along with facial asymmetry. Vertebral involvement can lead to scoliosis. Appendicular skeletal abnormalities that are commonly seen include “wind-swept” defor mity and “shepherd’s crook” deformity. Windswept deformities are those in which it appears that both legs have been swept to one side by a gust of wind. Shepard’s crook deformity refers to abnormal curvature of the femur or humerus. Fragility fractures are common. As treatment options are extremely limited, bone disease is typically the greatest source of mor bidity in individuals with MAS [5, 27]. ### 37.3.7 Rare Manifestations ### 37.3.7.1 Gastrointestinal Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMNs) have been described in patients with MAS. These are pancreatic mucin-producing cysts. IPMNs have also been associated with hepatic adenomas, hemangiomas, hamarto mas, focal nodular hyperplasia, biliary cysts and fatty liver in MAS [28]. These findings ## PDF page 998 | printed page 1002 can also occur independent of IPMNs. IPMNs are thought to form because of increased signaling in the JAK/STAT pathway [29]. Upper gastrointestinal polyps have also been described. Gastroesophageal reflux may manifest in childhood. When present, hepati tis and neonatal cholestasis generally wane with age in severity but are persistent [30]. Pancreatitis and diabetes mellitus have also been reported. Diabetes is thought to be caused by a combination of decreased insulin secretion secondary to recurrent pancreatitis and insulin resistance in overweight and obese individuals [10]. ### 37.3.7.2 Mass Cell Hypersensitivity Patients with MAS may have an increased risk of anaphylaxis, the exact etiology of which is poorly understood. The histamine 1 (H1) and histamine 2 (H2) receptors are coupled with G proteins [31]. The H2 receptor works with Gsα and cAMP for signaling [32–34], which has been associated with increased gastric his taminic activity and a predisposition for reflux. The H1 receptor, which is associated with allergy and urticaria, is coupled with a different G-protein (Gqα) pathway but there is known crosstalk between Gsα and Gq/11α. This may explain the increased wheal and flare responses to histamine observed in MAS patients [35]. ### 37.3.7.3 Multisystemic Involvement Rare cases of MAS have been described in which there is involvement of the heart, liver, kidneys, and other vital tissues. In all such cases, the condition has been lethal [36]. ### 37 ### 37.3.7.4 Malignancy There have been some rare cases of malignant transformation of areas of FD associated with previous radiation therapy and GH excess in adults with MAS. Therefore, radia tion therapy should be avoided in these patients as they are at increased risk of osteo sarcoma [37]. There have also been case reports of papil lary thyroid carcinoma in children with MAS in the setting of hyperthyroidism [38]. There is one report of a clear cell thyroid carcinoma in an adult patient [38]. Breast cancer risk is increased in women with MAS especially in those with thoracic FD lesions. Therefore, it is recommended to start screening mammo grams in the third and fourth decades of life [39]. Testicular carcinoma has been described at a very low incidence. Abnormal testicular ultrasound findings should be monitored closely [12]. IPMNs can be high grade or have worri some features on imaging that should be mon itored as it is not known whether or when malignant transformation will occur or when resection would be optimal [28]. Pancreatic adenocarcinoma has only been described in one patient in the literature [40]. GI and liver tumors have been rarely described [40]. ### 37.4 Diagnostic Criteria MAS is a clinical diagnosis. The criteria include having two or more classic clinical fea tures including CAL macules, FD and endo crinopathies (PP, hyperthyroidism, GH excess, hypophosphatemia or neonatal hypercorti solism). However, it has long been recognized that some patients with MAS have a forme fruste of the disease with only a single mani festation such as isolated FD or isolated peripheral PP. Patients previously thought to have isolated FD have also been found to have other features of MAS on careful review of history and physical exam [41]. ### 37.5 Genetic Testing There is low yield in identification of a somatic activating pathogenic variant in GNAS1 in peripheral blood lymphocytes. In contrast, genetic analysis of tissue with a suspected mutation has significantly increased accuracy and sensitivity [42]. Biopsies with fresh or fresh frozen samples are ideal but may need to be repeated if they contain more normal tis sue than tissue with the mutation. When undertaken, targeted analysis of exons 8 and ## PDF page 999 | printed page 1003 9 in lesional tissue using PCR sequencing based methods is recommended [43]. ### 37.6 Surveillance The initial evaluation in children with sus pected MAS should include a bone age x-ray and serum IGF-1, prolactin, GH, thyroid function tests, LH/FSH, and testosterone/ estradiol levels, as indicated. An elevated IGF1 or growth acceleration should prompt an oral glucose tolerance test to look for GH excess. Thyroid ultrasound should also be obtained periodically after age 3 years. For concerns of neonatal hypercortisolism, a chemical metabolic panel, 24-h urinary free cortisol, serum cortisol, and/or low dose dexa methasone suppression test may be employed [17]. As mentioned earlier, first bone scans should be performed by age 5 years as most FD lesions will be apparent and additional studies are not necessary after age 15 years [10, 11]. Patients with PP should have ongoing clinic follow-up and annual bone ages [11]. Annual evaluations by an ophthalmologist and audiologist are important for patients with craniofacial FD [10]. GI surveillance with imagining should be considered in those with a history of pancreatitis [29]. ### 37.7 Management ### 37.7.1 Precocious Puberty No single therapy has been found to be supe rior for the treatment of PP in girls with MAS. In addition, clinical trials are hampered by the extreme rarity of the disease and the remarkable phenotypic heterogeneity among affected patients. In the studies that have been conducted, girls typically serve as their own controls. Given the unpredictable nature of vaginal bleeding episodes, a period of obser vation is recommended following an initial diagnosis of MAS. If therapy is deemed nec essary, the goal is to block the effects of estro gen or to decrease its synthesis. Tamoxifen, a selective estrogen receptor modulator, has been shown to cause cessation of vaginal bleeding and a significant increase in predicted adult height in girls with MAS [44]. While an increase in uterine size was noted after treat ment for 1 year, long term follow-up of tamox ifen treated patients failed to identify any safety signals associated with its use [45]. The third-generation aromatase inhibitor (AI), letrozole, has also been shown to decrease rates of skeletal maturation, growth velocity, and improve predicted adult height, although ovarian torsion has also been reported with the use of this medication [46]. First- and sec ond-generation AIs have not been found to be efficacious in MAS, nor has the thirdgeneration AI, anastrozole [47]. Fulvestrant, a pure estrogen receptor antagonist, has been shown to decrease vaginal bleeding and rate of skeletal maturation [48]. However, the need for weekly injections is a significant drawback of this medication. Surgical intervention for ovarian cysts is typically discouraged as these almost always resolve on their own [9]. In boys, a combination of an androgen receptor blocker such as bicalutamide with a third-generation AI such as letrozole or anas trozole represents state of the art treatment [12]. In both boys and girls, surveillance for the onset of central puberty through periodic measurement of ultrasensitive LH or GnRHa stimulation testing is imperative. If secondary central PP ensues, a GnRH analog is added as adjunctive therapy. ### 37.7.2 Thyroid Methimazole is effective for the medical man agement of hyperthyroidism. Propylthiouracil is not recommended because of an increased risk of hepatotoxicity in children. Thyroidectomy is definitive treatment [21]. Radioablation is not recommended due to the potential for increased uptake by tissues bear ing a somatic activating GNAS mutation, which could theoretically increase the risk of malignancy [11, 14]. ## PDF page 1000 | printed page 1004 Table 37.2 Current therapeutic options for the endocrinopathies in MAS and associated side effects Endocrinopathy Treatment Precocious puberty Letrozole Tamoxifen Fulvestrant Hyperthyroidism Methimazole Total thyroidectomy Acromegaly Pegvisomant Somatostatin analogs Pituitary surgery Radiotherapy Hyperprolactinemia Cabergoline Bromocriptine Cushing syndrome Metyrapone Ketoconazole Adrenalectomy Hypophosphatemia Rickets/osteomala cia Phosphorus and calcium supplementa tion Calcitriol Hyperparathyroid ism Primary: Parathyroidectomy Secondary: Vitamin D supplementation ### 37.7.3 GH Excess ### 37 49 11 16 47 37.2 Side effects Ovarian torsion Uterine enlargement Agranulocytosis, acute liver failure Permanent hypothyroidism Injection site reactions, hepatotoxicity Cholelithiasis, hepatotoxicity High risk of sarcomatous transforma tion Dizziness, impulsive behavior, nausea Hypertension, hirsutism, hyperkalemia Hepatotoxicity, hypogonadism Adrenal insufficiency GI side effects Hypercalciuria, hypercalcemia ### 37.7.4 Bone Disease Medical treatment with bisphosphonates has been used in patients with MAS. It is also important to ensure that Vitamin D and cal cium supplementation are adequate in these patients. Denosumab, a RANKL inhibitor, has also been used to treat FD, but there is a rebound increase in fracture risk when this medication is discontinued in addition to a risk of hypercalcemia and increased bone resorption [21]. Surgery may be needed for management or prevention of fracture or deformities but is extremely problematic as it can worsen FD. Surgery may also be needed for manage ment of scoliosis as complications of restric tive lung disease can be life threatening.
