Patients who present in DKA have varying degrees of dehydration. The insertion of two larger peripheral catheters is recommended over central venous access due to the high risk of thrombosis in pediatric DKA [6, 7]. Volume should be expanded as required to restore adequate peripheral circulation [5, 8]. Isotonic fluid, such as normal saline, should be admin istered intravenously. Consensus guidelines recommend administering aliquots of 10–20 ml/kg over 1–2 h to be repeated as necessary [5, 8]. Once the patient’s circulation has been stabilized, the remaining fluid deficit should be calculated and replaced, along with main tenance fluids, as a continuous infusion spread over the next 24–48 h [5, 8] using 0.45–0.9% saline or a balanced salt solution. For ease of quick calculation, using the calculation of
paragraphs.heading: of Intravenous (IV) Fluid

paragraphs.text: 1.5× maintenance rate is often adequate for an estimated 10% dehydration. Historically, there has been concern that rapid IV rehydra tion leads to osmotic shifts and subsequent cerebral edema [9–12]. However, the available literature is inconclusive regarding the poten tial risk for cerebral edema with specific rehy dration techniques. Well-controlled studies identify no increased risk of cerebral edema based on IV fluid infusion rate or sodium con tent [13–17]. Given inconclusive data, the fluid administration described here is based on the widely accepted International Society for Pediatric and Adolescent Diabetes, Pediatric Endocrine Society, and American Diabetes Association guidelines [2, 5, 8].
paragraphs.heading: of Intravenous (IV) Fluid

paragraphs.text: with the insulin infusion, as a onetime subcu taneous dose per the patient’s home dosing or weight-based calculation (0.3–0.4 units/kg) for new-onset type 1 patients (see Fig. 40.1), which helps with the transition off of the insulin infusion once the acidosis resolves and decreases rebound hyperglycemia. This should be done in consultation with endocrinology ( Table 40.2).

Numerous electrolyte imbalances occur in acute DKA, but fortunately many of them resolve with insulin and rehydration. Potassium is the most unstable electrolyte dur ing DKA treatment. Extracellular acidosis causes upregulation of potassium proton pumps in the cellular membrane in order to transport hydrogen protons into the cells in exchange for potassium, causing elevated extracellular potassium. This extracellular potassium leads to increased serum potas sium, which is ultimately excreted in the urine. Thus, serum potassium levels may be high, normal, or low at any given point of DKA. However, total body potassium tends to be low secondary to obligatory losses from osmotic diuresis. Consensus guidelines recom mend adding 40 mEq/L of IV potassium when the serum potassium is within the normal range in a patient with DKA who has demon strated successful urination [5, 8]. If the patient presents with hyperkalemia, potas sium should be withheld from fluids until the serum potassium normalizes. If the patient presents with hypokalemia, replacement potassium should be initiated right away with administration of insulin [5, 8]. Insulin admin istration will cause potassium to shift from the extracellular to the intracellular space with a rapid decrease in serum potassium levels. In patients in severe DKA and prolonged potas sium losses, more than 40 mEq/L of potas sium may be necessary to avoid hypokalemia.
paragraphs.heading: Imbalance

paragraphs.text: Similar trends occur with phosphorus in DKA. Thus, the guidelines recommend con sidering replacement of phosphorus in the form of 20 mEq/L of IV potassium phos phate, with close monitoring [5, 8]. Therefore,
paragraphs.heading: Imbalance

paragraphs.text: the recommended 40 mEq/L of potassium could be administered as 20 mEq/L of potas sium phosphate and 20 mEq/L of potassium chloride or acetate.
paragraphs.heading: Imbalance

paragraphs.text: Hyperglycemia causes an osmotic shift of fluid from the intracellular to the extracellu lar space, leading to pseudohyponatremia. The actual sodium content can be calculated by adjusting for hyperglycemia as follows: corrected sodium = measured sodium + [(serum glucose − 100) × 0.016], as the mea sured serum sodium is decreased by 1.6 mmol/L (=mEq/L) for every 100 mg/dl blood glucose over 100 mg/dl [5]. Fluid resus citation with isotonic saline such as normal saline and standard insulin management of DKA will correct any remaining mild hypo natremia.
paragraphs.heading: Imbalance

paragraphs.text: Cerebral edema occurs in 0.5–1% of pediatric patients with DKA [13, 18]. The exact cause of cerebral edema is unknown and widely debated [19]. As discussed above, some have postulated that the rate and composition of fluid resuscitation contributes to cerebral edema [9, 10, 12]. Others postulate that insu lin administration can precipitate cerebral edema [20, 21]. Recent studies have found that dehydration and cerebral hypoperfusion asso ciated with DKA itself may be the cause [5]. Although no consensus on etiology exists, risk factors for cerebral edema in DKA include younger age, new onset of diabetes, as well as longer duration and more severe signs and symptoms before initiation of treatment [1]. Once cerebral edema occurs, mortality is around 20% and approximately 25% of survi vors have permanent neurologic sequelae [1, 21]. Symptoms and signs of cerebral edema include headache, change in consciousness, unequal pupils, emesis, incontinence, hyper tension, and bradycardia [1]. Morbidity and mortality from cerebral edema can be mini mized if treated promptly by reducing the rate of IV fluid administration and administering mannitol 0.5–1 g/kg IV per dose or 3% hyper tonic saline 2.5–5 mL/kg IV over 10–15 min
paragraphs.heading: 40.1.6 Adverse Events

paragraphs.text: [1, 5]. Treatment can be repeated every 2–4 h if symptoms persist [1]. It is important to note that imaging should not delay administration of hypertonic therapy when concerned for cerebral edema. The head of the bed should also be elevated to 30° and the patient’s head kept in the midline position.
paragraphs.heading: 40.1.6 Adverse Events

paragraphs.text: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic syndrome (HHS) is a complication of diabetes mellitus classically characterized by severe hyperglyce mia (plasma glucose >600 mg/dl), hyperosmo lality (serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg), and dehydration, without significant ketoacidosis (or ketonuria), although mild ketoacidosis may be associated. HHS is more common in type 2 diabetes mellitus, in which residual insulin action results in less lipolysis, and hence less ketosis, than is seen with DKA [5]. However, HHS can also be seen in type 1 dia betes following intake of high carbohydrate beverages or in children with learning disabili ties who are unable to ask for drinks [22]. Manifestations vary and can include tachy cardia, hypotension, hyper- or hypothermia, depressed level of consciousness, seizure activity, and/or focal neurological symptoms, among others [5]. Although rare in children, this syndrome is increasingly recognized in adolescents with type 2 diabetes mellitus [5].
paragraphs.heading: Hyperglycemic Syndrome

paragraphs.text: HHS is treated differently from DKA. Volume repletion is key and should be performed quickly and aggressively using normal saline, 20 ml/kg boluses to be repeated as needed, followed by fluid deficit plus maintenance of 0.45–0.9% NS IV infusion over 24–48 h. Individuals in a hyper osmolar hyperglycemic state are particularly prone to vascular collapse and venous thrombo sis, making fluid resuscitation extremely impor tant. Regarding insulin treatment, HHS necessitates less insulin than DKA, and therefore consensus recommendations advise holding insulin until glucose ceases to decline from fluid resuscitation, and then administering 0.025–0.05 units/kg/h of insulin (as opposed to 0.1 units/ kg/h as recommended for DKA). The aim is to decrease serum glucose by 75–100 mg/dl/h [5].
paragraphs.heading: Hyperglycemic Syndrome

paragraphs.text: Mixed HHS and DKA has also been seen with type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Fluid resus citation exceeds that normally required in typical DKA, and insulin infusion should be started per HHS guidelines, after the initial fluid bolus(es) and hemodynamic stability is achieved. Rates of cerebral edema are higher in mixed HHS/DKA, so frequent monitor ing of mental status and avoidance of excess fluid administration are essential [5, 23].

Ideally, care for a child or adolescent with DKA or HHS should occur at a specialty cen ter experienced with the treatment of diabetes mellitus in pediatric patients. If the initial pre sentation is not at such a facility, support from an experienced center should be obtained and arrangements made for safe transfer, if possi ble [5]. Severe DKA or HHS requires inten sive care monitoring for frequent electrolyte measurements and close neurologic assess ments. At some centers, mild DKA can be managed in a nonintensive care hospital unit experienced with DKA management. Insulin infusion should be continued until transition criteria are met for subcutaneous insulin. Acceptable criteria for transitioning a patient from an insulin infusion to subcutaneous insulin include a HCO3 ≥15 or normalization of the anion gap [24]. Mild DKA requires less frequent monitoring and has negligible neuro logic concerns.
paragraphs.heading: 40.1.8 Disposition

paragraphs.text: Adrenal crisis is an important cause of shock in children [25]. An adrenal crisis is a state of car diovascular decompensation caused by a severe glucocorticoid deficit with or without concur rent mineralocorticoid deficit and electrolyte abnormalities. Adrenal crisis occurs when the demand for glucocorticoid is not met. Such an imbalance commonly occurs when a patient with primary adrenal insufficiency (including Addison’s disease and congenital adrenal hyper plasia) or secondary adrenal insufficiency (hypo pituitarism) develops a routine illness, and glucocorticoid dosing is not increased as recom mended for such times. Additionally, illness in a patient in whom the hypothalamic-pituitary axis has been suppressed from chronic exoge nous steroid use (resulting in secondary adrenal insufficiency) can bring about an adrenal crisis. Rarely, it can be an initial presentation of undi agnosed primary or central adrenal insufficiency or due to under- or missed dosing of glucocorti coid therapy.
paragraphs.heading: 40.2.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: Patients with adrenal crisis can present with long-standing insidious symptoms or acute symptoms depending on underlying etiology [26]. If the crisis develops from a progressive loss of adrenal function, preceding symptoms can include depression, fatigability, weakness, anorexia, nausea, abdominal pain, constipa tion or diarrhea, and weight loss or failure to thrive [26, 27]. Primary adrenal insufficiency with insidious onset classically presents with a history of salt craving and orthostatic hypo tension due to mineralocorticoid deficiency. Salt craving in children can be elicited by ask ing about consumption of table salt or other high salt-containing foods. Salt craving does not occur in secondary adrenal insufficiency because the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system remains intact [27]. Insufficient corti sol synthesis in primary adrenal insufficiency causes an upregulation of proopiomelanocor tin, the precursor of both adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) and melanocortin, which can lead to increased skin pigmentation in
paragraphs.heading: 40.2.2 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: sun-exposed regions of the body as well as flexor surfaces and mucosal membranes [26, 28, 29]. Providers typically describe a “bronzed” appearance of the skin as if the patient has been suntanning.
paragraphs.heading: 40.2.2 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Some patients with adrenal insufficiency have no insidious symptoms, and the crisis develops acutely after a sudden physiologic stress. Sudden stress such as trauma, hemor rhage, acute infection, or a medical procedure may trigger an adrenal crisis [26].
paragraphs.heading: 40.2.2 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: If the patient has developed acute primary insufficiency from adrenal hemorrhage associ ated with bacterial sepsis (as in Waterhouse- Friderichsen syndrome due to meningococcemia), a petechial rash may be present and progress to frank ecchymoses.
paragraphs.heading: 40.2.2 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: 34 Several syndromes may be associated with adrenal insufficiency. Adrenoleukodys trophy is an X-linked syndrome in which progressive cerebral demyelination leads to neurological symptoms and primary adrenal insufficiency. A diagnosis of adrenoleuko dystrophy should be considered in a young male with cognitive regression and adrenal insufficiency [26]. Another cause of adrenal insufficiency is autoimmune-mediated destruction of the adrenal glands, which can present in conjunction with other autoim mune diseases. Type 1 or type 2 autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes may include adre nal insufficiency, hypoparathyroidism, hypo thyroidism, pernicious anemia, gonadal failure, alopecia, and vitiligo [26]. Other causes of adrenal insufficiency include con genital adrenal hyperplasia, which is an important cause of adrenal insufficiency in neonates and children [26]. In the United
paragraphs.heading: 40.2.2 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: States, classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency is diagnosed through the mandatory neonatal screening program, and presents with virilization or ambiguous genitalia in girls, while boys have normal genitalia. Left undiagnosed by 10–14 days of age, adrenal or salt-losing crisis occurs. Immediate confirmation with a 17-OH progesterone level, basic metabolic panel, and renin level and prompt initiation of hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone averts adrenal crisis. Adrenal hypoplasia congenita is a rare X-linked disorder due to DAX1 gene mutations, which results in adrenal insuffi ciency and hypogonadism [26]. Both entities are likely to present in infancy due to crises but are rarely not identified until later in life.
paragraphs.heading: 40.2.2 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Regardless of the course of symptom onset, patients with an adrenal crisis pres ent with tachycardia, hypotension, and hypoglycemia, with or without hyponatre mia, hyperkalemia, and metabolic acidosis. Depending on the severity of hypoglycemia and hyponatremia, patients can have
severely altered cognition or even seizure activity [26].

In the acute setting, diagnostic hormone concentration results are not often available. If an adrenal crisis is suspected, the provider should obtain a serum cortisol, ACTH, glu cose, and electrolyte panel and administer glucocorticoid therapy immediately without waiting for laboratory results [25]. Replacement glucocorticoid therapy must be administered emergently to prevent morbid ity and in some cases death. A cortisol level <18 mcg/dl during cardiovascular collapse is diagnostic of adrenal insufficiency and should be treated as such [36]. An elevated ACTH level drawn before glucocorticoid therapy suggests primary adrenal disease, and elevated 21-hydroxylase antibodies are consistent with Addison disease. An ACTH stimulation test is often performed of gluco corticoid therapy to confirm the diagnosis if basal testing is inconclusive.
paragraphs.heading: 40.2.3 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Normal saline boluses of 20 ml/kg should be administered until perfusion improves [25, 37].
paragraphs.heading: and Disposition

paragraphs.text: Uncertain age or BSA should be treated with a higher hydrocortisone dose, as excess hydrocortisone has negligible side effects, but underdosing will lead to continued hemody namic compromise. The initial hydrocorti sone bolus should be followed by administration of the same dose run as a
paragraphs.heading: and Disposition

paragraphs.text: continuous infusion over the next 24 h or divided into every 4–6 h doses. Thereafter, continued “stress dosing” of glucocorticoid therapy will be necessary until the patient has recovered from the underlying illness. Standard stress dosing for a moderate to severe illness is 50–100 mg/m2/day of hydro cortisone divided into every 4–6 h dosing. If hydrocortisone is unavailable, dexametha sone (1.5–2 mg/m2/dose) may be used; how ever, dexamethasone is not recommended for salt-wasting adrenal crisis as it does not have mineralocorticoid effect. Methylpredniso lone (10–25 mg/m2/dose) may be used in this scenario, though it has less mineralocorti coid effect compared to hydrocortisone [39].
paragraphs.heading: and Disposition

paragraphs.text: Hypoglycemia must be corrected. If the serum glucose level is <70 mg/dl, we recom mend administering an IV bolus of dextrose (see hypoglycemia management), which can be repeated as necessary [40].
paragraphs.heading: and Disposition

paragraphs.text: Hyperkalemia should be further assessed with an EKG to evaluate for peaked T waves and other abnormalities. Emergency treat ment for significant hyperkalemia includes calcium for myocardial stabilization, bicar bonate, and insulin and glucose infusion, although these are rarely needed in adrenal insufficiency [40, 41].
paragraphs.heading: and Disposition

paragraphs.text: Finally, concurrent illnesses such as bacterial sepsis should be treated as neces sary.
paragraphs.heading: and Disposition

paragraphs.text: Once stabilized, the patient will need close monitoring of neurologic as well as hemody namic status, usually in the intensive care unit. Adrenal crisis precipitating events such as sepsis often require intensive care unit man agement, too.
paragraphs.heading: and Disposition

paragraphs.text: Diabetes insipidus (DI) is the pathologic state caused by insufficient arginine vasopressin secretion or action. Vasopressin (also known as antidiuretic hormone, ADH) is a key regu latory hormone for maintenance of intravas cular volume. In the kidney, vasopressin binds to V2 vasopressin receptors which leads to upregulation of aquaporin channels, allow ing water to flow down the osmotic gradient from the tubular lumen into the hypertonic medullary interstitium, thus concentrating urine and increasing intravascular volume [42]. Vasopressin also causes vasoconstriction via V1 vasopressin receptors located on vas cular smooth muscle [42, 43]. DI is either a problem with the production of ADH, known as central DI, or with the kidneys’ response to ADH, referred to as nephrogenic DI. A lack of vasopressin, as in central DI, causes water loss through inappropriately dilute urine, as well as decreased intravascular tone. Nephrogenic DI, caused by aberrant function of the renal vasopressin receptors, is unre sponsive or hyporesponsive to vasopressin replacement. Despite these differences, the acute presentation and management of the decompensated state of DI—i.e., dehydration and hypernatremia—are the same for both central and nephrogenic DI.
paragraphs.heading: 40.3.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: Patients presenting with acute decompensa tion from DI or new-onset DI usually have a history of chronic or acute polyuria and poly dipsia. They may have a history of extreme water intake, including eating ice chips or even drinking from the toilet bowl, as well as newonset nocturia and urinary incontinence. Younger infants typically present with more nonspecific symptoms and signs, such as irri tability, vomiting (despite a vigorous suck), and recurrent fevers [44–46].
paragraphs.heading: 40.3.2 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: All patients with DI who are unable to maintain hydration by increasing water intake will become progressively dehydrated and hypernatremic due to excessive free water loss through urine. Hypernatremia and dehydra tion can be severe; the patient may present with altered mental status, seizure activity, shock, or even death [45].
paragraphs.heading: 40.3.2 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Patients may also present with complaints associated with the underlying pathology. Between 18% and 50% of children with central DI are found to have an underlying tumor such as a craniopharyngioma or germ cell tumor [45, 47, 48]. An additional 12–16% of patients with new-onset central DI have an infiltrative disease such as Langerhans cell histiocytosis [45, 47, 48]. With these intracranial processes, patients may report headaches or, in some cases, visual disturbances [47]. They may also exhibit addi tional signs of pituitary or hypothalamic dys function, such as short stature or delayed or precocious puberty, in addition to DI. Langerhans cell histiocytosis may also be asso ciated with fever, weight loss, rash, lymphade nopathy, ear drainage, pulmonary infiltrates, hepatosplenomegaly, and/or bone lesions [49].
paragraphs.heading: 40.3.2 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Congenital central DI can occur in con junction with syndromes displaying midline cerebral and cranial anatomic malformations (e.g., septo-optic dysplasia with agenesis of the corpus callosum, cleft lip and palate) [47, 50, 51]. Familial central DI, caused by muta tions in the AVP gene (named for arginine vasopressin) with an autosomal dominant or recessive inheritance pattern, can present throughout childhood and may be accompa nied by a positive family history [45, 52].
paragraphs.heading: 40.3.2 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Central DI may also develop secondary to an abrupt CNS insult such as trauma, hemor rhage, severe infection, or neurosurgery, espe cially transsphenoidal pituitary surgery.
paragraphs.heading: 40.3.2 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Hereditary nephrogenic DI is most com monly the result of an X-linked genetic defect causing an inactivating mutation of the renal vasopressin V2 receptor [53]. Nephrogenic DI may also arise from autosomal recessive or dominant inheritance mutations in the aquaporin 2 (AQP2) gene [45, 53]. Secondary nephrogenic DI may be due to medication administration. Medications commonly asso ciated with nephrogenic DI [45, 54] include:
paragraphs.heading: 40.3.2 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: –– Alkylating chemotherapeutic agents –– Aminoglycosides –– Amphotericin B –– Lithium
paragraphs.heading: 40.3.2 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Also note that diuretics or other medications which alter urine solute load can affect the concentrating ability of the kidney, but this is not usually a result of vasopressin receptor malfunction.
paragraphs.heading: 40.3.2 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: A patient presenting with concerns for decompensated DI should be evaluated emer gently with a serum sodium, serum osmolal ity, and urine osmolality. If a measured serum osmolality is not rapidly available, serum osmolality can be calculated using the follow ing equation: serum osmolality (mOsm/kg or mmol/kg) = (2 × sodium [mEq/L or mmol/L]) + (glucose [mg/dl]/18) + (BUN [mg/dl]/2.8) [55]. A serum osmolality >300 mOsm/kg and a serum sodium >145 mEq/L, with a concur rent urine osmolality <300 mOsm/kg, are diagnostic of complete DI [55, 56]. Serum osmolality >290–300 mOsm/kg or hyperna tremia, in conjunction with urine osmolality in the more moderate range of 300–600 mOsm/kg, raises concern for partial DI, in which case further diagnostics, such as water
paragraphs.heading: 40.3.3 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: deprivation testing, are necessary for a defini tive diagnosis [56].
paragraphs.heading: 40.3.3 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Patients with intact thirst can, in the face of the severe polyuria, compensate by drinking enough water and will not have a raised serum osmolality or hypernatremia but will have dilute urine. In order to differentiate excessive urine production from primary polydipsia, a water deprivation test will be necessary.
paragraphs.heading: 40.3.3 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Urine specific gravity correlates with urine osmolality, but is not as reliable as a direct measurement of urine osmolality [57]. Never theless, because specific gravity is often quick est to obtain in the clinical setting, its crude estimate of osmolality may be helpful. A urine
paragraphs.heading: 40.3.3 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: specific gravity >1.030 correlates with a urine osmolality >600 mOsm/kg and thus usually rules out diabetes insipidus, while a specific gravity <1.010 usually correlates with an osmolality <350 mOsm/kg and thus is highly suggestive of DI in a hypernatremic patient. Values ranging between 1.010 and 1.030 may represent partial DI [58].
paragraphs.heading: 40.3.3 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: At the end of a water deprivation test, when the serum is hyperosmotic and the urine rela tively dilute (specific gravity <1.030), a trial dose of vasopressin (1 unit/m2 SC) is administered to differentiate nephrogenic versus central DI [54]. A urine osmolality increase <50% after the test dose is highly suggestive of nephrogenic DI, whereas an increase >50% in 60 min indicates central DI [56]. Copeptin, a fragment of the vasopressin prohormone pre-pro-vasopressin, can be measured in the blood and has been used as a surrogate marker of vasopressin secretion to help distinguish central and nephrogenic DI. Baseline copeptin >20 pmol/L with polyuria and polydipsia is diagnostic of nephrogenic DI, while values <2.6 pmol/L after a water depriva tion test are consistent with central DI [59].
paragraphs.heading: 40.3.3 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Additional diagnostics may be necessary, including BUN and creatinine levels to evalu ate for renal injury associated with severe dehy dration, as well as intracranial imaging to uncover underlying pathology in a child with new-onset central DI [55]. Magnetic resonance imaging is the “gold standard” method for evaluating the hypothalamic-pituitary axis [55]. The imaging protocol should include sag ittal and coronal thin (≤2–3 mm) slices, T1and T2-weighted images, and contrast. Additional sequences of the remainder of the brain should be performed to evaluate for comorbid pathology. If MRI is unavailable or if there is concern for intracranial hemorrhage, a head CT scan with multi-slice helical coronal and sagittal images can provide adequate rapid evaluation of the suprasellar region [55].
paragraphs.heading: 40.3.3 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Initial treatment of the dehydration and hypernatremia is aimed at stabilizing the patient’s intravascular volume. Normal saline
paragraphs.heading: and Disposition

paragraphs.text: boluses of 20 ml/kg should be administered as necessary. When the patient is hemodynami cally stable, IV fluids must be administered cautiously, so as to gradually decrease the serum sodium and replete the free water defi cit. A widely used calculation for free water deficit is free water deficit (L) = 0.6 × weight (kg) × ([serum sodium (mEq/L)/145] − 1) [60]. Once the free water deficit is calculated and any previous fluid volume given for resuscita tion accounted for (i.e., subtracted from the total deficit), replacement fluid should be started, with the infusion rate calculated to replete the remaining deficit over 24–48 h. Hypotonic fluids, such as 0.45% normal saline or D5 0.22% normal saline intravenously or enterally (e.g., through a preexisting gastros tomy tube), should be used to replete the fluid deficit [61]. Additionally, urinary losses must be monitored closely and replaced periodi cally with 0.5–1 ml of hypotonic IV fluid (0.45% normal saline or D5 0.22% normal saline) for every 1 ml of urine volume. One should aim for a rate of sodium decline no greater than 0.5 mEq/L/h [62, 63]. A rate of decline >0.5 mEq/L/h has been associated with an increased incidence of cerebral edema and seizure activity compared to a rate of decline <0.5 mEq/L/h [63, 64]. The patient’s serum sodium should be measured every 2–3 h initially and then can be gradually spaced out. Adjustments to the infusion rate and/or saline content will need to be made on an indi vidualized basis because each patient’s recov ery can be very unpredictable. The patient must be monitored closely for signs and symp toms of cerebral edema including headache and altered cognition. Because of the close monitoring required, patients with significant hypernatremia and dehydration are typically managed in the intensive care unit.
paragraphs.heading: and Disposition

paragraphs.text: Use of DDAVP should be individualized. If a patient is known to have DI and has had a predictable response to DDAVP administra tion, his or her prescribed dose should be given as soon as possible. If the presentation is unequivocally central DI, a vasopressin infu sion can be started in the intensive care unit. Once the patient improves, the IV infusion can be stopped, and oral, intranasal, or subcutane ous DDAVP administered. Of note, infants
paragraphs.heading: and Disposition

paragraphs.text: with central DI are typically treated with a lowsolute diet and free water replacement, with/ without a thiazide diuretic—rather than DDAVP—due to their unpredictable response and higher risk of developing hyponatremia [65]. Sometimes, though, it may be reasonable to try very small doses of oral or subcutaneous DDAVP. Transitional and long-term treatment of nephrogenic DI will need to address exacer bating factors, and fluid intake must be opti mized, in consultation with nephrology.
paragraphs.heading: and Disposition

paragraphs.text: Thyroid storm is the state of clinical decom pensation associated with severe thyrotoxico sis. Although hyperthyroidism is relatively
paragraphs.heading: 40.4.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: common in the pediatric population (occur ring in 1:1000–1:10,000 children), thyroid storm is fortunately exquisitely rare [66–68]. Despite its rarity, thyroid storm is a medical emergency with significant mortality, and pro viders must be aware of its presenting fea tures, diagnosis, and management.
paragraphs.heading: 40.4.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: Thyroid storm presents with extreme fea tures of hyperthyroidism. Symptoms and signs of thyroid storm are listed below and represent a hypermetabolic state. On physical exam, a goiter and exophthalmos are tip-offs to preexisting hyperthyroidism in a patient who does not have a known diagnosis of hyperthyroidism.
paragraphs.heading: 40.4.2 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: 40.7 In neonates, a maternal history of Graves’ disease is significant. Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI) can be transmitted across the placenta to the fetus causing neo natal Graves’ disease. This can occur despite adequate control of maternal hyperthyroid ism, including mothers with a past history of Graves’ disease treated with radioactive iodine therapy or thyroidectomy who con tinue to have high TSI titers in their blood [70]. Affected fetuses often have intrauterine growth restriction and are born small for ges tational age [68, 71]. The affected newborn may show signs of thyrotoxicosis at birth, although it is important to note that thyroid storm itself is exceedingly rare. Alternatively, if the mother received antithyroid medica tion, the clinical manifestations of thyrotoxi cosis may be delayed until several days after birth, once the antithyroid medication clears the neonatal circulation [68].

paragraphs.text: Electrolytes (including calcium), glucose, BUN, creatinine, and liver function tests may reveal potential renal and hepatic end-organ dysfunction. An EKG is necessary when there is concern for a dysrhythmia or for certain electrolyte abnormalities (e.g., significant hypercalcemia). If cardiovascular compro mise is severe, echocardiography should be performed as soon as possible. If sepsis is sus pected, a complete blood count as well as blood and other appropriate cultures should be obtained and antibiotics administered. If ingestion is a possibility, a toxicology evalua tion should be performed as well. Finally, a patient with severe altered consciousness may warrant emergent intracranial imaging.

paragraphs.text: Initial treatment of thyroid storm is aimed at stabilizing the patient’s airway, circulation, and body temperature. Patients in thyroid storm are usually net fluid positive; therefore, resuscitation fluids should be administered cautiously.

Hypoglycemia is a common pediatric emer gency with significant morbidity and mortal ity. The reported prevalence in pediatric emergency departments ranges from 6.5 to 29 per 100,000 visits [78, 79]. Hypoglycemia can cause seizures, coma, permanent neurologic impairment, and, rarely, death. Timely diag nosis can prevent significant neurocognitive sequelae and be helpful in discovering the underlying etiology.
paragraphs.heading: 40.5.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: The most common presentation of hypoglyce mia is hunger, followed by altered neurologic function. A neonate or young infant may be irritable, jittery, and feed poorly [80]. An older patient may be anxious, confused, and/or trem ulous and complain of palpitations. Severe hypoglycemia can cause seizures or coma in patients of all ages [78, 81]. In addition to these neuro-adrenergic manifestations, the patient may have cholinergic-related complaints such as flushing, diaphoresis, emesis, and gastroin testinal distress [78, 81]. Additional features depend upon the underlying etiology—e.g., fever and signs of infection with sepsis. If hypoglycemia is due to an inborn error of metabolism that produces metabolic acidosis, the patient may have compensatory tachypnea.
paragraphs.heading: 40.5.2 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Important information to ascertain include the patient’s age, duration of symp toms, timing of last oral intake, prior episodes of hypoglycemia, chronic diagnoses, and med
paragraphs.heading: 40.5.2 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: ications (including the possibility of an acci dental ingestion or intentional overdose [e.g., of a beta-blocker, sulfonylurea, or insulin]).
paragraphs.heading: 40.5.2 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: It can be helpful to evaluate hypoglycemia based on the age and fasting status of the indi vidual. The most common cause of fasting hypoglycemia in toddlers is ketotic hypoglyce mia, which is associated with poor oral intake or prolonged fasting, usually in the setting of a concurrent acute illness, and is a diagnosis of exclusion [82–84]. These children have no iden tifiable underlying pathology in glucose homeostasis or their endocrine regulatory axes. On the other hand, neonatal hypoglyce mia, which occurs regardless of recent oral intake, is more likely the result of hyperinsulin ism, an inborn error of metabolism, or a defect in a counter-regulatory hormone pathway.
paragraphs.heading: 40.5.2 Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: categorized by the underlying mechanism of either increased glucose utilization or decreased glucose production.
paragraphs.heading: 40.5.3 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: The diagnosis of hypoglycemia is made with a low serum glucose level obtained in the setting of symptoms and signs of hypoglyce mia. Because rapid glucose determination is standard of care when assessing an acutely ill patient, this is frequently performed by emer gency medical services personnel prior to reaching the emergency department. If it was not done or needs to be verified, a point-ofcare glucose should be obtained promptly. If low, a confirmatory serum glucose should be obtained, but should not delay correction.
paragraphs.heading: 40.5.3 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Historically, there has been much debate regarding the biochemical definition of pediat ric hypoglycemia, and accordingly, several cut off levels are provided by various sources [71, 81, 84, 86]. In general, serum glucose less than 70 mg/dl is considered low blood glucose. When the serum glucose decreases below 65–70 mg/dl, counter-regulatory systems are acti vated, and the patient may develop signs and symptoms of hypoglycemia [81, 84]. When the glucose has declined below 50–55 mg/dl, all counter-regulatory systems are employed, and the patient will likely be symptomatic.
paragraphs.heading: 40.5.3 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Once hypoglycemia has been identified, additional diagnostic studies should be obtained to ascertain the underlying etiology and evaluate for any associated comorbidities. When possible, a panel of labs (commonly referred to as a “critical sample”) should be obtained prior to administering glucose. An appropriate laboratory panel obtained while the patient is hypoglycemic <50 mg/dl can effectively rule in or rule out many differential diagnoses. The panel should include serum glucose, insulin, c-peptide, growth hormone, cortisol, free fatty acid, beta-hydroxybutyrate, ammonia, and lactate levels, as well as urinary ketones [71, 81, 84, 86]. Note, if highly suspi cious for hyperinsulinism, a glucagon chal lenge should be administered while the patient
paragraphs.heading: 40.5.3 Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: is hypoglycemic (and assumedly stable). A rise in glucose ≥30 mg/dl after administration of 1 mg of glucagon IV or IM is consistent with hyperinsulinism.

Hypoglycemia must be promptly corrected with IV dextrose or oral glucose [e.g., juice, glucose tablets] for milder cases. A recom mended initial IV bolus dose for a child is 4 ml/kg of 10% dextrose. A neonate should receive 2 ml/kg of 10% dextrose by slow IV push [40]. The glucose level should then be rechecked, and an infusion of 10% dextrosecontaining fluid started at a standard mainte nance rate. If the serum glucose has normalized (and remains normal), no further dextrose boluses are needed.
paragraphs.heading: and Disposition

paragraphs.text: If the underlying diagnosis is known, spe cific therapy should be initiated. For example, hyperinsulinism can be treated with glucagon (neonate, infant, and child <20 kg, 0.02–0.03 mg/kg/dose; child or adolescent ≥20 kg, 1 mg/ dose IV/IO/IM/SC), if glucose or dextrose are not available or do not correct the hypoglyce mia [40]. Treat with stress hydrocortisone dos ing (as described in the adrenal crisis section) for adrenal insufficiency [28].
paragraphs.heading: and Disposition

paragraphs.text: Once stabilized, disposition must be indi vidualized. Some forms of hypoglycemia may be mild and respond to treatment quickly (e.g., ketotic hypoglycemia). Without addi tional comorbidities, most of these patients can be treated with dextrose-containing infu sions and are easily managed on a standard hospital unit. Other forms of hypoglycemia may present with severe acidosis, neurologic impairment, and/or respiratory compromise. These patients require close monitoring, with frequent adjustments in therapy, and need to be admitted to an intensive care unit for con tinued care.
paragraphs.heading: and Disposition

Misra (eds.), Pediatric Endocrinology, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-66296-6_40 ## PDF page 1039 | printed page 1044 ### 40.5 Hypoglycemia – 1061 40.5.1 Introduction – 1061 40.5.2 Clinical Presentation – 1061 40.5.3 Diagnostic Evaluation – 1061 40.5.4 Management and Disposition – 1062 ### References – 1065 ## PDF page 1040 | printed page 1045 ### 40.1 Diabetic Ketoacidosis ### and Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic Syndrome Key Points 5 Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is the most common endocrine emergency. 5 Common presenting symptoms and signs of DKA include polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, dehydration, abdominal pain, vomiting, and Kussmaul breathing. 5 Hyperglycemia (blood glucose >200), HCO3 <18, and venous pH <7.30 are consistent with DKA in the presence of classic symptoms and signs. 5 Management of DKA includes cau tious attention to intravenous fluid administration and insulin dosing. 5 Hyperglycemic hyperosmolar syndrome (HHS) is increasing in incidence; diagno sis is based on blood glucose >600, serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg, and absence of significant ketosis and acidosis. ### 40.1.1 Introduction Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is the most com mon endocrine emergency. DKA occurs when there is insufficient insulin available for cellu lar uptake of glucose. Free fatty acids are con verted to ketone bodies for alternative cellular fuel [1]. Excess buildup of acidic ketone bod ies, primarily beta-hydroxybutyrate and ace toacetate, causes metabolic acidosis [2]. Though traditionally thought of in patients with type 1 diabetes, DKA can also be seen in patients with type 2 diabetes, due to actual or relative insulin deficiency and dysregulated glucagon secretion, often precipitated by the stress of illness or infection. Approximately 30% of new-onset type 1 diabetes patients present initially in DKA, while approximately 11% of patients with new-onset type 2 diabe tes present in DKA [3]. In patients with an established diagnosis of type 1 diabetes, DKA is most commonly precipitated by missed insulin doses or illness [1]. Prompt treatment with hydration and insulin is key to the man agement of DKA. ### 40.1.2 Clinical Presentation Polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss are the cardinal symptoms of new-onset diabetes mellitus. DKA should be suspected in patients with complaints of abdominal pain, nausea, or vomiting. Clinical signs include ill appear ance, dehydration, tachycardia, and rapid breathing, also called Kussmaul respirations. Kussmaul breathing increases minute ventila tion to optimize exhalation of carbon dioxide and thus compensates for the metabolic acido sis from accumulated ketone bodies. There is often a fruity odor to the breath from exhaled ketone bodies. Worsening DKA can progress to altered mental status and coma if untreated. Risk factors for DKA as the initial presen tation of type 1 diabetes include lower socio economic status, lack of private insurance [4] younger age (<4 years) and no first-degree relatives with type 1 diabetes. ### 40.1.3 Differential Diagnosis 40.1 ### 40.1.4 Diagnostic Evaluation 40.2 Initial testing for DKA should include: 1. Point-of-care blood glucose and confirma tory laboratory serum glucose. 2. Venous (or arterial) blood gas. 3. Serum electrolytes (most importantly HCO3), blood urea nitrogen (BUN), and creatinine, as well as calculation of anion gap: (sodium + potassium) − (chlo ride + bicarbonate). ## PDF page 1041 | printed Urine dipstick for glucosuria and ketonu ria. 5. Serum acetone and beta-hydroxybutyrate are optional. 6. Electrocardiogram (EKG) if there is hyper- or hypokalemia. 7. Head computed tomography (CT) scan if there is altered sensorium concerning for cerebral edema (after giving mannitol or hypertonic saline). ### 40.1.5 Management ### 40.1.5.1 Administration ### of Intravenous (IV) Fluid Patients who present in DKA have varying degrees of dehydration. The insertion of two larger peripheral catheters is recommended over central venous access due to the high risk of thrombosis in pediatric DKA [6, 7]. Volume should be expanded as required to restore adequate peripheral circulation [5, 8]. Isotonic fluid, such as normal saline, should be admin istered intravenously. Consensus guidelines recommend administering aliquots of 10–20 ml/kg over 1–2 h to be repeated as necessary [5, 8]. Once the patient’s circulation has been stabilized, the remaining fluid deficit should be calculated and replaced, along with main tenance fluids, as a continuous infusion spread over the next 24–48 h [5, 8] using 0.45–0.9% saline or a balanced salt solution. For ease of quick calculation, using the calculation of 1.5× maintenance rate is often adequate for an estimated 10% dehydration. Historically, there has been concern that rapid IV rehydra tion leads to osmotic shifts and subsequent cerebral edema [9–12]. However, the available literature is inconclusive regarding the poten tial risk for cerebral edema with specific rehy dration techniques. Well-controlled studies identify no increased risk of cerebral edema based on IV fluid infusion rate or sodium con tent [13–17]. Given inconclusive data, the fluid administration described here is based on the widely accepted International Society for Pediatric and Adolescent Diabetes, Pediatric Endocrine Society, and American Diabetes Association guidelines [2, 5, 8]. ### 40.1.5.2 Insulin Therapy 3 5 8 40.1 ### Automatic table extraction — verify rendered original |Col1|Mild|Moder­

This should be done in consultation with endocrinology ( Table 40.2). ### 40.1.5.3 Correction of Electrolyte ### Imbalance Numerous electrolyte imbalances occur in acute DKA, but fortunately many of them resolve with insulin and rehydration. Potassium is the most unstable electrolyte dur ing DKA treatment. Extracellular acidosis causes upregulation of potassium proton pumps in the cellular membrane in order to transport hydrogen protons into the cells in exchange for potassium, causing elevated extracellular potassium. This extracellular potassium leads to increased serum potas sium, which is ultimately excreted in the urine. Thus, serum potassium levels may be high, normal, or low at any given point of DKA. However, total body potassium tends to be low secondary to obligatory losses from osmotic diuresis. Consensus guidelines recom mend adding 40 mEq/L of IV potassium when the serum potassium is within the normal range in a patient with DKA who has demon strated successful urination [5, 8]. If the patient presents with hyperkalemia, potas sium should be withheld from fluids until the serum potassium normalizes. If the patient presents with hypokalemia, replacement potassium should be initiated right away with administration of insulin [5, 8]. Insulin admin istration will cause potassium to shift from the extracellular to the intracellular space with a rapid decrease in serum potassium levels. In patients in severe DKA and prolonged potas sium losses, more than 40 mEq/L of potas sium may be necessary to avoid hypokalemia. Similar trends occur with phosphorus in DKA. Thus, the guidelines recommend con sidering replacement of phosphorus in the form of 20 mEq/L of IV potassium phos phate, with close monitoring [5, 8]. Therefore, the recommended 40 mEq/L of potassium could be administered as 20 mEq/L of potas sium phosphate and 20 mEq/L of potassium chloride or acetate. Hyperglycemia causes an osmotic shift of fluid from the intracellular to the extracellu lar space, leading to pseudohyponatremia. The actual sodium content can be calculated by adjusting for hyperglycemia as follows: corrected sodium = measured sodium + [(serum glucose − 100) × 0.016], as the mea sured serum sodium is decreased by 1.6 mmol/L (=mEq/L) for every 100 mg/dl blood glucose over 100 mg/dl [5]. Fluid resus citation with isotonic saline such as normal saline and standard insulin management of DKA will correct any remaining mild hypo natremia. ### 40.1.6 Adverse Events Cerebral edema occurs in 0.5–1% of pediatric patients with DKA [13, 18]. The exact cause of cerebral edema is unknown and widely debated [19]. As discussed above, some have postulated that the rate and composition of fluid resuscitation contributes to cerebral edema [9, 10, 12]. Others postulate that insu lin administration can precipitate cerebral edema [20, 21]. Recent studies have found that dehydration and cerebral hypoperfusion asso ciated with DKA itself may be the cause [5]. Although no consensus on etiology exists, risk factors for cerebral edema in DKA include younger age, new onset of diabetes, as well as longer duration and more severe signs and symptoms before initiation of treatment [1]. Once cerebral edema occurs, mortality is around 20% and approximately 25% of survi vors have permanent neurologic sequelae [1, 21]. Symptoms and signs of cerebral edema include headache, change in consciousness, unequal pupils, emesis, incontinence, hyper tension, and bradycardia [1]. Morbidity and mortality from cerebral edema can be mini mized if treated promptly by reducing the rate of IV fluid administration and administering mannitol 0.5–1 g/kg IV per dose or 3% hyper tonic saline 2.5–5 mL/kg IV over 10–15 min ## PDF page 1045 | printed page 1050 [1, 5]. Treatment can be repeated every 2–4 h if symptoms persist [1]. It is important to note that imaging should not delay administration of hypertonic therapy when concerned for cerebral edema. The head of the bed should also be elevated to 30° and the patient’s head kept in the midline position. ### 40.1.7 Hyperosmolar ### Hyperglycemic Syndrome Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic syndrome (HHS) is a complication of diabetes mellitus classically characterized by severe hyperglyce mia (plasma glucose >600 mg/dl), hyperosmo lality (serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg), and dehydration, without significant ketoacidosis (or ketonuria), although mild ketoacidosis may be associated. HHS is more common in type 2 diabetes mellitus, in which residual insulin action results in less lipolysis, and hence less ketosis, than is seen with DKA [5]. However, HHS can also be seen in type 1 dia betes following intake of high carbohydrate beverages or in children with learning disabili ties who are unable to ask for drinks [22]. Manifestations vary and can include tachy cardia, hypotension, hyper- or hypothermia, depressed level of consciousness, seizure activity, and/or focal neurological symptoms, among others [5]. Although rare in children, this syndrome is increasingly recognized in adolescents with type 2 diabetes mellitus [5]. HHS is treated differently from DKA. Volume repletion is key and should be performed quickly and aggressively using normal saline, 20 ml/kg boluses to be repeated as needed, followed by fluid deficit plus maintenance of 0.45–0.9% NS IV infusion over 24–48 h. Individuals in a hyper osmolar hyperglycemic state are particularly prone to vascular collapse and venous thrombo sis, making fluid resuscitation extremely impor tant. Regarding insulin treatment, HHS necessitates less insulin than DKA, and therefore consensus recommendations advise holding insulin until glucose ceases to decline from fluid resuscitation, and then administering 0.025–0.05 units/kg/h of insulin (as opposed to 0.1 units/ kg/h as recommended for DKA). The aim is to decrease serum glucose by 75–100 mg/dl/h [5]. ### 40 Mixed HHS and DKA has also been seen with type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Fluid resus citation exceeds that normally required in typical DKA, and insulin infusion should be started per HHS guidelines, after the initial fluid bolus(es) and hemodynamic stability is achieved. Rates of cerebral edema are higher in mixed HHS/DKA, so frequent monitor ing of mental status and avoidance of excess fluid administration are essential [5, 23]. ### 40.1.8 Disposition Ideally, care for a child or adolescent with DKA or HHS should occur at a specialty cen ter experienced with the treatment of diabetes mellitus in pediatric patients. If the initial pre sentation is not at such a facility, support from an experienced center should be obtained and arrangements made for safe transfer, if possi ble [5]. Severe DKA or HHS requires inten sive care monitoring for frequent electrolyte measurements and close neurologic assess ments. At some centers, mild DKA can be managed in a nonintensive care hospital unit experienced with DKA management. Insulin infusion should be continued until transition criteria are met for subcutaneous insulin. Acceptable criteria for transitioning a patient from an insulin infusion to subcutaneous insulin include a HCO3 ≥15 or normalization of the anion gap [24]. Mild DKA requires less frequent monitoring and has negligible neuro logic concerns. ### 40.2 Adrenal Crisis Key Points 5 An adrenal crisis is characterized by shock associated with severe glucocorti coid deficit. 5 Common presenting signs of adrenal crisis include tachycardia, hypotension, and hypoglycemia. 5 Fluid resuscitation and hydrocortisone are the mainstays of treatment for adre nal crisis. ## PDF page 1046 | printed page 1051 ### 40.2.1 Introduction Adrenal crisis is an important cause of shock in children [25]. An adrenal crisis is a state of car diovascular decompensation caused by a severe glucocorticoid deficit with or without concur rent mineralocorticoid deficit and electrolyte abnormalities. Adrenal crisis occurs when the demand for glucocorticoid is not met. Such an imbalance commonly occurs when a patient with primary adrenal insufficiency (including Addison’s disease and congenital adrenal hyper plasia) or secondary adrenal insufficiency (hypo pituitarism) develops a routine illness, and glucocorticoid dosing is not increased as recom mended for such times. Additionally, illness in a patient in whom the hypothalamic-pituitary axis has been suppressed from chronic exoge nous steroid use (resulting in secondary adrenal insufficiency) can bring about an adrenal crisis. Rarely, it can be an initial presentation of undi agnosed primary or central adrenal insufficiency or due to under- or missed dosing of glucocorti coid therapy. ### 40.2.2 Clinical Presentation Patients with adrenal crisis can present with long-standing insidious symptoms or acute symptoms depending on underlying etiology [26]. If the crisis develops from a progressive loss of adrenal function, preceding symptoms can include depression, fatigability, weakness, anorexia, nausea, abdominal pain, constipa tion or diarrhea, and weight loss or failure to thrive [26, 27]. Primary adrenal insufficiency with insidious onset classically presents with a history of salt craving and orthostatic hypo tension due to mineralocorticoid deficiency. Salt craving in children can be elicited by ask ing about consumption of table salt or other high salt-containing foods. Salt craving does not occur in secondary adrenal insufficiency because the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system remains intact [27]. Insufficient corti sol synthesis in primary adrenal insufficiency causes an upregulation of proopiomelanocor tin, the precursor of both adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) and melanocortin, which can lead to increased skin pigmentation in sun-exposed regions of the body as well as flexor surfaces and mucosal membranes [26, 28, 29]. Providers typically describe a “bronzed” appearance of the skin as if the patient has been suntanning. Some patients with adrenal insufficiency have no insidious symptoms, and the crisis develops acutely after a sudden physiologic stress. Sudden stress such as trauma, hemor rhage, acute infection, or a medical procedure may trigger an adrenal crisis [26]. If the patient has developed acute primary insufficiency from adrenal hemorrhage associ ated with bacterial sepsis (as in Waterhouse- Friderichsen syndrome due to meningococcemia), a petechial rash may be present and progress to frank ecchymoses. 30 31 33 40.3 34 Several syndromes may be associated with adrenal insufficiency. Adrenoleukodys trophy is an X-linked syndrome in which progressive cerebral demyelination leads to neurological symptoms and primary adrenal insufficiency. A diagnosis of adrenoleuko dystrophy should be considered in a young male with cognitive regression and adrenal insufficiency [26]. Another cause of adrenal insufficiency is autoimmune-mediated destruction of the adrenal glands, which can present in conjunction with other autoim mune diseases. Type 1 or type 2 autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes may include adre nal insufficiency, hypoparathyroidism, hypo thyroidism, pernicious anemia, gonadal failure, alopecia, and vitiligo [26]. Other causes of adrenal insufficiency include con genital adrenal hyperplasia, which is an important cause of adrenal insufficiency in neonates and children [26]. [34] States, classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency is diagnosed through the mandatory neonatal screening program, and presents with virilization or ambiguous genitalia in girls, while boys have normal genitalia. Left undiagnosed by 10–14 days of age, adrenal or salt-losing crisis occurs. Immediate confirmation with a 17-OH progesterone level, basic metabolic panel, and renin level and prompt initiation of hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone averts adrenal crisis. Adrenal hypoplasia congenita is a rare X-linked disorder due to DAX1 gene mutations, which results in adrenal insuffi ciency and hypogonadism [26]. Both entities are likely to present in infancy due to crises but are rarely not identified until later in life. ### 40 Regardless of the course of symptom onset, patients with an adrenal crisis pres ent with tachycardia, hypotension, and hypoglycemia, with or without hyponatre mia, hyperkalemia, and metabolic acidosis. Depending on the severity of hypoglycemia and hyponatremia, patients can have severely altered cognition or even seizure activity [26]. ### 40.2.3 Diagnostic Evaluation 35 40.4 In the acute setting, diagnostic hormone concentration results are not often available. If an adrenal crisis is suspected, the provider should obtain a serum cortisol, ACTH, glu cose, and electrolyte panel and administer glucocorticoid therapy immediately without waiting for laboratory results [25]. Replacement glucocorticoid therapy must be administered emergently to prevent morbid ity and in some cases death. A cortisol level <18 mcg/dl during cardiovascular collapse is diagnostic of adrenal insufficiency and should be treated as such [36]. An elevated ACTH level drawn before glucocorticoid therapy suggests primary adrenal disease, and elevated 21-hydroxylase antibodies are consistent with Addison disease. An ACTH stimulation test is often performed of gluco corticoid therapy to confirm the diagnosis if basal testing is inconclusive. ### 40.2.4 Management ### and Disposition Normal saline boluses of 20 ml/kg should be administered until perfusion improves [25, 37]. 2 28 ### Automatic table extraction — verify rendered original |Mechanism|Drug| |---|---| |Direct inhibition of cortisol

Vasopressin (also known as antidiuretic hormone, ADH) is a key regu latory hormone for maintenance of intravas cular volume. In the kidney, vasopressin binds to V2 vasopressin receptors which leads to upregulation of aquaporin channels, allow ing water to flow down the osmotic gradient from the tubular lumen into the hypertonic medullary interstitium, thus concentrating urine and increasing intravascular volume [42]. Vasopressin also causes vasoconstriction via V1 vasopressin receptors located on vas cular smooth muscle [42, 43]. DI is either a problem with the production of ADH, known as central DI, or with the kidneys’ response to ADH, referred to as nephrogenic DI. A lack of vasopressin, as in central DI, causes water loss through inappropriately dilute urine, as well as decreased intravascular tone. Nephrogenic DI, caused by aberrant function of the renal vasopressin receptors, is unre sponsive or hyporesponsive to vasopressin replacement. Despite these differences, the acute presentation and management of the decompensated state of DI—i.e., dehydration and hypernatremia—are the same for both central and nephrogenic DI. ### 40 ### 40.3.2 Clinical Presentation Patients presenting with acute decompensa tion from DI or new-onset DI usually have a history of chronic or acute polyuria and poly dipsia. They may have a history of extreme water intake, including eating ice chips or even drinking from the toilet bowl, as well as newonset nocturia and urinary incontinence. Younger infants typically present with more nonspecific symptoms and signs, such as irri tability, vomiting (despite a vigorous suck), and recurrent fevers [44–46]. All patients with DI who are unable to maintain hydration by increasing water intake will become progressively dehydrated and hypernatremic due to excessive free water loss through urine. Hypernatremia and dehydra tion can be severe; the patient may present with altered mental status, seizure activity, shock, or even death [45]. Patients may also present with complaints associated with the underlying pathology. Between 18% and 50% of children with central DI are found to have an underlying tumor such as a craniopharyngioma or germ cell tumor [45, 47, 48]. An additional 12–16% of patients with new-onset central DI have an infiltrative disease such as Langerhans cell histiocytosis [45, 47, 48]. With these intracranial processes, patients may report headaches or, in some cases, visual disturbances [47]. They may also exhibit addi tional signs of pituitary or hypothalamic dys function, such as short stature or delayed or precocious puberty, in addition to DI. Langerhans cell histiocytosis may also be asso ciated with fever, weight loss, rash, lymphade nopathy, ear drainage, pulmonary infiltrates, hepatosplenomegaly, and/or bone lesions [49]. Congenital central DI can occur in con junction with syndromes displaying midline cerebral and cranial anatomic malformations (e.g., septo-optic dysplasia with agenesis of the corpus callosum, cleft lip and palate) [47, 50, 51]. Familial central DI, caused by muta tions in the AVP gene (named for arginine vasopressin) with an autosomal dominant or recessive inheritance pattern, can present throughout childhood and may be accompa nied by a positive family history [45, 52]. ## PDF page 1050 | printed page 1055 Central DI may also develop secondary to an abrupt CNS insult such as trauma, hemor rhage, severe infection, or neurosurgery, espe cially transsphenoidal pituitary surgery. Hereditary nephrogenic DI is most com monly the result of an X-linked genetic defect causing an inactivating mutation of the renal vasopressin V2 receptor [53]. Nephrogenic DI may also arise from autosomal recessive or dominant inheritance mutations in the aquaporin 2 (AQP2) gene [45, 53]. Secondary nephrogenic DI may be due to medication administration. Medications commonly asso ciated with nephrogenic DI [45, 54] include: –– Alkylating chemotherapeutic agents –– Aminoglycosides –– Amphotericin B –– Lithium Also note that diuretics or other medications which alter urine solute load can affect the concentrating ability of the kidney, but this is not usually a result of vasopressin receptor malfunction. ### 40.3.3 Diagnostic Evaluation 40.6 A patient presenting with concerns for decompensated DI should be evaluated emer gently with a serum sodium, serum osmolal ity, and urine osmolality. If a measured serum osmolality is not rapidly available, serum osmolality can be calculated using the follow ing equation: serum osmolality (mOsm/kg or mmol/kg) = (2 × sodium [mEq/L or mmol/L]) + (glucose [mg/dl]/18) + (BUN [mg/dl]/2.8) [55]. If MRI is unavailable or if there is concern for intracranial hemorrhage, a head CT scan with multi-slice helical coronal and sagittal images can provide adequate rapid evaluation of the suprasellar region [55]. ### 40 ### 40.3.4 Management ### and Disposition Initial treatment of the dehydration and hypernatremia is aimed at stabilizing the patient’s intravascular volume. Normal saline boluses of 20 ml/kg should be administered as necessary. When the patient is hemodynami cally stable, IV fluids must be administered cautiously, so as to gradually decrease the serum sodium and replete the free water defi cit. A widely used calculation for free water deficit is free water deficit (L) = 0.6 × weight (kg) × ([serum sodium (mEq/L)/145] − 1) [60]. Once the free water deficit is calculated and any previous fluid volume given for resuscita tion accounted for (i.e., subtracted from the total deficit), replacement fluid should be started, with the infusion rate calculated to replete the remaining deficit over 24–48 h. Hypotonic fluids, such as 0.45% normal saline or D5 0.22% normal saline intravenously or enterally (e.g., through a preexisting gastros tomy tube), should be used to replete the fluid deficit [61]. Additionally, urinary losses must be monitored closely and replaced periodi cally with 0.5–1 ml of hypotonic IV fluid (0.45% normal saline or D5 0.22% normal saline) for every 1 ml of urine volume. One should aim for a rate of sodium decline no greater than 0.5 mEq/L/h [62, 63]. A rate of decline >0.5 mEq/L/h has been associated with an increased incidence of cerebral edema and seizure activity compared to a rate of decline <0.5 mEq/L/h [63, 64]. The patient’s serum sodium should be measured every 2–3 h initially and then can be gradually spaced out. Adjustments to the infusion rate and/or saline content will need to be made on an indi vidualized basis because each patient’s recov ery can be very unpredictable. The patient must be monitored closely for signs and symp toms of cerebral edema including headache and altered cognition. Because of the close monitoring required, patients with significant hypernatremia and dehydration are typically managed in the intensive care unit. Use of DDAVP should be individualized. If a patient is known to have DI and has had a predictable response to DDAVP administra tion, his or her prescribed dose should be given as soon as possible. If the presentation is unequivocally central DI, a vasopressin infu sion can be started in the intensive care unit. Once the patient improves, the IV infusion can be stopped, and oral, intranasal, or subcutane ous DDAVP administered. Of note, infants ## PDF page 1052 | printed page 1057 with central DI are typically treated with a lowsolute diet and free water replacement, with/ without a thiazide diuretic—rather than DDAVP—due to their unpredictable response and higher risk of developing hyponatremia [65]. Sometimes, though, it may be reasonable to try very small doses of oral or subcutaneous DDAVP. Transitional and long-term treatment of nephrogenic DI will need to address exacer bating factors, and fluid intake must be opti mized, in consultation with nephrology. ### 40.4 Thyroid Storm Key Points 5 Thyroid storm is a very rare life-threat ening illness in children. 5 There is no single clinical or laboratory abnormality that is diagnostic of thy roid storm. Several clinical features are considered when making the diagnosis, which can be made using a clinical score. 5 Thyroid hormone levels are not neces sarily higher in patients with thyroid storm (as compared to those without). Thyroid storm is thought to be caused by the abrupt availability of excess thy roid hormone and/or increased sensitiv ity to it. 5 There is often a precipitating acute event, such as infection, trauma, sur gery, stopping antithyroid medication, or very rarely after radioactive iodine therapy. 5 The mainstays of treatment are stabili zation of the airway and circulation; management of hyperthermia; use of beta-blockers, potassium iodide, stress dose hydrocortisone, and antithyroid medication; and judicious use of resus citation fluids. ### 40.4.1 Introduction Thyroid storm is the state of clinical decom pensation associated with severe thyrotoxico sis. Although hyperthyroidism is relatively common in the pediatric population (occur ring in 1:1000–1:10,000 children), thyroid storm is fortunately exquisitely rare [66–68]. Despite its rarity, thyroid storm is a medical emergency with significant mortality, and pro viders must be aware of its presenting fea tures, diagnosis, and management. ### 40.4.2 Clinical Presentation Thyroid storm presents with extreme fea tures of hyperthyroidism. Symptoms and signs of thyroid storm are listed below and represent a hypermetabolic state. On physical exam, a goiter and exophthalmos are tip-offs to preexisting hyperthyroidism in a patient who does not have a known diagnosis of hyperthyroidism. 69 69 40.7 In neonates, a maternal history of Graves’ disease is significant. Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI) can be transmitted across the placenta to the fetus causing neo natal Graves’ disease. This can occur despite adequate control of maternal hyperthyroid ism, including mothers with a past history of Graves’ disease treated with radioactive iodine therapy or thyroidectomy who con tinue to have high TSI titers in their blood [70]. The affected newborn may show signs of thyrotoxicosis at birth, although it is important to note that thyroid storm itself is exceedingly rare. The reported prevalence in pediatric emergency departments ranges from 6.5 to 29 per 100,000 visits [78, 79]. Hypoglycemia can cause seizures, coma, permanent neurologic impairment, and, rarely, death. Timely diag nosis can prevent significant neurocognitive sequelae and be helpful in discovering the underlying etiology. ### 40.5.2 Clinical Presentation The most common presentation of hypoglyce mia is hunger, followed by altered neurologic function. A neonate or young infant may be irritable, jittery, and feed poorly [80]. An older patient may be anxious, confused, and/or trem ulous and complain of palpitations. Severe hypoglycemia can cause seizures or coma in patients of all ages [78, 81]. In addition to these neuro-adrenergic manifestations, the patient may have cholinergic-related complaints such as flushing, diaphoresis, emesis, and gastroin testinal distress [78, 81]. Additional features depend upon the underlying etiology—e.g., fever and signs of infection with sepsis. If hypoglycemia is due to an inborn error of metabolism that produces metabolic acidosis, the patient may have compensatory tachypnea. Important information to ascertain include the patient’s age, duration of symp toms, timing of last oral intake, prior episodes of hypoglycemia, chronic diagnoses, and med ications (including the possibility of an acci dental ingestion or intentional overdose [e.g., of a beta-blocker, sulfonylurea, or insulin]). It can be helpful to evaluate hypoglycemia based on the age and fasting status of the indi vidual. The most common cause of fasting hypoglycemia in toddlers is ketotic hypoglyce mia, which is associated with poor oral intake or prolonged fasting, usually in the setting of a concurrent acute illness, and is a diagnosis of exclusion [82–84]. These children have no iden tifiable underlying pathology in glucose homeostasis or their endocrine regulatory axes. On the other hand, neonatal hypoglyce mia, which occurs regardless of recent oral intake, is more likely the result of hyperinsulin ism, an inborn error of metabolism, or a defect in a counter-regulatory hormone pathway. ### 40.5.3 Diagnostic Evaluation 40.10 28 78 79 84 85 Table 40.10 Some causes of pediatric hypoglycemia [28, 78, 79, 84, 85] Glucose metabolism Differential diagnoses Increased glucose utilization Hyperinsulinism Ingestion/Injection Insulin overdose Oral hypoglycemic agents Sepsis Decreased glu cose production Counter-regulatory hormone deficiency (e.g., growth hormone, cortisol) Hepatic injury (Reye syn drome) Inborn error of metabolism Ingestion Beta-blockers Ethanol Ketotic hypoglycemia ### Automatic table extraction — verify rendered original |Glucose

The diagnosis of hypoglycemia is made with a low serum glucose level obtained in the setting of symptoms and signs of hypoglyce mia. Because rapid glucose determination is standard of care when assessing an acutely ill patient, this is frequently performed by emer gency medical services personnel prior to reaching the emergency department. If it was not done or needs to be verified, a point-ofcare glucose should be obtained promptly. If low, a confirmatory serum glucose should be obtained, but should not delay correction. Historically, there has been much debate regarding the biochemical definition of pediat ric hypoglycemia, and accordingly, several cut off levels are provided by various sources [71, 81, 84, 86]. In general, serum glucose less than 70 mg/dl is considered low blood glucose. When the serum glucose decreases below 65–70 mg/dl, counter-regulatory systems are acti vated, and the patient may develop signs and symptoms of hypoglycemia [81, 84]. When the glucose has declined below 50–55 mg/dl, all counter-regulatory systems are employed, and the patient will likely be symptomatic. Once hypoglycemia has been identified, additional diagnostic studies should be obtained to ascertain the underlying etiology and evaluate for any associated comorbidities. When possible, a panel of labs (commonly referred to as a “critical sample”) should be obtained prior to administering glucose. An appropriate laboratory panel obtained while the patient is hypoglycemic <50 mg/dl can effectively rule in or rule out many differential diagnoses. The panel should include serum glucose, insulin, c-peptide, growth hormone, cortisol, free fatty acid, beta-hydroxybutyrate, ammonia, and lactate levels, as well as urinary ketones [71, 81, 84, 86]. Note, if highly suspi cious for hyperinsulinism, a glucagon chal lenge should be administered while the patient ### 40 is hypoglycemic (and assumedly stable). A rise in glucose ≥30 mg/dl after administration of 1 mg of glucagon IV or IM is consistent with hyperinsulinism. ### 40.5.4 Management ### and Disposition Hypoglycemia must be promptly corrected with IV dextrose or oral glucose [e.g., juice, glucose tablets] for milder cases. A recom mended initial IV bolus dose for a child is 4 ml/kg of 10% dextrose. A neonate should receive 2 ml/kg of 10% dextrose by slow IV push [40]. The glucose level should then be rechecked, and an infusion of 10% dextrosecontaining fluid started at a standard mainte nance rate. If the serum glucose has normalized (and remains normal), no further dextrose boluses are needed. If the underlying diagnosis is known, spe cific therapy should be initiated. For example, hyperinsulinism can be treated with glucagon (neonate, infant, and child <20 kg, 0.02–0.03 mg/kg/dose; child or adolescent ≥20 kg, 1 mg/ dose IV/IO/IM/SC), if glucose or dextrose are not available or do not correct the hypoglyce mia [40]. Treat with stress hydrocortisone dos ing (as described in the adrenal crisis section) for adrenal insufficiency [28]. Once stabilized, disposition must be indi vidualized. Some forms of hypoglycemia may be mild and respond to treatment quickly (e.g., ketotic hypoglycemia). Without addi tional comorbidities, most of these patients can be treated with dextrose-containing infu sions and are easily managed on a standard hospital unit. Other forms of hypoglycemia may present with severe acidosis, neurologic impairment, and/or respiratory compromise. These patients require close monitoring, with frequent adjustments in therapy, and need to be admitted to an intensive care unit for con tinued care. ## PDF page 1058 | printed page 1063 Case Studies and Questions Case 1 An 8-year-old male presents with 2 weeks of polyuria, polydipsia, and a 7 lb. weight loss.
